documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: 1. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve educational outcomes for learners? OQ64729
documents.text_cy: 1. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella deilliannau addysgol dysgwyr? OQ64729

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: My priority is high standards and high aspirations for every learner. That is why this Government has worked at pace to develop the 'Foundational literacy and numeracy plan'. The plan sets out a clear and ambitious programme of action to raise literacy and numeracy outcomes throughout this Senedd term and is our first step in delivering sustained improvements in educational outcomes for all learners in Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you for that answer, Cabinet Minister, but there's a clear link also between attendance and educational outcomes, and we know we've got a huge attendance problem in Wales, with over 100,000 pupils every year missing at least 10 per cent of their lessons in the last year for which we have figures. In fact, the attendance records that have been provisionally published for 2025-26 suggest that this attendance problem is actually getting worse, not getting better. There's been a fall in the average attendance to just under 91 per cent in 2025-26. What action is your Welsh Government taking to address these appalling figures—which seem to be on the slide, not getting any better—and why is it that we have such a persistent attendance problem when other parts of the UK seem to be getting their act together and getting kids back into school?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: It's because they have a Labour Government.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
I think that's pushing it rather at this point, but thank you for the contribution.

Of course, this is an important area for us. There has been, you're quite right, a slight reduction on the latest figures, and there are a number of actions we are taking to tackle that. We are aware that school attendance has gone up again incrementally post COVID but is nowhere near the rate pre COVID. We're also aware that the cohort we are now targeting is likely to require a considerable focus and probably considerable support to push that figure higher. 

One of the things we have included in our literacy and numeracy foundational plan is targets on attendance. You will see a 0.5 per cent increase year on year to bring that level up. There's also a focus on persistent absence, which is missing 10 per cent or more of school sessions. A 2 per cent increase year on year is what we expect there.

There are a number of other areas we are focusing on. You will have heard me speak about the national framework on behaviour, attendance and well-being we are now bringing together, in the recognition that no single intervention, albeit we have targets now too, will address those persistent absence problems. They are often complex issues and do require tailored support, which is why we are looking at this framework in the round and making swift progress on introducing that.

Another thing we have done is to look in more detail—. Because often what we find is that reliable, consistent data across Wales is sometimes hard to find, so we've published new school attendance code guidance to give us that greater consistency in recording absence across Wales, to help us to target our work around this area to make a difference and to increase those figures over time. Because I agree with you: you need to be at school to benefit from the education system. It is very much a focus for us. Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Can I start by declaring an interest? My wife works in an additional learning needs provision within a school in Conwy.

I thank the leader of the Welsh Conservatives for bringing this question forward. Minister, I was speaking to a teacher in Rhyl, and it was explained to me that the school in which that teacher worked can't afford pens or pencils, and staff are currently using their own money to buy learning resources. It's no surprise, then, that the Institute for Fiscal Studies has claimed that students in that local authority area are up to 23 months behind the national average. As we are seeing a shift towards greater school-level flexibility on learning approaches and a more interlinked learning approach, researchers from Cardiff University have warned that schools need significant investment in materials and learning resources to avoid the widening of educational outcome gaps between different parts of Wales. How can we expect teachers in my constituency to achieve the best outcomes for students when their schools can't even afford pens and pencils? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Obviously, funding for schools is a priority for us, which is why we were pleased last week, or was it the week before, that the supplementary budget did go through, with that £60 million earmarked for pressures in schools linked to ALN, but a recognition that schools and the education system is under pressure across Wales.

On the points you make about those flexibilities locally, I would refer you back again to the foundational literacy and numeracy plan, because that will show us, on a national and a local level, the direction we're going in. It will make it easier for us to align the support appropriately in different areas and different schools in Wales in order to make that progress. I've also announced an intention to conduct a targeted review of the curriculum to make sure that we can have a better understanding and provide better advice to schools about some of the areas we expect learners to have access to.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Cabinet Minister, we know that an education workforce that is supported and valued is essential for raising standards and improving outcomes for our learners. Therefore, I welcome the 3.5 per cent pay award, which is fully funded and ensures parity with England, as well as the additional investment that you've just mentioned to alleviate pressures associated with ALN. ASCL Cymru, which also represents school leaders, has accepted the 3.5 per cent pay award. Does the Minister agree that it is in the interests of both school staff and pupils for those who remain in dispute to engage constructively with these proposals and seek to find a resolution without resorting to industrial action?
documents.text_cy: Weinidog, rydym yn gwybod bod gweithlu addysg sy'n cael ei gefnogi a'i werthfawrogi yn hanfodol er mwyn codi safonau a gwella canlyniadau ein dysgwyr. Felly, rwy'n croesawu’r dyfarniad cyflog o 3.5 y cant, sydd wedi'i ariannu'n llawn ac yn sicrhau cydraddoldeb â Lloegr, yn ogystal â'r buddsoddiad ychwanegol rŷch chi newydd sôn amdano fe i leddfu'r pwysau sy'n gysylltiedig ag ADY. Mae ASCL Cymru, sydd hefyd yn cynrychioli arweinwyr ysgolion, wedi derbyn y dyfarniad cyflog o 3.5 y cant. A yw'r Gweinidog yn cytuno gyda fi ei bod hi er budd staff ysgolion a disgyblion fel ei gilydd i'r rheini sydd yn parhau mewn anghydfod i ymgysylltu'n adeiladol â'r cynigion hyn a cheisio dod o hyd i ddatrysiad heb weithredu diwydiannol? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you very much. Working closely with the workforce and ensuring that they are paid and supported adequately in the important work that they do is a core priority of mine. I'm very grateful for the work that ASCL has done with us, for example to move on the broader debate on school funding. When I came into my role in May, there were detailed discussions at that point in order to facilitate getting the same kind of pay award for teachers in Wales as compared to England, and that was a very firm ask from the unions.

I'm always open to speaking to anyone as to how we move this debate forward in terms of appropriate support for the workforce, and I'm particularly eager to discuss workload and what we can put in place in order to reduce that burden. I see that the leader of the opposition isn't here today. I've had conversations with her, and every teacher that I've met over a period of 20 years, discussing workload specifically. We need to move that debate forward, and I'm willing to speak to anyone who has forceful ideas as to how we can make that progress. My door is always open.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr. Mae gweithio yn agos gyda'r gweithlu i sicrhau eu bod nhw'n cael eu talu a'u cefnogi yn ddigonol ar gyfer y gwaith pwysig maen nhw'n ei wneud yn flaenoriaeth greiddiol i fi. Rwy'n ddiolchgar iawn am y gwaith mae ASCL wedi ei wneud gyda ni, er enghraifft i symud ymlaen y ddadl ehangach ynglŷn ag ariannu ysgolion. Pan ddes i i fy swydd ym mis Mai, roedd yna drafodaethau manwl yn y cyfnod hwnnw er hwyluso cael yr un math o ddyfarniad o ran codiad cyflog i athrawon yng Nghymru o'i gymharu â Lloegr, ac roedd hwnna'n ofyn pendant gan yr undebau. 

Rwyf wastad yn agored i siarad gydag unrhyw un ar sut rŷm ni'n symud y ddadl yma ymlaen ynglŷn â chefnogaeth addas i'r gweithlu, ac rwy'n benodol yn frwd iawn i drafod baich gwaith a'r moddion y gallwn eu rhoi yn eu lle er lleihau y faich honno. Dwi'n gweld nad yw arweinydd yr wrthblaid yma heddiw. Dwi wedi cael sgyrsiau gyda hi, a phob athro neu athrawes rwyf wedi cwrdd â nhw ers 20 mlynedd, yn trafod, yn benodol, baich gwaith. Mae angen symud y ddadl honno yn ei blaen, ac rwy'n barod i siarad ag unrhyw un sydd â syniadau grymus er hwyluso'r drafodaeth honno. Mae'r drws bob amser yn agored.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: 2. What is the Welsh Government doing to improve further education provision in Swansea? OQ64724
documents.text_cy: 2. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i wella'r ddarpariaeth addysg bellach yn Abertawe? OQ64724

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you for the question. We are investing more than £26 million through the Sustainable Communities for Learning programme to deliver modern, high-quality further education facilities across Swansea. This includes the refurbishment of Gower College Swansea’s Tycoch campus and the redevelopment of Ysgol Gyfun Gymraeg Bryn Tawe for both secondary and further education learners.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Can I thank the Minister for that reply? Perhaps I ought to say that I used to be a governor at Tycoch and my grandchild goes to Bryn Tawe, so I've got an interest, though not necessarily a financial one. I thought I'd bring that up for the record.

One of the issues I think we are all in agreement on is that we do not want young people at 16 to become not in education, employment or training. That means we must have adequate availability of courses in the further education sector. If young people do not continue in education or training at 16, then many will face a life of unemployment. Getting them at 18 to go back into taking up a course is going to be very difficult.

Gower College Swansea is doing its best to provide opportunities. I really would like to commend them, and I hope the Minister will as well. Gower College has over-recruited against the numbers funded, but they still have a waiting list for some areas. Will the Minister commit to funding further education so that there is a place in college for every young person who wants it in Swansea, so that we don't have people sitting at home who want to be learning?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
There are two points there, Mike. The first one is around NEETs. This is an area of great concern for me and the Government. We know the NEET cohort in Wales is increasing. Roughly 17 per cent of the 16 to 24-year-old age group are NEET. That's clearly not where we want to be. We have to put interventions in place to stop them becoming NEET. That takes different approaches. The Alan Milburn report showed that about 70 per cent of those who are NEET are economically inactive—that is, they are not ready for work. That is because they have several barriers in their own personal lives that stop them becoming employable. That could be around mental health issues, it could be additional learning needs, it could be childcare, transport, disabilities, and so on. I am going to lead an inter-ministerial group of people to look at the NEETs agenda and how we can bring different policy areas to play, which would obviously involve health, social services, transport and so on. So, that's the first part.

The second part is ensuring that no young person will be turned away from the course that they want to study. I am increasingly aware of the significant increases in learner numbers in FE in recent years, and I recognise that that adds funding challenges to FE colleges. I am committed to reviewing that increased level of participation and the financial pressures over the next month, as we have final figures coming through. We will consider providing additional funding over and above what Medr have already provided, £6.25 million, should that money be available, given the budgetary constraints that we are under.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you, Mike, for the question. Improving further education in Swansea must mean providing the skills local industry needs. Employers need courses shaped around their businesses, reliable partnerships with colleges and practical help. For a small business, taking on an apprentice requires a financial and resource-heavy commitment. Announcing an audit does nothing on its own to meet these costs. Since your Government took office, another group of young people have left school hoping to secure an apprenticeship and employment. Employers need immediate funding. Your manifesto promises better use of existing city and regional growth deal funding to support apprenticeships. Your Government is happy to waste our money to fund international projects like tree planting in Uganda, but it seems Welsh employers are being left to shoulder apprenticeship costs. These are our young people, they are our future. What new funding has Plaid made available to help businesses, particularly smaller employers, take on apprentices?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
I'll deal with the main and the most important parts of that question, if I may. If I can refer back to a skills summit we organised on 8 October in the Swansea.com Stadium, for the first time ever we brought employers, small and medium-sized and large companies together with education providers. It was a hugely successful event, where employers were telling us that they need to forge a better relationship with apprenticeship providers and vocational skills providers. Employers know what the emerging sectors are. They know what skills they need for the future. So, we need to develop a mechanism where they are telling providers what they need and that we match them both together.

Now, I heard my colleague the Minister for enterprise explain earlier on that we need to create more demand as well. And you heard him explain how we are going to do that through setting up a Welsh development agency and other programmes as well to support industry and SMEs to take on more apprenticeships. I believe that apprenticeships are a great pathway into work and into further and higher education as well. You can earn and learn at the same time. So, we are committed to supporting the apprenticeship scheme, and we will be working with employers to make sure that what they need, in terms of the skills level, matches what education providers can put on in FE colleges, universities and also through apprenticeship schemes.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. Reform UK spokesperson, Stephen Senior.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Llefarydd Reform UK, Stephen Senior.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, additional learning needs funding remains a contentious issue, with a debate scheduled next month in response to a petition. ALN funding by the Welsh Government is up 14 per cent on last year, and has more than doubled in eight years. Inflation over that period has been around 35 per cent. The percentage of the education budget assigned to ALN has risen from just below 15 per cent to nearly 19 per cent over the same period. At local authority level, there have been huge variations, with increases over the last decade ranging from 65 per cent to 297 per cent. One authority now spends more than a quarter of its education budget on ALN. These figures suggest that there has been a rapid change within Welsh education. Whatever is happening looks unsustainable in terms of funding. Minister, what are your thoughts on the reasons for this ALN spending trajectory?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Diolch yn fawr. Thank you for the question. I think we are dealing with two issues simultaneously here. I mentioned earlier on that I was pleased that £60 million had gone into the system this year, as a result of the supplementary budget, to support with immediate pressures. But you are quite right, in the longer term we need to arrive at a system that is more sustainable and is inclusive of the learners in Wales. I think every jurisdiction everywhere over a time, and particularly post COVID, has been dealing with increasingly complex demand from children and families trying to negotiate a range of issues that their learners are facing.

The education system, arguably, experiences changes in society faster than most of us sitting here and probably most of our services as well. So, we have made an effort now to focus on the sustainability of the ALN system over time. You will have seen that a proportion of what was agreed last week has been allocated specifically for that purpose, and we will work now quickly with local authorities and other partners to work our way to a more sustainable system over time. We need this to be a coherent continuum, we need it to be of high quality, we need it to be inclusive, with—and this is the crucial part I think—clearer national expectations of what this system should look like, stronger mainstream capacity, which in turn comes with demand for support, obviously.

One of the first steps is to understand in detail, with all our partners, what an inclusive system looks like and plot our way from here to that system and this commitment—. There is a great willingness amongst all our partners to work on this and we will do so with speed.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Okay, thank you, Minister. I see that later on there's a question regarding teachers leaving the profession. Surveys show that poor pupil behaviour is a factor. However, Plaid's recent programme for government, whilst acknowledging workload concerns, makes no mention of behaviour.

Staff working in schools have a legal right to use reasonable force to control or restrain pupils. Welsh Government guidance explicitly states that no school should have a 'no physical contact' policy. However, there are still occasions when school staff face lengthy investigations and possible suspension for having operated within the law. This can have a devastating impact on both them and pupil behaviour in the school, whenever staff, unsurprisingly, decide that no physical intervention is their best policy.

Minister, will you ask your officials to establish whether schools are advising staff on their legal right to use reasonable force and whether disciplinary processes are being initiated despite staff having operated within the law?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
It is obviously important that staff feel safe at school and are able to operate appropriately. It is clear that staff may use reasonable force where necessary to prevent harm, an offence, damage to property or serious disruption, but that intervention must necessarily, and I think we'd all agree on this, be proportionate and use the minimum force required. And it should never be used as a punishment. I think we can all agree on those principles. If there are examples, individual examples, that you have, then I would be glad to look at them.

But we are clear that that is the environment in which our workforce is working. It is also our expectation that restrictive practices are a last resort. And to go back to your first point around behaviour, the behaviour and well-being framework is a priority for this Government, and bringing together a greater national consistency around our expectations and around the support that will help the workforce and the learners in turn is a piece of work that is ongoing.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Okay, thank you, Minister. Finally, the national literacy and numeracy assessments are online and personalised to each pupil. So, they're rather like a flow chart, where the next question depends on the answers to the last one. These tests can be taken whenever the school feels it's appropriate. Pupils can take time out during the assessments, and pupils are permitted to repeat the exercise any time. This is not a standardised test where all pupils in a cohort take the same test at the same time of the year so that judgments can be made about pupil and school standards, including progress.

This is what the tests were originally designed to do when Leighton Andrews introduced them, and that is what happened when the tests were introduced in 2014. This adaptive system, as it's called, has been in place for a decade, but has clearly not led to any improvements in the Programme for International Student Assessment results. Minister, will you reintroduce standardised literacy and numeracy tests to be used by all pupils annually at the end of year 2 to year 9?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you. These are adaptive tests. The idea is that the learner engages with them, and it helps to indicate what the next steps in their development should be. That's how they've been constructed to operate.

We can use the data more broadly that this system gives us, to give us an indicator at year 6, which is what we're doing as part of this plan, and which gives us a place go to, then, as a national trajectory of improvement, and also to make sure that we can align the support available appropriately for those schools and for those learners. 

I'm not going to go back to the future. I am, however, going to have, during this Senedd term, a clearer expectation that we can communicate effectively to learners and to schools.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Welsh Labour spokesperson, Lynne Neagle.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Lynne Neagle.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you. Last week, as we've heard from Sera Evans, you announced a teacher pay award of 3.5 per cent following the consultation on the independent Welsh pay review body report. That announcement was made during an active industrial dispute, and the National Association of Head Teachers have now withdrawn from talks with the Government and announced that they are moving to a statutory industrial ballot. 

Why did you make that announcement while talks were ongoing, and do you think that is in keeping with the principles of social partnership?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you. I think, as I said in my earlier answer, I remain committed to the social partnership, and I'm always willing to talk to those social partners on issues that we have in common as concerns. 

I announced that fully funded pay award last week, following that consultation, because I wanted to respect the principle of no detriment, so that there'd be no difference between the pay increases here and those over the border in England. I know this has been a continuing debate over many years, to ensure that we remain in that alignment.

I think the previous education Minister will also be aware of the financial environment, and the budgetary environment we are now in, and I judged, at this point, that 4.25 per cent was not affordable when we consider the other priorities of this Government, and Wales more broadly, around, particularly, health service demand—the national health service—and other priorities that this Government is committed to.

The 3.5 per cent was important to me. It was important to most partners. But I remain committed to talking to anybody who wishes to examine areas of mutual interest and concern.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Well, thank you for that answer, and I'm fully in support of no detriment myself. And I do understand the financial constraints, but would point out that the Government still has a significant amount of unallocated resource as a result of the consequentials that were received by the UK Government. 

So, since May, we've had an industrial dispute with the Association of School and College Leaders, an escalating dispute with the National Association of Head Teachers, and the National Education Union have previously gone out to indicative ballot. I hear what you're saying about being willing to talk to partners, but it doesn't seem to me like those talks are going as well as we would want them to go, really. So, in light of that, what are you going to do to get social partnership with the education trade unions back on line?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
I think that the judgment on where each of these parties is depends, rather, on who you talk to at this point. I think we have, for example, had very helpful and fruitful discussions with ASCL, in particular, around some of these elements. 

The social partnership—I've been part of arrangements like this for many years—is very important to me. And it is a place where some of these pressing issues that the workforce has been calling for action on for many, many years—. It is a good place to resolve them, particularly on ALN, particularly on workload, recruitment, retention, behaviour, attendance—all these things that are very important to everybody who works in our schools and has an association with them. 

All of those issues, I am entirely open to engaging on them. But I would repeat my first point around the salary increases—the pay increases—that 3.5 per cent was as far as I felt able to go. But I am and remain committed to discussing any and all other issues.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: The Welsh Conservatives' spokesperson, Paul Davies.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Paul Davies.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. Before I ask my questions, I would like to put on record my thanks to Efa Gruffudd Jones for her work as Welsh Language Commissioner. She's been a robust advocate for the Welsh language, and I wish her well for the future.

Minister, the report of the Commission for Welsh-speaking Communities, 'Cymraeg in every community, strengthening the Welsh language', notes that workplaces should be considered as key locations for use of the Welsh language, and the report makes a series of recommendations with the aim of increasing the use of the Welsh language in those settings. What progress has the Welsh Government made in terms of implementing those recommendations, and what evidence do you have that more people are using the Welsh language regularly in their workplaces as a result of that?
documents.text_cy:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Cyn i mi ofyn fy nghwestiynau, hoffwn gofnodi fy niolch i Efa Gruffudd Jones am ei gwaith fel Comisiynydd y Gymraeg. Mae hi wedi bod yn eiriolwr cadarn dros yr iaith Gymraeg, a dwi'n dymuno'n dda iddi ar gyfer y dyfodol.

Weinidog, mae adroddiad y Comisiwn Cymunedau Cymraeg, 'Cyrraedd pob cymuned, cryfhau'r Gymraeg', yn nodi y dylid ystyried gweithleoedd yn fannau allweddol ar gyfer defnyddio'r Gymraeg, ac mae'r adroddiad yn gwneud cyfres o argymhellion sydd â'r nod o gynyddu'r defnydd o'r Gymraeg yn y mannau yma. Pa gynnydd y mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi ei wneud o ran gweithredu'r argymhellion hynny, a pha dystiolaeth sydd gyda chi fod mwy o bobl yn defnyddio'r Gymraeg yn rheolaidd yn eu gweithleoedd o ganlyniad i hynny?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you very much for the question. I would like to add my thanks as well to the Welsh Language Commissioner for her work.

We will, in December, be publishing a consultation on the Welsh language strategy, the Welsh Language and Education (Wales) Act 2025, and the Welsh language proficiency code. I would ask you to look at that point at what we will publish, because we will indicate what the trajectory is to ensure that the use of the Welsh language, access to the Welsh language, the Welsh language in our heartlands, the Welsh language in our schools, all tie together under one co-ordinated strategy that will be based on the concept that the Welsh language belongs to us all. In that context, we will show how we will reach those particular goals in terms of those opportunities, including the workplace. There will be detail showing that trajectory, including, therefore, more specific targets.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn. Hoffwn i ategu fy niolch innau hefyd i Gomisiynydd y Gymraeg am ei gwaith hithau.

Mi fyddwn ni, ym mis Rhagfyr, yn cyhoeddi ymgynghoriad ar strategaeth y Gymraeg, Deddf y Gymraeg ac Addysg (Cymru) 2025, a'r cod ar y gallu i siarad Cymraeg. Byddwn i'n gofyn i chi edrych ar y pwynt hwnnw ar yr hyn rŷn ni'n ei gyhoeddi achos byddwn ni'n dangos y taflwybr i sicrhau bod defnydd o'r Gymraeg, mynediad at y Gymraeg, Cymraeg yn ein cadarnleoedd, Cymraeg yn ein hysgolion ni, yn clymu at ei gilydd i un strategaeth gydlynus, yn seiliedig ar y cysyniad bod y Gymraeg yn perthyn i ni i gyd. Yn y cyd-destun hwnnw, byddwn ni'n dangos siẁd rydyn ni'n mynd i gyrraedd y nodau priodol o ran y cyfleoedd hyn, gan gynnwys y gweithle. Mi fydd yna fanylder yn dangos y ffordd ymlaen, yn cynnwys, felly, dargedau mwy penodol.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
I thank you for that response. I look forward to seeing that publication in December.

Now, the commission also came to the conclusion that the current budget for strengthening the Welsh language at community level was not sufficient, and it highlighted the need for greater support to help organisations to develop workplaces where the Welsh language is spoken. It also called for a review of the way in which public funding and support mechanisms can be used to support the aims of 'Cymraeg 2050'. In light of that, can you tell us what funding is currently available to support the use of the Welsh language in workplaces across Wales, and can you tell us whether you think that the current level of investment is adequate to deliver the cultural shifts that the commission anticipates in its report?
documents.text_cy:
Dwi'n diolch i chi am yr ymateb yna. Dwi'n edrych ymlaen i'r cyhoeddiad hynny ym mis Rhagfyr.

Nawr, daeth y comisiwn i'r casgliad hefyd nad yw'r gyllideb bresennol ar gyfer cryfhau'r Gymraeg ar lefel gymunedol yn ddigonol, a thynnodd sylw at yr angen am fwy o gefnogaeth i helpu sefydliadau i ddatblygu gweithleoedd lle siaredir y Gymraeg. Galwodd hefyd am adolygiad o'r modd y gellir defnyddio cyllid cyhoeddus a mecanweithiau cymorth i hyrwyddo nodau 'Cymraeg 2050'. Yn sgil hynny, a allwch chi ddweud wrthym ni ba gyllid sydd ar gael ar hyn o bryd i gefnogi defnyddio'r Gymraeg mewn gweithleoedd ledled Cymru, ac a allwch chi ddweud a ydych chi'n credu bod y lefel bresennol o fuddsoddiad yn ddigonol i gyflawni'r newidiadau diwylliannol a sefydliadol y mae'r comisiwn yn eu rhagweld yn ei adroddiad?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Perhaps I'll have to write to you with the detailed response to that first question. But on what will be needed in order to realise the ambition in the strategy that we will publish—it will be published for consultation in December, into next year—as part of that, in order to deliver that, we will be looking at what's needed in terms of resources to deliver it. Both things will go hand in hand.
documents.text_cy: Efallai y bydd angen i fi ysgrifennu atoch chi gyda manylder y cwestiwn cyntaf. Ond ar yr hyn a fydd yn ofynnol er mwyn gwireddu'r uchelgais yn y strategaeth y byddwn ni yn ei chyhoeddi—byddwn ni'n cyhoeddi ar gyfer ymgynghoriad ym mis Rhagfyr, i mewn i'r flwyddyn nesaf—fel rhan o hynny, er mwyn ei chyflawni hi, mi fyddwn ni'n edrych ar yr hyn sydd ei angen o ran adnoddau i'w gwireddu hi. Bydd y ddau beth yn mynd law yn llaw.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Question 3 [OQ64738] is from Vikki Howells. Unfortunately, the Member has been delayed on her way back from an event at Aberfan, so I'll move on to question 4, Anna Nicholl.
documents.text_cy: Mae cwestiwn 3 [OQ64738] gan Vikki Howells. Yn anffodus, mae'r Aelod wedi'i hoedi ar y ffordd nôl o ddigwyddiad yn Aberfan, felly symudaf ymlaen i gwestiwn 4, Anna Nicholl.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: 4. How is the Cabinet Minister ensuring community involvement in decisions about the future of Church in Wales maintained schools in Ceredigion Penfro? OQ64786
documents.text_cy: 4. Sut mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn sicrhau bod cymunedau'n cael eu cynnwys mewn penderfyniadau ynghylch dyfodol ysgolion a gynhelir gan yr Eglwys yng Nghymru yng Ngheredigion Penfro? OQ64786

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. Local authorities are responsible for decisions on the future of schools, and they must follow statutory procedures when bringing forward proposals. This includes consulting communities, providing sufficient information to enable people to come to informed views, engaging with relevant partners, including religious bodies, and having regard to the wishes of parents.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Awdurdodau lleol sy'n gyfrifol am benderfyniadau ynghylch dyfodol ysgolion, ac mae'n rhaid iddyn nhw ddilyn gweithdrefnau statudol wrth gyflwyno cynigion. Mae hyn yn cynnwys ymgynghori â chymunedau, darparu digon o wybodaeth i bobl allu dod i farn ddeallus, ymgysylltu â phartneriaid perthnasol, gan gynnwys cyrff crefyddol, a rhoi sylw i ddymuniadau rhieni.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch, Cabinet Minister. I'm concerned about the low level of confidence that parents, staff and governors in Pembrokeshire have told me that they have in the council involving them meaningfully in big decisions about the future of their schools. Examples include but are not limited to church schools. I wrote to the council back in September around decisions on the future of Cilgerran school, and I'm glad this is now resolved. But, Cabinet Minister, public trust and confidence is easily lost. As Pembrokeshire County Council now consults on proposals to close Tenby Church in Wales VC Primary School and neighbouring Greenhill school, replacing them with a new three-to-19 community school, can the Cabinet Minister assure us that she expects these decisions to be based on the meaningful involvement of parents and the wider community, including open and transparent information on all options available?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch. Local authorities are democratically accountable to their communities and are responsible for developing school organisation proposals. In so doing, they must comply with the requirements set out in the School Standards and Organisation (Wales) Act 2013, and the school organisation code, which is quite clear about the processes and involvement that is required in these cases. I do expect all proposers to comply fully with these statutory requirements and to engage openly and meaningfully with all those affected by any proposal. These decisions should be informed by the evidence gathered through consultation and taken in accordance with the legislative framework. You will be aware, because I've said it several times, that the role of Welsh Ministers in the statutory process means that I'm unable to comment on proposals that I may later be required to determine. But, in the context of all decisions, I would expect my first two points to be clear.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: 5. What assessment has the Cabinet Minister made of the financial pressures facing rural schools in Gwynedd Maldwyn? OQ64722
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa asesiad y mae’r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi’i wneud o’r pwysau ariannol sy’n wynebu ysgolion gwledig yng Ngwynedd Maldwyn? OQ64722

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. I seem to have lost you in my book. Wait a second. I'm sorry.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: We recognise the significant pressures across our schools and local authorities, and acknowledge the commitment of the education workforce in continuing to support learners. Decisions on the level of funding available to schools, including rural schools, are made by each local authority as part of their overall budget setting.
documents.text_cy: Rydyn ni'n cydnabod y pwysau sylweddol ar draws ein hysgolion a'n hawdurdodau lleol ni, yn ogystal ag ymrwymiad y gweithlu addysg i barhau i gefnogi dysgwyr. Mae penderfyniadau ynghylch lefel y cyllid sydd ar gael i ysgolion, gan gynnwys ysgolion gwledig, yn cael eu gwneud gan bob awdurdod lleol wrth bennu eu cyllideb gyffredinol.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. In Gwynedd Maldwyn, we're already seeing the consequences of the financial pressures on these rural schools. Both Gwynedd and Powys have closed rural primary schools and further closures are being considered or progressed. I understand smaller schools can cost more per pupil to run, but these schools are often at the heart of their communities. When one closes, it's not just the school building that is lost; children may have to travel much further, parents have to reorganise their lives, and villages lose something that is very difficult to replace. And, of course, transporting those children elsewhere comes at a cost as well. So, can I ask the Cabinet Secretary whether the Welsh Government is properly accounting for those wider costs and the impact on rural communities when assessing the funding pressures facing our rural schools? Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you very much. We understand just how important schools are for our rural communities, and in the context of smaller schools, for example, there are very detailed requirements in relation to consultation on any reorganisation that's proposed. The Member will also be aware that my colleague the Minister for rural resilience is looking at ways of nurturing and protecting the resilience of rural communities, and that considerations on sustaining services with a more dispersed population, for example, are part of those wider considerations. I think that the broader response is that, in looking at the needs of rural communities, there is a broader responsibility across Government in ensuring that we do understand the specific challenges faced by those areas and respond appropriately to them.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Rydyn ni'n gwybod yn iawn pa mor bwysig yw ysgolion i'n cymunedau gwledig, ac yng nghyd-destun ysgolion llai, er enghraifft, mae yna ofynion manwl iawn ynglŷn ag ymgynghori ynglŷn ag aildrefnu mewn unrhyw fodd. Mi fydd yr Aelod hefyd yn gwybod bod fy nghydweithiwr y Gweinidog dros ddygnwch gwledig yn edrych ar fesurau i feithrin a gwarchod dygnwch cymunedau gwledig, a bod ystyriaethau ynglŷn â chynnal gwasanaethau gyda phoblogaeth mwy gwasgaredig, er enghraifft, yn rhan o'r ystyriaethau hynny. Dwi'n credu mai'r ateb ehangach yw, o edrych ar y gofynion mewn cymunedau gwledig, fod yna gyfrifoldeb yn ehangach ar draws y Llywodraeth ar gyfer sicrhau ein bod ni'n deall yr heriau penodol yn yr ardaloedd hynny ac yn ymateb yn briodol iddyn nhw.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: The challenges facing rural schools like those in my constituency are a symptom of the broader challenges facing our rural areas, with an ageing population, families moving away and local authority services that are more expensive to run and more difficult to administer. For rural schools to flourish, we need high-quality jobs, adequate housing and effective public transport, and I'm very pleased to see the Government taking action on these matters. If rural communities prosper, then rural schools will prosper too. How, then, will the Community Schools Plus plan empower our rural schools, as well as empowering the communities to which they belong?
documents.text_cy: Mae heriau ysgolion gwledig fel y rhai yn fy etholaeth i yn symptom o heriau ehangach ein hardaloedd gwledig, gyda'r boblogaeth yn heneiddio, teuluoedd yn symud i ffwrdd, a gwasanaethau llywodraeth leol yn ddrutach i'w rhedeg ac yn anoddach i'w gweithredu. Er mwyn i ysgolion gwledig ffynnu, mae angen swyddi o ansawdd, cartrefi digonol a thrafnidiaeth gyhoeddus effeithiol, a dwi'n falch o weld y Llywodraeth yn gweithredu ar y materion hyn. Os bydd cymunedau gwledig yn ffynnu, yna bydd ysgolion gwledig yn ffynnu. Sut, felly, bydd y cynllun Ysgolion Cymunedol a Mwy yn grymuso’n hysgolion gwledig, yn ogystal â grymuso'r cymunedau maen nhw’n perthyn iddynt?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you very much. The Member may be aware that we are currently piloting the Community Schools Plus programme at the moment in order to look at developing our understanding of the challenges facing those schools and, as I said earlier, drawing on those different elements of policies and bringing them together. I am, of course, aware, too, that school transport is a particular priority for the Deputy Minister for Transport, that the Minister for rural resilience is also looking at these issues and I, too, am looking at the demographic challenges that will impact on how we provide services and education, particularly in rural communities and in Wales more broadly, too.

So, what I would encourage the Member to look at is the detailed work happening across a number of different areas, which we are progressing quickly, as areas that relate to her question but are not necessarily reserved to the education portfolio, and we have taken meaningful steps to ensure that we don't look at these issues in isolation.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: 6. What is the Welsh Government doing to support adult learners who are retraining for new careers? OQ64766
documents.text_cy: 6. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i gefnogi dysgwyr sy'n oedolion sy'n ailhyfforddi ar gyfer gyrfaoedd newydd? OQ64766

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: The Welsh Government is committed to lifelong learning and ensuring that adults can access opportunities to develop new skills, retrain and progress throughout their lives. Through personal learning accounts, employability programmes and further education opportunities, we support adults retraining for new careers to realise their potential and progress into sustainable employment.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch, Weinidog. People retrain for many reasons: after losing a job, returning to work after raising a family, or starting a new chapter following a career break. Others come to Wales with valuable qualifications and skills that go unrecognised, despite the contribution they could make to our Welsh economy. At the Inspire! adult learning awards, I met learners determined to gain new skills and contribute to their communities. For many, adult learning is more than education; it is a vital opportunity to rebuild their careers and their lives here in Wales. One of my constituents, Yassmein Hussein, completed 13 adult learning courses through Cardiff and Vale College and Cardiff Council, leading her to win the shared futures award at the awards. Yassmein's story shows what people can achieve when they have access to the right learning opportunities. But not everyone gets that chance, and many adults still face barriers to retraining. So, I want to know how the Welsh Government is ensuring that adults who want to retrain for a new career can access the learning opportunities and support they need to make that transition.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Well, like you, I was there in the Inspire! adult learning awards, and what a terrific night it was, to hear the remarkable stories of adult learners across Wales, many who have overcome very personal barriers to achieve in their learning. It really was an inspirational evening and, for me, it's one of the highlights of the year to go to that event. What it shows is that adult learning is about more than just gaining qualifications or skills. It builds confidence, it increases resilience and it improves well-being, and I was delighted to be there to share in Yassmein's success that evening.

In terms of your direct question, the Welsh Government is committed to ensuring that people of all ages have opportunities to learn throughout their lives. We do provide Medr with funding streams, which is allocated to further education colleges and other providers to support learners facing particular barriers. They may relate to disabilities, financial hardship, transport issues, childcare, mental health and well-being. This can include additional learning support, disability-related support, transport assistance, childcare, well-being services and so on, because we want to remove those barriers that stand in their way. Now, in particular, there is a community learning grant worth £6.5 million available to fund adult community learning in general, adult basic education, employability, English for speakers of other languages and well-being courses. These actually help people back into skills and work.

There is also a learning grant for learners over the age of 19, and also a personal learning account programme, which aims to help individuals upskill or reskill, as you mentioned, in priority sectors. So, the Welsh Government is absolutely clear that we do support adults in their retraining and upskilling, and want to be as supportive as we can. Because lifelong learning means exactly that: it never stops. So, we are 100 per cent committed to that programme.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to establish the reasons for teachers leaving the profession? OQ64775
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i ganfod y rhesymau pam y mae athrawon yn gadael y proffesiwn? OQ64775

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Improving recruitment and retention is one of my priorities. We already know that teachers leave the profession for a range of reasons, including workload, well-being and working conditions. We are drawing on national and international evidence and working with our social partners to take practical action to address these issues.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you, Minister. In March, the Welsh Government workforce plan admitted that they did not have data as to why teachers leave the profession. Estyn noted exactly the same concern 19 years ago. The latest figures from the Education Workforce Council show that more than 3,000 schoolteachers have left the register in the year up to March, the highest number in five years. But we don't know why. There is no national system in place to ask the teachers themselves why they have left. England and Scotland do that. Why doesn't Wales? Will the Minister ask the Education Workforce Council to start asking teachers who are leaving the register why they did so, so that we can understand how we can stop more teachers from leaving in the future?
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Weinidog. Ym mis Mawrth, cyfaddefodd cynllun gweithlu Llywodraeth Cymru nad oedd ganddyn nhw ddata ynghylch pam mae athrawon yn gadael. Nododd Estyn yn union yr un broblem 19 mlynedd yn ôl. Mae ffigurau diweddaraf Cyngor y Gweithlu Addysg yn dangos bod mwy na 3,000 o athrawon ysgol wedi gadael y gofrestr yn y flwyddyn hyd at fis Mawrth, y nifer uchaf mewn pum mlynedd. Ond dydyn ni ddim yn gwybod pam. Does yna ddim system genedlaethol i ofyn i’r athrawon eu hunain pam maen nhw wedi gadael. Mae Lloegr a’r Alban yn gwneud hynny. Pan nad yw Cymru? A wnaiff y Gweinidog ofyn i Gyngor y Gweithlu Addysg ddechrau gofyn i athrawon sy’n gadael y gofrestr pam yr aethant, er mwyn inni ddeall sut fedrwn ni stopio mwy o athrawon rhag gadael yn y dyfodol?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you. I don't think it's correct to say that we don't have any evidence. There are a number of reports that have looked into this specific problem—one quite recently carried out by Cardiff Met, for example, which was published in 2024. The OECD has also looked at these challenges in the context of work that they have done in Wales. One of the Senedd committees has also looked in detail at this issue.

They've all come to the same conclusion, to all intents and purposes, namely that the workload is excessive and is a heavy workload. There's also a feeling that society does not appreciate the efforts of teachers as it did at one stage in the past. I think that we all have a responsibility to examine how we speak about the education profession; we can all be of help in that context, at least. There are also questions about the professional pathway—in terms of promotions and so on, as you move through the system. Then, there are specific subject areas where it is especially difficult to recruit and retain teachers. There is a dependence as well on teachers who are perhaps qualified to teach one subject but are increasingly asked to teach another subject.

These are all issues that influence our ability to recruit and to retain teachers, and this has, clearly, been a priority for me over the recent period. That is why, for example, we provided those additional payments for recruitment to difficult-to-recruit subjects, and also are looking then at the broader requirements with representatives from the workforce itself.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: 8. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve pupil safety? OQ64768
documents.text_cy: 8. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella diogelwch disgyblion? OQ64768

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: The safety and well-being of learners is an absolute priority for the Welsh Government. We continue to work closely with schools, local authorities, the police and other partners to prevent harm, identify emerging risks and ensure that appropriate arrangements are in place to respond effectively when concerns arise.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you for that answer, Minister. In September, more than 300 pupils in the Caerphilly borough lost their free school transport because, as the council said, they fall within the two-mile measurement of the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008. Now, the problem with that is that the Measure is looking at distance but not incline. I've walked this route with campaigners and parents and children themselves—I went from Aberbargoed to Bargoed—and it's the incline that is the tricky part. During different weathers, whether it's the heat we experienced in the summer, or even cold winter days, when that road can be slippery, it does become a risk. Will the Government now look at reviewing the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008 and look to include the advice on inclines and the difficult weather paths that this could create?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. As I referred to in an earlier answer around school transport more broadly, this has been a challenge on many levels—access to Welsh-medium education, for example. The cost of transport has been an increasing concern and that's why, with my colleague the Minister for transport, we are looking at school transport in particular as an immediate priority and linking that, which may be of interest to you as well, to additional learning needs learners for whom this is a pressing priority. I can't commit this afternoon to looking at the learner travel Measure again, but, certainly, issues more broadly around access to school and transport to get learners there safely are right at the top of my colleague's agenda, I know.

documents.text: Thank you very much, Minister and Deputy Minister.
