documents.item: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
documents.text:
Diolch, Llywydd. One way to start is to have a bit of a laugh after that one, about not playing politics. I'd just like to thank everybody for their contributions to this debate today. Since being elected in 2016, I've always said that inaction is not an option, but the people of Newport and the surrounding area must not pay the price of costly options that this Government's report says won't solve the problem on the M4 around Newport.

What has been missing as well, for many Members who perhaps don't realise, is that this report was actually commissioned by the previous Labour Government and the Labour transport Minister at the time. So, what we're discussing, which the report is based on, is actually something that has come out from the previous Government. 

I realise that many Members might not have realised my contributions in the past Senedds, and that I did not vote to scrap the M4 relief road. I think that many Members here perhaps don't realise that. I spoke up at every opportunity throughout that time when it was being discussed, so just to be aware of that.

You might think that junction closures are quick fixes, but they will make next to no difference to congestion on the M4 and certainly cause havoc on local roads. And we've heard that from many Members across the Chamber today. 

Lyn Ackerman spoke earlier, and I think, from your contribution, Lyn, we weren't clear, and perhaps we could assume that you are not against the proposed junction closures. And also, to other Plaid Members as well, if you remember the time of a junction closure which was junction 41 around Swansea, that was temporarily closed by a Labour Government, but it was campaigned on by Plaid Cymru Members to reopen that junction at the time. And I would be interested to know—at the time, the Labour Government listened to Plaid Cymru Members—if the Plaid Cymru Government will listen to other Members in this Chamber, so I look forward to seeing that. 

Natasha, I absolutely do agree with your points on the junction closures. I went to visit a group of pensioners a couple of weeks ago, and the only thing they wanted to talk to me about was proposed junction closures, whether temporary or permanent. They were very, very concerned about that.

The other thing that has been missing from a number of people's contributions is a collective memory loss, that, actually, Plaid Cymru also voted to reject the M4 relief road at the time, and it was a Plaid Cymru Minister in 2009 who rejected the M4 relief road that put us back, and Plaid Cymru voted with the Labour Party, so not myself, to stop the M4 relief road last time.

Paul Rock, I should say, 'pen-blwydd hapus', first of all. I think we'd all like to say that to you, Paul, on your birthday. I have said that the black route is not an option, but I do think—and I would encourage you to look at the Arup report—when you talk about the freight that would go off, the Arup report also highlights that would only take up to 1 per cent of traffic off the road. So, just be aware of that, because there are a number of these issues that I think people haven't looked into, into that depth yet. But it would only take 1 per cent of traffic off the M4 around Newport.

Public transport absolutely does have a role to play, and Welsh Labour championed the Burns stations, and we now need to see that similar level of commitment to these stations from Plaid Cymru. The evidence is, though, clear that public transport interventions have to be delivered alongside a revised relief road, and that's the only option that provides resilience and reduces congestion.

We've heard some warm words from the Welsh Government today and I am hopeful of engagement with local people. I know the Deputy Minister has said again today about the importance of that, something I very strongly place an importance on. I feel, too many times over the years, the people of Newport's voice has not been heard to the extent that it should have been heard—[Interruption.] Pardon? Of all parties, as I said, of all parties. I have championed my constituents over that time, and I've spoken up, and I feel that these—. I would hope that the Government would also take that engagement with local people seriously. Unfortunately, we haven't seen that at the moment. Some decisions and options have been presented to local people, and they feel that they haven't had their say in all of this so far. So, I look forward to understanding, as does Natasha, how you will engage with local people throughout this time, because their voice absolutely needs to be heard.

This is why we in Welsh Labour believe that local people do need to shape this answer to the decades-old problem at the M4 around Newport, and we know that it shouldn't be an experiment that I feel like we're seeing today. The Welsh Government should begin work immediately on what an appropriate relief road could look like to meet the needs of a growing city. And that has changed: Newport is, as I said, the fastest growing city, it's a young city, so we have to be aware of that.

Mike Hedges talked about that this is not just a particular—. This, obviously, is an issue we're talking about today, but we do know there are other resilience issues around the road network in Wales. Mike mentioned the M4 around Swansea.

Ken talked about building roads better and investment in growth. I think an appropriate relief road would have the innovation to drive down and embed carbon and promote alternatives to private transport, and it should act as a template for responsible road building that others can follow. I think it's something that we can do to lead the world here.

Art mentioned—[Interruption.] I'd like to go to Art, sorry, James; I'm out of time otherwise. But I would like to mention Art, who contributed as well, who mentioned the homes that have been built, and mentioned the points in the report, and that the Government is at the moment planning to fail. But different funding options should be explored, as we have said. We need to listen to the local leaders who work with local communities to solve this problem. Give it to leaders who innovate and inspire an effective solution. So, let's put people above politics and vote for this motion today. Diolch.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: The next item is the short debate. Jason O'Connell.
documents.text_cy: Yr eitem nesaf yw'r ddadl fer. Jason O'Connell.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. It's good to see the Chamber so full for a short debate. I had no idea I was so popular. I'd like to give a minute's time in this debate to Joe Martin, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, Francesca O'Brien, Carrie Harper, Steven Rodaway and Kiera Marshall.

Llywydd, our town centres were once the bright and beating heart of our communities, where businesses thrived and families felt safe. But years of economic decline and political failure have let our town centres, sadly, rot. As a result, a new dangerous culture has emerged. From Newport to Rhyl, balaclava-clad young men, often dangerously riding illegal e-bikes, have been fuelling anti-social behaviour and making our streets feel unsafe. For these individuals, face coverings are a way to conceal their identity, to make it harder for authorities to hold them accountable. And while Governments across the UK turn a blind eye to this, Reform says, 'Enough is enough'.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
Face coverings have no place in British and Welsh society. Let's take a look at the city of Newport, the city that holds the unenviable title of the worst high street in Britain. Disaffected young people have run through businesses, causing a decimated high street and rundown shopfronts, leading to a loss of inward investment and hope for the future deserted, thanks, in part, to balaclava-covered youths running riot over those that are just trying to make a living—people who've worked hard, paid their taxes, and contributed to their communities. But this is not just about one Welsh city; this is a Wales-wide issue.

Plaid will say this is a pointless debate because it's a non-devolved matter reserved to Westminster. But that doesn't mean UK councils are powerless. Look at what Nottingham has achieved as an example. They introduced a targeted restriction against face coverings, and they've seen a 40 per cent reduction in city-centre anti-social behaviour. Newport City Council has voted to explore similar options, and I, alongside every Reform MS, will be encouraging all Welsh councils to do the same.

Adam Price disappointed me today with his response to spokespersons' questions. Imagine being a victim of crime, of violent theft or some kind of violent robbery, only to listen to Plaid's economy minister today saying balaclava bans are a gimmick, that businesses don't care. But the reality is that Plaid doesn't care. Plaid cares more about promoting foreign cultures than our own. They clearly don't care about keeping Welsh people and businesses safe.

When a Welsh person supports Reform, Plaid often accuses them of questioning their loyalty to Wales. But when foreign people who can't speak any British language enter Wales for a life on the welfare system, they are celebrated as trophies of the benefits of mass migration. They don't care about how a lack of integration by face-clad unknown people impacts Wales, our working-class communities. All they care about is supporting mass migration in all its forms, no matter the cost to our communities. We see this today. They defend balaclavas, all because they want some in our society to be able to hide their faces. Some will lazily say we're being Islamophobic, whatever that means. Some, no doubt, will roll out the old classic and shriek, 'Racists!' These tropes are tired, ineffective, and clearly wildly inaccurate, but I will address them.

Reform supports freedom of religion in all its forms. But where that freedom oppresses women and damages assimilation into Welsh communities, a line must be drawn. In Afghanistan, under Taliban rule, women are under a system of gender apartheid. They can't study above the age of 12, they can't speak loudly in public, and they're forced, by law, to wear the burqa. If they don't, they could be denied healthcare, they could be beaten, or even worse. For these women, raised under an extremist form of Islam, the burqa is a symbol of oppression. This symbol is what Plaid Members are attempting to back today: an extreme ideology that is anti British, anti women and against assimilation, forced on young girls and carried on into adulthood.

In numerous countries, the burqa is already banned. But we cannot allow this form of oppression to become the norm in Wales. Walk through any areas across Wales, and you will see it for yourself. The Muslim Council of Wales has tried to silence this debate today, saying we are hateful and divisive. So, I say again, and let me be very clear: Reform has no issue with the hijab, we have no issue or problem with Islam or Muslims, but we do have an issue with people living in our communities hiding their identities. We say the same thing to protesters that cover their faces, whatever their political persuasion. In modern Britain, we are polite people. We say 'hello' to our neighbours, and we do not hide our faces. That is our culture, that is our way, regardless of race, creed or religion. Reform wants safer streets and strong communities for our families to live, work and thrive. Diolch.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Face coverings, including the burqa, are anti British. Not all cultures are equal. We can't continue to import alien cultures into this country and expect integration. These oppressive beliefs are totally at odds with our history and culture. Banning these coverings is simple common sense. European countries like Denmark, Belgium and Austria have already banned them. We should do the same. Muslim countries like Kazakhstan and Tunisia have already banned face veils. France is currently on fire; this country could be next. We can't allow a parallel society to develop in this country, or we could be facing the consequences sooner than we think.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Carrie Harper.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I think we're all entitled to question Reform's real intentions when they raise a debate on face coverings, especially given, just in the last fortnight, a very similar debate was raised in the Scottish Parliament as well, which explicitly called for banning the burqa and the niqab, and we've heard the same statements here today. So, let's not pretend that this is about criminality and balaclavas. That's nonsense, and we can all see through that. This is a thinly veiled attack on the religious rights of women. That's blatantly obvious to everybody.

I think it's really ironic as well that Reform have chosen to frame this debate about values in the same week that we've had an ITV investigation exposing deep-rooted racism and sexism in your party. One of the worst things that I heard from that programme was then Reform councillor Chris Whelan talking about a fellow Reform candidate. He said, 'If she were my daughter, it would still be bath night on a Thursday'. Vile, disgusting and disturbing in the way it sexualised a child. There were multiple examples of sexism and racism in that programme, from the party that claims to want to protect women.

So, seriously, how can Reform lecture us about values when they're in the midst of a scandal about racism and sexism? How on earth can you claim to stand up for women when you are trying to dictate what Muslim women can and cannot wear? Complete hypocrisy—complete hypocrisy.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
The burqa and niqab are two of the many ways in which fundamentalist Islam is uniquely incompatible with western civilisation. They represent ideas that are oppressive, misogynistic and anti-British. Mass immigration was sold to the public with the assertion that those arriving would assimilate into British culture. That was a lie—we can't even see the faces of thousands of people who've moved here. If two Muslim women live in the same street and they both wear burqas, how are we meant to tell them apart? I can't believe this needs to be said, but being able to tell people apart is an important part of British culture.

Proponents will argue that they promote modesty and stop women from being sexualised. For thousands of years, the west achieved the same result—not by oppressing women, but by requiring men to employ an ounce of self-control. If the people who've moved here can't do that, they should live in countries where it's accepted that men can't control themselves. I've also seen children wearing face coverings; anyone who struggles not to feel lust when looking at a child should not be free to walk around in our society. There are countries where that might be normal. This is not one of them. Assimilation means losing religious face coverings, and to encourage that, they should be banned.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
We are being asked to debate about people on the basis of what we imagine their lives to be. Their lives are not fictional, they are real, and what we debate here deeply matters to them, and affects their perception of their home here in Wales. I want to focus my remarks on a territory I'm sure is familiar to Reform of civil liberties. Members opposite speak a great deal about this, but instead of advocating for freedom, they have brought us a list of things a woman may not do, and are asking the state to enforce it.

I want to add a bit of philosophy to help frame my remarks. I choose it deliberately because I feel it has some resemblance to this debate today. Burke's argument against revolutionaries was that a nation cannot be remade by decree, and this goes back as far as 1700. A society is not an arrangement between people who happen to be alive. It is a partnership between the living, the dead and those that are yet to be born. That is the essence of the social contract.

The liberties we hold in these countries were not granted to us by anyone in this room. They were fought for, often at huge cost. Lives were lost, people were imprisoned, and often people were hanged for them. We did not earn any of that, we inherited it, and it is our role as stewards of these liberties to protect them for future generations. We are not entitled to erode that liberty just because Reform finds it politically expedient.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
I am proud to be Welsh, proud to be British, and unapologetic in defending our culture. In Britain we show our faces. It builds trust and, more importantly, it keeps us safe. In certain Islamic countries, under Islamic law, girls from puberty must cover their faces, and some countries will arrest females above the age of nine for showing too much hair. Whether balaclava or burqa, face coverings have no place on our streets here in Wales. It is oppressive, and it is a risk to Welsh public safety. We have written to the First Minister urging him to make a much-needed representation to the UK Government.

This summer, the Prime Minister and the First Minister managed to meet together to ban the barbecue. While those on the left want us to ban the barbecue, we in Reform want to ban the burqa, or the balaclava. Face coverings are incompatible with our British way of life. It is an outright betrayal of the dignity and freedom of women.

Beyond this, we must look at banning cousin marriages and address religious attitudes towards women and homosexuals. Women's freedom and their safety here in Wales deserve urgency, which is why we must, at the very first possible opportunity, ban face coverings in public, and I urge every Member across this house to support this motion. Thank you.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
This summer, a Muslim woman in my constituency in Cardiff was subject to a physical violent attack in broad daylight. The attacker shouted at her about removing her headscarf, and continued to do exactly this while physically assaulting her. And this is just one example of an increasingly common occurrence where Muslim women are being targeted. This is exactly what the rhetoric that Reform is peddling is doing.

Reform claims to protect women and girls, but they don't really, do they? Because only over the weekend did we hear about one of Reform's own MPs say that Reform is chauvinistic and has a male issue. And today, they're trying to control what women wear, and it's quite frankly disgusting and creepy that they're trying to do this. Meanwhile in Wales, 31 per cent of our children live in poverty, the unemployment rate has consistently remained above the UK average, and in this context, it's bizarre that they've chosen to focus their taxpayer-funded time on a debate like this today.

To all the Muslim women—to all the Muslim women—who might be watching today, who might be feeling afraid and let down by this debate, Reform may claim that this attack on your faith is in line with British values, but it is not in line with Welsh values. Plaid Cymru stands with you, we will stand up for you, and we will always call out this hate where we see it.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: David Mills.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
Gosh, I don't know how to follow some of this. Thank you, Presiding Officer, and thank you, Jason O'Connell, for tabling the debate. We're a nation that prides itself on our tradition of constitutional liberty, which has always included freedom of expression to dress as one chooses, including garments that most people find offensive or objectionable, such as face coverings. This stands in opposition to the tradition on the continent where restrictions are commonplace. However, I think we need to re-examine our position on this, as the wearing of face coverings has become normalised in recent years, and consider banning them.

In Swansea, Neath and many other areas of Wales, there has been a growing problem with anti-social behaviour committed by youths wearing face coverings. No-one should have to tolerate this sort of hooliganism. We should recognise too that face coverings are not normal practice in any religion, and they're only employed by a tiny minority of ultra-conservative adherents. Whilst religious freedom is an important tenet of British values, our laws and cultural norms should not bend to the whims of an ultra-conservative minority. We should recognise too that many countries across Europe, the middle east and central Asia ban the use of face coverings and do not make religious exceptions. So, I agree with Jason that the use of face coverings is a growing issue and we must look to banning them.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: I call on the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality to reply to the debate—Sioned Williams.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr, Lywydd. Before I start, I just want to say, it's been a sad day today. I stood in Aberfan this morning. I stood side by side with that community, which came together in unity in the face of such adversity. But it's been a terrible, shameful, shameless end to a sad day. A sad day indeed when those benches bring into this Siambr—those who are here to represent the whole of Wales, all our communities, all our citizens—that which seeks to divide those communities. I've listened carefully to the contributions this evening. I've been disturbed by such an unsettling sound, because, Llywydd, you don't have to strain hard at all, do you, anymore, to hear the dog whistle that has too often pierced political debates in this Chamber since the election in May? [Interruption.] Yes, Vikki.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. On Saturday afternoon, like myself, the Member who tabled this debate this evening attended a concert at Afon Taf High School to mark 60 years since the Aberfan disaster. He, like me, listened to the powerful rendition of a song called 'Diversity' by the pupils of Ynysowen Community Primary School, which called for us all to embrace and celebrate cultural differences. Would you agree with me, Minister, that the Member who tabled this debate and a number of his party Members who also spoke could do well to heed the lessons in that song sung by those young people?

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
Absolutely, and properly represent their communities and the voice of their communities. Absolutely. That dog whistle varies in volume, it's always there, but it's getting louder. It lingers over those benches, a deliberately intangible thing that leaves too many wondering whether a line has been crossed. Llywydd, I am not afraid to speak up and say that, since May, that line has too often been crossed. It hides itself in plain sight: hateful speech dressed up as free speech over concerns—[Interruption.] No, we've heard enough from those benches, thank you very much. It lurks beneath what is disingenuously tonight presented as the language of common sense and—I'm not taking interventions—in today's case, British values. [Interruption.] Llywydd, can I carry on?

I want the Members who have spoken in support of this debate to know that not only do we hear you but we see you. We see you for what you are. We see you weaponising discontent, driving division and stirring hate. We see you in this debate conflating the intimidating behaviour of thugs—those whose protests can descend into disorder and violence, often in demonstrations directed against migrants or Muslims—with the very people who are targeted by that intimidating behaviour.

Llywydd, let me say clearly that I do not accept the premise that face coverings are in themselves contrary to our values. Such a catch-all position ignores the many legitimate reasons why face coverings are worn. People's rights to do so can, of course, be subject already to lawful and proportionate restrictions when necessary, including to prevent crime and disorder. But the justification comes from the situation and the behaviour, not from a judgment that covering one's face in itself is unacceptable and dangerous.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Will you take an intervention, Minister?

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Yes.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: We've heard a lot of nonsense tonight. What I haven't heard is any condemnation of the masked mobs who stormed RNLI stations across the south coast last month. Would you join me, Minister, in condemning those protesters and agree with me that a fine representation of British values is the decency and courage shown by the lifeboat crews out in the English channel saving lives, regardless of creed or skin or race or religion?

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
Absolutely. And the people of Neath showed—. We had a food fair recently where they were there out in the street. They had never had so much support and so many donations after those. The people of Neath came out and they spoke in support of the fine men and women of the RNLI.

One of the reasons for wearing a face covering is, of course, an important one that I am determined to use my voice to defend: religious expression. The values of our nation are centred not on exclusion but on respect, and we as representatives of our communities should respect people of every religion within them and we should never suggest that they are in any way less or inferior because they exercise their human right to freedom of religion. People of every religion or belief should feel that they belong in Wales. I do not accept that a face covering worn by an individual for religious reasons means they don't share British or Welsh values. Nor should we suggest that someone belongs any less because their religious practice differs from that of others.

Framing religious dress as contrary to British values without demonstrating any harm that justifies interference with fundamental rights risks deepening division rather than strengthening cohesion. But this is clearly Reform UK's aim here. The Jewish people of 1930s Germany were subject to the Nuremberg laws that stated they were no longer German, laws that led to their persecution and extermination by the state that stripped them of their German-ness, enabled by those who believed German-ness could not accommodate diversity. Who is the arbiter of Britishness or Welshness? Who decides that a woman who wears a face covering is less British or less Welsh? We have a moral duty and responsibility in this place to be careful about the language we use and the message we send and not to engage or encourage discrimination on the basis of race, religion or belief.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Could I ask the Minister to pause for a moment, please? There's a point of order being raised.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Just a point of order, Presiding Officer—[Inaudible.]—review, after what's been said in the last 60 seconds or so, to decide whether that's appropriate for the Chamber.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: What, stating history?

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: I am always happy to review the Record of Proceedings and return to the matter if—if—I consider a ruling is necessary. But the Minister can respond.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
Thank you. It was a statement of fact about what happened in Germany in the 1930s. The face coverings debate, when it is spoken about by Reform UK, is always referencing connection with religious dress. On 6 October, the deputy leader set out their position in this Chamber: they would ban the burqa and every full-face covering in public. The debate put forward on this subject in the Scottish Parliament also specifically references the burqa and niqab as the only face coverings mentioned. This dog-whistle politics, while almost always a disturbing undercurrent where Reform UK is concerned, pierces the surface of this debate and other debates more and more often.

But then there are occasions where the racism, sexism and misogyny of Reform UK is plain to see. ITV's exposure Undercover: A Year in Reform, broadcast just a few days ago, recorded Reform UK members and representatives describing Asian families as parasites. A Reform candidate in Wales who was employed by the Member that brought this debate to the Chamber was recorded using abhorrent racist terms. Unsurprisingly, it also exposed the misogyny and sexism within the party—so much for a party who so often claims to want to protect women and girls. And we, as women of all races and religions, stand as one against this behaviour, this language and the so-called values of your party.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: No-one should tell a woman what to wear. Respect for women means respect for every woman—respecting the fact that every woman can make her own choices. Home Office figures published last week showed a 13 per cent increase in religious hate crimes recorded by the police during the year up to March of this year. With a total of 11,419 recorded offences, there was a 15 per cent increase in hate crimes targeting Muslims. Respondents shared experiences of being physically attacked, threatened, spat upon and having their religious attire mocked and targeted.
documents.text_cy: Ni ddylai neb ddweud wrth fenyw beth i wisgo. Mae parch at fenywod yn golygu parch at bob menyw—parchu bod pob menyw yn gallu gwneud ei dewisiadau ei hunan. Roedd ffigurau'r Swyddfa Gartref a gyhoeddwyd yr wythnos diwethaf yn dangos cynnydd o 13 y cant mewn troseddau casineb crefyddol a gofnodwyd gan yr heddlu yn ystod y flwyddyn hyd at Fawrth eleni. Gyda chyfanswm o 11,419 o droseddau wedi eu cofnodi, o'r rheini roedd cynnydd o 15 y cant mewn troseddau casineb sy'n targedu Mwslimiaid. Rhannodd ymatebwyr brofiadau o gael eu hymosod yn gorfforol, eu bygwth, cael pobl yn poeri arnynt a gweld eu gwisg crefyddol yn cael ei gwawdio a'i thargedu.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: These crimes aren't just happening in faraway towns and cities, as we heard from Kiera Marshall, they're happening in our communities. When I visited a mosque in September, members of the Muslim community told me about the profound impact that Islamaphobia is having on them and how that attack, in which a Welsh Muslim woman had had her hijab torn from her head, was affecting their sense of safety and belonging.

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr. I'll be very brief. Would you not agree with this: that actually Reform UK's recent debates, including this one, are designed to divide and are designed to bring fear—[Interruption.]—to bring fear to our communities? And on this day, where you started, we should be in unity together. Would you not agree that this is shameful by Reform UK?

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text:
I absolutely agree that it's shameful. And what's also shameful is the claim that Muslim women are somehow voiceless and forced to dress against their will. That's as sexist as it is Islamaphobic. These experiences and the stubbornly high rates of hate crime don't happen by accident, they happen by design. They do so by deliberately pitting communities against each other for political gain, which is as shameful as it is hateful.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt, herself deemed 'un-German' and forced to flee her native land, warned that the death of human empathy is one of the earliest and most telling signs of a culture on the verge of descending into barbarism. What can stop that descent is the power and protection of universal human rights. So, if we are to talk about British values, let us talk first and foremost about those rights, those freedoms that are enshrined in British laws: the freedom of religion—everyone in Wales is protected by the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998—a freedom that Reform appear to have a problem with. Because the pattern is always the same: they claim to be champions of freedom—[Interruption.]—no, I won't—but only when it fits their narrow and singular definition, a dangerous, exclusionary definition. We must never be bystanders to bigotry and hatred.

And, Llywydd, this Government will always celebrate the plurality of our communities. We will always challenge those who claim that our differences divide us. Our values are demonstrated by how we treat one another. In her report on the war crimes trial of the Nazi Adolf Eichmann, Hannah Arendt suggested that his evil stemmed from an inability to think from the standpoint of someone else. That lack of empathy, that ability to see others as less, is what we must constantly guard against in this society. And that empathy must be expressed by those with power and influence through the language they use.

So, finally, Llywydd, at a time when racism and Islamaphobia, fuelled by deliberate political discourse, are becoming increasingly normalised, we should remind ourselves that we, as elected Members in this Chamber, hold a position of privilege and of power. Our words matter and we can't afford to stay silent. [Applause.]

documents.item: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
documents.text: That brings today's proceedings to a close. Thank you.
documents.text_cy: Daw hynny â thrafodion heddiw i ben. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Good afternoon, everybody.
documents.text_cy: Prynhawn da, bawb.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Good afternoon, everybody.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We will begin this afternoon with questions to the First Minister. Question 1, Lyn Ackerman.
documents.text_cy: Rydyn ni'n dechrau nawr gyda chwestiynau i'r Prif Weinidog. Cwestiwn 1, Lyn Ackerman.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 1. What assessment has the First Minister made of the uptake of annual health checks among adults with learning disabilities? OQ64798
documents.text_cy: 1. Pa asesiad y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o'r niferoedd sy'n manteisio ar wiriadau iechyd blynyddol ymhlith oedolion ag anableddau dysgu? OQ64798

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
With your permission, a brief statement from me on the incident in Newport this morning, just to say that our thoughts are very much with the children and families affected by that incident. We're grateful to the emergency services for their swift response and to everybody involved in supporting the children affected. This is an ongoing police investigation, so it would be inappropriate, I think, for me to comment further, but our thoughts are very much with those injured and those for whom this has caused anxiety today.

To the question, the uptake of annual health checks for people with a learning disability continues to show encouraging month-on-month improvement, increasing by more than 12 per cent since December 2025. Building on this momentum will be a key priority of the new learning disability transformation programme, helping to increase uptake further, identify health needs earlier and improve health outcomes.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, I welcome the inclusion of annual health checks in GP contracts and the new national pathway. Could you give me more detail on how the Welsh Government is working with the health boards and with GP practices to keep learning disability registers accurate, make invitations and appointments accessible, and how these figures can guide further support to increase uptake?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Certainly. We're working with health boards, with GP practices and NHS partners across the board to improve the quality of learning disability registers so that eligible people can be identified and offered that all-important health check. We're also supporting primary care staff through training, digital assessment tools and reasonable adjustments to make invitations, appointments and the health check process itself more accessible for people with a learning disability. Since annual health checks became part of the core GP contract, we have strengthened data collection in Government on both offers and completed checks. That information is important because it helps us to identify variation where it exists, helps us to target support where it is needed most, and also, so importantly, to share good practice to increase uptake right across Wales, which is what we're looking to see.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, once an annual health check identifies a need, responsibility should not fall on the individual to fight for treatment. People with learning disabilities need a clear, funded pathway to further tests, specialist assessment and treatment. Welsh Labour's Lynne Neagle cited £550 million over three years from Westminster for ALN. We know not all this money will be allocated to ALN, and much will go to other manifesto commitments and pledges. Last week, your finance Minister didn't, couldn't or wouldn't answer my question on Cynnal, but delivered another Plaid word salad with no answers. Show some transparency on what the rest of the £550 million is being used for. Will it support treatment protocols for people with learning disabilities? If not, please identify the specific NHS budget that funds this pathway. Thank you.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I think we've been pretty transparent that the bulk of the pressures that we face as a Government do indeed come from the NHS, from across the whole range of services that are provided, and that it's very important that we do provide, including the services that we are talking about in this question. The Member is quite right to identify the fact that the onus shouldn't be on the individual, and that is why we are putting those steps in place to strengthen the provision of how those invitations go out, to make sure that those individuals who need to be targeted for their well-being are targeted and brought into the system. This is a whole-system approach and not just one based on the finances.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I echo the points raised by the Member for Casnewydd Islwyn about the importance of these annual health checks. It's important that GPs make reasonable adjustments for these annual health checks as well, and that could mean anything from having a quiet space available for people waiting for their appointment to offering a longer appointment for some patients. Now, last week, I met with Mencap Cymru to hear about their 'I'm in' campaign, which highlights the importance of GP learning disability registers as a gateway to accessing annual health checks. Now, for many years, organisations such as Mencap Cymru have highlighted the importance of increasing annual health check uptake and ensuring they are delivered to a consistently high standard. So, therefore, First Minister, can you tell us what support does the Welsh Government provide to local health boards to help GP practices make reasonable adjustments so that these annual health checks are as accessible and as comfortable as possible for people with learning disabilities?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The Member is right that those reasonable adjustments that I referred to in my initial response are very, very important. Sometimes they can be small, but they can make a big difference. I also welcome the referencing by the Member of the work that Mencap Cymru is doing. And that's another good example, isn't it, of how this is something that many organisations, including the voluntary and the third sector, need to be involved in. We will work with health boards. We will work directly with GP practices also, to make sure that those reasonable adjustments are made. And I very much welcome feedback from an organisation such as Mencap Cymru on how we could make that system even better.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 2. How is the First Minister strengthening co-operation with the Republic of Ireland? OQ64788
documents.text_cy: 2. Sut mae'r Prif Weinidog yn cryfhau cydweithrediad â Gweriniaeth Iwerddon? OQ64788

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, I went to Dublin on my first overseas visit as First Minister back in June. I was very pleased on that visit to confirm my Government’s commitment to the joint Ireland-Wales statement for 2030. This is a partnership framework, which covers six priority areas, including climate and energy, economy and trade, culture and language. And, quite simply, Ireland is one of our most valued international relationships here in Wales. It is rooted in shared history, geography and values that I think we share, and I look forward to building on delivering the goals of that shared statement between our two nations.
documents.text_cy: Wel, i Ddulyn yr es i ar fy ymweliad cyntaf 'dros y môr', fel petai, fel Prif Weinidog, yn ôl ym mis Mehefin. Mi oeddwn i’n falch iawn o allu, ar yr ymweliad hwnnw, cadarnhau ymrwymiad fy Llywodraeth i i ddatganiad ar y cyd Iwerddon a Chymru ar gyfer 2030. Fframwaith partneriaeth ydy hwn, sy’n cynnwys chwech o feysydd blaenoriaeth, yn cynnwys hinsawdd ac ynni, economi a masnach, iaith a diwylliant. Ac Iwerddon, yn syml iawn, ydy un o’n cysylltiadau rhyngwladol mwyaf gwerthfawr ni yng Nghymru. Mae e’n gysylltiad sydd wedi’i wreiddio yn yr hanes, y ddaearyddiaeth, wrth gwrs, a’r gwerthoedd dwi'n credu rydyn ni’n eu rhannu, a dwi’n edrych ymlaen at adeiladu ar y gwaith o gyflawni nodau'r datganiad hwnnw rhwng ein dwy wlad.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch. I welcome the Ireland-Wales shared statement 2030, committing our nations to strengthening cultural partnerships and artistic exchange. In my constituency, Other Voices Cardigan has become one of the most vibrant and successful examples of that ambition. Since 2019, it has brought together Welsh and Irish artists, audiences and communities, thanks to support from the Welsh Government, the Irish Government and broadcasters. The festival has delivered significant economic benefits for Aberteifi, increased numbers visiting from Ireland to west Wales, and created lasting creative partnerships between musicians from both countries. Sadly, a late decision to reduce funding this year means the festival isn't taking place. So, a multi-year funding agreement is now vital to enable the festival to continue to plan for future years. So, will the First Minister explore this potential with his Irish counterparts to help secure the long-term future of Other Voices Cardigan and strengthen Wales-Ireland relations for years to come?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Other Voices has certainly been a valued cultural partnership for Wales, helping to showcase Welsh and international talent, while strengthening our relationship specifically with Ireland. Officials did meet the festival organisers last month, on 22 September, to discuss future proposals, with a further meeting, as I understand, scheduled for early November. And my officials in Dublin also are discussing future support with the Irish Government. We do remain open to discussions about future proposals. This will be, of course, subject to funding priorities and available budgets.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, collaboration from the Irish Republic is something that I, like you, strongly support, particularly on trade, Holyhead and the resilience of our links across the Irish Sea. But co-operation between two Governments is one matter; advancing a party political constitutional objective is quite another. Your Government's shared statement, as you just mentioned before, with Ireland, specifically refers to co-operation in areas for which the Welsh Government has devolved responsibility. So, will you give this Chamber a categorical assurance that Welsh Government offices, officials, public money and ministerial visits to Ireland will not be used directly or indirectly to promote Plaid Cymru's campaign for Welsh independence? And can you give that assurance today?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, we had a meeting recently that was a political meeting between a political party in Ireland and me as leader of Plaid Cymru in Wales on areas of shared responsibility. There are Government actions that we take that are around trade and that are around culture. Similarly, we have an agreement with the Scottish Government around climate change and renewable energy, and so on. The activities of this Government will be around those Government issues on which we can find common ground in order to pursue the interests of the people of Ireland and the people of Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We on these benches very much value greater co-operation and increased trade with Ireland. Around 1.5 million passenger journeys are made between Wales and Ireland each year through Holyhead port, making it a vital gateway between the two nations. Holyhead handled 4.3 million tonnes of freight between Ireland and Wales in 2024, which is more than any other Welsh port. The 2.4 km Holyhead breakwater is approximately 150 years old and needs work done to it. First Minister, closer co-operation with Ireland must be demonstrated through delivering not simply warm words. Your Government inherited a £40 million commitment to Holyhead breakwater, together with a clear warning that its failure could ultimately close the port. With Welsh-Irish connectivity, trade and around 700 local jobs dependent on resilient port infrastructure, why is there still no firm timetable, and when exactly will the refurbishment begin and be completed?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Work is progressing on the work that absolutely needs to happen to maintain this remarkable piece of engineering. For anybody who hasn't ventured to the far end of it, clear a decent amount of time, because it takes time, but it is something that is a genuine engineering marvel. That is an immediate challenge to the port of Holyhead, and action is being taken to remediate the damage caused by many years of Irish sea storms. The ongoing damage, of course, that we face is the damage of Brexit. The Member mentions the importance of the port of Holyhead, and we know the pain that has been caused in terms of limits on trade to the port of Holyhead. We're still seeing it now with the comings and goings on the border posts. This is disruption that has held back the development of the port of Holyhead. That is something that is in my mind when I say that we should be building closer relationships with our European friends, the closest of which is across the Irish sea—the Republic of Ireland.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I now call on the party leaders to question the First Minister. First, the leader of Reform UK, Helen Jenner.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar arweinwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Prif Weinidog. Yn gyntaf, arweinydd Reform UK, Helen Jenner.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I want to firstly pay tribute to the Aberfan tragedy, which took place 60 years ago tomorrow. We'll never forget the lives lost and the community forever scarred by this devastating event. I appreciate the Government is making a statement on this later today, and I welcome the opportunity to pay further tribute then.

Llywydd, we are coming to the end of a very long half term, but whatever fatigue we might be feeling here in this Chamber, quadruple that and you might get somewhere near to how our teachers are feeling. It's not just down to the day-to-day workload; teachers are under immense strain when it comes to managing students' behaviour. More and more teachers are reporting high levels of verbal and physical abuse from students, and many are beginning to feel unsafe at work. First Minister, we've heard a lot about this Government's new literacy and numeracy frameworks, but will your Government now commit to delivering a robust behaviour framework, and will it include zero tolerance on violence, which would protect school staff from the sort of abuse that isn't accepted in other public institutions, because what's currently in place across schools in Wales is clearly not fit for purpose?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I absolutely think that we should have that zero-tolerance approach towards violence. My Government has shown very clearly its support for the teaching profession, and the pupils, the parents and the wider school community that are affected when, sadly, we do see incidents of violence in schools, albeit, thankfully, very, very rare. Just as we have put clear frameworks in place to improve standards in schools, we have also clearly made it a priority to work across agencies to make sure that all those partners can work together to make schools the safe learning environment that we all want them to be.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, a well-known issue with behaviour in schools is linked to students having access to their mobile phones. At the end of July this year, schools across the border in England were given clarity on mobile phone use. What was initially guidance became law and, from the beginning of this academic year, a statutory mobile phone ban was in place. Yet, here we are in Wales, the first half term down, and teachers from my constituency are contacting me to say that the problems with phones are persisting, and headteachers are holding their hands up, saying there's nothing they can do because they're waiting for guidance from the Welsh Government. So, First Minister, when can teachers in Wales be given the same clarity as in England? When will this Government make a decision on whether or not to ban mobile phones from the classroom?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We already made a decision as a Government to act as quickly as we could. It was a suggestion that we might legislate on this. We took the decision that we didn't want to wait for legislation to happen and that we would press ahead with making it clear that we, as a Government, wanted action to be taken. That consultation is happening now, so we can move as quickly as we can to empower those school leaders to make the necessary choices around phones. We made it very, very clear as a Government that we expect that to happen, and that will be in the guidance.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
You're talking about empowering schools to make the necessary choices around phones, and that leads to this notion of guidance as opposed to bringing something into law. First Minister, the fact is that you are speaking, as you know, to a former teacher, and I can tell you that schools interpret guidance very, very differently. So, what we really need is leadership from this Government on this matter. It is vital that a consistent approach is enforced across all schools in Wales, not only to benefit teachers dealing with poor behaviour associated with phone use, but for the well-being and academic success of our students. I would like to read out a quote from a former year 11 pupil of mine, word for word:

'It's like you're distracted by your phone. You can't get anything done. I know the school says, "Keep your phone in your bag", but I know it's there, and if I hear it buzz, I just have to check it, and I can't focus on anything else. If they banned phones in schools, I know I'd hate it'—

she was very honest—

'but I'd keep thinking about all the things I'd be able to get done if they did.'

This is a 16-year-old GCSE student crying out for a boundary with phones for the good of her education. First Minister, the Government can't control what goes on in people's homes, but it can lead the way when it comes to removing the distraction of phones from schools. We've got the worst Programme for International Student Assessment scores in the UK and a mental health catastrophe on the way. So much of this can be linked to excessive phone use. So, First Minister, I ask will you today commit to an outright ban on mobile phones in schools and, if so, when can we see that happen?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We agree with the points that have been made. We agree on the damage that can be caused to a child's education through the existence of phones in schools. We agree also on the element of bullying that can be linked to mobile phone use, and that is why we took the decision not to wait for legislation and to take action sooner, because this Government expects schools to take the action of the kind that the Member outlines.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The leader of Welsh Labour, Ken Skates.
documents.text_cy: Arweinydd Llafur Cymru, Ken Skates.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'd also like to pay tribute to the community of Aberfan, as we remember one of Wales's worst ever tragedies.

First Minister, our democracy is facing unprecedented attacks through the spread of misinformation and disinformation. So-called bots and algorithms are a threat to open-mindedness, and I'd urge you to ask UK intelligence chiefs whether there's any evidence emerging of any recent interference in Welsh democracy. But, of course, the greatest defence against this is the objective truth provided by truly independent journalism. The BBC in Wales must be protected from the recently announced cuts. Our democracy needs impartial and independent news more than ever before, and I'm amazed that we haven't had an opportunity to debate or discuss the threats posed to the BBC in Wales. First Minister, what are you doing to save jobs at BBC Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I declare an interest previously declared, as a journalist myself, as a member of the National Union of Journalists, and, of course, we are all deeply concerned about any funding decisions at the BBC that impact not just journalism itself, but the way we tell our own story as a nation to ourselves as a nation and to the world. So, I'm very concerned indeed about potential cuts, and that is something that we will publicly make clear. On the other hand, we, of course, do not have a situation whereby broadcasting is devolved. I would like to be in the situation where broadcasting is devolved in order that we are able to put more protections in place for Welsh-based journalism, for the way that we're able to speak about our nation to ourselves and to the world. We will be taking measures to strengthen the voice of broadcasting in Wales, but we need to see that devolution, and I would welcome the support of the Member for that call.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
First Minister, I don't think we can wait for the devolution of broadcasting, and, indeed, devolution of broadcasting in itself will not protect BBC Wales from cuts being imposed by the board centrally in London. It needs protection right now. We shouldn't have radio silence from the Welsh Government over what's happening at the BBC. It's as though Ministers are content to sit on their hands whilst our democracy is weakened.

Now, another issue over which Plaid Cymru Members sat on their hands is the Hillsborough law. In the last Senedd term, your party abstained on a crucial consent motion. When the matter returns to this Chamber, will you commit to vote with Welsh Labour and support the fight for justice for the 97 and their families?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
The Member knows full well that we support the principle and the purpose of a Hillsborough law, and that the duty of candour is something that people should be able to expect.

On the comment that he made previously about a board in London making decisions on broadcasting in Wales, let's just, for example, replace that 'board in London' with 'a UK Government'. On how many issues is that UK Government making decisions in London that have a detrimental impact on us in Wales? And how many years have Labour sat on their hands on rail funding, rather than making decisions that could make a real difference now to the infrastructure that we need in Wales?

I hope there's a conversion happening here, where the leader of the Labour group is starting to see things my way. The evidence suggests otherwise. But this is precisely the case that we make. We need here in Wales to be able to make those decisions that build a better future for Wales ourselves, because we cannot depend on a board in London or, indeed, a UK Government to do the right thing for Wales themselves.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The leader of the Welsh Conservatives, Darren Millar.
documents.text_cy: Arweinydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Darren Millar.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Can I also put on record that our thoughts are also with those affected by the devastating events in Aberfan 60 years ago this week?

First Minister, it's vitally important that every single penny of taxpayers' money is well spent, and that includes on our national health service here in Wales. Unfortunately, more than £600 million has been paid out by the Welsh NHS in clinical negligence and personal injury claims over the past five years, £145 million of which was just in the last financial year alone. These are eye-watering figures, but they provide further evidence of the crisis engulfing the NHS here in Wales. Every single payout, of course—. Behind those payouts are families and individuals who've suffered loss or harm as a result of some tragic situation and failings in care. Now, our priority, I believe, has to be preventing these tragedies from happening in the first place, because every pound paid in compensation is a pound that could have been invested in delivering better care, better facilities for patients and better outcomes for them across the country. What action are you and your Government taking to get to grips with this issue?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I agree, Llywydd, with the points made by the Member that, when we lose money from the NHS in compensation payments, that is money that is lost from the front line of tackling the serious issues that we have within the NHS in Wales. We don't think of it centrally as a financial issue, because behind every one of those compensation claims you will have somebody that has suffered a loss of some sort, because of—. It could be a human error, it could be a deeper systemic issue within the NHS. All I'll say is that we are determined as a Government to root out those problems that are within our control. There will always be mistakes made, by very, very well-meaning and professional health workers, and the compensation system exists in order to address that and pay recompense where that is necessary. But we are a Government that is determined to root out those issues that are creating the unsustainability of the NHS, and perhaps the unsustainability that is leading to problems that could end up with a compensation payout.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I asked you for specific things about what you would do to try and tackle this, and I appreciate the words about your desire to get on and deliver some improved sustainability, but you didn't tell me any specifics in terms of action that you would take, and, unfortunately, the situation with compensation payments looks as though it's going to get a whole lot worse. The Royal College of Emergency Medicine has warned today that our emergency departments in Wales are in a precarious position and facing the prospects of a very, very difficult winter, largely due to a lack of hospital beds. And the latest Welsh Risk Pool talks about the financial forecasts in the future, and buried on page 733 of a 1,100-page pack of papers for the Velindre University NHS Trust board, it suggests that the annual cost in the year 2028-29 of negligence claims is expected to rise to more than £310 million per year. So, within three years, the Welsh NHS could be shelling out the equivalent of salaries for more than 8,000 nurses in clinical negligence claims. I'd rather see that money spent on preventing people from coming to harm and dying than on compensation.

So, can I ask you today, First Minister, to declare a health emergency? Everybody knows that we need to do that. Surge hospital numbers, recruit more doctors, nurses and paramedics, and then get on and deliver the safer care that people across Wales need.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I respect the consistency with which the leader of the Conservatives makes that call for declaring a health emergency. I want to impress this Senedd with the fact that I don't think we could be treating the NHS with a higher level of urgency than we are currently. Giving it a title in that respect doesn't work, doesn't make a difference. What we have done since coming into Government, in that very short time, is make that financial investment in speeding up flow through the system, the kind of governance changes that we believe will lead to better management and, hopefully, if we get this right, to reducing the number of errors that happen within the health service, and improving our ability to target what is going wrong across the health service.

The Member knows, having spoken on health for many, many years, that the problems we face within the NHS in Wales are multiple. Our task is to build that sustainability to create a system that works well together. I am satisfied that we are putting those steps in place now. Will it take time? Yes. But the example given on the need to bring down compensation payments is a very, very valid example of why keeping things as they were under previous administrations within the health service is not an option.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 3. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve the support provided to adopted and care-experienced children and young people? OQ64755
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella'r cymorth a ddarperir i blant a phobl ifanc mabwysiedig a'r rhai sydd â phrofiad o fod mewn gofal? OQ64755

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Everybody in Wales deserves access to high-quality care and support that is timely, effective and centred around their needs. Through investment in therapeutic support, early intervention, the removal of profit from care and the transformation of children’s services, we are committed to working with the 75 signatories to our corporate parenting charter to improve stability, strengthen relationships and deliver better outcomes for adopted and care-experienced children and young people.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
In the August 2026 report, Care Inspectorate Wales found that adoption support remained inconsistent, with waiting lists across almost every regional collaborative. The average number of days taken for children to move from the decision that they should be placed for adoption to actually being in place varied considerably across Wales, with the lowest figure of 248 days waiting in the Western Bay Adoption Service to a high of 450 days waiting in the Adoption Mid and West Wales collaborative. It is apparent that you want to build a united Wales, but in what modern nation is it acceptable for a child to wait an additional 202 days to get the outcome they need in one region compared to the other? This is not timely.

Having experienced the care system myself, both as a child and as an adoptive parent, I know the struggle first-hand. So, my question is simple: what specifically is this Government going to do to close these gaps and ensure equitable support nationwide?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Well, the Member's lived experience tells her why this is not acceptable, that people are waiting too long, and, as a Government, we want to close that gap. The Welsh Government funds the National Adoption Service. The national adoption commitment supports access to a range of universal targeted and specialist provision, which is important. But we have to be always looking at means to make sure that children have the support that they need sooner. It is not the situation that we accept things as they are.

We also have to accept that once we are able, hopefully, working with other partners, to speed up that initial part of the system, adoption is recognised as a lifelong journey, and support isn't limited to that point of placement, as much as we need to get that point of placement speeded up and the making of that adoption order. Children, young people and families can access and re-engage with adoption supporters as needs emerge, or as those needs change over time. But the Member is right. Through our work with the National Adoption Service and the funding that is going in—over £2 million of core funding per year—we have to make sure that that initial contact is made quicker.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, the previous Government had a programme of radical reform of care for care-experienced children and young people. That programme made progress, but I would argue that there is much more work still to be done. The programme benefited from the proactive involvement of successive First Ministers. Can I ask whether it is the Government's intention to continue that programme and whether you will personally be involved in it? Because I think that is a vital thing, that we all recognise that care-experienced children are all our children.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Absolutely, and I certainly appreciate efforts made by Ministers and First Ministers in the past to highlight this as an issue that we have come to, I think, understand as being one that we as elected Members need to take more seriously than perhaps we have done in the past. I certainly will work closely with my ministerial team. Programmes will change, programmes will develop, programmes will evolve, and that is very much what we want to do in partnership with others across this Senedd.

But we know that there's been a lot of attention given, for example, to the cliff edge of care—when young people, having gone through care, leave care and find themselves without that level of support that we should be able to give them. That's one example of why we need to work right across Government, including the First Minister, to show those young people that we are serious in our words and in our deeds in supporting them.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, many young people face a sheer cliff-edge situation when they turn 18 and prepare to leave care. It means moving from an established care system that they're familiar with to the uncertainty of independent living. That, quite understandably, can be really daunting because often they don't have the family network, safety nets or support that other young people have. Too many care-experienced young people face challenges with financing, housing, employment, education and their mental health. So, First Minister, I'd like to know: what is your Government doing to ensure that young people across Wales are as prepared as possible for this transition? And will you commit to ensuring support continues for as long as these young people need it, rather than simply ending it on their eighteenth birthday?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I'm grateful to the Member for again emphasising that cliff edge that we need to avoid. Action is being taken to provide longer term support for young people who have left care. That starts with the role of personal advisers and provision to ensure that all care leavers do have a personal adviser up to the age of 25. I think that's very, very important. We have re-established the Wales leaving care forum to share learning and inform our policy development on care leavers. And finally, perhaps—again, one of the areas where we have to work cross-departmentally on this—our programme for government specifically includes a commitment to embed a housing first, trauma-informed and person-centred approach to tackling homelessness. That's very, very relevant when it comes to making sure that we look after the housing needs of young people leaving care.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 4. What assessment has the First Minister made of the adequacy of staffing levels in NHS Wales? OQ64794
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa asesiad y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o ddigonolrwydd lefelau staffio yn GIG Cymru? OQ64794

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We have the largest NHS workforce Wales has ever had. We have a committed workforce. We have a skilled workforce. But we know that the state of the workforce can't be judged by numbers alone. That is why we are developing a new NHS workforce strategy now to support a sustainable workforce for the future. Our new digital and estate strategies will also support the modernisation of services to nurture a more productive and innovative workforce.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister, for that answer. Numbers do make a difference when it comes to general practitioner practices. Over the last 15 years, there's been a drop in GP numbers of some 20 per cent, from 1,845 to under 1,500 GPs now available within the Welsh NHS. You have a manifesto commitment to, obviously, put an extra 100 GPs into the service by the end of this Senedd term. How are those 100 GPs going to be allocated to the GP practices in Wales, given that, as a percentage, we have fewer full-time GPs working within the Welsh NHS, and yet patient numbers have gone up by a third for those full-time equivalent GPs?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Full-time equivalence is very, very important here, because we've been given statistics in recent years showing the number of GPs growing, when actually the number of full-time equivalent GPs has not increased at the same level. Yes, we have a pledge to recruit 100 new GPs. Essentially, we know that there are different pressures in different parts of Wales. We will need to make those decisions based on the specific pressures in different parts of Wales. We know, for example, that rural parts of Wales have faced problems in recruiting GPs. But it's not just rural areas either; post-industrial areas have experienced problems in recruiting GPs also. This is very much a part of that workforce strategy. Again, coming back to my initial point, it's not just about numbers; it's how those people are used, how they're individually able to work to the top of their training, but also that they're in the right place, doing the right things, to make sure that that NHS sustainability really does exist across the board.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I declare an interest as somebody who lives with diabetes and has worked in diabetes care. Our specialist diabetes teams in Wales deserve enormous credit for the progress they've made in giving people access to new diabetes technology. What we need to appreciate is that Wales has made that progress without the same dedicated injection of implementation funding that we have seen in England. That is a success story for Wales and, above all, for our NHS staff, but we must be careful that their success is not used as evidence that they can simply continue to do more with the same resources. First Minister, how will the Welsh Government build on that success and ensure that our specialist workforce has the investment it needs so that Wales can continue to improve access to life-changing diabetes technology? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The Member, Llywydd, is right to recognise the success of our specialist diabetes teams here in Wales, and I'm proud of the progress that those teams have made. We continue to support improvement in the delivery of diabetes care by using a carefully planned approach to NHS services. The Welsh Government itself sets national planning requirements on NHS organisations through the NHS planning framework and system measures. The expectations for planning diabetes care are set out in the quality statement for diabetes, which was updated earlier this year, in February. As part of our ongoing Tackling Diabetes Together programme, we're supporting health boards to ensure that type 1 diabetics can access hybrid closed-loop systems. This is the very latest technology recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. It's a good example of how we're using technology and using innovation in order to improve the outcomes for patients.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The NHS in Wales now employs more than 100,000 members of full-time equivalent staff across the organisation. Those staff are the backbone of our NHS, and they do vital work to provide the care that so many people in Wales depend on. But, too often, they are overburdened and under-resourced, and those problems are exacerbated when staffing levels are insufficient. Official statistics show that there are currently more than 5,000 unfilled posts across our NHS, with medical and dental vacancies nearing 9 per cent. Sickness absences are elevated, and many clinicians are reporting that staffing levels are currently inadequate to meet patient demand. What specific action is the Government taking to reduce our dependency on agency and temporary staff, so that we can recruit and retain more home-grown workers and deliver a measurable improvement for our patients in Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I welcome those comments. This is something that was a mantra of mine when I was a health spokesman in opposition. It is quite obvious why over-reliance on agency staff causes and exacerbates unsustainability within the workforce. It's something that my Minister has acted on, because dealing with that historic overuse of agency work absolutely gets to grips with how we make sure that we're not taking short-term decisions, but that we're thinking about the long term always. I think if there's one thing that previous administrations were failing on more than any it was—and it was well meant—'deal with the waiting times now, as quickly as possible'. It wasn't particularly successful, but also was not addressing the long-term problems. Making sure that we have long-term staffing in place, with a commitment to those areas of the NHS in which they're working, gives you that robustness that we need to improve services moving forward. This is part of that wider workforce planning agenda, as I said. We've been clear that workforce planning across NHS Wales must continue to strengthen. Workforce planning has often relied on just replacing existing vacancies and modelling based on current workforce numbers, rather than taking a broader look. That's a fundamentally different approach that we're taking as a Government.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 5. What steps is the Welsh Government taking to support people living with motor neurone disease in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni? OQ64781
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gefnogi pobl sy’n byw gyda chlefyd niwronau motor ym Mlaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni? OQ64781

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Motor neurone disease is a devastating illness that has a profound impact on those affected, their families and loved ones. We are committed to improving care and support for people living with the disease. Health boards are implementing the quality statement for neurological conditions to provide better, more consistent care for people with MND and other neurological conditions.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Motor neurone disease, as you said, is such a devastating, rapidly progressing condition, and, for those people who are living with it, time is really critical. I lost my auntie to MND a couple of years ago, and I saw first-hand the devastating impact that that had on her and our family as well. Around a third of people who are diagnosed with MND die within a year of that diagnosis, yet the MND Association tells us that securing funding for vital home adaptation can take just as long. And that funding is about so much more than just home improvements. It's about preserving people's independence, their dignity and also their quality of life.
