Constituents have contacted me about the difficulties that they face in securing these adaptations. People with MND shouldn't have to spend their precious time waiting for their homes to be made safe and accessible for them. So, Prif Weinidog, what steps are the Welsh Government taking to address the critical housing challenges faced by people living with MND in Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, the first thing I would say is that I'm sorry for your and your family's loss, and no doubt your own experience will make you an effective campaigner for those living with MND. People have a right to expect us to help them to maintain their independence and to continue to live at home with dignity. Home adaptations are a smart preventative investment, protecting independence and generally easing those pressures on health and care services. The Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014 codes of practice already enable local authorities to respond quickly where a person has a rapidly deteriorating condition, as with MND. To make this possible, Welsh Government continues to invest some £60 million to speed up and expand home adaptations, on top of funding to local authorities to deliver disabled facilities grants to their residents. In addition, the Welsh Government-funded Managing Better service, delivered by Care and Repair Cymru and partners, provides practical advice, support and home interventions for people with complex needs, including MND.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 6. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve public transport services in rural areas of Fflint Wrecsam? OQ64787
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella gwasanaethau trafnidiaeth gyhoeddus mewn ardaloedd gwledig yn Fflint Wrecsam? OQ64787

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Through expansion of pay-as-you-go on the rail network, our £26 million investment in bus grants and network north Wales, and £28 million of funding through the regional transport fund, we continue to invest meaningfully in public transport in north Wales. Transport for Wales have recently concluded a consultation on the bus network specifically across the region, and more than 1,000 people participated, showing just how important public transport is to communities across the region.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Residents in rural Flintshire villages such as Llanfynydd and Penyffordd feel increasingly frustrated by the lack of reliable bus services. They're sporadic at best, and they're also under threat. For any vibrant community, that simply isn't good enough. This is about more than bus timetables; this is about people's independence, it's their ability to get to hospital, to get to work, to see friends and family, to live their day-to-day lives. Some of you might think that Fflint Wrecsam is an urban area, but I can tell you there are rural pockets in my constituency that feel as excluded and isolated as any in Wales. For some, especially the elderly, these barriers of transport can leave them feeling isolated with limited options to get around. So, will the First Minister outline what work is being done with Transport for Wales to protect and improve rural bus services to ensure these communities can access public transport easily and effectively?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
The Member is right, Llywydd, these are people's lives, this is their ability to access services and to access leisure and so on, and I certainly recognise the vital role that bus services play in that, in connecting rural communities to work, education, healthcare and social opportunities, and those in urban areas to those opportunities too. Some £150 million is being invested in local bus services across Wales this year, helping to protect services and to improve connectivity, despite significant cost pressures right now across the sector.

We are working closely, though, with local authorities and Transport for Wales to improve access to public transport in rural areas, including through innovative solutions such as the Fflecsi demand-responsive services that have been introduced in Flintshire, as in some other areas. Alongside that, crucially, the bus reform programme that we'll be delivering will help deliver a more integrated and more accessible bus network that must better meet the needs of communities across Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to support high-street businesses in Gŵyr Abertawe? OQ64730
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gefnogi busnesau'r stryd fawr yng Ngŵyr Abertawe? OQ64730

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: High-street businesses are at the heart of thriving communities. We're backing businesses across Gŵyr Abertawe through town centre regeneration, alongside advice, finance, skills and digital support. In addition, our independent town centre taskforce is focused on practical options to revitalise town centres and create thriving places where businesses can succeed, and where eligible retail, hospitality and leisure premises will benefit from a permanent 30 per cent reduction in business rates from April 2027, something that has been widely welcomed.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister. Our high streets are being taken over by dodgy vape and barbershops. Last week, in my constituency, two vape shops were shut down due to their suspected involvement in trading illegal goods, including drugs. It's also come to my attention that many similar businesses have been placed on the visa sponsor list, which allows them to bring in so-called skilled workers into this country. What is the Welsh Government doing to support councils, trading standards and immigration enforcement to finally take action on this crisis, which is destroying our local high streets?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Our high streets have been in decline for many years. Where we have any examples of illicit businesses or businesses not behaving in the appropriate way, it has always been the case that trading standards are able to step in. We certainly do want to work with local authorities to make sure that our trading standards are able to step in, whatever the issues might be around trading misdemeanours or worse. What I am focused on and what we in Welsh Government are able to do is to bring that vibrancy back to our high streets, making sure that we do have that mix of businesses on our high streets, that mix of shops and leisure, and to create that footfall that brings our high streets back to, I think, what we all believe they should be, which are the centrepieces of communities.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 8. What action is the Welsh Government taking to ensure efficiency and waste reduction when delivering public services to achieve better value for money for taxpayers? OQ64796
documents.text_cy: 8. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i sicrhau effeithlonrwydd a gostyngiad mewn gwastraff wrth ddarparu gwasanaethau cyhoeddus er mwyn sicrhau gwell gwerth am arian i drethdalwyr? OQ64796

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Our focus is very much, Llywydd, on making every pound of public money work as hard as possible for the people of Wales. That means spending better, reducing duplication, simplifying how Government works and moving resources from administration towards front-line services, which I think is what people want to see. We're also taking a much stronger focus on outcomes, making sure public spending delivers real benefits for people and supports the priorities this Government was elected to deliver.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Minister, Welsh taxpayers are continually being asked to pay more, yet many feel they are receiving less in return. Does the Minister agree that rather than continually demanding more from Welsh taxpayers, the Welsh Government should first demonstrate that it can spend the money it receives responsibly? And will the Minister commit to an independent, comprehensive audit of Welsh Government spending, identifying wasteful projects, unnecessary bureaucracy and duplication of services, with a clear commitment to redirect those savings towards front-line NHS services, education and local communities, because surely the priority should be delivering value for taxpayers, not simply spending more money?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: In effect, I don't disagree with the central point made there, that our job is to spend money well, but your job is to hold us to account for the way that we spend our money. [Interruption.] That's what you've been elected to do. I became First Minister. And on an independent audit of the way Welsh Government spends its money, well, we have a national audit office for Wales, which literally does that. We are held to account in different ways through the democratic process, through committees here in the Senedd. Our task in putting together the budget now, for publication as a draft next month, is to make sure that, 'Are we eking the most out of the money that we are entrusted to look after and make the most out of?' That is our job; hold us to account for it.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 9. What consideration has the Welsh Government given to reforming the structure of health boards? OQ64795
documents.text_cy: 9. Pa ystyriaeth y mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi'i rhoi i ddiwygio strwythur byrddau iechyd? OQ64795

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Restructuring isn't an immediate priority for this Government. We are instead focused on improving delivery and outcomes, and addressing barriers to more effective institutional collaboration. To do that, we are directing health boards to shift towards prevention, community care and early intervention. We're also strengthening accountability arrangements and, crucially, we're reviewing regional joint working to support better joined-up care, which is vital. This underpins our determination to ensure that health board boundaries aren't barriers to better delivery of health and care.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you for that response, First Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn am yr ymateb, Brif Weinidog.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We've found on at least five occasions that you've described Betsi Cadwaladr as too large, too unwieldy and too distant from the people it serves. That was when you were the spokesperson for health for Plaid Cymru in opposition. And on 2 October this year, as Prif Weinidog, you said you were essentially in the same place as when you were a health spokesperson. You said we were in the last chance saloon with Betsi Cadwaladr, and that Wales must be ready to break up Betsi, which can only mean that, in your view, it's too large. Yet in recent weeks, Plaid Cymru Members have suggested that the answer to bed closures in Powys is to merge Powys Teaching Health Board with Hywel Dda University Health Board or even with Betsi Cadwaladr. That idea was nowhere in your manifesto, so I'm seeking to put on record that this is not something that Plaid Cymru are intending to do. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
As I said, there are no plans for restructuring. I will refer to what I have already said. Are we looking for better partnerships? Yes. Does that mean better partnerships between health boards? Yes. Do we look for a neighbouring health board where there's capacity to do something to step in and take the pressure off another? Yes. Innovations of that kind are very, very important. Do I stand by my comment over the years as—? I declare my interest as a patient of Betsi Cadwaladr. Do I have a sense that here we have a health board whose scale is an issue that you don't get elsewhere? Yes, I think that that is true, but the answer is to see if we can work around that.

Now, I have used the words 'last chance saloon', 'they are on notice'. Call it what you like, we have to give it a go. We did not come into Government saying, 'We're going to restructure the health boards.' What we did say we would do is deliver a more sustainable NHS service and care service for the people of Wales. If it means getting to grips with the organisation and shapes of boards in the future, we'll look at that. But let's crack on with the work that we have begun as a Government now. I believe it will reap results.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 10. Will the First Minister provide an update on the Government's plan to deliver 20,000 new social homes by 2030? OQ64783
documents.text_cy: 10. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf am gynllun y Llywodraeth i ddarparu 20,000 o gartrefi cymdeithasol newydd erbyn 2030? OQ64783

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Yes. Delivering 20,000 additional social homes by 2030 is a clear priority for this Government. Some £474 million is allocated for social housing this year. Local authorities across the Clwyd constituency have been allocated almost £100 million in social housing grants funding this year, and this new Government's supplementary budget has put forward plans for an additional £20 million nationally, which I hope will attract support. Together, this will contribute to the delivery of almost 1,300 social homes in Clwyd.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch. It was really, really good to hear you speak about Clwyd then, which is the constituency that I represent and where I have used available data to calculate that there are approximately 4,000 households on waiting lists for social homes there alone. So, it's evidently clear that we've got a severe lack of affordable housing here in Wales, and the plans to build 20,000 new social homes by 2030 is amazing and really welcome. However, it's really important to note that housing need varies widely by community, and even within communities, both in terms of volume and the type needed. Could the First Minister confirm that assessments of current housing stocks and needs across the different communities will be undertaken, and give assurances that those developments are to be aligned with the specific community needs?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I certainly recognise the demand for additional social housing, which is why, over the summer this year, we published a new version of the local housing market assessments tool and guidance. These are vital tools in understanding the local housing needs of the diverse communities within each local authority area, and they help ensure that local authorities bring forward developments that are aligned with those specific community needs. I believe that the record investment that we want to put in place demonstrates our commitment. I'll also make the point that it's not just building new homes either, and we will take an approach in a number of different ways in bringing property back into use, and so on, to address what is a problem that affects all parts of Wales and one that Government is equipped to deal with.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Finally, First Minister, question 11, Gareth Thomas.
documents.text_cy: Yn olaf, Brif Weinidog, cwestiwn 11, Gareth Thomas.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 11. How is the Welsh Government supporting the mental health of veterans in Wales who face investigation or prosecution relating to their service in Northern Ireland? OQ64774
documents.text_cy: 11. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi iechyd meddwl cyn-filwyr yng Nghymru sy'n wynebu ymchwiliad neu erlyniad mewn perthynas â'u gwasanaeth yng Ngogledd Iwerddon? OQ64774

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: No veteran should feel unsupported when facing significant personal challenges. We're committed to ensuring that veterans in Wales can access the mental health support they need. Veterans are entitled to priority access to NHS care, subject to clinical need, for service-related conditions. They can also access specialist support through Veterans' NHS Wales and the NHS '111 press 2' mental health service, which provides free confidential support 24 hours a day.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, soldiers from Wales answered their country's call in Northern Ireland. Some never came home, and this Remembrance Day we will rightly honour their memory. Those deployed as part of Operation Banner witnessed violence, experienced loss and lived under constant threat. For some reason, the scars, both physical and mental, have lasted a lifetime. Today, veterans face investigation or prosecution for events that did or did not take place decades ago. They are asked to account for a split-second decision when memories have faded, records have been lost and fellow soldiers, who could speak to them, have passed away. They've lived with years of uncertainty, questioning and public scrutiny. Those who served this country deserve to know that they will not face this ordeal alone. Yet Veterans' NHS Wales receives only £8 per veteran. Will the Welsh Government review the funding of Veterans' NHS Wales, so that the Welsh veterans receive the support they deserve? And will the First Minister take this opportunity to recognise the service and sacrifice of Welsh veterans who served in Northern Ireland?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I recognise absolutely those who have served in the armed forces and those who lost their lives in combat, of course. We are fully committed as a Government to the covenant, which we owe to those who have served in the armed forces. It is important for us to know, when we offer services to veterans, that those services are sustainable. That is part of building the sustainable NHS that I mentioned. On those mental pressures, if you like, that veterans face, as I say, there are those priority services. We have a continued focus on rolling out veteran-friendly GP accreditation, which I think is important. I will remind you also that the programme for government that we have commits to an open access, 'no wrong door' approach to mental health, and veterans very much are able to access this.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Brif Weinidog.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Questions now to the Counsel General. Question 1, Catherine Cullen.
documents.text_cy: Cwestiynau nawr i'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol. Cwestiwn 1, Catherine Cullen.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 1. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding the legal rights of adopted children to seek specialist support when their needs continue into adulthood? OQ64742
documents.text_cy: 1. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch hawliau cyfreithiol plant mabwysiedig i geisio cymorth arbenigol os bydd eu hanghenion yn parhau i oedolaeth? OQ64742

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I thank the Member for this question. Adopted people in Wales may request an assessment for adoption support services. Where needs continue into adulthood, they may also access wider health and social care support under the relevant statutory frameworks. We continue to work with partners to support adopted people throughout their lives.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Counsel General, for many adopted young people, turning 18 does not mean their need for support disappears; in fact, it can be the point when they need it the most. Adopted young people can face complex challenges around identity, trauma, attachment and mental health, yet as they transition into adulthood, the support available to them can become fragmented, leaving them struggling to navigate adult services at the time they need it. We wouldn't expect a young person to suddenly overcome the impact of early childhood traumas just because they've reached a certain age. So, will the Counsel General clarify whether existing Welsh legislation provides sufficient protection for adopted young people into adulthood, and whether the Government is considering introducing a statutory duty to ensure continuing specialist support up until the age of 25?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The legislative framework recognises that the impact of adoption may well continue throughout a person's life, as the Member recognises, and it does provide mechanisms for adopted people to access certain support services beyond childhood. Local authorities may assess adopted adults for adoption support services and, where appropriate, co-ordinate this with broader assessments under the Social Services and Well-being (Wales) Act 2014. Adult adopted persons may also access support through health, well-being and social care services where they meet the relevant statutory criteria. We continue to work with local authorities, the National Adoption Service and adoption partners to support adopted people and their families across Wales. It's very much a matter for local authorities primarily to ensure that these services are available—that is a hard fact, they should be available everywhere—but also it's their duty to ensure that people know about the access to these very important services. The current framework allows adopted persons to access support through both adoption legislation and, where relevant, as I've said, the wider adult social care framework. Local authorities are able to co-ordinate assessments where individuals have complex or overlapping needs.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I'd like to thank the Member for raising this question and raise a similar issue. Too often, foster children leaving care are not aware of their rights. I recently hosted care-experienced campaigner Sam Gardner to give a question and answer session with Senedd Members here. Sam shared his experience of the foster system, moving between 15 different foster placements and having to research and advocate for his own rights. Sam has six asks of the Welsh Government, and one is for young people leaving care to be made aware of their legal and local entitlement in a clear and accessible way. Currently, this information is a postcode lottery, leaving some care leavers more vulnerable to homelessness or problems with unsupported mental health. What legal advice could the Counsel General give to the Welsh Government on ensuring that there is a legal obligation to make sure that care leavers are aware of their rights and the support services that they can access?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I thank the Member for that question. Adoption support services include advice and information, and local authorities are required to maintain arrangements to provide those services to adopted people and others affected by adoption. The statutory framework places duties on local authorities to provide information, advice and adoption support services. Those duties are intended to help adopted people understand and access the support available to them. Local authorities must appoint adoption support services advisers, whose role includes providing information about available support services and how those services may be accessed.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Question 2 [OQ64747] has been withdrawn. Question 3, Jane Dodds.
documents.text_cy: Tynnwyd cwestiwn 2 [OQ64747] yn ôl. Cwestiwn 3, Jane Dodds.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 3. What assessment has the Counsel General made of the adequacy of Welsh Ministers’ legal powers to intervene in devolved public services? OQ64735
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa asesiad y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i wneud o ddigonolrwydd pwerau cyfreithiol Gweinidogion Cymru i ymyrryd mewn gwasanaethau cyhoeddus datganoledig? OQ64735

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The Welsh Ministers have a range of legal powers to intervene in devolved public services, and the use of those powers would be assessed on a case-by-case basis. We are committed to working in partnership to secure effective delivery of public services.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you very much for that repsonse.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn am yr ymateb.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: You very kindly responded to my questions on this issue before, but what I'm really specifically asking about is what powers the Welsh Government should have in order to intervene in health boards when there is a real challenge to the services that are being delivered. In England, the Secretary of State, since January 2024, has been able to call in NHS service changes and decide on them. In Scotland, major service changes require ministerial approval. Even in Wales, Ministers appointed commissioners to take over the South Wales Fire and Rescue Service, and can direct or challenge school closures. Yet, in Powys, families are simply being asked to accept community beds closing and care moving further from home, and the Government says it cannot weigh in and look at the merits of this decision. Cwnsler Cyffredinol, what advice would you give the Welsh Government on how Wales can gain those powers—the powers that England and Scotland have? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The law is quite clearly stated, as I mentioned before. I'm not being critical of the Member for raising it again. Clearly, there is a perceived problem, according to her, in Powys. But it is really for the local health boards. They are responsible for planning and delivering services for their local populations, including decisions about how services are configured. The Welsh Ministers expect health boards to make these decisions on the basis of evidence, and with proper regard to quality, safety and patient experience. Welsh Ministers do have powers to provide oversight and, where appropriate, intervene in the exercise of health board functions. But whether intervention is appropriate will depend on the particular circumstances, including any concerns about patient safety, governance, statutory compliance and the decision-making process. Those are the criteria. They're hard and fast, and that is the current law.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Like so many residents across Powys, I'm very concerned regarding the current health board proposals. But unlike other Members, I am more focused on ensuring residents respond to the consultation process than scoring political points. The day-to-day running of healthcare services is the legal responsibility of health boards. Does the Counsel General therefore agree with me that Ministers intervening in this work is legally unviable, inappropriate at a time when the consultation process is ongoing, and risks undermining the authority of the clinicians and healthcare experts who are entrusted to design these services?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: As I said just now, the Welsh Ministers' powers to provide oversight and, where appropriate, to intervene are very strictly delineated. They are intended to deal with issues such as governance, performance, patient safety or compliance with statutory duties. They do not ordinarily place Ministers in the role of determining the merits of local service change proposals. Responsibility for developing service change proposals, consulting affected communities, considering representations and reaching a decision rests with the relevant health board. Consulting on service proposals and reaching those decisions is exactly what the health board is there to do. Ministers would not ordinarily seek to pre-empt or to direct the outcome of a live consultation or decision-making process.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: It's probably no surprise, but as a Member with Powys in my constituency, I'm going to be asking the same kinds of questions. Counsel General, when a health board proposes cutting hospital beds in rural communities, despite serious concerns from patients, families and local representatives, surely Welsh Ministers should have the power to step in and stop it. That's exactly what we're seeing here with Powys Teaching Health Board at the moment and their proposals affecting hospitals in Ystradgynlais and Llandrindod Wells. These decisions can have devastating consequences for communities that already struggle to access healthcare. If Ministers don't have sufficient powers to intervene, isn't it time they were given them? This Welsh Government cannot keep ducking and diving and telling people that health boards make these decisions independently while expecting the public to hold you to account for the NHS. Surely accountability must come with the power to act.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I can but, again, relate the law. The law is there, it is clear: Welsh Ministers cannot intervene except in those specific examples that I've already referred to twice this afternoon. I understand the Member's concern—of course I do. There is always concern when there is talk of reconfiguration. That is always the case. What is vitally important is that the consultation is allowed to take its course. People should respond in their thousands to the consultation if they feel strongly about it. People from all walks of life have a right to be consulted and they should make their views known. At the conclusion of the consultation process, some decisions will be arrived at. At that time, there will be consideration of whether the consultation was full and fair, as expected, and within the usual guidelines. More than that, I really cannot say. As for the need for changing the law, with regret, I cannot answer that—that would be speculation outside the purview of my office.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I now call the party spokespeople to question the Counsel General. Reform UK spokesperson, Adrian Mason.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol. Llefarydd Reform UK, Adrian Mason.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. Good afternoon, Counsel General. The two-week time frame required under Standing Order 29.2 is not merely an administrative suggestion. It's in place to ensure that proper scrutiny of the relevant provisions of UK legislation can be conducted by committees. The Welsh Government's repeated failure to adhere to this time frame impedes proper scrutiny. Counsel General, in light of this, can you provide the Senedd with an update on the clear action planned to be taken by the Welsh Government to ensure that committees are able to effectively scrutinise legislation made by your Government in the interest of fair and accountable governance?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I share the Member's concern. I have been before a scrutiny committee when I heard very clearly this concern. The point is not lightly made; it's a good point, and I hear what he says. The problems of late have probably been because of the King's Speech. A bundle of 16 or 17 different Bills were proposed, many of which affected Wales. There has been a bit of a backlog. It's not a sufficient answer that I'm giving you. We must improve, because if we stymie the work that these committees do, then the whole process in this place will grind to a halt. Now, I fully hear what he says. We are taking active steps to improve the situation. It has not been good over the past couple of months—that, I fully accept. I don't make any excuses, but part of the reason was the election coming so soon, in conjunction with the King's Speech, and that is a big part of the problem. But things are now improving, they will improve, and we have our eye on this matter, because otherwise, as I've said, it will be damaging to the processes within this Senedd.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you, Counsel General. I know you wouldn't stand there making excuses—I'm quite fully aware of that. But considering Plaid Cymru's fierce commitment to promoting and preserving the Welsh language, which has rightly received support across the Chamber, of course, it remains unclear why the Welsh language versions of statutory texts are repeatedly attracting reporting points concerning inconsistencies between the English and Welsh texts. So, going forward, Counsel General, what is the Welsh Government doing to ensure that translation of statutory texts into the Welsh language are accurate, clear and contribute positively to the accessibility of Welsh law?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: There again, I regret to say that the Member is right. There have been problems on that score as well. We are redoubling our efforts now to ensure that there is, obviously, a better service provided. There have been several problems. Some of them, by the way, were nuanced. In other words, the translation may well have been correct, although translation is never as good as the original language—and that's not an excuse being put forward. Yes, there have been failings over the past year or so and we are putting them right. We are going through the various matters that need to be put right, and, looking to the future, we wish to assure the Senedd that we are really looking at this carefully and we will not be countenancing a repeat of what has happened over the last 12 months or so.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I thank you again for your honesty, Counsel General. In light of the often elusive nature of inter-governmental communications between the Welsh and UK Governments, can you commit to ensuring that, where it is appropriate, the Legislation Committee is provided with a clear record of discussions, negotiations and agreements reached on draft legislation? Whilst I do recognise, Counsel General, that the Welsh Government may consider these discussions are subject to privilege, there must be some exceptions to facilitate proper scrutiny. So, basically, to ensure that draft legislation can be scrutinised, of course, it is vital that both the Legislation Committee and the wider Senedd understands the context of these negotiations. So, Counsel General, transparency is of paramount importance if we intend to collaboratively create a clear, cohesive body of Welsh law for the remainder of the seventh Senedd. Would you agree?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Obviously, as the Member says quite rightly, there is some privilege involved, but I would suggest that I take back what he's just said to the appropriate colleague and speak in detail with them, and hopefully, at some other point, come back with a full answer. I don't want to dismiss this in any way; it's an important point and it therefore deserves important attention.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The Welsh Labour spokesperson, Mike Hedges.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Mike Hedges.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Diolch. Counsel General, last month, on level 7 apprenticeships, you said,

'What I can tell him, which may cheer him up slightly, is that level 7 apprenticeships at the bar and also solicitors are uppermost in this Government's mind. We are pushing forward on them and, indeed, I shall be making a speech on them in about a fortnight's time, during the Legal Wales conference.'

What progress has been made?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, a little progress; I made the speech. But it is an important matter, we are looking at it, but, of course, it comes down, at the end, to finance. There is no lack of will to do what's necessary. There are lots of young people now intending to qualify both at the bar and as solicitors, who have been through university, have done excellently and are not able to get a training contract or pupillage. This is, actually, a disgraceful situation. It's not unique to Wales; it's throughout England and Wales. But it's a matter we must address, and it's something that I engaged in various discussions about during that conference last week and I'm hoping that we might be able to take it forward at a quickened pace with the necessary finances in place.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Thank you for that answer. I'm sure we'll return to that next month. What I'll also say, of course, on that, is that you've got approximately £200 million underspent, sitting there available, so you could be looking to use some of that.

But I want to move on to the tribunal system. I know you said it is also high in your priorities, Counsel General. The proposed new Welsh tribunal structure is intended not only to bring existing devolved tribunals into a more coherent system, but also be capable of taking on additional jurisdiction in the future. Before any additional jurisdiction is transferred into the Welsh tribunal system, what safeguards do you believe need to be in place?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: That's looking far ahead, actually, but it has been left open for possible future development. My brief is to look at the six current tiers of Welsh tribunals and the appellate tier above them. That is what I'm concentrating on now. Clearly, the Member is right—in the future, at some point, there may be others that might be devolved, and we'd have to consider the safeguards when they are up for discussion. But it's nowhere near on the horizon at this moment in time, nor is it hidden from sight either. It's simply not on the agenda at the moment, and I say that with respect to the gentleman.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The Welsh Conservatives' spokesperson, Natasha Asghar.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Natasha Asghar.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Thank you so much, Presiding Officer. Counsel General, in April last year, the Supreme Court issued its landmark ruling in terms of sex, that 'man' and 'woman' refer strictly to biological sex only. Now, that ruling is crystal clear as far as I'm concerned, and anyone else with a shred of common sense will feel the same. Yet I fear certain Plaid Cymru politicians are still trying to get their heads around this. On the International Day of the Girl recently, the Deputy First Minister said, and I quote,

'On International Day of the Girl, we are reminded of the importance of ensuring people in Wales can manage their periods with dignity, confidence and pride'.

Now, Counsel General, I don't profess to be an expert in biology, but it is blindingly obvious that 'people' do not have periods; women and girls do, because to suggest otherwise would be absurd. Following the Supreme Court's ruling, the Equality and Human Rights Commission updated its code of practice, which came into force in August this year. It stressed that single-sex spaces should be just that—single sex. And only last week, NHS England announced it was issuing new guidance that patients should be assigned to single-sex wards based on their biological sex, which is a welcome move for me and my colleagues. So, Counsel General, how are you going to be ensuring the Welsh Government and other public bodies across Wales are following and implementing the law when it comes to protecting the rights of women and girls all across Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Again, that's an important issue and quite topical. We are going to observe the law, and the law is quite plain from the case to which she just referred. And it's a matter of drawing up our policies in accordance with that law. It's my duty to ensure that it does happen. The Government will, I am sure, adhere. I suppose the question is: when is it going to happen? Well, the sooner the better from my point of view, and if I have anything to do with it, which I will, I will certainly speak with colleagues about getting some proper, hard-and-fast policies, and so on, drawn up as soon as possible.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Thank you very much for your response, Counsel General. I do appreciate that.

I want to turn to Plaid Cymru's dangerous plans for independence. Now, Plaid tried to downplay their ambition to rip Wales out of the United Kingdom during the election period in May. But, as soon as the party was in office, the mask slipped, and this is visible to everybody across Wales. The moving boxes hadn't been quite unpacked and already the First Minister was calling up his nationalist pals in Scotland and also Ireland. Next thing you know, the leaders of Sinn Féin, a party deeply tied up to terrorists in the IRA, and the Scottish National Party in Scotland are making their way to Cardiff for a separatist summit, drawing up plans to tear up the United Kingdom.

Now, frankly, I know—and many other people will agree—that independence will be disastrous for Wales. There's no two ways about it. Financially, it will ruin Wales, with an annual deficit of around about £21 billion. It will severely compromise our national security, and it will leave Welsh families financially worse off, costing every resident upwards of £7,000 extra in taxes every single year. Frankly, I believe that we are stronger and much better off in the United Kingdom. So, Counsel General, what legal advice have you provided to Ministers about their independence plans? And for the avoidance of doubt, can you confirm that this Welsh Government does not have the legal competence to unilaterally legislate for independence or call for a binding referendum? And do you agree with me that, given Plaid has no legal standing when it comes to independence, their efforts would be much better spent on tackling issues that they are responsible for, such as NHS waiting lists, educational outcomes and boosting the economy? There's your question.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, the Member's had her say. Little of that has any relevance to my job and, therefore, I say with respect that I'm not getting involved in the politics.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 4. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding its legal responsibilities in relation to the independent inquiry into grooming gangs? OQ64725
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae’r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi’i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch ei chyfrifoldebau cyfreithiol mewn perthynas â’r ymchwiliad annibynnol i gangiau grŵmio? OQ64725

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The independent inquiry into grooming gangs is, as the Member knows, a statutory inquiry established under the Inquiries Act 2005. The Welsh Government has a dedicated legal team working constructively with the inquiry, providing information, evidence and witness testimony as required, and engaging fully with its processes in relation to devolved responsibilities.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you. The inquiry has confirmed that it will examine matters involving devolved services in Wales. You started to clarify the legal obligations there placed on the Welsh Government to co-operate with the inquiry. Will this include provision of relevant documents and evidence, and will there be any legislative changes necessary following its findings?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: We shall have to wait and see what the findings are, but, meantime, what I can assure the Member—it is an important point—is that we are fully engaged with the inquiry. The Welsh Government has applied for core participation status. The result of that application is awaited on a daily basis, but, even now, there is close liaison between officials of the Welsh Government and the grooming inquiry. There are separate strands to do with Wales and they will be fully addressed, and the whole gamut will be looked at very, very carefully. The list, as I've said, of core participants will be available shortly, but, as I say, we have a dedicated legal team working on it now, and they will continue apace, whatever happens. As for any legislation, we'll have to wait to see what the recommendations are and to evaluate them very carefully. It is a big subject and it's worthy of proper evaluation, and that is what the recommendations will get in due course.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 5. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the devolution of broadcasting to Wales? OQ64746
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch datganoli darlledu i Gymru? OQ64746

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: This Government is committed to working towards the devolution of powers over broadcasting, including powers to regulate, supervise and ensure accountability for broadcasting and also communications in Wales.
documents.text_cy: Mae’r Llywodraeth hon wedi ymrwymo i weithio tuag at ddatganoli pwerau darlledu i Gymru, gan gynnwys pwerau i reoleiddio, i oruchwylio ac i sicrhau bod atebolrwydd dros ddarlledu a hefyd dros gyfathrebu yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you very much for that answer. I would like to think that we can all agree that it is important that we have a strong broadcasting sector that reflects our country and our systems. We know that most people in Wales get their news from sources outside Wales, and it's important for democracy here in Wales that people are aware of what happens here. But it's also important to hear a Welsh voice and perspective on external affairs. Do you agree with me about the need to devolve broadcasting and that this would be an important step towards strengthening civic life in Wales?
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi am yr ateb. Mi fuaswn i'n hoffi meddwl y gallem ni i gyd gytuno ei bod hi'n bwysig i gael sector darlledu cryf sy'n adlewyrchu ein gwlad a'n systemau ni. Mae'n hysbys i ni fod y rhan fwyaf o bobl yng Nghymru yn cael eu newyddion o du allan i Gymru, ac mae'n bwysig i ddemocratiaeth yma yng Nghymru fod pobl yn ymwybodol o beth sy'n digwydd yma. Ond mae hefyd yn bwysig i gael llais a safbwynt Cymreig ar faterion allanol. A ydych chi'n cytuno efo fi am yr angen i ddatganoli darlledu a'i fod yn gam pwysig wrth gryfhau bywyd sifig yng Nghymru?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
The Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport has made statements to this Senedd on her work in this area in gathering evidence and seeking recommendations on the way forward. Indeed, the Minister has written to the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport declaring clearly this Government's commitment to pursue the devolution of powers over broadcasting, and asking for further dialogue on the issue.

And I would add that it is clear that an informed nation is crucial for democracy and also for public debate at local, national and international levels in order to understand what is happening around us and our role in it. The expert panel on broadcasting, the Institute of Welsh Affairs and the Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales have all acknowledged the need for a stronger voice for Wales on broadcasting issues. For the Welsh Government, the devolution of broadcasting is a key part of that journey.
documents.text_cy:
Mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Ddiwylliant a Chwaraeon wedi gwneud datganiadau i'r Senedd hon am ei gwaith yn y maes yn casglu gwybodaeth a cheisio argymhellion ar y ffordd ymlaen. Yn wir, mae'r Gweinidog wedi ysgrifennu at yr Ysgrifennydd Gwladol dros Ddigidol, Diwylliant, Cyfryngau a Chwaraeon yn datgan yn glir ymrwymiad y Llywodraeth hon i fynd ar drywydd datganoli pwerau darlledu, ac yn gofyn am ddeialog bellach ar y pwnc. 

Ac mi fuaswn i'n ychwanegu drwy ddweud ei bod hi'n glir bod cenedl wybodus yn angenrheidiol i ddemocratiaeth a hefyd i drafodaeth gyhoeddus ar lefelau lleol, cenedlaethol a rhyngwladol er mwyn deall yr hyn sydd o gwmpas a'n rhan ni ynddo. Mae'r panel arbenigol ar ddarlledu, y Sefydliad Materion Cymreig a'r Comisiwn Annibynnol ar Ddyfodol Cyfansoddiadol Cymru i gyd wedi cydnabod yr angen am lais cryfach i Gymru ar faterion darlledu. I Llywodraeth Cymru, mae datganoli darlledu yn rhan hollbwysig o'r siwrnai honno.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I'm sure you just made a political statement about the strong broadcasting sector required to be devolved, but, okay, I'll forgive you on that one.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Sorry, could you repeat that?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Yes, I thought you'd just made quite a political statement, because she asked you whether you agreed it should be devolved, and you said you did.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: [Inaudible.]—answer the question.
documents.text_cy: [Anghlywadwy.]—ateb y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Okay, fair enough. It's obviously currently largely reserved to the UK Parliament, so the question is: how do you assess the implications of such a change with broadcasting to the overall existing constitutional settlement? So, how does that work by taking something out of the constitutional settlement?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, if there was to be devolution of broadcasting, then that would be quite a major undertaking. The finances would have to be delivered with it. It's quite a huge undertaking, but it's something that has been talked about for a long time by various commissions and so on, and it's something that this Government is pursuing. It won't happen overnight, but, if it does, what has to be ensured is that such a move would be totally independent of others controlling it, but also, crucially, that all the necessary finances would come this way with it, if you can understand the rather crude language. It would have to be properly financed, otherwise it simply would not work.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 6. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding whether removing parents' right to withdraw their children from relationships and sexuality education is consistent with the European Convention on Human Rights? OQ64740
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch a yw dileu hawl rhieni i dynnu eu plant yn ôl o addysg cydberthynas a rhywioldeb yn gyson â'r Confensiwn Ewropeaidd ar Hawliau Dynol? OQ64740

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: As the Member will know, there was a High Court judgment in 2022 that held that the provisions of the Curriculum and Assessment (Wales) Act 2021 in respect of relationships and sexuality education were compatible with the rights protected by the Human Rights Act 1998.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Relationships and sexuality education, as you say, has been a compulsory element of the Curriculum for Wales since 2022. In its own words, the framework covers relationships, rights, equality and diversity. What parents may not be aware of, however, is that education is compulsory and in force in Wales from the age of three, including in funded nursery education. Moreover, unlike previous sex education arrangements, RSE is mandatory until 16, and parents do not have the general right to withdraw. Now, whatever our views on the ECHR may be, we are as lawmakers in the Senedd totally bound by the European convention on human rights. Article 2 of protocol No. 1 plainly states that

'the State shall respect the right of parents to ensure such education and teaching is in conformity with their own religious and philosophical convictions.'

So, quite simply, do parents in Wales actually still have the right to withdraw their children from RSE when it does not conform to their religious and philosophical convictions?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
I don't believe there is a decided case on that as such, but there is on the question of withdrawing from sexuality education. That education is meant to be appropriate for the child's age and maturity, and, of course, it's open to the parents also to teach their children about such matters. But in terms of a challenge, the purpose of the mandatory RSE is to keep children safe, to promote respect for others, help them establish healthy relationships and protect them from harmful content and people online. The 2021 Act expressly requires that the children can only be provided with RSE that is appropriate for their children's age and their maturity. 

As for a challenge on human rights matters, in the Isherwood case, Mrs Justice Steyn said that

'the content of the Code and the Guidance is consistent with the requirement to take care to ensure that RSE teaching is conveyed in an objective critical and pluralistic manner, and does not breach the prohibition on indoctrination. There is nothing in the Code or the Guidance that authorises or positively approves teaching that advocates or promotes any particular identity or sexual lifestyle over another, or that encourages children to self-identify in a particular way.'

'In my judgment,'

she said,

'both the Code and the Guidance reflect the general spirit of the Convention as an instrument designed to maintain and promote the ideals and values of a modern liberal democracy, including the values of tolerance, respect and equality.'

And that reflects the current law as we stand.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 7. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the compatibility of its policymaking with the Equality Act 2010? OQ64736
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch cydnawsedd llunio polisïau Llywodraeth Cymru â Deddf Cydraddoldeb 2010? OQ64736

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The Welsh Government is required to comply with equalities legislation within its policy areas. The Equality and Human Rights Commission acts as a regulator for ensuring compliance with equalities legislation across and beyond the public sector in Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you, Counsel General. The last Labour Government introduced a £5,000 grant for teacher training, but it was only available to student teachers from ethnic minorities, not on merit, but purely based on their skin colour. The current Plaid Cymru Government has carried on this scheme. Will the Counsel General agree to publish any legal advice given to the Welsh Government that they've received on this policy, and will he commit to ensuring that the Welsh Government makes any advice public, so that the people of Wales can see how their money has been spent on this piece of anti-white discrimination?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, as the Member knows, I cannot agree to publishing any legal advice, that is for sure, but on the general point she makes—again, an important point—the purpose of equalities law is to protect minority groups and those at risk of discrimination and also harassment. This aim fully reflects the Welsh Government's values. On 21 November 2025, the Welsh Government entered into a formal legal agreement with the Equality and Human Rights Commission, EHRC, under section 23 of the Equality Act 2006. This agreement presents a unique opportunity for the Welsh Government to strengthen the approach to assessing equality impacts, ensuring it is embedded consistently across the organisation. This will further build on and strengthen our approach to delivering policy and services for the people of Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 8. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding Welsh Ministers’ powers to call in planning applications for large-scale data-centre developments, including the statutory criteria under the relevant planning legislation and the legal duties that apply when such a request is received? OQ64745
documents.text_cy: 8. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch pwerau Gweinidogion Cymru i alw ceisiadau cynllunio i mewn ar gyfer datblygiadau canolfannau data ar raddfa fawr, gan gynnwys y meini prawf statudol o dan y ddeddfwriaeth gynllunio berthnasol a'r dyletswyddau cyfreithiol sy'n gymwys pan geir cais o'r fath? OQ64745

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The law on this matter is quite clear. Call-in powers are set out in section 77 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990. Examples of proposals that may be called in are set out in 'Planning Policy Wales'. The Welsh Ministers may call in an application where they deem it appropriate.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Given that several call-in requests for data centre schemes, including the one at the former Ferodo site near Caernarfon, are currently under consideration, what does the legal advice say about the statutory criteria under section 77 of the Town and Country Planning Act and the threshold of 'more than local importance', when issues such as grid capacity, energy demand or the absence of a specific national data centre policy are raised?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 9. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding the use of AI-enabled smart glasses in public buildings such as libraries and swimming pools given the ban in courts and tribunals? OQ64749
documents.text_cy: 9. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch defnyddio sbectolau clyfar a alluogir gan ddeallusrwydd artiffisial mewn adeiladau cyhoeddus megis llyfrgelloedd a phyllau nofio, yn sgil y gwaharddiadau sydd mewn grym mewn llysoedd a thribiwnlysoedd? OQ64749

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: New technologies, including smartglasses, can offer benefits and present challenges. Individual operators of public buildings are responsible for developing policies that take account of privacy and of safeguarding considerations that are appropriate to the use of each building and the needs of stakeholders, customers and the staff.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Courts and tribunals have restricted these devices, and, in fact, I've just heard the Cabinet Office banned them last week. I think we've learned that news from this Chamber travels rather fast. In fact, the Member's glasses opposite have been discussed in buildings 200 miles away. All these institutions have concluded that people in those spaces are entitled to know whether they're being recorded. The same question applies to a library, a leisure centre, a GP surgery or even a school, and these are places where people have no reason to expect they are being filmed. I'd be grateful to know whether the Welsh Government considers existing data protection law sufficient for this, or whether it intends to give further guidance to public bodies in Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: A tailored approach is needed, given the wide-ranging use and activities undertaken in public buildings. What is suitable in one setting may not be in another, and operators are best placed to make sensible policies based on their own responsibilities as data controllers and according to their individual risk appetite. Swimming pools are likely to be an example where particular care and greater restrictions may well be appropriate. The approach taken in courts and tribunals will be informed by the long-standing prohibition on recordings being made unless special permission has been given. So, local authorities and other public bodies are responsible for their own compliance with data protection requirements and also managing their own security risks. Following our own review of Welsh Government policy, we will consider if there is any guidance we can issue to public bodies.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 10. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding its role within the national inquiry into grooming gangs? OQ64737
documents.text_cy: 10. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch ei rôl yn yr ymchwiliad cenedlaethol i gangiau grŵmio? OQ64737

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The independent inquiry into grooming gangs is a statutory inquiry, established under the Inquiries Act 2005. The Welsh Government is working constructively with the inquiry and stands ready to provide information, evidence and witness testimony as required, while engaging fully with the inquiry's processes on matters within devolved responsibilities.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you, Counsel General. Young white women and children in this country were groomed, raped and trafficked, often by groups of mainly Pakistani men over decades. The worst injustice this country has seen, in my opinion. Wales needs its own inquiry. There are strong suspicions that it happened in Swansea, in my constituency, along with many other places in Wales. Section 29 of the Inquiries Act lets Welsh Ministers hold an inquiry into anything they have functions over. So, my question is simple, Counsel General: does the Welsh Government have the legal power to hold its own inquiry into how devolved services in Wales failed these children and young women—'yes' or 'no'?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Yes, but I would suggest that it's prudent now to await the decisions and recommendations of the present inquiry. What may come of that, I know not. It may be that a separate inquiry may be considered. I know not. I do not know. None of us knows what's going to come out of this inquiry. What I do know is that we have a specialist team that are working very, very closely with the inquiry team, and Welsh issues are being raised properly, as they should be. We've applied for core participation status, and the outcome of that application is expected very, very shortly. I can assure the Member—and it's an important point again—I can assure the Member that we are making every possible effort to ensure that the problems that occurred in Wales are properly evaluated, properly researched and are part of the inquiry. For the future, who knows? Let's see what the recommendations will be. But I can assure her that we do not take the issue lightly.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Finally, question 11. John Clark.
documents.text_cy: Yn olaf, cwestiwn 11. John Clark.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 11. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the legal implications of establishing a distinct or separate legal jurisdiction for Wales? OQ64744
documents.text_cy: 11. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynghylch goblygiadau cyfreithiol sefydlu awdurdodaeth gyfreithiol benodol neu ar wahân i Gymru? OQ64744

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The first thing I should say is that a distinct or separate legal jurisdictions are two separate things. We already have a distinct jurisdiction in Wales in as much as Welsh laws are used in Welsh courts, Welsh judges and so on. A lot of Welsh law has been created within this building. So, to that end, we have a distinct jurisdiction already. Turning to the separate legal jurisdiction, it's an entirely different matter altogether. The Welsh Government supports the formal establishment of a Welsh legal jurisdiction to provide greater legal clarity for practitioners and citizens as Welsh law continues to develop. This would not in practice require a separate judiciary or court system, nor the creation of a separate legal profession, qualifications or regulatory requirements.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: What legal advice has the Counsel General provided on the practical implications of moving from the existing distinct body of Welsh law to a fully separate jurisdiction, specifically for the single England and Wales legal profession, cross-border practices, access to justice, and legal certainty for businesses operating on both sides of the border?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, I've just answered that question; I've answered that question once. What is proposed would have no effect. What is happening on the ground has no effect on legal practitioners. If I give him an example, when I was at the bar, I was in a court in Manchester on a Monday, Wolverhampton on a Tuesday, Wrexham or Caernarfon on a Thursday and Friday. The regulations applying to children's law were completely different in Wales. But I'm not a genius and I managed it, and I'm sure our colleagues in England will continue to manage it. But the point is that as the corpus juris of Wales is growing, as the separate legal steps being taken within Wales are growing—and will grow, clearly, as we legislate—there will come a time for further consideration, but not a consideration of in any way changing the nature of the legal profession. The legal profession can rest assured—as can, importantly, the people of Wales—that people will be able to come and represent them whether they are in Wales or whether they practice across the border. Provided they're up to speed on Welsh regulation and Welsh law, there will be no bar to them practising.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you, Counsel General.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Gwnsler Cyffredinol.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: We'll now move to the business statement and announcement. I call on the Trefnydd, Heledd Fychan.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn yn nawr at y datganiad a chyhoeddiad busnes. Galwaf ar y Trefnydd, Heledd Fychan.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Thank you, Llywydd. There are no changes to this week's business, and draft Plenary business for the next three weeks is shown on the business statement, which is available to Members electronically, as usual.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Lywydd. Nid oes unrhyw newidiadau i fusnes yr wythnos hon. Mae busnes drafft y tair wythnos nesaf wedi'i nodi yn y datganiad busnes sydd ar gael fel arfer i'r Aelodau yn electronig.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Could I have a statement from the Trefnydd and the Welsh Government on what efforts are being taken to address rough-sleeping and homelessness in Wales? As we're coming into the winter time, it's becoming very concerning about how many people are sleeping out in horrendous conditions right now, and I'd be grateful if the Government could come forward on what we can do, and, hopefully, we can find consensus around the Chamber to address this, so we don't see more lives lost by rough-sleeping this winter.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Thank you for raising a matter that will be of great importance to a number of us, if not every Member here. I will certainly make the Cabinet Minister aware that you have raised this issue, namely Siân Gwenllian, and see what updates are available for all Members.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am godi mater fydd o bwys i nifer fawr ohonom ni, os nad pob Aelod yma. Mi fyddaf i'n sicr o wneud y Gweinidog Cabinet yn ymwneud eich bod chi wedi codi hyn, sef Siân Gwenllian, a gweld pa ddiweddariadau sydd ar gael i'r holl Aelodau.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: We have a shortage of housing available for rent. Houses that were previously privately rented have been converted into Airbnb properties. This housing shortage is made worse by the growth of Airbnb properties. These Airbnb properties take business away from guest houses and hotels; they create parking problems. It's not just a problem of tourist areas; it affects areas with older terraced housing, as well as properties at the seaside. There is control over houses in multiple occupation concentrations to stop areas becoming HMO areas. We need the same for Airbnb. I'm asking for a Government statement on what action they intend to take to control the growth of Airbnb, or are they going to let it just grow and grow?

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Thank you. I'm sure the Member will be aware that work was done between your party and my party through the co-operation agreement on this issue, and a number of measures were put in place that are within the gift of local authorities to implement. Certainly, this is a very live issue; it's also pertinent to the report presented to the previous Government, but we will be implementing those recommendations, in terms of, specifically, Welsh-speaking communities, but I do acknowledge that it is a problem, and that's why there has been co-operation to look for solutions in this area, and we will continue to look at that.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Dwi'n siŵr y bydd yr Aelod yn ymwybodol bod yna waith wedi'i wneud rhwng eich plaid chi a'm plaid i drwy'r cytundeb cydweithio ar y mater hwn, a nifer o fesurau wedi'u rhoi mewn lle sydd o fewn gallu awdurdodau lleol i fod yn medru eu gweithredu. Yn sicr, mae hwn yn fater byw iawn; mae o'n berthnasol hefyd wrth gwrs i'r adroddiad sydd wedi'i gyflwyno i'r Llywodraeth flaenorol, ond rydym ni'n mynd i fod yn gweithredu'r argymhellion hynny, o ran cymunedau Cymraeg yn benodol, ond dwi'n cydnabod mae hi yn broblem, a dyna pam mae yna gydweithio wedi bod i edrych am ddatrysiadau yn y maes hwn, a byddwn ni'n parhau i edrych ar hynny.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Trefnydd, I'd like to request a statement from the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality on the Welsh Government's support for people with learning disabilities across Wales. As I mentioned to the First Minister earlier, last week I met with Mencap Cymru to discuss their 'I'm In' campaign, which highlights the importance of GP learning disability registers as a gateway to accessing annual health checks. Of course, it's important that we have access to the relevant data to ensure that people with learning disabilities are accessing these vital health checks.

Another issue raised with me was the increasing difficulties that people with learning disabilities face when trying to access and use cash within their local communities. Now, in my view, organisations that receive public funding should be able to accept cash payments from the public, and access to cash continues to be an important way of promoting independence and inclusion for many people with learning disabilities. Therefore, I'd be grateful if we could have a statement from the Welsh Government on its position on support for people with learning disabilities, including measures to improve access to annual health checks and its approach to ensuring continued access to cash for those who actually rely on it.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for those questions and those requests. You will have heard the response of the First Minister earlier on today, but also you will be aware of the commitment of the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality in terms of these areas. She, in the previous Senedd, was the chair of cross-party groups that did look at a number of the issues that you've raised. I will ensure that she is aware that you have raised these further issues today and ensure that there is an update given to you on the work that is under way.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am y cwestiynau hynny a'r ceisiadau hynny. Mi fyddwch chi wedi clywed ymateb y Prif Weinidog yn flaenorol, ond hefyd mi fyddwch chi yn ymwybodol o ymrwymiad y Dirprwy Brif Weinidog a Gweinidog Cabinet dros Gyfiawnder Cymdeithasol a Chydraddoldeb o ran y meysydd hyn. Mi oedd hi, yn y Senedd ddiwethaf, yn gadeirydd grwpiau trawsbleidiol oedd yn edrych ar nifer o'r pethau rydych chi wedi'u codi. Mi wnaf i sicrhau ei bod hi yn ymwybodol eich bod chi wedi codi'r materion pellach hyn heddiw a sicrhau bod yna ddiweddariad i chi o ran y gwaith sy'n mynd rhagddo.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I'd like to ask for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability on the state of dog breeding in Wales and whether the Welsh Government intends to review the current regulatory framework. The RSPCA has raised concerns that dog breeding continues on a considerable scale in Wales and that existing legislation may no longer be fit for purpose. There have also been calls for a review of current laws, a centralised microchipping database, consideration of a national scoring system for breeders and whether a national representative body could provide greater support to responsible breeders. Given the importance of protecting animal welfare, while ensuring that responsible breeders have the support and the clarity they need, can the Welsh Government outline whether it will review the current regulatory framework to ensure it remains effective and fit for purpose and whether it will consider combining and streamlining the regulation into a single piece of legislation?

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising that issue. I would ask you, because there were a number of questions to the Minister in what you raised with me, to write to the Minister so that you can get a full response on those specific points. But what I can tell you is that animal welfare is something that's very important to this Government, and we will act in accordance with that.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r mater hwnnw. Mi fyddwn i'n gofyn i chi, gan fod yna nifer o gwestiynau i'r Gweinidog yn yr hyn wnaethoch chi'n ei godi efo fi, ysgrifennu at y Gweinidog fel eich bod chi'n gallu cael ymateb llawn ar y pwyntiau penodol hynny. Ond yr hyn fedraf i ddweud ydy bod lles anifeiliaid yn rhywbeth sydd o bwys mawr i'r Llywodraeth hon, a byddwn ni yn gweithredu yn unol â hynny.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Prynhawn da, Drefnydd. I'd like two statements, please. Last week I met coracle fishermen from west Wales. They were promoting their very, very unique craft. I don't know if you know—they are very small boats, they carry them on their back, and they only fish at night between Monday and Friday. However, the period of them being able to fish has been massively reduced by Natural Resources Wales. So, could I just ask what the Government is going to be doing in order to protect this important Welsh tradition?

The other statement is with regard to job opportunities for physiotherapy graduates. We're in this terrible place where we've trained physiotherapists and we can't give them jobs, and yet we are crying out for people to have the service of a physiotherapist. So, please, could you tell us what the Government's intentions are to ensure that physiotherapists get the jobs that they need to be able to deliver the services to the people of Wales? Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lywydd.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
I thank the Member for raising those two issues. In terms of the coracle, certainly, that is something that is part of our tradition as a nation, isn't it? It's unique, and, certainly, I would suggest that you do write specifically to the Minister, but, in terms of the heritage aspect, which I'm responsible for, I'll see what is relevant in terms of my portfolio.

In terms of the second point, with regard to physiotherapy, clearly we do acknowledge how concerning the situation is. You will see that there was an announcement made yesterday in terms of some of the posts with regard to nurses specifically. But we do acknowledge that there are other roles where the situation has been very concerning, and the lack of planning comes over clearly in that regard. We are committed to helping graduates to gain employment and to keep their skills within the health service here in Wales. They are skills that are very much needed. So, I acknowledge and recognise what you've raised and I will certainly be making the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care aware of the points that you've raised this afternoon.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr iawn i'r Aelod am godi'r ddau fater yna. O ran y cwrwgl, yn sicr, mae hwnna yn rhywbeth sy'n rhan o'n traddodiad ni fel cenedl, onid ydy? Rhywbeth unigryw yw, ac, yn sicr, byddwn i yn awgrymu eich bod chi yn ysgrifennu yn benodol at y Gweinidog, ond, o ran yr ochr treftadaeth dwi'n gyfrifol amdano fo hefyd, mi wnaf i weld beth ydy'r hyn sydd yn berthnasol o ran fy mhortffolio i.

O ran yr ail beth hefyd, efo ffisiotherapi, yn amlwg rydym ni yn cydnabod pa mor bryderus ydy'r sefyllfa hon. Byddwch chi yn gweld bod yna gyhoeddiad ddoe o ran rhai o'r swyddi o ran nyrsys yn benodol.
