Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Hoffwn i roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf i'r Aelodau ynghylch y gwaith o ddatblygu strategaeth ynni genedlaethol i Gymru. Mae ynni yn hanfodol i fywyd modern. Mae'r newid i system ynni carbon isel yn ganolog i'n huchelgais i gyrraedd sero net erbyn 2040, gan wynebu'r argyfyngau hinsawdd a natur gyda'n gilydd wrth gryfhau ein diogelwch ynni, gwella cynhyrchiant a chreu manteision parhaol i Gymru.

Mae ein huchelgais yn mynd y tu hwnt i gynhyrchu mwy o ynni. Mae angen i ni ddeall anghenion ynni'r presennol a'r dyfodol yng Nghymru a lle mae angen seilwaith, gan sicrhau'r defnydd gorau o'r hyn sydd gennym ni a sut y gellir cadw gwerth a grëwyd gan ein tir, gwynt, dŵr a moroedd mewn ffordd fwy teg i bobl a chymunedau Cymru. Asedau cenedlaethol yw adnoddau naturiol Cymru. Dylid cadw'r gwerth maen nhw'n ei greu fwyfwy yng Nghymru a'i ddefnyddio i gefnogi cymunedau a busnesau Cymreig a chenedlaethau’r dyfodol.

Bydd y strategaeth yn darparu llwybr clir i gyflawni ein polisïau, a fydd, unwaith y cânt eu gosod, yn darparu mwy o sicrwydd i ddatblygwyr a chymunedau, gan nodi sut rŷn ni’n bwriadu cyflwyno system ynni sy’n lân, yn cael ei berchnogi yng Nghymru ac yn fwy fforddiadwy. Felly, bydd y strategaeth yn cael ei harwain gan weledigaeth i gyflwyno system ynni sy’n cydbwyso ac yn cyflawni ein hamcanion ar gyfer hinsawdd a natur, yn cadw gwerth yng Nghymru, ac yn fwy fforddiadwy a gwydn.

Bydd ynni adnewyddadwy yn hollbwysig wrth i Gymru newid y mathau o ynni mae’n eu defnyddio, gan gynnwys technolegau arloesol fel ynni ffrwd llanw a morlynnoedd llanw. Ni all system ynni ddibynnu ar ynni anwadal yn unig. Mae arnom ni angen cynhyrchu ynni gwynt, ynni solar ac ynni morol sy’n cael eu hatgyfnerthu gan storio ynni, rhwydweithiau cryfach a chapasiti cadarn, carbon isel sydd ar gael yn ôl yr angen. Rhaid inni leihau dibynnu ar danwydd ffosil heb fesurau dal a storio carbon ynghlwm, wrth gynnal diogelwch cyflenwadau, gan gynnwys drwy dargedu rolau penodol ar gyfer storio a dal carbon, hydrogen carbon isel a bioynni lle maen nhw’n gwneud cyfraniad pendant a pharhaus.

Yn ei hanfod, mae'r strategaeth hon yn ymwneud ag adeiladu system ynni sy'n fwy glân, mwy fforddiadwy ac yn cael ei pherchnogi fwyfwy gan Gymru—system ynni all yrru adnewyddiad economaidd, cefnogi adfer natur a chadw mwy o'r gwerth a grëir gan adnoddau Cymreig gan bobl Cymru.

Bydd y seilwaith sydd ei angen ar gyfer y trawsnewid hwn yn arwain at newid, gan gynnwys effaith na ellir ei hosgoi bob amser. Ein cyfrifoldeb ni yw gwneud penderfyniadau ar sail tystiolaeth gadarn, yn unol â Deddf Llesiant Cenedlaethau’r Dyfodol (Cymru) 2015. 

Bydd ein strategaeth ynni genedlaethol newydd yn sefydlu cyfeiriad strategol ar ynni ar gyfer y Llywodraeth hon, gan nodi’n glir beth all Cymru ei gyflawni’n uniongyrchol, gyda fframwaith cyflawni ynni cenedlaethol yn darparu’r cyfeiriad hwnnw mewn rhaglen waith fanylach. Bydd yn nodi’r camau sydd eu hangen i gefnogi ein hamcanion ar gynhyrchiant a chyflawni ein cyllidebau carbon.

Byddwn hefyd yn gwneud ein gofynion yn glir i Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig, Ofgem, Gweithredwr y System Ynni Genedlaethol—NESO—ac eraill os yw’r penderfyniadau y tu hwnt i’n rheolaeth uniongyrchol ni. Mae yna raglen sylweddol o waith eisoes ar y gweill. Pwrpas y strategaeth yw gosod cyfeiriad clir ar gyfer y gwaith hwnnw, a sicrhau ei fod yn cyflawni blaenoriaethau'r Llywodraeth hon. Byddwn yn ymgysylltu ac yn ymgynghori wrth i bolisi gael ei ddatblygu.

Rŷm ni'n cynnig ffordd ymlaen sydd wedi ei seilio ar dystiolaeth a gweledigaeth realistig i gynyddu’r defnydd cyfrifol o dechnolegau ynni carbon isel cynaliadwy. Bydd y dull ar sail cynllun yn ein helpu ni i osgoi effeithiau ar gynefinoedd unigryw nad oes modd eu creu eto a thir amaethyddol o ansawdd uchel, lleihau effeithiau ar safleoedd gwarchodedig a nodi cyfleoedd i brojectau ynni gefnogi adfer natur.

I gefnogi hyn, bwriadwn ni newid y targed presennol, gan gyflwyno targed ynni sy’n seiliedig ar allyriadau. Bydd y targed diwygiedig hwn yn golygu na fydd ynni’n cael ei drin fel polisi trydan adnewyddadwy yn unig, neu fel polisi hinsawdd yn unig, a’i fod wedi’i osod o fewn gweledigaeth system gyfan. Bydd hyn yn darparu mesur mwy cyflawn o gynnydd tuag at ein cyllidebau carbon ac yn adlewyrchu’n well rôl ynni wrth ddatgarboneiddio adeiladau, gwres, trafnidiaeth a diwydiant. Yn ogystal â hyn, byddwn yn diwygio ein targed perchnogaeth leol fel ei fod yn cefnogi ein huchelgais i gadw mwy o’r gwerth wrth newid y mathau o ynni rŷn ni’n eu defnyddio yng Nghymru. 

Ni ddylid trin ynni fel mater hinsawdd yn unig. Mae’n seilwaith economaidd hanfodol ac yn ganolog i’n hamcanion i wella cynhyrchiant a hyrwyddo ailddiwydiannu yng Nghymru. Nid yw ein nod yn syml i ddatgarboneiddio’r economi, ond i ddefnyddio'r trawsnewid ynni i gryfhau sefyllfa gystadleuol Cymru, denu buddsoddiad, cefnogi diwydiannau strategol a chreu swyddi o ansawdd uchel. Dylid defnyddio ynni fel mantais gystadleuol i sicrhau bod busnesau Cymru'n ffynnu. Byddwn yn gosod camau gweithredu a fydd yn sicrhau ein bod yn cadw'r gwerth yng Nghymru.

Gall system ynni garbon isel ddibynadwy roi hyder i fusnesau i fuddsoddi a thyfu, cefnogi ein sylfaen ddiwydiannol, denu buddsoddiad newydd a chreu cyflogaeth fedrus a hirdymor. Mae hynny'n golygu nodi prosiectau ynni strategol bwysig, cydgysylltu cyflenwadau â phrif ganolfannau galw a chlystyrau diwydiannol, a datblygu'r sgiliau a'r cadwyni cyflenwi sydd eu hangen i droi buddsoddi yn swyddi gwerth uchel a chymunedau cryfach.

Mae'n rhaid datblygu ynni glân gyda phobl a chymunedau Cymru. Gall perchnogaeth leol gadw mwy o werth economaidd, cryfhau gwydnwch y gymuned a rhoi cyfran ystyrlon i bobl wrth drawsnewid. Nid cynnal seilwaith newydd yn unig y dylai cymunedau. Dylen nhw gael cyfleoedd gwirioneddol i siapio prosiectau a manteisio drwy berchnogaeth, buddsoddiadau, cyflogaeth a gwerth hirdymor i'r gymuned. Rydyn ni wedi dechrau casglu tystiolaeth ar berchenogaeth gymunedol drwy ein hymgynghoriad ar gynigion ar gyfer cwmni trydan cyhoeddus cenedlaethol sy’n eiddo i bobl Cymru, ac rŷn ni'n annog pobl Cymru, busnesau, sefydliadau cymunedol a phartïon eraill sydd â diddordeb i gymryd rhan yn hwn. Rydyn ni eisoes yn ystyried cyfleoedd eraill i ddatblygu’r polisi hwn o ran rhoi prosesau gorfodol ar waith, a byddwn yn ceisio tystiolaeth bellach ac yn ymgynghori ar faterion cysylltiedig unwaith y bydd gennyn ni eglurder ar dargedau.

Byddwn yn cyhoeddi strategaeth ynni genedlaethol lefel uchel yn ystod mis Tachwedd. Bydd yn cael ei datblygu ochr yn ochr â chynllunio strategol gan Weithredwr y System Ynni Cenedlaethol—NESO—a bydd y dystiolaeth a blaenoriaethau Cymru yn ganolog iddi. Bydd cyflawni hyn yn gofyn am gydweithredu ar draws y Llywodraeth. Mae penderfyniadau am dai, trafnidiaeth, cynllunio, yr economi, amaethyddiaeth a diwydiant i gyd yn effeithio ar y galw am ynni yn y dyfodol, a bydd y strategaeth yn cysylltu’r penderfyniadau hynny yn hytrach na’u trin ar wahân.

Mae’r trawsnewid yr ydym yn ei wynebu yn sylweddol, ond mae’r cyfle yr un mor sylweddol. Bydd strategaeth ynni genedlaethol yn darparu'r cyfeiriad a'r ddisgyblaeth sydd eu hangen i greu system ynni glanach a mwy diogel sy’n cefnogi cynhyrchiant, diwydiant cynaliadwy a swyddi da. Mae ein nod yn glir: ynni glân, fforddiadwy o dan berchnogaeth Cymru, sy’n cael ei ddarparu’n gyfrifol ac yn cael ei ddatblygu gyda phobl a chymunedau Cymru. Edrychaf ymlaen at weithio gyda’r Aelodau, cymunedau, diwydiant a phartneriaid ledled Cymru wrth inni symud y gwaith hwn yn ei flaen.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
Thank you for your statement, Minister. Across Wales, families have faced and continue to face some of the largest energy price increases anywhere in the developed world. Yet the statement today makes it clear that this Government is committed to one thing, and that's more bureaucracy. Minister, your new publicly owned energy company is no doubt in your mind a key tenet of your energy strategy, but it's just not needed. It's a waste of taxpayers' money, and just like the Welsh Development Agency 2.0, it's an exercise in Government by quango, committee, council, advisory body and any other bureaucratic body to avoid actually taking responsibility. Now, when this inevitably goes wrong, there will be a plethora of other agencies to take the burden of blame in your place. So, what are you doing? To transfer functions from public bodies that already exist and calling it progression—why should the public of Wales stand for that?

Yet again, and as usual, we have little detail on cost, nothing on timelines and nothing on actual delivery. Now, I understand that the consultation is still under way, but why shy away from letting the public know exactly how much of their money you intend to waste? And when do you plan to update the Chamber on the details? Now, this isn't the first time I've made these comments, and I would have hoped that these details would be available for us as opposition Members to scrutinise effectively.

Minister, we welcome offshore windfarms. We welcome solar panels on school roofs, warehouses, factories and on car parks. But we do not support renewable projects that ruin the Welsh countryside and the outstanding natural beauty of Wales. We are the custodians of this land, and we must take that responsibility seriously. We, in Reform, we certainly do.

Yesterday, travelling through Merthyr and the Cynon valley, I saw multiple wind turbines on green land and across our mountainside. They are an eyesore to local residents, and I've had many constituents raise that with me. In Newport, Candwr Solar Farm is proposed to be built on 300 acres of prime agricultural land. Plaid claim to support the countryside, to protect our environment, but you can't do that without protecting green spaces from windfarms and excessive pylons. Minister, in your statement, you mentioned working across departments. How will you work with the Minister for rural resilience to make sure that these spaces are protected?

While the statement offers warm words, it will not lower energy bills for Welsh people at a time when a staggering one in four are in fuel poverty. It says nothing about working with the housing Minister, about making homes more insulated in a nation with some of the oldest homes in the UK. It says nothing about the potential that nuclear solutions have to offer. And as I've already stated, it lacks the detail and accountability that leads to meaningful change for the Welsh people.

Now, Minister, in your statement, you mention changing targets on sources of renewable energy to emissions-based targets. But you haven't mentioned how you're working with the UK Government to make energy more affordable for Welsh people. How exactly are you doing that, what conversations are you having with the UK Government, and what actions are you taking towards this? And how can you call this a serious update on the national energy strategy for Wales without mentioning nuclear energy once? What is Plaid's attitude towards the nuclear industry? Diolch.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
I'm grateful to the Member for his questions. I think that he focused much of them on the proposal to create a single Welsh public energy company. That wasn't the main focus of my statement today, but I have to disagree with him, based on the evidence that actually demonstrates that public ownership of energy companies across Europe is a major factor in lowering energy costs. And that's also true not just in terms of national public ownership, but we have evidence even in Wales, where community ownership leads to direct benefit, including lower energy costs. So, I think that we just disagree on that, but I would urge him to look at the evidence. I think that we have to build a mixed economy in energy, and part of that is certainly ensuring that we have higher ownership in Wales. We've learned from our history in the past, haven't we, where we had an energy system, where we had the natural resource, but we didn't derive the benefit from it. Let's actually not make that mistake again and build up greater Welsh ownership in all its forms, including public ownership.

In relation to working across Government, I specifically mentioned housing and the need for a cross-Government approach. Absolutely, there is a need to have that holistic approach because energy touches so many different parts of Government function and responsibilities, and I can assure you that that will be at the heart of the Government's approach as a whole and indeed the national energy strategy.

In terms of technologies, I think we shouldn't just build a mixed economy with an important element of public ownership, but we need to have a mixed technology approach as well. And certainly, he's right to point to the importance of offshore wind. I think this week, Project Erebus, the first wave of this great potential that we have in floating offshore wind, is holding its community and business stakeholder event. There's a real opportunity there for Welsh businesses to benefit from that first of many projects, a 100 MW project, which is really significant, happening this week. But also, there is another stakeholder event for businesses at Wylfa, being held on Thursday, which I will be attending. There's a very important opportunity there as well in terms of the supply chain for Welsh businesses.

And certainly, at the heart of our work on the national energy strategy is working out what the likely possible contribution of different technologies is. Obviously, we will be basing that analysis on the decision that has already been made in relation to the contract for the three small modular reactors at Wylfa. That will be part of working out what possible contribution will be made in terms of energy generation and how that fits then with the likely energy demand that we are going to be seeing in the course of the period between now and 2040.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement. Wales has enormous potential to become a nation of clean energy. I'm sure you'll indulge me if I say that much of what you mentioned in your statement is only possible because of the actions that my party took in Government, launching Trydan Gwyrdd Cymru, the first state-owned renewable developer in the UK, and Ynni Cymru to support community-owned energy. We set renewable energy targets, including generating the equivalent of 100 per cent of our electricity consumption from renewable sources by 2035, boosted grid capacity and invested in tidal energy.

We took those practical steps too to speed up delivery, including reforming the planning system, shaving at least 12 weeks off the process for renewable energy projects of up to 50 MW, and helped more than 82,000 households benefit from energy efficiency and advised 210,000 households on how to save money on their energy bills. So, there's already a strong foundation for you, Minister, and this Government to build upon. But families do need action now, and businesses in Wales need certainty to invest. Regrettably, there was little in this statement by way of immediate action and the measures risk perhaps adding to investment uncertainty.

Your focus, I would argue, should be on outcomes. How many jobs will be created? How much investment will be secured? How much money will families save on their energy bills? Cabinet Minister, I want to ask about the rationale for replacing Welsh Labour's ambitious renewable electricity generation targets with an emissions-based target instead. As the demand for electricity increases, we need more clean energy generated. So, why is the Government creating more uncertainty by replacing these targets? What assurance can you give that this isn't a weakening of ambition? And what guarantees can you give that your new approach won't lead to less renewable electricity being generated in Wales?

At the same time, the Government's approach to electricity infrastructure risks creating additional uncertainty about how that energy will actually be delivered. The reality, of course, is that onshore wind is one of the quickest and most affordable ways of delivering clean energy at scale. And I can reassure the Member opposite, who represents the same constituency as I do, that windfarms are actually embraced within the south Wales Valleys and, in particular, the millions of pounds of community benefits that they bring. 

But with the ban on the use of large steel lattice pylons for new 11 kV to 132 kV lines, the Welsh Government has committed to a policy of undergrounding electricity infrastructure at 132 kV and below. And the significance, of course, of that policy is that it could increase the cost and complexity of building the electricity network needed to connect those renewable energy projects. While the policy aims to reduce the visual impact of pylons, it could slow grid expansion, increase costs for consumers and make it harder, eventually, to deliver Wales's clean energy ambitions. That is my party's concern.

Indeed, the Institution of Engineering and Technology estimated that undergrounding costs five times more per mile than overhead lines. So, what assessment, Minister, have you made of the additional costs of this policy? What impact could it have on the viability of renewable energy projects and the speed at which new infrastructure can be delivered? How will you ensure that these costs don't ultimately fall on households and businesses? And what guarantees can you give that families' energy bills won't rise because of the Welsh Government's outright ban on pylons?

Lastly, I recognise and acknowledge your comment that energy should not be treated only as a climate issue, and I do agree, but in addition to an economic issue, it's also a social justice one. Welsh Labour established our approach to social partnership, working hand in hand with trade unions to ensure that economic growth delivers fair work. So, I would urge you, Minister, to ensure that social partnership remains at the heart of the Government's approach to energy policy, so that the benefits of the energy transition are felt by workers and communities through the whole of Wales. So, finally, would you agree with Oxfam Cymru's challenge that we can make the transition to a green economy our primary vehicle for reducing structural poverty, advancing equity and fulfilling our duties as a globally responsible nation, and if so, could you please outline the next steps for taking these forward? Diolch.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
I'm very grateful to the Member for her questions. In relation to the shift in the target, the previous target by the previous administration was based around 100 per cent of the—a notional figure for Welsh consumption coming from renewable sources. The problem with it is that it ignored those emissions that were produced beyond that by fossil fuel sources. And so, you could hit the target and still have completely unabated fossil fuel generation, which there is in Wales. So, from a decarbonisation perspective, it didn't make any sense, because it didn't actually decarbonise the actual energy system in Wales. So, by aligning the climate and energy policy, it makes more sense to deliver the benefits of decarbonisation because you're actually looking at the emissions produced by the energy system in Wales. 

I would say as well, if you look, most objective observers would say that the policy of the previous administration was not successful. For almost a decade before the last Senedd election, there was very, very little development. You might think, 'Well, relatively speaking, that's—.' I'm quoting what industry observers have told me, all right? So, it wasn't successful in its own terms, is the point that I would make, certainly relative to developments elsewhere in Europe.

In relation to undergrounding, I think that that wasn't the main focus of this statement. We'll have more to say about that, but we've consistently set out our position, and we will have more detail to share on that in due course.

Where we do absolutely agree is on the need for a just transition. Certainly, social partnership is right at the centre of the emphasis, which was the common thread through everything I said, which is about local ownership, about things being done with communities, not to communities—you know, a just transition, absolutely. The key thing as well is that you don't want to do just transition, okay? Because an energy transition also needs to be a means by which we can get to grips with social inequality, where we can get to grips with poverty, and also use it as a driver for closing the prosperity gap for Wales. It can be a vehicle for all these other important policy goals. As well as its important role in delivering decarbonisation, what we are saying through the energy policy is it needs also to deliver on those wider social and economic objectives, and we are in agreement on that.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
Well, thank you for your strategy announcement again today, and I look forward to more meat on the bone as this goes forward. I'm not a lover of strategies, as people well know, but this is looking at the future of moving towards renewables. 

Now, interestingly, you've just said it mustn't be a just transition. During the co-operation agreement that you had with Labour, every other word on climate change policy was talking about a just transition. We believe, quite firmly, and it was the UK Conservative Government, first starting with Prime Minister Rishi Sunak, who pushed the move to the climate targets and everything back a little, in order to take people with them. And it's been continued by our leader, Kemi Badenoch MP, that we believe in the development of a sensible approach, and one that is not making a very expensive transition for those already facing an increased cost of living.

I'm very wary of the approach by this Plaid Cymru Government and the approach previously by the Welsh Labour Government, at a time when your own hypocrisy is so paramount, when you have actually, with Ed Miliband, supported the stopping of the oil and gas fields that were providing us with good energy sources, and under the Welsh Labour Government and the co-operation agreement, we saw numerous large-scale wind and solar farms approved across Wales. Those of us who live in Llandudno, and there are other Members here, actually face hundreds of turbines out in Llandudno bay, and yet we have the highest electric bills in the whole of north Wales and Wales.

So, there's got to be this sensible approach. If you look at Alaw Môn, the solar farm on Ynys Môn, 660 acres taken out of agriculture to facilitate generating 160 MW. Llanwern solar farm near Newport, 250 acres with a capacity of 75 MW. Clocaenog forest windfarm, 27 turbines. These developments disrupt our natural environment, affect the views enjoyed by visitors and residents, and take valuable agricultural land out of production.

Now you talk about, and we have got a climate emergency, but we've also got an energy security issue. Global fighting across the world is very paramount currently. Sorry, I thought you were looking at me then.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text: Not at all.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
We don't need more state-owned companies being established, nor do we need more large-scale wind and solar developments without proper consideration. What Wales needs is cheap, reliable energy to keep our existing factories running, help our businesses remain competitive and keep household bills low. These should be the priorities; they're my priorities for my residents. But none of this must come at the expense of Wales's food security. We need to strike a sensible balance between meeting our energy needs, protecting our countryside and preserving the agricultural land that helps to feed our communities. That's why we are reiterating our call for a moratorium on industrial scale solar and windfarm developments.

You've referenced using tidal stream and lagoons, and I actually agree with that, but it would be interesting to see how you as a Government put money behind that and make that an action, not just words.

Cabinet Minister, your strategy must also focus on restoring the marine environment. During the fourth carbon budget, I met with Lord Deben, and he noted that I was the only Member who had picked up on that we're not doing enough in our marine environment in terms of carbon sequestration, and I'd like to know what you're doing on that going forwards.

When people think of renewable energy now, they just think of solar, wind and tidal power. But Gwyndod power station on Ynys Môn is a significant asset that deserves to be focused on, and again is thanks to the UK Conservative Government, who actually purchased the land. It has the potential to provide energy, create jobs and strengthen our economy. We must ensure that nuclear energy is properly considered. I'm really pleased with Morlais and the work that's going on there. We must remember oil and gas production—to ignore it and then import inferior quality oil and gas is not what you should be looking at as a Government here. So, Minister, I hope you'll hear our calls from these benches, and I hope that we can have a sensible strategy going forward. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
I'm grateful to the Member for her comments. I would say that we're absolutely in agreement about the central importance of affordability, and I've mentioned that at several points during my opening remarks. I think that we have to start from a position of clarity that many of the levers and tools that are relevant when it comes to energy costs do lie with the Westminster Government, and so that is a limitation about our ability to affect energy prices in the broadest sense. But I think it's important that we do recognise, as I've done throughout my remarks, that addressing this issue of affordability, addressing the issue of energy costs, needs to be central to any energy strategy. It's relevant, obviously, to households the length and breadth of Wales.

You're absolutely right that it's a strange situation, isn't it, where we are energy exporters, we have a latent renewable energy potential of very, very significant scale, and yet at the moment, actually, the UK faces higher energy costs than most European countries, but within the UK as well we face some of the highest energy costs overall. We have to address that. We have to find ways of addressing that within the limitations that I describe. And so we have to, I think, look creatively at different solutions: turnkey solutions that can help us, for instance, with businesses and industrial users, as we have discussed at previous sessions, looking at private wire solutions, behind-the-meter solutions, combinations of storage and on-site generation, possibly in conjunction with the public energy company that we've described, as well as with other investors where that is relevant. So, let's look at that while recognising that some of those levers and tools are not in our hands. Many things that I've described are a means by which we can address that very question of affordability that you stressed as central to your contribution. 

In terms of carbon capture and storage, I did mention that as an important element, not least in the context of our industrial base in Wales. We have engaged with the UK Government and other UK stakeholders to emphasise the importance of carbon capture and storage in enabling us to decarbonise our industrial base, but also to address some of the issues in terms of economic and financial sustainability, as well as environmental sustainability as well. I specifically mentioned the importance of protecting productive agricultural land in the balanced approach that is at the heart of our planning approach in this context.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text: We'll now move to one-minute contributions. First, John Davies.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn at gyfraniadau un funud nawr. Yn gyntaf, John Davies.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Thank you, Minister. Wales's economy is, and always has been, one of extraction. It's an economy designed to export our resources for little or no reward, while private companies, mostly from the other side of the bridge, rake in the profits. People in Wales, therefore, live in poverty, and are affected by everything that poverty brings with it. We have a massive economic, social and climate change opportunity that is with us at the moment. Wales has a massive green energy potential. It's an opportunity to buck this pattern and to break the chains that we currently have.

Many Welsh community energy initiatives have already seized this opportunity, reversing the outflow of energy and retaining wealth in Wales. Volunteers typically spearhead these initiatives. We, as a Government, must support them, as this sometimes can be a complex process. By providing communities with ready-made turnkey community energy solutions, we can change things. We can enable communities to embrace new green technology, to consume locally produced energy and to embed—

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text: Could you ask a question, please?

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text: I will. What consideration has the Cabinet Minister given to such a turnkey Government-supported approach to community energy? Thank you.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text: I very much concur with the points made by the Member. Building on my earlier remarks, I think what we need to do in order to leverage that potential competitive advantage that we have in Wales, because of the renewable energy sources, both existing and nascent technologies that we have—. I think that it's a combination of approaches, some of which I've already described, in terms of planning industrial infrastructure with energy infrastructure, private wire arrangements, power purchase agreements, which can be done at a more attractive rate than the wholesale energy market, smart energy systems, using storage and flexibility, and as part of that, as you suggest, using public and community ownership. Putting all of that together in a package, in the way that you describe, is the way that we actually address the energy costs problem that we have at the moment and flip it. We could get to a place where we build energy as a source of competitive advantage for Wales, rather than what it is at the moment, which is a source of competitive disadvantage for too many businesses and industrial users.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text: Thank you, Minister, for your statement. I want to ask you a question specifically about energy being more affordable from this strategy—and maybe I'm misunderstanding it. I appreciate single home owners can go and purchase solar panels with a grant, possibly, and then they can see their energy bills reduced for that household. I also get about communities that can perhaps put a panel of solar panels on a nearby field and feed into that, and they get their own reduction in energy. But we are part of the national grid, so any energy that we produce, whether it's clean or fossil fuel, goes into a national grid. We're part of an energy market across the UK. We've got household prices fixed by the UK Government. We've got international fuel fossil markets that dictate that. So I'm trying to understand, with the community ownership and the national public energy company, what is the actual mechanism by which this strategy will eventually lower bills for the majority of Welsh people that go onto comparison sites and just choose a provider? The majority of people. How is that mechanism going to work when we have a national grid and the UK Government dictating energy prices? Diolch.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text: As I said in my earlier remarks, I think we have to recognise the fact that many of the levers and tools are not in our hands. That's not what we want, and we want to have more of those energy powers in our hands so that we can make a bigger difference to the people of Wales. But does the fact that we are constrained mean that we should do nothing? No, absolutely not. We've got to get creative here. The Member asks what can we do. The PPAs that I mentioned are one way in which, for instance, a publicly owned energy company can actually set its own price with a target community, with industrial users and business users. Offtake agreements are standard practice in energy. Sometimes sleeved agreements. So, even though you're sending the electrons into the national grid, you as a generator can have an agreement with a customer or set of customers. We've got to get creative here. Within the constraints that we have, we believe that we can find ways in which we can ensure that our energy generation, owned by the people of Wales in myriad different forms—local community ownership, Welsh private sector ownership and indeed Welsh public ownership—can mean that we are not left as victims, if you like, of decisions that are made by companies or indeed Government bodies elsewhere.

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
I thank the Cabinet Minister for his statement. I'm delighted that the Welsh Government agrees with us Greens that Wales has a huge untapped potential to be completely self-sufficient in green, safe, resilient energy generation, owned by our communities and our nation. We believe that Wales must aim to meet all of our energy needs from renewables by 2035, to reduce our carbon emissions and tackle global heating, but also to ensure energy independence from global price shocks, and to protect the poorest in our society from continuing energy poverty.547

I do have a concern about the loss of the explicit mention of renewables from targets. Because if we reduce carbon emissions, but create other problems, future generations won't thank us. And I would remind the Reform spokesman that nuclear power is expensive, won't deliver in time, and creates terrible risks for future generations. Can the Cabinet Minister provide reassurance that the shift in focus from renewable energy targets to reducing emissions will not lead to other significant environmental consequences for our children and grandchildren?

documents.item: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
documents.text:
As I said earlier, the motivation for the shift to a holistic target hopefully is one that the Member would be in sympathy with. Because it was a perverse situation where we weren't actually recognising the fact that we could hit the target because it was based on this notional consumption, whereas our energy generation system was creating masses of fossil fuel-based-emissions through fossil fuel generation. That makes no sense in environmental terms. And so, what we're saying is we want to decarbonise the energy system.

The other point to make is that we're adopting a holistic view, not just in the terms that I've just described, but also recognising the importance of looking at the entire energy system. Energy is also in the form of heating, isn't it? It's also in the form of how we power our transport system. So, it's not just decarbonising the electricity generation system, but also electrifying the entire energy system and doing it on a low-carbon basis, which allows us to hit our more ambitious net zero target of 2040.

documents.text: Can I thank the Minister for today's statement? Plaid Cymru's manifesto policy establishes a clear presumption on undergrounding new electricity transmission cables up to 132 kV. documents.item: 9. Legislative Consent Motion: The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network Information Systems) Bill
documents.text:
More from me, I'm afraid.

It's a pleasure for me to rise to my feet to move the motion in my name, I believe, or in the name of the Government. The motion recommends that the Senedd consents to the relevant provisions in the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill 2026 as set out in the legislative consent motion. The Bill will make critical national infrastructure more resilient by amending the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018. It broadens incident reporting requirements, strengthens regulators' information gathering and enforcement powers, and ensures that critical suppliers are brought within scope. These measures will help to protect essential services, including transport, energy, drinking water, health and digital infrastructure from a growing and increasingly complex cyber threat.

The Welsh Ministers are the designated competent authority for health services and for drinking water supply and distribution in Wales. In the water sector, the Drinking Water Inspectorate acts on our behalf. Therefore, a number of provisions confer, remove or modify functions exercised in devolved areas and may affect water companies operating wholly or mainly in Wales.

Although much of the Bill concerns matters that are reserved to Westminster, it also interacts with devolved responsibilities. The Senedd could not legislate for the Bill as a whole, and a UK-wide Bill offers the most coherent way to protect interconnected networks and services while recognising the responsibilities of Welsh Ministers and Welsh regulators. Welsh Government officials have engaged closely with the UK Government as the Bill has developed. I am satisfied that it provides appropriate safeguards. The need for an effective and coherent response to cyber threats across the United Kingdom justifies the powers that are delegated by the Bill. In these exceptional circumstances, these powers are proportionate and consistent with our principles on UK legislation in devolved areas.

I'm grateful to the Legislation Committee and the Economy, Energy and Connectivity Committee for their scrutiny. The Legislation Committee has agreed with our assessment of the provisions requiring consent, but the Economy, Energy and Connectivity Committee was unable to reach a position on the motion. We have responded to both committees and have set out why the Welsh Government now recommends consent.

The legislative consent memorandum did not include a recommendation on consent because it was laid shortly after the formation of the new Welsh Government. Time was needed to assess the Government's policies, the Bill's cross-cutting implications, and the application of our principles on UK legislation. I also acknowledge that the memorandum was not laid within the two-week deadline. We recognise the difficulties that this causes in terms of scrutiny, and we remain committed to the efficient discharge of the LCM process.

Members have raised concerns about delegated powers, including those relating to codes of practice and reporting. I agree that proper consultation and parliamentary scrutiny are essential. The UK Government has brought forward concessions in response to concerns raised in the House of Lords. We will assess the final amendments and will lay a supplementary legislative consent memorandum if required. Much of the operational and practical detail will follow through implementation and through secondary legislation, so it is not yet possible to assess all potential costs, including those for water companies and the Drinking Water Inspectorate.

We will continue to work with UK Government, regulators and affected sectors and will keep the Senedd informed. We will also continue to provide oversight with regard to health matters through the Welsh Ministers' statutory role as the competent authority and will support operators through the NHS Wales cyber resilience unit. In the water sector, we will work with the Drinking Water Inspectorate and water companies as the enhanced requirements are developed.

Llywydd, cyber attacks do not respect institutional or geographical boundaries—or even the deadline for me to complete my contribution [Laughter.] But, for those reasons, I recommend that the Senedd supports the motion and gives its consent to the relevant provisions in the Bill.

documents.item: 9. Legislative Consent Motion: The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network Information Systems) Bill
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I thank the committee for its work on this legislative consent memorandum. Last week, I spoke in the debate on the consent motion for the Armed Forces Bill. The committee's report on the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill contains many of the same themes. We received the Cabinet Minister's response to our report last Thursday. While the committee may disagree with the responses to some recommendations, we nonetheless welcome the timely responses and we encourage other Welsh Ministers to follow suit.

The committee agrees with the Welsh Government's assessment about the provisions in the Bill that require the Senedd's consent. However, in our report, we ask whether consent should also be sought for clause 37(7) of the Bill. Changes to the relevant consultation requirement under clause 37 could affect a code issued by the Secretary of State under clause 36, and the Cabinet Minister believes consent is needed for clause 36. But the Cabinet Minister considered that the regulation-making power in clause 37(7) falls short of meeting the consent test in Standing Order 29.1. He told us it is not possible to conclude at this stage that the regulation-making power would be used to make provision that would affect consultation with regulators on codes of practice. He was also unable to conclude that, as a result of the changes made to the consultation requirements, provision would be made that would affect how regulators in Wales exercise their functions.

The Welsh Government's view on whether the Senedd should grant consent to the relevant provisions in a Bill is an important part of the legislative consent process, because it helps the Senedd committees make an informed decision on a consent motion. This memorandum did not include a recommendation on consent. We eventually received the recommendation in a letter on 28 September, in which the Cabinet Minister said that, as a result of engagement with the UK Government, he could now recommend the Senedd does consent to the relevant provisions in the Bill. We acknowledge this letter in our report, but we were not given full details of the inter-governmental discussion, and so we asked for those details. It is disappointing that, in responding to our report, the Cabinet Minister has only gone as far as to say the Welsh Government is satisfied that the Bill provides appropriate safeguards. So, we still don't have the details we requested.

The Bill confers several delegated powers on the Secretary of State to act in devolved areas. Members will be aware that, in July, the Welsh Government published its principles on UK legislation in devolved areas. The fourth principle states that delegated powers in UK legislation, including Henry VIII powers, should be conferred on the Welsh Ministers alone. The principle further states that any departure from this position needs to be justified by exceptional circumstances on a case-by-case basis. The committee could not identify the exceptional circumstances. In the memorandum, the Cabinet Minister himself calls them broad delegated Henry VIII powers. Members may know that the House of Lords Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee performs a similar role to that of the Legislation Committee. That committee has deemed two powers in the Bill, which are relevant to the Senedd's consent decision, as unacceptable. Again, the Cabinet Minister's responses to the committee's fifth and sixth recommendations are disappointingly sparse on detail. We asked for an explanation for the apparent breach of the Welsh Government's principles in relation to each delegated power in the Bill that may be used in a devolved area. The Cabinet Minister does not consider that the Welsh Government's principles have been breached and the committee has not received the explanations it asked for.

As for the report of the House of Lords committee, we thought it was fair to give the Cabinet Minister an opportunity to reflect on the concerns of that committee, and we invited him to comment. The Cabinet Minister did not comment, stating that the UK parliamentary committee is entitled to its views and it's the responsibility of the UK Government to consider those views. The Cabinet Minister may wish to reflect on his written response to the committee's report in his closing remarks. Diolch.

documents.item: 9. Legislative Consent Motion: The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network Information Systems) Bill
documents.text: Thank you, Presiding Officer. Now, at a time when threats to our national security are growing, protecting Britain and Wales from cyber attacks has never been more important. We live in a world where a single cyber attack can bring businesses to its knees and cripple essential, life-sustaining services. Having spent over 30 years working across aerospace and in the defence industry, I fully understand the importance of national security. National security isn't something we can afford to get wrong. Now, Reform UK will always put the security of our country and its people first and foremost, and that is why we support this legislative consent motion. Thank you.

documents.item: 9. Legislative Consent Motion: The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network Information Systems) Bill
documents.text: I'm very grateful for the committee's scrutiny, as I said. I have very limited time, and so I think that what I will undertake to do is to give a full response, setting out the rationale as to a number of issues that were raised and why we do think, in this instance, our recommendation is consistent with the principles in relation to delegated powers. There were very particular circumstances, which I referred to in my opening remarks, in relation to the timing of this LCM that meant that we weren't able to bring forward our position on consent earlier. I am grateful for the recognition that, at least in response to the committee, we were timely in that response, but I will undertake to give a fuller response to the committee and Senedd Members in relation to all the matters that were raised.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Local authorities have a statutory responsibility to provide a comprehensive and efficient library service. The Welsh Government supports libraries in Clwyd through capital and revenue funding. In 2026-27, this includes awarding £349,000 to fund capital improvements in Colwyn Bay library and Rhyl library. Libraries across Clwyd have also benefited this year from over £50,000 of funding for smaller projects.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Thank you, Minister. A local authority in Clwyd in 2023 resolved to reduce library one-stop shop opening hours by 40 per cent. This was despite over 4,500 residents responding to the consultation—the most that the local authority had seen in years. Ninety per cent of those responses warned that the closure or reduction in hours would limit their ability to visit their local library, and 96 per cent of these submissions submitted negative comments about the proposal. The local authority went ahead because its hands, to a certain extent, were tied financially by the funding formula. The significant change has seen around £360,000 saved but severely limits residents' access to this important service. So, what steps are you taking to support local library services, and what discussions have you had with the Minister for local government on seeing a funding formula that specifically protects library services? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text:
The Member raises an important issue, I know, for many of our constituents across Wales. I do acknowledge the challenges that local authorities have faced because of the financial settlements of these past years and the impact that that has had on local libraries in particular. One of the things that we are doing as part of our work in developing the culture and sports strategy is looking at local services. I have had discussions already with some local government leaders in Wales and the Welsh Local Government Association, in order to try and truly understand how fragile some of these services are.

Central to our new strategy is ensuring equal access for everyone. So, we want to understand what these challenges have been over past years, what that has meant to services in terms of libraries across Wales. A large part of our next piece of work will involve looking at that long-term strategy in terms of what library services that work for our communities look like, recognising that the service doesn't always meet our ambition in all parts of Wales at the moment.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Libraries are essential services for young and old, often going far past the borrowing of books by providing warm spaces and tackling social isolation. The Public Libraries and Museums Act 1964 places a statutory duty on councils in England and Wales to provide a comprehensive and efficient library service. However, discussions with people in the sector suggest that a lack of clarity around what this actually means creates ambiguity and can lead to library provision being treated as discretionary rather than a legal duty. I think you have gone some way to answering the question in terms of that long-term strategy, but would the Government consider looking to give more clarity on what constitutes a comprehensive and efficient library service and provide councils with greater certainty about their statutory responsibilities?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: I thank the Member for that further question. In Wales, we have a public library standards framework, which is the measure that is used to decide whether the quality of libraries has been met or not. This is a very live issue. I am aware of the concerns that exist across Wales, and one of the things that I am looking at is what responsibilities and powers I have under that Act if those services do not reach the mark in terms of quality. As the work of developing the new strategy goes forward, we will also be publishing specific plans looking at every sector, including libraries, in order to provide more clarity, yes, to local authorities, but also to the people of Wales.

Dwi'n ymwybodol o'r pryderon sydd ledled Cymru, ac un o'r pethau dwi'n edrych arnyn nhw ydy beth ydy'r cyfrifoldebau a'r grym sydd gen i o dan y Ddeddf honno os nad ydy'r gwasanaethau hynny yn cyrraedd y safon ddisgwyliedig. Wrth i'r gwaith o ddatblygu'r strategaeth newydd fynd rhagddo, byddwn ni hefyd yn cyhoeddi cynlluniau penodol sy'n edrych ar bob sector, gan gynnwys llyfrgelloedd, er mwyn rhoi rhagor o eglurder, ie, i awdurdodau lleol, ond hefyd i bobl Cymru.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: 2. How is the Welsh Government protecting and promoting national monuments in Gwynedd Maldwyn for future generations? OQ64676
documents.text_cy: 2. Sut y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn diogelu ac yn hyrwyddo henebion cenedlaethol Gwynedd Maldwyn ar gyfer cenedlaethau’r dyfodol? OQ64676

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Cadw protects and promotes nationally important monuments in Gwynedd Maldwyn through designation and through providing expert advice, guidance and support to the owners for their conservation. Cadw also promotes our heritage by managing the national monuments in its care and ensuring public access to them, in accordance with this Government's commitment to provide fair access to all of our cultural and heritage sites.
documents.text_cy: Mae Cadw yn gwarchod ac yn hyrwyddo henebion o bwysigrwydd cenedlaethol yng Ngwynedd Maldwyn drwy eu dynodi a thrwy ddarparu cyngor arbenigol, arweiniad a chymorth i'w perchnogion ar gyfer eu cadwraeth. Mae Cadw hefyd yn hyrwyddo ein treftadaeth drwy reoli'r henebion cenedlaethol sydd yn ei ofal a sicrhau mynediad cyhoeddus atyn nhw, yn unol ag ymrwymiad y Llywodraeth hon i hyrwyddo mynediad teg i'n safleoedd diwylliannol a threftadaeth.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: You will be aware that Llansilin in the Gwynedd Maldwyn constituency is the home of Sycharth, the ancient court of Owain Glyndŵr and one of the most significant sites of our national heritage. Unfortunately, however, it is disgraceful that the current state of the site doesn't reflect its historic and national importance. There are problems such as overgrowing foliage, lack of access and even a lack of mention of the site on the Cadw website. On the other hand, Powys council has already rejected proposals for more signage on the road to promote the site. Can I ask, therefore, how the Welsh Government can work with Cadw and Powys County Council to ensure that Sycharth is promoted as a site of national importance for future generations?
documents.text_cy: Fe fyddwch yn ymwybodol fod Llansilin yn etholaeth Gwynedd Maldwyn yn gartref i Sycharth, llys hynafol Owain Glyndŵr ac un o safleoedd mwyaf arwyddocaol ein treftadaeth genedlaethol. Yn anffodus, fodd bynnag, mae'n gywilyddus nad yw cyflwr presennol y safle yn adlewyrchu ei bwysigrwydd hanesyddol a chenedlaethol. Ceir problemau megis gordyfiant, diffyg mynediad hygyrch, a hyd yn oed diffyg crybwyll i'r safle ar wefan Cadw. Ar y llaw arall, mae Cyngor Sir Powys eisoes wedi gwrthod ymdrechion am fwy o arwyddion pwrpasol ar y ffyrdd i hyrwyddo'r lle. A gaf i ofyn, felly, sut y gall Llywodraeth Cymru gydweithio â Cadw a Chyngor Sir Powys i sicrhau bod Sycharth yn cael ei hyrwyddo fel safle o bwysigrwydd genedlaethol ar gyfer cenedlaethau'r dyfodol?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising the issue of Sycharth. Just to be clear, I do consider Sycharth to be a monument of national importance that has a very significant place in Wales's history and in our identity as a nation. The monument is open to the public. There are interpretation signs on the site. After a conservation programme carried out with funding by Cadw, work has gone ahead since concerns were raised a few years ago. However, I am on the record as saying that I would like to see more being done to promote Sycharth before I was in this role, and I'm still of that opinion. Even though the rural location and nature of the site do present some problems in terms of physical access and the way it's presented, I have asked Cadw to look into how we can make the story of this site more prominent, because it is just so important in terms of our history. You will also be aware that Sycharth isn't for sale at the moment. It has a lifetime tenancy. Cadw is working in partnership with the estate that owns Sycharth to ensure that it is maintained and kept in good condition and that public access continues.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi Sycharth. I fi fod yn glir, dwi yn ystyried bod Sycharth yn heneb o bwys cenedlaethol sydd â lle arwyddocaol yn hanes Cymru ac yn ein hunaniaeth ni fel cenedl. Mae'r heneb ar agor i'r cyhoedd. Mae yna arwyddion dehongli ar y safle. Yn sgil rhaglen o waith cadwraeth a gynhaliwyd gyda chyllid gan Cadw, mae yna waith wedi mynd rhagddo ers i bryderon gael eu codi rai blynyddoedd yn ôl. Ond, mi ydw i ar y record yn dweud y byddwn i'n hoffi gweld mwy yn cael ei wneud i hyrwyddo Sycharth cyn i fi fod yn y rôl hon, a dwi'n dal o'r farn honno. Er bod lleoliad gwledig a natur y safle yn peri rhai heriau o ran mynediad ffisegol a'r ffordd y mae'n cael ei gyflwyno, mi ydw i wedi gofyn i Cadw ymchwilio i sut y gellir gwneud stori'r safle hwn yn fwy amlwg gan ei fod o mor, mor bwysig o ran ein hanes ni. Fe fyddwch chi hefyd yn ymwybodol nad yw Sycharth ar werth ar hyn o bryd. Mae o'n destun tenantiaeth gydol oes. Mae Cadw yn gweithio mewn partneriaeth efo'r ystâd sy'n berchen ar Sycharth i sicrhau ei fod yn cael ei gynnal a'i gadw mewn cyflwr da a bod mynediad i'r cyhoedd yn parhau.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Following on from that question about protecting our historic heritage for future generations, last week, I had a meeting with Historic Houses Wales. A great deal of our heritage is actually in private ownership. I know from personal experience of living in a grade II listed house just how expensive these properties can be to maintain, particularly when there are restrictions on making improvements to reduce running costs. Can I ask the Cabinet Minister what practical support is available through Cadw for private owners who are helping to preserve our historic heritage, and how is she working with colleagues across Government to make sure these buildings remain viable for future generations?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: I thank the Member for that further question. I and Cadw officials did meet with Historic Houses Wales last week, and officials will be having further discussions with them in relation to how we can proceed with any support work and to look at any possible options. Clearly, there is an opportunity also for them to contribute as part of the development of our new strategy.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am y cwestiwn pellach hwnnw. Mi wnes i a swyddogion o Cadw gyfarfod efo Historic Houses Wales yr wythnos diwethaf, ac mi fydd swyddogion yn trafod ymhellach efo nhw o ran sut mae mynd rhagddo efo unrhyw waith cefnogaeth ac i archwilio beth yw'r opsiynau posib. Yn amlwg, mae yna gyfle iddyn nhw hefyd gyfrannu fel rhan o ddatblygiad y strategaeth newydd.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. The Reform UK spokesperson, Louise Emery.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf nawr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Llefarydd Reform UK, Louise Emery.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Diolch. Minister, I had a question to the First Minister on 29 September about business rates and music venues—and I welcome the 30 per cent reduction—that talked about the cliff edge that happens at the £51,000 business rate edge. I want to keep this issue front and centre of your mind when you're in discussions with the finance Minister. A lot of cultural activities require public money to exist, and we don't want music venues to join that list. They want to be self-sufficient, they don't want to rely on grants, and this is a way we can help them. So, can I ask will you address the exclusion of music venues with the finance Minister, including consideration of a business rates taper approach in the future? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Thank you. You will appreciate that these are questions to me, and you may want to ask that question of the finance Minister in the next set of questions. But, certainly, in terms of the future of music venues, it is one of the reasons why that 30 per cent was announced, in order to support smaller venues. We will also be looking at this as part of the new culture strategy. In terms of the future of music in Wales in its entirety, some responsibility for music lies with Creative Wales, and some of the responsibility for music falls to the Wales Arts Council. There is some ambiguity on occasion as to who is responsible for this sector in Wales, because, clearly, it's important for the Welsh economy too, along with our town centres and so many communities the length and breadth of Wales. What we as a Government to determine to do is to work on a cross-ministerial and cross-portfolio basis in order to ensure that the new strategy does take into account the benefit of music, yes, in terms of health and well-being, the culture of Wales, but also in terms of our economy. So, this is a very live issue.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Fe fyddwch chi yn gwerthfawrogi mai cwestiynau i fi ydy'r rhain, ac mae'n bosib holi'r Gweinidog cyllid yn y set nesaf o gwestiynau o ran hynny. Ond, yn sicr, o ran dyfodol lleoliadau cerddoriaeth, mae o'n rheswm pam mae'r 30 y cant yna wedi'i gyhoeddi, i gefnogi lleoliadau llai. Mi fyddwn ni hefyd yn edrych ar hyn fel rhan o'r strategaeth diwylliant newydd. O ran dyfodol cerddoriaeth yng Nghymru yn ei chyfanrwydd, mae peth cyfrifoldeb am gerddoriaeth rŵan efo Cymru Greadigol ac mae peth cyfrifoldeb am gerddoriaeth yn dod o dan Gyngor Celfyddydau Cymru. Mae yna amwysedd weithiau o ran pwy sy'n gyfrifol am y sector hwn yng Nghymru, oherwydd, yn amlwg, mae'n bwysig o ran economi Cymru hefyd, ac i ganol ein trefi ni a chymaint o gymunedau ledled Cymru. Yr hyn rydyn ni'n benderfynol, fel Llywodraeth, o wneud yw gweithio yn draws-weinidogol, trawsbortffolio i sicrhau bod y strategaeth newydd yn cymryd i ystyriaeth fudd cerddoriaeth, ie, o ran iechyd a lles, o ran diwylliant Cymru, ond hefyd o ran yr economi. Felly, mae hwn yn fater byw.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Diolch. Now, I'd like an update on the national museum in Cardiff. Now, we know that we got some funding for roof repairs earlier this year, and you came to our culture committee and expressed concern about water entering galleries containing our national collections. We've got winter approaching, and it's important that we have essential maintenance that carries on. But I want to know what progress there's been on the funding and repairs and what timetable and funding are in place to complete the urgent works, because we could be in a position where not only that our collections are at risk, but that the museum actually has to close.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Thank you for that question. As I said when I appeared before the committee, and as you have mentioned, I am extremely concerned about National Museum Cardiff, and I am looking forward to receiving proposals for the possible redevelopment from the national museum. I haven't received the details to date. What we have been doing is working very closely with Amgueddfa Cymru to try and understand what the position is and what the needs are, and we have allocated up to £4.8 million in capital funding in this financial year to support the most urgent remedial work and to help to secure the collections. These are questions that I too have been asking of Amgueddfa Cymru, and I look forward to receiving an update on them and to sharing that information more broadly when I have it.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn hwn. Fel roeddwn i'n dweud wrth fod gerbron y pwyllgor ac fel rydych chi wedi sôn, dwi'n bryderus dros ben ynglŷn ag Amgueddfa Genedlaethol Caerdydd a dwi'n edrych ymlaen i dderbyn cynigion ar gyfer yr ailddatblygu posib gan Amgueddfa Genedlaethol Caerdydd. Dwi heb gael y manylion hynny hyd yma. Yr hyn rydyn ni wedi bod yn ei wneud ydy gweithio'n agos iawn gydag Amgueddfa Cymru i geisio deall beth ydy'r sefyllfa a beth ydy'r angen, ac mi ydyn ni wedi dyrannu hyd at £4.8 miliwn mewn arian cyfalaf yn y flwyddyn ariannol yma i gefnogi'r gwaith gwella mwyaf brys ac i helpu i ddiogelu'r casgliadau. Mae'r rhain yn gwestiynau dwi hefyd wedi bod yn eu holi i Amgueddfa Cymru, a dwi'n edrych ymlaen at gael diweddariad arnyn nhw ac i fedru rhannu'r wybodaeth yna'n fwy eang pan fydd y wybodaeth gen i.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Okay. Finally, I want to talk about the Tour de France. It's coming to Wales next summer, starting in Welshpool and finishing in Cardiff. We want it to be a successful event to showcase Wales, to help the local economy and be a great event for all of us to attend. But events of this scale cost money to host. We totally accept that; that's the deal. But we want transparency around these costs now and in the build-up to the event, and in the legacy funding afterwards. Now, I know you've announced the £4.5 million legacy fund, and I've got a query about that and then a question about the hosting fees. The legacy fund comes from the brilliant basics fund, or is administered through the brilliant basics fund, which is to provide small tourism infrastructure projects. Is this additional money, the £4.5 million, noting that it's going to be ring-fenced for cycling infrastructure, or is it just part of the brilliant basics fund, so it's going to come out of that original pot? That's my first question. And secondly, on the hosting fee, which public body has paid for this? Thank you.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: I'm happy to provide additional information. The first part of your question should be referred to another minister, Adam Price, as it's not part of my portfolio. There is close collaboration on a cross-ministerial basis on the Tour de France. You will also appreciate that we inherited the Tour de France, and one of the things that I'm on the record as having said is that these are things that any government should look at before bidding for any major event. All of that information should be known before we even make that application. That clarity isn't there. So, at the moment, what we are doing is working on a cross-ministerial basis to better understand what different pots of money are in different portfolios currently, and also, in terms of looking at the legacy, how we can co-ordinate all of that work in order to ensure the greatest possible impact and the greatest possible legacy from all of this. But, for me to be clear, as we as a Government proceed, this is the kind of change that you will see—we will be looking at detailed planning before making applications, and not, as we saw under Labour, doing the thinking once something has been delivered for Wales.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n hapus i ddarparu gwybodaeth ychwanegol. Mae rhan gyntaf eich cwestiwn chi at Weinidog arall, sef Adam Price; nid yw'n rhan o fy mhortffolio i. Mae yna gydweithio agos ar y funud yn draws-weinidogol o ran y Tour de France. Fyddwch chi hefyd yn gwerthfawrogi ein bod ni wedi etifeddu'r Tour de France, ac un o'r pethau dwi ar y record yn dweud ydy bod rhain yn bethau y dylai unrhyw lywodraeth edrych arnyn nhw cyn mynd am unrhyw ddigwyddiad mawr. Mi ddylai'r holl wybodaeth yma fod yn wybyddus cyn i ni hyd yn oed roi'r cais i mewn. Dydy'r eglurder yna ddim yna. Felly, ar y funud, yr hyn dŷn ni'n ei wneud ydy gweithio'n draws-weinidogol i ddeall yn well ba symiau gwahanol sydd mewn gwahanol bortffolios ar y funud, a hefyd, o ran edrych ar y gwaddol, sut ydyn ni'n cydlynu'r holl waith hwnnw i sicrhau bod yr impact mwyaf a'r gwaddol mwyaf yn dod o hyn. Ond, i fi fod yn glir, wrth i ni fel Llywodraeth fynd rhagddi, dyma'r math o newid fydd, sef edrych ar gynllunio manwl cyn i ni roi cais i mewn, ac nid, fel rydym ni wedi gweld o dan Lafur, yn meddwl wedyn ar ôl i rywbeth ddod i Gymru.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: The Welsh Labour spokesperson, Mike Hedges.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Mike Hedges.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. I want to raise a question on esports, which, as most people I think know, is short for electronic sports, which refers to organised competitive video gaming where individuals or teams compete in specific games for prizes, ranking or prestige. Esports have developed from a casual hobby into a structured global industry with leagues, governing bodies, teams, sponsors and dedicated venues. In Wales, the industry is growing rapidly. From my days of being a college lecturer, it was very popular. Esports Wales runs multiple official tournaments throughout the Welsh esports league, and the student esports championships. These events include seasonal leagues, open tournaments and school and college competitions, with structured formats and prize money. Will the Minister dedicate some of the money given to support the creative industries to esports as part of a comprehensive esports strategy?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: I thank the Member for being someone that does raise esports frequently, and I agree with you—we do need to do more in terms of esports. There hasn't been enough of a strategy or enough appreciation of their importance here in Wales. Through Creative Wales, we have supported a number of joint projects with Esports Wales. A number of these projects have developed digital skills, technical skills, broadcasting skills, and have raised awareness and strengthened pathways to the future. I will meet shortly with Esports Wales, and I look forward to carrying on that discussion. Clearly, as the work goes ahead, I am very content to update the Member, and also all Members of the Senedd, on this work.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am fod yn rhywun sydd yn codi esports, a dwi'n cytuno efo chi—mae angen gwneud mwy o ran e-chwaraeon. Does dim digon o strategaeth wedi bod na digon o werthfawrogiad o'i bwysigrwydd o yma yng Nghymru. Drwy Cymru Greadigol, rydyn ni wedi cefnogi nifer o brosiectau ar y cyd ag E-chwaraeon Cymru. Mae'r prosiectau hyn wedi datblygu sgiliau digidol, technegol a darlledu, wedi codi ymwybyddiaeth o yrfaoedd creadigol a chryfhau llwybrau i gemau sgrin a chyfryngau digidol. Mi fydda i yn cwrdd ag Esports Wales cyn bo hir, a dwi'n edrych ymlaen at fynd â'r sgwrs yna'n bellach. Yn amlwg, wrth i'r gwaith fynd rhagddo, rwy'n hapus iawn i ddiweddaru'r Aelod, a hefyd holl Aelodau'r Senedd, ar y gwaith hwnnw.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text:
Thank you very much for that answer. As you may remember, in November 2024, the then Minister for Culture, Skills and Social Partnership, Jack Sargeant, took part in a landmark event in the Senedd to promote Wales's thriving esports industry and the Government's commitment to providing the safest and most engaging environment for young gamers. At the event, the Minister said that esports

'is a priority sector for the Welsh Government and I’m keen do all I can to support its growth and gain an international reputation for Wales as a centre for this rapidly growing industry.'

Esports Wales have garnered significant success in recent years, with notable achievements, such as winning a gold medal in the Rocket League open competition at the Commonwealth Esports Championships. The team also secured a silver medal in the eFootball women's competition and a bronze in the eFootball open competition. I was very pleased, in the event we had here, to see Peter Fox in action playing esports. Are esports a priority for this Government, and have they a date for another esports event at the Senedd?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text:
I thank the Member. I hope that I have responded to that question in my first response. Yes, I do think that they're important, and I think more needs to be done. And unlike Ministers in the past, I don't just believe in warm words—I believe in taking action and putting a strategy in place. So the fact that you're still asking that question, despite the commitment being made by a previous Labour Minister in 2024, says it all, I'm afraid, in terms of the portfolio I've inherited.

Certainly, we do need to do more. I give you that commitment, and I will discuss further with Esports Wales. I also attended that event, and I took part in some of those esports. No, I wasn't very good at them, but it was very good to see esports in action here in the Senedd.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch i'r Aelod. Dwi'n gobeithio fy mod i wedi ateb rhan o'r cwestiwn yna yn fy ymateb cyntaf, sef ydw, dwi'n credu eu bod nhw'n bwysig a dwi'n credu y dylid gwneud mwy. Yn wahanol i Weinidogion yn y gorffennol, dwi ddim yn credu mewn geiriau cynnes yn unig—dwi'n credu mewn gweithredu a chael strategaeth yn ei lle. Felly, mae'r ffaith eich bod chi'n dal i holi'r cwestiwn hwnnw, er i'r ymrwymiad gael ei wneud gan Weinidog Llafur blaenorol yn 2024, yn dweud y cyfan, mae arnaf ofn, o ran y portffolio dwi wedi ei etifeddu.

Yn sicr, mae angen gwneud mwy. Dwi'n rhoi'r ymrwymiad hynny, ac mi fyddaf yn trafod yn bellach efo Esports Wales. Mi wnes i hefyd mynychu'r digwyddiad hwnnw a chymryd rhan mewn rhai o'r esports. Na, doeddwn i ddim yn dda iawn, ond roedd yn dda iawn gweld esports ar waith yma yn y Senedd.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Welsh Conservative spokesperson, Paul Davies.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Paul Davies.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Minister, last week, a member of Amgueddfa Cymru staff said that the national museum had become increasingly dysfunctional and described a culture of managed decline, individual posturing, and a lack of professional stewardship of the national collection. They also raised the fact that any additional public funding provided, as part of the centenary of the museum, could fail to deliver its objectives unless the issues identified were examined and addressed properly. Minister, what is your response to those concerns? And following on from your earlier responses, what kind of discussions have you had with Amgueddfa Cymru to secure public confidence in the governance and management of our national collections?
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Weinidog, yr wythnos diwethaf, dywedodd aelod o staff Amgueddfa Cymru fod yr amgueddfa genedlaethol wedi dod yn fwyfwy camweithredol yn ystod y blynyddoedd diwethaf. Disgrifiodd ddiwylliant o ddirywiad rheoledig, ystum unigol, a diffyg stiwardiaeth broffesiynol o'r casgliad cenedlaethol. Roedd hefyd wedi codi y gallai unrhyw gyllid cyhoeddus ychwanegol a ddarperir, fel rhan o gynlluniau canmlwyddiant yr amgueddfa, fethu â chyflawni ei amcanion bwriadedig, oni bai bod y materion a nodwyd yn cael eu harchwilio a'u mynd i'r afael â nhw yn iawn. Weinidog, beth yw eich ymateb chi i'r pryderon hyn? Ac yn dilyn ymlaen o'ch atebion cynharach, pa fath o drafodaethau ydych chi wedi eu cael gydag Amgueddfa Cymru i sicrhau hyder y cyhoedd o ran llywodraethu a rheoli ein casgliadau cenedlaethol?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text:
I thank the Member for raising this issue. I am aware of that article that was published on Nation.Cymru. It also included a response from Amgueddfa Cymru. I certainly am very alive to the questions that are being raised. I, like all of you, want to ensure value for money. I want to ensure the safety of our national collections, and I want to ensure a future for our national museums. There are questions in terms of the situation that I have inherited, and I am pursuing those. There are very live issues in terms of ensuring that we understand how National Museum Cardiff has reached this position where so much expenditure is needed.

I want to learn lessons so that we can avoid making the same mistakes going forward. But the commitment I give you is that we are working with Amgueddfa Cymru on developing proposals for the future. And central to everything that we want to do, as I said, is ensuring the future of our national museums and safeguarding our national collections, because they belong to the people of Wales—not the Government, not the museum, but the people of Wales, and Amgueddfa Cymru is answerable to the people of Wales.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r mater hwn. Mi ydw i'n ymwybodol o'r erthygl a gyhoeddwyd ar y wefan Nation.Cymru yr ydych yn cyfeirio ati. Mi oedd o hefyd yn cynnwys ymateb gan Amgueddfa Cymru. Mae yna gwestiynau byw iawn o ran sicrhau ein bod ni'n deall sut mae Amgueddfa Genedlaethol Caerdydd wedi cyrraedd sefyllfa lle mae angen cymaint o wariant hefyd.

Dwi eisiau dysgu gwersi fel ein bod ni'n gallu osgoi'r rheini wrth fynd rhagddo, ond yr ymrwymiad dwi'n ei roi i chi ydy ein bod ni'n gweithio gydag Amgueddfa Cymru ar ddatblygu cynigion i'r dyfodol.
