documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Reform calls for more democratic powers to be put in the hands of local taxpayers. Where Welsh councils propose council tax increases above 4.99 per cent, residents will have the right to approve or reject them through a local referendum. This policy would finally put Welsh taxpayers on an equal footing to their English counterparts. If council leaders want to implement inflation-busting council tax rises year on year, it is only right that they justify it directly to the people who pay—the people who they supposedly work for.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
For too many people across Wales, opening the annual council tax bill is something they absolutely dread. Families are struggling with the cost of living. They're working hard to pay their mortgages whilst grappling with energy bills and weekly shopping, yet they're also being asked to find more and more money every year to pay their council tax. In my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, a standard band D bill in Cardiff has risen from around £1,637 in 2022-23 to over £2,000 this year—an increase of almost 23 per cent. And it's not just my constituency. Let us look at the figures elsewhere. In 2025-26, Wrexham and Flintshire increased council tax by 9.5 per cent, Pembrokeshire by 9.35 per cent and Ceredigion by 9.3 per cent. In Conwy, residents have faced successive increases of 9.67 per cent, 8.95 per cent and a further 6.5 per cent this year. And on Ynys Môn, the council's band D charge has risen more than 31 per cent since 2022. On average, that's over £425 more each year added to their council tax bill. Staggering. Yet, the Plaid Cymru-led council on Ynys Môn reported a budget underspend, totalling over £8 million across the last three financial years, and holds £19 million in general reserves. Surely, it is reasonable to ask whether residents were charged more than was necessary.

It isn't just about the money they haven't spent. It's also about the stupid decisions they've committed to spend on. A few weeks ago, the Isle of Anglesey County Council passed a motion to spend £1.1 million swapping household black bins for smaller ones. Only one councillor voted against that proposal, and I am proud to say that that was a sole Reform Cymru councillor—[Interruption.] There'll be more than one soon. A lonely voice of common sense in a crowded room of nonsense. Let me be clear, of course councils face genuine pressures, from social care to schools, roads and waste collection—these all need funding. We understand that and we want to see them fairly funded, but that does not mean that ever-higher council tax bills should be accepted as the norm. Wales has 22 principal local authorities, so let me ask a straightforward question: do we really need 22 separate back offices when councils could work together to save money? Do we need duplicated payroll systems, separate IT contracts and independent procurement arrangements when sharing services could deliver better value? Could councils combine their purchasing power to secure better prices, reduce duplication and free up money for front-line services, such as social care? This is not an attack on local government employees. They are common-sense questions about the political leadership of Welsh councils.

Greater efficiency is one reason Reform wants to introduce a democratic lock on annual council tax increases above 4.99 per cent. We see this policy working as an active deterrent against wasteful and unnecessary spending. If Welsh councils want to raise tax above this threshold, they must make a convincing case through a local referendum. It is up to local people to decide whether their money is being spent efficiently. Consider a household paying £2,000 a year in council tax. A 4.99 per cent increase would add £100 to its bill and an 8 per cent increase would add £160. During a cost-of-living crisis, every pound matters. In England, councils are generally required to seek approval through a local referendum if they want to increase council tax beyond the relevant threshold. So, why shouldn't Welsh taxpayers have the same democratic safeguard? Our objective isn't to force councils to make indiscriminate cuts or undermine essential services, it is to challenge unnecessary duplication, improve procurement, review administrative overheads and encourage councils to work together, wherever that delivers savings.

We would also expect greater transparency so that residents can see how their money is spent, what savings have been achieved and why any proposed council tax increase above the threshold is necessary. The people of Wales work hard for their money. They deserve responsible spending, effective services and a fair deal from local government. The answer to every budget pressure cannot simply be another inflation-busting increase in council tax. Plaid Cymru talk about a new deal for Wales, but what the people of Wales really need is a fair deal from all layers of Government within Wales. It's time for the Welsh Government to set the bar.

But I know what will happen. Like every other major issue in Wales, Plaid will say it's somebody else's job to fix, someone else's responsibility. 'Council tax is a local matter for councils.' We've heard it before. This is where Reform is different. We will stand up for Wales and fight the corner of local people. We will make sure their voices are heard loud and clear. We will set the standard, and in this case, that means giving taxpayers the final say on high council tax increases. If Members here today want to help people with the cost of living, put your money where your mouth is and back this democratic lock. Their money, their decision.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
I want to address why referendums on council tax increases above 4.99 per cent would be utterly unfeasible. Now, I'm not going to get into a debate about whether we should be lowering council tax or not. I'm going to be looking at the practical aspects of whether a referendum would work or not. So, before I start, let's be honest, Reform UK Wales is what you name yourself, not Reform Cymru. Reform Cymru does not exist.

Anyway, in 13 years, across over 300 English authorities, one referendum has been held: Bedfordshire's police and crime commissioner in 2015. It failed. In England, council taxes can be increased without holding a referendum, and that power has been used regularly. If a mechanism designed to trigger local votes produces no local votes, it is not facilitating local democratic choice.

What a referendum does is two things. The first is a ceiling becomes a floor. A council that might have raised council tax by 2 per cent or 3 per cent in an easier year raises it by the maximum every year because the cap compounds. Forgone revenue cannot be recovered later, so the rational response is to build up the reserves that you have and to take the maximum annually and build a buffer. The second is where that cap bites: services are cut rather than referendums held. Birmingham, Nottingham, Croydon, Thurrock and Woking have all issued section 114 notices in recent years, effective local bankruptcy in a system with referendums and still no referendums. It is clear that even though this mechanism exists in practice in England, it is either barely used or superseded because circumstances are so dire.

So, let me turn to why this would operate differently and worse in Wales. A referendum costs a local authority somewhere between £150,000 and £600,000 to run. That is not a large sum against the total budget, but the total budget is the wrong denominator. Between 80 per cent to 85 per cent of a council's spending is committed to statutory duties, teacher salaries, statutory social care, waste collection, additional learning needs. We all know that these need to be accounted and budgeted for. A referendum cannot be taken from those. It comes from discretionary services or from unallocated reserves.

For Cardiff, I'll admit that is absorbable within central contingencies, but for Merthyr Tydfil, a £300,000 cost represents a materially different proportion of unallocated general reserves. In some Welsh authorities, that is between 5 per cent and 7 per cent of the entire safety net in a single hit. In service terms, that is a library, youth provision or a year of community transport. The motion sends it to Merthyr, it doesn't send it to Cardiff.

Then there is the tax-based vulnerability, which this motion appears not to have considered at all. In wealthy English shire counties, a 4.99 per cent rise generates substantial revenue, because a high proportion of properties sit in bands E to I. In Welsh Valleys and much of rural Wales, over 70 per cent of properties sit in bands A to C. The same percentage rise yields a fraction of the revenue. This means a lower income authority must raise it by a higher percentage simply to generate the same money. It is therefore pushed towards a referendum threshold, precisely because the tax base is so weak, and we know that of Wales. So, the authorities most likely to be forced into a referendum are the ones least able to afford to be. It's not Cardiff, it's not the wealthy English shires, it's Blaenau Gwent and Merthyr Tydfil, and they would spend a significant fraction of the additional yield on the ballot itself. And then there is the risk of losing it, which is not a small risk, and that would mean that libraries would shut, youth provisions would go and community transport would be axed. Stand-alone referendums outside of a general election cycle typically see turnout of between 15 per cent to 25 per cent. A referendum on a single percentage figure for council tax would certainly fall below that: you're looking at 5 per cent to 10 per cent. There is no candidate, no campaign, no competing vision, simply a number put to the public on a Thursday in February. And the motivational asymmetry is severe: a resident angry about a tax rise will turn out to vote 'no'; a resident who accepts that social care and libraries need funding rarely feels strong enough to turn out for 'yes'. The result is not a referendum on the budget; it is a referendum amongst the people most opposed to it.

There is a serious debate to be had about council tax and the funding settlement and about the burden on households. This is not this debate. In England, this policy produced one referendum in 13 years, a queue of bankrupt councils—Reform have looked at that and decided Wales should have some more.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
I'm pleased to support the motion tabled by my colleague Llŷr Powell, but I want to approach it from a slightly different angle, because I've been a town councillor myself, and know something about setting budgets and council tax precepts.

I know it's not always easy; the constituency I represent covers parts of four council areas—Gwynedd, Wrexham, Powys and Denbighshire—and each faces its own challenges. But there's one thing they all have in common: every year, people receive their council tax bill and almost without fail it's gone up again. For someone on a good income, another £100 or £150 might not seem particularly significant, but, for a pensioner or someone living on a fixed income, that's money they've got to find from somewhere, and the trouble is that these increases don't happen in isolation; they build up year after year. A 5 per cent increase this year is added to all the increases that have gone before it, and next year's increase is calculated on top of that. That's why I think we need to look at what people are paying today compared with five or 10 years ago, rather than just looking at the latest percentage, because household incomes certainly haven't kept pace.

Now, having been a town councillor, there's something else I think that's worth explaining. When your council tax bill arrives, you might reasonably assume all that money is going to your county council, but it isn't. Part of it goes towards policing, and, depending on where you live, there's also a contribution to your town or community council. Fire and rescue services are funded through council budgets too. In fact, the police element alone accounts for roughly £1 in every £6 on the average council tax bill in Wales, and that's not an amount your county council decides. I mention this because I think people deserve to know exactly who is responsible for the different parts of their bill, and, if we're going to introduce a referendum threshold, we need to be clear about which increase it applies to.

Now, I don't want anyone to think I'm suggesting councils have an easy job; they don't. Social care costs are rising, schools are under pressure, and councils are being asked to deliver services with increasingly stretched budgets. But that brings me to something else that matters. Is the way we fund local government in Wales actually fit for purpose? Because delivering services in large rural counties like Powys, Gwynedd and Denbighshire is very different from delivering them in a city. You've got smaller communities spread over much greater distances. School transport costs more, providing services costs more, and, in many cases, there simply aren't the economies of scale that larger urban areas can achieve. So, we need a funding system that recognises those differences, not a one-size-fits-all approach that assumes every council faces the same circumstances.

The Welsh Government has a responsibility to get that right, because, if we're going to hold councils accountable for the money they ask residents to pay, we must also hold the Welsh Government accountable for the funding decisions that affect them. None of this changes the position of the person who has to pay the bill—they don't get to choose whether their income goes up enough to cover another council tax increase, they just have to find the money, and that's why I support giving them a greater say when particularly large increases are proposed. It doesn't mean councils can never put council tax up by more than 4.99 per cent; it means that, if they believe they need to, they should be prepared to explain why and put that decision to the people who are going to pay for it. I don't think that is unreasonable, because, ultimately, this isn't about figures on a spreadsheet or arguments between politicians, it's about what people have left in their pockets at the end of the month, and I think those people deserve a say. So, I'll be supporting this motion and urge other Members to do the same. Diolch, Lywydd.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
I've never heard people speak in a debate with so much ignorance. I will just respond to one thing. There's the Welsh purchasing consortium, where local authorities get together to buy things cheaply between themselves.

Local government provides many of the key services provided by the public sector in Wales—not just refuse collection, but hundreds of services, from road maintenance to trading standards. No local authority makes increases in council tax because they want to punish their electorate—that would be perverse and self-defeating. Council tax rises are driven by the need to meet demand, meet their statutory obligations and council tax payers' wishes. We must consider that budgetary pressures on local authorities are not a simplistic mathematical exercise. Why 4.99 per cent? I know it makes a good headline. Can Reform publish the calculations behind it? Which services would they consider scrapping? Are they seeking statutory services to be made non-statutory in order for councils to legally stop services? In Reform-led Kent, the budget financial risk register reveals an immediate exposure of £411 million—that's it, £411 million—indicating the scale of uncertainty facing Kent's finances. Risks include potential overspends, underfunded services, the pressure of increasing demand in social care, and infrastructure upkeep. This level of risk raises a question about the council's ability to manage its reserves and avoid more drastic cuts in coming years, gambling with services for the vulnerable and the council's finances.

The previous Senedd's Finance Committee received evidence from witnesses about the differential rates at which inflation affects and has an impact on their budgets. Local government in Wales has many financial pressures outside of its control. Education is a major area of expenditure and teachers' pay and pension increases need to be met in full. Education is the key to moving children out of poverty.

I want to discuss three major financial pressures on local government in detail. The estimated pressure for local government services for this year was £599 million. Social services alone account for almost half of that, equating to over £200 million all told. The provision of social care is critical to the health and care system operating effectively, and plays a key role in achieving positive health outcomes. Investing in social care leads directly to reducing pressure on the NHS, both in terms of keeping people out of hospital and helping people to return home at the appropriate time, reducing delayed transfers of care.

Wales has an ageing population and people are living for longer with complex care needs and dementia. This will continue to increase pressure on care services. The Welsh Local Government Association stress that social services face acute and widening financial challenges, with more than 81,000 people relying on care and support. Care Forum Wales says the sector is under immense strain, grappling with persistent workforce pressures, unsustainable fee rates and increasing employer costs. A committee was shown that fees for nursing care can vary by as much as £9,000 a year between neighbouring authorities. For those who fully fund their own care, so-called 'self-funders', average weekly costs are around £1,156 for residential care and £1,394 for nursing care. The older people's commissioner highlights how funding pressures fall unfairly on service users, with inequitable fee structures and top-up fees leaving many self-funders effectively subsidising publicly funded care home placements.

Workforce pressures: staffing pressures remain a major concern, with chronic vacancies and ongoing recruitment and retention difficulties, despite the introduction of the real living wage for social care workers. More than a quarter of domiciliary care workers are on zero-hours contracts. Social Care Wales's workforce survey in 2025 found that one in five social care employees aim to leave the sector within the next 14 months, citing low pay, poor conditions and limited progression.

The Welsh Government does not currently publish data on waiting times for social care services, but stakeholders report long and growing delays, including waits for assessment for care packages, equipment and occupational therapy. Age Cymru research found that nearly one in four older people were waiting more than 30 days for a care assessment and one in six were waiting more than 30 days for care to be put in place after the assessment.

Another major area of pressure is additional learning needs. We've talked about it a lot here, and everybody was saying how we need more money for additional learning needs. Where do you think it's going to come from? Schools across Wales are at breaking point. A significant number of school budgets are currently in deficit, and, for many, that crisis is driven almost directly—[Interruption.]—by severely underfunded provision. Schools that had substantial surpluses have seen that money used for ALN provision. [Interruption.] If you want to intervene, please do, and I'll try and educate you. The school system failed. [Interruption.]

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.member: Aelod o'r Senedd / Member of the Senedd
documents.text: Excuse me. Have you got Mark Drakeford sitting there or something?

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Do you think that the taxpayer, local tax payers, should pay for everything, Mike? How high do you think the council tax should go up every year, because, under Labour, it's going up and up and up?

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: I can understand—. I understand your position: you want to privatise everything. You want the parents to pay for everything. You want them to pay for everything and you don't want the taxpayer to pay for it. [Interruption.]

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Please, Mike, conclude, if you can.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Well, we'll find out next May how few of you will survive in local government, and we'll find out in three years' time how few of you are here. Can I suggest you start looking at council by-elections and, if you go back, how long it is since you last won one?

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Janet—[Interruption.] Please. We're trying to listen to the contributions from the floor. Janet Finch-Saunders.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Cor blimey, I'm on my hobby horse now, I'm afraid. Now, this may shock some, but I have to begin by congratulating Reform. [Interruption.] Not because you've come up with a brilliant idea of a new policy, but because once again you've demonstrated an impressive talent for taking good Conservative ideas and applying the Reform logo to them. Now, as they say, imitation is the sincerest form of flattery. But let's just remind people in this Chamber who weren't here years ago—. I'll just remind you that you did that, of course, with your pre-election manifesto launch, which was a direct copy-and-paste job of good Conservative policies.

Now then, it was a Welsh Conservative manifesto pledge to fix council tax, and has always been a solid manifesto pledge not only to fix council tax, but to reduce council tax. Indeed, it was the Conservatives who have long noted the importance of low council tax, and, in 2011, I was proud to have been elected here when the Right Honourable David Cameron, Conservative Prime Minister, actually provided a three years' council tax freeze—£50 million—to the Welsh Government, Labour propped up by Plaid Cymru. But guess what, folks? They did not pass those moneys on to secure reductions in council tax, instead spending it on their own pet projects.

We as a party, we fight to keep all taxes low. It is the solid foundation of the Conservative Party to allow those who work hard, and our cash-strapped pensioners, to have more money in their pockets, not just at the end of the week or the end of the month, but day in, day out. Now, we have long advocated—. And I can name the Secretaries, Cabinet Secretaries, Ministers that have been in post here—there isn't one that we haven't raised with, on these benches, the idea of a 5 per cent cap on council tax increases. If you look at our own local authority in Conwy, over the past three years nigh on 10 per cent—9.8 per cent; 9.6 per cent—and people are getting less. We've got more weeds than ever before, toilets closing down, we've got litter on our streets, and people genuinely wonder what on earth they pay their council tax for.

Now, this system already exists in England, where referendums are required for what Government determines to be excessive council tax increases. The principle has been established for more than a decade and it does provide an important democratic safeguard. What is perhaps most remarkable is hearing this proposal from Reform, a party whose own councils in England have discovered that campaigning against tax rises is rather easier than governing in those councils. So, you say one thing before an election—. And this is pre-local government election talk and spin. [Interruption.] No, we mean it, every day. It's not a come-day, go-day. We believe that there should be a referendum on council tax. And, of course, we've made these same arguments for years; long before you were ever a twinkle in Nigel Farage's eye. [Laughter.]

Across Wales, residents are facing average council tax rises—average—of 7.2 per cent. But, as I've mentioned, there are others who have the audacity to try getting 10 per cent. Now, after 26—actually, it's 27 now—years of a Welsh Labour Government, propped up by Plaid Cymru, the council tax system in Wales is broken. [Interruption.] Yes. From you, Sarah, any day; yes.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Do you accept that there have been instances where councils have been allowed to increase the council tax without a referendum and, actually, some of the worst examples are in Reform-led councils, including Worcestershire, at 9 per cent?

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
Sarah, you are right to point out that Reform say one thing and do another. Now—[Interruption.] The figures, I won't repeat them again, but—. A £600-plus increase in the average band D council tax bill in Wales over the past five years. The annual band D council tax bill in Conwy County Borough Council being £2,472 and in Kensington and Chelsea, £1,643. How can that be right?

After more than two decades of Labour-led Government, with Plaid Cymru support, residents are paying more, but are not necessarily seeing improvements in services they deliver. I would ask, Cabinet Secretary, please have a look at ensuring that referendums are brought into Wales for council tax increases of 5 per cent or more. I think that way it would be very fair for our residents, our hard-working families, and, indeed, our cash-strapped pensioners. Diolch.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Before I start—. Mike, I've got to take the bait. You talk of ignorance; we are standing up for taxpayers. Ignorance is your party sitting on its hands for 27 years and doing nothing but cripple our local government. So, let's start—[Interruption.] Yes, of course.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Do you want to go around telling elderly people they can't have home care support because you want to save money?

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
Twenty-seven years of failure. We're putting taxpayers first, Mike, that's what we're doing. And this is an incredibly effective tool. We've already seen it work in England. [Interruption.] Not a single local authority dares go to the electorate this year in England because they recognise that people are under enough financial pressure. Unsurprisingly, these rules have already made careful financial management in local authorities the preferred option, compared to simply asking residents to pay evermore taxes. Inflation-busting tax rises are no longer the default option in England. Currently, these protections offered to English taxpayers are not afforded to Welsh taxpayers.

Our residents in Wales are paying more than average. Over the last decade, residents in Denbighshire have seen their council tax rise by 61.9 per cent; in Flintshire, 75 per cent; Wrexham, 76 per cent; and in Conwy, 84 per cent, in a decade. The inflation rate over the same period was 34 per cent. Despite those excessive increases, this financial year, all of those local authorities increased council tax by above inflation again. And this pattern is set to continue because our local authorities are fighting with their hands tied behind their backs.

As my colleague Cai Parry-Jones has highlighted, we need council mergers. Welsh Labour was wrong to reject the offer made by Conwy and Denbighshire to merge; stopping a proposal that could have seen savings of over £1 million on middle and front-line services, over £2 million on back-office functions and the creation of a single management team that could have saved thousands.

Then we come to the funding formula. We are told that data is fundamental in driving budget allocations through the revenue support grant. But, again, local authorities are being failed in Wales. The formula uses data, Members, that is older than me. It comes from the 1991 census. Unsurprisingly, the WLGA have explained that calls from local authorities have grown for a thorough independent external review to be undertaken. I agree, and we need to see the Government get on and do this, and bring forward the proposals for the formula change urgently.

But why make this change now? There needs to be a wake-up call in this Chamber, Members, about the level of debt that local authorities are carrying. Conwy council has around £230 million of debt; Flintshire, £360 million; and Wrexham over £0.5 billion in debt. This situation is only going to get worse. From my time as a county councillor, I know that when these loans are taken, they are assumed—[Interruption.] I'll take a second intervention.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Can you explain to me, then, given those levels of debt, what does a cap do to reduce those levels of debt that you complain about?

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Thank you, Alun. If you let me get through, I'll explain why we need the cap now, before the burden of debt cripples taxpayers.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: Which is already there.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: What about public services? How do you pay for them?

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
The situation is getting worse. Councils borrow the debt on repayment terms expected to be 10, 15 or 20 years or more, but the repayment periods are only, often, five years. So, this means that when the loans mature, new deals need to be made and, with current interest rates, they're often much higher than originally forecast, meaning financing often falls to local authorities to find the extra money to continue to finance these debts. These debts are a ticking financial time bomb. 

The solution is not more excessive council tax rises, which is the option that many local authorities will turn to, not more reliance on borrowing, not the decline in offers for mergers. It is not continuing a funding formula system based on data that is older than me. The solution is fundamental reform of local government in Wales. That must start with greater protection for our taxpayers. Council tax referenda will do just that. They will raise awareness of the serious state of our local government finance, they will challenge the cabinet and officers to work in a more effective way, and give voters the final say on the financial direction of their local area. Members, I urge you to support this motion.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
I think we all know that communities are really struggling in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis, and, of course, nobody wants to pay more council tax, especially in these circumstances, and the pressures that are on people at the moment are very real. We recognise that, and that's why this Plaid Cymru Government has prioritised supporting our communities by extending free school meals, expanding free childcare and cutting business rates by 30 per cent for thousands of businesses across the country.

But we also have to recognise, as others have said, that county councils deliver essential services that people rely on every single day, from social care and children's services to schools, highways and waste collections, and those services cost money to run. I was a county councillor in Wrexham for almost 20 years, so I've seen first-hand how difficult budget decisions can be, and I know many of us here understand that reality.

I can assure Reform that no county councillor wants to increase council tax, but councils have statutory responsibilities. They have to protect vulnerable children, care for older people, and maintain essential services. And let's remember that councils have had to deal with the consequences of austerity for the last 16 years, as well as rising demand and also increasing costs. And why 4.99 per cent? What happens if the cost of delivering statutory services rises by more than that? What happens if a referendum rejects the increase needed to maintain those services? Which services would Reform cut? Would it be social care, children's services, support for people with disabilities? Because those are the difficult questions Reform have to answer.

And let's look at Reform's own record across the border as well. Every major council controlled by Reform in England with responsibility for services like education and social care increased council tax this year. When Reform ran Worcestershire County Council, you increased council tax by almost 9 per cent. There wasn't a referendum. So, why is it acceptable for Reform councillors in England to raise council tax by 9 per cent without a referendum, while you're demanding that councils here in Wales face a referendum for anything above 4.99 per cent?

There's a wider point about local democracy here as well. We already elect councillors to make these decisions on behalf of our communities. And in just a few months' time, people right across Wales are going to have the opportunity to hold those councillors to account at the ballot box. Now, of course councils should be challenged, they should be transparent about their budgets, they should explain why increases are necessary, and they should consult meaningfully with residents about their priorities. But we should also recognise that every council faces different pressures, different levels of need, and different financial circumstances.

So, it might sound simple to draw a line at 4.99 per cent, but running a council isn't that simple, as Reform's own councillors in England have found out. Despite promising to root out waste, the reality is there isn't some vast army of diversity officers whose salaries can fund our schools and social care. And when you're responsible for delivering services and protecting the most vulnerable, you can't just ignore the financial realities. And I think the people of Wales deserve to know what Reform's proposals would mean in practice, which services—.

I took your intervention. 

Councillors have to make difficult decisions, but that's how local democracy works. That's what accountability means. Political leadership isn't just about the promises you make. It's about being responsible for the consequences of your decisions. And the consequences of what Reform are proposing here today could be very, very serious for our councils delivering essential services, and, importantly, for the communities who rely on them.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
Well, we all get that brown envelope, don't we, through the post, or sometimes it's an email nowadays? Council tax is not voluntary, is it? It arrives every year and households have got to find the money to pay for it. When a council wants to raise the bill by more than 4.99 per cent, Reform UK believes that the people paying for it should have the final say. This motion does not ban a higher increase, it simply says: make the case, publish the consequences and ask permission.

The Welsh average band D council tax rose by 7.7 per cent in 2024-25, and by a further 7.2 per cent in 2025-26. Over the last five years, council tax rises across Wales have accelerated significantly, with the Welsh average increasing 7.2 per cent in 2025-26. And nowhere is that seen more than in north-east Wales where I live. In Flintshire, the council tax increase for 2025-26 was 9.5 per cent, and in Wrexham, residents faced an increase of approximately 8.9 per cent. These rises came on top of substantial increases in previous years. Where does it stop? Yet both councils continue to face severe financial challenges in themselves.

From a Flintshire and Wrexham perspective, the situation has become increasingly difficult to manage. Both authorities are forecasting budget deficits in excess of £25 million, as pointed out by Cai. Adult social care, there are issues, demand for services, additional learning needs provision, homelessness services and expensive out-of-county placements continue to grow faster than the funding available to support them.

Councils have had to make difficult decisions for well over a decade now—I'm aware of that. Flintshire and Wrexham have delivered millions of pounds of expenditure reductions since about 2010, but there comes a point where efficiencies are exhausted and residents are simply asked to pay more to cover a growing funding gap.

Before Flintshire approved its recent budget, residents were consulted. Many expressed concern about the rising council tax increases to bridge budget shortfalls during the continuing cost-of-living crisis. Despite these concerns, local people had no binding vote on the outcome—no binding vote, and that's important. When you speak to residents across Flintshire and Wrexham, you hear a common message: council tax keeps rising, but many people believe services are being reduced.

I've seen it myself. Your bins—they don't get emptied every week now. There are all sorts of places where we're seeing things cut. Potholes in the road, local road infrastructure—there are loads of issues. Whether every criticism is justified or not, the perception is clear: people are paying more and feeling they are receiving less in return. That's why local democracy comes into its own. Of course, supporters of the status quo argue that local elections are sufficiently accountable. I disagree with that. A local election provides a general mandate. A referendum provides a specific mandate for an exceptional tax increase.

And, of course, we must be honest about council finances. Reserves are not a magic pot of money that can simply solve every problem. Some reserves are earmarked, yes. Some are legally committed. And some can only be used for specific purposes. Flintshire, for example, reports significant levels of usable reserves, but much of that money is allocated for identified risks and future commitments. However, transparency is absolutely essential. If councils—

Reserves are not a magic pot of money that can simply solve every problem. Some reserves—[Interruption.] No. Some reserves are earmarked, some are legally committed and some can only be used for specific purposes. [Interruption.] I did.

There's one thing I would like to mention, by the way, and it just came to me when Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was speaking, and I just wanted to finish on that, actually. On 2 October 2014, under the provisions of the Local Government Act 1972, a referendum was held in the town of Flint on the question to reinstate in-patient beds. The referendum drew 3,500 residents to vote, with 99 per cent saying 'yes'. So, referendums do work in towns, completely.

I've missed some of the speech out, because I realise I'm actually going on now. This is local democracy in action, and I urge Members to support the motion. Thanks very much.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
Llywydd, I welcome this opportunity to contribute to this debate on the proposal for a regime of council tax referenda similar to those seen in England. Plaid Cymru does not believe that the Welsh Government should impose arbitrary and fixed national targets on council tax rises, which disregard local circumstances and volatile and diverse economic contexts. Annual decisions about local taxes should be made by locally elected councillors who are accountable to the communities that they serve.

Of course, local decisions need to consider the cost-of-living pressures facing households, just as our national decisions will prioritise actions to reduce the financial pressures facing families. But council tax helps to fund schools, social care services, housing services, policing and all of the local services that our communities rely on every day.

There are many comparisons that have been made during this debate, many of them with England, but there is one comparison that hasn't been made. Despite the referendum policy in England, average band D council tax in Welsh councils is £109 less than in England. So, taxpayers in Wales pay less council tax than council tax payers in England, and they continue to do so even though they have that policy in place in England.

Local referenda under this motion would come with significant costs and bureaucracy needlessly, at a time when resources are better directed at protecting front-line services. Only one local referendum has ever been called under this policy in England, in Bedfordshire, with the police and crime commissioner, and it was estimated that that referendum cost around £600,000 to taxpayers.

Nid yw Llywodraeth Cymru yn credu y dylid gosod targedau cenedlaethol penodedig a mympwyol ar godiadau yn y dreth gyngor, sy'n anwybyddu amgylchiadau lleol a chyd-destunau economaidd amrywiol. documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
Of course, over the past few years, several local authorities in England have been granted permission by Whitehall to exceed referendum limits, that limit of 5 per cent. There are several references already made to this. For example, one of the exceptions granted was in February of this year for Reform-led Worcestershire County Council, and they received permission to increase council tax by 9 per cent, which is higher than any increase seen across Wales this year. The average increase in Wales this year at council level was 4.8 per cent, which is the lowest average increase since 2022. The increase chosen by councils was as low as 3.6 per cent in some cases, demonstrating accountability for their own choices on that local level.

Working with the previous Government in passing the final budget for this year, Plaid Cymru helped to secure a stronger budget settlement for local government, delivering an increase of £282 million in the final settlement, ensuring that every council receives an increase of more than 4 per cent, by supporting the funding floor. This additional investment helped to ease immediate pressures on councils and contributed to lower council tax increases the length and breadth of Wales.

Llywydd, as I have mentioned several times in this Siambr, the Welsh Government faces an incredibly difficult budgetary position in the next financial year, with a real-terms decrease in both our resource and capital budgets. And local authorities, too, face increasing spending pressures across the services that they are responsible for. That's why our draft budget next month will prioritise front-line public services, and I hope that we can work across parties in this Senedd to deliver an adequate settlement for local government.

Because it's not an arbitrary cap that we need, dictated to local authorities by a finance Minister sitting in Cathays Park. That's not what will protect local taxpayers and the services that they rely upon. It's sufficient funding for public services that we need, for the Welsh Government settlement from the UK Treasury in the first instance, and then in that settlement to local authorities passed on by this Senedd. Both settlements will be the greatest influence on the level of council tax levied next year by our county councils.

Llywydd, this debate also highlights a wider principle. We believe, as a Government, in autonomy and accountability, be it for local authorities or for us as a Senedd and for us as a Welsh Government. That's why Plaid Cymru has long argued that Wales needs greater fiscal powers, including in relation to taxation. With stronger budget settlements and flexible revenue-raising powers, we would be better placed to shape our budgets, strengthen public services and provide more sustainable funding for local government over the longer term.

Just as we oppose the arbitrary fiscal limits imposed on us by Westminster, we also oppose placing arbitrary restrictions on local authorities when they set their own budgets and their own council tax levels. Members should reject this motion to preserve the democratic accountability of local authorities and work with us to deliver the high-quality services that people across Wales deserve.

Anyone who believes in devolution of power from the centre to the local level is going to oppose tying the hands of those who decide on that local level, those who are elected democratically on that local level. I urge the UK Chancellor once again to use this upcoming autumn budget to protect public services from higher inflation, enabling us to provide the additional funding that local services need. It will then be the responsibility of all of us in this Chamber to work together constructively to agree a settlement that gives local government the resources and certainty it needs to continue delivering the vital services that it is responsible for.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text: I call on Francesca O'Brien to reply to the debate.

documents.item: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I thank everyone who has participated this afternoon for all the contributions, and for the humorous interjections, shall I say. It certainly kept us entertained this afternoon. Our motion rests on a simple principle: if a council wants to raise council tax by more than 4.99 per cent, it should ask the people who pay for it. England has had that rule for years, Wales currently has no limits.

If I can turn to Cai, who is sitting behind me, who opened the debate and highlighted the council tax bill that every year each and every one of us and those that we represent in our constituencies absolutely dread, because, like I say, there is no limit. We do not know what's going to hit that doorstep. He also highlighted that in his own constituency, they have seen rises of over 23 per cent, which is absolutely scandalous. We talk about the cost of living. How are families going to be affording that increase?

He has also highlighted some of the misspending, shall I say—£1.1 million on changing the size of black bins. If that's a government's priority, I seriously question it. Janet, I'm glad you highlighted that it was the one Reform councillor. Thank goodness for that one Reform councillor who objected to that stupid notion.

We also had Andrew, who shared his experience of being on a town council and highlighted the vital services that the fire service does in our communities. I'm sure the Cabinet Minister would agree that the fire service have had their hands full this year with the wildfires and they do a sterling job. I met with them recently and they are under huge financial pressures. I know in our own constituency in Gower and Swansea, they're actually taking on more financial burden from the Welsh ambulance service with the co-responder unit in Reynoldston. So, again, they've taken on more pressures, more statutory duties without the resources. I think it's important to mention the fire service and also the police service, which also contribute to the council tax bill. I don't think many of the public realise that is included.

Tom, I know you were another councillor as well in north Wales. The borrowing amounts are eye-watering that councils are having to do. Again, it goes back to those statutory duties. We are putting those councils' backs against the wall. I know, speaking of when I was a Swansea councillor, we were lucky we had a fantastic responsible finance officer who borrowed at the right time. But I am equally aware that not all councils, not all 22, borrowed at the same rates that we did in Swansea.

Nigel, I think you hit the nail on the head about transparency for the public. Referendums do work. I think we need to be held accountable. If we are elected to serve our public, we are civil servants. We are there to serve. We should be held accountable and have the transparency at every opportunity—[Interruption.] Well, we are. We're there to serve the public, so whether you like it or not, we're not here to pat each other on the back and be in an echo chamber. We're there serving the people.

To the speakers across the floor, Sarah, I ask the Member, you stood on the Reform manifesto back in May. Did you mislead the public then, or are you misleading them now on your new stance on council tax reform? And what a referendum actually does do—I know you argued against it and you don't think it works. Again, going back to Nigel's point, they can work, actually. I'm a believer in democracy. It's giving the people a democratic right; our country is based on a democratic right. Also, with councils, if they've got a limited amount of budget, they need to sharpen that pencil and make priorities work as well. So, it gives people that power.

Mike, I always love your interventions. I know we represent the same constituency, but I am glad you mentioned procurement, because when I was last on Swansea Council, procurement was a little bit odd, because we actually imported, in one constituency, in Merthyr, 99 per cent of our chicken from China and Thailand. That's a great example of how procurement doesn't work, so I disagree with you on procurement there.

Carrie, I know you also mentioned—. I need to go over my notes. Mike and Carrie both mentioned Reform councils. Actually, they do work. I know you don't like to admit it, but in County Durham, Reform's first budget raised council tax by less than 2 per cent, with no rise at all in core charges. So, across the nine councils where Reform hold a majority, the average increase was under 4 per cent, against nearly 5 per cent in parts of Wales and parts of England. Our councils also face the same pressures of social services. But we in Reform have the willingness to go through the budget line line by line.

Janet, you were doing so well. And yes, I'm so glad you recognise we are a twinkle in Nigel's eye. Absolutely. [Laughter.] It's shining bright from over there. It is, absolutely. But you highlighted some really good points, Janet—the fact that there's a lot of money coming into Wales, but with statutory duties, that money is not always going down to local councils, and that is a worry that many of the councils are facing for next year. In my shadow Minister post, I've met with a lot of councils over the course since May, and they're all worried about the budget. You've got the growing cost of social services, which is spiralling out of control, the additional learning needs—they are all worried how they're going to make it work. So, that is something I'm a little bit worried about, because that's been the topic of debate the last couple of days of the supplementary budget—not enough is going to ALN—but that's a different debate for another day. But let me go on to—[Interruption.] Well, it's £60 million out of, what, £233 million that was coming from Westminster? So, yes, and I'm sure the headteachers are pleased with that.

I will end the debate. We need to bring back trust in local government, Llywydd, and councils should be able to communicate with the public and justify the reasons for the increases in council tax. That should be the social contract between the public and politicians. Our motion says if a council wants to raise more, they should make the case and win the local vote. Plaid Cymru told voters its budget deal would prevent unaffordable rises. If they really believe that, then surely they've got nothing to fear from letting residents decide. Put your money where your mouth is. People across Wales are not asking for miracles. They want their council taxes spent with care, and before it goes up sharply next year, we should be asking: do we need a referendum? This motion gives them that right, and I urge Members across the floor to support it. Diolch, Lywydd.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: We'll move now to item 8, the short debate. I call on David Mills to speak to the topic that he has chosen.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn nawr at eitem 8, y ddadl fer. Galwaf ar David Mills i siarad am y pwnc a ddewiswyd ganddo.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: Shall I start?

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: Yes.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
Thank you, Presiding Officer. I'm pleased to have the opportunity to open the debate today. I will be giving a minute of my time to John Clark, Paul Rock, Anna Nicholl and James Evans. I want to begin by outlining why I am personally invested in this issue. I have been a lifelong environmentalist. I run a farm where I've dedicated a significant amount of my land to habitat restoration and tree planting. Prior to farming, I have a background in conservation and countryside management. I have also run an organic, environmentally conscious farm in France, where I saw first-hand the value of good land management, protecting biodiversity and working with nature rather than against it.

The ease of operating in France has helped me identify where we have gone wrong in Wales. For me, environmental stewardship has never been an abstract political concept; it is something I live and practice every day. It's about the condition of the land you pass on to the next generation, it is about the wildlife that inhabits your fields and hedgerows and it's about the health of our rivers, the quality of our soil, the responsibility we all have to leave our countryside in a better condition than we found it. And it was precisely because of that commitment that I became increasingly frustrated with the bureaucracy I encountered in Wales. Too often, I found a system more interested in penalising conservationists for breaching some trivial rule buried deep in a dense guidance document, rather than encouraging landowners to do the right thing for the environment. The spirit of the guidance should be more important than a strict, legalistic interpretation where conservationists can be fined for petty reasons. People who want to restore habitats, plant trees and improve biodiversity should be treated as partners, not potential rule breakers. That experience helped spur me to stand for elected office, and that brings me to the purpose of today's debate.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
Environmental stewardship should not belong to one political party, one ideology, or one side of the Chamber. It should be a common cause. For small c conservatives, environmental conservation is central to our political philosophy. Yes, too often the tradition is overlooked because the debate about the environment has become almost entirely dominated by carbon reduction, which, whilst important, should not dominate Government action over other concerns. Many to the right, myself included, object to the direction of current environmental policy, but we should not allow that disagreement to be mistaken for indifference towards the environment itself. I believe climate change is a serious, potentially existential challenge that must be addressed, and we cannot simply ignore the evidence to pretend that a changing climate presents no risks, but we must distinguish between the challenge we face and the policies Governments choose to pursue in response to it.

I have profound concerns about the approach to net zero. The UK can impose ever more ambitious targets on itself and introduce costly regulations, but climate change is a global problem driven by global emissions. The effectiveness of our response must therefore be judged in a global context. My concern is that policies pursued in the name of net zero will make little difference to the global climate trajectory if they are not matched by meaningful international action, while not imposing enormous costs on ordinary people here at home, because those costs are not borne equally. We should not ask people on the lowest incomes to shoulder disproportionate costs for policies whose global impact depends on what the rest of the world does, when the UK's impact is so minuscule.

If the United Kingdom reached net zero by next week, would the climate stop changing? Of course it would not. That does not mean we should abandon efforts to reduce emissions, it means we should pursue them sensibly, in concert with other countries, and in a way that is economically sustainable and commands public support.

We should also be honest about the need to adapt to the changes in climate we face. We need resilient infrastructure, effective flood prevention, healthy soils, restored peatlands, and landscapes better equipped to withstand drought, wildfire and extreme rainfall. We must also consider the standardisation of air conditioning in homes and schools, and fund agricultural science that looks at how crops may have to adapt to a changing climate.

Mitigation and adaptation must go hand in hand, but my concern is that the single-minded focus of carbon targets has distracted us from other pressing environmental problems—problems where we could make tangible difference to people's lives and the natural world around us.

As we have been racing towards ever more ambitious carbon targets, our rivers and our seas have been filling with sewage. Natural Resources Wales reported that Dŵr Cymru was responsible for 155 pollution incidents in 2024. That was the highest number of sewage pollution incidents recorded by the company in a decade. We should be just as determined to stop sewage entering our rivers as we are to meet carbon targets.

Another area where we should be able to find common ground is the protection of our habitats and our beautiful landscapes. Species are disappearing, habitats are under pressure and too many landscapes are failing to reach their ecological potential. Tree planting, habitat restoration, healthier soils and protecting native species can all make a real difference, but this must be done in partnership with farmers and landowners, not through top-down diktats. We should reward long-term stewardship rather than simply measuring compliance with administrative requirements. We also need tougher penalties for environmental crime and better policing. While law-abiding citizens face increasingly costly waste disposal, criminals are dumping toxic waste and despoiling our countryside with apparent impunity.

Michael Sheen's recent documentary Buried has highlighted the illegal dumping of forever chemicals and acid sludge across England and Wales. In March, Natural Resources Wales reported that nearly 50,000 fly-tipping incidents had been recorded in Welsh local authorities in the previous year—an increase of almost 15 per cent. That's about 133 incidents every day. We need effective investigations and meaningful penalties. This is not about punishing well-meaning landowners for missing a clause in a regulation; it's about ensuring that those who wantonly destroy our natural environment face prison.

Presiding Officer, this brings me back to the central argument of this debate: environmental policy should not be judged solely on carbon targets, but by whether our rivers are cleaner, our habitats are recovering, our wildlife is thriving and our countryside is protected for future generations. Achieving this means working with farmers, landowners, conservationists, volunteers, communities and businesses. Good environmental policy need not be prohibitively expensive. Often, the best solutions are practical, locally led and rooted in an understanding of the landscapes. We can disagree about net zero and the pace of decarbonisation, but surely we can agree that sewage should not pollute our rivers, that endangered species should be protected, illegal dumping should be punished and those restoring habitats should be encouraged rather than obstructed. These aren't left-wing or right-wing objectives; they're commonsense objectives.

I'm confident the new Minister for climate change and rural resilience shares my desire to put sound land management and the protection of our natural inheritance at the heart of environmental policy, and I look forward to hearing how he intends to deliver that. Our responsibility as custodians is to ensure the next generation inherits a natural environment richer, healthier and better protected than the one we inherited. That's what environmental stewardship means to me. I look forward to hearing the other contributors to the debate. Thank you.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
We're told that even though Britain only emits 1 per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, whilst China and India emit 40 per cent, we should pursue net zero as an example. Ironically, our main emissions cuts have come from exporting steel and other heavy industries to those same countries. But they cannot follow our example; they cannot export their emissions to themselves, and the goods we now import are often produced under weaker environmental rules.

Net zero in its current form is ideologically driven, it is damaging our economy and it will not deliver its aims. We need to look after the environment without crippling our industry or sacrificing our energy security. Nuclear power offers that practical path. It's carbon neutral, highly reliable and statistically the safest form of large-scale energy. Yes, the upfront costs and build times are significant, but the long-term benefits outweigh them. It's time to stop delaying. Let's re-industrialise, invest in nuclear and protect both our economic and environmental future. Thank you.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: My constituents see and smell the wildfires; the rising threat of flooding is constantly at their door. Our farmers are worried about the viability of their businesses and their communities; people are concerned about how they can afford to heat their homes, pay their bills and feed their families. We can ease pressure on household costs by helping people to move to sustainable energy and fossil-fuel-free heating. So, it's very disappointing to see the UK Government's support for heat pumps evaporating before our eyes. Heat pumps lower heating bills, but people need to be supported to make the change. Also, Wales is blessed with extraordinary natural resources. We have the potential to generate all the renewable energy our nation needs, so that we can reduce energy bills, make families less vulnerable to rising fuel costs and cut carbon emissions at the same time. This is about delivering greater energy security, warmer homes and a more sustainable future for our children. So, when we put social justice at the centre of climate action, and we put climate action at the centre of social justice, we don't have to choose between helping people and helping the planet, we must, and we can, do both.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
I'd like to thank David Mills for bringing forward this debate and giving me a slot to speak.

Environmental stewardship should be common ground across this Chamber, not because the challenges are easy, but because they affect every community in Wales. As a member of the climate change committee, I'm acutely aware of the scale of those challenges. Nearly one in five assessed species in Wales is now threatened with extinction, and species abundance has fallen by around 20 per cent in a generation. In Ceredigion Penfro, those pressures are felt in the rivers, peatlands and coastal habitats that define our communities. We're fortunate to be home to the Dyfi UNESCO biosphere, Cardigan Bay and some of Wales's most important marine and terrestrial wildlife habitats. They're not only environmental assets, they're economic assets too.

This debate should not simply be about what we stand to lose; it should be about what we stand to gain. The transition to a low-carbon economy presents major opportunities for Wales—opportunities to create jobs, attract investment, strengthen energy security and support thriving rural economies. The same is true for nature recovery. Whether it is tackling agricultural pollution, restoring peatlands, improving river quality or supporting sustainable food production, there are solutions that can work for nature and for people. We need to move beyond denial, beyond blame and beyond the sense of hopelessness that too often creeps into these discussions. Instead, we need leadership, we need collaboration—and I agree that should extend to international collaboration—and we need the confidence to seize the opportunities that come from responding to the climate and nature emergencies together. Because, if Wales gets this right, environmental stewardship will not just protect what we value, it will help build a more resilient, prosperous and sustainable future for all our communities. Diolch.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: I'll be short, because I know we're running out of time. As probably the third longest serving Member still left in this Chamber this afternoon, we've been through a lot of different changes, from 'Brexit and our land' to 'Sustainable Farming and our Land', and we've always talked about sustainability through that. I asked the Cabinet Minister a question the other day about the optional and collaborative layers, about ring-fenced funding, and he body-swerved the question quite remarkably, actually. But it'd be quite interesting to know from him, through those optional and collaborative layers, how much are you going to ring-fence for things like biodiversity, for increasing wildlife, for making sure that wildfires are addressed, and flooding. So, through your answer, Cabinet Minister, it'd be quite nice to see if you don't body-swerve the question again.

documents.text: Minister, a challenge.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: I call on the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability to reply to the debate—Llyr Gruffydd.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd i ymateb i'r ddadl—Llyr Gruffydd.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: Thank you very much, Llywydd. Could I start by thanking the Member for tabling this debate and giving us the opportunity to discuss this topic once again, and also to the other Members for their contributions this afternoon? We don't always agree in this Chamber, but I do agree with the central proposal behind today's debate, which is, of course, that environmental stewardship is not the responsibility of just one party. It is not the responsibility of one sector or even one generation. It's a shared responsibility, and the potential benefits of that reach every community in Wales, whether that is clean rivers, healthy soils, productive farms, nature recovery, clean energy, stronger local economies. These aren't competing priorities. They are all connected, in my view, and that understanding, of course, is at the heart of this Government's programme for government. It shapes our approach to farming, water, clean energy, rural resilience. It also shapes the way that we create the conditions for sustainable growth, and, of course, we focus on practical delivery—not stewardship as a theory, but stewardship in practice, on the ground.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
We're developing, as Members know, Wales's first climate and nature action plan. It'll bring together actions across government and across society to restore nature, to strengthen climate resilience, to support sustainable development, setting out a pathway towards our ambition in relation to net zero, but also substantive nature recovery as well. And a just transition will be baked into our approach, so that we avoid some of the mistakes that have happened in the past where some communities have been damaged and left behind by much of this.

And I would refer to an example that I've used previously when it comes to this. Retrofitting homes is one policy that's being put forward as a means of reducing carbon emissions. But, of course, it isn't a binary policy, because retrofitting homes provides people with support for the cost-of-living crisis because it will lower bills. More energy-efficient homes will mean lower energy bills. Retrofitting homes means jobs. People will need to be employed to retrofit those homes, bringing further economic benefits. It'll give people warmer homes to live in. And that, in itself, I think is something that we should aspire to. But there are health benefits from that as well, because we will see, as a consequence of people not living in cold and damp homes, fewer children being raised in those homes and consequently suffering from respiratory challenges. We will see fewer winter excess deaths amongst our older population. So, net zero isn't binary. It's an opportunity to bring a number of additional benefits with it.

And environmental stewardship as well can't sit within one portfolio. Decisions on housing, on transport, on food production, on skills, on economic development, public investment, they all matter. Every part of Government has a role here. And that ambition, of course, has to be backed up then by strong governance and accountability. And the Environment (Principles, Governance and Biodiversity Targets) (Wales) Act 2026 creates, doesn't it, the independent Office of Environmental Governance Wales to monitor environmental law, and hold public authorities to account. Statutory biodiversity targets will provide the long-term focus and transparency needed to halt and reverse biodiversity loss. And we'll develop those, by the way, using science and evidence. Taken together, the legislation, the independent oversight and targets give us a strong foundation for long-term nature recovery.

Now, farmers are at the heart of much of this approach, but not just only farmers. There's a wider societal piece that's playing out here as well. But farmers do manage, of course, most of the land in Wales and they play a vital role as stewards of our countryside. Many of the habitats and landscapes we value depend on that active management. They produce our food, they sustain rural businesses and communities, and help shape the landscape that defines Wales very often.

Too often, these debates present a choice, don't they, between food production and nature recovery. Well, the sustainable farming scheme is built on a simple principle: resilient ecosystems and sustainable food production can and should go hand in hand. And this year, as we know, more than 8,000 farm businesses, around half of all eligible farms in Wales, have joined the universal layer of the SFS. Now, that is a strong foundation on which to refine the scheme and develop future optional and collaborative actions. And the reason I didn't directly answer the points raised is because we haven't made those decisions yet. Those discussions are still ongoing, because I want to hear the voices of those around the table in stakeholder groups, and I want to understand what the options are. But when we have made the decision, you will be amongst the first to know.

So, as I've said, this whole process is evolution, isn't it? It's evolution, not revolution. Farmers need certainty because they plan over many years—we know that—and that's why I've committed to over £1 billion over three years, to a multi-year funding cycle for the SFS, giving the sector that long-term certainty it needs to be able to help it to plan and invest with confidence. But support must also be practical. Good stewardship should not come with unnecessary bureaucracy, and, as you know, I have commissioned an independent review of the bureaucratic burden on family farms to identify where there is unnecessary complexity and to recommend practical improvements, because by reducing duplication and simplifying processes, we can then help farmers focus on what really matters most, which is the point I think that you're making: running successful businesses, producing food and caring for the landscapes that they manage.

But individual action, of course, is only part of the answer. Flooding, water quality, wildfires and nature recovery don't stop at field boundaries, and that's why collaboration matters here as well. Through the collaborative layer of the sustainable farming scheme, we are looking to create those opportunities for farmers, land managers and communities to work together across landscapes and across catchments. The integrated natural resources scheme is demonstrating the value of collaboration as well across those larger landscapes and catchments, to improve water quality, to restore habitats, to reduce flood risk, of course, which is important here as well, and to strengthen that climate resilience that we need to build. We're now looking at how we can build on that approach and strengthen the support for that collaborative action in the future.

Ffermio Bro supports co-ordinated action within our designated landscapes, helping farmers and land managers deliver local priorities for nature recovery, for ecosystem resilience and climate action. Its funding has increased from £1.9 million in 2025-26 to £7.5 million from 2026-28. Together, these schemes hopefully will shape future collaborative delivery through the sustainable farming scheme and other means, enabling action at a scale that no individual holding can achieve alone.

We're also looking to restore Wales's natural assets as well. Peatlands are among our most important carbon stores, and wildlife habitats too. The national peatland action programme has restored over 4,000 hectares and has improved the habitat across a further 9,000 hectares here in Wales. That work supports biodiversity, yes, it does store carbon, whether we like it or not, but it also improves water management and it strengthens resilience to drought, flooding and wildfires—again, the multilayered benefits of some of these actions that we're taking. It's practical delivery for climate and nature together.

But restoration can't be limited to individual habitats or protected sites. Nature recovery is needed across productive farmland, yes, but in our towns and communities as well. And, of course, Government can't deliver all of this alone. Through Nature Networks, we've announced more than £10 million for the next funding round. The fund has already supported more than 125 projects, improving protected sites and ecological connections across Wales.
