documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text: You mentioned wildfires and peatland. I know there are other Members in the Chamber who represent Blaenau Gwent, for example. If you look at Llangynidr, for example, it's almost lost all of its peatland. It would just be interesting to hear from the Government exactly what you're going to do in terms of restoration and the partners you're going to work with up there to make sure the peat is restored. Because if you want to hold water back, that is a way of doing it.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
Yes, you're right. I will be coming on to wildfires specifically in a minute, but that has to be a collective effort. You will know that a summit is being held, and I'll say a little bit about that in a minute and then we can maybe develop that a little bit. I've lost my train of thought now, which is always the risk when you take interventions.

Woodland and tree planting—that's it. That also does have an important role to play. Through the national forest programme, of course, we're expanding and connecting woodland across Wales, restoring habitats, improving access to nature as well, and strengthening climate resilience while supporting communities and the Welsh timber sector as well, which is critical in this context also. We're also supporting landowners and communities through various woodland creation and restoration grants, helping deliver the right tree in the right place so that it benefits biodiversity, water quality, carbon storage and landscape resilience.

Community groups, local authorities and volunteers are also restoring nature in our towns and villages, which is an important area that I wish to see more work done with. We want everyone to experience and benefit from nature close to home and that matters, again, for health and well-being, for children and families and for communities that maybe have not always enjoyed equal access to good-quality green space.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
Llywydd, there is increasing urgency to carry out this work, of course, as Wales experiences the effects of a changing climate. This year, we have seen the drought, the heatwaves and the devastating wildfires that were referred to earlier, as many communities continue to face flood risks now as the winter closes in. Climate change isn't a challenge for the future; it is the reality that faces us right now and we must foster resilience where we can before these crises emerge. And that means natural flood management measures, it means peatland restoration, healthier soils and habitats; improved catchment management schemes; and creating communities, of course, that are more ready to face future risks.

The First Minister will convene a climate change and resilience summit for Wales on 22 October. That will bring together partners to learn from recent events and to strengthen preventative processes, which will assist with readiness for events such as these in future, and help with the response when we face these challenges moving forward. I see that event as the trigger for starting to put those pieces together from the point of view of addressing the consequences of what's already happened, but also to make us more ready as we move forward for future events that will happen—I'll say that they will happen rather than 'could happen', because we know what the trajectory is.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
So, we continue to invest heavily in flood risk management with over £85 million made available to risk management authorities in Wales this year, and that's not simply about delivering individual interventions, is it? It's about strengthening collaboration, improving our understanding of what works, sharing lessons to support future natural flood management and resilience activity as well, across Wales. And flood risk cannot be managed by any one organisation acting alone—I would reiterate that point again—and that's why, of course, we're refreshing the membership of our flood and coastal erosion committee, so that it can use its expertise and support Government in advising on policy strategy and long-term resilience. And that means, of course, working closely with risk management authorities, obviously, but Natural Resources Wales, Dŵr Cymru, Hafren Dyfrdwy, landowners, businesses and local communities as well. And community engagement is central to this approach, ensuring that local knowledge and lived experience help shape decision making and that resilience planning for the future.

And the same principle of course applies to water quality. People rightly expect cleaner rivers and healthier water environments, and Government, regulators, water companies, land managers and communities all very much have a role there as well. We're progressing water reform, as Members will know, including proposals for a Welsh economic water regulator, with stronger powers to drive investment, reduce pollution and secure long-term improvements. Stewardship succeeds when responsibility is shared and when action is co-ordinated. And it's not only a rural agenda, by the way; as I said earlier, access to nature supports health and well-being, green spaces strengthen communities, and environmental investment can support jobs and local economies. That's why our programme for government includes action on skills, ensuring that Wales has the workforce to deliver on our ambitions, while supporting, of course, good jobs and growth.

documents.item: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
documents.text:
So, Llywydd, today's debate has shown, I think, that Members may disagree on individual policies, and it's quite fair for that to happen, but that there is also common ground here. We all want healthy rivers. We want nature restoration, productive farms, resilient communities, a Wales that is more prepared for floods, drought and wildfires, and environmental action that supports jobs and prosperity. But the challenge, of course, is turning that common ground into practical action. That calls for more than just individual projects or short-term initiatives. It demands a long-term commitment, clear accountability and policies that work together. It also requires us to acknowledge the knowledge and the experience of farmers and land managers, communities and environmental organisations across Wales. Good stewardship must shape the way that we support the agriculture industry, the way that we manage water, restore nature, develop clean energy and strengthen communities.

But this all, of course, means supporting those who manage our land and our natural resources, listening to those people who know their areas best and working together to ensure long-term resilience. It means acknowledging that stewardship does not fetter prosperity, but that it is a fundamental component of it. Healthy ecosystems support productive farms, resilient supply chains, safer communities and a stronger economy in Wales. That is the journey that's ahead of us: shared stewardship; practical delivery; and a Wales that is more resilient, healthier and prosperous.

Therefore, I hope that Members in all parts of this Chamber will be able to work together to help the Government to achieve this vision. Thanks.

documents.text: 1. What assessment has the Government made of whether current school transport arrangements meet the needs of pupils with additional learning needs in Afan Ogwr Rhondda? OQ64716

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Good afternoon. Whilst it's for the local authorities in Afan Ogwr Rhondda to assess the school transport needs of all pupils, we as a Government are of course keen to see effective provision that meets everyone’s needs. documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister. Rhondda Cynon Taf council has retained discretionary school transport for some of its most vulnerable learners, including those with additional learning needs. documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Parents across Afan Ogwr Rhondda are deeply concerned about their children's school transport arrangements. A hundred and twenty-five people described feeling anxiety, vulnerability, stress or fear as a result. We, as I say, have been discussing with the WLGA those kinds of pressures that we realise are on local government, at the same time as making the case to the UK Government on the issues that they can take decisions to address—on fuel costs, for example. documents.text: First Minister, I'm proud to support a grass-roots campaign in Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg to stop the proposed small modular reactor nuclear project in the Llynfi valley by Last Energy. documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, I want to raise a deeply disturbing case from our capital city. In March this year, 29-year-old Mohammed Abbas arrived in Britain on a small boat from France. By June, he was in custody facing criminal charges. In July, he was convicted of offences including assaulting a police officer and sentenced to 300 hours of community service. He was subsequently placed in Home Office-funded accommodation in Cardiff. Just two days later, at 2 o'clock in the morning, he entered a family home and committed sexual offences in the presence of two young girls, both under the age of 16. He has since pleaded guilty to four further offences and is awaiting sentencing. Those two young girls should have been safe in their own home. First Minister, what discussions have you had with the Home Office about this case? What assurances have you sought about the safeguarding of communities hosting asylum accommodation? And will you now commission an urgent review of the arrangements between Welsh public services and the Home Office to ensure that a case like this is never repeated?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I think I would refer the Member to the safeguarding work that this Government is doing in general, making sure that we are strengthening the provisions that we put in place as a Welsh Government to safeguard the citizens of Wales. What has been described to me—and it's not a case that I am familiar with myself—is criminality. What has been described to me are the actions of an individual that all of us would condemn and that the legal system should be empowered to deal with.

I know that it is always the case that Reform seeks only to comment on those elements of criminality that emerge from people who have come into the UK, but that really doesn't help us when it comes to the core issue here, which is to make sure that we in Wales, in the public sector, in the Welsh Government, have safeguarding measures in place across the board that make sure that we de-risk and that we look after those vulnerable people within our society.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:

First Minister, last week your Deputy Minister for Transport announced yet another 18-month study into congestion on the M4 around Newport, alongside proposals that could see motorway junctions closed. Let's not forget it was the Labour Government who scrapped the relief road, wasting well over £100 million of taxpayers' money in the process. Closing motorway junctions doesn't make the traffic disappear; it simply moves the problem elsewhere, and restricts emergency services trying to carry out their duties. First Minister, Newport needs a long-term solution that improves capacity, not measures that redistribute congestion into residential communities. So, I'll ask you a straightforward question and I expect a straightforward answer: does your Government intend to press ahead with building an M4 relief road around Newport during this Senedd term—yes or no?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I described in the Senedd last week the multiphase approach that we are taking to addressing an issue that previous administrations chose not to. documents.text: Well, it's a 'no', and it's a shame to see that you're determined to continue Mark Drakeford's war on motorists. Nothing changes, does it? The cosy Cardiff consensus continues. Now you're in power, it's Labour who are nodding along as your Government sends millions of pounds abroad while our NHS suffers. When you said you'd deliver change, people expected you to change more than just the seating plan in the Chamber. And I know a few things about seating plans. documents.text: Diolch, Llywydd. First Minister, some here will doubtless work tirelessly to destroy and sabotage devolution, but Welsh Labour firmly believes in making it work for the people of Wales, and we're proud to have fought for and secured an extra £60 million for children with additional learning needs for this financial year. Absolutely, First Minister, and Welsh Labour will never fold. It's now reached around £200 million for the taxpayer—money that is coming from education budgets. Now, it may come as a surprise to the vocal crew on the other side of this Chamber, but their leader at a UK level, when he went to Kent, said that spending on home-to-school transport was ridiculous. Actually, he used more profound terms. He said that the way that he would cut it is to stop providing it, to make parents drive or walk their children to school. Is that the policy of Reform here, First Minister, do you think?

And, First Minister, would you agree to a more sensible approach, a more intelligent approach, one that was started by the Welsh Labour Government, where we composed an expert panel, a cross-party, cross-departmental group, to look at how we can reduce costs for home-to-school transport whilst improving the amount of home-to-school transport that can be provided to young people?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I certainly agree with the comments made that there is an ideological drive to push down public transport by the Reform benches, and they don't seem to care who that impacts. I think we have seen in recent weeks around the ALN funding issue that we are able to reach a positive place through co-operation, and I'm always interested in looking at how we can co-operate across the Senedd in finding ways to spend public money well on ALN needs, on public transport and on learner transport. It is through that co-operation that we will get better results.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Leader of the Welsh Conservatives, Darren Millar.
documents.text_cy: Arweinydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Darren Millar.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Look, Labour didn't fold, they collapsed. Isn't that the case?

First Minister, people across Wales are facing a cost-of-living crisis, yet senior managers in the public sector and in publicly funded organisations are enjoying pay packets that people in our country could only dream of. And what's really galling is that the worse their organisations seem to perform, the better the pay packet seems to be.

Let's take Transport for Wales, for example. Last year, it was one of the worst performing rail companies across the whole of the United Kingdom in terms of cancellations, yet its chief executive is earning nearly £0.25 million every single year. Then there's Cardiff Airport. It currently receives £20 million per year in annual subsidy from the Welsh Government just to stay afloat, yet its latest financial statements show that its highest paid director received a package of more than £275,000 per year. And in north Wales, Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has the worst performing emergency departments and longest waiting times in the country, yet its chief executive is earning a salary of £262,500 per year. It's scandalous. 

So, do you agree with me, First Minister, that these salaries are now completely out of control, they bear no relationship to the performance of their organisations, and that no-one in the public sector or in a publicly funded organisation should be rewarded for failure?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I must say at the outset that there's a real irony here, isn't there, that the Conservatives choose to focus on high salaries when tax cuts for the highest earners are always among the driving forces of the Conservatives' agenda, which does nothing whatsoever to help people in Wales who are living with the challenges of the cost-of-living crisis.

Across the public sector, we need to make sure that we have the right people in the right place. That does absolutely involve paying them the right sums of money. But all I can tell you is that this new Government, through our work on effectiveness and efficiency, will do everything that we can to make sure that the public pound in Wales is driven as far as it possibly can be. Securing that value for money is at the heart of what this Government is trying to achieve for Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Look, we all know why you are not in favour of performance-related pay and that's because you'd all be skint, wouldn't you, frankly, if it was based on the performance of your Government so far. Let's look at a decision. You say that you want efficient and fair services for taxpayers, let's take a look at a decision that you took last week, as a Government, on your Government website. On 7 October, you approved a salary of more than £200,000 per year for a chief executive of Natural Resources Wales, and a package that would be worth more than that. That's another organisation that has faced serious criticism over its performance: failures to tackle illegal dumping; slow progress in delivering flood defences; and sewage discharges into Welsh waterways, which people have been protesting outside the Senedd about even today. Yet, your Government has decided to offer its next boss a salary that is much higher than even your own—

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: A question, please, Darren.
documents.text_cy: Cwestiwn, Darren.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: These unacceptable salaries for public sector fat cats have gotten out of control and must stop. So, can I ask you today, First Minister: will you introduce a public sector pay restraint Bill to prevent excessive salaries for senior managers paid by the public purse, to make sure that there's fairness for taxpayers and to ensure that pay reflects performance and doesn't reward failure?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Pay absolutely should reflect performance. But I again point to the irony here. We have to make sure that we get value for money from, yes, at times, high wages within the public sector. But compare like for like. Where were the Conservatives calling for the bankers to pay their part of the bill for the financial collapse that is still causing pain for families in Wales today? Where are the Conservatives when it comes to making sure that public spending is able to help those people in communities the length and breadth of Wales, with two out of every five children in Wales living in poverty? I'm afraid that this is faux outrage from the Conservatives. And on performance-related pay, the Conservatives have precisely nothing to show for 27 years in this Parliament.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 3. What measurable improvements in the efficiency and effectiveness of the Welsh Government does the First Minister expect to deliver during this Senedd? OQ64721
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa welliannau mesuradwy o ran effeithlonrwydd ac effeithiolrwydd Llywodraeth Cymru y mae'r Prif Weinidog yn disgwyl eu cyflawni yn ystod y Senedd hon? OQ64721

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Our programme for government sets clear priorities. We will drive efficiency and effectiveness by focusing on these priorities, working collaboratively across Government with a clear focus on outcomes for the people of Wales. We're committed to being the most transparent Government since devolution. And the first iteration of our digital dashboard, for example, which measures progress against our top priorities, was issued this summer.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
First Minister, taxpayers don't measure Government efficiency by how many strategies, reviews or initiatives you announce; they measure it by what actually improves and what it costs them.

Your Government has promised measurable outcomes, progress milestones, plans for plans, greater productivity and so on, so will you actually put the numbers against those promises? Will you publish clear targets showing how much taxpayers' money you intend to save, and which areas of Government will become more efficient and by when? And when programmes or public bodies repeatedly fail to deliver value for money, will you actually reform, merge or scrap them? Because Government efficiency cannot just mean spending more money more efficiently; sometimes, it actually means having to spend less.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, neither does spending less mean that you are being more efficient or more effective, that's what my response would be to that. You spend what you need to spend, not a penny more. You drive that efficiency, you drive that effectiveness. That's the programme that the Government is engaged with now in looking at budgets for the coming years. We have a set budget. Reform voted against fair funding for Wales, but we will work within the budget that we have. And in spending every pound sensibly, in looking at how we get the most out of every pound, that is how we drive outcomes. Because I absolutely agree with the Member that it's not measuring how much you spend, it's what you do with the money. And that also goes on whether you're putting efficiency drives in place for ideological reasons, or whether you're doing it in order to get more out of the system. Let's focus on what we're trying to achieve always for the people of Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Effective Government is underpinned by taking a collaborative, cross-sector and holistic approach to policy development and decision making. It recognises that many of the challenges facing Wales cannot be addressed by individual departments working in isolation. Because for too long, previous Governments have operated in silos, failing to look at the bigger picture and tackle shared challenges through joined-up action. Take prevention, for example. Prevention cuts across health, housing and culture. Food policy connects social justice, public health and rural resilience. Creating high-quality jobs needs co-ordination between the economy and education. So, Prif Weinidog, I'd like to know how this Plaid Cymru Welsh Government is already working collaboratively across ministerial portfolios in a tangible and measurable way that will genuinely make a difference to the lives of the people of Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
This is a programme of work that we put in place in the early weeks of this new Government. The programme for government is built around a set of priorities. To deliver on those priorities and all those other areas that the Welsh Government is responsible for will take a whole-Government approach. Cross-Government working we really want to be a part of our DNA as a Government.

I tasked the Cabinet Minister for Government effectiveness to ensure that the Government works collectively across portfolios to deliver meaningful outcomes. Here are three examples. On climate change, yes, there's a Minister responsible, but it belongs to all of us, so we've put the structures in place to make sure that we're working collaboratively on climate change. Prevention is another one that cuts across the work of so many departments. Tackling poverty is another one of those.

I'd also make the point, Llywydd, that it's not how we work co-operatively within Government alone that matters. Effective delivery also depends on strong collaboration with others—local government, for example, businesses, the third sector and, crucially, communities across Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, you've spoken about the importance of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of the Welsh Government. You've even appointed a Minister for the task. My constituents and the people of Wales need more than just warm words, new strategies and talking shops. They actually want to see improvements in the areas that matter most to them and they want to see their money spent wisely. We've all heard about these ambitious targets and pie-in-the-sky plans from your Government. In fact, you've filled 70 pages with pipe dreams and packaged it up as a programme for government full of ideas but very light on delivery. So, First Minister, what specific measurable targets are you going to be setting during this Senedd term to reduce waste, improve productivity, slash NHS waiting lists and improve educational outcomes across the board? Thank you.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
We can point to a whole host of targets that are already in place, from the first meaningful economic target that we've had in maybe a quarter of a century, on halving the productivity gap with the rest of the UK within a decade. That's setting our sights high, but we need that kind of target. We know about the targets on the longest waiting times in the NHS. We have a very clear path towards raising standards in numeracy, literacy and so on.

I'd refer the Member to the answer I gave a few moments ago. Yes, we want to be efficient in our use of public money in everything that we do. And yes, we have already found ways that we, I believe, can deliver more for less in a whole host of different ways, and I think that's very important.

But to ideologically drive down spending for the sake of it doesn't help the people of Wales. What helps the people of Wales is using money wisely, carefully and setting a clear trajectory for the kinds of changes that we want to deliver for them. With childcare, we know what it is that we're trying to deliver. We know what we have to do. We're getting on with the job.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 4. What action is the Welsh Government taking to resolve the health visitor pay and grading dispute at Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board? OQ64682 [R]
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i ddatrys yr anghydfod o ran tâl ymwelwyr iechyd a graddio ym Mwrdd Iechyd Prifysgol Cwm Taf Morgannwg? OQ64682 [R]

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I recognise the vital role that health visitors play in supporting children and families across Wales. Responsibility for their pay, grading and employment rests with the health board as the employer. But we have engaged with the health board and the trade union, making clear our expectation that all parties should work constructively towards a swift resolution. We will continue to support those efforts while ensuring appropriate arrangements remain in place to safeguard children and families.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
First Minister, I accept the health visitor dispute began before you took office, but it has continued under your Government, affecting vulnerable children and families in my constituency. In March, Heledd Fychan, who now sits in your Cabinet, asked the previous First Minister to intervene. Luke Fletcher reminded the Government that it was, in his words,

'setting the policy and funding the services.'

Then, on 17 April, you signed a letter calling for band 6 health visitors to be upgraded to band 7. Yet your Cabinet Minister for health continues to describe this as a local employment dispute between Unite and the health board, with no fixed timetable for resolution. First Minister, you now set the policy, you fund the services, and you signed the call for band 7. So, I ask you plainly: will your Government provide the funding necessary to deliver band 7 for these health visitors? 'Yes' or 'no'?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: This is a dispute, as the Member rightly points out, that this Government inherited, and yes, I did say that I wanted this dispute to be settled very quickly. I say now, also, now that I'm in Government, that I want this dispute to be settled quickly—for the health visitors, for the health board and for the people that they serve. It is clear that this is a matter that can only be resolved in dispute resolution between the employer and the employee, between the health board and the health workers. What we can do in Government is ensure that there is real clarity on roles and bands and pay structures nationally, and that is exactly what the review instigated by the Cabinet Minister for health is setting out to do.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Prif Weinidog, I think it's important to challenge the suggestion that nothing has been done on this issue. Plaid Cymru Members have repeatedly raised the dispute with the health board in the Senedd and through the Health and Social Care Committee. The health Minister has engaged with both sides and consistently called for a resolution. The Minister has also been clear that this is not a dispute he can simply impose a settlement on, and the frustration felt by the health visitors is shared across this Chamber. What this long-running dispute does raise, however, is wider concerns about governance and accountability. When concerns can persist for years despite scrutiny and repeated calls for resolution, we must ask whether the warning signs should have been identified much earlier. What lessons is the Government drawing more widely about strengthening leadership and accountability across NHS Wales to prevent disputes reaching this stage in future? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I agree that it is important that there's a real understanding of where resolution for this dispute lies. Where disputes persist and affect service delivery, wherever that might be, health boards must demonstrate how concerns have been managed, risks monitored, and the necessary actions taken to maintain safe services.

The Cabinet Secretary has therefore sought further assurance from the health board on safeguarding arrangements and health visiting capacity, with an expectation of full transparency and robust oversight, just to make sure that children and families remain protected.

More broadly, NHS organisations must have strong governance to identify and respond to emerging risks, whatever they might be. The new accountability and support framework published just two weeks ago strengthens accountability, oversight and improvement support, while a forthcoming well-led framework will further strengthen leadership right across the NHS.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: There's obviously no denying that the dispute has been running for far too long. Many of us have been outside on the picket lines and have spoken to constituents who are really frustrated; it's a massive women's workforce, particularly. But I do welcome some news that it looks like, potentially, some progress is now being made towards resolving the dispute. But does the First Minister accept that the lesson from this dispute is that the Welsh Government must now understand and accept its own role in using social partnership as a vehicle to bring employers and trade unions together and to drive that early resolution of disputes rather than allowing them to become so entrenched?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: It's hard for me to comment on what would have happened in the early days, because that was under a Labour Government. Do I believe that we should lean heavily on social partnership? Yes, absolutely. That comes to the resolution of local disputes, it comes into play on issues of national disputes. I believe in the concept and the principle of social partnership. There are certainly learnings from this issue, where we can all ask could things have been done sooner. I hope, as the Member does, that that resolution, which we all wish to see happening, is coming closer.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Steve Bayliss highlighted the letter that you signed as leader of Plaid Cymru during the election campaign. There was a key ask in that letter, and it's stated quite simply: 'Honour agreed processes and upgrade all band 6 health visitors to band 7.' Do you still agree with that statement that you made back in April now that you're First Minister?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: It is not as simple as that. This is a resolution that can only come from dispute resolution between the employer and the employee. What we need to ensure, as I said, is that we have absolute clarity now on pay structures and banding, as that relates to health workers wherever they are in Wales, because that consistency of application is crucial to make sure that we avoid this kind of dispute in future. There's work that has been instigated by the Cabinet Minister for health, and I trust that that not only comes into play now, but that it will be of use when it comes to, potentially, nipping other disputes in the bud in future through social partnership.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
At the start of September, my mother passed away. She had spent her entire career working as a health visitor. For her, this work wasn't just a job, it was her calling. My mum's identity, from when she first started training in 1951, was shaped around her time as a health visitor. Even in retirement, you could tell from the way that she spoke and interacted with people that being a health visitor was really part of who she was and what she was meant to be doing. This is the case for so many people for whom their career is a vocation.

Does the First Minister agree with me that, very often, when a career is a vocation for a person, they are often not remunerated according to the value of the kind of work they do for society or in comparison with other equivalent professions? And furthermore, does the First Minister agree that this is an issue that disproportionately affects professions dominated by women, like health visiting, more than it does professions dominated by men?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: There is no question that health visitors are driven by vocation. I've met those who are currently involved in this particular dispute. They want to get back to work. That's the core of this from their point of view. Yes, we are talking about women, largely, here, but I think what we need to show always is an appreciation of that commitment that people right across the public sector show towards their work that goes over and above, by some way, what they are contracted or paid or the hours that they are meant to work. We look right across the public sector and show our appreciation to those people who care for those within their communities. I'll also take this opportunity to wish your family well after your recent loss.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 5. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve access to essential public services in town and city centres across Wales? OQ64706
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wella mynediad at wasanaethau cyhoeddus hanfodol yng nghanol trefi a dinasoedd ledled Cymru? OQ64706

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The Government believes in the future of our town and city centres. They're at the heart of local identities, our culture and our communities. We refuse to accept their decline and want to reinvent and repurpose those town and city centres for the future. Public services are very much part of that. We want our town and city centres to be places where people can easily access the services they need. We're also investing in better transport links and regeneration schemes and using our town centre taskforce to consider what further action is needed.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, First Minister. Strong cities and towns depend not only on attracting investment but also on ensuring that people can continue to access essential services they rely on every day. In Swansea, the city centre post office in the Quadrant is due to close in February 2027. While a replacement is being explored, no new location or opening date has been confirmed, and the alternative branches do not provide the same range of services. For older residents, disabled people and many small businesses, that would represent a significant loss. First Minister, your Government has rightly committed to supporting thriving high streets and regenerating our towns and city centres. How will the Welsh Government work with partners to safeguard access to essential services, including a full-service post office, as part of a wider regeneration plan for Swansea city centre and communities across Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, post office provision in itself is a reserved matter for UK Government, but I certainly do recognise the importance of maintaining access to a full-service branch in Swansea city centre, particularly for older and perhaps disabled people and small businesses too. I understand that Post Office Ltd has committed to finding replacement host businesses for branches like the one in Swansea affected by the TG Jones closures. Alongside this, our town-centre taskforce will consider how essential public services, as I say, can support thriving town and city centres. Across Wales, we will continue to support co-location, accessible transport and business rates relief, which we announced recently, so that regeneration sustains the kind of everyday services that communities rely on, and, at the same time, attracting, hopefully, new investment into these town and city centres.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 6. What progress has the Welsh Government made in addressing congestion on the M4 around Newport? OQ64681
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa gynnydd y mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi'i wneud o ran mynd i'r afael â thagfeydd ar yr M4 o amgylch Casnewydd? OQ64681

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: People are rightly frustrated by congestion on the M4 around Newport and want to see progress, so last week we brought clarity where there has been uncertainty, I think, for too long. We've taken a clear decision that road and engineering improvements must be part of the solution, and we're getting on with the practical improvements now while we develop that long-term solution.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Thank you, First Minister. I know you've spoken about this earlier, but it's one of those things that I think is going to crop up again and again and again for the next few years, because everyone in this Chamber knows the issues on the M4 around Newport all too well, yet too few of us here acknowledge there is only one proper solution, and that is a relief road.

Some of the alternative suggestions, such as junction closures, are certainly very concerning, and would see huge volumes of traffic pushed into the city, Newport, stifling the local economy there, which is of great concern to many people already, and I know the Minister will be talking to people over the coming months, but there is concern.

And the suggestion to encourage HGVs to use the A465 will supposedly reduce traffic on the M4 by 1 per cent. Now, that's great, but it will then move that same 1 per cent on to already challenged areas like the Hardwick interchange at Abergavenny, which, based on traffic this week, is really, really struggling to cope.

So, let's not send Newport's congestion on a sightseeing tour of Wales. We know the answer is a relief road, First Minister. I note your earlier answer, but if the smaller engineering fixes don't solve the congestion problem—

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Question, please, Peter.
documents.text_cy: Cwestiwn, plis, Peter.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: —will you finally reconsider a relief road, or have you ruled out the only long-term solution, regardless of evidence?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
The Member is referring to what was known as the black route, of course. It is no longer a protected route. When the decision was taken to cancel that particular route, that option was essentially taken off the table, or at least for a very, very, very long time, and we're not prepared to wait that long. And I think we've made it clear that we do think road relief is a part of the solution, and that is why we need to do that careful planning and engineering work to make sure that we understand what is the best solution to pursue, because it's become very, very clear to me—and I've been personally engaged on this, because I have an interest in unblocking this issue for the people of Newport and for the wider south Wales economy—that it will take a host of different things. It will mean—and this is good news for the people of Newport—strengthening public transport. It is important, it will contribute.

Taking traffic on other roads where there is capacity is something that's very, very important, and it could be something as simple as making sure that we provide better provision for HGV drivers, something that I know from my own constituency, with how important that is around Holyhead. So, what I say is, this is live now, this is happening. We're pressing ahead with a multiphase scheme that will crucially take into consideration the views of, and will happen in partnership with, the people of Newport. Will there be challenges in this transformation to a twenty-second century Newport? Yes, but we want to face those challenges and put solutions in place with the people of that city, because there is a city and a broader region that have a lot to benefit from getting this right. Inaction is what we saw up until now; that's not an option now.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to ensure that patients in north-east Wales who rely on NHS services in England receive timely treatment, effective information sharing and clear accountability? OQ64687
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod cleifion yng ngogledd-ddwyrain Cymru sy'n dibynnu ar wasanaethau'r GIG yn Lloegr yn cael triniaeth amserol, y caiff gwybodaeth ei rhannu'n effeithiol, a bod atebolrwydd clir? OQ64687

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Patients in north-east Wales deserve timely, joined-up care, whichever side of the border provides it. We are strengthening cross-border partnerships, streamlining referrals and improving information sharing between NHS Wales and NHS England. Our aim is clear: better co-ordinated care, clear accountability and fewer avoidable delays, so patients receive the right treatment, in the right place, at the right time.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, First Minister. In Fflint Wrecsam, cross-border healthcare is an everyday reality. The Health and Social Care Committee heard evidence a couple of weeks ago that patients can face different waiting time arrangements depending on which side of the border they are treated, that some are left chasing records, test results and appointments themselves, and that there are concerns Welsh patients could become invisible as the NHS in England restructures.

So, with more than 13,000 Welsh patients registered with English general practitioners and over 20,000 English patients registered with Welsh GPs, what concrete assurances can you give that cross-border patients will not face longer waits, poorer co-ordination or unclear accountability when things go wrong? And will your Government commit to publishing regular data on cross-border waiting times, complaints and patient outcomes so that patients don't fall through the gaps?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I'm very glad that the Member pointed out that statistic about traffic for primary care and in which direction it goes. And it's a little-known fact that there are more people from England coming into Wales to see a GP than the other way around. What that tells me is that we need to get this right for people on both sides of the border. I'm a patient in the north of Wales too. It is part of our landscape that there are elements of care that we might get at a specialist children's hospital in Liverpool or a neurosurgery department at Walton and so on. We are committed to making sure that we improve that cross-border working.

I'll give you an example on information sharing: we are working on improving the transfer of referrals, improving the sharing of clinical records, test results and prescribing information. Digital interoperability work is focused on making sure that care becomes safer, becomes more co-ordinated, reducing the need for patients to chase information and so on. In terms of those waiting times, the key thing is that it is the patients that we look after and make sure that we trace their journey through the NHS, wherever that treatment takes place, and for many patients, parts of their treatment will be in the north of Wales and parts of it will be in the north-west of England.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 8. What action is the Government taking to improve and integrate public transport links in Sir Fynwy Torfaen? OQ64704
documents.text_cy: 8. Pa gamau mae'r Llywodraeth yn eu cymryd i wella ac integreiddio cysylltiadau trafnidiaeth gyhoeddus yn Sir Fynwy Torfaen? OQ64704

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We are taking action across Wales to improve and integrate provision across bus, rail and active travel. We are working closely with Transport for Wales and local authorities, including in Sir Fynwy Torfaen. We are implementing bus franchising and making better use of assets across bus and rail, which will be key to delivering better integrated services that reflect passenger demand and the priorities of communities.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, Brif Weinidog. The transport Minister's announcement last week shows that this Government is willing to tackle transport issues that have previously been kicked down the road. Now, this is an opportunity to vastly improve public transport throughout Monmouthshire and Torfaen. Because when people have the option of quick, frequent and reliable public transport, they'll take it, especially if it's convenient and affordable.

Now, previous south Wales metro reports have proposed upgrading to transport services, with more frequent trains between Abergavenny and Cardiff and rapid bus transport from Monmouth to Newport. So, will this Government's fresh look at transport in the south-east of Wales look to provide convenient and affordable public transport, including, if I may, rapid bus transport between towns in Sir Fynwy Torfaen, more frequent trains between Abergavenny and Cardiff, and more reliable trains to and from Chepstow, Severn Tunnel Junction and the much-anticipated Magor and Undy station? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The Member describes exactly what we all should be trying to achieve in making public transport so accessible and cheap and easy to use that it becomes a no-brainer. We want to make it easier to choose public transport for everyday journeys across the wider M4 corridor by integrating bus and rail into one cohesive network. Bus reform is an important of it. That'll support co-ordinated planning and management of public transport by Transport for Wales, in collaboration with local authorities. That should mean more efficient aligning of transport options. TfW is already working with local authorities in the south-east to review the bus network plan. We'll launch a programme of public engagement in the region next year. Yes, we will consider the potential for more frequent train services, including on routes from Abergavenny and Chepstow to Cardiff, and, yes, we want to see the delivery of those new stations in the south-east of Wales without further delay.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 9. What assessment has the First Minister made of the accessibility of addiction recovery services? OQ64705
documents.text_cy: 9. Pa asesiad mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o hygyrchedd gwasanaethau o ran adfer o gaethiwed? OQ64705

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We are committed to this agenda. I know the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health wants people to be able to access high-quality addiction recovery services where needed. Some £68 million has been invested annually in substance misuse services, with most funding allocated to area planning boards to commission services based on the needs of those localities. Accessibility is a key consideration, with boards needing to provide regular assurance to Welsh Government on both delivery and performance.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch. I recently visited the Salvation Army in Rhyl, an open-access organisation with a welcoming home-from-home feel, offering a warm space alongside physical and emotional support to anyone seeking help. I was privileged to speak with two amazing volunteers, Chris and Mandy. Both have experienced their own journeys through recovery and now use their lived experiences to support others. Their experiences, alongside those of the others that were there, with accessing services highlighted to me significant challenges individuals experiencing addiction can face when trying to access and retain support. Chaotic living circumstances, mental health difficulties, fear, shame and the physical and cognitive effects of substance use can make it difficult for people to engage with rigid appointment times, overly structured recovery programmes and services that may not accommodate the reality of their lives.

The stigma faced by people experiencing addiction can further hinder recovery, and this stigma doesn't always disappear when in recovery. How can the Government build on the support being offered in Wales to ensure that people experiencing addiction have access to more effective support, and what work can be done to reduce the stigma around addiction?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, we certainly do recognise the challenges faced by people recovering from addiction, and we value the vital contribution of organisations such as the Salvation Army in supporting recovery. We also recognise, absolutely, the stigma that can be a significant barrier to individuals seeking help and sustaining recovery afterwards. Through investment in local treatment and recovery services, we're working to make sure that people can access the right support at the right time. The Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health will continue to engage with people with lived experience, service providers and the wider sectors, so that we can be properly informed as a Government of future action in these areas.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Finally, First Minister, question 10, Anthony Slaughter.
documents.text_cy: Yn olaf, Brif Weinidog, cwestiwn 10, Anthony Slaughter.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 10. What plans does the Welsh Government have to deliver its commitments to ensure that everyone has a safe and affordable home? OQ64698
documents.text_cy: 10. Pa gynlluniau sydd gan Lywodraeth Cymru i gyflawni ei hymrwymiadau i sicrhau bod gan bawb gartref diogel a fforddiadwy? OQ64698

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, we've allocated over £450 million for social housing alone this year, providing the investment needed to increase supply and help more people access a safe, secure and affordable home. Local authorities across the Caerdydd Penarth constituency have been allocated over £82 million in social housing grant funding this year. Together, this will contribute to the delivery of over 1,100 additional homes.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, Brif Weinidog. There are currently over 10,000 people in temporary accommodation across Wales, including over 2,000 children. I welcome that the Government has set out its ambition to deliver 20,000 new social homes by the end of this Senedd. However, the latest data from Shelter Cymru suggests that there at least 94,000 households currently on a waiting list for a social home.

Will the First Minister commit to publishing a new housing strategy as soon as possible, including the Government's plans for ending homelessness? What steps will you be taking to ensure that everyone in Wales is supported to access a safe and affordable home?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I appreciate the work that the Member does around the issue of housing. Some of the statistics that he mentions are pretty sobering, and we are under no illusion as a Government as to the scale of the challenge that we are facing.

We propose to address this, and look forward to co-operating with him and others on this. We propose to take action, not only in making sure the necessary investment goes in on building more social homes, but that we legislate too, that we put legislative steps in place to make sure that we are emphasising our belief as a Government that people should have that fundamental support in making sure that they have a roof over their heads and somewhere to live safely. This is something that I know drives my housing Cabinet Minister every day in her work.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Brif Weinidog.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Item 2 now, the business statement and announcement. And I call on the Trefnydd, Heledd Fychan.
documents.text_cy: Eitem 2 nawr, y datganiad a chyhoeddiad busnes. Galwaf ar y Trefnydd, Heledd Fychan.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Thank you, Llywydd. There is one change to this week's business. The debate on the legislative consent motion on the Armed Forces Bill has been extended to half an hour, in recognition of the interest shown by Members. Draft Plenary business for the next three weeks is shown on the business statement, which is available, as usual, to all Members electronically.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Lywydd. Mae yna un newid i fusnes yr wythnos hon. Mae'r ddadl ar y cynnig cydsyniad deddfwriaethol ar Fil y Lluoedd Arfog wedi ymestyn i hanner awr, i gydnabod y diddordeb a ddangoswyd gan yr Aelodau. Mae busnes drafft y tair wythnos nesaf wedi'i nodi yn y datganiad busnes, sydd ar gael, fel arfer, i'r holl Aelodau yn electronig.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
I'd be grateful if, when budget deals or statements are made in the future, that they're made to the Chamber, and not to the press in advance. 

But on to—. I request a statement, if possible, Trefnydd, from the Minister for education, based on AI and coding. There's a new study that's coming out that shows Wales quite low, behind other parts of the UK, in terms of where we are with coding in our schools. Given that it's going to be a huge part of young people's futures, would the Government come forward with a statement to tell us what their plans are to get children up to date with the future, like other nations?

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Thank you. On the first point, you will be aware that those processes will be followed in relation to the budget, and there will be an opportunity for everyone to express their view on the supplementary budget once again. Nothing has been broken in terms of the ministerial code in terms of what happened today; this is how Parliaments work. If Reform were a party that is serious about the future of this Senedd, and wanted to seriously discuss getting the best settlement for the people of Wales, you'd understand how parties collaborate in this Chamber and beyond.

In terms of AI, it's hugely important that we are alive to the advantages and risks related to AI, and I know that this is an issue that the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy does take as an issue of great importance. There will be updates, and, as you know, the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy is taking questions in this Senedd next week.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch. O ran y pwynt cyntaf, mi fyddwch chi’n ymwybodol bydd y prosesau yna yn cael eu dilyn o ran y gyllideb, ac mi fydd yna gyfle i bawb i fod yn rhoi barn ar y gyllideb atodol unwaith eto. Does yna ddim byd wedi’i dorri o ran y cod gweinidogol o ran yr hyn ddigwyddodd heddiw; fel hyn mae Seneddau yn gweithio. Ac, efallai, pe byddai Reform yn blaid sydd o ddifrif ynglŷn â dyfodol y Senedd hon, ac eisiau trafod o ddifrif a chael y setliad gorau i bobl Cymru, fe fyddech chi’n deall sut mae pleidiau yn cydweithio yn y Siambr hon a thu hwnt.

O ran AI, mae’n bwysig iawn ein bod ni yn fyw i’r manteision a’r risgiau sydd yn gysylltiedig ag AI, a dwi’n gwybod bod hwn yn fater y mae’r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni yn ei gymryd fel mater sydd o bwys mawr. Mi fydd yna ddiweddariadau, ac, fel y byddwch chi’n gwybod, mae’r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni yn derbyn cwestiynau yn y Senedd hon yr wythnos nesaf.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Trefnydd, while the Welsh Government has rightly highlighted support for households facing energy bills, businesses across Wales are also grappling with energy costs themselves and rising overheads. Will you request a statement, please, from the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy on the effects of higher energy prices on Welsh businesses and what further action the Government intends to take to support those firms throughout all of those pressures?

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Thank you. I will certainly make the Cabinet Minister aware that you've raised this issue. Of course, the Cabinet Minister for Finance is present here, and you'll be aware of some of the steps that have already been taken by this Government to support businesses. Obviously, if there are any specific businesses that you are concerned about, then it's always important that Members do raise these concerns with the Ministers, but I will certainly make him aware of what you've raised.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Mi wnaf i yn sicr wneud y Gweinidog Cabinet yn ymwybodol eich bod chi wedi codi’r mater hwn. Wrth gwrs, mae Gweinidog y Cabinet dros Gyllid yma, ac mi fyddwch chi’n ymwybodol o rai camau sydd wedi’u cymryd gan y Llywodraeth hon eisoes i gefnogi busnesau. Yn amlwg, os oes yna fusnesau penodol rydych chi’n pryderu amdanyn nhw, mae wastad yn bwysig bod Aelodau yn codi’r pryderon hyn gyda’r Gweinidogion, ond mi fyddaf i'n sicr yn ei wneud o’n ymwybodol o’r hyn rydych chi wedi’i godi.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Trefnydd, I'd be grateful if we could have a statement from the Welsh Government on its overview of local authorities across Wales. A special investigation by the Cambrian News in my constituency has unearthed a number of troubling concerns regarding Ceredigion County Council and its purchase of Llettytwppa Farm, including questions over governance and oversight, allegations of conflict of interest, and the use of significant sums of public money for a project that reportedly has attracted only a small number of students.

Now, I believe that, given the serious nature of the concerns, it's vital that there is a statement from the Welsh Government outlining what oversight mechanisms are available to ensure proper governance and accountability of local authorities in Wales, and to confirm whether the Welsh Government believes any further investigation is warranted in this particular case. The people of my constituency need assurances that public funds are being spent appropriately by the local authority and that decisions are being taken transparently and appropriately. So, I'd be grateful if a statement could be issued by the Welsh Government on this important issue as soon as possible.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising this issue. I don't know, from what you've outlined, if you have written to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning; clearly, she is in the Chamber and will have heard your comments. You will also be aware that there are formal processes to be followed in relation to any concerns, including with the ombudsman, if concerns have been expressed. I hope that the Member will raise these concerns through those appropriate channels, so that what has been set out can be looked into if there are concerns.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r mater hwn. Dwi ddim yn gwybod, o'r hyn roeddech chi'n ei amlinellu, a ydych chi wedi ysgrifennu at y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Lywodraeth Leol, Tai a Chynllunio; yn amlwg, mae hi yn y Siambr ac wedi clywed hyn. Mi fyddwch chi hefyd yn ymwybodol bod yna brosesau ffurfiol i'w dilyn ynglŷn ag unrhyw bryderon, gan gynnwys gyda'r ombwdsmon, os oes yna bryderon wedi eu mynegi. Dwi'n gobeithio bod yr Aelod yn codi'r pryderon hyn drwy'r ffyrdd priodol hynny, fel bod yr hyn sydd wedi ei nodi yn cael ei ymchwilio iddo fo os oes yna bryderon.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: British job losses from AI last year were twice the international average. I'm particularly concerned about the impact of this on younger people and particularly entry-level jobs. We already have one of the highest amounts of young people in Wales not in education, employment or training. I'm also concerned about how we ensure that the gains from AI are spread equally across our communities in Wales and not just felt in the pocket of big businesses. We know that there is generally concern among people in Wales with AI. In my constituency, there's been huge pushback against a data centre in Pontyclun, which will have little, if any, benefit for the local community, and I know this isn't unique just to my constituency. So, I wonder if the Government would make a statement on its strategy towards AI, including mitigating job losses, the development of data centres and also ensuring equitable gains from AI as well.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Certainly. You will have heard the Cabinet Minister talking about the advantages, but also the risks, of AI, and, certainly, there is a recognition, in terms of a number of sectors, when it comes to those risks to jobs that could be lost entirely, or skills. For example, in my portfolio, in terms of music, actors and so on, there are a number of concerns. We're also looking at what the advantages are, and we want that advantage. The Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy is in Boston this week, meeting business investors and the diaspora community. So, we are looking at the opportunities and the jobs that could come from AI as well, so that it's not just extractive, as we are seeing. Certainly, I will raise the fact that two Members—perhaps more by the end of this session—have raised AI with me, in order to ensure that we do update you and also engage with Members as this work goes ahead.
documents.text_cy: Yn sicr. Mi fyddwch chi wedi clywed y Gweinidog Cabinet yn sôn ynglŷn â'r manteision, ond hefyd y peryglon, ac yn sicr mae yna gydnabyddiaeth, o ran nifer o sectorau, o ran y pryderon hynny ynglŷn â swyddi a allai gael eu colli'n llwyr, neu sgiliau. Er enghraifft, yn fy mhortffolio i, o ran cerddoriaeth, actorion ac ati, mae yna nifer fawr o bryderon. Rydym ni hefyd yn gweld beth ydy'r manteision, ac rydym ni eisiau cael y budd hwnnw. Mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni yn Boston yr wythnos hon yn cwrdd â buddsoddwyr busnesau a'r gymuned diaspora. Felly, rydym ni yn edrych ar y cyfleoedd a'r swyddi sydd i ddod gydag AI hefyd, fel dyw o ddim jest yn extractive, fel rydym ni'n ei weld efo pethau. Yn sicr, mi fyddaf i'n codi bod yna ddau Aelod—efallai y bydd yna fwy erbyn diwedd y sesiwn hon—wedi codi AI gyda mi, er mwyn sicrhau ein bod ni'n eich diweddaru chi a hefyd yn ymgysylltu efo Aelodau wrth i'r gwaith hwn fynd rhagddo.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Trefnydd, I'd like to request a statement from the First Minister on the Welsh Government's overseas offices—the network of 20 offices across 11 countries, with an annual running cost of around £4.7 million. Members from more than one party have asked since 2021 for office-by-office costs and benefits, most recently David Mills, on 6 October. The Government has said it cannot break them down. In February, the Government told the Economy, Trade and Rural Affairs Committee it would not release office-by-office investment results, citing data protection and Office for National Statistics rules, and offered only network-wide figures. A Senedd committee has also reported that written information on the wider £58 million international budget was frequently incomplete and unclear, with irreconcilable amounts. Will the Trefnydd ask the First Minister to make a statement on this?

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I think it is very important that the Member should reflect on which Government you're referring to. You're talking about the Labour Government in your contribution there, whereas we are a new Government, in post since May. So, many of the questions were raised through scrutiny—and I was a member of the committee that undertook that scrutiny work—of the previous Government. Work is ongoing, and is being led by the First Minister, in terms of a new international strategy, which is looking at all of the offices, and looking at how we as a Government engage internationally too. He's been very clear that he wants us to be a Government that engages on the international stage because of the benefits to Wales of doing so. As the work on the strategy is updated, of course, there will be opportunities for Members to be questioning the First Minister and to be engaging and scrutinising.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n meddwl ei bod hi'n bwysig iawn bod yr Aelod yn adlewyrchu ar ba Lywodraeth rydych chi'n cyfeirio ati. Rydych chi'n sôn am y Llywodraeth Lafur yn eich cyfraniad chi yn y fan yna, lle rydym ni'n Llywodraeth newydd ers mis Mai. Felly, mae nifer o'r cwestiynau a godwyd gan graffu—ac mi oeddwn i'n rhan o'r pwyllgor a oedd yn gwneud y gwaith craffu hwnnw—i'r Llywodraeth flaenorol. Mae'r gwaith yn mynd rhagddo, dan arweiniad y Prif Weinidog, o ran strategaeth ryngwladol newydd, sydd yn edrych ar yr holl swyddfeydd, o ran edrych ar sut rydym ni fel Llywodraeth yn ymgysylltu yn rhyngwladol hefyd. Mae o wedi bod yn glir iawn ei fod o eisiau i ni fod yn Llywodraeth sy'n ymgysylltu'n rhyngwladol oherwydd y buddion a ddaw i Gymru o hynny. Wrth i'r gwaith ar y strategaeth gael ei ddiweddaru, wrth gwrs, mi fydd yna gyfle i Aelodau fod yn holi'r Prif Weinidog ac i ymgysylltu a chraffu.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Can I call for two statements today, please? Can I have a statement in relation to the noise assessment work that needs to be done on the A55 in the Llanddulas area from the Deputy Minister for Transport? This is a priority area for noise reduction. Residents in that community have lived with lots of noise from the A55 for many years. We've been told that a noise assessment is going to be done, but there's no indication as to the timeline for that work or when any follow-up work might be completed, in terms of capital investment for noise barriers. So, I think it is something that I would like an update from the Minister on.

Secondly, can I call for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care in relation to medical speciality training for next year? I've been contacted by a group of doctors who are internationally trained, who have many years of experience in the Welsh NHS and want to go on to further their careers, but their experience in the NHS is not currently recognised within the framework as giving them priority access to that training. I do think this is something that the Welsh Government could take action on to address some of the gaps in our workforce in the NHS, and I'd be grateful for a statement.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Thank you. The Deputy Minister for Transport is here in the Chamber. What I would ask you to do in terms of the A55 is to write to him, and I'm sure that there will be an update for you on that.

In terms of the second statement that you request, I will raise this with the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care. Since you have met specifically with members of the workforce, then I think it would be a good idea for you to write to him as well, because it is important that they get that response. I understand, from what you say, that you have written, so I will ask him to ensure that he writes back to you.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch. Mae'r Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth yma yn y Siambr. Yr hyn byddwn i'n gofyn i chi ei wneud o ran yr A55 ydy ysgrifennu ato fo, a dwi'n siŵr bydd diweddariad i chi o ran hynny.

O ran yr ail ddatganiad rydych chi'n gofyn amdano fo, mi wnaf i godi hyn efo'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Iechyd a Gofal. Gan eich bod chi wedi cwrdd yn benodol gydag aelodau'r gweithlu, dwi yn meddwl byddai fo'n syniad pe byddech chi'n gallu ysgrifennu ato fo hefyd, oherwydd mae'n bwysig eu bod nhw'n cael yr ymateb hwnnw. Dwi'n deall, o'r hyn rydych chi'n ei ddweud, eich bod chi wedi ysgrifennu, felly mi fyddaf i yn gofyn iddo fo sicrhau ei fod o yn ysgrifennu nôl atoch chi.

documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Can I ask for a statement from the Deputy Minister for Transport on Network Rail's plans to close the railway between Holyhead and Chester for four weeks in January to carry out repair works along the line? This is a line that thousands of people rely on, and therefore the impact that this will have on passengers in Bangor Conwy Môn and north Wales will be significant. However, many people who use these services regularly remain unaware of the disruption that lies ahead. I'm pleased to see that Network Rail has now published further information about the work, but I would like to request a statement from the Deputy Minister outlining the support that the Welsh Government can provide between now and January to spread the word, ensuring that local residents are aware of the situation and have the opportunity to make alternative travel arrangements. Thank you.
documents.text_cy: Gaf i ofyn am ddatganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth ar gynlluniau Network Rail i gau'r rheilffordd rhwng Caergybi a Chaer am bedair wythnos ym mis Ionawr er mwyn cynnal gwaith atgyweirio ar hyd y llinell? Mae hwn yn rheilffordd y mae miloedd o bobl yn ddibynnol arno, ac felly bydd yr effaith y bydd hyn yn ei chael ar deithwyr ym Mangor Conwy Môn a gogledd Cymru yn sylweddol. Serch hynny, mae nifer fawr o bobl sy'n defnyddio'r gwasanaethau yma yn rheolaidd yn parhau yn anymwybodol o'r tarfu sydd o'u blaenau. Dwi'n falch o weld bod Network Rail erbyn hyn wedi cyhoeddi rhagor o ddeunydd gwybodaeth am y gwaith, ond hoffwn ofyn am ddatganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog sy'n gosod allan y gefnogaeth y gall Llywodraeth Cymru ei rhoi rhwng rŵan a mis Ionawr i ledaenu'r gair, fel bod trigolion lleol yn ymwybodol o'r sefyllfa ac yn cael cyfle i baratoi cynlluniau teithio amgen. documents.item: 2. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising this issue. I appreciate that this will cause temporary disruption in terms of the service for travellers while the railway is closed.
