Is the Labour leader in Wales now suggesting that he, if he were in Government, would take away those elements of universalism that have been so well embraced by the people of Wales in recent years?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, the First Minister knows full well that we would never ever do that, and it's simply a deflection from the truth. Because I can reveal what the cost to the taxpayer would be in giving millionaires and the highest earners free childcare: it would amount to about £15 million per year. For every person earning over £100,000 a year, they would benefit from Plaid Cymru's Government to the tune of £5,650 per child per year. As I say, that amount will total £15 million per year, paid for through cuts elsewhere. It's not fair, it's not progressive, and it's certainly not left wing. You're standing up for millionaires, you're not standing up for Wales. And indeed, you're standing beside the Tories in wanting the same policy. So, who stole this policy from whom? Did you steal it from the Tories, or did Kemi Badenoch steal it from yourself? And why won't you use £15 million a year instead to support those who are facing the toughest of times in the cost-of-living crisis, not the richest?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The Member knows, of course, that it's not millionaires that we're talking about here through universalism, but it's hard-working families, medium earners, middle earners who the Member says should be excluded from childcare. I just don't believe that. I believe in the principle of universalism that Labour used to believe in. What has Labour become if Labour now are genuinely asking us to engage in a fundamental debate on the question of universalism? We could allow, could we not, millionaires to buy their own health services, and we wouldn't mind, right? Let's have just a health service for those who can't afford it. I don't believe that is the best way forward. I don't believe in having a two-tier health service. I believe in the principles laid down by Aneurin Bevan I think that are as relevant today as they were when he established the NHS. So, whether it's on free school meals, or on free prescriptions, or on bus passes, or on the NHS itself, universalism is a principle that brings us together as a community, as society, and we will pursue this in the interest of the people of Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Leader of the Welsh Conservatives, Darren Millar.
documents.text_cy: Arweinydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Darren Millar.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Can I put on record that the thoughts of my party are with the Jewish community in Wales and around the world as we mark the anniversary of the 7 October attacks this week?

First Minister, Wales is in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis. At a time when households are struggling with prices, last week the cost of alcohol in Wales went up, with a massive increase of 30 per cent in minimum alcohol pricing. And that doesn't affect just people who have alcohol problems, it affects everyone, including those people who are responsible drinkers, hitting them in their pockets too. What consideration has the Welsh Government given to the economic impact of the change in minimum alcohol pricing, especially on retailers close to the Welsh border, who are now seeing their customers nipping across into England in order to do their shopping to avoid these extra costs?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I was part of the committee in the Senedd before last that assessed the pros and cons of introducing minimum alcohol pricing. There were others here who were on that committee with me. And what we concluded was that, just as with cigarettes, the impact of pricing can have a positive impact on the choices that people make in relation to their use of alcohol. It's not a ban of alcohol, it's a trigger to make people think. That is the principle that led to the increase now—exactly these arguments that if it's about making sure that alcohol is as cheap as it possibly can be, that is not in the interest of the health of the people of Wales. It really isn't. And I think there has been a greater understanding in recent years, as happened with smoking decades ago, that we can no longer ignore the detrimental impacts of alcohol on health. And this measure is one step where we can try to redress the balance there.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Look, we all know that left-wing Governments make choices that drive people to drink. [Laughter.] But then, pushing the price of booze up isn't, I think, the right thing to do, particularly during a cost-of-living crisis. We've seen fuel prices go up, energy prices have just gone up and now the cost of booze in Wales is up. Now, people who enjoy a responsible tipple across Wales are absolutely furious by this decision. The evidence from the Welsh Government's own evaluation undertaken in January 2025 shows that, actually, this policy isn't working. Those people who are already alcohol dependent and problem drinkers are still alcohol dependent, still have problems with booze, and actually they're now even worse off because they're giving up food, they're not putting the heating on, in order to pay for more expensive alcohol.

So, can I ask you, can I urge you, to look at that evidence? Instead of pushing up shopping bills, instead of punishing responsible drinkers, instead of retailers losing out because of this policy, why don't you scrap this policy altogether and get on instead with investing in support for problem drinkers, including better access to alcohol rehabilitation services in Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
The truth of the matter is that, when we discussed this at source, back then in committee, it was about doing both. There was a recognition that this wasn't a measure that would stop alcoholics from obtaining alcohol, because they are addicted to alcohol. That is not what this is about, and I agree that we need to be strengthening support for people who have alcohol abuse problems.

For the Member, though, to point to this decision being about the impact of the cost of living, I would ask him to reflect on the actions of successive Conservative Governments on a UK level, which decided to go down the route of austerity, hitting ordinary people in their pockets every single day in all aspects of their lives, rather than punishing the bankers who had put us in that position at that time. There are many decisions that Governments can take where we consider the impact on the pockets of the people that we represent. Minimum alcohol pricing is about health.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 3. What is the Welsh Government doing to ensure that its childcare offer is flexible and meets the needs of parents? OQ64647
documents.text_cy: 3. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i sicrhau bod ei chynnig gofal plant yn hyblyg ac yn diwallu anghenion rhieni? OQ64647

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Funded childcare must be flexible for families and deliverable for providers. We're working with local authorities and registered providers to expand provision sustainably and move to a simpler system that's easier for parents to navigate. As we introduce our universal childcare offer, we will ensure that it will enable longer and more flexible sessions.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, Brif Weinidog. I'd like to give an example of how the current system isn't flexible for parents. One nursery I know of in Cardiff can only provide Flying Start provision for 2.5 hours a day for the children who are eligible, but, meanwhile, the same nursery group in Newport can provide Flying Start in blocks so that parents can return to work part-time and use their Flying Start hours all in a couple of days. Parents in Cardiff aren't offered the same opportunities. Currently, funded childcare provision is too fragmented. It's a postcode lottery between local authorities and even different sides of the street. Too many who need it cannot access it.

Labour are complaining about a universal childcare offer. We've heard it again today—Labour complaining about universal childcare. The party of Aneurin Bevan and universal healthcare is complaining about universalism. They've lost touch with their roots. Meanwhile, Reform in England are closing publicly funded nurseries. So, does the First Minister agree with me that the universality of this childcare offer is key, so that parents can get back to work and not a single child slips through that gap in provision?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
That universality is very, very important and, as we've touched on already today, it is a broader principle that we should value.

On flexibility, as we introduce a radical, an ambitious, new national childcare offer, we're working to create a simpler, more streamlined system that gives parents more flexibility and easier access to funded childcare across Wales. Universal provision, of course, supports every child to get the best start in life, and thousands of low-earning families who've previously been locked out of any childcare or early years support will benefit as a result of our policy. Current guidance allows childcare sessions to be combined. We know this flexibility is interpreted and applied differently, and we are working to, as we roll out the childcare offer, partner with local authorities and others to make sure that that consistency does become the norm across the board.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Prif Weinidog, last week your Deputy First Minister told me that childcare must be flexible for families and deliverable for providers. Yet, when I asked what this expanded offer will actually cost, she told me that the figures will only become clear in the forthcoming draft budget. But flexibility has a price tag. Longer hours, greater capacity, rural provision and the workforce to deliver it cannot be paid for with aspiration. So, how can your Government promise parents a flexible childcare offer when it still cannot tell them or this Senedd what the fully modelled policy will cost? Surely you cost the flexibility before you promise it, rather than promise it first and work out the bill afterwards. Because however flexible the promise, First Minister, the budget remains stubbornly inflexible. Eventually, the numbers will have to add up. So, please reassure us that Welsh parents will not be left quite as baffled by your childcare maths as your Deputy First Minister apparently was by mine.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Well, I fundamentally disagree with that take from the Member. We've made it clear. In fact, we have put the money in for the first phase, which is the rolling out of the 12.5 hours in every part of Wales within this first financial year. It's £55 million, and that is—. Well, that's happening. The money has gone. It's £55 million. Working towards the end of roll-out in a Government term, you're talking about a significant sum, £300 million to £400 million, depending on uptake and so on. There are lots of different factors. But this was meant to be, and is being, done in a phased way, which is the only way that it can be done. It's not just because of the money; one of the big challenges that we are facing, and dealing with, is workforce. We visited a nursery in Rhyl last week, and there's real excitement about how to bring more young people into the profession, which we will need to do in significant numbers to roll out this childcare offer, which will transform lives.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, we've heard from Kiera Marshall very clearly that access to childcare is heavily dependent on where you live; Flying Start is a great example. So, you are declaring—your Government says—that its new offer will be flexible and responsive to parents' needs, which is great, but is that really going to take effect? We talked about rural-proofing earlier. Will rural-proofing enable this to happen in our rural communities? Can we truly see a levelling-up and a universality, as you said, of childcare in those most hard-to-reach areas like I represent?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: As you mentioned rural-proofing and Flying Start, I'll maybe bring those two together. Flying Start has done a great job in helping families who are struggling to make ends meet in some parts of Wales. I know of parts in my own constituency, and many others will have their own experiences of families who are outside Flying Start areas, in rural areas who are unable to get that kind of support. What we're doing in building on Flying Start, not cutting it, is making sure that we are expanding this universally to all people, universally to all areas, because we have identified this as something that could be the underpinnings of education, of job opportunities and tackling poverty. We're not setting simple targets for ourselves here. We're stretching ourselves because we think it's important, and rurality is very much a part of the mix.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 4. What assessment has the First Minister made of the impact of professional sport on the Welsh economy? OQ64617
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa asesiad y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o effaith chwaraeon proffesiynol ar economi Cymru? OQ64617

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Professional sport makes a significant contribution to the Welsh economy. It brings visitors into our communities, supports local businesses, creates jobs and showcases Wales to a global audience, at home and abroad. I'll take the opportunity to congratulate Elfyn Evans again on waving the flag in Sardinia on Sunday. But, from the Tour de France Grand Départ to Euro 2028, Wales has shown that it is able to attract world-class sporting events. What we need to do always is make sure that those events leave a lasting legacy for communities across Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister. I agree with you. Sport can have a huge impact on the economy, as we've seen in places like Swansea—when they made the Premier League, tens of millions of pounds put into the economy there—and here in Cardiff, when they were a part of the Premier League. We've seen success with Wrexham now, having an impact on their economy, in Newport, and with other sports as well, like when the Ryder Cup came to Wales, and we've seen it when the wrestling was in Cardiff. But what future plans has the Welsh Government got to encourage more of these large-scale events that can bring better, high-paying jobs during those periods and that can boost our hospitality industry, but not only to current areas that are seeing that—how about if we can attract more of these large-scale events to other parts of Wales yet to be showcased around the world?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I believe in the principle of seeing what we can do to attract events. We've got the Women's Champions League final as well coming to Cardiff. It's not always Government that delivers them. Government can be a facilitator. Government can be a conduit for making them happen. We want to work with others when they see opportunities to bring global sporting events to Wales. Like having overseas offices, it is all part of that—[Interruption.] It is all part of that work of raising Wales's profile on the world stage, and the benefits that flow from that are multiple. This soft diplomacy, plus the hard numbers of where we can attract, through sporting events, international inward investment, is something that we should embrace, all of us here, because Wales can only win from this.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Prif Weinidog, I'd like to focus on the people behind the sports. Every sporting journey is built on dedication, discipline and enormous personal sacrifice, whether or not an athlete ultimately reaches the highest level of success, or even achieves financial success. Being an elite athlete is a unique way of life because, for many, their lives are structured around training, competition, travel, performance targets, coaches and team mates, often from a very young age. Education and career opportunities can be shaped around that commitment too, making the transition out of sport particularly challenging. While just a small number go on to gain financial security, many athletes make significant sacrifices without that sustainable living that comes afterwards. Yet many do leave sport with valuable skills in leadership, resilience, discipline, teamwork and performing under pressure, skills that can only benefit the wider Welsh economy and inspire future generations. So, Prif Weinidog, what support is the Welsh Government providing to support athletes transitioning into sustainable careers when they leave professional sport?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Llywydd, I know the Member speaks from her own experience working in sports governance before being elected here. But I'd say that, through our investment as a Government in elite sports, we support partners, including Sport Wales and other governing bodies, to help athletes prepare for life beyond sport, through education, through training and through career development opportunities. There are so many of them—Welsh Athletics, Swim Wales, Hoci Cymru—they all support athletes to gain coaching, officiating and leadership qualifications alongside their sporting careers. Many former elite athletes go on to become coaches, performance managers, board members and ambassadors within their sports. The Football Association of Wales is particularly good at being a centre of excellence for preparing the coaches of the future, not just for Wales, but for other nations too. And developing that pipeline is key, I think, to ensuring that the skills, the experience and the inspiration gained through representing Wales or competing in elite sports continue to benefit our economy, our communities and our sporting success in future.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I'm a Swansea City Association Football Club supporter and I remember the effect that playing in the premiership, winning the league cup and qualifying in Europe had on the image of Swansea. I drove down Mumbles Road one Saturday morning and a huge crowd of Chelsea supporters were walking towards the city centre. They had stayed in Swansea overnight, paid for accommodation, food and drink, helping our economy. The Ospreys, when they have European games against French and English opponents, also generate a substantial number of overnight supporters, with the same effect. Does the First Minister agree with me that the success of professional sport is beneficial for our economy, and that Swansea needs Swansea City back in the premiership and a successful Ospreys team? [Laughter.]

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Right then, I'm going to have to be careful here. 'Yes' is the answer to the question. I have no doubt that professional sporting events, which happen week in, week out, of course, through professional sport in football and rugby, can bring huge, huge benefits, and supporting those hospitality sectors that support those coming to support their teams, that's something that we should encourage always.

Do I want to see Swansea City being promoted to the premier league? Absolutely, yes. As a Cardiff City Football Club fan, they can only go up if we go up as well. And let's make it Wrexham also. Because, genuinely, I think the success of Welsh football currently—. I see Jayne Bryant looking at me here—I wish Newport all the very, very best too, and all league of Wales teams. [Laughter.] But, no, I think the success of our football teams is something that we can all celebrate, whichever colour we individually choose to wear.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
First Minister, as you said, professional sport plays an important role in supporting local economies by creating jobs and generating investment in our communities. One good example is the expansion of the Novira Cymru Premier football league to 16 teams, with new branding, improved broadcasting and a stronger media presence, which has raised the profile and visibility of the league, which is indeed very welcome.

Now, this season, Haverfordwest County Association Football Club has adopted a hybrid model, combining full-time professional players with part-time players. The aim is to provide a pathway for local talent into senior football, while also further improving the club's competitiveness, building on its recent qualification for European competition, which has happened twice in recent years. So, in light of the economic impact that clubs can have on their communities, what further steps can the Welsh Government take to promote the Novira Cymru Premier football league and the clubs that actually compete in it, particularly in developing home-grown talent, strengthening their commercial profile and helping more Welsh clubs compete successfully on the European stage?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Llywydd, I hope you've built lots of time into this, because everybody wants to name their local football team now, I think. But I wish Haverfordwest well.

I'm quite excited about premier football in Wales. Currently, there's been a lot of investment and there seems to be a real vibrancy around football at its highest level in Wales. I congratulate the work that the Football Association of Wales are doing. We engage with the Football Association of Wales in many different ways in supporting grass-roots sport, and we are happy to engage in any way that could see the Welsh Government supporting and facilitating the kind of investment that I know the FAW are determined to bring into Welsh football.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 5. What progress has the First Minister made on improving timely access to NHS care? OQ64675
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa gynnydd y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud o ran gwella mynediad amserol at ofal y GIG? OQ64675

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Our programme for government commits us to cutting waiting lists and building a health and care service fit for the future. Backed by £145 million of additional investment, we're taking immediate action to reduce waits for diagnosis and treatment, while accelerating the wider transformation of services, with a stronger focus on prevention, care closer to home and the needs of individuals and communities.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, I'm sure you'll agree with me that when it comes to dentistry, it's important to drill into the data. Recent data shows that only 40 per cent of people were treated under an NHS dentist, a 40 per cent drop since 2020. It is very difficult for anybody now to access NHS dental treatment. Your own health Minister admitted in a committee recently that he faces a 60-mile round trip to see his dentist. When the flawed new dental contract came into force on 1 April, five practices in my area of Monmouthshire Torfaen stopped providing NHS care. Access to NHS dentists is absolutely vital, otherwise Wales will face more dental problems further down the road. What are you going to do about it, First Minister? Will you finally involve practising dentists to try and help solve this problem? The lack of accessibility to NHS dentists is now out of control.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
The lack of accessibility to dentists is something that deeply worries me. I lost my NHS dentist a long time ago, as many of us here have, I know. What we're in the process of doing now is reviewing the contract. We need to make sure that we have a system that works for the patient and for the dentist, who we want to work within the NHS system in Wales.

There's more beside that. We need to be making sure that we have that pipeline of dentists coming through the system. That is why work led by the now Minister for local government, when she was in opposition, to bring a new dental school to Wales is something that is so key. The problems in dentistry are plain for all to see. I do believe we have a window in which we can try to act now, but be in no doubt about the scale of the challenge that we face around dentistry, because of the legacy of a lack of attention to this over many years, I fear.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 6. What are the Welsh Government's plans for addressing poverty in this Senedd term? OQ64674
documents.text_cy: 6. Beth yw cynlluniau Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer mynd i'r afael â thlodi yn nhymor y Senedd hon? OQ64674

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Throughout our ambitious programme for government, we commit to take action to reduce financial pressures facing households, working to break the cycle of poverty that too many find themselves in. Our new child poverty strategy will set clear targets and milestones to drive ambitious, deliverable change. We'll also seek to introduce the Cynnal child payment pilot. This Government will help those in crisis, while taking longer term, strategic action to prevent people falling into poverty in the first place.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: It's fascinating that your answer did not explicitly state whether you're talking about absolute poverty or relative poverty, and they are very different metrics. Absolute poverty focuses on the welfare of the poorest people in our society, something I want to see all Governments focus on. The other, relative poverty, is in reality a type of inequality, focused on the gap in wealth between people, and that can be a very dangerous metric. As Margaret Thatcher said, those who focus on inequality above absolute poverty would rather the poor were poorer so long as the rich were even less rich, reducing the gap. First Minister, do you accept there is an important difference in the two measures of poverty? To avoid confusion in future, will you and your Government, when referencing poverty, state clearly whether you're talking about absolute poverty or the socialist obsession that is inequality?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I think the fact that the Member wants an academic discussion rather than a discussion about how we as a Government can really help those who are in dire need of that help from Government says a lot. The fact that he quotes Margaret Thatcher in an argument on tackling poverty speaks even further volumes. We have a series of measures that we have put in place. Our poverty strategy, setting the meaningful targets that the sector and others have called for, is going to be a really important part of that. We haven't had a trajectory for some years in Wales on where we need to go in terms of tackling poverty. What I know is that the problems are real. That's why the universal childcare offer cuts to some of the biggest challenges that families are facing, and why the Cynnal direct payment can be the beginnings of something that genuinely puts a safety net beneath some of our poorest families in Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 7. How will the Welsh Government support social prescribing capacity in Afan Ogwr Rhondda? OQ64651
documents.text_cy: 7. Sut bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi capasiti presgripsiynu cymdeithasol yn Afan Ogwr Rhondda? OQ64651

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: This Government is committed to supporting social prescribing across Wales, including in Afan Ogwr Rhondda, helping people to improve their health and well-being through community-based support and by focusing on prevention. As recently as yesterday morning, the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health, Nerys Evans, visited an excellent project for social prescribing that is nature based, namely Grow Well at the Dusty Forge in Ely, here in Cardiff. We are investing in an independent evaluation to assess outcomes for individuals, communities and front-line services and to try and better understand how social prescribing can improve well-being and support sustainable services.
documents.text_cy: Mae'r Llywodraeth yma wedi ymrwymo i gefnogi presgripsiynu cymdeithasol ledled Cymru, yn gynnwys yn Afan Ogwr Rhondda. Mae hynny'n golygu helpu pobl i wella eu hiechyd a'u lles drwy gymorth yn y gymuned a thrwy ganolbwyntio ar atal. Mor ddiweddar â bore ddoe, mi wnaeth y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Iechyd Cyhoeddus ac Ataliol, Nerys Evans, ymweld â phrosiect rhagorol presgripsiynu cymdeithasol sy'n seiliedig ar natur, sef Grow Well, a hynny yn Dusty Forge yn Nhrelái yma yng Nghaerdydd. Rydyn ni'n buddsoddi mewn gwerthusiad annibynnol i asesu'r canlyniadau i unigolion, cymunedau a gwasanaethau rheng flaen, ac i drio deall yn well sut y gall presgripsiynu cymdeithasol wella lles a chefnogi gwasanaethau cynaliadwy.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Thank you for your response, First Minister. For social prescribing to be effective, we not only need the ability to make referrals, but we also need a strong and sustainable network of community organisations that have the resources to be able to accept them. Recently, I met Kate from the Gilfach Goch Community Association, which provides a wide range of support to about 1,500 local residents, with the demand continuing to rise.

Institutions like this are exactly the sort of places people get referred to, but one of the concerns I hear again and again is that funding streams can lean heavily towards capital funding, with much less flexibility in terms of the revenue funding needed to pay staff, cover operational costs and keep services running. A building isn't much use if there aren't people and resources to keep the doors open and provide the services inside. 

So, could the Government consider how more flexibility could be built in between capital and revenue funding in grant programmes in the future, so that organisations like the Gilfach Goch Community Association have the capacity and stability they need to meet the growing demand, and so that—many large words here today—social prescribing leads to continuous support that underpins this Government's preventative agenda? Thank you.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch am eich ymateb, Brif Weinidog. Er mwyn i bresgripsiynu cymdeithasol fod yn effeithiol, nid yn unig mae angen y gallu i wneud atgyfeiriadau arnom, ond mae hefyd angen rhwydwaith cryf a chynaliadwy o sefydliadau cymunedol sydd â'r adnoddau i allu eu derbyn. Yn ddiweddar, cwrddais â Kate o Gymdeithas Gymunedol Gilfach Goch, sy'n darparu ystod eang o gymorth i dros 1,500 o drigolion lleol, gyda'r galw yn parhau i gynyddu.

Sefydliadau fel hyn yw'r union leoedd y mae pobl yn cael eu hatgyfeirio iddynt, ond un o'r pryderon rwy'n eu clywed dro ar ôl tro yw y gall ffrydiau cyllidol ogwyddo'n sylweddol tuag at gyllid cyfalaf, gyda llawer llai o hyblygrwydd o ran y cyllid refeniw sydd ei angen i dalu staff, talu costau gweithredol a chadw gwasanaethau i fynd. Ychydig o ddefnydd sydd i adeilad os nad oes pobl ac adnoddau i gadw drysau ar agor a darparu'r gwasanaeth ynddo.

Felly, a all y Llywodraeth ystyried sut y gellid ymgorffori mwy o hyblygrwydd rhwng cyllid cyfalaf a refeniw mewn rhaglenni grant yn y dyfodol, fel bod gan sefydliadau fel Cymdeithas Gymunedol Gilfach Goch y gallu a'r sefydlogrwydd sydd eu hangen arnynt i ddiwallu'r galw cynyddol, ac fel bod presgripsiynu—lot o eiriau mawr heddiw—cymdeithasol yn arwain at barhad cymorth sy'n sail i agenda ataliol y Llywodraeth hon? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Thank you. It's good to hear about the work of the centre in Gilfach Goch. I agree that social prescribing, done effectively, does depend on strong community organisations that are sustainable and have the capacity to meet ever-increasing demand. The voluntary sector is key to that Welsh model. I certainly accept that the pressures around short-term budgeting and the lack of flexibility on occasion in terms of staffing and running costs can create problems.

We as a Government will continue to work with partners and to consider how possible changes to funding arrangements in future could better support that capacity and the stability available to these organisations, so that they can deliver our preventative agenda. Because the Government doing this is not the whole story; the story is that the Government sets the tone, and we need partners to do that work on the ground.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch. Mae hi'n dda clywed am waith y ganolfan yn Gilfach Goch. Dwi’n cytuno bod presgripsiynu cymdeithasol effeithiol yn dibynnu ar sefydliadau cymunedol cryf a chynaliadwy sydd â chapasiti i ateb galw sydd yn cynyddu o hyd. Mae'r sector wirfoddol yn allweddol i'r model Cymreig yna. Dwi’n sicr yn cydnabod bod y pwysau yna o gwmpas cyllidebu tymor byr a diffyg hyblygrwydd weithiau o ran arian staffio ac arian rhedeg yn gallu creu problemau.

Mi fyddwn ni'n parhau fel Llywodraeth i weithio efo partneriaid ac i ystyried sut y gall newidiadau, o bosib, i drefniadau cyllido yn y dyfodol gefnogi yn well y capasiti a sefydlogrwydd sydd gan sefydliadau er mwyn iddyn nhw allu delifro ein hagenda ataliol ni. Achos nid y Llywodraeth yn gwneud hynny ydy'r stori gyfan; y stori ydy bod y Llywodraeth yn gosod y tôn, ac mae angen partneriaid arnom i wneud y gwaith ataliol ar lawr gwlad.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 8. What assessment has the First Minister made of whether the current learner travel framework is delivering fair access to education across Wales? OQ64650
documents.text_cy: 8. Pa asesiad y mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi'i wneud ynghylch a yw'r fframwaith teithio presennol i ddysgwyr yn darparu mynediad teg at addysg ledled Cymru? OQ64650

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Effective learner travel provision is vital to ensure that children and young people can access the education that they need. I understand there are also challenges for local authorities, given very real budget pressures. This is why we've committed to a joined-up approach to learner travel in our programme for government and why we've already delivered on our first 100 days commitment to review learner travel in Welsh-medium education in particular.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The statutory threshold remains 2 miles for primary schools and 3 miles for secondary pupils. In communities such as Islwyn, the reality of their journey can be very different, depending on the terrain, the roads and whether there is a genuinely safe walking route. Will the First Minister look at whether the current framework is producing fair and consistent outcomes for children across Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I certainly appreciate that journeys for pupils are different depending on their individual circumstances. We're looking at the existing framework in the context of the budgets available to us. The Deputy Minister for Transport has himself highlighted learner travel as one of his key priorities. We'll consider this as a Cabinet, because it does cut across portfolios.

I know that decisions are made on a local level by local authorities, some of whose decisions to deem walking routes safe do raise questions and anxiety. But these are decisions for those local authorities. It is for local authorities to assess whether a walking route is safe, taking account of the conditions learners would encounter on that journey to school at that time of day, and so on.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 9. What action is the Welsh Government taking to support survivors of childhood abuse who experience further trauma when accessing historical social work, health or police records? OQ64653
documents.text_cy: 9. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gefnogi goroeswyr camdriniaeth yn ystod plentyndod sy'n profi trawma pellach wrth geisio cael mynediad at gofnodion gwaith cymdeithasol, iechyd neu'r heddlu hanesyddol? OQ64653

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: For many survivors, accessing historical records is important in understanding their childhood, but the process can be deeply distressing. We know that. We are supporting public services to adopt trauma-informed approaches, so that people are treated with dignity, compassion and sensitivity. This work is reinforced through our trauma-informed Wales framework and our strategy for preventing and responding to child sexual abuse. Both recognise the lifelong impact of abuse and place survivors' voices at the centre of improvement.
documents.text_cy: I lawer o oroeswyr, mae cael mynediad at gofnodion hanesyddol yn bwysig er mwyn deall eu plentyndod, ond mae'r broses yn gallu peri gofid mawr. Rydyn ni'n gwybod hynny. Rydyn ni'n cefnogi gwasanaethau cyhoeddus i fabwysiadu dulliau mwy ystyriol o drawma, fel bod pobl yn cael eu trin efo urddas, tosturi a sensitifrwydd. Mae'r gwaith yma yn cael ei ategu gan ein fframwaith Cymru sy'n ystyriol o drawma a'n strategaeth ar atal ac ymateb i gam-drin plant yn rhywiol. Mae'r ddau yn cydnabod effaith gydol oes cam-drin ac yn rhoi lle canolog i leisiau goroeswyr wrth wella gwasanaethau.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister. Victims and survivors tell us that, when they raise concerns about victim-blaming language or missed opportunities to protect them within historical social work, health or police records, they are often told that these attitudes were simply a product of the time and would not be acceptable today. However, for survivors living with post-traumatic stress disorder, physical ill health and the lifelong consequences of abuse, the impact is very much felt today. Many access these records in an attempt to piece together their life story and to better understand their experiences, only to find that the files leave them with more questions than answers. For professionals, these may be historical records, but for survivors, the trauma is not historical at all. What more can the Welsh Government do to ensure survivors are met with recognition, trauma-informed support and meaningful acknowledgement of the harm these records can still cause?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We recognise that the language, the assumptions or professional judgments contained in some historical records can be distressing and certainly can compound the impact of past trauma. Through the trauma-informed Wales framework and that strategy for preventing and responding to child sexual abuse, we are supporting services to respond with dignity, with compassion, with sensitivity, recognising, as I say, that the effects of abuse can be lifelong. We're also continuing to support life journey work for children in care, care leavers and adopted children, helping them to understand their personal history and experiences in a way that is sensitive, that is meaningful and that, crucially, is centred on their voice. These are matters that the Government is determined to take steps forward on, for very good reason, because we are talking about people who face vulnerabilities, and they deserve to sense that support from Government in all ways.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Brif Weinidog.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: We'll move now to questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution. The first question is from Donna Cushing.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn nawr at gwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Effeithiolrwydd Llywodraeth a'r Cyfansoddiad. Cwestiwn 1, Donna Cushing.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: 1. Will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the proposed National Commission for Wales? OQ64628
documents.text_cy: 1. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet roi diweddariad ar y Comisiwn Cenedlaethol arfaethedig i Gymru? OQ64628

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: The Welsh Government is committed to establishing a national commission for Wales and is taking forward the final arrangements necessary for its establishment. I will make a further statement to Senedd Members in due course, setting out the commission’s remit, membership and next steps.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. Devolving the Crown Estate to Wales is very broadly and strongly supported all across the country. Every single one of our 22 unitary authorities in Wales have recently voted in favour of bringing powers over the Crown Estate to Wales. Since 2017, Scotland has had powers over its own estate, which lets the Scottish Government retain and reinvest the income generated. According to Crown Estate Scotland, in one 12-month period, it generated an economic impact of £2.1 billion and supported 17,000 jobs. We, on the other hand, are not so lucky. The profits generated from the Welsh part of the Crown Estate flow back to the UK Treasury, with a share allocated to the royal household. The income from retaining the full value of leasing our land and sea bed could be transformative for Wales, generating energy and reinvesting in our communities. Given that the demand is already so strong and supported all across Wales, what is the next step for making the case for devolution of the Crown Estate to Wales and making sure we get a fair settlement in line with Scotland's?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I thank the Member for the question. The case is very clearly made for the devolution of the Crown Estate. If you look over the past decade, there have been hundreds of millions of pounds of profits made by the Crown Estate in Wales. We believe that money should be invested in Wales and in Welsh energy and in supporting Welsh families and communities. The Welsh Government has established an expert group on the devolution of the Crown Estate and the future of the Crown Estate, which is building the evidence case. I expect a final report from the group to be published next summer. Then they will move forward to work on the broader issues of energy devolution.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: 2. What assessment has the Cabinet Minister made of the impact on Government effectiveness of the Welsh Government's relationship with trade unions? OQ64620
documents.text_cy: 2. Pa asesiad y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'i wneud o effaith perthynas Llywodraeth Cymru ag undebau llafur ar effeithiolrwydd y Llywodraeth? OQ64620

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: As a Government, we recognise the value that trade unions bring to Government effectiveness. They provide structures for meaningful dialogue, negotiation and problem solving, enabling early intervention that saves time and money. Social partnership ensures workforce voices are heard early in decision making and remains the most effective way to address Wales's challenges.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Thank you, Minister, for your response. You might have noticed I've written a number of times to you—I've kept your office busy—and I've written to your office a number of times via written questions, and I thank your office for supplying information on that. From that information gathered, it has shown that, over the previous Labour Government, over the course of five years, around £13 million was provided to trade unions. In addition to that information, it has also shown that they have also funded up to 10 equivalent full-time posts. What I do find a little bit concerning is that there's no definite time spent on trade union work and that of their civil service work. My question to you is, Minister, will your Government be spending any more taxpayers' money on political trade unions?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: As I said in my first response, this Government remains committed to social partnership. It is something that we believe in, in principle and on principle. There will be Members across this Chamber who have led organisations and who have managed organisations with trade unions and built effective relationships with those trade unions. We will make no apology for supporting trade unions, for working with them. There will be times, as everyone knows, when we will not see eye to eye on everything with those trade unions, but a strong and happy workforce is an effective workforce, and I'm proud to say that this Government will work with our trade union partners.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. First, the Reform UK spokesperson, Iain McIntosh.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Yn gyntaf, Llefarydd Reform UK, Iain McIntosh.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Before I address the Minister, I just wanted to correct the record on something the First Minister said earlier, when he suggested that all Reform Members want to take down the Welsh flag. I can't call that a lie, but I would like to say it's deliberately misleading, because we don't want to do that. I would like to suggest that he perhaps concentrates on his own Members, some of whom seem intent on merging the Welsh flag with the Palestinian flag. I'll leave that there. Thank you. [Interruption.]

To address the Minister: Cabinet Minister, how much taxpayers' money has the Welsh Government committed to pursuing Welsh independence, including establishing the new national commission and seeking powers to hold an independence referendum? Even a recent poll commissioned by the pro-independence organisation Yes Cymru found that only 32 per cent of likely voters would consider supporting independence. So, there is clearly no blanket support for independence across Wales at all. At a time when the NHS, our schools, councils and front-line services are under enormous financial pressure, do you really believe that this is an appropriate use of taxpayers' money, and will you please publish the full projected cost of pursuing this agenda over the course of this Senedd term?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Well, I welcome the Member to his new position on the Reform frontbench. Had he been at a previous question time, he would have heard me say from this position that this Government is committed to delivering on its priorities for the people of Wales—on childcare, on child poverty, on the economy, on educational standards and on tackling waiting lists. Those are our priorities. That mission is underpinned by standing up for Wales, and we make no apology for seeking devolution of the Crown Estate, for the very reasons we've heard outlined earlier, for improving our rail services, and for making our communities safer by devolving policing. That is our agenda as a Government, as I set out in my oral statement on the priorities on the constitution.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. You answered a question I didn't put to you, but, anyway, I'll try again with a different one. Mine was about devolution, but anyway—sorry, about independence. 

Cabinet Minister, how are Wales's taxpayers actually supposed to know whether the Welsh Government is delivering value for their money? Billions of pounds are spent every year across numerous programmes, projects and initiatives, but spending money is not the same as delivering results. So, will you publish clear performance data showing what every Welsh Government programme is supposed to achieve, how much it costs, whether it is on time, and, crucially, whether it is actually working? Now, when a programme repeatedly fails to deliver results or value for money, will you reform it or scrap it altogether, rather than continuing to pour taxpayers' money into something that simply isn't working?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: There's a simple answer to that question, which is 'yes', because, as a Government, we are committed to outcomes. We have been critical of previous Governments who have poured money into projects and focused on inputs and outputs rather than outcomes that people can feel in their daily lives across the country. Part of my role is to challenge and to work with every one of my Cabinet colleagues to look at those Government programmes, to ensure that we are both getting value for taxpayers' money and ensuring that we're delivering outcomes for people right across Wales, whether that's on childcare, on the economy, on education—change that people can feel.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Okay. Thank you for that one. Cabinet Minister, I would also like to know why does the Welsh Government keep creating more bureaucracy instead of reducing it. Since 2018, 16 new devolved public bodies have now been created, whilst only five have been replaced or abolished, but now your Government wants to actually create even more. Now, every new body means more boards, more senior executives, more administration and, unfortunately, more cost to the taxpayer. So, when are you actually going to start reducing the machinery of Government? Will you identify which arm's-length bodies duplicate work that is already being done elsewhere, publish what each one costs, and commit to merging or abolishing those that are simply not necessary? Government efficiency shouldn't mean managing even more bureaucracy; it really should mean having the courage to get rid of it if isn't working.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Again, I thank the Member for the question. This Government has a very limited set of bodies that it seeks to set up. There has been widespread debate about the national economic development agency. There is widespread consensus across this Chamber that the Welsh economy is not performing as it should, and an arm's-length, business-driven development agency is a clear way forward there. However, I share the Member's scepticism for the proliferation of bureaucracy, for more bodies for bodies' sake. You will be aware that the Government publishes the budget and the grant letter for every Government sponsored body on an annual basis. Where there are efficiencies to be gained, I will certainly pursue them. Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: The Welsh Labour spokesperson, Huw Thomas.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Huw Thomas.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Thank you, Llywydd. Many comments have been made over recent weeks on constitutional issues. I want to focus on what's important to the people of Wales, and that's why I want to ask questions on the programme for government.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Lywydd. Mae yna lot o sylwadau wedi cael eu gwneud dros yr wythnosau diwethaf am faterion cyfansoddiadol. Dwi eisiau ffocysu ar beth sydd yn bwysig i bobl Cymru, a dyna pam dwi am holi cwestiynau ar y rhaglen lywodraethu.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Minister, the programme for government, which you have overall oversight for, is full of references to collaboration and it's also very strong—there's a whole section on it—about supporting teachers. But, last week, an overwhelming majority of school leaders voted to support industrial action in response to your Government's priorities and policies. Ninety-three per cent of NAHT members voted, and 72.5 per cent of them indicated they would be prepared to take industrial action. Why does the Minister think the programme for government has been so poorly received by school leaders? Can you confirm that intensive negotiations with NAHT are now taking place, and what progress is the Government making?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I think what we're seeing across the public services in Wales is a legacy of a decade and more of austerity that has seen cuts and challenges, and public services that are genuinely facing crisis point. I am very pleased that my colleague the Minister for education has been engaging effectively with a range of teaching unions. There's been more progress with some than others. I said in my earlier answer that trade union colleagues and us will not always agree. Those negotiations are ongoing, and I'm sure we would all wish to see a positive conclusion to those negotiations. My colleague the Cabinet Minister for education has focused on raising standards in our schools, and if we are to achieve that, it must be done in collaboration and co-operation with both the teachers and those who lead our schools.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Diolch, Weinidog. I applaud the answer you gave earlier in response to Reform's attack on trade unions, and I should declare myself a member of many of them, including Unite, because I'm going to come on to this. You talk about social partnership, you talk about Government efficiency, and there's a clear link between both, but at your own party conference this weekend, you had a delegation of health visitors from Cwm Taf, who are Unite members, who've been on strike. They heard a political priority from the First Minister that he would resolve their dispute, and they believe he's lied. Those are their words—that he's failed to keep his promise. As the Minister responsible for keeping the Government's priorities, do you regret the First Minister's failure to keep his promise? We now have the longest running nursing strike in NHS Wales history. To secure efficiency of the NHS, what will you do to resolve the issue?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
As my colleague will know full well, the Cabinet Minister for health is responsible for the health service and our health priorities, and has set out our approach and our encouragement to all of those partners in the debate in Cwm Taf, to reach a negotiated conclusion. We very much hope that will happen at the soonest time possible.

The point more generally about the NHS is an important one. People right across Wales are currently being let down by a service that has not invested significantly enough in tackling waiting lists. We have invested, as the First Minister said earlier, £145 million in bringing down waiting lists, because the impact of that on individuals, on families, on workplaces right across Wales is unconscionable, and those are our priorities as a Government.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: The Welsh Conservatives' spokesperson, Sam Rowlands.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Sam Rowlands.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. As the Cabinet Minister for effectiveness, what actions are you taking to guarantee that your Cabinet colleagues are effectively ensuring value for money in the departments across the Welsh Government?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: One of the areas that we are looking at as a centralised Cabinet office in the Government is looking right across our Government priorities and ensuring that there is effective delivery on those and there is effective value for money. I know my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Finance has been engaging with Cabinet colleagues about their budgets for the year ahead, working closely with them to ensure that there is value for money at the heart of those programmes. Government effectiveness is about value for money, it is about delivering outcomes for people, and it comes back to the question posed earlier: if there are programmes that are not delivering measurable, tangible outcomes for people in communities right across Wales, then we should indeed reconsider them.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
Thank you for your response, Cabinet Minister. You'll know, in July, that your colleague the Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport announced that the Welsh Government will be setting up a new shadow broadcasting and communications authority as a first step in trying to pull powers over broadcasting away from the UK Government. And you'll know, of course, that broadcasting has never been devolved, so setting up the shadow authority is clearly an example of this Plaid Cymru Welsh Government working outside of its constitutional boundaries. And, of course, as the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution, I'm sure you were the first to object to these plans at the earliest opportunity.

At the same time, your colleague also announced that tens of thousands of pounds have been set aside to fund the shadow authority in its first year. And, of course, because it's not a devolved matter, there's no funding from the UK Government to enable this to happen, meaning every penny spent on the shadow authority has to be redirected from an area the Welsh Government does have responsibility for. So, Cabinet Minister, do you think that this is an effective use of taxpayers' money that the Welsh Government is spending tens of thousands of pounds on something it has no responsibility for?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I think if anyone had seen the evidence from colleagues in the media, in BBC and in S4C, to the culture committee in Westminster and in other places on the challenges facing the media landscape, and the very real challenges facing the media landscape right across Wales, they would understand that broadcasting in Wales would be in a stronger place if it was indeed devolved. That is why this Government is committed to the devolution of broadcasting, so that we can have effective media, so that we can have effective scrutiny of this Government, amongst other things. That is what we support, and we make no apology for supporting that.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: 3. What assessment has the Cabinet Minister made of how statistics can support more effective government and public sector decision making across Wales? OQ64626
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa asesiad y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'i wneud o'r modd y gall ystadegau gefnogi o ran gwneud penderfyniadau mwy effeithiol gan y llywodraeth a'r sector cyhoeddus ledled Cymru? OQ64626

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Diolch, Safa. Trustworthy statistics play a vital role in effective decision making across Wales. They help us understand where need is greatest, target resources effectively and judge whether outcomes are improving. As a Government, we are committed to using high-quality evidence to shape policy and delivery, and to publish clear outcomes that strengthen accountability.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Diolch, Cabinet Minister. Evidence-based decision making is central to delivering effective public service and ensuring the best use of public money. In healthcare, for example, we know that additional capacity can sometimes be needed to reduce waiting times. Audit Wales has highlighted that insourcing and outsourcing can help reduce long waits, but that it can also place additional pressure on NHS finances down the line, whilst opportunities remain to improve productivity within NHS services. So, Cabinet Minister, how is the Welsh Government ensuring that decisions on improving and delivering effective public services are not just informed by immediate cost savings or short-term deliveries, but also on sustainability, long-term outcomes and capacity building?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr. The Member, from her professional background, speaks clearly from experience. I believe there is more work to be done in the NHS on improving productivity. I also believe that throwing money at a problem as a sticking plaster is not a long-term solution. Decisions should be informed by evidence on outcomes, value for money and long-term sustainability, not simply the upfront costs. Health economics is an important part of that evidence base, helping decision makers understand what delivers the best outcomes from available resources. For example, health economics is being used in our work as a Government to bring care closer to home, often referred to as Community by Design, including community resource teams, virtual wards, integrated community hubs for health and social care.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Minister, good workforce data should, obviously, allow Governments to anticipate pressures rather than respond when they reach crisis point. How will your Government's data on recruitment, retention and workforce pressures to engage with our trade unions earlier actually help prevent some of those pressures ultimately escalating into industrial disputes? And talking of understanding our workforce, it is important, of course, for me to also reference that TUC Cymru has consistently gathered evidence about the experiences of workers in Wales because good policy obviously does start with good data. And I think that some of the mentions in relation to funding and social partnership—. Of course, Wales union learning fund funding provides funding for unions to encourage and support work-placed learning specifically, and it's about skills, and, of course, the TUC has very cleared referenced that 100,000 workers in Wales have benefited as a result of that funding in recent years.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr. Thank you to the Member for their question. I also pay tribute to the work that she did in a previous life with TUC Cymru, doing very important work on behalf of trade unions in Wales. The focus of the question on recruitment and retention is an important one in the health service. There is work on a workforce strategy being undertaken currently, both by Welsh Government and our colleagues in Health Education and Improvement Wales. Getting these data right and planning for the long term is crucial, because we need the right staffing in the right places, with the right mix of skills, in order to deliver long-term, sustainable success for our health service.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Good afternoon, Minister, and thank you to Safa for the question.
documents.text_cy: Prynhawn da, Weinidog, a diolch hefyd i Safa am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: You said in your response to Safa that trustworthy statistics and evidence is vital to the delivery of services, but that must also include listening to residents: 9,700 people in Powys have objected to the proposals ahead of them. But I also want to talk about a recent Healthcare Inspectorate Wales—and you've talked about that body—inspection of Gwaun Cae Gurwen Surgery. It found that 85 per cent of respondents rated their experience as 'poor', while 73 per cent did not feel listened to or involved in decisions about their healthcare—a very high proportion of patients for that practice, yet the inspection did not identify failings that fully reflected the level of dissatisfaction reported by patients. We know that Healthcare Inspectorate Wales can make recommendations and seek improvements, but there are questions about how much leverage sits behind those recommendations when services fail to improve. So, Minister, I really want to hear this answer—an answer, please: for more effective—

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: A question, please. [Inaudible.]
documents.text_cy: Cwestiwn, plis. [Anghlywadwy.]

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Yes, well, I'm pre-empting it. [Laughter.] For more effective public sector decision making, who has the power to ensure that clear evidence of poor service actually results in action?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
I thank the Member for the question and for highlighting some of those very local issues. Clearly, I'm not abreast of the precise nature of the issues in Gwaun Cae Gurwen, but if the Member would like to write to myself or my Cabinet colleague the Cabinet Minister for health, I'm sure we can look specifically at that.

I think there is a broader question here about how Government listens, takes concerns on board and what those avenues are for citizens right across the country to make progress when those concerns are not being listened to. We've heard various examples over the last hour or so from colleagues across this Chamber. It is something that we need to be clear about, and there is almost certainly a case for ensuring that that is as effective as possible, and it's one of those areas I'd be happy to look at.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: 4. What discussions has the Cabinet Minister had with the Cabinet Minister for Finance about delivering the Government's priority of working to improve levels of local procurement? OQ64638
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa drafodaethau y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'u cael gyda Gweinidog y Cabinet dros Gyllid ynglŷn â chyflawni blaenoriaeth y Llywodraeth o weithio i wella lefelau caffael lleol? OQ64638

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I have regular discussions with the Cabinet Minister for Finance on public procurement and its contribution to the Welsh economy. These discussions have included strengthening Welsh supply chains, improving access to opportunities for Welsh businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises and social enterprises, and increasing expenditure with Wales-based suppliers towards our 70 per cent ambition.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Thank you. I understand the importance of small businesses across the region being offered the opportunity to grow. Such growth in small businesses is critical to Wales for expanding employment opportunities and in terms of improving their productivity. I see local procurement as one such area of opportunity we should be encouraging and supporting. Therefore, how is your department tracking data to ensure that small and medium-sized businesses are successfully winning local contracts?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I thank the Member for the question. The point is very well made. We need to support our small and medium-sized enterprises, and in my view, we can do more as a Government to support those small and medium-sized enterprises. We track supplier and contract award data through our procurement systems and business intelligence reporting and supplier information, including SME status where available, is drawn from core procurement platforms and analysed through departmental dashboards. And what this enables us to do is monitor the participation and success of SMEs in winning contracts, assess trends over time and identify opportunities to increase access to public sector procurement for local businesses.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Claire Johnson-Wood.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I think my question's been answered. Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Thank you very much.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Thank you very much. Questions 5 and 9 are grouped. Question 5, Andrew R.T. Davies.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Mae cwestiynau 5 a 9 wedi'u grwpio. Cwestiwn 5, Andrew R.T. Davies.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: 5. How is the Cabinet Minister improving the delivery of the Government's policies? OQ64633
documents.text_cy: 5. Sut mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn gwella'r ffordd y mae polisïau'r Llywodraeth yn cael eu cyflawni? OQ64633

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: 9. What action is the Cabinet Minister taking to ensure that the Government is able to deliver its priorities for the people of Wales? OQ64613
documents.text_cy: 9. Pa gamau y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod y Llywodraeth yn gallu cyflawni ei blaenoriaethau i bobl Cymru? OQ64613

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
Presiding Officer, I understand that you have given your permission for questions 5 and 9 to be grouped.

In my role, I am focused on strengthening delivery across Government. Through our programme for government, we have set clear priorities. I am working to keep our efforts focused on those priorities, support joined-up working and maintain a clear focus on outcomes.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
Thank you, Minister. You highlighted there your priorities for delivery. During the election campaign, the now First Minister signed a letter that has been quoted many times in this Chamber regarding the health visitors' dispute in the Cwm Taf health board area. The key line in that letter was:

'upgrade all Band 6 health visitors to Band 7'.

There's no ambiguity there. The First Minister put his name to that letter. How are you getting on in delivering that pledge, or wasn't it a pledge, and it was misleading in its kindest form and an outright lie in its cruellest form?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: I think Members should be very careful in this Chamber of accusing colleagues of misleading the Chamber or—

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Well, have you delivered it?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: —misleading people. Our manifesto in the election, upon which we stood, upon which we fought the election and won the election, was based on prioritising bringing waiting lists down, on tackling waiting lists, prioritising the health service and developing productivity within the NHS. That is our priority and I will remain focused on that priority.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Cabinet Secretary, before entering this Senedd, I served our communities as a police officer, a teacher and I worked in the NHS. And I now see daily the immense pressures on hospitals, care homes, schools, businesses and front-line staff, especially in my constituency of Fflint Wrecsam. Our communities are closely linked, as you know, with Chester, Merseyside and the wider north-west, and people want practical improvements, not further constitutional distraction. Can you explain how this Government can claim to be effective if time and civil service capacity are spent pursuing constitutional ambitions while front-line public services remain under so much pressure in the area? Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
Thank you to the Member, and I'm very well aware of those thriving and important cross-border relationships in the north-east to the north-west of England, and also in the south-east to the south-west of England, and we support those important relationships.

I think the broader question relating to Government priorities is very clear in my mind. Our priorities are childcare, child poverty, the health service, schools and the economy. And on each of those, we intend to make progress. As the Cabinet Minister for the constitution, specifically charged with looking at constitutional issues, there are a range of areas—railways, the Crown Estate, policing—where I believe we can make progress, working with the UK Government, to deliver better services for people in Wales. And that remains the core focus of my work as a Government Minister and a core focus of our work as a Welsh Government—delivering better public services, whether it's in schools, health or education.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister. From childcare to business rates and support with the cost of living, this Government is already tackling the issues affecting people across Wales. I'm pleased to see us collaborating across different portfolios and reducing the work carried out in Government silos, which is something that has been needed for many years.

Now, as noted after the first 100 days, the Government is investing £100 million in tackling waiting lists in the NHS. It's vital for people across Wales, and, of course, in Gŵyr Abertawe, that the Government succeeds in tackling this huge problem, which has faced Wales for far too long. How will the Government ensure that these investments will provide the most effective, and, more importantly, continuous benefit, while delivering the programme for government? Thank you.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch, Weinidog Cabinet. O ofal plant i gyfraddau busnes a chymorth efo costau byw, mae'r Llywodraeth yn mynd i'r afael â'r problemau sy'n effeithio ar bobl hyd a lled Cymru. Dwi'n falch o'n gweld ni'n cydweithio ar draws gwahanol bortffolios a lleihau'r gweithio sy'n cymryd lle mewn seilos llywodraethol—rhywbeth dŷn ni wedi'i eisiau ers blynyddoedd maith.

Nawr, fel y nodwyd ar ôl y 100 diwrnod, mae'r Llywodraeth yn buddsoddi £100 miliwn i daclo rhestrau aros y GIG. Mae'n hynod o bwysig i bobl ar draws Cymru, ac, wrth gwrs, yng Ngŵyr Abertawe, fod y Llywodraeth yn llwyddo i fynd i'r afael â'r broblem fawr hon, sydd wedi wynebu Cymru ers llawer rhy hir. Sut bydd y Llywodraeth yn sicrhau bod buddsoddiadau fel hyn yn darparu'r budd mwyaf effeithiol, ac, yn fwy pwysig, parhaol, wrth gyflwyno'r rhaglen lywodraethu? Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
documents.text: Well, I thank the Member very much for the question, and I know that he has served the NHS for many years, and very effectively, in Swansea. There is a common theme to these questions, isn't there, that, with this additional funding that the Government's providing in childcare, in the health service, in the economy, we need outcomes for the people of Wales. And therefore, we need to look in great detail, as my colleague the Cabinet Minister for health has done, at what exactly those plans are. Are they plans that will deliver for the longer term? Do they ensure that there is collaboration between the health service and the care service provided through local authorities in order to ensure that the care package is complete, to ensure that some of the challenges in the system are addressed? Do they look, as our colleague earlier referred to, to the longer term with the workforce? So, all of those issues have to coalesce, and we always have to ask the question as to whether this money is going to deliver real change in the long term, not just in the short term. Thank you.
documents.text_cy: Wel, diolch yn fawr i'r Aelod am y cwestiwn, a dwi'n gwybod bod yntau wedi gwasanaethu'r NHS am flynyddoedd lawer, ac yn effeithiol iawn, yn Abertawe. Mae yna graidd i'r cwestiynau yma, onid oes, sef, gyda'r buddsoddiad ychwanegol mae'r Llywodraeth yma yn ei roi yng ngofal plant, yn y gwasanaeth iechyd, yn yr economi, mae angen canlyniadau i bobl.
