documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: We are all aware that Flying Start has some limitations. Its delivery can vary between local authorities and some families are left out, but the figures also show that the programme is one that families are using. So, in 2025-26, 98.5 per cent of eligible children were offered Flying Start childcare, with 85.4 per cent taking up that offer. The programme also delivered 211,000 health contacts to families across Wales. I'm concerned that, in moving towards a universal offer, we could lose sight of the targeted support that Flying Start provides to some of Wales's most disadvantaged families. Flying Start is more than childcare. It provides health visiting, parental support and help with speech, language and communication. So, will the Government give this Senedd a clear guarantee that, as the universal childcare offer expands, families currently benefiting from the wider Flying Start package will not lose vital services or see them diluted? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
I can absolutely give you that guarantee. Obviously, we do see a lot of families taking up the Flying Start offer, but, because it's limited geographically, there are many families, especially, we know, and there are more children in poverty who live outside Flying Start areas than actually live within Flying Start areas. So, this is why we're getting to grips with this model, because it isn't as effective as it could be.

This is a Government that has prevention at its heart in everything we do, and we absolutely recognise the contribution that the other elements, besides childcare, of Flying Start can provide. So, we recognise the huge contribution that that workforce, specifically on the non-childcare elements of Flying Start, provide and the importance of their work. So, the end goal is a childcare and an early years system that includes that preventative element that is easier for families to navigate and is clearer for partners to deliver, and is better able to support all children who need that intervention.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. The Reform UK spokesperson, Cristiana Emsley.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf y nawr ar lefarywyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Llefarydd Reform UK, Cristiana Emsley.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Deputy First Minister, I want to put you on notice from the outset: my questions today will be direct, so I respectfully ask you to address the questions rather than the person asking them.

In June, I wrote to you asking seven specific questions about the implementation and protection of women's sex-based rights in Wales. For the first time, I'm making that correspondence public. I asked what action your Government would take, what timetable you would follow, what instruction would be issued to public bodies, how women's sex-based rights would be protected in practice, and whether existing Government policies and guidance would be reviewed. You answered none of those seven questions directly. You are the Cabinet Minister responsible for equality and human rights. More than three months later, women are entitled to something more than general assurances. Women do not need another statement of principle; they need implementation. So, I'll ask you again: what has your Government actually done to implement women's sex-based rights in Wales? What has changed? What instructions have been issued? And by what date can women expect those rights to be protected consistently in practice?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: I think there's a fundamental misunderstanding here. The Equality and Human Rights Commission's code of practice for services, public functions and associations, which came into force on 5 August, means that we have to comply with our legal duties as a Government in respect of the Equality Act 2010. All bodies and service providers must themselves ensure that they're complying with the law. The Welsh Government of course expects all organisations to comply with the law, and we've clearly stated that. But the application then means careful consideration of the guidance in each situation. It is the responsibility of all the bodies and service providers to do that. The EHRC is the regulator to ensure that that is happening. They are responsible for monitoring compliance with equality and human rights law, ensuring that public authorities and other duty bearers meet their obligations. That isn't a responsibility of the Government.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
I'm sticking to the parliamentary code of practice, so I can't answer back. 

Deputy First Minister, in June, when I scrutinised the cost of your childcare—

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: You can. You can use your second question to do that.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: No, I've got a lot to go through today, but the law is the law and the judgment was issued on 16 July. So, hiding behind the EHRC is not going to cut it. [Interruption.] Shall I carry on with the second question?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Perhaps you can write to the EHRC to get clarity.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
In July, when I scrutinised the cost of your childcare commitment, you told this Chamber that my questioning baffled you. You even suggested that I should do a little bit of reading. Well, I remain baffled by your bafflement, because scrutiny eventually extracted something rather important. Your £375 million mid point became a potential funding range of £250 million to £500 million a year. I would be delighted to do a little bit more reading if your Government would finally publish the numbers. 

Deputy First Minister, let us leave the personal remarks behind and deal with the maths. What is your Government's latest fully modelled annual cost of delivering this commitment? What provisions are you asking the finance Minister to make in the forthcoming budget? What measurable benchmarks will you use to demonstrate that hundreds of millions of pounds of taxpayers' money has delivered the promised outcomes? Because the budget cannot be baffled by the maths and eventually the numbers have to add up.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
The figures will become clear in the forthcoming draft budget. You will be able to scrutinise that, the committees will be able to scrutinise that, and, of course, questions can be asked here of Ministers around their spending plans. 

You're asking about progress. In terms of the money that we've already spent, you'll know that there was £55 million in total allocated in the supplementary budget, which we have put to work in terms of expanding childcare and also with some capital grants to enable that to happen. So, 78.9 per cent of all two-year-olds are now offered childcare. Over 13,000 new two-year-olds have been offered a childcare place. Over 9,900 new two-year-olds attended their funded childcare, and over 2,000 of those children attended funded childcare in a Welsh-medium setting. 

As I said, we are now expecting, and I've had assurances from local authorities—. Many Members in the Chamber will probably see this happening now—their local authorities putting out that offer to parents of that age group. That's happening progressively in the way that we said it would. And then, by the end of the financial year, all two-year-olds in Wales, in every single local authority, will be offered 12.5 hours of funded childcare. I think there are quite a lot of statistics there for you.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Deputy First Minister, I have another piece of correspondence that I'm making public for the first time today: our exchange about the veterans and armed forces covenant. In June, I asked you for something very simple, namely measurable outcomes—has veteran homelessness fallen, have healthcare waiting times improved, are veterans finding employment more successfully, and are they accessing housing more quickly. Your response listed programmes, pathways, meetings and future work, but, Deputy First Minister, an activity is not an outcome. A programme existing is not evidence that it is working.

You told me that specific performance measures were something you were planning to raise with the UK Government, that the UK veterans strategy offered a potential way forward, and that further measures would be explored. We are now several months further on, so I'm asking you again: can you give this Senedd just one measurable outcome showing that veterans in Wales are materially better off because of the armed forces covenant on housing, homelessness, healthcare or employment? Will you now commit to publishing Welsh performance measures against which you, as the Minister responsible, can actually be held accountable?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
We are of course, as I'll reiterate again, absolutely committed to upholding the principles of the armed forces covenant, ensuring fair access to healthcare, housing, employment, education, skills and training for veterans and their families. The covenant is absolutely a social justice issue, reducing the potential for disadvantage from serving in the armed forces. By and large, service in the armed forces does lead to positive outcomes. I have submitted a legislative consent memorandum to the Senedd in respect of the Armed Forces Bill, including its plans for broadening the armed forces covenant.

The covenant, of course, doesn't specify outcomes or targets. It's about consideration. It's about understanding why there needs to be a specific way of working, to be adapted insofar as the services that veterans may come in contact with, to reduce that disadvantage and to afford a special consideration. It's clear that plans for broadening the armed forces covenant will impact the way we work, and so we need to consider policy now across a broad range of areas through that armed forces lens. We already have the ways and means to do that in other areas, of course, through our integrated impact assessment process.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Welsh Labour spokesperson, Lynne Neagle.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Lynne Neagle.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. I'd like to return to Flying Start. The First Minister said in response to my colleague Ken Skates yesterday that she wants to build on Flying Start and make it available everywhere. But as I said to you, and as we've heard previously today, Flying Start is so much more than childcare. It is that enhanced health visiting, speech and language, and parenting support. I would argue that that focus on strong parent-infant relationships is one of the most defining things you can do to transform lifelong good mental health from babies growing into adults.

The letter that went out from the Welsh Government to local authorities asking them not to use the term ‘Flying Start’ to describe Flying Start childcare has caused some concern. Indeed, there have been some suggestions, which I hope aren't true, that different local authorities have received different letters. I will ask you today: will you publish the letter that has gone to local authorities so that Senedd Members can understand what local authorities are being told about Flying Start?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
I just want to reflect first of all that there seems to be the suggestion that there's some kind of malign motivation behind the fact that we want to evolve this model, and there absolutely isn't. Local authorities, of course, have been engaged with us from the very beginning. There’s a WLGA representative on the expert group, and has been from the early days of this Government, because we started work on this commitment, as you would expect, immediately after the Cabinet was formed. They have always been fully in the loop.

As regards the moving away from that model, that's absolutely not what this is about. It's about evolving what it is. The main reason why we want to call something Welsh Government-funded childcare is for the very reason, as I outlined earlier, that people, now we’re making a universal offer, don't think they're eligible, because they're so used to the Flying Start geographical cliff edge that means that somebody in one street is eligible and somebody on the other street isn't. So, what we wanted to do in the promotion of our rolling out of universal childcare is make that clear. That was the sole motivation: it was a communication to make it clear to parents that they were now eligible for that universal offer.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you for that clarification. I think it would be useful if you could commit to publishing the letter for transparency. I don't think anybody is suggesting malign intent; I and others are worried about a programme that provides a package of support for babies at a really critical time in their lives. You've talked about evolving the programme, and I recognise what's been said about the number of children living in poverty that aren't able to access it, but, for me, the solution to that is to look at how it's delivered, rather than to alter the four-element basis of Flying Start. When you talk about evolving Flying Start, is it your intention to offer that range of services to more children by looking at how that is delivered? What assurance can you give that nobody who is receiving that service now will lose it, and that, actually, more people will have the opportunity to access that range of support in that critical first 1,000 days?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: That is absolutely our intention. You will know, as the former Chair—. I think you conducted an inquiry when you were Chair of the Children, Young People and Education Committee in the Senedd before last. I think you did an inquiry on outreach and on how that approach wasn't reaching all those in need. So, I know that you understand this well. We've used that Flying Start model as the current vehicle for the first phase of our expansion of childcare, but, of course, we have to make sure that the support that is available is available for all children, for all the reasons that your committee inquiry pointed out. At the same time as delivering that universal childcare offer, we have to look at options to enhance the early years support that we're providing, to make sure it does get to all those children. The majority of children in poverty in Wales do not live in Flying Start areas, and therefore are not able to avail themselves of it. When I say 'enhance', that would mean that the children within those Flying Start areas who are currently receiving that support absolutely will not be losing out.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Welsh Conservative spokesperson, Natasha Asghar.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Natasha Asghar.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Thank you so much, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, many households across Wales are struggling with rising living costs, yet too often the response from your Welsh Government is to request more powers and expand dependency, rather than creating opportunity. Recent debates around welfare reform and our ballooning benefit bill have highlighted the need to ensure that support reaches those who genuinely need it, whilst also helping others into sustainable employment. At the same time, Wales continues to have some of the lowest wages and highest levels of economic inactivity in the United Kingdom.

My Welsh Conservative colleagues and I argue the best route out of poverty is through lower taxes, economic growth and job creation, not an ever-growing reliance on the welfare state. Cabinet Minister, what assessment has the Plaid Cymru Government made of whether your anti-poverty policies are actually reducing long-term welfare dependency rather than simply managing or, at worst, masking the symptoms of poverty? Thank you.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Diolch. The Member is absolutely right as regards economic prosperity. Making sure that we have well-paid jobs and jobs that pay fairly and have fair work conditions is absolutely key to making sure that we can lift families out of poverty. But I do reject the narrative around dependency on benefits. People are eligible for those benefits because their income is currently not sufficient to make sure that they are able to live with dignity and meet their essential needs. I think there is a fundamental difference of values and principles between us on this. We will absolutely make sure that every penny that this Government spends—and, obviously, the Member knows that welfare policy is not devolved to Wales—goes to those who most need that support. And of course, we will not be quibbling about who is eligible for that support. If they are in need, if they are in poverty, if they are disabled and need our help, then we will help them.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Thank you for that response, Cabinet Minister. Tackling child poverty is one of your Government's key stated priorities. However, despite nearly three decades of Labour-led Governments here in Wales, some that your party even helped prop up, too many families remain dependent on benefits, foodbanks and emergency support. Your own portfolio includes responsibility for co-ordinating measures to tackle child poverty and engagement with UK Government on such matters. Yet many working families tell us that what they need is not another strategy or warm words—they need better paying jobs, affordable childcare and stronger economic growth.

The Welsh Conservatives have proposed such measures by extending free childcare, reducing the tax burden on working households to ensure that they keep more of what they earn, whilst also calling for a dedicated poverty action plan, focusing on children and fuel poverty. Given the continued rise in reliance on the welfare state amongst many Welsh households, can you, Cabinet Minister, explain how your Government's approach differs from treating poverty after it occurs, instead of addressing the actual cause that keeps families trapped with it in the first place?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Well, I'm glad that you agree with me and I hope you were listening carefully to the action we are taking on affordable childcare. That's why it's one of our main priorities as a Government and one of the main policies that, of course, I'm working on. It's a transformational, complex policy, but we absolutely know that it is fundamental to making sure that we can make those costs less for families and also give them the opportunity to be able to get back into the labour market and also increase their hours and get back into training and education.

On the point on how we're doing things differently, well, I have already said and set out, and reiterated this in my scrutiny session in committee last week, that I am not going to be throwing the baby out with the bath water as regards the child poverty strategy. But I do think that it needs a tighter focus and I do think that it needs measurable targets and milestones for us to make sure that what we are doing is having the desired effect and the intended effect.

So, I have already started work on developing and focusing in on what that more honed child poverty strategy can look like, and, as I said, including thinking about how we can evaluate as we go along, making sure we measure our progress. So, we will be working on that, we're developing it with stakeholders, considering, then, how to report on that progress to show what impact we are having. And I've already met with our external reference group and I've also met across Cabinet as well. We've got a cross-Cabinet taskforce on this very issue to make sure that we are aligned on our ambitions for that strategy and the types of targets we think will be useful to guide our work.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: 3. Will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the roll-out of the Welsh Government’s childcare offer in Powys? OQ64599
documents.text_cy: 3. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet roi diweddariad ar gyflwyno cynnig gofal plant Llywodraeth Cymru ym Mhowys? OQ64599

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you very much for the question. Using the additional funding we announced earlier this year, I am delighted that Powys is able to roll out the first phase of the Government funded childcare offer of 12.5 hours of quality childcare for all two-year-olds from January 2027.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn. Gan ddefnyddio'r cyllid ychwanegol y gwnaethon ni ei gyhoeddi yn gynharach eleni, rwyf wrth fy modd bod Powys yn gallu cyflwyno cam cyntaf y cynnig gofal plant a ariennir gan y Llywodraeth o 12.5 awr o ofal o ansawdd i bob plentyn dwy oed o fis Ionawr 2027.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you very much for that positive update. There is always a concern in mid Wales that everything goes to urban or city areas. An assurance, therefore, that our rural areas will also benefit from this important development in childcare would be appreciated. Thank you very much.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am y diweddariad positif yna. Mae gwastad yn bryder yn y canolbarth fod pob dim yn mynd i'r ardaloedd trefol neu ddinesig. Byddai cael sicrwydd, felly, bydd ein hardaloedd gwledig yr un mor gymwys ac yn elwa o'r datblygiad pwysig yma ym maes gofal plant yn cael ei werthfawrogi. Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you. Yes, flexible childcare is crucial, I think, in order to support families with the cost of living, across Wales and in every area, in order to enable parents, as I mentioned, to take up more opportunities to work, to study or to increase their hours, and, of course, to give the best possible start to every child too. So, we are developing that childcare offer, and the priority, as I mentioned, was the offer of 12.5 hours for all children across Wales—and Powys has demonstrated that they will be making progress on that very soon, so I am delighted. And the applications system is expected to open to all families in Powys by the end of November.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Ie, mae gofal plant hyblyg yn hanfodol, dwi'n meddwl, er mwyn cefnogi teuluoedd gyda chostau byw, a hynny ar draws Cymru ac ar draws pob ardal, er mwyn galluogi rhieni, fel roeddwn i'n sôn, i fanteisio ar fwy o gyfleoedd i weithio, i astudio, neu gynyddu eu horiau nhw, ac, wrth gwrs, er mwyn rhoi'r dechrau gorau hefyd i bob plentyn. Felly, rŷn ni'n datblygu'r cynnig gofal plant yna, a'r flaenoriaeth, fel roeddwn i'n sôn, oedd cynnig y 12.5 awr yma i bob plentyn ar draws Cymru—ac mae Powys yn dangos eu bod nhw'n mynd i fod yn gwneud cynnydd ar hynny yn fuan iawn, felly, dwi wrth fy modd. Ac mae disgwyl i'r system geisiadau yna agor i bob teulu ym Mhowys erbyn diwedd Tachwedd.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. I welcome the principle of extending childcare, but there does seem to be a rather large gap between announcing an entitlement and families actually benefiting from it. Powys County Council has itself estimated that the parents of more than 1,000 young children in the county could be missing out on free or reduced-cost childcare. And, of course, in a county as large and rural as Powys, eligibility is only half the issue. There also has to be a suitable provider within a reasonable distance of where a family lives. So, Cabinet Minister, as you roll out this offer, what are you doing to ensure that Powys County Council not only identifies those families who are entitled to support, but has sufficient childcare provision for them actually to use it?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you very much for that supplementary question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn am y cwestiwn atodol yna.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: We are committed to ensuring that childcare expansion works for families in all parts of Wales, and that's including rural communities, where provision can be more dispersed and can be more fragile. So, we already have some flexibility in the system through guidance, through funding and local authority planning. But we are, as a part of this expansion programme, actively looking at what more can be done to ensure childcare hours and transport solutions and capital investment all respond to the specific needs of rural communities. So, local authorities use childcare sufficiency assessments and annual action plans to identify those gaps in provision, including those rural challenges, and we continue to support practical solutions, then, such as co-locations with schools and community hubs. We also recognise that childminders are really important as well in rural communities, and so we're working with partners, including Cwlwm, to support workforce development, business sustainability and provider capacity.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: 4. What assessment has the Cabinet Minister made of the impact of the closure of Caerphilly post office? OQ64598
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa asesiad y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'i wneud o effaith cau swyddfa bost Caerffili? OQ64598

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Post office services play a vital role in supporting communities. These matters, of course, are reserved and are the responsibility of the UK Government, and that Government has stated that their aim is to retain as many branches and services as possible.
documents.text_cy: Mae gwasanaethau swyddfeydd post yn chwarae rôl hanfodol wrth gefnogi cymunedau. Mae'r materion hyn, wrth gwrs, wedi'u cadw'n ôl o fewn cylch cyfrifoldeb Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol, ac mae'r Llywodraeth honno wedi datgan mai ei nod yw cadw cymaint o ganghennau a gwasanaethau â phosibl.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Minister, can I thank you for your response? I, along with the leader of Caerphilly County Borough Council, have taken part in direct meetings with the Post Office to secure a suitable replacement in the town centre, but we are encountering a wall of excuses. The reason given by the Post Office as to why alternative sites are unsuitable do not stack up, because the excuse is that they are simply unsuitable—one site, across the road from the post office that had been there, to my knowledge, for at least 73 years, was because there is unsuitable parking. Minister, can I please ask you if you could commit to making direct representations to the Post Office executive to challenge these reasons for site rejections? We do need transparency on when the town centre will finally get its service back. I do feel that if the local Senedd Member—sorry, one of the local Senedd Members—and the leader of council can't get answers, I'm sure, they may listen to you, Minister. I know that I certainly would. [Laughter.]

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you, Lindsay, for the question. First of all, I want to acknowledge the concern when a community loses services. I know a number of us have seen this in our communities over the years, on the high street in terms of banks specifically, and, in the same way, sometimes, when post office services come to an end.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Lindsay, am y cwestiwn. Yn gyntaf oll, rwy'n moyn cydnabod y pryder pan fo cymuned yn colli gwasanaethau. Dwi'n gwybod bod nifer ohonom ni wedi gweld hyn yn ein cymunedau dros y blynyddoedd, ar y stryd fawr o ran banciau yn benodol, ac, yn yr un modd, weithiau, pan fo gwasanaeth post yn dod i ben.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: I just want to let the Member know that I actually met with the Post Office, with Post Office Ltd, yesterday. Again, as I said, they provided reassurance to maintain the network, as is their duty. I'm pleased to say that the Post Office Ltd confirmed to me that they have—because I did raise this topic specifically around post office services in Caerphilly—received expressions of interest to run the post office service in Caerphilly, and these are now currently being reviewed. So, that process, from expressions of interest to being, typically, open, takes up to six months. So, I hope that that will give your constituents assurance that we, hopefully, will see that post office service resume in your area.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: I thank the Minister for the answer there. The other concern that people are passing to me in terms of post office closures—whether it's Caerphilly or throughout the constituency—is, once the post office closes, it's the lack of being able to get ID, identification; it's the additional services that the post office uniquely provides to communities. I appreciate what you said on Caerphilly there, but what about other parts of Wales and my constituency that have lost that service, and now people are unable to get identification, because of simple things like the proofreading, the assistance, that the post office provides? What help can the Welsh Government provide to constituents there?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
I fully recognise those concerns. I'm sure that they are familiar to us all. Those services are crucial to our communities, particularly for people who perhaps can't use public transport or there is no transport available to take them to the next town. They are an important part of our town centres and high streets, and that is the Government's view, most certainly.

But, again, issues related to post offices are not devolved to Welsh Ministers. As I mentioned in an earlier response, the UK Government's commitment to post offices includes plans to retain the size of the network as it is, and that means looking for new businesses to offer those services when individual post offices close. But it also includes a commitment to locate post offices in town centres, where possible. Because, as I said, I agree—we know that post offices increase the number of visitors to the high street, as well as providing those crucial services.

Our programme for government does include a commitment to look at those options to rejuvenate our town centres, and that links to our work in terms of the town-centre taskforce that we've established. So, I'm sure that ensuring that post offices can be part of vibrant high streets could be part of that work too.
documents.text_cy:
Rwy'n cydnabod yn llwyr y gofidiau yma. Dwi'n siŵr, eto, eu bod nhw'n gyfarwydd i ni i gyd. Mae'r gwasanaethau yn rhai hanfodol iawn i'n cymunedau ni, yn enwedig i bobl sydd, efallai, ddim yn medru defnyddio, neu does yna ddim argaeledd, trafnidiaeth gyhoeddus ac yn y blaen, er mwyn mynd i'r dref nesaf. Maen nhw'n rhan bwysig o'n canol trefi a'n strydoedd mawr, a dyna yw safbwynt y Llywodraeth, yn sicr.

Wrth gwrs, eto, dyw materion sy'n ymwneud â swyddfeydd post ddim wedi eu datganoli i Weinidogion Cymru. Fel y soniais i yn yr ateb cynharach, mae ymrwymiad Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol i swyddfeydd post yn cynnwys cynlluniau i gadw maint y rhwydwaith fel y mae, ac mae hynny'n golygu chwilio wedyn am fusnesau newydd i gynnig y gwasanaeth pan fydd swyddfeydd post unigol yn cau. Ond mae hefyd yn cynnwys ymrwymiad i leoli swyddfeydd post yng nghanol trefi, lle y bo'n bosibl. Achos, fel roeddwn i'n dweud, dwi'n cytuno—rŷn ni'n gwybod, onid ydyn ni, fod presenoldeb swyddfa bost yn cynyddu nifer yr ymwelwyr â stryd fawr, yn ogystal, wrth gwrs, â darparu'r gwasanaethau hanfodol yna.

Mae ein rhaglen lywodraethu ni yn cynnwys ymrwymiad i archwilio'r opsiynau yna i adfywio canol ein trefi, felly, wrth gwrs yn gysylltiedig â'n gwaith ni o ran y tasglu canol trefi rŷn ni wedi ei sefydlu. Felly, dwi'n siŵr y byddai sicrhau bod swyddfeydd post yn gallu bod yn rhan o strydoedd mawr bywiog yn gallu bod yn rhan o'r gwaith yna.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: 5. What is the Cabinet Minister doing to tackle the unique rural challenges associated with child poverty in Ceredigion Penfro? OQ64603
documents.text_cy: 5. Beth mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn ei wneud i fynd i'r afael â'r heriau gwledig unigryw sy'n gysylltiedig â thlodi plant yng Ngheredigion Penfro? OQ64603

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: We recognise that rural families can face additional barriers, including restricted access to employment, services and transport, as well as higher costs. That is why our programme for government includes a commitment to legislate for rural-proofing, helping to deliver better outcomes for children living in poverty in rural areas.
documents.text_cy: Rŷn ni'n cydnabod bod teuluoedd mewn ardaloedd gwledig yn gallu wynebu rhwystrau ychwanegol, gan gynnwys mynediad mwy cyfyngedig at gyflogaeth, gwasanaethau a thrafnidiaeth, ynghyd â chostau uwch. Dyna pam mae ein rhaglen lywodraethu yn cynnwys ymrwymiad i ddeddfu ar gyfer prawfesur gwledig, er mwyn helpu i sicrhau canlyniadau gwell i blant sy'n byw mewn tlodi mewn ardaloedd gwledig.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Diolch, Cabinet Minister. A 2023 report by the Bevan Foundation found that Ceredigion ranks second in child poverty levels across Wales, with Pembrokeshire not far behind. Crisis has also highlighted that many families in my constituency face significant gaps between their incomes and essential living costs, leaving them at greater risk of poverty and financial hardship.

Whilst child poverty exists across Wales, it's often less visible in rural and coastal constituencies. One example in my constituency is Aberporth, a beautiful and vibrant village that many Members might know as a holiday destination, but also where one in four children live in poverty. In these communities, community action can make a real difference to people's lives—for example, the incredible range of activities that are run from the renovated Aberporth village hall that provide not just practical support, but friendships and social support that are invaluable to people.

So, will the Cabinet Minister consider what more can be done to strengthen our community infrastructure as part of your efforts to address child poverty?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Thank you very much. I think that using that example you used there in terms of Aberporth, somewhere that I'm sure a number of us have visited—a very beautiful place, a pretty place, but there is something hidden, isn't there? And Welsh Government recognises that rural poverty quite often is less visible than poverty in our towns and cities, but it's no less real. We are determined as a Government to ensure that children and families in rural communities have the support they need.

Every child in Wales, wherever they may live, should have the same opportunity to succeed. So, we want to ensure that our commitment in terms of our policies shows that, and that we take that into consideration in everything that we do. So, we recognise that many families are facing specific challenges, as I've mentioned earlier, in terms of lower pay and higher transport and energy costs, and so on, and also sometimes it's difficult to access the services and support they require.

So, that's why we have ensured that support is available to families throughout Wales in our tackling poverty programme, which is worth about £5 million and includes that specific support for rural communities and centres, such as the Member mentioned, to plan and to help those who are facing the greatest financial pressures.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr. Dwi'n meddwl bod defnyddio'r enghraifft yna y gwnaethoch chi ddefnyddio fanna o ran Aberporth, rhywle dwi'n siŵr bod nifer ohonom ni wedi ymweld ag e—lle hyfryd, lle mor bert, ond mae yna rywbeth cudd, yntefe? Ac mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cydnabod bod tlodi gwledig yn aml yn llai gweladwy na thlodi sydd yn ein trefi a'n dinasoedd ni, ond dyw e ddim yn llai real. Rŷn ni'n benderfynol fel Llywodraeth o sicrhau bod plant a theuluoedd mewn cymunedau gwledig yn cael y cymorth sydd ei angen arnynt.

Dylai pob plentyn yng Nghymru, lle bynnag maen nhw'n byw, gael yr un cyfle i lwyddo. Felly, rŷn ni eisiau sicrhau bod ein hymrwymiad o ran ein polisïau yn arddangos hynny, a'n bod ni'n cymryd hynny i ystyriaeth ym mhopeth rŷn ni'n ei wneud. Felly, rŷn ni'n cydnabod bod llawer o deuluoedd yn wynebu heriau penodol, fel rydw i wedi sôn yn gynharach, o ran enillion is a chostau teithio ac ynni uwch, ac yn y blaen, ac mae'n anodd hefyd weithiau cael mynediad at y gwasanaethau a'r cymorth maen nhw eu hangen.

Felly, dyna pam rŷn ni wedi sicrhau y cymorth yma i deuluoedd ledled Cymru yn ein pecyn cymorth trechu tlodi, sydd yn werth bron £5 miliwn, sy'n cynnwys y cymorth penodol yna i gymunedau gwledig a chanolfannau, fel yr oedd yr Aelod yn sôn amdanynt, i gynllunio a helpu'r rhai sy'n wynebu'r pwysau ariannol mwyaf.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you to Anna for the question. Deputy First Minister, on 22 September the First Minister told the Senedd that Cynnal was going to be piloted and it is happening, yet your programme for government says that you will 'seek to' pilot Cynnal. The distinction there really matters, Minister, because 'we're going to' is a commitment, while 'seek to' is not. So, for families in Ceredigion Penfro, I have two straightforward questions: will Ceredigion Penfro be included in the Cynnal pilot? And on your childcare commitment, on what date will families in Ceredigion Penfro be able to access the allocated funded hours per week? Families need to know not just what this Government intends to do, but when they will actually receive the support. Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
I'd like to clarify the reason why it says 'seek to pilot': it's because there's a very important decision that needs to be made by the UK Treasury, because what we don't want to do with Cynnal is make families worse off. We want to make them better off. So, that means the UK Treasury has to give a benefit and tax disregard. We heard some encouraging signs in an interview with Andy Burnham during the Labour conference on that. It's something, of course, that I've been pressing on with the UK Treasury, and so of course has the Cabinet Minister for Finance, because we want them to allow us to—. We have the powers to pilot the payment, but what we don't have are the powers over that tax and benefit disregard. So, that's why we are saying 'seek to pilot', because we don't have—. We wouldn't want to do something if we didn't have that assurance from UK Treasury that it wouldn't make families worse off. 

We are preparing to implement that pilot. We've commissioned an expert team to help lead on that design, thinking about then, obviously, again, the monitoring and evaluation. We want it to be effective. We've already met four times, and we're meeting again in a few weeks' time. It's been an intense piece of work. It's an intense process because we do want to make sure that we can get this payment out to families—a payment that has proven so successful in Scotland in lowering rates of child poverty—out to children who are in need as soon as we possibly can.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: And the final question, question 6, Carrie Harper.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: 6. What action is the Welsh Government taking to tackle child poverty? OQ64596
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i fynd i'r afael â thlodi plant? OQ64596

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Tackling child poverty is central to our programme for government. We are already delivering on our commitments on free school meals and the childcare offer, as well as developing our Cynnal child payment. Our new child poverty strategy will include clear, measurable targets to improve outcomes for children and families.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
Diolch yn fawr iawn. In my constituency of Fflint Wrecsam, there are currently 12,786 children living in poverty. In Caia Park, where I live, we have one of the highest levels of deprivation, not just in the constituency, but one of the highest levels across Cymru. We all know that children who grow up in poverty are far more likely to find themselves categorised as not in education, employment or training later in life, becoming trapped in a cycle of poverty. It's vital that we break that cycle, isn't it, and ensure that every child gets a fair chance to succeed.

We know that progress is possible. The only nation in the UK where child poverty rates are improving is Scotland. And Scotland acts as an example to all of us in Cymru in terms of what can be achieved when Governments have the tools to do more for their own people. The Scottish child payment and their additional powers on welfare are making a tangible difference there. So, my question in many ways follows on from Paul Marr's, which you very eloquently just answered, in terms of the progress the Government is making in implementing Cynnal, our Welsh child payment pilot, and ensuring that under a Plaid Cymru Government, child poverty statistics finally start moving in the right direction.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text: Thank you very much for that question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
documents.text:
We are, as I said, already making progress on the preparation of that implementation of the Cynnal pilot, the Welsh child payment. We have heard views and evidence on how such a payment could make a real tangible difference to families, so we want to make sure that we design a pilot that can demonstrate that. That expert group I was referring to earlier, which I'm co-chairing with Steffan Evans from the Bevan Foundation, is meeting regularly, as I said, to help with that design, help with the implementation, so it launches on a real sound and evidence-based footing as soon as that preparation is complete.

On the tax and benefit disregards, I met with Baroness Sherlock, who's Minister of State in the Department for Work and Pensions, to discuss our ambitions around child poverty more broadly, and also the Cynnal payment. She has agreed to work with us to explore how we can ensure those payments do not impact on tax and benefits. And also, on the implementation piece, it's around how we can share DWP data as well, for delivery purposes. So, our officials are working together to take this forward.

documents.text: Thank you, Deputy First Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Ddirprwy Brif Weinidog.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: We'll move now to item 2, questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability. Question 1, Natasha Asghar.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 2, cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd. Cwestiwn 1, Natasha Asghar.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: 1. What action is the Welsh Government taking to protect community green spaces in Newport and Islwyn? OQ64574
documents.text_cy: 1. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i ddiogelu mannau gwyrdd cymunedol yng Nghasnewydd ac Islwyn? OQ64574

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Obviously, our community green spaces matter for people, for nature and the places where people live. We are investing in programmes that protect and improve them, including in Newport and Islwyn. I want to build on that work, particularly in communities where access to good-quality green space is most limited.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Thanks so much for your response. Cabinet Secretary, over the summer, I met up with a group of residents in Newport who are concerned that they are poised to lose the only community green space in their area, and a plan has been drawn up by Newport City Council. Constituents of mine, particularly dog walkers, children and families, make full use of a parcel of land just off Ruskin Avenue in Rogerstone North, but that could soon come to an end if the local authority rubber-stamps the plan to turn the community green space into an allotment site. To be clear, no-one is against allotment sites or developments, but not only would that take away a vital community asset, it's simply not the right site, with fears about even more traffic in the area, as residents are already experiencing and facing that sort of problem.

Cabinet Minister, more than 200 residents have signed a petition calling for the site in Rogerstone North to be ruled out. I've written to the council myself highlighting the residents' concerns and calling for the site to be dropped, and the decision now rests with the local authority. So, will you join me in putting pressure on Newport council to protect this community green space by removing it from the authority's allotment plans?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Thank you for raising this issue. I am aware, actually, of the concerns that residents have raised on this particular issue. You will also know that this is a matter for Newport City Council; it wouldn't be appropriate for me to intervene in what is and should be a local decision. But I think the wider principle here is important. Communities need both accessible green spaces and opportunities to grow food. But it is important, of course, that those local decisions have to reflect the value that people place on these spaces, and access to nature shouldn't depend, really, on where you live. I want more people to have good-quality green spaces close to home, particularly, as I said in my initial answer, where access is currently poorest.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Minister, Wales needs both renewable energy and secure domestic food production. Welsh planning policy already gives considerable weight to protecting our best and most versatile agricultural land. Can you explain how the protection works alongside the Government's drive for renewable energy, so that we increase green generation without unnecessarily losing our most productive farmland?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Thank you for the question. Obviously it's about striking the right balance, isn't it? We know that there is a demand for energy, we know that there is a demand for food, and consequently there will be, sometimes, conflicting demand for land. The planning system is there to try and protect the integrity of those demands in a way that strikes the right balance. Sometimes, planning authorities get it right, other times, maybe, people will disagree, and that's the nature of the situation that we're facing.

You will know—and I am straying into the territory of other Ministers here—that work is ongoing to look at planning policy, particularly in relation to energy infrastructure. There is also work happening on a new national energy strategy for us here in Wales. I will entrust that work to my Cabinet colleagues, and I am confident that they will get it right and also confident, of course, that all Members here in the Senedd will have an opportunity to scrutinise that when the time is right.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
We are very similar in the questioning, Lyn, so I'll try and skirt around some of the other parts of it.

Cabinet Minister, it's not just community green spaces at risk in Casnewydd, but also agricultural land. Currently, plans see 578 acres of farmland given over to solar development at the Candwr and Craig y Perthi sites. Residents have raised serious concerns about flood risk, traffic, landscape damage and impact on wildlife, including the important lapwing habitat on the Gwent levels, particularly around Bishton, which is their only site. What cumulative assessment has the Government made of the impact that these developments will have on food production, biodiversity and local flood risk? And does the Cabinet Minister believe that removing hundreds of acres of agricultural land is compatible with the Government's stated commitment to food security?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Well, thank you for the question. As you say, it's similar to the question that has been asked, and I feel that the answer may well be similar as well. But it is about striking that balance, I think, and, as I say, the planning system should, when it functions properly, take all of those considerations in the round and, hopefully, bring forward the right balance. But we are looking at planning policy in this energy space and we are working as well on the new energy strategy for Wales, much of which will not only deal with solar, but with the additional infrastructure that goes with some of these projects.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Access to green spaces and nature is so important to our physical and mental well-being. The Road to Nature project in Newport is a great example of what can be done, and the incredible work of the Friends of the Road to Nature group, Newport City Council and the wider community has absolutely transformed what was a real criminal dumping ground for rubbish a few years ago, and that's now a haven for wildlife. Biodiversity is absolutely thriving there, and willow emerald damselflies were recorded for the first time in recent weeks, following the completion of a pond dipping area. This area is a real shining example of a community working together for nature restoration. So, will the Welsh Government commit to supporting and funding more projects like this in Casnewydd Islwyn, as well as other parts of Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Thank you for drawing attention to that particular scheme. I always believe that this kind of work is most effective when you empower local communities to take action like that, and, of course, we have backed that commitment with practical investment through Local Places for Nature, for example, because that scheme alone has created or improved thousands of green spaces and pollinator sites across Wales. In Newport and Caerphilly particularly, 28 community garden packages were delivered in the last year, creating nature gardens, orchards, food-growing areas, but wildlife habitats as well. Another 70 nature gardens are planned by the end of this year.

So, there's a lot happening, backed up by the £16 million that the Government has allocated to Local Places for Nature this year. It's very commendable, the work that's happening, and what we really want to see is how we can replicate that as widely as possible across the whole of Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: 2. What discussions has the Cabinet Minister had with the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy about the impact of pylons on rural communities? OQ64568
documents.text_cy: 2. Pa drafodaethau y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'u cael gyda'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni am effaith peilonau ar gymunedau gwledig? OQ64568

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: I have regular discussions with my Cabinet colleague. In the coming weeks, I know that the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy will set out our plans to turn our manifesto commitment for the undergrounding of new electricity circuits in Wales into a new planning policy.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Farmers in Carmarthenshire have reported Green GEN Cymru contractors arriving on their land without warning, with one recent incident reportedly requiring police attendance. This is causing real anxiety and frustration among farming families. Will the Minister raise these reports urgently with the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy and stand up within Government for the rural communities affected? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Thank you for drawing our attention to that. I'm always concerned when there are any circumstances that require police attendance and police involvement. There's a certain way of doing things, and I think decent courtesy means that that should always be adhered to. I won't be drawn on commenting on any specifics, because I'm sure you can understand that I'd be straying into difficult territory.

But we do expect all developments planned in Wales to have regard to all relevant planning policy, to be sensitively designed and implemented to avoid and to definitely minimise impacts, at least on communities and the environment, but also to maximise the benefits, because I think there are two sides to this coin. When you get it right, it releases a lot of opportunities economically, et cetera, but when you get it wrong, then those are the risks that sometimes appear.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: What conversations has the Cabinet Minister had regarding the national policy statement for electricity network infrastructure with UK Government Ministers?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Well, that isn't really a role of mine within my portfolio. Clearly, it has a relevance to the energy Minister and it will have a relevance to the planning Minister as well. So, maybe you'd like to direct your question to them when the opportunity arises.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. Reform UK spokesperson, Laura Anne Jones.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Llefarydd Reform UK, Laura Anne Jones.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Diolch, Deputy Presiding Officer. Firstly, Minister, I want to say 'diolch' to you too for your recent announcements, finally injecting some common sense into Labour's ridiculously rigid nitrate vulnerable zones rules. It's of course welcome and long overdue, as are advance payments for the basic payment scheme and the sustainable farming scheme after such a difficult summer.

But bringing forward that money does not give farmers a penny more overall, and it does not address the downward trajectory of the basic payment scheme. Lawfully, we are all, of course, aware that you have to bring down BPS payments, but it is in your power, Minister, as to how much. Many are struggling on the 60 per cent of the BPS original 2025 value. Now dropping it to just 40 per cent would literally signal the end of most family farms in Wales. As I am, you must be aware that the majority of the 51 per cent remaining on the BPS are those small family farms that you claim to want to protect. Pushing ahead with this cut, with SFS remaining wholly unsuitable, inflexible and unworkable, is playing literally Russian roulette with their livelihoods. Minister, you need to make the SFS workable, and fast, and you need to put protections in place to help those that remain on the BPS. So, would you consider dropping the BPS by just 1 per cent, as opposed to the further 20 per cent, unless of course you do want to be the Minister responsible for the genuine end of family farms across Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: I'm under no illusion about the difficult transition that we're on at the minute, from the legacy BPS programme through to the new sustainable farming scheme. It's a journey that we will continue to travel on. You said that the SFS is wholly inflexible. Well, I'd like to think that some of the decisions and announcements that I've made of late shows that we can make it flexible and more workable for more farmers, so we will continue to do that. I will not entertain dropping the transition by just 1 per cent, but I am of course considering making the SFS truly more accessible to as many farmers as possible.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: I hope you're more than considering it because it's absolutely completely unworkable, and you know that as well as I do. Not only is dropping the BPS funding by 1 per cent the right thing to do, but by not doing that and pushing ahead with this 20 per cent cut, you're putting our Welsh heritage, our Welsh culture and Welsh language at risk, as well as our national security. You said all the right things in opposition, Minister, didn't you? But now you seem to be struggling to say them and do them as the Minister. I know you've agreed with me in the past that the BPS trajectory needs to be a much more gradual, tapering trajectory—your words, not mine. Now you're in Government as the Minister able to do this, you're backtracking. You said in black and white in this Chamber that you thought that it should be a more just transition—again, your words. So, tell me: will you do it?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
'Just transition' is exactly what we are trying to achieve here. You say that we've done nothing; we've committed £1 billion over the coming three years to farming to make sure that those farmers who aren't sure about coming on board with the SFS can see that there actually is a quantum of funding there that they can access, that they can utilise, to make their businesses and their farms more resilient. Now, some will choose not to do that and I appreciate that. My job is to make sure that as many people as possible who wish to come on that journey can do so. I'm focused on doing that because that is the just transition that we need to see.

But it isn't only about money as well, of course. We have introduced the review into red tape, which will be, hopefully, a great benefit to farmers who are grappling with the amount of paperwork that they're dealing with. You mentioned the control of agricultural pollution changes. We have been pragmatic, we have been practical, and, where we can do that, we will do that. But, ultimately, we are on this journey transitioning into the sustainable farming scheme and we need to keep our focus on getting there.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Well, you're putting family farms in Wales at risk, Minister, by saying that. I hope that you do recognise that, currently, on the SFS, people cannot get on it whether they want to or not.

I'd like to bring back to what Sarah Edwards, one of my colleagues, has just asked you in the Chamber. I, too, am aware of the extremely worrying circumstance that Green GEN Cymru surveyors appear to be arriving unannounced on farms to survey land, with huge machinery, and, not only that, they are not even adhering to their own biosecurity measures, with no checks in place to ensure that they are. This is genuinely concerning. This is not about whether you agree with windfarms or not, Minister. Most of these farms have had bovine TB or are at high risk of it. This is not a theoretical concern either; the High Court has already found Green GEN lacking in terms of their biosecurity measures. Without the right measures in place here, there is a real risk of disease like TB being spread farm to farm, and I'm not even mentioning the other environmental concerns that the people of the Towy valley have. Don't you agree with me, Minister, that we cannot have a situation where rural communities in west Wales have to spend hundreds of thousands of pounds to ask a court to help them to merely protect their own farms? Farmers need protection in place. They need support on this, Minister. Green GEN Cymru and contracted surveyors need to adhere to the rules to protect our farms. Will you work with the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy to ensure this happens, please, and perhaps even visit the Towy valley to meet with the communities there that are so concerned? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Thank you. I won't get drawn on particular court cases, et cetera—you'll understand that I can't comment on those—but you make a very valid point about biosecurity measures, and I will write to the company and others to make sure that they are reminded of their responsibility particularly to respect those.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: The Welsh Labour spokesperson, Vikki Howells.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Vikki Howells.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Cabinet Minister, over lunch today we both attended WWF Cymru's briefing on the implications of extreme weather events such as wildfire and flooding, where we heard from speakers including representatives of the fire service and the farming sector. A key takeaway from that session for me was the vital role that nature-based solutions have to play in protecting communities and farm businesses from the impacts of climate change-related weather events. Given the shared commitments of our parties to increase the use of nature-based solutions across Government action, I'm wondering what steps you might intend to take to mainstream their use in the coming months. Both WWF Cymru and the Fire Brigades Union have come forward with funding proposals to ensure Wales is more resilient and better prepared for extreme weather impacts, and a key element of this proposal is seeking commitment to an extreme weather resilience fund that could look to inject tens of millions of new money into the expansion of preventative spend on nature-based solutions. We're at that time of year when everyone is talking about the budget, so, as those conversations go on, will you commit to making it a priority to expand nature-based solution investment within your portfolio?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Well, not only within my portfolio, as I think there's a huge responsibility across Government on all of us to lean more heavily on nature-based solutions, because we can mix concrete to our heart's content, but, unless we work with the grain of nature, we will always ultimately lose that battle. So, we do have to recalibrate our approach, and we absolutely are committed to those nature-based solutions. The wildfire summit in a few weeks' time will offer, hopefully, the starting gun for some particular work streams around that. I have some particular thoughts around how the sustainable farming scheme and land management can actually support that as well, particularly given the way that farmers stepped up to help fight some of the wildfires that we saw over the summer. Flooding as well, of course—we know there's talk of improving catchment or retaining water through various means in the uplands, et cetera. But key to all of this as well, of course, is it still needs funding, it still needs finance, because the interventions will cost. So, yes, Government has a role to play. Other authorities clearly have a role to play. But nature finance as well, I think, is a key area where we need to be focusing on. I very much intend to build on the work of the previous Government to really focus on that area over the coming months.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Cabinet Minister, I'm really encouraged by your answer there, and I look forward to seeing these developments over the coming months. I think there's particular potential within the optional and collaborative layers of the SFS for that as well.

Turning to another matter, a review of the code of practice for the rearing of game birds for sporting purposes in Wales is overdue, with animal welfare organisations such as the League Against Cruel Sports concerned that this is an issue that is being overlooked. This is perhaps borne out by the data. There were no inspections of game bird farms in either 2023 or 2024 and just four since 2025, and those uncovered two breaches of the code of practice. We also have shocking evidence from Animal Aid site visits of three game bird breeding farms in Wales that found conditions falling far below the standards that we all expect. What assessment has the Welsh Government made of the treatment and welfare conditions of game birds bred and reared to be shot for sport, and what plans do you have to ensure that the code is reviewed to ensure it is fit for purpose?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Thank you for that. I'm not 100 per cent sure where we are on that. I am aware, if I'm correct, and I don't wish to mislead the Senedd, that a review is happening of the evidence at the minute. I'm awaiting advice from officials. Maybe, if you'd allow me, I will write to you to give you an update of where we are, because it is an area that clearly needs to be addressed.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: The Welsh Conservatives' spokesperson, Andrew R.T. Davies.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Andrew R.T. Davies.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Yay. [Laughter.]

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. I like a fan next to me. [Laughter.]

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Yes, she's very good. She never does it to me. [Laughter.]

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
You announced at the Royal Welsh Show the national food strategy, which you have got a group working on at the moment, and I commend you for doing that, because it's something that has been missing. But it's really vital that both ends are joined up—the farm gate and the retailer selling to the consumer. Are you confident that you've got the mix right on that group? Because, when I look at the people on there, there doesn't seem to be a major retailer, who, at the end of the day, passes the bulk of the food on to the consumer. And I don't believe you've got a major processor on there either. And those are two key ingredients that are required to build a sustainable chain of supply here in Wales. I hope it'll be successful.

And the other thing that is required is your ability to use legislation to drive improvements in public procurement and nutritional standards. You supported my colleague Peter Fox's Bill when it came to the floor of the Senedd. Will you commit today, as a Minister, that whatever the food strategy group recommends, and if it requires legislation to support those recommendations, you will pilot that through the Senedd as a Government Minister?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Thank you. There were a couple of questions in there. I haven't got the list in front of me of the membership of that group, but we are, you're right, looking at a whole food system, from gate to plate and beyond—well, no, where does it go after that? I'm not sure. [Laughter.] But, certainly, there is a need to make sure that all voices are heard around that table. And I know, of course, that the group itself will be utilising work streams that will draw on experience of others also through other fora and networks. And I know that the chair has engaged widely, to say the least, already, beyond what has been brought together around that particular stakeholder group.

It will have a number of work streams. We want to look at areas around the red meat supply chain in Wales. We want to look at horticulture and growing horticulture, and we want to look at food in schools initially. Those are some of the areas that will be prioritised in the first place. So, clearly, if we're looking at the red meat supply chain, then processors and others will be a big, big part of that conversation.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
I didn't hear you refer to the legislation, and I'd be grateful if you'd reply back to me on that, because, as I said, you did support the food Bill when it first came here. Sadly, the Government at the time rejected it. I think it's an important instrument to use to drive up nutritional standards and also local procurement.

But I'd also like to raise with you the point that I raised with you in committee the other day about the fertiliser tax that's coming in in January of this year. That could potentially be devastating to the ability to procure fertiliser to grow the crops for next year's harvest. And at a time when the uncertainty in the middle east is driving up fertiliser prices to double what they should be at this time of year for forward buying, it seems madness to me to actually introduce a fertiliser tax. Will you now lobby the Westminster Government—the point I made to you in committee—to hold that off for at least 12 months, as the National Farmers Union were asking, so that that situation, hopefully, in the middle east can get back to a sense of normality, so that that price pressure can come out of the system and farmers can purchase the fertiliser they need with confidence that there isn't this supertax being applied to it?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Well, after the session we had in committee, I made sure that I did write to the UK Government to make these representations, to make sure that any implications for Welsh agriculture are properly considered and any negative consequences are avoided. My understanding is, of course, that most of the fertiliser coming to the UK is from the EU—so they wouldn't be affected by the carbon border adjustment mechanism—mainly from the Netherlands, Norway, Germany, and Belgium. But there is some coming from beyond, and we need to guard against any negative consequences stemming from that.

To come back to your previous question as well, if we need to legislate on certain areas, we will. I think we need to wait and see what they recommend. I would prefer action that doesn't require legislation in order to get on with it more quickly, but where we do need to legislate, we won't shy away from that.

And on strengthening procurement policy as well, I know that there will be the publication of a new statement on public procurement policy from this Welsh Government soon, and I'm sure the relevant Minister will publish that when it's ready.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: 3. What action is the Welsh Government taking to ensure that groundwater sources that could be affected by major developments are appropriately protected and monitored? OQ64604
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod ffynonellau dŵr daear, y gallai datblygiadau mawr effeithio arnynt, yn cael eu diogelu a'u monitro'n briodol? OQ64604

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Protecting groundwater is essential for safeguarding drinking water supplies, the environment and Wales's long-term water resilience. Planning and environmental permitting processes require risks to groundwater to be assessed and managed. Where risks are identified, Natural Resources Wales can then require mitigation measures, monitoring and ongoing controls to protect water resources.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text: Diolch. Access to clean and safe groundwater is essential for protecting public health, supporting agriculture and safeguarding our natural environment. As major developments come forward across Wales, it is vital that local communities can feel confident that groundwater sources are being properly monitored and protected. Can you outline how the Welsh Government is working with Natural Resources Wales and the local planning authorities to ensure that groundwater resources are robustly monitored, protected and transparently assessed before major developments are approved?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
Thank you for that question. I know that this is a challenge that could occur in a number of different contexts. I hope you'll be reassured that the Welsh Government is working with Natural Resources Wales and local planning authorities through the planning and environmental permitting systems to make sure that groundwater risks are identified and that they are properly assessed and managed before major developments proceed.

We set the national planning policy framework that local planning authorities apply when determining applications, and Natural Resources Wales provide specialist technical advice on groundwater risks as a statutory consultee. Planning authorities can draw on their hydrogeological expertise when they consider whether further investigation or any mitigation or monitoring is needed before a decision is taken. 

Where evidence identifies a specific local risk, local planning authorities and NRW can use their respective planning and permitting functions to make sure that proportionate monitoring and controls are in place during construction and operation. But, ultimately, we will work closely with those bodies to support the consistent and effective application of groundwater protections as a number of different development pressures—and environmental risks, no doubt—evolve.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
documents.text:
This links back to the Member's question, but I want to go a bit more local. The Welsh Water treatment works in Gowerton serves around 58,000 constituents across Gŵyr Abertawe. However, concerns have been raised that proposed housing developments in Gowerton and surrounding areas could place unsustainable pressure on waste water networks and storage capacity.
