documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr. Sarah Rees.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
Diolch. Here in Cymru, we had a proud tradition of peace activism. Many of us can trace our family history back to a woman who signed the Welsh women's peace petition. St Fagans held a powerful exhibition tracing that journey from the women who organised for peace in the aftermath of the first world war to the women of Greenham Common who sacrificed so much in their campaign against nuclear weapons. Once again, we find ourselves living through turbulent times with devastating conflicts unfolding across the world. And, of course, there remains a pragmatic need for defence, and we must engage honestly with that reality.

I welcome the work that this Plaid Cymru Government is undertaking to develop an ethical defence investment framework. It presents a real opportunity to build on the Scottish Government's human rights due diligence approach, which evaluates businesses before they receive public grants or investment, and to establish a gold standard for ethical investment here in Wales. This framework is the first of its kind in Cymru, and Wales can be world-leading in setting clear expectations that public money should never support companies linked to human rights abuses or violations of international law. It allows us to stand on the shoulders of those women who came before us and carry forward their commitment to peace, justice and ethical leadership. Whether the conflict is in Gaza, South Sudan or Ukraine, we should be clear in our determination that no weapon manufactured, even in part, in Wales should ever be used in a way that breaches international human rights law.

Global responsibility is not just about following money. It is about ensuring Wales is never complicit in human rights abuses, and that our economic choices reflect our commitment to peace, justice and international solidarity. But we must also be honest about the wider questions this debate raises. Defence spending is often presented as an economic opportunity, but what kind of economy do we want to build here in Wales? The people of Wales elected this Plaid Cymru Government with a mandate for a different kind of economy, an economy that places our people and communities at its heart. They voted for an economic model rooted in ownership and community wealth, ensuring that wealth generated in Wales remains in Wales, building stronger communities, creating opportunity and delivering prosperity that is shared by all. If that is our ambition, then we must also ask who owns Wales's arms and defence manufacturing facilities and whose interests they serve. In many cases, ownership rests with large multinational corporations and private firms whose primary responsibility is to shareholders—

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text: Will you take an intervention?

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
No, I won't. 

Rather than to communities in which they operate. When we talk about wealth leaking from Wales, this is exactly what we mean. Wealth created by Welsh workers and Welsh communities flowing out of Wales, rather than being reinvested in the places that need it most. That also raises questions about who gets to make decisions with profound consequences for peace, security and human rights. Those decisions should be guided by the public interest, ethical responsibility and respect for human rights, not by commercial priorities alone.

And there is the question of jobs. We must be willing to ask whether it’s right that military bases and defence manufacturing facilities are concentrated in civilian communities and what the consequences of those choices are. A leaked Russian strike list by a senior Senator shows a map of UK military and industrial sites, with Merthyr Tydfil as a potential target due to the General Dynamics facility there. Hosting facilities in Welsh communities inevitably ties the safety and everyday lives of civilian towns to international conflict. This is a reality that we can't ignore. Is it fair that some of our poorest communities are expected to shoulder those risks while being denied the investment they need to thrive? Is it fair that working-class people are presented with a choice between employment in the defence industry or economic insecurity? Is that really a choice at all?

The work this Government is undertaking on an ethical defence investment framework is both necessary and timely. I wish to thank the Welsh Conservatives for bringing forward this debate because it gives us an opportunity to reflect on the kind of Wales we want to build. I believe there is one principle on which we can all agree: any investment connected to defence must be consistent with international law and fundamental human rights. As we shape Wales's future, those values must remain at the heart of the decisions we make.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
It gives me great pleasure to take part in this afternoon's debate and to highlight the contribution being made by the defence sector in west Wales. Now, our motion recognises the importance of the defence sector, particularly during this time of geopolitical uncertainty. In Ceredigion Penfro, and contrary to the previous speaker, we are proud of our military heritage, proud of the men and women who serve our country, and proud of the role our communities continue to play in supporting our armed forces and the wider defence industry.

The Ministry of Defence maintains a substantial operational and testing presence in west Wales, and this, of course, includes the MOD Aberporth range, located near Cardigan, which provides a vast and secure safety area for the testing and evaluation of air-launched weapons and uncrewed aerial systems, ensuring that these are safe, effective and fit for operational use. As I understand it, the range employs around 200 skilled staff and makes a significant contribution to the local economy. The facility supports a wider supply chain of local businesses, contractors and service providers, which, of course, helps to sustain jobs and investment across the region. These are important roles that provide career opportunities and help retain skilled workers in west Wales. MOD Aberporth has established itself as a centre of excellence in aerospace and defence innovation, particularly in the rapidly developing field of uncrewed and autonomous systems. And I believe this supports innovation, research and technological advancement, which, in turn, strengthens our national defence.

Of course, the presence of the defence sector in west Wales is not limited to Aberporth. Cawdor barracks in Brawdy has long been an important part of the region's military landscape and also makes a significant contribution to both our national security and, indeed, to the local economy. The barracks have provided employment opportunities for military personnel, civilian staff and local contractors, and the service families are a cherished part of the local community. There has been some discussion around the future of the barracks, with proposals to develop it as the UK's host site for the deep space advanced radar capability programme, known as DARC. This would be the UK's first dedicated military space tracking radar system and it would help the UK contribute towards space security by providing greater levels of UK-sourced data for the National Space Operations Centre.

I appreciate there are strong-held views for and against the DARC programme, but in my view, Cawdor barracks has an opportunity to be at the forefront of this very important technology. It would provide jobs for up to 100 UK military and civilian personnel onsite and it would also deliver further supply chain opportunities for the local area. For example, there will be significant opportunities during the construction phase. And so, if the DARC programme does proceed at the Cawdor barracks, I believe it would continue Pembrokeshire's proud tradition of supporting our military and protecting our nation.

The final sub-point in our motion calls on the Welsh Government to work with the UK Government to explore opportunities to strengthen investment in the defence sector here in Wales. I also want to make a brief point about Milford Haven, and the announcement last year that it was identified by the UK Government as one of 13 potential sites for new munitions and energetics factories. We are now waiting for further details from the UK Government on the next steps in that selection process, and whether the Milford Haven site will ultimately be chosen. But the fact that it has been shortlisted as a potential site reiterates the area's strategic importance.

At a time when strengthening the resilience of our defence supply chains is becoming increasingly important, it is encouraging to see west Wales being recognised for the role it can play in bolstering our defence. Of course, it would be remiss of me not to also highlight the importance of the Castlemartin training area and firing range, which is regularly used for live firing and tactical battle group-level exercises that are an essential part of ensuring our soldiers are prepared for all combat eventualities.

My constituency has a strong military history. Pembroke Dock's naval dockyard was one of the most important shipbuilding sites in Britain during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Angle airfield was a fighter station belonging to No. 10 Group Fighter Command, and a succession of squadrons passed through Angle, flying Supermarine Spitfires, Westland Whirlwinds and Hawker Hurricanes. St David's, Britain's smallest city, was a submarine listening post in world war one and a radar station in world war two. That's just a few examples, but there are many, many more. We in west Wales are proud of our contribution to our defence sector and to our armed forces, and we will continue to make an important contribution in the future. So, I urge Members to support our motion.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
Reform heartily supports today's motion that's before us today. Wales has a proud defence tradition, and our aerospace and defence sector directly employs 16,000 people. The UK defence investment plan commits £298 billion over the next four years, with almost 60,000 industry jobs created. The investment is coming, the jobs are coming, the contracts are coming, and thank God we are part of our United Kingdom, so we can access these opportunities. The question for this Government is simple: how many of these opportunities are coming to Wales? Because Wales must not simply watch this investment happen elsewhere. We have to fight for our share of it.

I know personally what this industry can offer. I started my career with a three-year apprenticeship at the Ministry of Defence at St Athan. It was one of the best decisions I ever made. I earned while I learnt, I gained skills, experience, and it became the foundation of a 30-year career in aerospace and defence. I later joined General Dynamics, where I had technical teams that led the installation of complex communication systems in military platforms. And that's the power of what a good apprenticeship can do. It doesn't simply give somebody their first job, it can give them a career. It's a foundation for success, it can transform their prospects, and when we get it right, it can transform whole communities as well.

That's why Wales needs an ambitious defence industrial strategy. We have the workforce, we have world-class companies, we have universities, engineers, manufacturers, and the supply chains. What we need is a Government determined to bring those strengths together and compete relentlessly for investment. And that means stronger relationships with the MOD and industry, closer ties with decision makers in Westminster, not ideological division or the pursuit of independence. More apprenticeships, more technical skills, and fighting for every factory, every contract and every skilled job that Wales can secure.

Look at Merthyr Tydfil: General Dynamics has already demonstrated what high-quality defence manufacturing can bring to the heart of the Valleys. We're thrilled that Marshall Land Systems has seen the potential that Merthyr holds and is establishing its new facility there, employing hundreds, and that's exactly the sort of investment Wales should be pursuing. We should make sure that Welsh SMEs and supply chains benefit from this investment too. But this is where the Government needs to answer a very serious question. At the precise moment Britain is embarking upon one of the biggest periods of defence investment in generations, this Government is developing an additional bureaucratic Welsh ethical framework for defence investment—more  unnecessary red tape.

Now, we are told, of course, that this will not create more barriers to defence investment, but this claim doesn't pass the commonsense sniff test. And here's the contradiction: this Government says Wales needs defence investment, they say they want the jobs. Yet instead of focusing on how Wales can attract that investment, Plaid wants to put an ethical defence framework at the centre of its approach to this crucial industry. We all want responsible investment, but Plaid's framework is an ideological purity test, putting political conditions ahead of jobs, growth and the economic opportunities Wales desperately needs.

And while this Government is busy putting barriers on defence investment, Russia's foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov, is openly questioning the future of the United Kingdom, seeking to divide, weaken, disrupt, just as Plaid are trying to do for our union. Now let that sink in: a country that poses a direct threat to our national security sees the break-up of the United Kingdom as an opportunity. And yet Plaid is determined to pursue the very ambitions that Russia sees as being in its interests.

Now, this motion today should be a wake-up call for Plaid Cymru. Wales should be leading the way in strengthening Britain's defence, not undermining the very country that protects us. Plaid needs to stop putting ideology before our national interests and start putting Welsh workers first. Back this motion today, back our national defence, and let's get these defence jobs into Wales and back our communities. Diolch.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
I very much welcome this debate today. I support the motion and also support many of the points raised in the amendment. Indeed, I particularly welcome the reference to the importance of respecting human rights, of upholding international law and international solidarity. I would also say that national solidarity is just as, if not more, important. A divided nation is a weak and vulnerable nation, and we must demonstrate unity to our enemies as much as we possibly can.

Now, Llywydd, the defence sector is interwoven with many other sectors in Wales, including aerospace, automotive, AI, glass, electronics, fabrics and advanced materials. So, investing in defence provides investment across the economy, and, crucially, in jobs that require the highest levels of skills and provide the best opportunities for career progression, especially for young people leaving universities and college. In my constituency, the defence sector is particularly important, as many Members will be aware. Fflint Wrecsam is home to a huge number of businesses, producing items that are then used by our armed forces and our allies. It represents a huge, huge proportion of employment across the constituency. So, without defence businesses, we would be so much poorer, not just so much weaker. Defence is just that—a means of protecting against aggression, against attack, against harm, and, crucially, against invasion. But we must never, never use our defence capabilities for aggressive intent, nor should we allow those who use what our defence sector produces and provides, whether it be intelligence, weapons, vehicles or kit.

Now, to the point in the motion referring to geopolitical instability, I would refer Members to NATO's assessment of global security at present: we are not living in war, but we are not living in peace either. We are living in the most vulnerable time since the cold war, with Russia in particular growing its military might. It's doing so not for the purpose of defence, as we can see in Ukraine; they are doing it for more nefarious purposes. I do believe that a strategy here is definitely needed. It's needed in order to take maximum advantage of the UK Government's increasing investment in defence, and I believe that the Scottish National Party in Government are looking at creating their defence strategy as well. I welcome and also agree with what Paul Davies had to say on the DARC programme. I do believe that this is essential for our defence and for jobs.

We also, whether we like it or not, invest in our intelligence services, our armed forces, and their families. I was with veterans at Caffinaafi in Connah's Quay just last Friday. It's a brilliant hub—I'd recommend it to all Members. It's a brilliant hub for veterans, for service leavers, reservists, cadets, serving personnel and, of course, their families. I spoke with a number of the veterans there. They didn't go into the forces and their loved ones didn't support them in the forces in the hope of war, or in the anticipation of invading another country. They took the action they did to defend people here, in our communities and around the world, for a better, safer, freer tomorrow.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
Let's be absolutely clear about what we are talking about here today: we are talking about an industry that employs thousands of people across Wales, one that supports some of our most highly skilled jobs, and an industry that drives innovation, supports apprenticeships and contributes billions of pounds to our economy. And yet, at a time when the world is becoming increasingly volatile, we have a Welsh Government that is reluctant to engage in the opportunities that this sector presents. Some members of their own party have even been heard to say that we should move the arms industry out of Wales, because they do not want to have the guilt or the feeling of complicity in death.

Plaid Cymru's approach risks weakening our defence industry at precisely the moment when we should be strengthening it. We cannot allow Wales and the United Kingdom to become vulnerable in a time of geopolitical instability. The Welsh Government's own figures tell us that the combined defence and aerospace sector directly employs around 16,000 people, with a turnover of £3.7 billion and approximately £1.5 billion in gross value added. And when we include security in space, these figures rise to around 18,500 people and £5 billion in turnover and £2 billion in GVA. These aren't insignificant figures. These numbers represent family apprenticeships, families paying their mortgages. They represent the very best of engineers, innovators, technicians and highly skilled workers who are contributing to Wales and the United Kingdom's safety.

And we see that contribution in my own constituency of Bridgend and the Vale of Glamorgan. We have a proud tradition and history of contributing to Britain's defence sector and war effort. In the Vale, RAF St Athan played a major role during the second world war, training thousands of flight engineers, with more than 22,500 British Commonwealth and allied personnel passing through the site between 1941 and 1951. The area was also directly involved in the wartime scientific work, including radar research at St Athan, while Porthkerry Country Park in Barry was occupied by the British and American forces preparing for D-day. In Bridgend, the contribution was on an enormous industrial scale. The royal ordnance factory was one of the largest munition-filling factories in Britain during the second world war, and employed 40,000 people at its peak, making a major contribution to the production of ammunition and the war effort. That tradition of defence manufacturing continues today through businesses such as Spectrum Technologies in Bridgend, which designs and manufactures industrial laser systems for customers including the Ministry of Defence and the US Government Department of Defense. And as we heard from Darren a little earlier, IrvinGQ makes parachutes and ejector seats also in the constituency of Bridgend.

From the factories and airfields of the second world war to the highly skilled defence manufacturing and aerospace businesses of today, Bridgend and the Vale have constantly played their part in keeping Britain safe. The defence sector provides skilled employment opportunities for our young people and supports a wider supply chain. That is why I welcome the work that is being done to develop the defence training college in Wales, because if we want young people to have opportunities, we need to give them the route into highly skilled careers. We know that there is a skills challenge across Wales, so we want to use the defence sector to address this skills challenge. Wales currently receives around 3 per cent of the UK Ministry of Defence expenditure. There is an opportunity to increase that, but we will not get that investment by turning our backs on the sector. And we certainly will not get it by allowing ideology to come before jobs, skills and economic interests of communities, such as my constituency in Bridgend and the Vale of Glamorgan. We should be ambitious for Wales. We should be saying to defence companies, 'Come to Wales, invest in Wales, employ Welsh workers, train Welsh apprenticeships and develop the technologies of tomorrow here in Wales', because supporting the defence sector means supporting our economy and building skills in the workforce across the whole of Wales, and we should be proud of that. And at a time when our allies are strengthening their defences and the threats facing the United Kingdom are becoming increasingly complex, Wales cannot afford to stand on the sidelines. We should be competing for that investment, we should be creating those jobs and we should be making sure that Wales plays its key role in keeping Britain safe. That is why I will be supporting today's motion and rejecting the Government amendment, and I urge all colleagues here this evening to do the same.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
As a veteran myself, I have to say I am thankful to our defence industry, which allows us to operate in dangerous environments efficiently, effectively and safely. I have to say I'm somewhat baffled by some of the arguments I've heard on Plaid's side of the Chamber. It's bizarre. So, I want to support a motion that allows Wales to build more, make more and win more of the skilled work that helps keep this country safe. I want a young person leaving school to see a future in Welsh engineering. I want graduates to have the opportunity to remain in Wales, and I want Welsh businesses competing for defence contracts to believe they have a Government that is firmly behind them. There is nothing shameful about earning a living helping Britain to defend itself. Our engineers, our manufacturers and our apprentices deserve respect. Being proud of Wales should mean being ambitious for the people who work here.

Defence is reserved to the United Kingdom Government. The Senedd does not direct our armed forces or control the MOD's procurement programmes. But Welsh Ministers have a responsibility for education, training and business support. Those powers matter. Use them properly and we can help Welsh firms compete. Use them badly and we risk putting obstacles in their way. Reform's Welsh manifesto already commits to expanding high-quality technical education and apprenticeships and working with employers to match training to the needs of the Welsh economy. This is a commitment I want applied to the opportunities in defence. Bring defence employers and higher education closer together. Give school leavers a route into skilled work, graduates an opportunity to build their careers here, and experienced workers the chance to retrain.

On 20 February, the UK Government and Wales Office announced their intention to work collaboratively to establish a defence technical excellence college in Wales by September 2027. What's the location? Is it in Swansea? Please say it is. But wherever it is based, we need a clear delivery plan. What funding has been agreed? Is September 2027 still achievable? How will the college work with defence employers? When can students find out what they can study and how to apply? For somebody considering a career in defence, those are details that matter. They should be able to see a route from training into employment here in Wales.

The same practical approach is needed for smaller businesses. A Welsh firm with the skills to produce to a military specification should have a fair opportunity to win the work. There should be support to help it prepare a bid, help it to meet the security requirements, and help to put it in contact with the MOD and major defence contractors awarding work. Give them a clear pathway, then show us whether that support is helping Welsh businesses win contracts and take on staff. Reform would introduce a Welsh industrial strategy built around secure, affordable energy, as our manifesto commits. I want defence manufacturers and their suppliers included in that ambition, with opportunities to invest, expand and employ more people.

That brings me to the Government's proposed ethical framework. On 22 September the Minister said that, wherever legally and practically possible, the new Welsh Government investment support decisions for defence activity should not be finalised until the framework is published and its implementation considered. Existing contractual commitments remain unaffected. Discussions can continue. Decisions needed sooner can go to the First Minister. I have to agree with Darren Millar, as, I have to say, asking businesses to wait while the rules are being developed is the wrong signal to industry. Before committing to expansion and recruitment, employers need to understand the conditions attached to that support. Minister, a company deciding where to invest needs an answer. An order book cannot be organised around your consultation timetable. Set clear standards and, in doing so, explain what this approach will achieve and how you will prevent avoidable delays. Plaid talks about standing up for Wales. Here's the opportunity to demonstrate it. Give Welsh employers clarity and Welsh workers a fair chance of securing the next investment. A Reform Government would be fearless in its support for the Welsh defence industry.

We should equally be focused about the weapons and civilian harms. Some weapons are restricted in their use. Others are prohibited because of their effects. With weapon systems, how they are deployed and used matters enormously. The UK's export licensing criteria already address the risk of equipment being used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law. Welsh Ministers need to explain what their framework will add and why that benefit justifies any further bureaucracy, administration and expense. Delays could encourage businesses to invest elsewhere.

I can't say this framework hasn't already cost Welsh jobs. I can demand that Ministers assess the risk to investment and employment. Welsh workers deserve to know that their livelihoods are being properly considered. I want Wales to play a confident part in a strong United Kingdom, with skilled people making equipment we can rely on and businesses capable of competing for work. I want this motion to lead to apprenticeships someone can apply for, a contract a Welsh business can bid for and a stronger Welsh defence industry. Deliver the training, help firms win contracts and give investors clear answers—

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text: Steven, could you conclude now, please?

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text: This is the last sentence. Our ambition should be Welsh apprentices qualifying, Welsh factories securing orders and Welsh families building their futures here. This is the opportunity before us, this Government should be getting on and delivering it. Thank you.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
There's some irony here that only last week, when we were scrutinising and challenging your ethical defence framework, the aircraft went down at RAF Valley. I would hope that everybody on these benches is glad that those two pilots were able to eject and that they're well now after receiving treatment for minor injuries. I'm incredibly proud of that base. I'm also incredibly proud of the defence industry across Wales and the United Kingdom. And I'm incredibly proud of those who serve, and have served previously, in our armed forces—those who have lost their lives so that we have the freedom of speech here in this place. I've enjoyed so many excellent contributions today, bar one. I will leave it at that.

It should be noted that the ejection seats in that aircraft were made by Martin-Baker, a company based in Denham. The company's own data notes that these seats have saved almost 8,000 aircrew lives around the world, but it is shocking to note that this essential business has been subjected to vandalism and factory occupation by Palestine activists simply because the Israeli air force utilise their ejection seats. This type of behaviour should be firmly reprimanded and these essential companies should be protected.

This crash last week served rightly as a reminder to us all of the risks that each and every one of our brave servicemen and women take in protecting our country. And when I say 'our country', I mean the United Kingdom, to include Wales. Our vital defence sector uses a wide range of high-value skills that makes it naturally an ideal partner for schools, colleges and universities. It also employs over 18,500 people, has a turnover of more than £5 billion and contributes around £2 billion of gross value added to the Welsh economy. This industry contributes significantly to both our Welsh economy and our nation's safety. It provides highly skilled employment, supports supply chains across Wales and creates opportunities for collaboration between industry and education. Following the crash last week, when I got out of this Senedd, even though I had to go on somewhere, I made a point of contacting RAF Valley, sending them my best wishes and assuring them of our 100 per cent support.

Unlike the Welsh Government, some within Plaid Cymru in particular want to move the arms industry out of Wales due to what they describe as a feeling of complicity in death. Other Plaid Members use the pretence of an ethical defence framework that will push back defence spending in Wales. This is absolute madness at a time—well, it's madness at any time, but particularly now—when we are under such global threat. This is also reflected in the ideological blacklist that's set out in the form of the ethical framework for Welsh Government engagement with the defence sector. There's one that already exists in the United Kingdom Government. The Conservatives understand the importance of this sector because of the global unrest and have instead set out a plan. We would increase defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP.

It is also important to remember that, in the last Senedd term, the Welsh defence growth deal memorandum of understanding was signed. This agreement allocated £50 million to Wales from £250 million of UK-wide investment in regional growth as part of growing investment in defence. Following this, the regional defence and security cluster was established. This helps Welsh businesses, universities and colleges access Ministry of Defence contracts, develop their supply chains and grow their share of defence spending. It also connects businesses with Wales's eight universities and further education colleges, making use of their research and their expertise in areas such as cyber security, optoelectronics and artificial intelligence. The UK Government has pledged to work collaboratively with the Welsh Government to establish a new defence technical college by September 2027. This will train the next generation of defence engineers and help support Britain's growing autonomous capabilities. There is a clear opportunity here for Wales, Cabinet Secretary. We have a strong—. We were in committee this morning—

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text: Would you conclude now, Janet, please?

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text: Yes, I will. It's essential we have productivity in Wales. We are lagging behind because of the previous Welsh Labour Government, supported by you. The evidence is clear: the defence sector is a vital component. We need the Welsh Government to commit to ensuring this industry has the support and what it needs to thrive here in Wales. I hope that you have a change of heart and that you support this motion today. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
Hopefully, we're getting to that point where we've got some common ground across the Chamber in relation to how important defence is to our economy, and the aerospace sector as well, but the measure of success can't simply be about how much money we spend on defence, it must be about what investment delivers for Wales, for our workers, and for our communities.

We already have so many enormous strengths, which many of us have talked about. At BAE Systems in Glascoed, around 500 people work in defence manufacturing, alongside an apprenticeship programme delivering the next generation of skilled workers. At Airbus Broughton, we have world-class aerospace manufacturing and thousands of highly skilled jobs. The UK Government has announced a £50 million Welsh defence growth deal, with Welsh workers expected to be involved in designing, testing and manufacturing new technologies. The investment includes funding a specialised college designed to train the next generation of defence engineers. Yesterday's UK Government announcements on Great British Grid also matter. If we want Welsh manufacturing to expand, to attract investment and create jobs, businesses need that infrastructure to do it. Faster grid connections can help unlock that growth. This is what joined-up industrial policy should be about: investment, infrastructure and skills working together to create good jobs.

My challenge is really simple: if defence spending is increasing, Wales must secure its fair share of the jobs, skills and investment. This means using procurement to strengthen Welsh supply chains, creating apprenticeships and ensuring that public investment supports fair pay, secure employment and opportunities to progress. Governments, employers and trade unions must be around the table together, because investment shouldn't simply deliver more jobs, it should deliver good jobs, decent conditions and a strong voice for workers.

We don't need to start from scratch. The Wales Union Learning Fund gives us a model to build upon. It supports union-led workplace learning and workforce development through Wales's social partnership approach. It's an approach that was very much championed by the Welsh Labour Government, putting workers and trade unions and skills at the heart of our economy. Let's build on that as defence investment grows, upskilling today's workforce and ensuring the next generation of defence jobs are Welsh jobs.

But this can't become a false choice between investing in defence and investing in the things our communities need. Building homes, investing in our NHS, schools and care services and protecting our national security are not competing ambitions. A strong country needs each and every single one of them, because security isn't only about defence, it's about having a decent home, a good job, strong public services and confidence in the future. Now we must move beyond talking shops and frameworks. We need delivery and we need it urgently—delivery that means good jobs and good futures, delivery where workers and communities can see and feel the economic benefit, and delivery that ensures that no worker and no community is left behind.

So, let's judge defence investment not simply by how many billions are spent but by what those billions leave behind: more skilled workers, stronger Welsh businesses, good secure jobs and stronger communities. Welsh industry should have its fair share. Welsh businesses should have their share. But above all, Welsh workers and Welsh communities should feel the benefit: good jobs, good futures, prosperity that stays here in Wales with nobody left behind.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. I welcome the opportunity to respond to this motion, because it gives me an opportunity once again, following the oral statement I made last week, to place on the record what's at the heart of this Government's view, namely that Wales has always sought to be a nation that combines economic ambition—and I think there is consensus on that there—with social responsibility. On that basis, of course, we are developing the ethical defence investment framework, because we don't see these two things—economic ambition and ethical values—as being contrary to each other; we see them dovetailing together and supporting each other.

I understand that there is a difference of opinion on some of the elements we've discussed this evening, but there is broad recognition on the importance of the sector. We've all been quoting the same figures, haven't we? What's important is not just the size of the sector but also the related sectors, because it's more than just the core defence sector. I agree with the broader point that Shavanah Taj has just made. We need to think about security in that broader sense, including the resilience of our infrastructure and so on; that is part of security, and there are important economic opportunities for us in that direction too.

But the defence sector and related sectors—aerospace and so on—are not only important employers, but they are also growing significantly. Our amendment, which sets out the most recent figures, which contradict the figures in the original motion, shows that—in just a short period of time, just 12 months, there has been a significant increase in terms of employment in the sector.

It's important to note also that one figure that is worth quoting is the percentage of MOD procurement that Wales gets at the moment—3.6 per cent. We have 5 per cent of the population, so it's less than the percentage share of the population. In terms of our manufacturing sector, because it is larger as compared to the rest of the economy, we in Wales have something like 6.5 per cent of the whole manufacturing sector of the UK. So, 3.6 per cent of defence procurement and 6.5 per cent of manufacturing. Over 6 per cent of members of the armed forces are here, and we as a Government are entirely committed to the armed forces covenant for those who are serving now, and for our veterans

We have contributed more than our population share to the armed forces, and yet only 3.6 per cent of the procurement budget is coming to Wales. So, there is a fundamental unfairness there, which is reflected in other parts of public procurement across the UK in terms of the use of public money. I think it is something that unites us, namely that Wales should get fair play and that companies from Wales should have their fair share of those opportunities. Why? Well, because these sectors do create high-value employment: high salaries, they maintain wide supply chains and give people across Wales the opportunity to develop higher level skills and to have worthwhile careers. We do have the manufacturing base here, of course: aerospace, electronics, cyber security, and so on. So, we are in a position where there are opportunities. There is potential there, and we certainly want to ensure that we deliver that potential.

Of course, it's important to note that we as a nation can't ignore changes to the geopolitical map across Europe and beyond. Governments are considering how they can be more resilient and safe and how to strengthen their industries. And Wales will need to be able to take advantage of those economic opportunities that will come from greater investment in that context, whilst also remaining true to our own values and responsibilities. And I think that is where there is perhaps some disagreement between us.

There was reference to the defence growth plan. That is a contribution towards creating more opportunities for companies in Wales. That will place Wales in a position to make the most of the opportunities that will come in manufacturing, advanced digital technologies, cyber capability, autonomous systems and dual-use innovation. And of course, skills will be crucial, as we have heard, to our future success. We as a Government, of course, are committed to understanding the skills needs more generally. That's why we're going through the national skills audit, but it is pertinent in the context of defence too.

Mae yna botensial yna, a rŷn ni yn sicr eisiau sicrhau ein bod ni'n gwireddu'r potensial hynny.

Wrth gwrs, mae'n bwysig nodi, gallwn ni ddim fel cenedl anwybyddu'r newidiadau i'r dirwedd geowleidyddol ar draws Ewrop a thu hwnt. A dyna lle mae yna rywfaint o anghytundeb rhyngom ni.

Roedd yna gyfeiriad at y cytundeb twf amddiffyn. Mae hwn yn gyfraniad tuag at greu mwy o gyfleon i gwmnïau yng Nghymru. Bydd yn rhoi Cymru mewn sefyllfa i allu gwneud y gorau o'r cyfleoedd a ddaw ym meysydd gweithgynhyrchu, uwch-dechnolegau digidol, gallu seiber, systemau ymreolaethol ac arloesi dau ddiben. Ac wrth gwrs, bydd sgiliau yn hanfodol, fel rŷn ni wedi clywed, i'n llwyddiant yn y dyfodol. Dŷn ni, fel Llywodraeth, wrth gwrs, yn ymrwymedig i ddeall yr anghenion sgiliau yn gyffredinol. Dyna pam ŷn ni'n mynd trwy'r broses o'r archwiliad sgiliau cenedlaethol, ond mae e'n berthnasol yng nghyd-destun amddiffyn hefyd.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text: I've sat here and obviously listened to your contribution for six and a half minutes. Can you just answer the questions about how long this pause in investment is going to take? If I accept what you're saying, and I do accept what you're saying, that you want to attract more of the MOD procurement to Wales so that we get our fair share, don't you accept that by pushing companies away with this pause, you're sending absolutely the wrong message in terms of trying to attract that money into Wales at this critical time, when businesses are making investment decisions? Don't you accept that that's a problem? And if you do, how long is this review going to take? How long is this pause? Who's undertaking the review? Which individuals are involved? Are you engaging the industry? Answer those questions.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
Thanks. Well, I answered all of those questions in the oral statement I made last week. We said that we would publish the framework in the autumn—[Interruption.] I did. It's being developed, as I said just last week, by the Welsh Government in engagement with the defence sector—which was one of your questions—and with other stakeholders too. It doesn't mean that we won't be supporting the sector; it relates to providing clarity and assurance and a clear, transparent framework.

As I said last week, it aligns with what is happening globally with governments. The leader of the Labour group made reference to Scotland. Scotland has an ethical framework for the defence sector. The Northern Ireland Government has an ethical framework for the sector. The UK Government, as we heard from a Reform Member, has a framework. We were the only Government in the UK that didn't have a framework. We are putting that right so that we have a clear framework, so that, yes, we can ensure that Welsh companies benefit from the opportunities that exist, but on a firm foundation that is consistent with the values that are so important to our democracy here in Wales.

Mae gan Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol, fel y clywom ni gan Aelod o Reform, fframwaith. Ni oedd yr unig Lywodraeth yn y Deyrnas Gyfunol a oedd heb fframwaith. Rŷn ni'n gwneud yn iawn am hynny fel bod gennym ni fframwaith clir, fel ein bod ni, ie, yn gallu sicrhau bod cwmnïau o Gymru yn elwa ar y cyfleon sydd yna, ond ar sail gadarn sydd yn gyson â'r gwerthoedd sydd mor bwysig o ran ein democratiaeth ni yma yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'm grateful to all Members who've contributed to the debate in this Chamber this evening. I think it shows the importance of the defence sector in Wales to all parts of Wales. I will start my closing of this debate, Llywydd, by addressing the Cabinet Minister's opening remarks in relation to the ethical defence framework, because it became clear through the debate that Members across parties have serious concerns about the implications of this, the delays it will induce and the consequences in Wales and more widely as a result. It clearly sends a message out that the defence sector is not properly supported by this Welsh Government. And I hope, Cabinet Minister, that you'll reflect on the concerns that Members have raised in this place, because we want to see that investment here in Wales, we want to see those jobs created here in Wales so that we can see prosperity here in Wales as well.

I did welcome the Cabinet Minister's remarks, Llywydd, in recognising the importance of the defence sector here, in particular growth industries around cyber security, aerospace, advanced manufacturing. I was pleased to hear from colleagues in Fflint Wrecsam. Ken Skates mentioned Airbus, and I was pleased to be able to visit there recently with Darren Millar and see the incredible work that they do in my own constituency—a real highlight for Wales is the work that Airbus do. And they've just recently announced another 480 new jobs in the area. Again, a fantastic example of what aerospace does in Wales.

And this growth and investment has been enabled by the skilled workers we have here in Wales, working with the UK Government and Welsh Government-backed Wrexham and Flintshire investment zone, alongside the support from local authorities. We heard in the debate, Llywydd, from Paul Davies about the strategic importance of west Wales and the opportunities for defence investment there, and we heard from the Reform spokesperson about the difference that the armed forces and the apprenticeship that he had made in his life and his career. And these are examples of why the Welsh Government should be directing more support to the defence sector right now, not pontificating and tying up the sector in red tape. And with the announcement of the ethical defence framework, potential investors and workers in the defence sector are facing nothing but uncertainty and delays. And that, Cabinet Minister, is what Members have raised in this place with you this evening.

These investments, as we've heard from Members also, are the things that make a very real difference day in, day out. We heard from Janet Finch-Saunders, didn't we, of the real-world impact of defence investment here in Wales. And when we talk about the defence sector, I think sometimes it's really easy to be fixated on the materials being produced—extremely important, of course, but let's not forget what is actually being defended. Darren Millar mentioned this with reference to the cold war in his opening remarks. It's our freedoms that are being defended; it's our values that are being defended; it's our democracy, our economic security, it's our resilience that's being defended by the defence sector. It's our way of life, it's the equalities that we enjoy as a nation, it's our peace that is being defended by the defence sector. And peace has to be fought for. We see it in the world that we live in today that peace is not something to be assumed. We have to fight for peace. And it's a fundamental. The highest priority of any Government is the peace of their nation. And it's this social responsibility of peace that we must fight for as a nation as well. That is our responsibility when it comes to our country. It's so important that we defend our values.

This debate comes precisely at a time when we are realising the growing need for investment and action. In short, Llywydd, because the world on our doorstep is getting more and more dangerous, we in this Senedd should be giving the defence sector our full backing, enabling manufacturers to be able to expand in Wales, provide good jobs to skilled workers and bolster the UK's defences. This is fundamental to the security of Wales, the security of the United Kingdom and the security of our allies abroad. That's why I urge all Members to back our motion and show your support for the defence sector here in Wales. Diolch yn fawr iawn.
