documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: 1. What are the Welsh Government's priorities for improving access to public transport in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64484
documents.text_cy: 1. Beth yw blaenoriaethau Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer gwella mynediad at drafnidiaeth gyhoeddus ym Mhontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64484

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you for the question, Vikki. We want to make it easier for more people to travel on buses and trains in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr. That means better connections between bus and rail, keeping fares fair and providing reliable services. The south Wales metro is central to this work. We are also investing in improving local bus services and improving interchanges such as Merthyr.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn, Vikki. Rydyn ni eisiau ei gwneud hi’n haws i fwy o bobl deithio ar fws ac ar drên ym Mhontypridd Cynon Merthyr. Mae hyn yn golygu bysiau a threnau sy’n gweithio’n well gyda’i gilydd, prisiau teg, a gwasanaethau sy’n dod ar amser. Mae metro de Cymru yn rhan bwysig o’r gwaith hwn. Rydyn ni hefyd yn rhoi arian i wella bysiau lleol a llefydd fel gorsaf Merthyr.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Minister. Now, capping bus fares at £2 for adults was a key pledge in my party's manifesto from May, building on our work in Government, where we introduced £1 bus fares for young people and provided free bus travel for older people and people with disabilities. Now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced that, from January 2027, single bus fares in England will be capped at £2 for adults. This will, of course, mean a Barnett consequential for the Welsh Government. So, will you use this to introduce a similar £2 cap for fares in Wales? And if not, will you explain why bus users in Wales should lose out?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: This Government is committed to buses being a key part of the transport infrastructure, especially for those people who maybe cannot afford and don't have access to a private car. We've made sure that the bus fare for young people is continued and that's a commitment throughout the term of this Government. It was in the programme for government that we talked about yesterday. We're looking forward to seeing the consequentials come in, but, as an ex-Minister, you know that the consequentials come into the Government, the Government then decides on the priorities it sets to that. You've seen the priorities in the programme for government yesterday. But if I can give you one reassurance, I think that bus services are one of the key things that this Government will be differentiating itself for over the next four years, because we recognise the importance of them to those people who are furthest away from their own transport solutions.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Minister, many people in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr still struggle to access jobs, education and healthcare because of poor transport links. Given the significant amount of public money already spent on transport projects in Wales, can the Cabinet Secretary please explain why so many communities remain poorly served, and what steps will be taken to improve reliability and accessibility before asking taxpayers to fund further major schemes? Thank you.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you for the question, David. I think the key thing for this is actually starting to recognise the truth of the matter. We've got a Transport for Wales service that's hitting its time targets ahead of everyone else in the UK. The latest statistics show that Transport for Wales was hitting over 80 per cent within three minutes of its required time. So, it is providing the service it needs to provide. The second part of this is about making sure we have the funding to be able to invest in that infrastructure. If I remember, when we talked about rail devolution when I came to this Siambr relatively recently, the benches behind me were against us having extra rail devolution, which is for precisely the same reasons that you're asking the questions. We want to make sure that people can access jobs, healthcare and just make society work. I'm just going to reiterate a point I made to Vikki a few seconds ago. This is important for us in terms of not just rail transport, it's important to us from a bus perspective as well, and I think that's going to be key for these four years ahead.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Parents and children across Rhondda Cynon Taf are concerned about the impact of the council's decisions, which is a Labour-led council, to make school transport as complex as possible for children who just want to know whether they're going to get to school safely. The impact of this decision is significant. It affects local people who can't get on the bus because it is full of school pupils on their way to school and pupil attendance has been gravely affected. More concerning still, children can't go to the school they want to go to, including Welsh-medium schools, because there are fewer buses available or because of changes to the terms of the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008. Deputy Minister, will you make a statement today supporting parents in RCT who want to make the Labour-led council prioritise the safety of children?
documents.text_cy: Mae rhieni a phlant ar draws Rhondda Cynon Taf yn pryderu am effeithiau penderfyniad y cyngor, sydd o dan arweiniad Llafur, i wneud cludiant ysgol mor gymhleth â phosib i blant sydd jest eisiau gofyn, 'A ydw i'n mynd i gyrraedd yr ysgol yn ddiogel?' Mae canlyniadau'r penderfyniad yma yn sylweddol. Mae'n effeithio ar bobl leol sydd ddim yn gallu mynd ar y bws oherwydd ei fod yn llawn disgyblion ar y ffordd i'r ysgol ac mae presenoldeb disgyblion yn yr ysgol wedi'i effeithio'n ddifrifol. Yn fwy pryderus byth, mae plant yn methu mynd i'r ysgol maen nhw eisiau, gan gynnwys ysgolion cyfrwng Cymraeg, oherwydd bod llai o fysiau ar gael neu oherwydd newidiadau i delerau'r Mesur Teithio gan Ddysgwyr (Cymru) 2008. Dirprwy Weinidog, a wnewch chi wneud datganiad heddiw yn cefnogi rhieni Rhondda Cynon Taf sydd am wneud i'r cyngor, sydd o dan arweiniad Llafur, flaenoriaethu diogelwch plant?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you for the question, Lis.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn, Lis.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I think there are a couple of things here. One, it's very complicated. I think one of the things that learner travel has shown me is that this is probably the biggest difficult problem I've got on my horizon, excepting that I've got the M4 and the Menai on that as well. So, it shows the complexity of it. And I think it's been shown by this Government that we've taken this on as a cross-portfolio opportunity, because, as you say, this affects—. We're talking about education and Welsh learner education, but also post-16 education. And one of the things that I found most disconcerting is that, ultimately, learner travel and learner transport should be an enabler of people's education; it should not be a disenabler. So, this Government is keen and it was in our 100-day commitment. We've started work on it, particularly in relation to the Welsh language first, but then we're going to be focusing on post-16 education and, following that, it'll be additional learning needs learner transport as well.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: 2. How will the Welsh Government's energy policy support its efforts to achieve its net-zero targets? OQ64525
documents.text_cy: 2. Sut y bydd polisi ynni Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi ei hymdrechion i gyflawni ei thargedau sero net? OQ64525

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: The Welsh Government’s national energy strategy will take a whole-systems approach, replacing the previous renewable electricity generation target with an emissions-based energy target. This will help identify where action delivers the greatest contribution to our ambition of achieving net zero by 2040.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you, Minister. Minister, releasing carbon dioxide into the atmosphere causes temperatures on earth to rise, and that isn't good for any of us. And we need to achieve whatever reduction in emissions is necessary to secure the long-term future of mankind. That's why, in its current formulation, net zero is so frustrating. Deindustrialisation and a reliance on China and India are not long-term solutions. Renewables, again, are not a long-term solution, neither is burying our heads in the sand about the economic and geopolitical problems created by net zero. The only long-term solution to the challenges that we face, both as a nation and as a species, is nuclear power. So, I'm excited about the development of small modular reactors at Wylfa. After that, Minister, what's next for nuclear power in Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I just would point out to the Member that I think the context is key here, isn't it?  So, the situation in Wales where we have unique assets—latent potential in many cases in terms of green energy—is that, actually, green energy is the means for our reindustrialisation, not our deindustrialisation. I'm specifically referring to, for example, our globally significant potential in terms of floating offshore wind, and the well-known, unique natural advantages we have in terms of tidal technologies, for example. We could, therefore, not just generate the electricity through those technologies, but also capture the supply chain and build up a manufacturing base on that level.

In relation to his point about nuclear, I would just point out that, actually, the move towards an emissions-based target includes not just renewable sectors, but also other low-carbon technologies that include nuclear, alongside carbon capture and storage.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm pleased to hear the Minister's reference to reindustrialisation. I welcome that. I would also agree on the importance of the nuclear industry in achieving that. Last week, I visited Hinkley Point, which is a nuclear power station that is being built with a great deal of Welsh steel, and there's an opportunity to go further, beyond the new project in Wylfa, in expanding nuclear in Wales.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n falch o glywed cyfeiriad y Gweinidog at ailddiwydiannu. Dwi'n croesawu hynny. Byddwn hefyd yn eilio pwysigrwydd y diwydiant niwclear i gwblhau hynny. Yr wythnos diwethaf, bues i lawr yn Hinkley Point, pwerdy niwclear sydd wedi ei adeiladu gyda pheth helaeth o ddur Cymreig, ac mae yna gyfle i fynd ymhellach, y tu hwnt i'r prosiect newydd yn Wylfa, o ran ehangu'r diwydiant niwclear yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: But on the net-zero target set by Welsh Government for 2040, we welcome that target. We will push you on it. But that target is meaningless unless the Minister is prepared to deliver the renewable energy infrastructure needed to achieve it, and you referenced renewables in your earlier answer. Do you accept that Wales cannot reach net zero in that time frame without a major expansion of onshore wind as well as offshore wind, and that that in itself cannot be delivered without grid infrastructure and pylons to connect it? And if you do accept that premise, will you commit to supporting that infrastructure and those projects, even where those decisions prove difficult and locally unpopular?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I'm grateful to the Member for his question. There are a number of elements to that question, but, of course, everything is connected at the end of the day, isn't it?

With the national energy strategy, one of the major elements will be setting out the different contributions that will be made by each form of technology, and then, of course, at a spatial level—so, that's one aspect—and setting out what the different elements will contribute. The decision with regard to Gwyndod, to all intents and purposes, has already been made, and that's the basis on which all of the energy stakeholders across Britain are planning.

That element has to be a part of the mix, but, certainly, we do accept that there is a contribution to be made by onshore green energy, and there are implications in terms of ensuring that the infrastructure with regard to grid connection is there to facilitate that to happen in the most efficient way with regard to our systems and our economy, recognising, of course, that there is a need in any planning framework to strike the right balance in terms of the interests and voice of the community.
documents.text_cy:
Rwy'n ddiolchgar i'r Aelod am ei gwestiwn. Mae yna nifer o elfennau yn fanna, ond, wrth gwrs, mae popeth yn gysylltiedig ar ddiwedd y dydd, onid ydy? 

Gyda'r strategaeth ynni genedlaethol, wrth gwrs, un o'r elfennau mawr fydd gosod mas y gwahanol gyfraniadau fydd yn cael eu gwneud fesul technoleg, a wedyn, wrth gwrs, ar lefel gofodol—so, bydd hwnna’n elfen—a gosod mas beth mae’r gwahanol elfennau yn cyfrannu. Mae’r penderfyniad gyda Gwyndod, i bob pwrpas, wedi’i wneud, a dyna’r sail y mae’r holl randdeiliaid ynni ar draws Prydain nawr yn cynllunio arni.

Felly, mae’r elfen yna, wrth gwrs, yn gorfod bod yn rhan ohono fe, ond, yn sicr, rŷn ni’n derbyn bod cyfraniad gydag ynni gwyrdd ar y tir, ac mae yna oblygiadau wedyn o ran sicrhau bod y seilwaith o ran cysylltiadau grid yno i helpu hynny i ddigwydd yn y ffordd fwyaf effeithlon o ran ein systemau ni, a hefyd o ran ein economi, gan, wrth gwrs, gydnabod bod yna angen gydag unrhyw fframwaith cynllunio i gael y balans yn iawn o ran y llais a'r buddiannau cymunedol hefyd.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Good afternoon, Minister.
documents.text_cy: Prynhawn da, Weinidog.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I'm really pleased to hear from Reform UK that there's not a rejection of the net-zero targets, which we have previously heard. So, I'm hoping that there's been a bit of a change on those benches over there. But I would like just to come back on the point that was made by Joe Martin in relation to selective forms of energy, because what we should be doing is everything. The world is on fire. We've seen the wildfires across Wales this summer, and, actually, we have at our fingertips the opportunity to deliver a whole raft of renewable energy, and here in Wales, as you've said, we've got a real opportunity.

Very different to my friend on my right—you're not on the right, I know—. We've talked about this before, but I would like to give you another opportunity, just to be clear on this, that, in developing onshore wind, your commitment still is to undergrounding those transmission cables, because that's what our communities want. I'm hoping you'll confirm that, and also that we're looking at how communities can own that onshore wind as well. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I'm grateful to the Member for her question, and she is absolutely right, of course, that our national energy strategy will be looking particularly at those technologies where Wales is well placed, in terms of its natural assets, in the way that I described, to develop. But we need to be mindful, of course, of nascent technologies, which are at different stages of maturity at any point. So, this area never stands still, and we need to be building the capacity for Wales to be a test bed for some of those technologies that are on the horizon as well. 

In relation to grid infrastructure, can I take the opportunity as well to say—I should be able to recite this without looking at my notes—that we are clearly committed to delivering our manifesto commitment in relation to the distribution network of 132 kV and below, which is in favour of undergrounding, with only exceptions in terms of overhead, through low wooden poles, or other similar, equally unintrusive infrastructure?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you. I now call the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. The Reform UK spokesperson, Jason O'Connell.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi. Llefarydd Reform UK, Jason O'Connell.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Minister, this week marks three years since the introduction of the default 20 mph limit across Wales. That's three years that motorists have been treated as a problem, and three years since this institution has ignored all the calls to overturn this disastrous policy. The cost is 1 billion extra minutes to car journey times across Wales each year. That's 1 billion minutes, and a policy estimated to cost up to £9 billion to the Welsh economy. And, after all of that, Welsh road deaths are still rising throughout the varying speed zones. Now, Minister, every one of those deaths is a tragedy. Road safety deserves a strategy that's more than just changing road signs. For years, when Labour was in Government, your party backed this single-minded approach. You defended it, you backed it, and now the data tells us it's clearly not working. So, Cabinet Minister, will you finally listen to the data and the hundreds of thousands of people who continue to speak out against this policy and end this experiment?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I hesitate to thank you for the question, Jason, but I will do out of courtesy. At the business statement last week, you were reminded to use data carefully, and you used the same data now as you used then. This data doesn't relate to 20 mph. Let's give you the actual data: in 2025, there were 1,469 collisions on roads with 20 mph and 30 mph speed limits combined, which is 2 per cent higher than in 2024, when there were 1,445. But it is the second lowest annual number ever recorded in Wales. So, this proves that, when we've reduced speed limits, it's actually reduced collisions. And I've heard it from people over the other side of the Siambr, and I appreciate it. This saves children's lives. This is a policy that this Government supports. We recognise there were ways we could have done it better; we talked about that throughout the last term, and I think we'd say the same thing again. However, we've got to make sure we follow the evidence, and when the evidence gets polluted by words that aren't actually true, it distorts things. The one thing that I'm sure that I'm going to make sure I do is that I am evidence led; I'm not going to be just led by rhetoric that is from the benches behind.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I'm pretty sure I heard the data tell me there that accidents were going up, but that's the data for you.

Cabinet Minister, you can dispute all the figures you like, but you can't dispute your party's own record. This goes far beyond the 20 mph default limit. For years, major road projects have been frozen, cancelled or ruled out while congestion's got worse and motorists have been left in traffic up and down Wales. Your own leader made his priorities perfectly clear during the election campaign. He said that Plaid would keep the default limit and that it would not be reviewed. So, let us be clear: while we accept that this is a policy that you inherited from the previous Government, it's an approach you actively supported. You spent years telling the people of Wales that this was all about safety, when in fact, as most people know, up and down the country, it was all about the pursuit of damaging net-zero dogma. Absolutely. Without the proper infrastructure investment, frustrated Welsh motorists would have no choice but to use public transport—isn't that right, Minister? So, rather than punishing motorists as a transport strategy, will you actually invest in the proper road infrastructure that Wales actually needs?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Do you know, it's great when you see young people in the Chamber looking down, and looking down at what we're talking about today? It's with them in mind that I support this policy, because, ultimately, this is not about dogma, this is about safety and particularly children's safety. So, this is something that this Government supports; I think it sounds like it's got support from across other parts of the Siambr. Because, when it comes to dogma, there's no party more interested in dogma than the party behind me when they're talking about things like this. Ultimately, I care more about those children who are up there than I do about answering questions that are like this.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Oh, you don't care about answering questions from an elected Member. Shocking.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Another cop out. But the good news is we also care about young people. We want to make sure they have jobs well into the future and our economy thrives. Absolutely. Now, in June, you stood in this Chamber and made a very clear commitment to review the position on the M4 relief road. You said this would not be another review that kicks the can down the road—the can would likely end up in a traffic jam anyway. You said you would return to the Senedd early in autumn with your Government's way forward. Well, Cabinet Minister, rather depressingly, it is autumn. You ruled out a completely viable black route, but the people sitting in congestion around Newport every day don't know what this Government is going to do about the traffic. So, it's time to come clean. Before the election, your party promised a solution on the M4. But I know, and you know, that you have nothing. You were just trying to waste time while you figure it all out at the last minute. In fact, you've taken so long, we've done the work for you. We've revised the costings for the M4 relief road, and £2.8 billion is the updated cost. We are more than happy to continue the work, secure the funding, take over your brief and get the job done ourselves. So, Minister, can you tell us what is your solution to the congestion on the M4? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: The Member is well aware that we're going to be coming back to this Siambr on 6 October with an update based on evidence. The reason we want evidence is to make sure that we make the right decisions and we don't—. We're not kicking the can down the road, we're actually making the right decisions based on what the evidence tells us. As he knows, as do other transport spokespeople in this room, I've made sure that I'm going to share that evidence ahead of this meeting, so we'll be in the position that this Siambr will be able to talk about things that actually are important, that actually matter. Because then, hopefully, we'll come to some consensus. The M4 isn't straightforward. Let's be honest. The M4, as a road, was built as part of the infrastructure around Newport. So, it's not just about the M4—this is about intra-Newport issues as much as it is about the M4. That's what this Government is going to do. I look forward to debating that on 6 October when we can talk about evidence.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Welsh Labour spokesperson, Shav Taj.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Shav Taj.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Minister, data centres, I've written to you about them many a time, and, obviously, they're not new, but their use—principally because of AI and its expansion—is going to be important. There are critical challenges around that, potentially opportunities as well, in terms of jobs and growth and all the rest of it. To that end, it was really good to have a response from you. When I wrote to you, you responded about a new strategic policy framework for data centres in Wales. I think that's really critical, and of course it would be great to now, I guess, understand from you what the Government's intentions are on the basis of that framework. Will you commit that any framework will ensure positive community and environmental impact as being a guiding force? I'm sure that you would, hopefully, agree with me that we need to ensure that communities that have that infrastructure do then actually receive tangible local benefits through good jobs, good apprenticeships and genuine community wealth building.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm really grateful to the Member, not just for writing to me, as she's described, but also for raising this subject here in the Siambr, which gives me an opportunity to address some of the issues that are relevant to this area. As she's aware, we have commissioned work that is ongoing in this area. It's important to acknowledge that with the huge growth of data centres, related digital infrastructure and the wider context, of course, of AI, edge computing and related technologies, we do need to have a robust policy framework that is futureproofed and that also recognises the need to enable us to have the advantages that can flow from the investments that are happening in digital infrastructure across the world but to do so in a way that balances those with the legitimate concerns that people have at a community level and more broadly in terms of energy use, in terms of water, in terms of land use et cetera. So, we will be setting this out as soon as we can so that we can have that discussion across the Siambr and more widely across civil society in Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you, Minister. Obviously, we can't have a thriving economy in Wales without stronger connections between jobs, opportunities and communities. That's why the UK Labour Government invested £14 billion in Welsh rail, and Cardiff parkway is a really important part of that strategy. My constituents in St Mellons know that the construction is going to take time, and they're going to need some reassurances about the direct benefit to the community, of course, but every day some of that news—. They're still waiting. So, can you now update us on when we will see the first shovel in the ground on Cardiff parkway, in my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm grateful to the Member for that question as well. We were wondering whether we could do a little bit of choreography. But I think that the key here, and obviously we're aware of that specific opportunity, is we're keen to see investment in our railway infrastructure the length and breadth of Wales, including in Cardiff. The one thing that we need, and maybe we can work together on this, is to turn that £14 billion promise that, you know—. The promise was very welcome, but what we need now is to turn that into an action plan with budgetary commitments and a timetable. And then we'll not only be able to deliver Cardiff parkway and wider investment across Cardiff and south-east Wales, but the length and breadth of Wales. So, let's work together on that.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Welsh Conservative spokesperson, Janet Finch-Saunders.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Janet Finch-Saunders.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. And pen-blwydd hapus, Cabinet Secretary. Minister, there is potentially a very expensive problem with the Global Centre of Rail Excellence. Now, my colleague Andrew R.T. Davies yesterday raised it, and I'm not sure that the answer that you gave yesterday actually addressed the very fundamental point of such an amount of wasted taxpayers' money. When the Welsh Government announced this scheme, the Global Centre of Rail Excellence—sounds good, doesn't it—it explicitly stated that Celtic Energy would gift all the land necessary for the project, yet the site was subsequently described as having been purchased by GCRE, and it was transferred before restoration of the former Nant Helen opencast mine had been completed. So, will you tell us today, plainly, was the land gifted or purchased? If it was purchased, how much did GCRE pay, and what restoration liabilities did the previous and now this current Welsh Government-owned company take on when it acquired the site? Most importantly, if the money available for restoration is not enough to finish the job, exactly who does pick up the bill, Celtic Energy or the Welsh taxpayer?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I'm grateful; thank you for your birthday wishes. In relation to the specifics on GCRE, there were some specific questions, and, if the Member is happy, I would prefer to take those back so we can ensure that, whatever information we can, we provide accurately, because I don't have all of that at my fingertips here.

But what I can say is that we as a Government reviewed the situation, we commissioned specialist advice in terms of where we are now, as the First Minister was saying, in terms of the opportunity. We've received that specialist advice, and we are now in the process of reviewing and discussing with other potential investors what the potential is. There is an incredibly important employment site here, and we're looking both at the Global Centre of Rail Excellence option, but looking at it in the round as well.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
Diolch. I hope you can answer this one. Minister, the original plan was that £70 million of public money would help unlock around £330 million of private investment. For years, we were told there was serious private sector interest. GCRE talked about credible bidders and international interest, even from the middle east and America. And as recently as March last year, the First Minister at the time told this Senedd that GCRE was in detailed discussions with a potential funder, yet the private investment still hasn't materialised and the rail testing centre still hasn't been built.

So, what exactly went wrong? Was there ever an investor genuinely prepared to put up the money needed to build the project, and, if so, why did they walk away? Because, at this moment in time, it does look as though your Government has inherited a large hole in the ground, a project nobody is prepared to invest in, and, potentially, a very large bill for putting the site back as it was. How much more taxpayers' money are you prepared to put into this scheme? Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you for that further question in this area. There's not much, really, I can add usefully at this stage. I'm sure the Member will be mindful of the fact that we need to actually drill down into the detail, look at the potential interest that has been expressed by an investor, and then make a decision in the full possession of all of that information that delivers the best public value that we can, both in economic and employment terms, in a very, very important region of Wales, which is deserving of our support to the full extent that is possible. And once we have that information, we will make a decision and we will bring that decision, of course, back to the Siambr.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: 3. What role will community energy projects play in Wales's transition to net zero? OQ64557
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa rôl fydd prosiectau ynni cymunedol yn ei chwarae yn nhrawsnewidiad Cymru i sero net? OQ64557

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Our national energy strategy will recognise the vital role of community energy in achieving net zero. The Welsh public energy company will help unlock that ambition, scaling up the number of community energy projects, installing renewables and storage and using them to provide lower cost power and heat to people.
documents.text_cy: Bydd ein strategaeth ynni genedlaethol yn cydnabod rôl hanfodol ynni cymunedol wrth gyflawni sero net. Bydd cwmni ynni cyhoeddus Cymru yn helpu i gyflawni’r uchelgais honno, gan gynyddu nifer y prosiectau ynni cymunedol, gosod systemau ynni adnewyddadwy a chyfleusterau storio a'u defnyddio i ddarparu pŵer a gwres am gost is i bobl.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you very much. It's excellent to hear that you share my view that community energy has a crucial role to play as we move towards our ambition of a net-zero Wales. Of course, at the heart of our principles as we develop community energy projects is that they align with local need, and it's important to ensure that the planning process reflects that. A perfect example of an industrial development that is contrary to our principles in my constituency is the Menai data centre scheme on the former Ferodo site near Caernarfon. It's a project that will swallow great amounts of energy and water, will have a damaging impact on wildlife and will cause sound and light pollution locally. But, more than anything, the huge scale of the project means that it will be sure to destroy our local landscapes and views, while offering very few local benefits. So, how can you ensure that the energy supply for data centres doesn't have a negative impact on the local area?
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Mae'n wych clywed eich bod chi o'r un farn â fi fod gan ynni cymunedol ran hollbwysig i'w chwarae wrth inni symud tuag at ein huchelgais o Gymru sero net. Wrth gwrs, wrth galon ein hegwyddorion wrth inni fynd ati i ddatblygu prosiectau ynni cymunedol yw eu bod nhw'n cyd-fynd â'r anghenion yn lleol, ac mae'n bwysig sicrhau bod y broses cynllunio yn adlewyrchu hynny. Enghraifft berffaith o ddatblygiad diwydiannol sydd yn mynd yn gwbl groes i'n hegwyddorion ni yn fy etholaeth i yw'r cynllun canolfan ddata Menai ar hen safle Ferodo yn ardal Caernarfon. Mae'n brosiect fydd yn llyncu llwythi o ynni a dŵr, yn cael effaith ddinistriol ar fywyd natur ac yn achosi llygredd sŵn a golau yn lleol. Ond, yn fwy na dim, mae graddfa anferthol y prosiect yn golygu y bydd yn siŵr o ddifetha ein tirwedd a'n golygfeydd yn lleol, gan gynnig ychydig iawn o fanteision yn lleol. Felly, sut y gallwch sicrhau nad yw cyflenwad ynni canolfannau data yn cael effaith negyddol ar yr ardal leol?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm grateful to the Member for that supplementary question. I think that you get to the core of the principles of our economic policy, namely that developments in terms of our economy or our energy system have to be planned for the benefit of the people of Wales. We have seen in our past as a nation, of course, the opposite of that happening, and developments taking place at the expense of local interests. We're not willing to see the same mistakes being made again. So, that's why we put an emphasis on community energy. We have made a commitment in terms of ensuring a minimum, at least, in terms of the local ownership of major projects, and in the particular context you referred to in terms of data centres, if I could echo what I said earlier, we as a Government will be bringing a policy framework forward that will address the quite understandable fears that exist across Wales where there are recommendations made in terms of data centres that don't give due consideration to the interests of local people or the local environment.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n ddiolchgar i'r Aelod am y cwestiwn atodol. Rydych chi'n mynd, dwi'n credu, at hanfod egwyddorion ein polisi economaidd, hynny yw, fod datblygiadau o ran ein heconomi ni neu o ran ein system ynni ni yn gorfod cael eu cynllunio er budd pobl Cymru. Rydyn ni wedi gweld yn ein gorffennol fel cenedl, wrth gwrs, y gwrthwyneb yn digwydd, a datblygiadau'n digwydd ar draul buddiannau pobl leol. Dydyn ni ddim yn barod i weld yr un camgymeriad yn digwydd eto. Felly, dyna pam rydyn ni'n rhoi pwyslais ar ynni cymunedol. Rydyn ni'n rhoi ymrwymiad o ran sicrhau isafswm, o leiaf, mewn prosiectau mawr o ran perchnogaeth leol, ac yn y cyd-destun penodol y gwnaethoch chi gyfeirio ato fe o ran canolfannau data, os caf i ategu'r hyn a ddywedais i'n gynharach, mi fyddwn ni fel Llywodraeth yn dod â fframwaith polisi gerbron sy'n mynd i'r afael â'r ofnau digon dealladwy ar draws Cymru lle mae yna argymhellion o ran canolfannau data sydd ddim yn rhoi'r priod ystyriaeth i fuddiannau pobl leol na'r amgylchedd lleol.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Cabinet Minister, there's a world of difference between genuine community energy and simply expecting rural communities to host enormous commercial energy developments. Across Wales, communities are being asked to accept industrial-scale windfarms, pylons and other infrastructure, while too often the electricity profits and the economic benefits flow elsewhere. So, if your Government wants at least 1.5 GW of renewable energy capacity to be locally owned by 2035, will you guarantee that community energy really means community ownership, community consent and tangible benefits for the people who live there, including lower energy costs, rather than simply imposing ever more large-scale development on rural Wales and calling a community benefit fund compensation? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm grateful to the Member for his question. As I said a moment ago, I think that building, financing and facilitating community energy that is 100 per cent community owned is an important element of our policy. For larger schemes, we have said that we are committed to mandating a minimum level of community ownership of those schemes. I would say, more broadly, as well, a key principle of our national energy strategy will be taking an approach that I would characterise as more planned in relation to the spatial development of energy, rather than what we've had previously, which is, essentially, a market-led approach, which has led to concerns in communities, legitimate questions, like whether cumulative impact is properly being addressed. So, I think, by taking a planned approach, and getting the balance right between the necessity for decarbonising our energy system, recognising the range of technologies, including onshore renewables and their role in that, but giving confidence to communities as well that this is being done in a planned way, with them, and is not being imposed upon them with little benefit accruing to communities and to the people of Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: 4. What action is the Cabinet Minister taking to improve economic outcomes in Ceredigion Penfro? OQ64513
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa gamau y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn eu cymryd i wella canlyniadau economaidd yng Ngheredigion Penfro? OQ64513

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Improving economic outcomes in Ceredigion Penfro means backing local businesses, strengthening rural economies, and creating better paid jobs. We're delivering our commitment to support Welsh firms, align skills with employer needs, invest in infrastructure and procurement, and ensure communities across west Wales share in economic growth.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Minister, thank you for your response. Yesterday, you told this Chamber that new defence-related investment decisions should, where possible, wait for your ethical defence investment framework. Yet Ceredigion Penfro should be benefiting directly from the £50 million defence growth deal, with Ministry of Defence Aberporth offering skilled jobs, investment and opportunities for local business. So, a simple question, Minister: are the defence growth deal and Aberporth both exempt from that pause? And if not, can you guarantee that not one job or contract, and not one pound of investment in Ceredigion Penfro will be lost or delayed as a result? West Wales needs certainty and investment now, not another framework standing in the way. Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm grateful to the Member for his question. I think I set it out clearly yesterday that we, obviously, are working at pace on the framework. The framework, actually, is a solid foundation for us to work with the sector in Wales, and we'll be working with companies in the sector as part of the process of developing it. Where there are decisions that—. We are trying—. Obviously, where it's possible to defer, partly out of respect for this Senedd, really—. But where it's not possible, in situations where decisions, for practical reasons, have to be made before the framework is finalised, we have allowed that exceptional flexibility, partly for the reasons that the Member describes, that we do not want to lose opportunities in cases that, actually, would be well within the framework. So, we have that flexibility, and I can assure him, as the economy Minister, I will be mindful of the need to use that flexibility where necessary.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Question 5 [OQ64492] by Tom Montgomery has been withdrawn. Therefore, question 6—Anna Nicholl.
documents.text_cy: Mae cwestiwn 5 [OQ64492] gan Tom Montgomery wedi'i dynnu'n ôl. Felly, cwestiwn 6—Anna Nicholl.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: 6. How will the Cabinet Minister ensure that the benefits of the Welsh Government's new national energy strategy are retained within local communities? OQ64542
documents.text_cy: 6. Sut y bydd y Gweinidog Cabinet yn sicrhau bod manteision strategaeth ynni genedlaethol newydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn cael eu cadw o fewn cymunedau lleol? OQ64542

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: We are determined that the communities hosting energy developments are genuine beneficiaries. The national energy strategy will identify the clean energy that Wales needs and how more of this can be owned through minimum community ownership requirements and investment from the new Welsh public energy company.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
Diolch. I welcome this Government's commitment to a renewable energy strategy that retains value in Welsh communities. The net-zero economy is already a significant and high-value component of the Welsh economy. There are particular opportunities in Ceredigion Penfro, with 1,600 jobs in the sector in Pembrokeshire alone already, and billions set to be invested in upcoming projects. This ranges from successful community-owned projects, such as Cwm Arian, to large-scale initiatives, like the Celtic Freeport.

Net zero is now an integral part of Welsh industry, and we've got huge potential to develop this further. The transition to net zero is a major economic opportunity, but I also welcome what the Minister has said here, that there needs to be a proper, planned strategy as to how we do this, both spatially and to balance the benefits for our economy, our communities and the environment. So, could the Cabinet Minister describe, as more energy infrastructure is developed in our rural communities, how Government will now ensure genuine benefit through local ownership jobs and skills and lower energy bills?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm really grateful for the question—part of an emerging theme this afternoon. It's such an important opportunity for us nationally and locally to make sure that we create an energy system where we benefit from the energy resources that we have. We can do that at different scales; we can do it through the Welsh public energy company at a larger scale, publicly owned, delivering benefit across the whole of Wales, for the people of Wales; we can do it through supporting community ownership, of which there are some good examples in the Member's constituency already. One of the reasons for doing that is precisely to get to grips with the energy costs problem that we face. Wales has some of the highest energy costs relatively compared to other parts of the UK. The UK has some of the highest energy costs in Europe. There's good evidence that community ownership actually is a means by which you can begin to deliver lower costs to households. And similarly, a publicly owned energy company, which is free not to follow the market price in energy, but to say, 'Let's actually engage in contracts with large-scale industrial users in Wales to create a Welsh energy advantage using our renewable energy resources, but for the benefit of our economy', that's precisely why we're creating a Welsh public energy company, and we're supporting public ownership and local ownership in a variety of ways at different scales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I welcome the Welsh Government's guidance published in June on behind-the-meter energy systems, and I was pleased to see the Government recognising the potential for businesses to generate, use and sell locally produced energy. These are exactly the sorts of arrangements that can deliver real economic benefit to Welsh communities and ensure that solar panels are installed on industrial units rather than prime agricultural land.

I have heard from business owners who tell me that the financial return from exporting surplus electricity to the grid can be low, that it's so low that it simply does not provide enough incentive to install solar panels on large commercial or industrial buildings. Suppliers setting their own export tariffs turns this on its head. So, can the Minister outline what they are doing to actively promote private-wire and licence-exempt arrangements, allowing businesses to sell surplus power directly to neighbouring businesses at an agreed price?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I'm really grateful to the Member for his question. He's absolutely right: I think that private-wire, behind-the-meter opportunities are actually one of the ways in which we can do what I just described, really, which is to create that energy advantage, particularly in the context of businesses. Because it can be done, there is a means to do it, but we've got to get organised to see where we can build that out at scale to facilitate businesses, because if they can avoid the network costs—. Although there's been some movement from the UK Government on network costs to large industrial users, by and large, there's still a huge network cost element. If we can devise different ways, it could be on-site microgeneration in some circumstances; in larger scales, there could be local energy systems, which are behind the wire, which could actually provide low-cost energy for a wide range of businesses. There's some work we've got to do with some of the stakeholders in order to ensure that the arrangement that you just described in terms of connection, maybe with the grid, can be part of it. So, we're working on it. It's absolutely one of the areas where, if we work smart, we could build that Welsh energy advantage, which will be such a critical determinant of our economic success.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: 7. Will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the performance of the Development Bank of Wales? OQ64545
documents.text_cy: 7. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet roi diweddariad am berfformiad Banc Datblygu Cymru? OQ64545

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: The Development Bank of Wales continues to deliver finance and investment support to businesses across Wales. The bank has reported strong performance during the year and remains a key economic development partner. Its 2025-26 annual report will be published later this month, setting out its full performance and economic impact.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: While of course I support ethical guidelines of conduct for the Development Bank of Wales, I worry about the politicisation of the bank and that investment decisions are based more off the whims of the Welsh Government rather than sensible financial criteria. For example, climate change is now a political priority that's been forced on the bank by the Government to meet mad net-zero targets. In the programme for government announced yesterday, we heard new economic criteria and possibly restrictions on defence investments for the bank. We have already had plenty of controversy with the bank in recent years, with concerns over political donations and alleged blacklisting of certain businesses. Can the Minister confirm whether the new defence ethical framework announced yesterday will apply to the Development Bank of Wales, and, if so, when? And will the Government publish a consolidated ethical and policy criteria that the development bank is expected to follow so that businesses and the Senedd can now understand how investment decisions are being made and scrutinise any further changes? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
I intend to issue the bank's remit letter in the coming weeks, which will set out clear priorities for the bank, supporting this Government's ambitions for investment, productivity and growth. That's a standard approach that every Government uses. There's nothing to see there. It's how every Government relates to arm's-length bodies, setting out the way in which the arm's-length body can deliver to the wider ambitions of the Government, particularly in the economic sphere.

Of course, we would expect the ethical framework that we are setting out in the defence sector to be cross-Government. It's there to govern the use of public money, including by the development bank, and it will also govern the development agency. Again, it's fairly normal. There are policies around fair work, for example. You would expect these to be reflected across the whole range of agencies.

I was at the launch of the development bank's Economic Intelligence Wales 'Productivity Heroes' report, and there's fantastic news here; let's remind ourselves of that. Over 1,700 high-growth firms are delivering higher productivity, higher employment and higher profits for those businesses so that they can continue to reinvest in their future trajectory of growth. I recognise scrutiny is an important part of our work here, but also let's not lose the opportunity to celebrate Welsh economic success. Because there are great things happening in Wales, and some of it is down to the work of the development bank.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: Thank you. The final question to you, Minister. Question 8—Elfed Williams.
documents.text_cy: Y cwestiwn olaf i chi, Weinidog. Cwestiwn 8—Elfed Williams.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: 8. What action is the Welsh Government taking to maximise the local economic opportunities arising from the Gwyndod project in Bangor Conwy Môn? OQ64550
documents.text_cy: 8. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i wneud y mwyaf o’r cyfleoedd economaidd lleol sy’n deillio o brosiect Gwyndod ym Mangor Conwy Môn? OQ64550

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: The Welsh Government is working closely with Great British Energy—Nuclear and Rolls-Royce SMR to maximise local benefits from Gwyndod. We are helping Welsh businesses to access supply chain opportunities and working with education partners to enable local people to develop the required skills that will be required for the project.
documents.text_cy: Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cydweithio'n agos gyda Great British Energy—Nuclear a Rolls-Royce SMR i sicrhau'r manteision mwyaf posibl i'r gymuned leol o Gwyndod. Rydym yn cefnogi busnesau Cymru i ddefnyddio cyfleoedd y gadwyn gyflenwi ac yn gweithio gyda phartneriaid addysg i alluogi pobl leol i ddatblygu'r sgiliau sydd eu hangen ar gyfer y prosiect.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text: I thank the Cabinet Minister for that response. On my visit to the Gwyndod site last week, it was clear that this is not only an opportunity to secure energy for decades, but also a once-in-a-generation opportunity for the economy of Ynys Môn and north-west Wales. If we want local people to truly benefit, we need to start to prepare now. That means working with local colleges to ensure that apprenticeships and the required skills are in place, and, importantly, that they have the funding to deliver those. It also means giving fair opportunities to local businesses to get work through the supply chain. Will the Minister therefore commit to ensuring that jobs, skills and local businesses will be at the heart of the Welsh Government's strategy for Gwyndod? Thank you.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Gweinidog Cabinet am yr ymateb. Ar fy ymweliad â safle Gwyndod yr wythnos diwethaf, roedd hi'n amlwg fod hwn nid yn unig yn gyfle i sicrhau ynni dibynadwy am ddegawdau, ond yn gyfle unwaith mewn cenedlaeth i economi Ynys Môn a'r gogledd-orllewin. Os ydym am i bobl leol elwa go iawn, mae angen dechrau paratoi nawr. Mae hynny'n golygu gweithio gyda'r colegau lleol i sicrhau prentisiaethau a'r sgiliau fydd eu hangen, ac, yn bwysig, sicrhau bod ganddynt y cyllid i wneud hynny. Mae hefyd yn golygu rhoi cyfle teg i fusnesau lleol ennill gwaith drwy'r gadwyn gyflenwi. A wnaiff y Gweinidog felly ymrwymo i sicrhau mai swyddi, sgiliau a busnesau lleol fydd wrth galon strategaeth Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer Gwyndod? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy
documents.text:
Certainly, this is a golden opportunity in terms of the economy of the whole of Wales, and also regionally and locally. We want to maximise the benefits of that opportunity across the range of dimensions in terms of skills. The Learning and Work Institute has been commissioned to carry out a skills review for Wales. In this context, Great British Energy—Nuclear has been invited to contribute to the call for evidence, so that the needs of the specific workforce for Gwyndod can be at the heart of the strategy that will emerge. The nuclear skills centre and a working group has been drawn together to bring together industry, the Welsh Government, local government and community representatives around a co-ordinated approach, to ensure that we have the system that we need in place to ensure that local people can derive the maximum benefit from the opportunities available.

In terms of the supply chain for local businesses, Welsh Government officials will be playing a central role in the Gwyndod suppliers event—and I'm pleased to publicise this more widely—that will be held over two days in Coleg Menai in Llangefni, on 22 and 23 October, alongside GBE-N and Rolls-Royce SMR. So, there is a great deal of work being done, but that's an overview of what's possible. It's another example, because the decision has already been made, of Wales's importance not just in terms of renewable energy—there are many opportunities in that regard in north Wales—but that we are also there at the beginning of this new technology of SMRs in the United Kingdom, and Wales is in a very good position to benefit economically from these for generations to come.
documents.text_cy:
Yn sicr, mae hwn yn gyfle euraid o ran economi Cymru gyfan, a hefyd yn rhanbarthol ac yn lleol. Rydym ni eisiau gwneud y mwyaf o'r cyfle hwnnw ar draws yr amrediad o ddimensiynau o ran sgiliau. Mae'r Sefydliad Dysgu a Gwaith wedi cael ei gomisiynu i wneud archwiliad sgiliau cenedlaethol ar gyfer Cymru. Yn y cyd-destun yma, mae GBE-N wedi cael ei wahodd i gyfrannu at y galw am dystiolaeth, fel y gall gyfynion y gweithlu penodol ar gyfer Gwyndod fod yn ganolog i'r strategaeth a ddaw yn ei sgil. Mae canolfan sgiliau niwclear Cymru a grŵp llywio wedi'u sefydlu i ddod â diwydiant, Llywodraeth Cymru, llywodraeth leol, darparwyr a chymunedau ynghyd o amgylch dull cydlynol, i sicrhau bod gyda ni y system sydd ei hangen er mwyn sicrhau bod pobl leol yn cael y mwyaf o'r cyfle sydd yno.

O ran y gadwyn gyflenwi ar gyfer busnesau lleol, bydd swyddogion Llywodraeth Cymru yn chwarae rôl ganolog mewn digwyddiad cyflenwyr Gwyndod—mae'n falch gen i geisio hysbysu hynny yn fwy eang—a fydd yn digwydd dros ddau ddiwrnod yng Ngholeg Menai yn Llangefni ar 22 a 23 Hydref, ochr yn ochr â GBE-N a Rolls-Royce SMR. Felly, mae yna lot mwy yn digwydd, ond dyma ryw fraslun o'r hyn sy'n bosib. Mae'n enghraifft arall, gan fod y penderfyniad wedi cael ei wneud, o sut mae Cymru yn bwysig nid yn unig o ran ynni adnewyddol—ac mae yna lot o gyfleoedd fanna yng ngogledd Cymru—ond ein bod ni hefyd yno ar ddechrau technoleg newydd o ran SMR ym Mhrydain, ac mae Cymru mewn safle arbennig o dda i elwa yn economaidd o hynny am genedlaethau i ddod.
