documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: We will now move on to item 2, questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language. The first question is from Becca Martin.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 2, cwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Addysg a'r Gymraeg. Cwestiwn 1, Becca Martin.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 1. Will the Cabinet Minister ensure that adults who wish to learn Welsh have access to more opportunities to develop their language skills? OQ64524
documents.text_cy: 1. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet sicrhau bod oedolion sy'n dymuno dysgu Cymraeg yn cael mynediad at fwy o gyfleoedd i ddatblygu eu sgiliau iaith? OQ64524

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you very much for the question. The good news is that more people are learning Welsh than ever before, and it's wonderful to see interest growing amongst people of all ages and of all backgrounds. The Welsh Government is investing over £18 million in the National Centre for Learning Welsh this year to create opportunities for adults and young people to learn Welsh. The centre provides online provision, face-to-face provision and hybrid provision across all levels to its learners.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn am y cwestiwn. Y newyddion da yw bod mwy o bobl yn dysgu Cymraeg nag erioed o'r blaen, ac mae'n braf gweld diddordeb yn tyfu ymysg pobl o bob oedran ac o bob cefndir. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn buddsoddi dros £18 miliwn yn y Ganolfan Dysgu Cymraeg Genedlaethol eleni i greu cyfleoedd i oedolion a phobl ifanc i ddysgu'r iaith. Mae'r ganolfan yn cynnig darpariaeth ar-lein, wyneb yn wyneb neu hybrid ar draws pob lefel i'w dysgwyr.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch. It's widely accepted that one of the most effective ways for a child to learn the Welsh language, or any language, is through immersion. Simply put, the more Welsh a child hears and uses, the more likely they are to develop the language effectively. The trochi method, or immersion, can also foster a deeper understanding of, and a connection to, Welsh culture and history. However, for too many children, this immersion stops at the school gates. Many children come from English-speaking homes, which is the case in my home, and may have limited opportunities to hear or use Welsh within their wider communities. This is particularly prevalent in north-east Wales, where I am an elected representative. I'm regularly told that the issue is not a lack of desire to learn Welsh, but a lack of opportunities for adults to develop their language skills to a conversational standard. Will the Minister work with partner organisations and external agencies to provide additional opportunities for adult learners to use the language they have, helping to create stronger Welsh-speaking communities and in turn support the next generation of Welsh speakers?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Diolch yn fawr iawn. Thank you very much indeed. Immersion teaching has been with us in Wales for many years, and it's the proven way of ensuring that children acquire the Welsh language, the target language, in the most effective way possible. This was based on work that was done in Canada, where they have immersion programmes. We know that children from non-Welsh-speaking backgrounds acquire the Welsh language fluently through immersion schools. But what we need as well is support for the parents, like yourself, who are learning with their children. I know the national language centre does provide funding and support for parents through various programmes, so that they can learn with their children at the pace their children are developing.

This is equally important in terms of helping parents to help their children with homework, which is one of the barriers that many parents have about putting their children into Welsh-medium schools: 'How can I help with homework?' I can provide many answers to that. First, it's not their parents' homework anyway, but I could go on and on. But where they feel that they can help, learning Welsh is important and helps develop a bond between parents and their children through that second language. I think that sends a positive signal to families about the importance of bilingualism and living in a bilingual Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: As a Welsh language learner, I'm delighted to have the opportunity to learn Welsh in the Senedd.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: I'm Sarah Edwards, and I'm learning Welsh.
documents.text_cy: Sarah Edwards ydw i, a dwi'n dysgu Cymraeg.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Can the Cabinet Minister comment on what provisions are being set out by the Welsh Government to upgrade Welsh language learning facilities in my own constituency of rural Carmarthenshire? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Congratulations for learning Welsh. You live, like I do, in a county where the Welsh language is an important part of the community.
documents.text_cy: Llongyfarchiadau mawr am ddysgu Cymraeg. Rŷch chi'n byw, fel fi, mewn sir lle mae'r Gymraeg yn rhan bwysig o'r gymuned.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Carmarthenshire, which we share in terms of our constituency, is a predominantly Welsh-speaking area, and it is great that people like you are learning the language. The national centre that I referred to earlier on provides funding, and the Welsh Government gives them £18 million to provide funding for courses that are tailored to the needs of people, whether that is in the community, in the Senedd, in workplaces, and online as well. As a former Welsh language tutor myself, I know how important it is for those courses to be available in workplaces in particular, but also in the community.

The joy of the workplace is that a place like the Senedd does give you opportunities not only to learn the language, but to use the language as well, as you have effectively done this afternoon. I would encourage all Members and all staff members in the Senedd, and other workplaces across Wales, to learn the language and be supported in a sensitive and effective way by those of us who are Welsh speakers by engaging with you and practising the language with you. Because learning Welsh is a virtuous cycle in many different ways. It's to do with confidence, it's to do with opportunity and it's to do with developing skills. That cycle needs to be continued and developed until you become fluent to use the language in all kinds of different ways in life. Da iawn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 2. What are the Welsh Government's priorities for schools in Pembrokeshire for the next 12 months? OQ64510
documents.text_cy: 2. Beth yw blaenoriaethau Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer ysgolion yn Sir Benfro dros y 12 mis nesaf? OQ64510

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you very much for that question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Our priority is to raise standards for every child, wherever in Wales they go to school. We want to see sustained improvement in literacy and numeracy, more children and young people making good progress from where they start, and more school leavers earning useful qualifications ready for further study, training or work.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you for that response, Cabinet Minister. There are some serious concerns regarding the future of faith education in our schools in Pembrokeshire, following a number of controversial decisions that have been taken by Pembrokeshire County Council in recent months. As you may be aware, the council decided in May to remove the voluntary controlled status of Ysgol Cilgerran Church in Wales school. This was followed in June by a decision to close Manorbier Church in Wales VC School, while proposals are also being considered to discontinue Tenby Church in Wales VC Primary School.

These decisions have raised some serious concerns amongst parents, governors, church representatives and local communities about the long-term future of faith-based education in Pembrokeshire. So, Cabinet Minister, do you agree with me that no faith school should be lost or lose its status against the will of its school community? And can you tell us what action the Welsh Government is willing to take to support schools that wish to retain their faith status in Pembrokeshire and, indeed, across the whole of Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you very much for that question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: I'm aware obviously of the plans that he raises with me in terms of school organisation proposals from Pembrokeshire County Council. He has been here far longer than I have and will be equally aware that I am unable to comment on the merits or otherwise of any local authority proposals, which may later be referred to Ministers for determination.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
I'd just like to say 'thank you' to my constituency Member, because it is something that is very close to my heart—church schools. So, I just wanted to get that out there.

Policies promoting inclusive physical activity are welcome and many disabled pupils and their families continue to report barriers to meaningful participation in school sports, such as wheelchair-bound children being made to take timings for their peers rather than actively taking part. Can you therefore outline what specific measures the Welsh Government is taking to monitor participation rates amongst disabled learners, how it evaluates whether policies are translating into outcomes on the ground and whether it will commit to publishing data, so that Members can assess if disabled pupils are participating in curriculum-based sport at the same rate as their non-disabled peers? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch. Thank you. And I too want to see all pupils in Wales being able to engage in all aspects of the curriculum, including, obviously, sport and physical activity. We know how important that is for their development, for their health, for their inclusion in school and in society, and I think I've referred in previous answers to our focus on that inclusion. We want our system and access to curriculum to be available for all our learners. I don't have to hand the numbers that she asks for, but I can look into that and share that with her. But I can assure her that all pupils will be a focus of all our work in terms of education standards and the accessibility of the curriculum for learners across Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. Reform UK spokesperson, Stephen Senior.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf nawr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Llefarydd Reform UK, Stephen Senior.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, let's just have a little look back over 20 years of the Programme for International Student Assessment in Wales. Back in 2006, Jane Hutt:

'we can learn from the best and most effective practice'.

We move on to Leighton Andrews, who, to his credit, had a bit of a crack at this, quite forthright. He talked about 'systemic failure'. A few more years to Huw Lewis—'no quick fixes'. Kirsty Williams, who was in post for quite a while:

'it will take time for Welsh education reforms to be reflected in PISA results'.

Well, a Liberal did get one prediction correct there. Jeremy Miles:

'a renewed national focus on reading, numeracy and science'. 

And then, obviously, a few years later, yourself:

'not where we want them'.

I should say, during that period, I actually was partly responsible for administering PISA in a couple of schools in Wales, so I know a little bit about it. It's a grim tale, Minister. It feels like groundhog day for the younger Members. Perhaps that's a film well worth watching. We feel stuck in a loop. My question is: why should we think that this Welsh Government's announcements will make any difference?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you for the gallop through PISA in Wales that I think most of us are familiar with and has got us to a place where we don't want to be. What is different about this plan is its focus on nought to 16 as the first element in that. We recognise that the very earliest years have an impact on learners' development in schools. We're tying it in very firmly with all the interventions that we are making in that space, in order that we can apply the support for those learners and for staff that is appropriate. I'm also—and this too is new—looking at a baseline for entry into schools, a year 6 indicator, which I and others will be able to be held to account for the trajectory we are making in literacy and numeracy, and we also want to see improvements in qualifications outcomes at 16.

What I am keen to do is to make live in our schools system the ability to demonstrate what we are doing, what you can hold me to account on, and the clarity that we give school staff about those expectations. The plan will be published in detail for consultation, in terms of what those expectations look like, very soon. And we will be able to see, on literacy and numeracy specifically, in which direction we are going, and that is different from the responses in the past.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you, Cabinet Secretary. I hear what you're saying, but there's nothing new in baseline assessment. Perhaps it'll be different from what we've had previously. [Interruption.] Yes. I mean, we can go back to 1998, and there was the literacy and numeracy framework, which never got adopted—didn't see its way through devolution.

Putting that to one side, I'm going to talk about the Curriculum for Wales, because the Curriculum for Wales will be cited as having the potential to improve pupil outcomes. But last week, the Scottish Government announced its largest ever review of the curriculum up there in over 15 years, because of their poor PISA results. And unfortunately, for those who don't know, the Curriculum for Wales was largely based, not exclusively, but largely based on their Curriculum for Excellence in Scotland, as it was called. Its DNA runs right through our curriculum here. I describe it as the mashed potato of the curriculum—it's bland and of little nutritious value.

Minister, since we've not yet seen the impact of the new curriculum on PISA results, and Scotland has, my fear is that matters are going to get worse, and potentially a lot worse. Will you follow the lead of Scotland and announce your own review of the Welsh school curriculum?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
I think, to go back to your first point, on the literacy and numeracy framework, one was introduced in Wales, but the sustained focus on it was not maintained. And I said last week that one of the factors that does make a difference in jurisdictions across the world is that sustained focus, which is what we are offering.

On Curriculum for Wales, you are right that there are similarities in the way these have evolved, but while we might learn from Scotland in some respects, you will find that a lot of the emerging research now suggests that they might very well learn from us too.

I have announced that I will begin a targeted review of the curriculum, in order that we have greater clarity around expectations regarding the content of that curriculum. I don't want to start again, because 15 years of further reform would not be helpful, and the curriculum is being applied well in very many schools—I have seen that. So, there will be a review; I will come back and explain how that will work and the timeline for it. There is a need for a review, but I think that we are not in the same place as Scotland, and that lessons work both ways.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Okay. Finally, you touched on qualifications at 16—I'm just going to touch on those at 18. There are those who believe that PISA results are stand-alone and don't contribute to anything in particular, because we've got GCSE and A-level results. Let's just look at A-level results, because you can't really compare them to England any longer, because both GCSEs and A-levels, whilst they're branded the same, have not got the same structure, and have not necessarily got the same gradings either.

But we do have comparative data for university entry, and I'm just going to focus on Cambridge University. This is not the complete picture, but when we look at some of the data published by Cambridge University, going back over a decade, a few things come to light. During the last three years, there were 325 applicants from Wales to Cambridge, and 21 per cent of those were ultimately successful. If we roll back a decade, we're at 260 applicants, so fewer applicants, but 30 per cent were successful. And I should point out the success rate for Scotland last year was just 12 per cent, and that's a real worry, because we've adopted that curriculum. It's the trend that matters—there are more applying, but fewer are successful.

My question to you, Minister, is: would you commission—because I've only had a snapshot there—some independent research to see whether fewer students from Wales are successful in their applications to the competitive universities and the competitive courses?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
There are two points there to take up, I think. Looking at the trajectory and progression of students into post-18 and post-16 education is part, I think, of my colleague's review, and that will feature in that regard.

I think, on GCSEs and A-levels, it is important to remember that none of the pupils, the learners, who have done Curriculum for Wales have yet gone through these qualifications. So, drawing lessons about Curriculum for Wales with these particular cohorts may not be as helpful as we need at this point.

I think, also, it's important to remember that the consistency of testing—. PISA is one test and it tells us valuable things, and I want to draw on the detail and the granular detail of what that tells us, particularly how good we are at stretching our most able learners. I want to look at that and feed that knowledge and information into our plan. What is also clear, though, is that it doesn't measure everything. GCSEs measure something slightly different. A-levels, in which we perform, actually, very well, measure something else. So, I think it is important and is a responsibility to think of all these results in the round, while also being clear about what our expectations are, particularly around foundational skills, which is what our plan is about.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Welsh Labour spokesperson, Lynne Neagle.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Lynne Neagle.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Diolch. If I could start by respectfully saying to the Cabinet Minister that the work on age-related expectations and, indeed, a lot of what's in the literacy and numeracy plan was begun under the previous Government and therefore is a continuation of that work. But what I wanted to ask about today was school support staff. And I know you understand how vital school support staff are, and, indeed, I think they are the glue that holds the schools together. But on too many occasions, we know that school support staff are asked to help with complex medical issues in schools, including things like attending to catheters and feeding lines.

I know that guidance is being developed on supporting learners with healthcare needs, but there is a lack of clarity on when that guidance will be published. Again, I know that this is a challenging area, because it involves the interface between health and education. But it is crucial that we get that guidance in place, so that children with complex health needs don't face barriers in school, and so that school support staff aren't asked to do tasks that they're either not trained for—

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Can we have a question, Lynne?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: —or certainly not remunerated for. When can we expect that guidance to be available?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
On one thing I do agree with you: the support staff in our schools do an enormously positive and important job. And any teacher and, indeed, any learner you talk to will attest to that. 

She's also quite right that these are issues that need to be considered across portfolios. Health in particular and arguably, also, preventative health are going to be key partners in deciding how the education system and how we support support staff, but, more crucially also, the learners, in this work. I can't give her a timeline at this point, but I can assure her that, in pursuit of the breaking down of silos that I think every Minister on this bench has mentioned over the past few weeks, that is one of the very clear areas of focus that we have. Because, again, to go back to an associated point to yours, making sure that all our learners are able to make the best progress that they can, and that they are well supported whatever their needs are, is a priority for us.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you. You may be aware that a safeguarding letter was issued by Estyn to Ysgol Heol Goffa special school in Llanelli following the inspection last year, and that that was around issues around healthcare support in school. Now, a letter that the Cabinet Minister for health sent to one of the people who made representations about the school indicated that the guidance would be published some time in 2027, whereas your last written answer to me said that

'this work is at an early stage and...we are not yet in a position to confirm a timescale for the publication of revised guidance.'

So, there is a difference there between what two Ministers have said. Now, I entirely agree with you about the dangers of silos. And I wonder whether you would agree with me that this is not just a matter for local authorities and health boards, and that if this work is to be done, it has to be driven at Government level by the Cabinet Ministers responsible, in both health and education. What assurance can you give that you will be working closely with the health Minister's team to make sure that that interface between health and education, when it comes to children's education, is absolutely seamless?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Yes, that is an assurance I can absolutely give her. Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: The Welsh Conservatives' spokesperson, Sam Rowlands.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Sam Rowlands.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, what is your view on the impact of school closures on communities, parents, teachers and learners across Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you for the question. I'm afraid I have to refer you to the previous answer that I gave to your colleague, in that, obviously, these are decisions for local authorities. There are clear codes that govern the process that need to be followed in order to look at school organisation, and, particularly in relation to smaller schools, you will see a commitment in our manifesto to make sure that those codes are well applied. But I cannot, as Minister, comment on any particular plans in any local authority in Wales, as I am conscious that some of these decisions may at some point be referred to Welsh Ministers.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister. I appreciate the position you take on that, but, as you point out, on the process, it's important throughout that this is being adhered to properly, because communities are concerned when school closures and mergers are threatened for schools in their areas. You'll be aware, in my own constituency, that Flintshire council has proposed the merger of four schools into one superschool, with communities at the periphery of that, such as in Saltney, with St Anthony's school, and in Mold, with St David's school—where my colleague Darren Millar is the Member for—particularly concerned about the impact from the distance of the site that's being proposed.

The point here, Cabinet Minister, is that the consultation for the proposal has been rejected by more than 96 per cent of respondents. Schools are at the heart of our communities, and their closures have a particularly stark impact on rural areas, where schools serve as important community buildings and set habits of a lifetime for travel to and from school. Councils should not be imposing school closures on communities that do not want them. Instead, closures should only be considered where there's significant evidence, considerable public support and action to mitigate impacts on those communities. So, within the powers that you do have, Cabinet Minister, will you commit today to supporting parents, teachers and learners in disputes over school closures?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. I can't commit to that, for the reasons that I mentioned earlier on. But I think your question does illustrate the importance of schools in our communities, and I wouldn't dispute that for a second. They are key institutions in all our communities. We all have a vested interest in their success and in the success of the learners who are in those schools. So, while, obviously, for your constituents this will be an issue that they will want to pursue with you and with others, I will leave it there.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 3. What is the Welsh Government doing to ensure that young people in Caerdydd Penarth have equal access to Welsh-medium high school education? OQ64509
documents.text_cy: 3. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i sicrhau bod gan bobl ifanc yng Nghaerdydd Penarth fynediad cyfartal at addysg ysgol uwchradd cyfrwng Cymraeg? OQ64509

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch. Cardiff Council is implementing its Welsh in education strategic plan to ensure sufficient Welsh-medium secondary education in all areas of Cardiff. I understand that the council is currently developing strategic, long-term options for Welsh-medium secondary school provision, and we should await the outcomes of that work.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. Diolch. I know a family in Butetown whose daughter must leave the house by 7.30 a.m. every morning to get to Glantaf high school in time for registration—just one of many young people and their families whose decision to continue Welsh-language education wasn't and isn't straightforward. Travelling through an already broken transport system from one side of the city to another is not sustainable. It is expensive and difficult for parents, and stressful for vulnerable 11-year-olds starting high school. Many who want to stay for after-school clubs can't due to the lack of safe transport options home. The lack of access to Welsh-medium education for Grangetown, Butetown and the surrounding areas disproportionately impacts those on the doorstep of this very Siambr. I stand with the campaigners who call this a social injustice. It is structural discrimination against the most multicultural communities in our city. The public sector has a duty under the Equality Act 2010 to address the imbalance, irrespective of any discussions as to the viability of Callaghan Square—

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Sorry, Anthony, can we come to a question?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: —as a potential site. I'm aware, Minister, that you have previously expressed support for a fourth Welsh-medium secondary school in the city. While acknowledging Cardiff Council's ongoing role, what assurances can the Minister give to local families in south Cardiff of the Welsh Government's commitment to securing a Welsh-medium secondary school in de Caerdydd? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr. The Welsh Government's commitment to developing Welsh language schools and opportunities for learners across Wales is clear. It is expressed, again, in our manifesto. We are consulting very soon in this autumn term on the broader strategy around Welsh and the implementation of the Welsh language and education Act—Deddf y Gymraeg ac Addysg (Cymru) 2025. I may not have translated that wholly accurately. That is a focus for our work as a Government, and I would invite him to look in detail at that consultation when it is issued. Additionally, we have just conducted a rapid review of the Welsh in education strategic plans that all local authorities are required to develop to demonstrate how they propose to develop these options for all learners in Cardiff and elsewhere.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Minister, it's vitally important that Wales's unique culture is not only preserved but nurtured. Access to Welsh-medium education for those who want it will be an important part of that process. More than that, bilingualism is literally good for the brain. It leads to better executive function, better memory, problem solving, and even delays dementia onset by an average of around five years. Of course, Wales isn't the only country that recognises the importance of language in the transmission of culture. There are examples that we can learn from from across the globe. I'd be interested to know if the Welsh Government has learned or is trying to learn anything from Catalonia and the Basque region in successfully promoting bilingualism.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. I know my predecessors and I are very keen to learn from examples of successful bilingual countries and cultures across the world. It always strikes me as interesting that we consider this in some way unusual. In most places in the world, bilingualism is an accepted part of life—it's just the way things are. Learning from those countries, learning from those jurisdictions, has always, I think, been important to this Government and the previous one. Certainly, I can commit to continuing that interest in the way things are done elsewhere and to learn appropriately from that.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
The Member mentioned the Basque Country. May I refer the Minister to ysgol Groes-wen, also in Caerdydd Penarth, which is an innovative example here in Wales, on a model that has been adopted from education plans in the Basque Country and which is developing bilingualism through having two streams, Welsh and English? I want to recognise the Minister's support locally for a fourth Welsh-medium secondary school in south Cardiff. I also appreciate the personal conflict that exists in her role as a Minister.

But, having said that, can I just raise once again this issue of site? She will know in her role as the Minister the practical challenges in ensuring a fourth secondary school, in terms of the growth in numbers and the sustainability of other schools in Cardiff. But that aspiration exists in the council and in this Chamber, I believe, to see a fourth secondary school to respond to some of the concerns that have been raised on easy access across the city to Welsh-medium education. So, whilst the council proceeds with the preparatory work in terms of a business plan, I have written on the issue of the site at Callaghan Square. Cardiff south has developed a great deal and there are not many sites—
documents.text_cy:
Mae'r Aelod wedi crybwyll Gwlad y Basg. A gaf i gyfeirio'r Gweinidog tuag at ysgol Groes-wen, hefyd yng Nghaerdydd Penarth, sydd yn enghraifft arloesol yma yng Nghymru, ar fodel sydd wedi'i gymryd o gynlluniau addysg yng Ngwlad y Basg, sydd yn tyfu dwyieithrwydd drwy ddwy ffrwd, Cymraeg a Saesneg? Dwi eisiau cydnabod cefnogaeth y Gweinidog yn lleol i'r ymgyrch dros bedwaredd ysgol Gymraeg yn ne Caerdydd. Dwi hefyd yn gwerthfawrogi'r conflict personol sydd nawr yn ei rôl fel Gweinidog.

Ond, wedi dweud hynny, allaf i jest godi eto y mater yma o'r safle? Fe fydd hi'n deall yn ei rôl fel Gweinidog yr heriau ymarferol sydd yna o ran sicrhau pedwaredd ysgol, o ran twf niferoedd a chynaliadwyedd ysgolion eraill yng Nghaerdydd. Ond mae'r dyhead yna yn y cyngor a, dwi'n credu, yn y Siambr yma hefyd i weld pedwaredd ysgol i ateb y consýrn sydd wedi cael ei godi ynghylch access rhwydd ledled y ddinas i addysg Gymraeg. Felly, tra bo'r cyngor yn mynd rhagddo â'r gwaith o baratoi cynllun busnes, dwi wedi ysgrifennu ac wedi cyfeirio at yr issue hyn gyda'r safle yn Callaghan Square. Mae de Caerdydd wedi datblygu yn sylweddol a does yna ddim llawer o safleoedd—

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Huw, can you move to a question, please?
