documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Elin Jones has just left the Chamber, unfortunately. Will you work with the Minister for finance to take that site off the market, as it belongs to the Welsh Government, so that the option exists and we can unlock a new secondary school in south Cardiff?
documents.text_cy: Mae Elin Jones newydd adael y Siambr, yn anffodus. A wnewch chi weithio gyda'r Gweinidog cyllid i dynnu'r safle yna oddi ar y farchnad—safle sy'n eiddo i Lywodraeth Cymru—fel bod yr opsiwn yna i ddatgloi ysgol Gymraeg yn ne Caerdydd?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you very much. Thank you also for recognising that this situation can be quite complex for someone like me, who also, of course, lives in Grangetown. However, having said that, I'm aware, I think, that the Member wrote to the Minister for finance, and I am confident that she will respond shortly. I would like to note on this point that we haven't received any correspondence officially from Cardiff Council on this issue, and perhaps that would be something to look at.

But to return to my previous answer, developing Welsh-medium education in every local authority in Wales, increasing the number of pupils who can have easy access to Welsh-medium education, and that learners in our system, whatever school they attended, can leave the school aged 16 as confident, proficient Welsh speakers are central to this Government's vision for the Welsh language. There will be very extensive consultation on the variety of ways in which we will be moving in that direction through the period of this Government term.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr. Diolch yn fawr am gydnabod hefyd fod y sefyllfa hon yn gallu bod yn ddyrys i rywun fel fi, sydd hefyd, wrth gwrs, yn byw yn Grangetown. Ond, wedi dweud hynny, rwy'n ymwybodol, rwy’n credu, fod yr Aelod wedi ysgrifennu at y Gweinidog cyllid, ac rwy'n hyderus y bydd hi'n ateb hynny yn fuan. Fe fyddwn i yn nodi ar y pwynt hwn nad ydyn ni wedi cael gohebiaeth swyddogol gan Gyngor Caerdydd ar y mater hwn, ac efallai fod hwnna’n rhywbeth i edrych arno fe.

Ond i fynd nôl at fy ateb blaenorol, mae datblygu addysg Gymraeg ym mhob awdurdod lleol yng Nghymru, cynnydd yn nifer y disgyblion sydd yn gallu cael mynediad rhwydd at addysg gyfrwng Gymraeg, a bod dysgwyr yn ein system ni, pa bynnag ysgol maen nhw wedi mynd iddi hi, yn gadael yr ysgol yn 16 yn siaradwyr hyderus o'r Gymraeg yn ganolog i weledigaeth y Llywodraeth hon ar gyfer y Gymraeg. Bydd yna ymgynghori helaeth iawn ar yr amryw ffyrdd y byddwn ni'n symud i'r cyfeiriad hwnnw dros gyfnod y Llywodraeth hon.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Everybody should have access to Welsh-medium education. Sadly, I missed out on this when I was growing up and I'm now having to learn as an adult. At the moment, our constituency of Caerdydd Penarth is only served by one Welsh-medium secondary school. We know that communities in the south of Cardiff are travelling further to access Welsh-medium education, which is disincentivising parents and guardians from sending their children to Welsh-medium education. I am mindful, though, that responsibility for the planning of local schools does rest with local authorities and that statutory procedures have to be followed. So, I was wondering if the Cabinet Minister could confirm what communication she's had with Cardiff Council in relation to this matter.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Specifically—I think I mentioned this in my earlier answer—on the location, I haven't. But, of course, alongside what is happening is that we are looking at the Welsh in education strategic plans, and these have now been submitted, the review has concluded, and we will be communicating with all local authorities in October to discuss the progress that has been made and the national picture that we can glean from those plans aligned, then, with the priority we as a Government give to developing Welsh language education. Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 4. What is the Welsh Government doing to improve educational standards in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64522
documents.text_cy: 4. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i wella safonau addysgol ym Mhontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64522

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Diolch. Improving educational standards for learners in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr, and indeed in every community across Wales, is a core mission of this Government. Last week, I published the foundational literacy and numeracy plan, which represents an important first step in our vision for an education system that works for all learners and supports key partners to succeed.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister. We can't ignore the clear link between social deprivation, child poverty and educational attainment, which I think are all areas that successive Governments have failed to address. The latest PISA results should be a wake-up call for this Government. Wales is bottom of the UK in maths, reading and science. Maths has fallen significantly, and your own Government acknowledges that Wales has constantly lagged behind other UK nations. But nowhere should that failure concern us more than in communities such as the one I represent in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr. Your own deprivation figures show that 83 per cent of areas in Merthyr Tydfil are among the most educationally deprived areas of Wales. So, Cabinet Minister, those statistics aren't just something to read on a Government spreadsheet; they represent children whose future opportunities depend upon the education they receive today.

Now, I appreciate the PISA records aren't yours to own, as they're based on 2025 results, and Labour spent years reforming the curriculum, changing qualifications and moving away. However, it's not lost on anyone on this side of the Chamber that Plaid Cymru supported that, so you can no longer blame the system you inherited. So, the question is: do you commit to working across Government departments to ensure that socially deprived areas in Wales are prioritised to make sure that we close the gap between those and any educational achievements for PISA? Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Diolch yn fawr. Spending time litigating previous Governments' records is not how I intend to use my time, because I want to move forward from here, so I have no intention of starting today. I think you will see a commitment across this Government particularly to tackle the impact of poverty on children across Wales, both in schools and more broadly in our society. That's why the childcare offer, for example, is such a focus for us. You will see, in each of our portfolios, I think, a strategic commitment to tackling the impact of poverty in Wales on children and on societies and on families across our country, including in your constituency.

You will see also, in the foundational literacy and numeracy plan that I published last week, that there is in that explicitly a commitment to looking at our success in delivering this plan in terms of how well we are getting to grips with those gaps, because some of these statistics are alarmingly and stubbornly high and have been for a very long time. And I hope you will have heard, over the past few weeks, how important that is, in all its complexity, for all of us.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Welsh-medium education succeeds when every child learns in the way that's appropriate to them as individuals, of course. I have a grandson who's living with autism. He's in a Welsh-medium school and he's getting excellent support, I have to say—it's excellent and I'm very grateful for that. Unfortunately, not every family is in that same situation, because this isn't true across other areas in Wales. Having additional learning needs shouldn't mean that learners have to give up their right to Welsh-medium education. Every child and young person, whatever their needs, should be able to access the support and provision that they need through the medium of Welsh. So, will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the Welsh Government's plans to ensure that additional learning needs provision through the medium of Welsh is just as accessible, inclusive and effective as the provision through the medium of English?
documents.text_cy: Mae addysg Gymraeg yn llwyddo pan fydd pob plentyn yn dysgu yn y ffordd sydd yn addas iddyn nhw fel unigolion. Mae ŵyr gyda fi sydd yn byw gydag awtistiaeth. Mae mewn ysgol Gymraeg ac mae'n cael cefnogaeth ffantastig, mae'n rhaid imi ddweud—hollol wych—a dwi'n ddiolchgar iawn am hynny. Yn anffodus, dyw pob teulu ddim yn yr un sefyllfa, achos dyw hyn ddim yn wir mewn ardaloedd eraill yng Nghymru. Ni ddylai cael anghenion dysgu ychwanegol olygu bod yn rhaid i ddysgwyr roi'r gorau i'w hawl i gael addysg drwy'r Gymraeg. Dylai pob plentyn a pherson ifanc, beth bynnag fo'u hanghenion dysgu, allu cael mynediad at y cymorth a'r ddarpariaeth sydd eu hangen arnynt drwy gyfrwng y Gymraeg. Felly, a wnaiff Gweinidog y Cabinet roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf am gynlluniau'r Llywodraeth i sicrhau bod darpariaeth anghenion dysgu ychwanegol drwy gyfrwng y Gymraeg yr un mor hygyrch, cynhwysfawr ac effeithiol â'r ddarpariaeth drwy gyfrwng y Saesneg?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you very much. I think we've heard in the past weeks from some of our colleagues as well about the personal impact that some of these difficult decisions have had when suitable support hasn't been available for ALN through the medium of Welsh, and for learners in Welsh-medium schools as well. We have looked at this in detail, in particular at that provision from the perspective of students in Welsh-medium schools, and certainly it is a priority for us. I can send you some more details about the timetable, perhaps, outside of this meeting this afternoon, but I want to assure you that we do realise that this is a particular problem and that supporting families who would like to have Welsh-medium education for their children and get that support that they need is certainly something that we would judge our success on over the period of this Government.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Rwy'n credu ein bod ni wedi clywed yn yr wythnosau diwethaf gan rai o'n cydweithwyr hefyd amboutu'r impact personol mae rhai o'r dewisiadau anodd yma wedi'i gael pan nad oes modd cael y gefnogaeth addas ar gyfer anghenion dysgu ychwanegol yn y Gymraeg, ac i ddysgwyr mewn ysgolion Cymraeg hefyd. Rydyn ni wedi edrych yn fanwl ar hwn, yn benodol ar y ddarpariaeth hynny o safbwynt dysgwyr mewn ysgolion Cymraeg, ac mae e'n sicr yn flaenoriaeth i ni. Mi allaf i anfon mwy o fanylion ynglŷn ag amserlen, efallai, iddi y tu allan i'r cyfarfod y prynhawn yma, ond rwy'n moyn ei sicrhau hi ein bod ni yn sylweddoli bod hwn yn broblem benodol ac mae cefnogi teuluoedd sydd yn dymuno cael addysg Gymraeg i'w plant a chael y gefnogaeth sydd ei hangen arnyn nhw yn sicr yn rhywbeth y byddwn ni yn barnu ein llwyddiant arno fe dros gyfnod y Llywodraeth.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. I'm highly aware of time and I would like to get at least halfway through the questions. So, I won't be able to call any additional contributions from here on in, unfortunately. We'll move to question 5—Andrew R.T. Davies.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Dwi'n ymwybodol iawn o amser, a hoffwn i gyrraedd o leiaf hanner ffordd drwy'r cwestiynau. Felly, fyddaf i ddim yn gallu galw unrhyw gyfraniadau ychwanegol, yn anffodus. Symudwn ymlaen i gwestiwn 5—Andrew R.T. Davies.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 5. What action is the Cabinet Minister taking to support school budgets in Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg? OQ64533
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa gamau y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn eu cymryd i gefnogi cyllidebau ysgolion ym Mhen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg? OQ64533

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Decisions on the level of funding available to schools are made by each local authority as part of their overall budget setting. I'm committed to working collaboratively with local authorities to consider how education funding is used most effectively.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Minister, what are your asks of the finance Minister in supporting your portfolio? Many schools in Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannwg are in a deficit situation and are looking to you as a new Minister to secure additional funding in the current budget settlement round. So, could you identify, given your experience in the education sector, especially as a former representative of the National Association of Head Teachers, what your asks are of the finance Minister, so that headteachers can have confidence that they will see more resource in the new financial year?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Diolch. I can assure him certainly that education is a priority for the entire Government, and that I, as an advocate for support for it in all aspects, will be delivering with determination. I think it is important to note the funding settlements that are in place at the moment. He may remember, in the last budget negotiations, that an additional £112.8 million was sourced for local government, which resulted in £6.56 billion in core funding for local authorities, and that is an increase of 4.5 per cent.

I know that there are issues around funding in education and in our schools. I am determined to work with all partners to try and resolve some of the more outstanding issues, and assure him that the Vale of Glamorgan and all the other 21 authorities will be in my mind as I do that, because, as I said, we recognise the importance of education, and success in delivering for our learners is a key measure of our success as a Government.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 6. How does the Welsh Government support adult learners in Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64486
documents.text_cy: 6. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi dysgwyr sy'n oedolion ym Mhontypridd Cynon Merthyr? OQ64486

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Wel, diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Welsh Government supports adult learners across Wales through investment in further education, community learning, personal learning accounts, employability programmes and essential skills provision. Working with local providers, including Coleg y Cymoedd and Merthyr college in your constituency, we are helping adults to gain skills, progress in work and access lifelong learning opportunities.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Well, Deputy Minister, it is, of course, Adult Learners Week this week, and I was really grateful to the adult learners who met me in Coleg y Cymoedd in Aberdare on Monday, who spoke about their experiences of re-entering education.

We know that there's considerable demand for adult education, but figures that I've seen from Adult Learning Wales suggest that demand in 2026-27 outstrips their funding by almost 10 percent, and that means that around 850 potential learners are missing out. I'm told by Adult Learning Wales that they could put additional funding to use immediately, upskilling workers and allowing for more flexible delivery. So, how is Welsh Government making meeting this demand a priority?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Well, again, you make a really important point. Let me just agree with you that, with adult learning, the benefits are so wide-ranging. It supports the development of skills, improves health and well-being and is a catalyst for social engagement and integration. It also shows that well-paid work, through developing skills, is the best route out of poverty, and helping people to gain the skills they need to thrive and work is a clear priority for this Welsh Government. And I'm looking forward to the awards ceremony this evening as well, the Inspire! adult learning awards. It is, for me—and I've been to many over recent years—one of the highlights of the year, when you see the outstanding achievements of learners whose passion, commitment and dedication I think demonstrates the transformative power of lifelong learning.

But, to answer your question briefly, we are keeping a very close watch on the increased enrolments in FE colleges in particular. We know that that creates funding pressures for FE colleges. And I'm aware that Medr have given £6.25 million in this financial year, which straddles half the academic year, to help FE colleges, but we are monitoring the situation with Medr, and, if funding allows, we will try and support the FE sector but also adult learning in general as best as we can.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 7. What progress has the Welsh Government made on surveying the condition of school estates across Wales? OQ64531
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gynnydd y mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi'i wneud o ran arolygu cyflwr ystadau ysgolion ledled Cymru? OQ64531

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: We are committed to improving the condition of the school estate in Wales so that every learner is educated in a safe, sustainable and high-quality environment. To do this, the Welsh Government works in partnership with local authorities, who are responsible for school repairs and maintenance. Condition surveys are used to identify schools in need of the most urgent repairs and upgrades, and we are committed to working with colleagues to ensure the most effective use of resources.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
A high number of schools across my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf are facing a maintenance backlog. Scaffolding has surrounded Roath Park primary since 2021, Marlborough Road primary since 2022 and Albany primary since 2023. The condition of a number of comprehensives is substandard and very close to being further downgraded, including the second-hand Welsh-medium comprehensives ysgol Bro Edern and ysgol Plasmawr.

Most worryingly, parents at Albany Primary School were advised the week before this term started that their children would be sent out to three different schools because of dry rot. This late notice was despite Estyn warning in October 2025 that the site management arrangements at Albany Primary School, and I quote,

'give cause for concern and have been brought to the attention of the local authority.'

What discussions has the Cabinet Minister had with Cardiff Council regarding the condition of their school estate, and the council's response to Estyn in particular, and whether earlier intervention could have avoided Albany primary's closure and the severe disruption caused to pupils' education?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. The Welsh Government only holds very high-level information on school conditions, so I think this is an issue that will need to be pursued with the local authority. But I will say that we did commit to conducting that survey of school buildings, and that work is continuing now, to recognise the fact that we know that there is a significant issue across Wales with school buildings. We are going to prioritise those that are categorised as C and D, which are the buildings that are in the worst conditions according to what we currently hold in terms of data. I think, more broadly, a focus on this to ensure that our school buildings really are appropriate for our learners and the opportunities we want to give them is what sits behind making that priority a manifesto commitment.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you. And the final question to you, Minister, question 8—Francesca O'Brien.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. A'r cwestiwn olaf i chi, Weinidog, cwestiwn 8—Francesca O'Brien.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: 8. How is the Welsh Government working with local councils to ensure adequate funding for education? OQ64517
documents.text_cy: 8. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn gweithio gyda chynghorau lleol i sicrhau cyllid digonol ar gyfer addysg? OQ64517

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: We recognise that schools and local authorities continue to face a range of financial pressures. I am committed to listening to, engaging with and working collaboratively with local authorities to ensure our decisions make a real difference for learners.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text:
Diolch, Minister, for your answer. Just three months into this financial year, Swansea Council has already overspent by £13.7 million over its budget. It has imposed a vacancy freeze and severe spending restrictions. The council's finance director warns that its general reserves are already below, and I quote, 'the absolute minimum of acceptability', end of quote, and the council is now considering using its reserves. Of course, once these reserves are spent, they are gone, and its schools buildings programme is £73 million more than it can afford, so fewer schools will get the investment that they were promised.

One of the fastest growing pressures on councils is additional learning needs. Wales received additional funding for ALN on the back of increased spending in England, but your supplementary budget kept that money in Cardiff Bay, rather than sending it to councils and schools that actually support these children. So, when you bring your revised plans forward this autumn, Minister, will you commit to passing that ALN funding directly to local authorities so councils aren't forced to drain their reserves to fill that spending gap?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you very much. These are conversations that are ongoing with local authorities. I met, in fact, with the Welsh Local Government Association yesterday to discuss a range of factors that are impacting local authorities at the moment. To return to the ALN spending, I agree with you that this is a pressing priority for local authorities and for our schools, which is why we made those commitments around funding in the supplementary budget. She will be aware that that was not successful, but that is continuing work and there remain opportunities for that funding to be sent to local authorities and schools to address some of these issues.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and Welsh Language
documents.text: Thank you very much, Ministers.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi, Weinidogion.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: We will move now to item 3, questions to the Senedd Commission. Question 1—Kiera Marshall.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 3, cwestiynau i Gomisiwn y Senedd. Cwestiwn 1—Kiera Marshall.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 1. How does the Commission ensure there are sufficient facilities for expressing breast milk on the Senedd estate? OQ64539
documents.text_cy: 1. Sut mae'r Comisiwn yn sicrhau bod digon o gyfleusterau ar gyfer tynnu llaeth o'r fron ar ystad y Senedd? OQ64539

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: The Senedd Commission is committed to ensuring that we are inclusive to everyone who works on or visits the estate. We have facilities available for those who need to express milk following the birth of their child. The quiet rooms can be used for expressing milk, and fridges are available to store the milk. These can be found on the ground floor in Tŷ Hywel in B block, opposite the committee rooms, and one in the Senedd on the Neuadd level. In addition, people can access the first aid rooms, where privacy, seating or couch facilities are provided. All these facilities are lockable and can be marked as occupied. For Commission staff, managers and HR support return-to-work planning after maternity leave in a number of ways, including a new and expectant parent risk assessment, covering practical arrangements such as quiet rooms, hygiene facilities and secure refrigerated storage.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you for that. I just wanted to flag some of my lived experience, because as a mother of a young baby, I had the experience of trying to find a suitable place to pump on the Senedd estate. I was initially offered the medical room you mentioned, but it only had a bed in it, and you can't pump lying down, and I do need a desk and chair to work, and I couldn't possibly lose two hours of my working day. I was then offered the quiet room, but if you look on the internal intranet, this room is listed as a place for prayer and contemplation, so that wasn't appropriate. I then had to use a printing room, which had no lock on the door, until I got in touch with the Senedd estate, and it also had no access then to the fridge that was in the medical room. So, given that the Senedd aims to be family friendly and inclusive, I was surprised that these facilities don't seem to support pumping on the estate, and the NHS does recommend breastfeeding up until two years, when most parents will have returned to work. Only 32 per cent of babies are still being breastfed at six months, despite all of the known benefits. So, I was wondering if you would look at creating a space for pumping that enables people to work at the same time, and confirm to me that no member of staff or Member will face the same circumstances I was in.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: I really welcome that feedback from your own experience, and thank you for sharing that with us. I'm more than happy to take that back to officials and to facilitate, if necessary, discussion with my officials so that they can look at that. One of the opportunities as to what we can do now to improve that—and we do want to be, very much, that best practice in terms of the workplace—the other thing going forward is how we respond to the family friendly and inclusive parliament review, which had recommendations specifically with regard to family friendly support, breastfeeding and so on. So, if you're happy, I'll facilitate those discussions and we can look at how we can improve it now.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Questions 2 and 7 are grouped. Question 2 first—Joe Martin.
documents.text_cy: Mae cwestiynau 2 a 7 wedi eu grwpio. Felly, cwestiwn 2 yn gyntaf—Joe Martin.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 2. What are Commission's plans regarding the expansion of Tŷ Hywel? OQ64535
documents.text_cy: 2. Beth yw cynlluniau'r Comisiwn o ran ehangu Tŷ Hywel? OQ64535

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 7. Will the Commission provide an update on the Bay 32 project? OQ64558
documents.text_cy: 7. A wnaiff y Comisiwn roi diweddariad ar brosiect Bae 32? OQ64558

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Diolch, Joe. Bay 32 is the Commission’s project to secure fit-for-purpose accommodation beyond the expiry of the Tŷ Hywel lease, which happens in 2032. A competitive procurement concluded that the best value option is a major refurbishment and renewal of Tŷ Hywel, with the potential for Commission ownership. Equitix is the preferred bidder and its proposal includes more than £50 million of landlord investment—landlord investment—in the building. This is planned to include increasing the amount of useable space in Tŷ Hywel by 25 per cent. The project is now in detailed design during a pre-development phase with capped costs to the Commission. Because the building must remain operational during major works, temporary accommodation will be needed for Members, staff and for services. So, the Commission will consider options for managing any relocation, before considering the full business case later this year. The works are currently expected to begin from early summer 2027 and last for up to three years.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you, Commissioner. Rent on Tŷ Hywel currently costs £2.7 million per year. Can you give any indication of what that might rise to once the proposed construction is complete?

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: I'm pleased to reiterate what I said in my opening remarks. First of all, the project is now in a capped cost pre-development phase. It's pegged. There's a clear understanding and expectation from all of the Commissioners who were involved in taking this forward, and an understanding from the potential project delivery partners as well. The other thing, reiterating but expanding a little bit on what I said earlier, is that we ran a competitive process. So, the Commission had a real choice of options of how to do this very important work for all of us and the constituents who come here to meet us as well. So, we tested the markets and secured what we believe is a very strong proposal for the long-term future of Tŷ Hywel. But one other thing I would say to you, Joe, and to other Members, is that we're keen that the project continues to be shaped by Member feedback, in providing those spaces that allow you and others to carry out your parliamentary roles. So, no decision has been taken yet to proceed, of course, with construction; the full business case is yet to be brought forward. We look forward to engaging with Members, and also with political groups as well, on the proposals as they're developed.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you, you've answered a couple of questions in your statement, so I just wanted to ask: will the landlord be paying for the costs relating to moving us and staff members, or is it just for the improvements to Tŷ Hywel? Thanks.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text:
So, the cost of what is known as the 'decant strategy', and the different options on that that Commissioners are currently considering, is within the cost we've already described. So, we're not looking at an escalating cost; we're looking at managing it within the budgets we've already put for it. And, as I say, this pre-development phase, we've got capped costs for this. So, I hope that's an assurance to the Member. And, I have to say, there's very robust challenge from the Commissioners, all of them, in terms of keeping this within the cost envelope that we've anticipated.

Ideally, going forward, we'll have a good building that is refurbished and fit for now and for years to come, that enhances the experience for Members and for people who visit here, and we can also do that in a very cost-effective way. Because at the moment—Members shouldn't be under any misapprehension as to what we are facing—if we don't proceed with this, the status quo option includes forking out for repairs to the existing building, into the millions of pounds. So, what we're trying to do is avoid that eventuality.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 3. What assessment has the Commission made of the impact of the ongoing backlog of payments from the Civil Service Pension Scheme on its current and former employees? OQ64546
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa asesiad y mae'r Comisiwn wedi'i wneud o effaith yr ôl-groniad parhaus o daliadau o Gynllun Pensiwn y Gwasanaeth Sifil ar ei gyflogeion presennol a chyn-gyflogeion? OQ64546

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text:
Diolch, Lindsay. Responsibility for administering the civil service pension scheme transferred from MyCSP to Capita on 1 December 2025. The change was intended to modernise the service, but the transfer included a substantial volume of cases affecting some retirement quotations and new pension payments. The Cabinet Office and Capita established a recovery programme to prioritise urgent and hardship cases, clear outstanding work, and restore contracted service standards.

The Commission currently has fewer than five former employees who have retired since Capita became the administrators, one of which has accessed the hardship loan scheme introduced by the Commission, in line with Cabinet Office guidance, to mitigate the financial impact, and we continue to monitor the situation and seek assurances that outstanding cases are resolved very quickly.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you, Commissioner. I have been contacted by three constituents—probably three of the five—regarding the unacceptable and worrying delays and backlogs they're dealing with from Capita, the managing company of the civil service pension scheme. Capita has issued a statement saying that they have everything in place to begin clearing the backlog. However, they will not provide a timeline for when every case will be cleared, nor will they provide a date for my constituents on their individual cases, and that is important. I've met people who have worked all their lives in the service of the public, and they now face serious financial hardship. They shouldn't have to go for financial loans at that time of life because their public pensions, of course, were outsourced to a private company unable, let's be honest, to manage those pensions. Has the Commission had any discussions with the Cabinet Office in Westminster or the civil service pension scheme regarding the retired former employees from the Senedd? And if not, can you please commit to doing this?

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you very much for raising this issue.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am godi y mater yma.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text:
It raises serious issues and, I agree, the situation is completely unacceptable. The welfare of former employees is paramount to what this Commission is looking to do.

In answer to your question, the chief executive has written to the managing director of Capita Pensions Solutions earlier this year to raise the concerns that you've raised, and former members of staff have raised, about the impact the backlog was having on Commission staff. To date, we haven't had a response to that, and that is also unacceptable.

But, in turning to what the Commission has done to support your constituents and others, in addition to administering the hardship loan, the human resources service continues to provide ongoing communication to affected retired staff, and the welfare of former employees has remained our primary concern. So, we will be keeping that under review and, where possible, furthering it as well.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you. Question 4 [OQ64493] from Tom Montgomery is withdrawn, so, question 5 from Francesca O'Brien.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Mae cwestiwn 4 [OQ64493] gan Tom Montgomery wedi'i dynnu'n ôl, felly, cwestiwn 5 gan Francesca O'Brien.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: I thought my name was Tom, then. Diolch, Presiding Officer.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 5. Pa gamau y mae'r Comisiwn yn eu cymryd i ddiogelu lles Aelodau a'u staff? OQ64516

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text:
Diolch, Francesca. The Commission takes the welfare of Members and their staff very seriously, and we provide practical, accessible support across well-being, employment, health and safety, dignity and respect, safeguarding, and, of course, security. This includes confidential employee assistance and occupational health services, tailored HR guidance and training, and security advice and measures. The Hwb brings information and face-to-face support together in one place, with a weekly virtual drop-in for support staff, whatever their location.

The Commission's phased learning framework treats personal resilience, well-being and maintaining a healthy work-life balance as continuing development needs rather than one-off induction topics. Training is repeated, reinforced and extended through the Senedd term, with provision adapted to Member and support staff learning needs and delivery preferences. 

And just finally, the Members' security team provides support to Members on a wide range of personal safety and security matters, including advice and guidance, the implementation of security measures at homes and offices, practical support and advice relating to social media security, and the reporting and management of security-related incidents.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Diolch for the description there. If I can provide some context to my question, and the scene I want to picture: Members of this Chamber and their support staff come into the Tŷ Hywel building each day to carry out their work freely, often in areas where members of the public are excluded unless they're chaperoned around the building. However, what's become quite clear is that we do have journalists, dare I say, lurking along the corridors in areas that we don't know. Some could be on the radio. We don't know who they are, or what they look like. I can give an example of that, if I may: just before the summer recess, going into the ladies' bathroom on level 2 and meeting a very chatty lady as I came out of the cubicle—and I know we all like a good chat, and I'm one for those—however, she asked for my number, when I believed perhaps she was support staff for one of my colleagues, and it was actually a journalist. So, I do think there are lines being blurred here between the access that they have to our workspace and kind of being led down a garden path, shall I say? I don't think that's appropriate, and I do wonder whether we can consider that they are put in a certain restricted area and not have free access to where we work, including the bathrooms as well.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text:
Thank you for that. It's helpful with that supplementary. The Commissioners, of course, keep constantly under review the access and the privileged access to different parts of not just the Senedd building, but also here within Tŷ Hywel as well. There are different levels of pass holders, and there's an expectation as well that there's an accompaniment of visitors into certain areas by pass holders—just to remind colleagues as well. But we do keep this under review, and we do keep a refresh on it. So, I take on board the individual example that you're saying. Perhaps we can discuss it further in terms of what area that was, what precise location that was.

But we do also want the building to be able to be accessible to people who want to ask us questions as elected representatives and for constituency members who visit us, and for legitimate lobbyists who come here from health organisations, et cetera, et cetera. So, point taken. I'm happy to discuss the individual location that you mentioned and, of course, Commissioners will always keep this under review.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising this important point. I hope that the Member and also everyone else in this Senedd agrees with me that we also, as Members of the Senedd, must take responsibility for looking after each other, whatever our party. This is especially important when the online world is becoming ever more violent towards politicians, especially young women. Therefore, as I speak about the online world, I'd like to ask what the Commission is doing to support Members of the Senedd and staff who see their well-being being negatively impacted because of the increase that we have all seen in online abuse, especially with AI as well, and deepfakes, just as an example for you.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r cwestiwn pwysig yma. Dwi'n gobeithio bod yr Aelod a hefyd pawb arall yn y Senedd yma'n cytuno â fi bod yn rhaid i ni hefyd fel Aelodau o'r Senedd gymryd cyfrifoldeb i edrych ar ôl ein gilydd, pa bynnag blaid. Mae hyn yn enwedig o bwysig pan mae'r byd ar-lein yn dod yn fwy treisgar tuag at wleidyddion, yn enwedig menywod ifanc. Felly, wrth i fi siarad am y byd ar-lein, hoffwn wybod beth mae'r Comisiwn yn ei wneud er mwyn cefnogi Aelodau o'r Senedd a staff sydd yn gweld eu lles yn cael ei effeithio'n negyddol oherwydd y cynnydd rydyn ni i gyd wedi gweld mewn cam-drin ar-lein, yn enwedig gydag AI hefyd, a deepfakes, jest fel enghraifft i ti.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr iawn. I would refer Members very strongly not just to the Hwb, but to the security team presence as well, for all the advice and assistance they can give. Of course, there is an interaction that we have, not just as individual Members, but through our security people, including the observation and monitoring. It's not monitoring in a NASA style, but keeping an eye on what's happening online. There is engagement as well with police across Wales. This is an issue that affects all Members, because it can be quite a hostile environment out there. But I would strongly say to Members and their staff that if they have individual instances, they should bring them to the attention of our security people, because they want to hear about it and we need to be notified of it.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you. Question 6 [OQ64482], tabled by Janet Finch-Saunders, is withdrawn. Question 7 was grouped with question 2. So we'll move to question 8. Jane Dodds.
documents.text_cy: Mae cwestiwn 6 [OQ64482], a gyflwynwyd gan Janet Finch-Saunders, wedi'i dynnu yn ôl. Mae cwestiwn 7 eisoes wedi'i grwpio gyda chwestiwn 2. Felly symudwn ymlaen i gwestiwn 8. Jane Dodds.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 8. What safeguarding checks does the Commission require of Members of the Senedd before they undertake activities involving children and young people? OQ64547
documents.text_cy: 8. Pa wiriadau diogelu y mae'r Comisiwn yn gofyn i Aelodau o'r Senedd eu gwneud cyn iddynt ymgymryd â gweithgareddau sy'n ymwneud â phlant a phobl ifanc? OQ64547

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Diolch, Jane. Responsibility for safeguarding arrangements within Members' offices rests with the individual Members, as Members of the Senedd are individually elected and they're not Commission employees. Members need to have their own safeguarding policy appropriate to their role as office holders and employers, as they are responsible for their activities. The statutory disclosure and barring framework is reserved to the UK level.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you very much for that response.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn am yr ymateb.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: During my first term as a Senedd Member, I was really surprised that I could go into any school, any youth club, any provision where a child, a young person or a vulnerable person lived or worked without any checks, without any need to show any documentation. On all of those visits, I was accompanied by somebody, but it wouldn't take a genius and it wouldn't take much imagination for somebody quite powerful, who is a Member of the Senedd, to say, 'I'd like to do this on my own'. I do believe it is the Senedd's responsibility to ensure that Senedd Members, who have access and are in powerful roles to influence other people—. It should take the responsibility. There is no reference to this in any recent documentation, and I raised it in the last Senedd. I wonder if the Senedd Commission could take this forward, even on a voluntary basis, to look at how Members could get a DBS check, which doesn't give you an absolute safety mark, but it is a tool in the toolbox that ensures that this Parliament is not putting children, young people and vulnerable people at risk by allowing Senedd Members to do their duties. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Thank you. There are a couple of points for consideration here. First of all, the statutory disclosure and barring framework is reserved to UK level, so broadening eligibility for things such as enhanced checks would require action by the UK Government. I'm aware that political parties operate, on a voluntary basis, their own approach to candidates, and it differs from party to party. We watch with interest the different proposals that are emerging currently at a UK level from some individual MPs. Some of them are looking at a statutory basis for changing this, and some at a non-statutory basis. The basic test, as you mentioned, in terms of DBS, as opposed to the enhanced test, has some limitations with it in terms of what it provides. My understanding is that DBS checks are legally designed as a tool for employers or for licensing bodies to assess the suitability of an applicant for a specific workplace role. MSs, of course, not unlike MPs, are not employees, but independent constitutional office holders chosen directly by voters. But it is an interesting area, and we're watching the discussions going on in Westminster at the moment. But the responsibility rests with UK statute.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 9. What action is the Senedd Commission taking to ensure a range of news media platforms are available on the Senedd estate? OQ64544
documents.text_cy: 9. Pa gamau y mae Comisiwn y Senedd yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod amrywiaeth o blatfformau cyfryngau newyddion ar gael ar ystad y Senedd? OQ64544

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Members and staff are able to access all major news outlets using the Senedd IT network on laptops and other Senedd Commission-issued devices. With regard to the internal broadcasting network, this matter is subject to ongoing discussion by Commissioners, and I’m sure Commissioners will gladly report back to their respective groups in due course. All major newspapers are delivered to the Senedd's library and can be accessed by Members and staff.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text:
Thank you for that answer. I think we've been here before, haven't we? When the Commission considered this issue in July, it argued that Sky News alone provided proficient plurality on the Senedd's television system. I would respectfully suggest that, in the time since GB News was removed from the Senedd's system, the media landscape has changed. Since the departure of Laurence Fox, GB News has continued to grow its audience and broaden its reach. It now reaches over 1 million viewers per day and, in 2025, overtook Sky News as the UK's largest commercial news channel by average viewing figures.

Whether Members agree with GB News or not is beside the point. It is an Ofcom-regulated broadcaster watched by millions of people across the United Kingdom. I'm sure that everybody on this side of the Chamber is a fan of GB News. Excluding it from the Senedd's internal television system risks creating the impression that some lawful viewpoints are more acceptable than others. In the interests of pluralism, free expression and informed democratic debate, will the Commission now review its policy and reconsider the inclusion of GB News on the Senedd estate? Diolch.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Catherine, you are right indeed, we have been here before. At the last Senedd Commission questions, there was quite a lengthy discussion on this. I can't really add much to my opening response. Perhaps it's worth highlighting for the record that press freedom is a principle that we all share. It remains central to the integrity and openness of the democratic institutions here in Wales. This principle, by the way, is reflected, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, in our policy on press passes to the estate as well. It is also reflected in the fact that all the major news outlets can be accessed on the Senedd IT network—on laptops and other Senedd Commission devices—and in the access to all major newspapers in the Senedd library. But as I said earlier, the matter is subject to ongoing discussions by Commissioners, and out of respect to them and those discussions, it's difficult for me to add to my earlier remarks.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: The final question, question 10, Gwyn Williams.
documents.text_cy: Y cwestiwn olaf, cwestiwn 10, Gwyn Williams.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: 10. Will the Commission consider alternative routes linking Tŷ Hywel to the Siambr to help alleviate bottlenecks during Plenary? OQ64548
documents.text_cy: 10. A wnaiff y Comisiwn ystyried llwybrau amgen sy'n cysylltu Tŷ Hywel â'r Siambr i helpu i leihau tagfeydd yn ystod y Cyfarfod Llawn? OQ64548

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Diolch, Gwyn. Ease of access to the existing routes from Tŷ Hywel to the Senedd building, and significant improvements to how the buildings connect for Members and other users, is actively being looked at in detail as part of the Bay 32 project. The Commission is not, however, currently considering any further alternative physical bridges, for example, to the Senedd building from Tŷ Hywel. There are two link bridges that provide access from Tŷ Hywel to the Senedd building—one via the first floor staff restaurant and one on the second floor. Access from the first floor link bridge is via lifts only. The second floor link bridge directly joins the Senedd building, with no lift required. Direct access is also available at ground floor level via the Senedd building courtyards.

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr. I would humbly suggest, as a new Member, as many of the people here are—. The level of the canteen, which is marked M, and the first floor and the stairwell on the other side, as you said in your answer, can only be connected via a lift. It does seem to be, at busy periods, a bottleneck of people. I have lost count of the number of long-serving staff, including a very nice lady called Sam, who works in the tea room here—. She has said that she has lost count of the number of times that she has suggested a flight of steps connecting that level with the stairwell on the other side. And there is some space to the side. So, would the Commission agree that this is a bottleneck and that a simple addition of a flight of steps would ease congestion? Would you look into it further so that I can report back to Sam in the tea room?

documents.item: 3. Questions to the Senedd Commission
documents.text: Now we're put right on the spot, because if Sam is keeping an eye on this, my goodness. As I mentioned, the proposals we're looking at for developing and enhancing the facilities here include those routes from one part of the building to the other—from Tŷ Hywel to the Senedd. So, it's under consideration by the Commissioners in the plans going forward. It won't be immediate—I can't promise that. Meanwhile, we're all going to have to work hard to avoid that last-minute bottleneck where we're all jammed in with Sam, with very important services and goods being taken across at the same time that we're rushing down for the bell. Diolch.

documents.item: 5. 90-second Statements
documents.text: Item 5, 90-second statements. Kiera Marshall.
documents.text_cy: Eitem 5, datganiadau 90 eiliad. Kiera Marshall.

documents.item: 5. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Diolch. This week is Adult Learners' Week, and I'd like to pay tribute to all the adult learners across Wales. It's sometimes difficult to step back into education, so it's so important that there's support there for them. The impact of adult learning is life-changing, and extends far beyond education. It improves health and well-being, and is fundamental to Wales's economic growth. It enables adults to access upskilling and reskilling and enhance their lives in ways that we will never understand. 

The adult community learning programme in particular offers people an important route into education, supporting people to access learning in a setting and at a pace that is right for them. Tonight, the Inspire! adult learning awards are going to take place, and I'd like to congratulate Hannah from my constituency in Caerdydd Penarth who will be receiving the new Welsh speaker award. 

Hannah will be recognised alongside 10 other award winners who are all being celebrated for their commitment, dedication and achievements—learners who have changed their lives through adult education. I hope these stories, and thousands like them across Wales, can encourage more people to embrace the message of Adult Learners' Week—to never stop learning. Diolch.

documents.item: 5. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Last Friday marked International Equal Pay Day, a UN awareness day of gender inequality and the gender pay gap between men and women. Sadly, this is a pressing issue for Wales. The latest state of the nation report on gender equality by the Women's Equality Network Wales exposed that the gender pay gap in Wales has widened to 9.7 per cent. On average, female employees earn £15.78 per hour, whilst male employees earn £17.48. Compared to men, women are over three times more likely to be out of the job market due to caring responsibilities. Women are also three times more likely to work part-time, which is limiting to earnings and progression. And women are more likely to work in sectors and roles that are lower paid, such as health and social care. We need change. 

Barriers to economic equality, like unequal caring responsibilities and gender stereotypes, must be challenged. Women must be supported to access better paid jobs, skills and training programmes throughout their careers, and we must have robust and inclusive policies on flexible working, harassment, menopause and parental leave. This International Equal Pay Day, I urge all colleagues across the Senedd to champion gender equality and help create a Wales free from gender discrimination. Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 5. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Next month, Wyeside Arts Centre in Builth Wells celebrates an incredible milestone—50 years of bringing arts and culture to the heart of rural mid Wales. The fiftieth birthday weekend brings that history to life, with Welsh music, poetry, art and community participation. At its centre is Cymuned Gwy, a new bilingual work commissioned for the anniversary, inspired by the River Wye and the people who live alongside it. Wyeside is a small, independent charity, but its contribution is anything but small. Open six days a week, it provides cinema, live performance, music, exhibitions and opportunities for people to come together across a large rural area. 

Places like Wyeside offer far more than entertainment. They are places where people meet, participate and belong. The anniversary, as well as looking forward and back, has amazing plans to introduce to people as well, which will improve accessibility, and new facilities that will serve mid Wales for decades to come. Alongside this celebration, we know there is a serious challenge. Despite operating all year round, generating much of its income, and being supported by a small team of volunteers, Wyeside continues to face a significant revenue shortfall. I congratulate everyone who has sustained Wyeside over 50 years, and encourage colleagues to join the celebrations from 9 to 11 October, to see its plans for the future, and help ensure it remains at the heart of mid Wales. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 5. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
It's Migraine Awareness Week, and I want to recognise people across Wales living with a condition that is too often dismissed. Migraines affect one in seven people in the UK. It's a neurological condition that can cause severe pain, sickness and sensitivity to light and sound. Its impact reaches far beyond an attack. It affects work, family life and mental well-being. 

The Migraine Trust's latest survey found that nine in 10 respondents had felt disbelief about the severity or the impact of their migraine. Nearly a third had experienced this from their colleagues or their managers. More than three quarters say that the disbelief has damaged their mental health. Nobody should have to fight to be believed while already struggling with pain. The trust's 'Believe me' campaign carries a simple message to us all: listen, take migraine seriously and offer practical support. To people living with migraine in Gŵyr Abertawe, and across Wales: your experience matters. Pain does not have to be visible to deserve understanding, and a little patience and compassion can make a difference. Diolch.

documents.item: 6. Welsh Labour Debate: Further education
documents.text: We'll move on now to item 6, the Welsh Labour debate on further education. I call on Lynne Neagle to move the motion.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn nawr at eitem 6, dadl Llafur Cymru ar addysg bellach. Galwaf ar Lynne Neagle i wneud y cynnig.

documents.item: 6. Welsh Labour Debate: Further education
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Can I draw Members' attention to my register of interests and the fact that I'm an adult learner in Cardiff and Vale College?

Today, I want to focus on one of Wales's greatest success stories and one that too often does not receive the recognition it deserves: our further education colleges. Across Wales, colleges are changing lives every day. For young people, they are the chance to take that first step after school and progress to work, an apprenticeship or to university. For adults, they are access to lifelong learning, and for employers, they are the support they need to upskill their workforce, improve productivity and compete for new business.

Across Wales, colleges have shown that they are innovators and are ready to meet new challenges. In north Wales, they are helping to drive the new tertiary alliance with our university sector. In south-west Wales, the four colleges have come together to form a new partnership to maximise opportunities from the Celtic Freeport. And in south-east Wales, colleges have pioneered new ways of supporting learners, including the junior apprenticeship programme I was so proud to support in Government. The evidence of their value is clear.

This year, colleges across Wales have seen record levels of demand, with every college reporting increased participation. More learners than ever are choosing further education as their route into skills, qualifications and careers. Demand is particularly strong in vocational and technical subjects, such as construction, engineering and health and care—precisely the sectors we know are critical to Wales's future prosperity. Colleges are also providing opportunities for those who need them most. They are supporting thousands of learners who are returning to education, improving literacy and numeracy and rebuilding confidence after difficult experiences in school or elsewhere.

This is a Welsh success story, but it is fragile, and more learners means more pressure on space and on budgets. And the pressures are urgent, with ColegauCymru estimating the sector will have enrolled a record 50,000 young people this academic year. At a time when we are in the middle of a crisis with the number of young people who are not in employment, education or training, and when we are weeks away from the publication of the Milburn review, there has never been a more important time to invest in further education.

So, rising participation is a good news story. It is a sign that colleges are succeeding, it is a sign that further education is delivering for Wales and it is an opportunity for Wales. However, record demand brings with it a significant challenge. We know that funding has not kept pace with participation. Last year, I was able to put an additional £20 million in to support participation in the sector, but this year, the shortfall is estimated by both the sector and by Medr to be around £23.5 million. To stop even more learners missing out on places, colleges have been forced to make the difficult choice of moving funding from adult part-time provision to pay for full-time learner numbers. This all means there are around 5,000 learners who are studying for whom the sector isn't receiving any funding. Hundreds of learners have not got a place at all, and hundreds more did not get their first-choice course because of a shortage of places.

As well as pressure on places, it is also stretching vital support, such as well-being services, mental health support, financial hardship provision and learner travel. I hope Members know my own personal commitment to supporting learners with additional learning needs, and I am concerned about the impact of underfunding. Early data from ColegauCymru suggests an additional 65 per cent increase in learners with individual development plans, and it is essential that they can access the funding they need.

Looking ahead, the pressures in 2027-28 are even greater. The sector estimates that at least £40 million will be required in the 2027-28 academic year simply to maintain existing participation levels and respond to sustained learner demand. Pay and other inflationary pressures will push this even higher. If that funding is not available, the consequences could be significant. We risk more young people becoming disconnected from education and training. We risk job losses in the sector and cuts to support services. We risk cutting progression routes to our universities and stopping young people from taking that first step on their career paths. And we risk cutting off the skills pipeline that businesses need to compete and grow.

That is why this motion is important. It calls for a clear assessment of the consequences of failing to fund increased participation in further education. We need to understand the impact on learner pathways, on not in education, employment or training levels, on staff, on learner support services, and on progression into employment and higher education. Further education colleges take a much greater proportion of learners from lower income backgrounds. It is vital that we understand the impact on deprived communities across Wales. For many young people, particularly those with the fewest qualifications, college is their second chance, and they have very few options if they don't get a place. We owe it to the young people and to the adults who rely on further education to ensure our colleges have the resources they need.

Llywydd, this debate is ultimately about opportunity. When people want to learn, train and improve their prospects, our response should not be to limit opportunity, our response should be to understand the consequences of inaction and ensure that Wales continues to invest in success. Our colleges have demonstrated their value. They are helping young people realise their potential, supporting employers and strengthening communities across Wales. Now we must ensure that the resources available to them reflect the vital role they play. I urge Members to support our motion. Diolch.
