documents.text:
Llywydd, the Member is absolutely right that we want to protect essential services, and most of us at one time or another have been involved in various campaigns around particular services in different places. I think the principles that we need to bear in mind always are that we provide timely services in the appropriate location. There will be different stories in different parts of Wales, but those are the principles that tie us together.

Decisions on clinical services are taken by the health boards themselves. I know that the health board in this particular instance has looked at eight out of nine of the services that it provides and consulted on them, and put in place changes that it believes would provide better services to be delivered over the best part of a decade. These aren't overnight changes. And it's important to remember that these are changes that can take time. But my appeal always is for health boards, when they make those changes, when they consult, and afterwards, to ensure that people feel that they are engaged properly on those decisions. But there will be, clearly, different applications of different services in different parts of Wales. It's about getting that balance of appropriate services that will always put the patient first.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you to Paul Davies for the question. First Minister, 35 per cent of Ceredigion households and 23 per cent in Pembrokeshire rely on oil heating, among the highest rates in Wales. Public Health Wales warns that cold homes increase cardiovascular and respiratory risks, particular for older and vulnerable people. As your Government moves towards net zero, how will you ensure that rural households are not forced to ration heating because of the cost of that transition, and will you guarantee that keeping people warm and healthy comes before hitting arbitrary deadlines? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I will accept that there is a healthcare link there, Llywydd, and I'm being very, very generous. We know that a healthy home, a healthy environment, is important for people's health, so the Member is absolutely right in that respect.

On oil heating in particular, of course, these are measures that are reserved. We have consistently appealed to the UK Government to make the right decisions when it comes to the options that it has at its disposal, but that we haven't as a Welsh Government, to relieve the pressure on households in rural Wales in particular that are particularly dependent on off-grid oil. It is a principle that ties this Government together, that we think cross-departmentally, and the Member is right: we need to think housing, we need to think energy, we need to think health when it comes to the well-being of the people that we represent.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, I'd like to agree that protecting services at Bronglais and Withybush hospitals remains vital for communities across Ceredigion Penfro. However, in rural areas, we also need innovative ways of bringing healthcare closer to people's homes. Integrated care centres in Cardigan and Aberaeron show what can be achieved when we bring services together, and, again, bring them closer to people, taking the pressure off hospitals. Having recently visited GP services in Fishguard, I know that there is strong local support for a similar approach there. Indeed, my colleague Elin Jones has previously worked with local councillors to make the case for an integrated care centre for Fishguard. So, will the Welsh Government commit to working with Hywel Dda University Health Board and local communities to explore how towns such as Fishguard could benefit from integrated care facilities, ensuring rural communities are not left behind as healthcare services evolve?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Many of us represent rural areas here, and the health of somebody in a rural part of Wales is as important as somebody in an urban part of Wales. We need to make sure that we have equitable healthcare, but it does mean that a different approach is needed. I'm really interested in the work that is developing—already has begun—into creating a centre of excellence on the delivery of rural healthcare in Bronglais Hospital, which could benefit all parts of Wales, not just Ceredigion Penfro.

The programme for government commitment is clear. We want to ensure that integrated care is delivered closer to home, with prevention in particular at its core, to support earlier diagnosis, reduce admissions and delays in discharge. We have many ideas on how, in general, the delivery can be improved in rural areas, but health officials, I know, are engaging with the health board and Pembrokeshire County Council specifically on the development of that integrated centre in Fishguard.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I now call on the party leaders to question the First Minister. First, the leader of Reform UK, Helen Jenner.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar arweinwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Prif Weinidog. Yn gyntaf, arweinydd Reform UK, Helen Jenner.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, you so often stand on your soapbox and arrogantly claim that you and your party are the ones fighting injustice and standing up for Wales. Yet, you and your party had the chance last week to tackle rape gangs and to stand up for Wales by backing our Reform motion to help bring closure for women and girls by uncovering the extent of rape gang activity in Wales. But, instead, you voted, shamefully, against it. How on earth can women and girls expect you to have their best interests and safety at heart?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Let me take this opportunity to congratulate the new leader of Reform in Wales on her election to the role. She is certainly a bold politician. Anybody who says she came into politics because she was impressed by the principles of Nigel Farage certainly has to be seen as bold.

There is nothing that is more important to any of us, hopefully, than safeguarding people that we have a duty of care for. That is why my Government at this moment is working on strengthening safeguarding and how it protects vulnerable people, including women and girls, potentially trafficked people, in all parts of Wales. That is something my Government is actively getting on with.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: You had the opportunity for a Wales focus there. Ironically, normally, we like to stand out, don't we, from the rest of the United Kingdom, but, in this case, you are happy to be absorbed into the UK inquiry. First Minister, the evidence suggests that rape gang activity may have been covered up by authorities to avoid racial tensions, and if we don't get to the bottom of what is among the most sickening organised criminal activities of our time, we cannot expect to prevent the risk of many more crimes of this nature. Last year, the Welsh Government said there was no current widespread issue with grooming gangs in Wales, and one of your current Ministers was accused by a grooming gang victim of downplaying her experience. Let's just have a look at the last 11 weeks alone: we've had two men imprisoned in Cardiff, five people convicted in Rhyl, and eight men across south Wales charged as part of Operation Oak, all relating to grooming gang-type activity. First Minister, can you really look me in the eye and say that you didn't let down victims last week by voting against wanting a grooming gang investigation in Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I can look you in the eye every single day of the week and tell you that we have a Government that isn't interested in scoring political points about what is a very, very sensitive issue, and is interested in getting on with finding solutions. Now, we said that we needed to understand the scale of the problem in Wales. Work was done to understand the scale of the problem in Wales, and it is apparent, obviously, that we have issues here that we need to get to grips with in order to safeguard people, which is why my Government is giving all support to the inquiry that is currently looking at the lessons that can be learnt. She may want to make this a constitutional issue; I make this about the safety of people in Wales, and that is the difference between her and me.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
First Minister, making sure victims' voices are heard—that is not political point scoring.

Speaking of uncovering the truth, First Minister, I've got a couple of quotes to read to you today:

'Reform would look at the nation of sanctuary and say Welsh people come first when prioritising council housing, and that is really, really important to me.'

Let me read you my second quote:

'Millions are being wasted on the tree-planting project, which is absolutely incredible, that we are sending money in Wales to Uganda.'

First Minister, these were things said by a Senedd Member that now sits on your benches. Do you agree with these comments, 'yes' or 'no'?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: What I admire is that somebody would have the bravery to stand up to this Reform group in the Senedd and say, 'I now can see you for what you are.' That is precisely what Sarah Cooper-Lesadd did last week. I firmly believe that, in politics, it is up to all of us to show that we are able to change, that we are able to see the light, politically, if you like, and so many other people are doing the same. We have now a scandal-ridden Reform party that is collapsing in chaos around the new Reform leader in Wales. The Member said yesterday that she is all for unity and continuity, but her party is incapable of showing either. Perhaps she can tell us how much of the £72 million arising from the latest Reform scandal she hopes will come to Wales. Maybe she hopes it will be Barnettised.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 'Yes' or 'no'? Okay. Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
First Minister, today we remember the deaths of hundreds of people in the Gresford mining disaster. It was a horrific disaster that devastated the community, and I'm sure you, First Minister, will also remember those who died. More than 260 bodies were recovered, but 253 remain entombed. Unfortunately, it wasn't just men that died; boys died in that disaster as well. It clearly was one of Wales's darkest days.

Research by Wrexham.com shows that, whilst the Plaid Government was questioning the need and rationale for an extra £100 million to be spent on additional learning needs, it was at the very same time asking councils how much more they'd be spending on additional learning needs this year. Now, the data was published just before the supplementary budget vote on your own website. And that figure, in total, for all councils and all schools in Wales was an extra £96.3 million—almost exactly the £100 million that Welsh Labour was saying was required to stabilise the system across Wales, and for which you received a major UK Labour Government windfall. Now, does this revelation, uncovered as I say by Wrexham.com, demonstrate that disadvantaged children risk coming second to this Plaid Cymru Government, behind free childcare for millionaires?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Let me, firstly, associate myself very much with the comments as we remember the Gresford disaster, and we send our thoughts to the community, for whom the pain of that day is still felt in many ways. 

On additional learning needs, I remind the Labour leader that he was intending to spend £9 million, had they won the election. My party's manifesto made it a pledge to put ALN on a sustainable footing. We had a discussion, running up to the supplementary budget, where we were putting £100 million plus on the table, including £40 million for this year—for this year—which is what we gauged, working with officials and others, could actually be spent to take the pressure. That money is still on the table, and I appeal to the Member again: help us to get it out of the door to help those families and the schools and local authorities who need that money spent.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
First Minister, the £9 million that you refer to was before the UK Government budget. Once the UK Government budget had taken place and confirmation that more than £300 million was made available, the then education Minister, Lynne Neagle, was planning to spend an extra £100 million on additional learning needs, had we been re-elected.

Now, I can provide clear, irrefutable evidence of how disadvantaged and disabled children will pay the price for your uncosted pledges. Clwb Cwtsh, which is the only provider of school holiday play for children with complex needs in north Wales, has just been told by the Plaid Government that funding for its services will end. The previous Labour Government here funded that provision, which is, as I say, for children with complex needs. I'm afraid, unless your Government makes a u-turn on this, changes its mind and provides the funding to Clwb Cwtsh, it will be lost. So, can I urge you to reconsider the decision to end funding for this provision? Otherwise, I'm afraid disabled children will be paying the price for free childcare for millionaires.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I ask the Member to look again at when they were promising £9 million, and it was very much after that money was made available. And there are principles here about the ability for us to set directions here in Wales. I am familiar with Clwb Cwtsh. I don't know why the previous Labour administration didn't put its funding on a permanent basis. The Member might be able to shed some light on that. I do understand also that it fills an ALN gap. The Member is asking for £30,000 for that; I have £40 million on the table that I have sought, and continue to seek, agreement with the Member on. That money includes money that would directly go to Flintshire council, so I'm imagining that the leader of Flintshire council would be keen for the Labour leader here to help us get that money out of the door.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The leader of the Welsh Conservatives, Darren Millar.
documents.text_cy: Arweinydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Darren Millar.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Llywydd. First Minister, last week, the UK Government published the inflation figures. They showed that inflation was up, with prices rising by 3.1 per cent in the year to August, and of course economists forecast that that increase in inflation will continue to rise to above 4 per cent around the end of this year, in the coming months. And that's going to be as a result of the energy price cap going up, the increase in fuel prices eventually coming through. Now, many households in Wales are facing the pinch in their pockets, and they desperately need help. One thing that your Government could do to help people here in Wales is to take action on council tax. Can I ask you, First Minister, instead of making yet more demands for more power, why don't you help people with their council tax demands? Why don't you initiate a cap on council tax and legislate, with the powers that you already have, so that people require a referendum in order to give local residents a say for any increase above that cap?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
I understand that the leader of the Conservatives wants to replicate policy in England. I'm interested in what works for Wales and it's about what works for council tax payers, Llywydd, and it's what works within the bounds of the finances of Welsh Government. And I remind the Senedd that we will be facing a real-terms cut in the day-to-day spending that we have available in the next financial year.

Council tax is set, of course, by local authorities and it's important that it is. I would remind the Member that, in a recent budget deal before we came into power, we made sure that there was a baseline for an increase in funding for councils, and a big part of that was to protect council tax payers, which I agree is something that's very, very important indeed.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
You know, I was listening to the radio this morning and I heard one of the commentators talking about it being a bad week for NATS; I thought they were talking about the Welsh nats, but actually, they were talking about the National Air Traffic Services, as it happens, and the chaos at our airports. [Laughter.]

One of the things that I want to see is fairness for council tax payers in Wales. You often talk about the need for fair funding between the England and Wales settlement—I get that, I completely get that and we support you on fair funding—but we need fair funding in Wales and we need fairness in council tax bills for people who have to struggle to pay them each and every year. The average band D council tax bill in Wales has risen by more than £600 over the past five years, and some residents have faced hikes of over 50 per cent over that period. It's totally unacceptable. We need urgent action to protect people from the sorts of excessive rises that some people have been having. So, can I urge you again: introduce a cap, legislate so that people have to have referendums for anything above that cap and do one more thing too—let's have a review, an independent review, truly independent of the local government funding formula, to make sure that there's fair funding to all parts of Wales, not just places favoured by the previous Labour Government.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Let's be positive and concentrate on the things that we agree on. Absolutely, we want to review, and looking at my local government Cabinet Minister, that is something that is happening under this Government, because it's important that people understand and feel that the decisions taken by Wales are equitable.

The other element that I agree with him on is that we need fair funding for Wales. We have lived under successive Conservative Governments and now Labour Governments that are still not engaging on that need to get the fundamentals right when it comes to fair funding for Wales. And you can't separate the two. It is an absolute truism that a lack of fair funding at the top will come down in the end to the money in the pockets of people the length and breadth of Wales, including through pressures on council tax. We want to be able to help in many ways that we can.

And on the rather glib start, if you're going to say it's a bad week for nats, actually choose a week that is a bad week for this Government. We're about to publish our programme for government, which is about transforming Wales, putting the health service on a firmer footing, raising education standards, halving that productivity gap with the rest of the UK, creating great job opportunities, the most generous childcare offer anywhere in the UK in dealing with child poverty, and standing up for Wales, always, which is something I'm not hearing from any other party in this Chamber.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 3. What is the Welsh Government doing to prepare for adverse and extreme weather events this winter? OQ64508
documents.text_cy: 3. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i baratoi ar gyfer digwyddiadau tywydd garw ac eithafol y gaeaf hwn? OQ64508

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I know the Member agrees with me that the evidence is clear: climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather. We are committed to building stronger, more resilient communities across Wales in that changing context. We're working closely with partners, including through the Wales resilience forum and local resilience forums to prepare for winter risks, to strengthen response arrangements and learn from recent extreme weather events. We're also making communities more resilient to flooding through continued investment in infrastructure and nature-based solutions.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Thank you. Last week, First Minister, you issued a statement saying that you will convene a resilience summit focusing on wildfires—very much welcomed. Yet, we must be ready for all of the escalating risks of a changing climate. This includes extreme cold, winter flooding and severe storms this coming winter. The Met Office has warned of a heightened risk on the horizon due to an unprecedented El Niño event this year, only highlighted in shocking headlines yesterday, recording the record breaking of 150 years of records. Weaknesses in our infrastructure and our resilience, such as recently witnessed in Gwaelod-y-garth, will only become more apparent in the coming months.

Wales is dangerously unprepared for the predicted onslaught of extreme weather conditions. Climate response must be integrated as our first line of defence. Welsh Government allocated in its supplementary budget just £1 million for emergency preparedness. Establishing a climate shock fund would be a vital step forward in demonstrating that the Welsh Government is serious about protecting communities this winter, with or without UK Government support. What discussions has the First Minister had with the UK Government on funding these emergency measures? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Thank you for the question. I think the world is largely unprepared for the challenges that we face. The question is how can we accelerate our preparedness. You will see in the programme for government today that climate change isn't seen as a priority in and of itself; it's one of the priorities that binds us all together as Government Ministers, because this has to be addressed across all portfolios.

Resilience—I talked about this last week—is an issue that I have tried to focus a great deal on since I came into the role of First Minister, understanding the various elements that contribute to the resilience, or lack of, in some ways, that we have as a society. Wildfires happen to be the one that has grabbed our attention, which is why we need to make sure that we're tightening up those resilience elements around that in the summit on 22 October. But the Member is right; flooding is something that many communities will be concerned about. There are other concerns too—the effects of heat, the effects of cold and so on.

It is something that we work across the UK on. I want to ensure (a) that Wales gets its fair share of resilience funding, civil contingency funding, across the UK, and that's something I'm eager to pursue. But the Member has my word that I will absolutely be looking at how we work between Welsh Government and UK Government to get the support that Wales needs to prepare for this wide range of threats that we face in future.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, I recognise that £85 million has been invested in flood risk management this year, but Rhondda Cynon Taf's investigation into storm Dennis has found that Blaenllechau was flooded from the steep hillside above it, that felling on Welsh Government-owned Natural Resources Wales-managed woodland may have contributed to surface water run-off, and that modelling suggested three of the four culvert networks lacked adequate capacity. This August, a major wildfire burned around 150 hectares of Llanwonno mountain, above Blaenllechau and Ferndale. So, before the winter rain arrives, will you ensure that Natural Resources Wales and RCT carry out a co-ordinated inspection of that hillside, its drainage and culverts, with the Mining Remediation Authority checking any relevant higher category coal tips within or below that affected area, and report the findings and any remedial work required to the Senedd by the end of October? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
There is, of course, an ongoing programme of works that need to happen, some of them under the auspices of Welsh Government or its agencies, Natural Resources Wales, some that are the responsibility of local authorities. I have no doubt that, as we face the challenges of the winter, there needs to be just a double-checking of the robustness of those measures being put in place. I would say that, as well as making sure that your culverts are able to deal with run-off, there are other questions and innovations that we need to be looking at in how you slow down that run-off. Clearly, hot weather—hard ground—makes the situation more difficult. I'm really interested in how we manage the land, working with farmers to try to limit run-off, and so on.

We have to be aware that there are no silver bullets, there are no single measures that can be taken as we face these threats. They are multiple, and the need to be strategic in the way that we approach this is important, which is why the wildfire summit, in particular, looking at that threat, brings in so many different partners who will be able to contribute to making our resilience that much stronger. But I'm sure that your message will have been heard by the local authorities and others today.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, Monmouthshire has faced catastrophic flooding in recent years, and I was pleased that you were able to visit Monmouth and Abergavenny before the Senedd elections to speak to some of the local people affected, as well as to those finding solutions—long-lasting solutions—upstream. The scenes from last year’s flooding, especially those from Monmouth, will be etched in the memory of everyone who saw them for a long time. These once in 100 years events are getting more and more frequent, and we must now assume that they could happen at any time. As we've heard, the approaching El Niño event is on the horizon, with extreme weather events already anticipated, so, with this in mind, how is the Government improving flood preparedness for this winter? And in the longer term, how can we learn from the experiences of Monmouthshire residents to improve flood management for their community and for all of Wales? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I was pleased, along with the Member, to speak with some of the individuals who were affected by the pretty devasting flooding that they experienced in Monmouth. The Member's right that it is about learning lessons. It's not just about cleaning up; that's the first step. It's about trying to make sure that lessons are learnt for those localities in order to avoid and avert flooding, but lessons for elsewhere too, and I know that Monmouthshire County Council is preparing its section 19 flood investigation report following the devastation of storm Claudia, and the flood investigation report is almost complete, I understand, and will be published in October. But, wherever those floods are, the learnings are ones that we can try to make sure that they are applicable in other parts of Wales too.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, my colleague Jayne Bryant, asked you, during your oral statement last week, whether the Welsh Government would consider bringing in a climate resilience fund to help us mitigate the impacts of extreme weather. You didn't really answer her directly, and nor did you answer Anthony Slaughter when he raised a very similar point in his opening question. Now, there's widespread support for this from stakeholders that we on the Welsh Labour benches have engaged with over the summer recess. And with resources for agencies involved in climate mitigation measures being really stretched, this is one way to safeguard those funds and make sure they're channelled in the right way. So, is this something that your Government can explore setting up ahead of your wildfire summit next month?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: No attempt to avoid the question. There are, in effect, a number of funds, aren't there, on which a Government can draw to deal with emergencies. What you want to make sure is that those funds themselves are resilient. I absolutely am ready to consider whether we can bring together funds in one place, in the same way as the Government is looking at how we can put preventative health funds under one banner, so that we can measure better what the various elements of those funding capacities are. So, absolutely willing to consider that. At the end of the day, it's making sure that we have the tools to do the job that we need. There's more than one way of doing that, but let's put that in the mix too.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 4. Will the First Minister provide an update on progress relating to the development of a new national food strategy? OQ64561
documents.text_cy: 4. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf am y cynnydd o ran datblygu strategaeth fwyd genedlaethol newydd? OQ64561

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Will the First Minister provide an update on progress relating to the development of a new food strategy and how that could start to deal with food poverty in Afan Ogwr Rhondda?
documents.text_cy: A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog egluro'r cynlluniau sydd gan y Llywodraeth ar gyfer strategaeth fwyd a sut y gall hynny ddechrau lliniaru tlodi bwyd yn Afan Ogwr Rhondda?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I am very pleased that significant and early progress has been made on developing our new national food strategy. An expert working group has been formed already, and terms of reference have been published. Plans are also in place to fast-track immediate discussions on food in schools, which is important, and edible horticulture as well, and the meat supply chain. There will be two interim reports that will be published before the final report by autumn next year.
documents.text_cy: Dwi yn falch iawn bod cynnydd sylweddol a chynnar wedi cael ei wneud ar ddatblygu ein strategaeth fwyd genedlaethol newydd ni. Mae gweithgor arbenigol wedi cael ei ffurfio yn barod, a chylch gorchwyl wedi’i gyhoeddi. Mae yna gynlluniau ar waith hefyd i fwrw ati i gynnal trafodaethau ar unwaith ar fwyd mewn ysgolion, sydd yn bwysig, cynnyrch garddwriaethol bwytadwy, a'r gadwyn gyflenwi cig. Mi fydd yna ddau adroddiad interim yn cael eu cyhoeddi cyn yr adroddiad terfynol erbyn hydref y flwyddyn nesaf.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister. Over the summer months, I've met with a number of organisations who are involved in food poverty and food insecurity. From frontline provision to community pantries and growing schemes, everyone seems to be saying the same thing: the number of people who are working and using these resources is increasing, contributions are declining, and groups of people who have never sought support before are starting to do so now. How does the Government intend to engage with these local organisations, who see the impacts on the ground, in developing its national food strategy?
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Dros gyfnod yr haf, dwi wedi cwrdd â nifer o sefydliadau sy'n ymwneud â thlodi bwyd a diffyg diogeledd bwyd. O ddarpariaeth rheng flaen i bantrïoedd cymunedol, cynlluniau a chynlluniau tyfu, mae pawb yn dweud yr un peth: mae nifer y bobl sy'n gweithio ac yn defnyddio'r adnoddau hyn yn cynyddu, mae cyfraniadau'n lleihau, ac mae grwpiau o bobl sydd erioed wedi gofyn am gymorth o'r blaen yn dechrau gwneud hynny nawr. Sut mae'r Llywodraeth yn bwriadu ymgysylltu â'r sefydliadau lleol hyn, sy'n gweld yr effeithiau ar lawr gwlad, wrth ddatblygu ei strategaeth fwyd genedlaethol?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I'm very pleased to have that question. It gives me a chance to explain a little bit about how the group is going to be operating. There are four pillars to that piece of work: one of them is the environment, one is the economy and rural development, there is a food security element, and then the other element is health and well-being. We can see there, can't we, where we need to make sure that local groups can feed into this. The working group does include a local food partnership in order to make sure that the voice of community organisations is heard. So, it is something that we were determined to build into this piece of work from the beginning, for the reasons that the Member referred to.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n falch iawn o gael y cwestiwn yna. Mae’n fodd i egluro mymryn am sut mae’r grŵp yn mynd i fod yn gweithredu. Mae pedwar piler i'r gwaith: un ohonyn nhw yr amgylchedd, un ohonyn nhw yr economi a datblygu gwledig, mae yna elfen diogelwch bwyd, a'r elfen arall ydy iechyd a llesiant. Rydym ni'n gallu gweld yn fanna, onid ydyn, lle mae angen gwneud yn siŵr bod grwpiau lleol yn gallu bwydo i mewn i hyn. Mae'r grŵp gweithredu'n cynnwys partneriaeth fwyd leol er mwyn gwneud yn siŵr bod llais sefydliadau cymunedol yn cael ei glywed. Felly, mae o'n rhywbeth roedden ni'n benderfynol o adeiladu i mewn i'r gwaith yma o'r dechrau, am rai o'r rhesymau roedd yr Aelod yn cyfeirio atyn nhw.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch. Alun, you extended the question a little bit from what was on the order paper, just to be aware, because this isn't an Afan Ogwr Rhondda-specific question. So, can I bring in now Claire Johnson-Wood, to explain why?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch. First Minister, what Welsh farmers need is a Government that understands and prioritises, not yet another 'expert panel' kicking the can down the road. Given that under the previous Labour-Plaid administration the sustainable farming scheme significantly increased regulatory complexity, can the Welsh Government please give assurances that the national food strategy will not place additional bureaucratic burdens on farmers and producers that they do not need at this time?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: I haven't heard anybody accusing this agriculture Minister, this rural resilience Minister, of kicking any can down the road when it comes to supporting the agriculture sector. I heard nothing but a sigh of relief from a sector that believe that they have a Government that's willing to engage with it in a positive way, that security of that over £1 billion over the course of this Senedd in order to give assurances and confidence to the sector. And on where they fit into the food strategy, they are members of the working group that is bringing together this food strategy, and as I said, rural development and the economy, which includes agriculture, is one of the core pillars of this work that we're undertaking.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Next—. I do apologise. Peter Fox.
documents.text_cy: Nesaf—. Mae'n ddrwg gen i. Peter Fox.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, I welcome the food strategy, and I was pleased to read the published terms of reference for it last week, and I look forward to the expert panel being put in place. I am frustrated in many ways that we've lost four months because, actually, most of the evidence that is needed around that area has been in place, because there are huge similarities between what you're putting forward and what I was considering a couple of years ago. Within my proposals back then, there were clear, measurable targets against food goals. Can we expect to see really robust, measurable targets against your food pillars, and can I ask you: would you consider anchoring your food strategy into legislation, recognising the importance this will have for our future generations?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Can I pay tribute, Llywydd, to the work that the Member has done in this field in trying to bring in a piece of legislation that would underpin a robust food sector and protect issues relating to food production and nutrition and so on in Wales? We haven't lost four months, of course, because this work is already under way. This was one of the early actions of the Minister, to appoint a chair. The work is ongoing.

I'm not going to be prescriptive in telling a chair who is much more of an expert in this field than I am of the approach that he should take. You know me: I tend to take the approach of, 'Let's see what the evidence tells us.' If there's a suggestion that legislation could be a part of the approach on one particular element of what we're trying to do, well, let's have a sit down and see how we could formulate that legislation. But it's also true, we know, that you can act without legislation. I'm about outcomes, at the end of the day: let's progress in the way that gives us the best result.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 5. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i gefnogi pobl hŷn gyda chostau byw? OQ64527

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Supporting people with the cost of living, as we know, is a real priority for this Government. We're ensuring that measures to tackle poverty reflect older people's needs and make support for older people simpler, fairer and also more accessible. Through our £4.84 million tackling poverty support fund, local authorities will provide crisis support, including emergency food aid, alongside preventative help also tailored to local communities, to stop people, including older people, from falling into poverty where we can avoid that.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thanks for the answer, First Minister. So, while I recognise there are a number of schemes available, and I knew you'd refer to some, of course you would, but the Older People's Commissioner for Wales tells us that one in six older people in Wales are living in relative income poverty, with one in five going without heating and a quarter skipping meals or eating less. How can we imagine that situation? It's happening in Wales. These figures suggest that despite the support available, too many older people are still struggling, particularly those living on fixed incomes and those who may fall just outside eligibility for means-tested assistance. So, what further action will your Government take to ensure that support actually reaches older people, and how will you measure whether it is succeeding?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
The Member is quite right. I have the results here of Age Cymru's 2026 annual survey, and more than half of respondents identified cost-of-living pressures as being the biggest challenge that they face—and for some, it will be a significant challenge.

There are things that we can do. The nearly £5 million that was announced in the past few days can really help people who are particularly vulnerable. There are a host of issues around travel and the continuation of bus travel and so on that we can wrap together as support for older people. But also we have to, when it comes to the main pressures, recognise that there is a need for all of us to put pressure on the UK Government here, especially on fuel. We've had a question already on the pressure of the cost of fuel in rural areas in particular. There has to be a coming together of all the potential levers—some of which are in our hands, but not all of them. And, at the end of the day, we also need a fresh approach on the question of public service funding because it is the most vulnerable people, including older people, who bear the brunt of it.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Can I support the Member in his questions on this topic, First Minister? We know that many older people at the moment are struggling with the cost of living, and particularly with the impact of a fixed income on many older people in our communities. We also know that, historically, people have been able to access advice services in their communities through organisations such as Citizens Advice and other fantastic organisations like that, who can support our older people to ensure that they are making the best use of any welfare support available to them and other types of support as well. So, I wonder, First Minister, if you're able to outline how you see those types of services in the future and what support the Welsh Government can give to organisations like the citizens advice bureaux to ensure that that advice is available to them in a timely way, and in an accessible way as well? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: We all have worked with Citizens Advice, with CAB, haven't we, and appreciate the work that they do on the ground in all parts of Wales in helping vulnerable people? I advise people to turn to your friends in CAB. Part of the funding that was announced in the past few days was specifically around advice; I think that's important to note. There is £36 million grant funding in place for the single advice fund for the period from April last year and for three years from then. That's about providing integrated advice services. I would hope that those providing services under that grant are able to reach as many people as they can. But the Member's right: reaching out with advice to people is key. We've made some funding available now and we are so lucky in Wales that we have those partners, and in local government too, who work so hard on this front.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 6. What consideration has the Welsh Government given to ensuring that the costs of remediating illegally dumped waste are paid by the people responsible, rather than by taxpayers? OQ64553
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa ystyriaeth y mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi’i rhoi i sicrhau bod costau adfer safleoedd lle mae gwastraff wedi’i waredu’n anghyfreithlon yn cael eu talu gan y rhai sy’n gyfrifol, yn hytrach na chan drethdalwyr?​‌ OQ64553

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: In line with the polluter-pays principle, those responsible for illegal activity should bear the costs of the clean-up. That's true for illegal dumping today, as it should be for historic contamination, if I could add, too. We are committed, as a Government, to reducing the burden of illegal dumping on taxpayers and on landowners, and landfill disposals tax ensures that those responsible for unauthorised disposals pay 150 per cent of the standard tax rate.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. In Fflint Wrecsam, you may be aware that communities continue to deal with both the historic legacy of illegal waste dumping and the current active sites that are causing ongoing problems for residents in my constituency. Time and again, we see the companies responsible for these environmental crimes avoid accountability by entering liquidation and walking away from the costs of remediation. This leaves local communities to deal with the consequences and risks shifting the burden of cleaning up onto the public purse. How will Welsh Government work with the UK Government, local authorities and relevant public bodies to address this ongoing issue?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: It is an issue that blights many communities and, as I say, communities should not have to bear the consequences of waste crime, and neither should the taxpayer, and we're committed to supporting regulators to pursue those who are responsible: funding Natural Resources Wales's waste crime work is important; supporting multi-agency work to tackle organised criminality, because this is criminality; sharing intelligence where we can; and co-ordinating enforcement action. This is also an issue on which we are eager to work with UK Government and, indeed, Governments across the UK. The Welsh Revenue Authority wants to build those links with His Majesty's Revenue and Customs and so on, to strengthen the system, to close loopholes and ensure waste crime does not pay. Of course, when it comes to historic contamination, something that has received significant publicity recently, we have to make sure that every avenue is pursued to deal with this, as one of our lasting post-industrial legacies.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to reduce river pollution levels in Carmarthenshire? OQ64555
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i leihau lefelau llygredd afonydd yn Sir Gaerfyrddin? OQ64555

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: My Government's determined to improve the health of our rivers. We're funding the west Wales nutrient management boards, which deliver targeted action across the Tywi, Teifi and Cleddau catchments. We're also establishing a new nutrient efficiency and resilience group to strengthen national leadership on nutrient pollution and co-ordinate action across sectors. Together, we believe these measures will support river restoration, improve water quality and build long-term environmental resilience.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
Diolch, First Minister. People whose livelihoods depend on Carmarthenshire's rivers, including members of Carmarthen Coracle and Netsmen's Association, tell us they have never seen such a poor season, with the return of only six sewin from May to June this year. Their experience makes clear that river pollution must be treated with a far greater urgency. I urge you to read the Royal Society's recent report on chemical mixtures in British waterways. Quote: 'Regulators are flying blind.' Unquote.

In Carmarthenshire, Natural Resources Wales seem to be flying blind. Our rivers are being contaminated by harmful chemical mixtures, including organics, ammonia, microplastics, cadmium and mercury, with no understanding of their interactions or the harm done. Will you acknowledge that the Welsh Government lacks a credible plan to clean up our rivers, and set out how it will meet its political duty to protect our waters and rivers and special areas of conservation?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: This is work that is under way, and it's very important that it is. We know that river pollution, sea pollution, is something that is of real concern to people the length and breadth of Wales, and it certainly is to me. The vision for a reformed Welsh water sector will be published later this autumn, so we're nearing that point where we have a point to move forward from. We know that river pollution has multiple causes. It requires action across all sectors. It involves industry, it involves agriculture, it involves the water companies themselves. It's about making sure that we have good, solid regulation, made in Wales—that's what I want. It's by having that attitude that we can move forward to having cleaner rivers in Wales.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 8. What is the Welsh Government doing to address NHS waiting times in Blaenau Gwent Caerfilli Rhymni? OQ64559
documents.text_cy: 8. Beth mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wneud i fynd i'r afael ag amseroedd aros y GIG ym Mlaenau Gwent Caerfilli Rhymni? OQ64559

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The Welsh Government is investing £145 million to help health boards reduce waiting times and improve access to treatment. This supports delivery of our planned care plan, which sets out a clinically led approach to eliminating the longest waits, increasing capacity and improving outcomes. An expert group is also advising on the development of up to 10 surgical and diagnostic hubs to provide faster, more efficient care for patients, including those in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, a constituent has come to me who is now unable to work because he has a hernia. He's been waiting close to 36 weeks for his surgery. He's living in pain. He feels it affects his family life, his relationship with his children, all because he's waiting to be seen. During the election, you looked down a camera and told the people of Wales that these waiting lists will see an impact within months. We learnt during recess from your health Minister that months could take up to, now, years. [Interruption.] So, the Minister was wrong when he said that waiting lists will take years to address, was he? That's what he said. So, what can you tell the people of Wales? Do you regret saying it's going to be months, because from reports last week, waiting lists are going up and not down? So, will you apologise to the people of Wales for your statement at the election?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text:
That's exactly what I've said throughout. This is an issue of seriousness that means we put it at No.1 on the list of our priorities coming into Government. It was somewhat missing in Reform's pledges for Government, were they to be in this position. I have said about the most extreme over-two-year waits that they have to go. They have to be eliminated. I said they'll go in months. That goes, a year from coming into Government they are gone. That's months. Well, months is not more than a year. So, a year after we come into Government, I expect them to have gone. I stick to what I have said throughout, okay?

I consider us right now to be beginning the work. We came into Government in May. We've had two months of figures. It's during that time that we have started putting money in that will, in months, bring us the benefits, not for us as Senedd Members, but for the people that we serve: people who are on long waiting lists who shouldn't be, staff across the health boards who want to be able to care and not have to have those that they're concerned about waiting two years or more. We stick to what we said. I've said it throughout. I say it again today.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: 9. How will the Welsh Government ensure that women can access opportunities in major growth sectors, including advanced manufacturing, clean energy, and information technology? OQ64494
documents.text_cy: 9. Sut y bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn sicrhau bod menywod yn gallu cael mynediad at gyfleoedd mewn sectorau twf mawr, gan gynnwys gweithgynhyrchu uwch, ynni glân, a thechnoleg gwybodaeth? OQ64494

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Our productivity mission, as a Government, is about unlocking the talents of the whole workforce, and ensuring economic opportunity is everywhere and open to everyone. We aim to work with employers, education and training providers, and others, to ensure women can enter and progress in sectors such as advanced manufacturing, clean energy and digital technology where, of course, many women are already having a huge impact.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: First Minister, thank you for that answer. I welcome the Welsh Government's focus on growth sectors and its commitment to fairness in the workplace. But to ensure, in the Valleys that I represent, that women directly benefit from these opportunities, could you expand any further on how you will agree to work alongside local authorities and industry partners to explore the targeted apprenticeship pathways for women in our former coalfield Valleys, please?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: It absolutely is about partnership working, and we will continue absolutely to work with employers, local authorities, training providers and others to make sure that those opportunities are there for women in these sectors. We want more women to access apprenticeships, to develop higher level skills and progress into well-paid careers that many women thought were closed to them not that long ago. Well, they are not closed to any women, and through apprenticeships, Careers Wales, Working Wales, we're helping women in communities like Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni to identify those opportunities and ambition to increase female participation in advanced manufacturing, digital and clean energy. That's the kind of Wales we want, where opportunity genuinely is open to all. There have been some positive signs, but we've got more to do.

documents.text: And finally, First Minister, question 10, Cai Parry-Jones.
