documents.text: 10. Will the First Minister provide an update on the implementation of the Senedd Cymru (Member Accountability and Elections) Act 2026? OQ64560
documents.text_cy: 10. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf am weithredu Deddf Senedd Cymru (Atebolrwydd Aelodau ac Etholiadau) 2026? OQ64560

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: The Welsh Government is working closely with the Standards of Conduct Committee and the Business Committee to ensure that Members whose conduct falls far below that which is expected of elected representatives can be robustly held to account.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Part of this Act places a duty on your Government to bring in rules banning false or misleading statements of fact, made before or during an election, to affect who is elected. It also lets your Government set out what does and does not count as a statement of fact. If it is, in fact, true that a candidate misrepresents their own beliefs to win votes, and that becomes clear after polling day, will your Government treat that as a false statement of fact?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: This is a sour grapes question, Llywydd, I believe. I think it references a decision taken by a Member of this Senedd who has seen a new approach to politics. This is a party that misled people in the Brexit vote. It knows all about misleading people. I and my Government stand by the determination to make sure that we have in Wales an honest politics, the kind that seems alien to many on his benches.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: Thank you very much, First Minister. I'm speaking very slowly now—
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn, Brif Weinidog. Rydw i'n siarad nawr yn araf iawn—

documents.item: 1. Questions to the First Minister
documents.text: —as we wait in high expectation for the Counsel General to appear on the benches. If Members will just bear with us for a moment, as soon as we are ready, we will commence.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: We will move now to item 2, questions to the Counsel General. The first question is from Jane Dodds.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn nawr at eitem 2, cwestiynau i'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol. Cwestiwn 1, Jane Dodds.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you very much, Llywydd. Good afternoon, Counsel General.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn, Lywydd. Prynhawn da, Gwnsler Cyffredinol.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 1. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding its legal powers to intervene in service reconfiguration decisions taken by local health boards? OQ64489
documents.text_cy: 1. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynglŷn â'i phwerau cyfreithiol i ymyrryd mewn penderfyniadau ad-drefnu gwasanaethau a wneir gan fyrddau iechyd lleol? OQ64489

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I thank the Member for that question. I am aware of her concerns with regard to reconfiguration in the area she represents, but it is up to local health boards, as they are responsible for service reconfiguration decisions and for engaging with communities and stakeholders, including Llais. Welsh Ministers are not the routine decision maker in such matters. Intervention generally would be considered only where there is evidence of significant concerns regarding decision-making processes, governance, statutory compliance or, crucially, patient safety.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you for that response.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am yr ymateb.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Sections 26 to 28 of the National Health Service (Wales) Act 2006 clearly give Welsh Ministers the power to intervene where a health board is failing to perform its functions adequately, and to remove board members, which we saw in the Senedd last term. Section 12 of the same Act allows Ministers to direct health boards on their functions more generally. While there appears to be some confusion over the 2006 Act, and the social care Bill in 2020, Vaughan Gething at the time was relatively clear that the Bill did not affect Ministers' powers under sections 26 to 28. That is a bit of a mouthful, I'm aware, of lots of sections. I ask for a clear answer, and I'm very happy to take a response in writing to this: is there anything in law that prevents Welsh Ministers from intervening under sections 26 to 28 where a board has lost public confidence in this way, or is the truth that Ministers could act and are choosing not to? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
I thank her for that further question, but the truth is that the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care has been very clear that any proposals for service change must be informed by evidence and with full regard to quality, safety and patient experience. In addition, it's expected that health boards engage with people openly and transparently about these service changes. As she probably knows, Llais also has a statutory role in representing the views and interests of people who use health services and may raise concerns regarding service change proposals. I do repeat that Ministers do retain statutory powers, to which she has referred, to direct local health boards and formally intervene where there's a failure in governance, performance and exercise of local functions by local health boards.

Those powers, clearly, are to safeguard patients and are intended to address significant patient safety concerns, failures in consultation or decision making, breaches of statutory duties or wider governance concerns. Therefore, with respect, political opposition, public concern or the controversial nature of a proposal would not, of itself, ordinarily justify intervention. These powers are safeguards for addressing failures by local health boards in discharge of functions and they are not a mechanism for reconsidering the merits or demerits of any clinical service decision. That is clearly the position as far as the law is concerned. But I would add that during a consultation, surely it's better to wait for the conclusion of the consultation before coming to any thoughts about any possible legal avenue.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I'd like to thank Jane Dodds for bringing this matter up. Powys is a large and sparsely populated rural county, where removing in-patient provision from community hospitals can mean substantially longer journeys for patients and their families. When a health board considers a major service reconfiguration, what legal duties must it take into account regarding rurality, equality and access to services? And what remedies are available if those duties have not been properly discharged?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I can only repeat what I've just said, and no doubt the Member has heard what I've said. That's clearly what the law says. I would, again, suggest to him that it might be better to wait for the outcome of the consultation and then to decide was it a fair consultation, was it a consultation that people would expect at law, and, whatever the conclusions are, are the conclusions safe as far as patients are concerned and other considerations. But I think it's rather early now to say, 'Let's look for a challenge', until the consultation has been completed and conclusions have been reached.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 2. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the devolution of youth justice? OQ64502
documents.text_cy: 2. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi ei roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ar ddatganoli cyfiawnder ieuenctid? OQ64502

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Youth justice should be devolved to Wales. That's the plain truth. It should be an important early step towards the devolution of justice in full. As a starting point, the UK Government’s proposed reforms offer the Welsh Government an opportunity to have greater influence over, and responsibility for, overseeing and funding youth justice services here in Wales.
documents.text_cy: Fe ddylai cyfiawnder ieuenctid gael ei ddatganoli i Gymru. Dyna ydy'r peth plaen i'w ddweud. Dylai fod yn gam cynnar pwysig tuag at ddatganoli cyfiawnder yn llawn. Fel man cychwyn, mae diwygiadau arfaethedig Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig yn rhoi cyfle i Lywodraeth Cymru gael mwy o ddylanwad a chyfrifoldeb am oruchwylio ac ariannu gwasanaethau cyfiawnder ieuenctid yma yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Diolch, Gwnsler Cyffredinol. Many have called for youth justice to be devolved to Wales, including the Brown commission, and I'm glad that this Plaid Cymru Government also wants to see that happen. Currently, a child in the justice system in Wales has one foot in each world. Their school, healthcare and social workers are devolved, yet their court and their custody are not. That jagged edge means different systems, different governments, and it's the child who tends to slip through the gaps. The UK Government is proposing, like you mentioned, reforms to the youth justice system. From April 2027, Wales is due to take on some funding for remand and early intervention. That's a start. It's funding, but it's not powers. Decisions on how the system works will still be made in Westminster, even though Wales delivers the majority of it. Does the Counsel General agree that the UK Government has a duty to work with Wales, not around it, on reforms to a system that Wales largely delivers? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
I thank the Member for this important question. The case for devolving justice and policing to Wales is open and shut, in my view. She referred to the various commissions. They've all said the same thing. They were arm's-length commissions, they decided what is best for Wales, how we could deliver better for Wales, and that is their conclusion. The commission found that devolving justice would enable more responsive, joined-up and effective services, as the Member alluded to, better aligned to the needs of people and communities in Wales and more closely integrated with devolved responsibilities such as health, social care, education and housing. In particular, the most recent commission found that youth justice should be among the starting points for fuller devolution. This Government's priorities are clear: where there are opportunities to improve the delivery of those priorities by securing further powers, then we will take them, to ensure the right foundations are laid for a system that is joined up—which the Member refers to—preventative, and fit for Wales.

I will conclude by saying that I agree entirely with her question. The Welsh Government position has been communicated to the Minister for youth justice, Jake Richards. The reforms being progressed by the UK Government potentially offer the opportunity to provide greater Welsh Government responsibility and influence in relation the strategic oversight and funding of local youth justice services. But it is important that the result is that Wales has sufficient powers and responsibilities to simplify and create strategy, governance and oversight arrangements. Our priorities are clear: where there are opportunities to enable more responsive, joined-up and effective services to be aligned, then of course we will go for them. I thank her for the question; it is an important one. There is a lot of ongoing work.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Counsel General, there is a fundamental difference between improving youth justice and simply devolving it. Wales already has strong pre-court diversion and comparatively low levels of youth custody. Yet the Government's own advisory work identifies inconsistent police management, staffing pressures, funding uncertainty and rising school exclusions. Indeed, its own youth justice advisory panel asked the questions Ministers must answer: how will devolution improve outcomes for children rather than simply change who is responsible? Because transferring responsibility across the border does not solve a problem. Changing the nameplate on the door is not reform. Counsel General, what objective test has the Government been advised must be met before further youth justice powers are devolved? If Ministers cannot demonstrate better outcomes for children, victims and the public, what is the legal or constitutional justification for transferring those powers at all?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The Member asks about legal tests. I would surmise that those legal tests were uppermost in the minds of all three commissions when they decided wholeheartedly to suggest that there should be devolution of justice. One of the problems that we have, which was alluded to in my answer to the previous question, is that we need joined-up responsibility in the whole area. It's not simply one function. It's not one service. It's an amalgam of the services. By having piecemeal devolution in these areas, it does nothing for the services and, arguably, we are letting our young people and families down. It's not a constitutional nicety. That is why we want to prioritise moving forward on this. And that is why, presumably, all three commissions, together, decided in that way as well.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I now call the party spokespeople to question the Counsel General. First of all, Reform UK spokesperson, Adrian Mason.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol. Yn gyntaf, llefarydd Reform UK, Adrian Mason.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Here we are again, Counsel General. You and I have to walk a narrow line in our exchanges. We're here in our legal capacity in this instance in an immensely political Chamber. So, no trick questions.

Constitutional change can have long-term consequences, of course. When the Government considers seeking additional powers for Wales, what tests do you believe should be applied before a proposal is taken forward? Should those tests include a clearly identifiable difficulty, evidence that transferring powers is the best way to address it, a workable delivery plan and sustainable funding, and clear accountability? Where services operate across the England and Wales border, should the effect on those cross-border links also be addressed and made clear before any changes take place?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
I think the overall priority of this Government is to improve the lot of the people of Wales. If that means prioritising further devolution in some areas, so be it. It's not devolution for devolution's sake. That would be unfortunate, and probably prone to several problems. 

There is, for example, an argument, occasionally, for cross-border understandings. These are exceptions to which we refer in our approach to UK legislation. That's only sensible, because we are looking at services for people on both sides of the border, actually, but our priority is people here in Wales.

If the test we apply shows that we can improve services for the people of Wales by going for further devolution, then that is the driving force, that is the reason why we are doing it. There's no other reason, because, as I said earlier on, change for change's sake—and the Member said this, and he's right—change for the sake of change takes you nowhere. Change for the sake of improving services does.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you. I want to move to the tribunal system. I know it's high in your priorities, Counsel General. So, the proposed new Welsh tribunal structure is intended not only to bring existing devolved tribunals into a more coherent system, but also be capable of taking on additional jurisdictions in the future. Before any additional jurisdiction is transferred into the Welsh tribunal system, what safeguards do you believe should be in place? In particular, how would we protect judicial independence, access to specialist expertise, consistent rights of appeal, and the handling of cases across the England-Wales border? And would you expect the costs and practical impact of each proposed transfer to be fully assessed before it takes place?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, there are some figures being looked at at the moment, but, clearly, as with any new major change, it cannot be known fully at the very beginning. But as regards cross-border function, I don't see that that is an issue in this case. It was, because I know of several cases where people in the tribunal system wished to appeal, and they happened to have their cases dealt with in Welsh, and they had to go over the border and could not obtain Welsh translation facilities, so they had to speak in their second language very often. So, that was one thing that needs putting right, and it will be put right in this case. All these tribunals, bar one or two, are existing. They are currently being run as best we can ensure that they are, but it will be far better to have the six of them designated properly, with a fully professional clerical service and administration, and then topped by a limited-form court of appeal within Wales for tribunal appeals. It's a logical step forward. The senior judiciary—not known for radical constitutional change—are all in favour of it, and we do have their full support in going forward, which makes me think it's the right thing to do.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Let's move now to the rail network—another one that is coming down the line, excuse the pun. Counsel General, the Government has set out a pathway towards full devolution of rail services and infrastructure, while also accepting that the Welsh network must remain integrated within the wider United Kingdom, of course. From a legal and constitutional point of view, what would need to be settled before such a transfer could take place? In particular, how would responsibility for long-term infrastructure liabilities, cross-border routes, for example, funding and dispute resolution be divided between Welsh Ministers, the Welsh Government and Great British Railways? And should funding and liability be settled as an integral part of any transfer rather than being left to subsequent negotiations?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, the transfer to which the Member refers does not apply to the tribunals Bill scenario. That's the first thing to say. As for further devolution, that clearly is a political matter. I am not part of the political machine as such. I am engaged by the Welsh Government on legal matters. If and when we come to a position where I'm asked my advice about the points that he very properly raises, then I will give my clear advice at that stage. At this moment in time, I can't assist any further.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The Welsh Labour spokesperson, Mike Hedges.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Mike Hedges.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Diolch. What discussion has the Counsel General had with the Law Society regarding securing fully funded level 7 solicitor apprenticeships in Wales? Level 7 solicitor apprenticeships are a well-established route to qualifications in England, allowing aspiring solicitors to earn while they learn and avoid taking on significant tuition debt. In Wales, however, aspiring solicitors still cannot access an equivalent funded route. The uptake of level 7 solicitor apprenticeships in England has grown, with more than 5,000 people starting an apprenticeship between 2018 and 2025. We cannot allow Wales to be left behind, can we?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: That is a very good question, and I fully agree with the Member on what he says. What I can tell him, which may cheer him up slightly, is that level 7 apprenticeships at the bar and also solicitors are uppermost in this Government's mind. We are pushing forward on them and, indeed, I shall be making a speech on them in about a fortnight's time, during the Legal Wales conference. So, as he is interested, I'll send him a copy of the speech, and he can see that we are doing what we can.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you very much for that answer. Let's see if I can keep being on a roll. Access to justice is a core component of the rule of law and yet many areas of Wales are facing a growing crisis in access to legal services. Described as legal deserts, these are areas where the presence of solicitors is so limited that people cannot easily obtain legal advice or representation when they need it. The Law Society has produced a report that draws on the latest data available, including solicitor distribution, demographic trends and the impact of legal aid funding pressures. The findings include severe geographic inequality in solicitor density, rising solicitor retirements without adequate replacements, the attrition of legal aid providers, and increasing numbers of unrepresented litigants in civil, criminal and welfare cases. What are the Counsel General's views on this report?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I've read the report, obviously. It's an important report, and it's been a fairly long-standing problem in many areas in Wales. In fact, it's been described, in terms of north and mid Wales, as an advice desert, and I do know of pockets of deserts, if you like, within urban areas as well. It's partly because solicitors have left the legal aid work, it's partly because there are fewer of them, it's partly because they are drifting away to larger firms who are privately funded. That is the picture. It is something that is creating a huge amount of difficulty for people who wish to access legal advice who are unable to obtain legal aid and who, therefore—and by the way, the qualification for legal aid has been cut back drastically as well in many areas—are left with private funding that they cannot afford. So, it is a big issue. What I can say is that I have no doubt that, during the forthcoming conference to which I referred, it will be a live issue and there will be further discussions. Something needs to be done, I fully accept that. It's been going on for far too long and it's reaching a situation now where it's becoming critical.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: The Welsh Conservatives spokesperson, Paul Davies.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Paul Davies.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. Counsel General, I want to return to the issue raised by the Member for Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd and ask some further questions around what the Welsh Government can do to intervene and stop service reconfiguration decisions taken by local health boards. I listened very carefully to your earlier answers. Now, I'm sure you'll agree that health board service reconfiguration is a contentious issue in most parts of Wales, including, of course, in west Wales, which has a long history of service reductions, relocations and reconfigurations that have led many residents to feel that healthcare provision is increasingly being moved further away from their communities. In my view, when there is such strong public opposition to the health board's decisions, the Welsh Government has a moral responsibility to get involved and put a hold on controversial plans that do not carry the will of the people. So, Counsel General, you've confirmed here today that Ministers can intervene under the National Health Service (Wales) Act 2006, but can you tell us what role you have as the Welsh Government's legal adviser in any process that would involve intervention? And can you confirm that a Government can legally intervene on any health board decision under this Act?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, the first thing to say—. The Member referred to a moral case. I'm not an arbiter of morality. My job is law—simply law—and the legislation is quite clear. I know that it will disappoint the Member. I fully appreciate that this is a very emotional subject. I fully appreciate that; I don't live in a bubble—I understand. Nevertheless, the law is clear and it relates to failure of governance, failure of performance and the exercise of functions by local health boards. If one or other of those are engaged, then there would be a case for intervention by Welsh Ministers. Currently, I do not see it. It has not been reported that there is any problem in any of those three cases. But I would suggest to him, as well, that he should allow the consultation to take its course, and then a step back can be taken to consider what kind of consultation it was, what the conclusions are, and whether the conclusions deliver a service fit for his constituents. That's the acid test. And then, if there's a problem with that, clearly something could be done. But up until at that point, there is nothing that Welsh Ministers can do under any legislation that I have seen, and I say that with respect, not to be pejorative.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: You see, many people across Wales will find it difficult to understand why Ministers appear powerless to act when there is overwhelming public concern about major service changes that could significantly affect access to healthcare. Therefore, Counsel General, can you outline the legal thresholds, then, you believe must be met before the Welsh Government will intervene in a service reconfiguration decision taken by a health board? Furthermore, do you believe the current legal set-up provides the Welsh Government with sufficient powers to protect communities from reconfiguration decisions that lack public confidence?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Again, I'm not trying to be unhelpful, but I'm not going to speculate about thresholds, and I cannot, because I do not have the information in front of me. And I'm not going to speculate about the law, either. But what I will say to the gentleman is this: if he feels the law needs amending, strengthening or whatever, why doesn't he prepare a Bill and then present it to the Senedd and see how far it goes?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I'm asking your opinion.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, I cannot give you my opinion on anything other than the law. The law is plain, and I told you and I've explained where Ministers would be engaged, and currently they're not. But it is a prerequisite for that consultation to take its course, in my view, and then people may look again objectively at what the findings are.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 3. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Government regarding maintaining the Senedd’s legislative competence where the Welsh Government and UK Government's views differ? OQ64507
documents.text_cy: 3. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae’r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi’i roi i’r Llywodraeth ar amddiffyn cymhwysedd deddfwriaethol y Senedd lle mae safbwyntiau Llywodraeth Cymru a Llywodraeth y DU yn wahanol? OQ64507

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Well, of course, the role of Welsh Government is to defend the devolution settlement, but also to ensure that things such as the Sewel convention are observed, and to defend and extend the relationship, one hopes. In July of this year, I published the Welsh Government's principles on UK legislation in devolved areas, and this includes a commitment that the UK legislation in devolved areas will only be used where the legislation protects or strengthens the devolution settlement and does not introduce new constraints on devolved competence. I am very clear, as is this Government, that we are focused on enhancing the devolution settlement and, with that, the Senedd’s legislative competence, rather than simply maintaining it. However, where there are attempts to limit or constrain the Senedd’s legislative competence, these will be firmly resisted, and this includes opposing the imposition of any further reservations or restrictions in the Government of Wales Act 2006, as well as securing relevant consents and carve-outs to ensure that devolved provisions conferred by UK parliamentary Acts can be removed by the Senedd at a later date. And I think key to all of this is the principle of legislative consent as set out clearly in the Sewel convention. This is essential to our devolution settlement and safeguards the Senedd’s role as the Welsh national legislature. As Counsel General, I am clear that the Sewel convention must be respected, particularly where there are any attempts to reduce or restrict the Senedd’s legislative competence via UK legislation.

Now, the Government's view is we would like it to have statutory underpinning. That is not forthcoming at the moment. There are discussions going on. Meantime, what is currently happening is there's a detailed discussion about a firm, proper solid memorandum of understanding on Sewel. It's probably second-best to having it on a statutory footing, but it is being undertaken and discussed as we speak now. So, something is happening. I fully appreciate the force of the question. It is vital that we ensure that Sewel is respected, as it has been disrespected so often of late.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I'm sure that, as a former Member of Parliament, the Counsel General is well acquainted with the concept of parliamentary sovereignty. Will the Counsel General acknowledge that the Senedd's legislative competence is defined by the Parliament of the United Kingdom and that the Senedd lacks the legal capacity to legislate on matters explicitly reserved to Westminster? Schedule 7A reserves the union. Does the Welsh Government accept that a Senedd Bill for independence or for an independence referendum would be outside the competency of the Senedd?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I've already said that I'm not a political animal, quite different from some of my colleagues. It's not a question I can answer, with respect.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 4. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding the adequacy of Welsh electoral law in respect of artificially generated content in devolved elections? OQ64487
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ynglŷn â digonolrwydd cyfraith etholiadol Cymru mewn perthynas â chynnwys a gynhyrchir yn artiffisial mewn etholiadau datganoledig? OQ64487

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I thank the Member for this question, which is a current hot potato, if I could describe it that way. Ofcom regulates certain online services under the UK Government’s Online Safety Act 2023, including standards to minimise disinformation. The Welsh Government will continue to work closely with partners to protect the integrity of devolved elections and the safety of candidates, and support access to reliable information, through vote.wales. We are very much alert to the threats to democracy from online disinformation and malinformation.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Seven years ago, the BBC's The Capture imagined footage of a public figure fabricated convincingly enough to destroy them. It was dystopian and it was fiction then, but today all it takes is a free app and 90 seconds. A councillor in Kent told LBC this week she is thinking of quitting politics altogether due to sexualised images of her being flyposted all around lamp posts around her home and the council building she works in. It makes her feel watched, she said, and unsafe in the town she represents. Other women have said they are now considering whether they should stand at all. This is a real cost, not for one councillor, but for every single woman who decides the abuse is not worth it. Wales goes to the polls in May 2027, and I know the Government really does take this seriously. So, does the Counsel General consider that the existing Welsh electoral law reaches artificially generated material of this kind, and what steps is the Government considering before those elections?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Well, again, I thank the Member for this important question. I do know, actually, that women and people from ethnic minority backgrounds are unfortunately particularly targeted by harassment and abuse. This misogyny is appalling and should be condemned by all decent campaigners. I know that the police welcome reports of any potentially unlawful material or behaviour in political campaigns. Whilst this does not take away the very real problem of abuse, anyone considering standing for election should know there is support out there. Now, that's the crucial point, I think. Ahead of next year's local elections, we are funding Elect Her to support female candidates in Wales. The programme includes a digital self-defence and self-care toolkit, including resources to support candidates to create their own digital self-care plan and strategies for dealing with online abuse. The Deputy First Minister is considering how the Welsh Government's diversity and inclusion guidance for political parties can be strengthened. So, it is an issue very much on the table at the moment. I would say that politicians and candidates should always report any harmful online material to Ofcom and also the police as appropriate. All digital campaign material must clearly show who it is being promoted by. These digital imprints ensure that there is accountability for all official campaign material. Thank you.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Counsel General, under Wales's electoral law voting system, voters get one vote for a political party and its list of candidates, so there's a very clear statement of accountability. What happens when a candidate asks voters to back one party, gets elected on that party's manifesto and then walks away from those commitments? The voter doesn't have to change their vote—[Interruption.]

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: We're trying to listen—

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: They can't choose another candidate—[Interruption.]

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Colleagues, we're trying to listen to the question. I think the Counsel General is trying to listen.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. Yet, the Member keeps their seat, alongside their very generous salary. Now, some learned legal minds, such as yourself, could consider that to be fraud by misrepresentation. So, Counsel General, does Welsh electoral law provide any legal protection for voters where a candidate's conduct after election departs from the political representation they were elected under? Does Plaid Cymru still consider that politicians who mislead constituents should be criminalised? And have you considered that, in order to protect Welsh democracy, the Member should do the right thing and resign? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I regret, Llywydd, that I haven't got my wellingtons with me. [Laughter.] I've never heard such a load of muck in a long time. And I'm not getting involved in the politics of it, but is the Member seriously saying that nobody within Reform has ever switched sides during the currency of an election?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: We've all been elected.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: No, I'm not—. I'm the legal officer. I thank him for that question, but it's not for me. Thank you very much.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Right. Now, we're going to try and move ahead and get some more questions in further down the list, if we can, with everybody's help.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Therefore, question 5, Mair Rowlands.
documents.text_cy: Felly, cwestiwn 5, Mair Rowlands.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 5. What assessment has the Counsel General made of people's ability to access legal services and justice through the medium of Welsh? OQ64495
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa asesiad mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi ei wneud o allu pobl i gael mynediad at wasanaethau cyfreithiol a chyfiawnder drwy gyfrwng y Gymraeg? OQ64495

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Forgive me, Mair, I couldn't find you for just a moment there.

The ability to access legal services and justice through the medium of Welsh is an important part of access to justice in Wales. As I engage with the legal profession and also the wider justice sector, I will continue to explore how we can improve access to justice for communities across Wales, including Welsh speakers.
documents.text_cy:
Maddeuwch imi, Mair, doeddwn i methu eich ffeindio chi am funud bach.

Mae gallu cael mynediad at wasanaethau cyfreithiol a chyfiawnder yn y Gymraeg yn rhan bwysig o fynediad at gyfiawnder yng Nghymru. Wrth imi feithrin cysylltiadau efo'r proffesiwn cyfreithiol a hefyd y sector cyfiawnder ehangach, mi fyddaf i'n dal ati i edrych ar sut y gallwn ni sicrhau gwell mynediad at gyfiawnder i gymunedau ar draws Cymru, gan gynnwys siaradwyr Cymraeg.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you, Counsel General. In February, the Law Society reported on the legal deserts in Wales, outlining how access to legal services declines outside the M4 corridor. While Cardiff has 12.3 solicitors for every 1,000 residents, in north Wales, the figure is closer to 2.3 per 1,000. This geographical inequality has a fundamental impact on Welsh-speaking communities in Bangor Conwy Môn and across north Wales in terms of access to legal services and justice through the medium of Welsh. Will the Counsel General outline the Government's plans to address this inequality?
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Gwnsler. Ym mis Chwefror, fe adroddodd Cymdeithas y Cyfreithwyr ar yr anialwch cyfreithiol yng Nghymru, gan amlinellu sut mae mynediad pobl at wasanaethau cyfreithiol yn gostwng y tu allan i goridor yr M4. Tra bod gan Gaerdydd 12.3 cyfreithiwr i bob 1,000 o drigolion, yng ngogledd Cymru, mae'r ffigur yn agosach at 2.3 mewn bob 1,000. Mae'r anghydraddoldeb daearyddol yma'n cael effaith sylfaenol ar gymunedau Cymraeg ym Mangor Conwy Môn ac ar draws y gogledd i gael mynediad at wasanaethau cyfreithiol a chyfiawnder drwy gyfrwng y Gymraeg. A wnaiff y Cwnsler amlinellu beth yw cynlluniau'r Llywodraeth i fynd i'r afael â'r annhegwch hwn?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Of course, access to justice means more than just access to the courts. People must understand their rights, get reliable advice at the right time and participate effectively in legal processes that have an impact upon them. The ability to use the Welsh language in legal cases is an important principle within the justice system in Wales. Arrangements are in place to support Welsh-medium cases, including translation, interpretation and bilingual documentation as necessary.

Wales, of course, is a bilingual nation, but in asking what specifically can be done, this is now a very live issue. It is an issue that will be raised in various conferences over this winter. The deficiencies in the provision of providing advice through the medium of Welsh has been too apparent to all, but also, by the way, through the medium of English in many areas too. But it is particularly bad in the case of the Welsh language, because, more often than not, we are talking about rural areas, and rural areas have been described as 'legal deserts'.

So, there is a great job of work to be done, and it is part of my job description to ensure that access to the law is possible through the medium of both languages. It's something that's at the forefront of my mind, and something that I will be working on in the coming months.
documents.text_cy:
Wrth gwrs, mae mynediad at gyfiawnder yn fwy o lawer na mynediad at y llysoedd yn unig. Mae'n rhaid i bobl allu deall eu hawliau, cael cyngor dibynadwy ar yr adeg iawn a chymryd rhan yn effeithiol mewn prosesau cyfreithiol sy'n effeithio arnyn nhw. Mae gallu i ddefnyddio'r Gymraeg mewn achosion cyfreithiol yn egwyddor bwysig o fewn y system gyfiawnder yng Nghymru. Mae trefniadau yn bodoli i gefnogi achosion drwy gyfrwng y Gymraeg, gan gynnwys cyfieithu, cyfieithu ar y pryd a dogfennaeth ddwyieithog pan fo angen.

Mae Cymru, wrth gwrs, yn wlad ddwyieithog, ond o ofyn beth, yn benodol, y gellid ei wneud, mae hon, rŵan, yn ddadl fyw. Mae hi'n ddadl sy'n mynd i godi mewn gwahanol gynadleddau dros y gaeaf yma. Mae diffygion darparu cyngor yn y Gymraeg wedi bod yn rhy amlwg i bawb, ond hefyd, gyda llaw, mewn sawl man drwy'r Saesneg hefyd. Ond mae'n dwysáu yn achos y Gymraeg, oherwydd, yn amlach na pheidio, dŷn ni'n sôn am gefn gwlad, ac mae cefn gwlad, ar hyn o bryd, wedi cael ei ddisgrifio fel 'anialwch cyfreithiol'.

Felly, mae yna job o waith mawr o'n blaenau ni, ac mae o'n rhan o'm swydd ddisgrifiad i i sicrhau bod mynediad at y gyfraith yn bosibl drwy'r ddwy iaith. Mae'n rhywbeth sydd yn fy meddwl i, ac mae'n rhywbeth y byddaf i'n gweithio arno fo yn y misoedd i ddod.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: My question has some crossover with the question that Mike Hedges asked earlier.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 6. What assessment has the Counsel General made of the impact of pressures on legal aid provision on access to justice in Wales? OQ64498
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa asesiad y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi'i wneud o effaith pwysau ar ddarpariaeth cymorth cyfreithiol ar fynediad at gyfiawnder yng Nghymru? OQ64498

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Pressures on legal aid provision in Wales are a very serious concern. Reduced provision means many communities cannot access the legal help they need. Although legal aid is reserved to the UK Government, we will always look for opportunities to bring these problems to the attention of the Ministry of Justice.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr iawn. We know how vital legal aid is to helping those in need and ensuring that everybody has the right to adequate legal representation. A report by the House of Lords select committee last year concluded that there are people who are both unable to access legal aid and unable to afford to pay for legal services privately. As the Law Society have noted, proposals put forward by the UK Government have not addressed the distinct issues facing the legal sector in Wales and that the part or full devolution of justice, if implemented and funded appropriately, offers significant potential opportunities to the people of Wales. What advice has the Counsel General given the Welsh Government on the adequacy of legal aid in Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Well, it is a matter that the Welsh Government are acutely aware of, and it's partly because of the narrowing of the scope of legal aid alongside tighter eligibility criteria. That's had a very significant impact over many years on the justice system across England and Wales. I'm particularly concerned that people in many parts of Wales are unable to access local legal advice because legal aid fees are no longer sufficient to support sustainable provision. In Wales, reduced provision has contributed to legal advice deserts, leaving some communities without local access to specialist legal help. For example, the Law Society's heat maps show that 82 per cent of the people of Wales have no access to a legal aid-funded local welfare provider, and no less than 88 per cent have no education law provider.

These pressures are acute everywhere, but particularly so in rural, post-industrial and lower income communities, similar to the area that the Member represents. Where alternative sources of advice may be very limited, and without early legal advice, problems can escalate, increasing pressures on devolved services including health, housing and social care. Through the regional advice networks, we are supporting closer collaboration between private law firms and not-for-profit advice providers so that people across Wales can access the advice they need. Although, as I've said before, legal aid is reserved, we will work closely with the Ministry of Justice, the UK Government and legal professions in Wales to ensure Wales's needs are clearly understood and are reflected in the response to these pressures.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: This feel slightly strange, asking a question to the person next to me. [Laughter.]
documents.text_cy: Mae hwn yn teimlo ychydig bach yn od, gofyn cwestiwn i'r dyn drws nesaf. [Chwerthin.]

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 7. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the devolution of justice? OQ64506
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gyngor cyfreithiol y mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol wedi ei roi i Lywodraeth Cymru ar ddatganoli cyfiawnder? OQ64506

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I'm pleased you're not fighting with the man next to you. [Laughter.] The devolution of powers over policing and justice has been recommended in a series of independent commissions, dating back to the Silk commission in 2014. Those commissions, all three of them, considered the legal implications, among others, in arriving at their clear conclusions. I will be working closely with colleagues as we continue to work towards this objective.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n falch nad ydych chi'n cwffio efo'r dyn drws nesaf. [Chwerthin.] Mae datganoli pwerau dros blismona a chyfiawnder wedi bod yn argymhelliad mewn cyfres o gomisiynau annibynnol, sy'n dyddio'n ôl i gomisiwn Silk yn 2014. Mi wnaeth y comisiynau hynny, y tri ohonyn nhw, ystyried y goblygiadau cyfreithiol, ymhlith eraill, wrth ddod i'w casgliadau clir. Mi fyddaf i'n gweithio'n agos efo cydweithwyr wrth inni barhau i weithio tuag at hyn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you, Counsel General. The need to devolve justice has been outlined several times in this Chamber by the Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales and by the Law Society. We know that the current system deteriorates outcomes for people in Wales. And I've been frightened, truth be told, that 40 per cent of the funding comes from the Welsh Government, although justice has not been devolved. That isn't sustainable. So, does the Counsel General agree that devolution of justice is vital to improve outcomes for those who go through the system?
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Gwnsler. Mae'r angen i ddatganoli cyfiawnder wedi ei ddangos droeon yn y Siambr yma gan y Comisiwn Annibynnol dros Ddyfodol Cyfansoddiadol Cymru a chan Gymdeithas y Cyfreithwyr. Dŷn ni'n gwybod bod y system bresennol yn gwaethygu canlyniadau i bobl Cymru. A dwi wedi cael braw, a bod yn onest, fod 40 y cant o'r cyllid yn dod wrth Lywodraeth Cymru, er nad ydy cyfiawnder wedi'i ddatganoli. Dydy hynny ddim yn gynaliadwy. Felly, ydy'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol yn cytuno efo fi fod datganoli cyfiawnder yn angenrheidiol i wella'r canlyniadau i'r rheini sy'n mynd drwy'r system?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: I have no doubt when I agree with the Member on that point, and the devolution of powers over policing and justice is a priority of this Government. The case for the devolution of justice and policing to Wales, as is the case in Scotland and the north of Ireland, is clear. That's a clear conclusion, as the Member said, of the Silk commission, the Thomas commission, and, more recently, the Independent Commission on the Constitutional Future of Wales. Those commissions did find that the devolution of justice would allow for more accountable, co-ordinated and effective services that align better with the needs of the people and communities of Wales and that are integrated more closely with devolved responsibilities, such as health, social care, education and housing. The First Minister has informed the UK Prime Minister that this is a main priority of the Welsh Government, and Ministers will try and secure progress on this, including through the police reform Bill, which is in the pipeline. I would have thought that that is an excellent opportunity to start the process of the devolution of policing, and it is an opportunity that we as a Government will grasp with both hands. Diolch.
documents.text_cy: Does gen i ddim amheuaeth pan wyf yn cytuno efo'r Aelod ar y pwynt yna, ac mae datganoli pwerau dros gyfiawnder a phlismona yn flaenoriaeth i'r Llywodraeth hon. Mae'r achos dros ddatganoli cyfiawnder a phlismona i Gymru, fel yn yr Alban a gogledd yr Iwerddon, yn glir. Dyna gasgliad clir, fel y dywedodd yr Aelod, comisiwn Silk, comisiwn Thomas, ac, yn fwy diweddar, y Comisiwn Annibynnol ar Ddyfodol Cyfansoddiadol Cymru. Mi wnaeth y comisiynau hynny ganfod y byddai datganoli cyfiawnder yn galluogi gwasanaethau mwy atebol, cydgysylltiedig ac effeithiol sy'n cyd-fynd yn well ag anghenion pobl a chymunedau Cymru ac wedi'u hintegreiddio'n agos â chyfrifoldebau datganoledig, fel iechyd, gofal cymdeithasol, addysg a thai. Mae'r Prif Weinidog wedi rhoi gwybod i Brif Weinidog y Deyrnas Unedig fod hyn yn brif flaenoriaeth i Lywodraeth Cymru, a bydd Gweinidogion yn ceisio sicrhau cynnydd, gan gynnwys drwy'r Bil diwygio'r heddlu sydd ar ddod. Mae hwnnw, feddyliwn i, yn gyfrwng ardderchog i gychwyn ar y broses efo datganoli'r heddlu, ac mae o'n gyfle rydym ni fel Llywodraeth yn mynd i afael ynddo fo efo'r ddwy law. Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Finally, question 8—Kiera Marshall.
documents.text_cy: Yn olaf, cwestiwn 8—Kiera Marshall.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: 8. How is the Counsel General promoting access to justice for rape survivors? OQ64490
documents.text_cy: 8. Sut mae'r Cwnsler Cyffredinol yn hyrwyddo mynediad at gyfiawnder i oroeswyr treisio? OQ64490

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
While criminal justice, as the Member knows, is largely reserved, the Welsh Government works with policing, the Crown Prosecution Service, courts and specialist services to improve access to justice for rape survivors. Through the violence against women, domestic abuse and sexual violence agenda, we fund advocacy, counselling and support services, including independent sexual violence advisers, helping survivors access information, support and justice.

I would further say that the Government has invested in specialist support services throughout the piece. More needs to be done, I hasten to add, and we recognise that access to justice is about more than court outcomes. Survivors must be able to access timely support, information and advocacy so they can make informed decisions and recover from the impact of abuse.

And with regard to the university sector, all learners, including university students, should be able to study in safe environments free from violence, abuse, harassment and intimidation. Whilst universities in Wales are autonomous, we expect them to take robust action to ensure safe and supportive teaching environments. Medr's new staff and learner welfare condition has introduced clearer expectations on well-being, safety and protection from harassment and misconduct, including sexual violence. Officials are working closely with Medr and universities and sector partners to strengthen prevention, reporting and support, improve consistency and transparency and support providers to create safe cultures where concerns are taken seriously. I would suggest to the Member that she writes to my colleague the Deputy First Minister on this matter, and I am sure that she will get a full and substantive response on the current steps being taken.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Thank you for that. I was pleased to see the UK Government announcement that specialist courts to deal with rape and sexual offences are to be introduced across England and Wales, and, hopefully, this begins to tackle the shamefully low prosecution rates of rape in the UK, which has, effectively, been decriminalised.

However, we also must look at prevention, not just justice. I met with a group of young women at Cardiff University, so I was glad to hear you talk about the university sector. They're called Time to Act, and they've been campaigning to eliminate sexual assault and sexual harassment from campuses, alongside supporting survivors. In England, as you'll know, there are currently regulatory consequences for institutions that fail to prevent and to tackle harassment and sexual misconduct. Students in Wales don't have this equivalent protection, so I was wondering if you would, potentially, look at what avenues are available for the Welsh Government to legislate and prevent sexual harassment and violence on university campus.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text:
Well, I hear what the Member says, and I appreciate the work that she's doing in the area. It's certainly very important, and I can speak from my own personal knowledge of work I do at the university in Aberystwyth. It's high on the agenda at that university and, I have no doubt, in every university in Wales, and so it should be. So, things are moving, albeit slower than all of us would want, but they are moving in the right direction. And our job, it seems to me, is to pressurise and ensure that the continued improvement in this area is to be seen by all.

If I add one final thing, on the issue of rape generally—horrific as it is—there has been an announcement that there will be, from 1 October, designated courts dealing with rape. That will lessen the backlog, and that will include specialists available to help and back up individuals but also things like separate entrances and waiting rooms, basic protections of that kind. This is something, I believe, to be welcomed. I would also say, on a more positive note, that the backlogs in Wales are considerably better than they are elsewhere in the UK, and we need to maintain that, but this, again, will assist, I believe.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Counsel General
documents.text: Thank you very much, Counsel General.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi, Gwnsler Cyffredinol.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: We'll move now to item 3, the business statement and announcement. I call on the Trefnydd, Heledd Fychan.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 3, datganiad a chyhoeddiad busnes. Galwaf ar y Trefnydd, Heledd Fychan.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. Two oral statements have been added to today's agenda, namely 'New Ambition for Wales', the programme for government, and also the Welsh defence ethical framework. Draft Plenary business for the next three weeks is shown on the business statement, which is available to all Members electronically.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Mae dau ddatganiad llafar wedi eu hychwanegu at yr agenda heddiw, sef 'Uchelgais Newydd i Gymru', y rhaglen lywodraethu, a hefyd fframwaith moesegol amddiffyn Cymru. Mae busnes drafft y tair wythnos nesaf wedi'i nodi yn y datganiad busnes sydd ar gael i'r holl Aelodau'n electronig.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Trefnydd, I'd be grateful if I could have a statement on local train overcrowding. Transport for Wales's service for Bridgend to Rhymney is currently the third most overcrowded service between peak hours in the UK. That service now is affecting commuters, affecting their transport into work. It's not very easy for elderly people to get a seat, and it's something that my constituents are raising with me quite often. So, I'd be grateful, Trefnydd, if the Minister sitting here could come forward with something so that we can address the overcrowding on Welsh trains. Diolch.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising that matter. Fortunately, the Deputy Minister for Transport is here, and he'll be writing to you. I would encourage you also to share any information that you have, and encourage any Member here to always share information where services need further attention from us as a Government.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r mater yna. Yn lwcus iawn, mae'r Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth yma, ac mi fydd o'n ysgrifennu atoch chi. Byddwn i'n eich annog chi hefyd i rannu unrhyw wybodaeth—annog unrhyw Aelod yma i wastad rhannu gwybodaeth lle mae gwasanaeth angen sylw pellach gennym ni fel Llywodraeth.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Last week, I was glad to be joined by my Welsh Labour colleague Ken Skates at Llanwern steelworks in my constituency. Llanwern is strategically important to Wales and the whole of the UK, and it must not be lost in the wider debate on the steel industry. Steel making is in Newport's DNA, and it should have a proud future, but the workers that I spoke to last week were concerned about that future and that it's under threat from cheap galvanised steel imports. The Welsh Government must work with the UK Government to protect steel jobs in Wales and engage with the unions to support the workforce. So, Trefnydd, can we have a statement from the Welsh Government confirming that you will do everything in your power to ensure a sustainable future for the steel industry in Wales?

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Well, I thank the Member for raising an issue that is, of course, hugely important. You will be highly aware, I'm sure, that the Deputy First Minister, when she met with the new UK Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, over the summer, expressed this new Government's concerns about the lack of action taken by the Labour Government in not securing a future for steel in Wales and ignoring the steel industry here. Certainly, the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy is in the Chamber and has heard what you had to say, and, as always, we are more than willing to have discussions with local Members where necessary. But, unambiguously, I can say that we do see a future for the steel industry, and we do want to work with those who are concerned about this issue, and, of course, are constantly making the case at a UK level for the UK Government to give sufficient attention to the steel industry here in Wales.
documents.text_cy: Wel, diolch i'r Aelod am godi mater sydd, wrth gwrs, o bwys. Mi fyddwch chi'n ymwybodol iawn, dwi'n siŵr, fod y Dirprwy Brif Weinidog, pan wnaeth hi gyfarfod gyda Phrif Weinidog newydd y Deyrnas Unedig, Andy Burnham, dros yr haf, wedi mynegi pryderon y Llywodraeth newydd hon ynglŷn â'r diffyg a wnaed gan y Llywodraeth Lafur o ran peidio â sicrhau dyfodol iawn i ddur yng Nghymru, a diystyru hefyd y diwydiant dur yma. Yn sicr, mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni yma yn y Siambr ac wedi clywed yr hyn rydych chi'n dweud, ac, fel bob amser, rydyn ni'n barod iawn i drafod gydag Aelodau lleol lle mae angen hynny. Ond, yn ddiamwys, mi fedraf i ddweud ein bod ni'n gweld dyfodol i'r diwydiant dur, eisiau gweithio gyda'r rheini sy'n pryderu am hyn, ac, wrth gwrs, yn gwneud yr achos drwy'r adeg i Lywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig roi sylw digonol i'r diwydiant dur yma yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Trefnydd, continuing on the theme of trains, I'd like to request a statement from the Deputy Minister for Transport on the delivery of rail services in west Wales. I'm regularly contacted by constituents from across Ceredigion Penfro who express concerns about the frequency, reliability and overall availability of rail services in the region. They want to see more regular and dependable train services operating across all rail lines in west Wales throughout the week, because for too long west Wales has not received the level of attention it deserves when it comes to rail connectivity and service delivery, and I believe there should be a review of rail provision in the region to assess whether current services are meeting the needs of local communities, and indeed to identify where improvements are required. Therefore, I'd be grateful if the Welsh Government could provide a statement outlining what steps it intends to take to improve the delivery, frequency and reliability of rail services in west Wales so that we can understand how it plans to address the long-standing concerns of passengers in Ceredigion Penfro.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising those issues. Dirprwy Lywydd, of course, every Member will have heard previous statements, including statements on priorities, including those from the Deputy Minister for Transport. We too share that vision in terms of ensuring that public transport is available in every part of Wales, and that vision includes the work in train to look at that provision. As that work continues, the Deputy Minister will be providing updates to the Senedd and will, of course, be very willing to engage with Members, who will want to make the case for their constituencies.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r materion hyn. Ddirprwy Lywydd, wrth gwrs, mi fydd pob Aelod wedi clywed datganiadau blaenorol, gan gynnwys datganiadau blaenoriaeth, gan gynnwys gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth. Mi ydym ni hefyd yn rhannu'r weledigaeth honno o ran sicrhau bod trafnidiaeth gyhoeddus ar gael ym mhob rhan o Gymru, ac mae'r weledigaeth honno yn cynnwys y gwaith sy'n mynd rhagddo er mwyn edrych ar y ddarpariaeth honno. Wrth i'r gwaith hwnnw barhau, mi fydd y Dirprwy Weinidog yn rhoi diweddariadau i'r Senedd hon, ac, wrth gwrs, yn barod iawn i ymgysylltu efo Aelodau, fydd eisiau gwneud yr achos dros eu hetholaethau nhw.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Trefnydd, we just heard questions to the Counsel General about the legal position surrounding health service reconfiguration. Last week, Powys Teaching Health Board decided to press ahead with consultation on proposals that could remove in-patient beds from a number of our community hospitals. There is considerable concern across Powys and many of us are far from convinced that the voices of local people or their elected representatives are being heard. Will you therefore arrange for an urgent statement from the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care setting out the Government's position, what discussions he has had with the health board, and, crucially, whether he is prepared to intervene?

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising this issue. Clearly, it's an issue that was raised last week as well, and, as I outlined at that time, dealing with that initial engagement, that's what the health board is doing. No decisions have been made. And what I would ask every Member who has constituents who have been affected by the possibilities raised in this consultation to do is to become involved in the consultation, and to encourage others to engage, and to be clear that the health board has yet to make any decision on its clinical services plan.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r mater hwn. Yn amlwg, mae hwn yn fater a godwyd wythnos diwethaf hefyd, ac, fel gwnes i amlinellu'r adeg honno, ymgymryd gyda'r ymgysylltiad cychwynnol y mae'r bwrdd iechyd. Does dim penderfyniadau wedi'u gwneud. A'r hyn byddwn i'n gofyn i bob Aelod sydd gydag etholwyr wedi'u heffeithio gan y posibiliadau yn yr ymgynghoriad hwn wneud yw ymwneud â'r ymgynghoriad, ac annog eraill, ac i fod yn glir nad yw'r bwrdd iechyd wedi gwneud unrhyw benderfyniad ar ei gynllun gwasanaethau clinigol.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Trefnydd, we know that many people were preparing for surgery when they heard, by word of mouth or by social media, that their surgeries under the Welsh Gender Service had been paused during the Senedd's summer recess. One of my constituents was actually in hospital for surgery when they were told that their operation was cancelled, with no further support provided since then. You'll know that I've written, with other Members, to the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee, who were responsible for this decision, asking about the evidence that informed this decision, the lack of communication with patients, and how patients' voices were not heard.

I know that this decision was made by a medical body, rather than a political one, but I'd like to request a statement outlining how the Government will ensure that this community will be listened to, how their concerns will be central to any further decisions made about trans healthcare, and how they will be supported. Diolch.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising such an important matter. I'm sure that many of us will have heard from friends, from constituents, who've been impacted, and have heard about the very powerful impact that this has had.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi mater eithriadol o bwysig. Dwi'n siŵr bod nifer ohonom ni wedi clywed gan ffrindiau, gan etholwyr, sydd wedi'u heffeithio, a chlywed am yr effaith dirdynnol mae hyn wedi'i gael.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Please be assured that this Government stands with the trans community and will continue to protect and promote trans rights in line with our commitment to a welcoming and inclusive Wales. Members will be aware that a debate is tabled tomorrow by Anthony Slaughter. There will be an opportunity then to ask questions of the Cabinet Minister for health, and he will also be responding in full then.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
To be fair, you, like me, Trefnydd, have been an advocate for ensuring children and young people get to school safely and happy, and I'm sure that you'll agree with me that the first priority of governments at every level should be to protect children's and young people's well-being and not leave them anxious and worried. This policy of getting as many pupils as possible onto public buses rather than school buses is majorly flawed. It may work in urban areas, but it certainly doesn't work in rural areas, where routes like the Usk to Monmouth are long and winding, with national speed limit roads. Children packed in like sardines, standing for 40 minutes, is just not acceptable, and I'm sure you'll agree with that. But, sadly, this was the case in Monmouthshire on the first day of term, with multiple parents and pupils contacting me, with issues—similar issues, actually—flagged all over Monmouthshire and Torfaen. How can we possibly be in a situation where children have to have their own seat and even wear a seat belt for school trips, but this is acceptable?

Cost-cutting exercises by councils—and we all know they're strapped for cash—should never come at the expense of children's safety and well-being. Trefnydd, on that note, I would like to request an urgent statement from the Cabinet Minister responsible as to when this policy will be reviewed to ensure all children and young people get to school safely, on time and ready to learn. Diolch.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising this issue. It is a very live issue as part of our discussions as a Government. It's a cross-portfolio issue. I'm pleased that the Deputy Minister for Transport is here. We have had discussions even this week, as Ministers, looking at the impacts in terms of barriers to people's access to education, and that does affect how much money families have too. This is a very live issue. The work is ongoing. As there are updates, the Deputy Minister will, of course, engage with Members of the Senedd who are concerned about this issue.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am godi'r mater hwn. Mae o'n fater sydd yn fyw iawn yn ein trafodaethau ni fel Llywodraeth. Mae'n fater traws-bortffolio. Dwi'n falch bod y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Drafnidiaeth yma. Rydyn ni wedi cael trafodaethau hyd yn oed yr wythnos yma, fel Gweinidogion, yn edrych ar yr effaith o ran rhwystro pobl rhag cael mynediad at addysg, sydd yn effeithio ar faint o arian sydd gan deuluoedd, ac ati. Mae hwn yn fater byw. Mae'r gwaith yn mynd rhagddo. Wrth fod yna ddiweddariadau, mi fydd y Dirprwy Weinidog, wrth gwrs, yn ymgysylltu efo Aelodau o'r Senedd sydd yn poeni am y mater hwn.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
Trefnydd, can I call for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy on access to banking services in Wales? I appreciate that banking is not a devolved matter, but banking services really do matter to people across the country, particularly in communities that don't have access to a bank. I've been blessed in my own constituency to have two banking hubs, which are serving the communities of Abergele and Prestatyn, but there are other communities, places like Llangollen that lost its last bank a couple of years ago, that don't have a bank present. At the moment, the FCA, the Financial Conduct Authority, simply do assessments of access to cash, rather than access to banking services.

Shortly after the election, the UK Government did announce a review of access to banking services. That consultation finished over the summer. I wonder whether the Welsh Government has made a submission to that about the particular circumstances in Wales, particularly given our rurality, to make sure that people have access to these vital services. If it hasn't, is there any way we can work together to make sure that we make a call and a demand for legislation in this area, to ensure that banking services are available?

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Thank you. I'm sure that you're not the only one and I know that we've been part of campaigns in the past when banks have been at risk, and have seen the impact when they have gone from those places, and what impact that has then had on some of the most vulnerable residents or the oldest people in that society. This is also an issue that the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality has been raising, because this is a social justice issue: ensuring those services. I am very pleased that the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy heard what you said just then. We will consider that, and I'm sure that the Minister will engage with you.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Dwi'n siŵr nad chi yw'r unig un a dwi'n gwybod ein bod ni wedi bod yn rhan o ymgyrchoedd pan oedd banciau mewn perygl, ac wedi gweld yr effaith pan maen nhw wedi diflannu, a beth oedd effaith hynny wedyn ar rai o'r trigolion mwyaf bregus neu'r rhai hynaf yn y gymdeithas. Mae hwn hefyd yn fater y mae'r Dirprwy Brif Weinidog a Gweinidog Cabinet dros Gyfiawnder Cymdeithasol a Chydraddoldeb wedi bod yn ei godi, oherwydd mae hwn yn fater o gyfiawnder cymdeithasol: sicrhau'r gwasanaethau hynny. Dwi'n falch iawn bod y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Fenter, Cysylltedd ac Ynni wedi clywed yr hyn rydych chi wedi ei ddweud rŵan. Fe wnawn ni ystyried hynny, a dwi'n siŵr y bydd y Gweinidog yn ymgysylltu â chi.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: Given the significant impact of storm Bert in November 2024, when the community centre in Aberfan and the leisure centre in Merthyr Tydfil opened their doors to support residents who had had to evacuate because of the destructive floods, many constituents across Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr are very concerned about the increasing risk of flooding over the coming winter. The Taff and Cynon rivers pose a serious threat to homes, businesses and community infrastructure. Given these concerns, I would like to ask for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability outlining how the Welsh Government is strengthening Wales's preparedness for floods over the winter months. This should include details about current resilience planning, support at a community level, the readiness of infrastructure, and any additional measures being taken in order to safeguard areas that are at risk in our region. Given the scale of recent events, clarity and assurance for residents is crucial.
documents.text_cy: Yn sgil effeithiau difrifol storm Bert ym mis Tachwedd 2024, pan agorodd canolfan gymunedol Aberfan a chanolfan hamdden Merthyr Tudful eu drysau i gefnogi trigolion a oedd wedi gorfod gwacáu yn ystod y llifogydd dinistriol, mae llawer o etholwyr ar draws Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr yn bryderus ynghylch risg gynyddol llifogydd dros y gaeaf sydd i ddod. Mae'r Afon Taf a'r Afon Cynon yn peri bygythiad sylweddol i gartrefi, busnesau ac isadeiledd cymunedol. O ystyried y pryderon hyn, hoffwn ofyn am ddatganiad gan y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Wydnwch Gwledig a Chynaliadwyedd yn amlinellu sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cryfhau parodrwydd Cymru ar gyfer llifogydd dros gyfnod y gaeaf. Dylai hyn gynnwys manylion am gynllunio gwydnwch presennol, cefnogaeth ar lefel gymunedol, parodrwydd seilwaith, ac unrhyw fesurau ychwanegol sy'n cael eu cymryd i ddiogelu ardaloedd sydd mewn perygl yn ein rhanbarth. Gan ystyried maint y digwyddiadau diweddar, mae eglurder a sicrwydd i drigolion yn hanfodol.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
I thank the Member for raising that issue, and it was spoken about earlier today in First Minister's questions. I should declare that I share a constituency with you and I have been a strong advocate of taking action in terms of supporting communities who face this continuing risk. I've seen the impact that this has, not just when the floods happen, but any time it rains heavily, and that continuing fear that people have that they are going to suffer further flooding and the impact that that will have on their day-to-day lives.

The Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability will be making a statement in these next weeks about preparing for the winter. And certainly, what we have seen now, with this extreme weather, is that we have to do this work throughout the year, because one of the challenges that we have seen is that some of the storms happen earlier or later in the year, and that then that preparedness is needed. Certainly, that statement will be coming in the next few weeks. And I think, from what the First Minister said earlier today, that the work that we can do as each Member of the Senedd, in terms of supporting communities with that resilience and advocating for them, is incredibly important.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text:
I'm raising this as an MS for Carmarthenshire, but I need to declare that I am also the Chair of the Local Government, Housing and Planning Committee. Trefnydd, can I ask for a statement from the Welsh Government on nutrient neutrality and its impact on housing delivery in west Wales?

Following Natural Resources Wales's marine assessment and subsequent planning advice to councils last year, social and affordable housing schemes across Carmarthenshire and Pembrokeshire face significant delays. I have been contacted by one contractor who builds almost exclusively for affordable social housing, and he has an order book of £30 million-worth of secured work that has now stalled. Its turnover has halved, it supports approximately 80 staff and 320 subcontractors, from groundworkers and bricklayers through to merchants, plant hire firms and delivery drivers. Everyone accepts in this Chamber the need to protect our rivers and estuaries, but nutrient pollution comes from a wide range of sources across whole catchment areas. These delays are affecting both families waiting for homes and the firms ready to build them.

So, can we have a statement on what has replaced the marine nitrates development taskforce, what further mitigation measures are being considered, and when these housing schemes can realistically move forward? Thank you.

documents.item: 3. Business Statement and Announcement
documents.text: I thank the Member for raising that issue. The Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning will have heard your calls and the issues that you've raised. And I will discuss with her the most appropriate way of responding to those, be that a statement or by correspondence.
