documents.text: And the final question, Minister, is from Francesca O'Brien.
documents.text_cy: A'r cwestiwn olaf, Weinidog, Francesca O'Brien.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: 9. What assessment has the Welsh Government made of the effectiveness of its relationship with the Welsh Rugby Union? OQ64445
documents.text_cy: 9. Pa asesiad mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi'i wneud o effeithiolrwydd ei pherthynas ag Undeb Rygbi Cymru? OQ64445

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: As a new Minister, I have set about trying to build a constructive relationship with the Welsh Rugby Union, ready to challenge when that's needed, and ready to work with them, whilst also respecting their independence. We engage regularly on shared priorities and the development of the game, including participation, facilities, grass-roots development and major events.
documents.text_cy: Fel Gweinidog newydd, dwi wedi mynd ati i geisio perthynas adeiladol gydag Undeb Rygbi Cymru, yn barod i herio pan fo angen, yn barod i gydweithio hefyd, tra'n parchu ei annibyniaeth. Mi ydym ni'n ymgysylltu'n rheolaidd ynglŷn â blaenoriaethau a rennir a datblygu'r gêm, gan gynnwys cyfranogiad, cyfleusterau, datblygu ar lawr gwlad a digwyddiadau mawr.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text: Diolch, Drefnydd. This year, the Welsh Government supported the WRU with a grant of more than £400,000 from Sport Wales this year alone, an £18 million loan and historic funding of close to £5 million over the years. That is a significant amount of taxpayers' investment in Welsh rugby, which is fantastic. Given that scale of support, can the Trefnydd confirm whether any conditions have ever been attached to that funding to safeguard the future of the Ospreys specifically, and also the future of grass-roots clubs across Swansea and Gower, who depend on a strong regional side for player pathways, as we've discussed in previous questions, coaching and community sport? Has any taxpayer money gone to the WRU with no strings attached, leaving my constituents' rugby clubs with no protection if the Ospreys are the region to go? I say that as a family member who has lost players who played for the Ospreys and they've gone over the border, and we're losing that young generation. So, I think I echo everyone on behalf of Gŵyr Abertawe, but I want to know: are there any strings attached to those loans? Thank you.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
documents.text:
Well, as I have emphasised during the session, these are independent issues, and it's through Sport Wales that we fund any body. Certainly, if you do have concerns, I can ask Sport Wales to provide more information to you. I think what is very clear from today's session is that there are a number of questions from Members related to the WRU. I'm very eager to work together with Members in relation to any concerns that you have, and I'm very happy to raise these directly with the Welsh Rugby Union. When I was a sports spokesperson, I was quite prepared to ask questions and challenge as well, and, as a Minister, I'm still prepared to do that.

I'm very pleased that so many of you are worried about the future of the game in Wales with such passion, and, if we can all work together, then I think that this is a good place to start.
documents.text_cy:
Wel, fel dwi wedi pwysleisio yn ystod y sesiwn hwn, mae'r rhain yn faterion annibynnol, a drwy Chwaraeon Cymru rydyn ni'n ariannu unrhyw gorff. Yn sicr, os oes gennych chi bryderon, mi fedraf i ofyn i Chwaraeon Cymru fod yn darparu rhagor o wybodaeth i chi. Dwi'n meddwl yr hyn sydd yn glir iawn o sesiwn heddiw ydy bod yna nifer o gwestiynau gan Aelodau ynglŷn ag Undeb Rygbi Cymru. Dwi'n awyddus iawn i gydweithio efo Aelodau ynglŷn ag unrhyw bryderon sydd gennych chi, a dwi'n hapus iawn i fod yn codi'r rhain yn uniongyrchol efo Undeb Rygbi Cymru. Pan oeddwn i'n llefarydd ar ran chwaraeon, mi oeddwn i'n ddigon parod i ofyn cwestiynau a herio hefyd, ac, fel Gweinidog, dwi'n barod iawn i wneud hynny.

Dwi'n falch iawn bod cymaint ohonoch chi yn pryderu am ddyfodol y gêm yng Nghymru gydag angerdd, ac, os cawn ni weithio gyda'n gilydd, yna dwi'n meddwl bod hwnna'n le da i ddechrau.

documents.text: Thank you very much, Minister.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: 1. What lessons has the Cabinet Minister learnt since failing to pass the first supplementary budget for 2026-27, and how will this inform the Welsh Government's approach to future budgets? OQ64442
documents.text_cy: 1. Pa wersi y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'u dysgu ers methu â phasio'r gyllideb atodol gyntaf ar gyfer 2026-27, a sut y bydd hyn yn llywio dull gweithredu Llywodraeth Cymru o ran cyllidebau yn y dyfodol? OQ64442

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
There are lessons for Government and political parties from the supplementary budget vote. In a Senedd with no overall majority, co-operation and responsible decision making are essential as we look forward to future budgets. The Government wants to engage constructively across the Senedd to ensure that budgets are a blend, as I see it, of three component parts: funding for the delivery of effective public services, funding for priorities brought into Government by Plaid Cymru, and funding for other priorities from other political parties.

In order to produce a blended budget that can command a Senedd majority, my only plea across the Chamber is that we have a common understanding also of the financial envelope available to us. We are facing the most challenging budget settlement of this decade in 2027-28, with a real-terms reduction of around 0.7 per cent in resource funding, and even greater reductions in capital budgets. The financial envelope for next year's budget is especially tight, and will require a particular discipline for this Government and for all of us who want to play a constructive part in passing Wales's annual budget.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Fair play, that's a fair answer, finance Minister, and thank you for giving so much information. One thing is critical: what was shown in the draft budget was that there was little dialogue of meaningful consequence with the other political parties, and hence the budget never passed. Can you confirm today whether you've begun those discussions with the political parties, or are you just in exclusive talks with a particular group in this Senedd? I appreciate the discussions are confidential, but I think it's a matter of public interest to understand exactly which parties the Government will work with and those parties you won't.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
I'm not sure whether I will always welcome a question from Andrew R.T. Davies as Cabinet Minister for Finance, but today in particular, it was particularly useful for me to see that your question, constructed in this manner, allowed me to outline some of my thoughts on how I see the future of budget discussions. And, yes, we are keen, as the First Minister has said, to have discussions with all political parties. We are very conscious of the fact that we are a minority Government. If that supplementary budget vote was useful in anything, it was useful in reminding us, as a Government, that we need to command a majority to pass any budget in this place.

So, I look to all Members here to consider our roles in a different way perhaps to how we have considered our roles and participation in budgets of the past. In fact, the Welsh Conservatives have an advantage over all other political parties here. You're almost the continuity party in this Senedd, because you are an opposition party and you've played—[Interruption.] You're consistently an opposition party; I do not prejudge the future. But Reform is a new party in this Senedd, Labour is a party in opposition for the first time and Plaid Cymru is a party in Government, and there are new roles for all of us to play in that. But I hope that as we continue discussions over the next few weeks and months—. And those discussions are happening, and I want now to use pace and to think about how we can have those discussions across political parties and individuals in this Chamber to bring ideas into this big melting pot that is the annual budget. So, I hope that we can do that in a more meaningful way than we have done coming out of the election before the summer. And I think that's a challenge that all of us have to rise to, and me, in particular, as the finance Minister.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: During the supplementary budget process, we, at Reform, were clear that one of our key red lines was the removal of Wales's international spending commitments. Now, the finance Minister today has spoken about the challenges that lie ahead with the budget, and, over the weekend, she said that there may well be some cuts in some areas of budget, when speaking to the media. Given that cuts are clearly on the table, will the finance Minister commit today to cutting Government spending in foreign countries before she considers cutting spending in Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I take no red lines into this budgetary process, genuinely, in terms of the work that I'm doing within Government and the need, as I outlined in my initial statement, for this Government to be disciplined in how our Ministers are looking at their portfolios. A 0.7 per cent real-terms decrease in the budget is a real challenge for the Ministers in the exercise of their portfolios. So, I take no red lines into my discussions across all budget areas. But, obviously, there are manifesto commitments and ideas that this party, Plaid Cymru, brings into Government, and I am sure, as we discuss with Members and parties across the Chamber, that we can have a frank discussion about what is possible and where our common priorities lie. So, no red lines, but an open door for discussions.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: One of the most common things I've heard since being elected is the difficulties the public sector and third sector are facing with short-term and single-year funding. It's clear that throwing money at an issue isn't going to solve the root cause of it, and, for a long time, it felt like that was the case. After 26 years of the previous Labour administration, as we know, one in three children are still living in poverty, our waiting lists are at their highest and there's been little behavioural change in walking and cycling rates, despite the promotion of active travel—all issues that we've inherited from Labour. So, does the Cabinet Minister agree that genuine, lasting change is more likely to be delivered through long-term, sustainable funding, with clear accountability for results?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Yes, I certainly agree that, in looking at budgets, we need not just to look at those spending lines as they are drafted on a spreadsheet, but we need to look properly at where our outcomes can be improved, and you've listed some of the areas where we need, as Wales, to be doing better, and, certainly, as a Government, we're committed to doing so. So, looking at outcomes, effectiveness and value for money all go hand in hand as we seek, as a new Government in place, in advance of making our own budget and putting it together, as we are looking at efficiencies within Government and outcomes of where we want to prioritise our funding. That piece of work is being undertaken as a budgetary process, but especially in light of our appointment of a Minister with exact responsibility for effectiveness and outcomes of Government action. And that lasting change, of course, that you spoke of, does require something that is more agile and meaningful than annual budgets—so, a commitment to looking to a multi-year budget, but, of course, within the spending review of the allocations to us as a Government. Looking to a multi-year budget is something that I'm looking to propose as part of our budget processes here.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Mike Hedges.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you very much for calling me. I didn't know I was down for this, but—[Laughter.]—that will not stop me making some comments. I think that when we look at budgets and we look at where we are, then it's all about priorities, isn't it? You and I have different priorities. My priority is additional learning needs for children. Yours is to have a Welsh broadcasting authority. You've every right to have those different priorities, but do you understand why we have a different one?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I don't think we have different priorities, Mike; I think we share that priority of needing to spend more on additional learning needs. We were prepared and we voted for that in the supplementary budget. I don't think these are competing positions. We need to strike that note and work on the balances of where we can land this together. So, let's not polarise this in question No. 1 to me at the start of a budget process. Let's see if we can work together on this.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: 2. How is the Welsh Government using its financial levers to support the tourism industry in Ceredigion Penfro? OQ64430
documents.text_cy: 2. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn defnyddio ei galluoedd ariannol i gefnogi'r diwydiant twristiaeth yng Ngheredigion Penfro? OQ64430

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: The Wales tourism investment fund, and other initiatives, invest almost £60 million directly in Wales. Many businesses receive non-domestic rates relief or they will benefit from the expanded lower multiplier from 2027 onwards, as I announced yesterday. We are also consulting on potential changes to the 182-day threshold for self-catering properties.
documents.text_cy: Mae cronfa buddsoddi twristiaeth Cymru, a mentrau eraill, yn buddsoddi bron i £60 miliwn yn uniongyrchol yng Nghymru. Mae llawer o fusnesau'n derbyn rhyddhad ardrethi annomestig neu byddant yn elwa o'r lluosydd is estynedig o 2027 ymlaen, fel y cyhoeddais i ddoe. Rŷn ni hefyd yn ymgynghori ar newidiadau posib i'r trothwy 182 diwrnod ar gyfer eiddo hunanarlwyo.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Cabinet Minister, yesterday's announcement of a 30 per cent cut in business rates for some of the smallest hospitality accommodation and leisure venues is certainly a welcome step forward. However, there is plenty more that the Welsh Government can do to support the tourism industry in Ceredigion Penfro, including reducing the devastating 182-day occupancy threshold for self-catering businesses. Now, I appreciate that the Welsh Government's consulting on this, but the consultation states that there will be a limit to the extent of any reduction in the threshold, arguing that a substantial decrease in the threshold could incentivise an oversupply of self-catering properties. In light of this, can you clarify what the Welsh Government considers to be the minimum viable occupancy threshold? And in the interests of transparency, will you commit to publishing the evidence underpinning that position, so that business owners can understand the parameters that the Welsh Government is considering in this important consultation?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
Well, it's always been something that's been a topic of debate in this Senedd, and within Plaid Cymru too, in terms of what is that point where you're striking the balance in the housing market between the housing stock available for people to live in and also the housing stock available for the tourism and self-catering sector, and striking that balance, so that one doesn't have a negative impact on the other, getting that balance right, is important. And that is what we hope to deliver through consulting on this.

I've already had discussions with representatives of the self-catering sector, who, clearly, do believe that the balance is at a lower point than the 152 days in the consultation, and you perhaps feel the same. Now, I am open to having that discussion. I sense that the response to the consultation will demonstrate that the sector itself, and those within the sector, do believe that we need to go deeper than what's contained within the consultation, but the Government does want to strike the right balance. We don't want to create further problems for ourselves by setting this threshold too low. But I am eager that we reach a position where this system that impacts our housing sector, but also our self-catering and tourism sectors, reaches a point where it can be a permanent solution in this area. So, I'm open to discuss this with you too in terms of how we get the outcome to this consultation to reach a point that has majority support in this place.
documents.text_cy:
Wel, mae e wastad wedi bod yn rhywbeth sydd wedi bod yn bwnc trafod yn y Senedd yma, a chyda Plaid Cymru hefyd, lle mae'r pwynt yna lle mae'r cydbwysedd yn y farchnad dai yn gorwedd rhwng y stoc dai sydd ar gael i ni ar gyfer pobl i fyw ynddyn nhw, a hefyd y stoc dai sydd yna ar gyfer y sector twristiaeth a hunanarlwyo, ac mae cael y balans yna, fel nad yw un yn effeithio'n negyddol ar y llall, cael y balans yna yn gywir, yn bwysig. A dyna beth ŷn ni yn gobeithio ei gyflawni drwy ymgynghori ar hyn.

Dwi eisoes wedi trafod gyda rhai sy'n cynrychioli'r sector hunanarlwyo, sydd, yn amlwg iawn, yn credu bod y balans yn gorwedd yn is na'r 152 o ddiwrnodau yna sydd yn yr ymgynghoriad, ac rŷch chi hefyd, mae'n bosib, yn teimlo yr un fath. Dwi'n agored i gael y drafodaeth yna. Dwi'n synhwyro y bydd yr ymateb i'r ymgynghoriad yn dangos bod y sector ei hun, a'r bobl sydd yn y sector, yn meddwl bod eisiau mynd yn ddyfnach na'r hyn sydd yn yr ymgynghoriad, ond fe fydd y Llywodraeth eisiau taro'r balans cywir. Dydyn ni ddim eisiau creu bwgan arall i ni ein hunain drwy osod y trothwy yma'n rhy isel. Ond rwyf i'n awyddus ein bod ni'n cyrraedd sefyllfa lle mae'r gyfundrefn yma sydd yn effeithio ar ein sector tai ni, ond hefyd ar ein sector hunanarlwyo, ein sector twristiaeth ni, yn cyrraedd pwynt lle mae'n gallu bod yn ganlyniad parhaol wedyn i'r pwnc yma. Felly, dwi'n agored iawn i drafod gyda chi hefyd ynglŷn â sut y mae cael y canlyniad i'r ymgynghoriad yma i gyrraedd rhywle sydd yn rhywbeth sydd yn cynnal mwyafrif y gefnogaeth yn y lle yma.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Minister, what financial support will you prioritise to attract visitors to Ceredigion and Pembrokeshire outside of the summer months, so that tourism can sustain year-round jobs and give young people greater opportunities to work locally?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: A year-round tourism economy is something that I definitely want to see, both for the constituency that we both represent, but also for Wales generally. I think we've seen significant progress on that over the last few years, but there is more to do still on that. We have our investment priorities, and looking at how we can attract tourists for an extended period of the year is part of the criteria in how we invest in that. Also, we need to make sure that the business rates system that we have, and other taxation aspects, are also ensuring that those businesses that support the hospitality sector are able to be all year round. There's no point having businesses that are only open for a particular part of the year. We need businesses that are open all year long, so that they can provide the opportunity for tourists to benefit, but also, what benefits tourists also benefits the communities they serve. So, I'm particularly hopeful that the positive sign that the Government was able to give yesterday for such a wide array of businesses that do support the tourism sector, of a 30 per cent reduction in business rates from next April, is a positive sign for the tourism sector generally that this Government backs it.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. Reform UK spokesperson, Cai Parry-Jones.
documents.text_cy: Galwaf yn awr ar lefarwyr y pleidiau i holi'r Gweinidog Cabinet. Llefarydd Reform UK, Cai Parry-Jones.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Last weekend, on BBC Politics Wales, you said you were, quote, 'quite shocked' by the financial pressures facing the Welsh Government and the reality of the Welsh budget when you came into the role of finance Minister. So, Minister, what specifically about the state of the Welsh finances came as a surprise to you after taking office?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: There are two aspects to this; I've spoken, actually, twice on the politics show on both of them. One was the in-year challenges that the Welsh Government inherited as a result of the budget that was laid last year and passed last year. The pressures in particular from within the NHS are considerable, and they were considerably more than I expected them to be. They are a challenge within the financial year that I'm trying to manage as we speak. But also, in a world where—and we've heard it again today—the inflationary pressures in our wider society and economy mean that the budget next year, at the moment, is 0.7 per cent less in real terms, that is very challenging in the context of the wage inflation that is within our public services as well. So, those were two aspects that were particularly challenging for public services in Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
I don't understand how that was a shock when you became finance Minister, because it was already known that there would be a reduction, unless you just didn't do your research before becoming finance Minister.

Anyway, Plaid Cymru went into the Senedd election saying that their manifesto was fully costed. Given these shocks you now have, can you confirm to us that your manifesto would not be labelled 'fully costed' if you had the information you have today?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
It was fully costed, but the job of work that we have to do as a Government, and I've alluded to it already, is the discipline now that Ministers have to face in allocating within their priorities how they marry the priorities that a governing party brings into Government with the day-to-day running of public services. 

I spoke of the three components of the budget as I see them: the effective running of public services in Wales and how we fund those in the budget settlement that we have as a Senedd and Government; and then the priorities that the Plaid Cymru Government, as voted for by the people of Wales, bring into that; as well as then, of course, the ability that other political parties will want to influence that budget as a third component part of it. So, putting all of that together in one blended melting pot is what we're doing as we speak. Doing that at a time of more financial flexibility would have made it an easier and more constructive piece of work to undertake. It is going to be a challenging piece of work. As I've hopefully set out today, I hope that we're all up for that challenge as a Senedd together.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you. You've spoken about cuts, but not taxes. However, actions speak louder than words. From April, the Welsh Government has introduced a higher business rates multiplier for larger premises. Is this the direction that you think this Government is going to go towards in dealing with the financial issues? Are you considering other tax rises, including income tax?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I accept that there is a higher ask of those businesses across the business rates portfolio that have the higher rateable values. The bit you didn't mention in your question was those up to 20,000 businesses that will benefit from lower taxes as a result of the announcement yesterday and the support for retail premises as well. I think the premise of your question is, though, that this is not just about how we allocate the public funding that's available to us, but how we also use our taxation system to ensure, yes, that we're using it to fund public services, because taxation is what enables public services to be run, but also how we get that balance right in terms of supporting our economy. All of those together, again, are part of the considerations when we need to think about where we strike this balance.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Welsh Labour spokesperson, Huw Thomas.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd Llafur Cymru, Huw Thomas.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. I'm afraid that Cai Parry-Jones has been copying my homework, because I too was going to ask about your comments on Politics Wales. It came as a surprise to me too to hear of your shock in looking at the pressures facing the Welsh Government.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Mae arnaf i ofn fod Cai Parry-Jones wedi bod yn copïo fy ngwaith cartref i, achos roeddwn i hefyd yn mynd i'ch holi chi am eich sylwadau chi ar Politics Wales. Roedd hi'n syndod i fi hefyd glywed am y sioc roeddech chi'n ei theimlo o ran y pwysau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei wynebu.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Cai has made reference to some of the commentary around the pressures facing Welsh Government in its next budget. The IFS, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned in the election campaign about the extremely challenging fiscal outlook facing the next Government, and yet your own party leader assured voters that Plaid Cymru had a fully costed programme for government. It does start to feel now like these were simply making promises without preparing for the consequences. I don't want to repeat Cai's question, so let me ask, therefore: if the Government faces a choice between funding its manifesto promises or making cuts to core public services and projects, how will it decide?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I think that that question is a truly interesting one, and is truly a question that faces us as a Government, who are in Government for the first time. We've inherited budgets that have been planned by other parties and previous Governments, although we as a party did support aspects of those budgets. It is true to say that we as a Government and Ministers within that Government are looking across all the Government budgets at present to see what's working effectively, what needs to change, and where there are cuts. By the way, you'll get to know this, I'm not a Minister for finance who is afraid to use the word 'cuts'. In some places, cuts are a good thing. In other places, they're not. But I'm not going to avoid using that term.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n meddwl bod y cwestiwn yna yn un gwirioneddol ddiddorol, ac yn wirioneddol yn gwestiwn sydd yn ein hwynebu ni fel Llywodraeth, sy'n Llywodraeth am y tro cyntaf. Rydym ni wedi etifeddu cyllidebau sydd wedi cael eu cynllunio gan bleidiau eraill a Llywodraethau o'n blaenau ni, er ein bod ni fel plaid hefyd wedi cefnogi agweddau o'r cyllidebau hynny. Mae'n wir i ddweud ein bod ni fel Llywodraeth a Gweinidogion y Llywodraeth yma yn edrych ar draws holl gyllidebau'r Llywodraeth ar hyn o bryd i weld beth sydd yn gweithio'n effeithiol, beth sydd angen ei newid, a lle mae toriadau. Gyda llaw, byddwch chi'n dod i wybod hyn, dwi ddim yn Weinidog cyllid sy'n ofni defnyddio'r gair 'toriadau'. Mewn rhai llefydd, mae toriadau yn beth da. Mewn llefydd eraill, dydyn nhw ddim. Ond dwi ddim yn mynd i osgoi defnyddio'r term.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
I'm not going to be one of those Ministers who avoids the term 'cuts' at all times and tries to say 'efficiencies' or other ways of describing it.

So, all of these factors are in the melting pot, as I see it, at this time. That overview of the whole budget of Government is currently a disciplined process that the Ministers are looking at, so that we reprioritise spend in terms of some of the priorities that Plaid Cymru has brought in to Government, but also that we look to see which budget areas are properly delivering the outcomes that another Member spoke of earlier. Because we really have to look at where the outcomes are best achieved, rather than just looking at headings on budget lines at all times.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Diolch, Weinidog. I'm sure you would concede that difficult budget decisions and cuts are rarely felt equally. Women, disabled people, minority ethnic communities, children and those already experiencing poverty are often placed most at risk when public spending is constrained. Under the previous Welsh Labour Government, there was the budget improvement and impact advisory group, bringing organisations representing those communities directly into the budget-setting process. We've now been told by equality stakeholders that the group has not met under this Plaid Cymru Welsh Government and they've had no assurance about its future.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Will you commit, Minister, to re-establish this group and also commit to meaningful engagement with equalities organisations when planning your budget, and not to simply consult once the major decisions have been made?
documents.text_cy: A wnewch chi ymrwymo, Weinidog, i ailsefydlu'r grŵp yma a chomitio i ymgysylltu ystyrlon â mudiadau cydraddoldeb wrth gynllunio'r gyllideb, ac nid i simply ymgynghori ar ôl i'r penderfyniadau mawr gael eu gwneud?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I am willing to commit to look at this issue. It's not an issue that I'm completely familiar with. I do see the value in it and I am aware that my fellow Ministers are very aware that the impact of any budgetary changes need to be assessed and need to be viewed through that lens you're talking about. We don't want to see the most disadvantaged or needy people suffering as a result of any budgetary changes. So, that's something we want to regard as a key factor in terms of how we undertake these budgetary assessments. So, I'll look specifically at the group that you just mentioned to see how we can progress that discussion with those experts.
documents.text_cy: Dwi yn fodlon ymrwymo i edrych ar y mater yma. Dyw e ddim yn fater dwi'n hollol gyfarwydd ag e. Dwi yn gweld y gwerth sydd yna a dwi'n ymwybodol iawn bod fy nghyd-Weinidogion yn ymwybodol iawn bod impact unrhyw newidiadau cyllid angen cael eu hasesu ac angen mynd drwy'r lens yna rŷch chi'n sôn amdano. Dŷn ni ddim eisiau gweld taw'r bobl fwyaf difreintiedig neu anghenus fydd yn dioddef o unrhyw newidiadau i'r gyllideb. Felly, mae hwnna'n rhywbeth rŷn ni'n mynd i eisiau iddo fod yn ffactor allweddol yn sut rŷn ni'n gwneud yr asesiadau cyllidol yma. Ac felly, mi wnaf i edrych yn benodol ar y grŵp rŷch chi newydd sôn amdano i weld sut gallwn ni fod yn dwyn y drafodaeth yn ei blaen gyda'r arbenigwyr yna.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Welsh Conservatives spokesperson, Sam Rowlands.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Sam Rowlands.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, how do you ensure that taxpayers' money is not wasted?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Well, I think, by doing the job of work that I outlined just earlier. We're a new Government, we have a new lens and, hopefully, a new energy into wanting to make the best use of the Welsh pound and to make sure that we are outcomes led in how we take our financial decisions. I recognise that we have a particular opportunity to do that in our first annual budget, and therefore there is considerable impetus from me, and from my Cabinet colleague on effectiveness of Government delivery, to be looking at how we ensure that the budgets that we will put to this Senedd are as outcomes focused as they can be and, as I've spoken of already, that they're not just lines on a spreadsheet, but they're actually meaningful in terms of what they will be delivering.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
Well, thank you for your response, Cabinet Minister. Last week, the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy released a written statement informing Members that the Welsh Government is going to write off £684,000 in unpaid rent owed by P.V. France Limited, a significant amount of taxpayers' money. There may be some specific reasons why that business went into difficulty, but what concerns me is how that debt of nearly £700,000 was allowed to reach such an extraordinary level in the first place. The Welsh Government, we understand, agreed to multiple payment plans, yet the arrears continued to build time after time. The company eventually entered administration, was dissolved, and now that money, nearly £700,000, seemingly cannot be recovered. 

At a time when we're being told that the public finances are incredibly tight, as I'm sure they are, how can the Government justify allowing almost £700,000 of taxpayers' money to be lost in this way? And as the Minister responsible for holding those purse strings, how will you prevent this from happening again in the future?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Well, it concerns me too that that level of debt was allowed to accrue without the Government being able to monitor it in an effective way, and I'm aware from cases in the past, not particularly this one, that this can happen. Government is always about investing properly in economic development and in running public services. Sometimes, that investment needs to happen in a context where there is risk, and Ministers need to balance that risk. But making sure that we have the right financial controls in place in a risky situation or not—. We need to make sure that those financial control measures are in place, because £700,000 is, as you could describe, or I could describe, money that would have been better spent elsewhere.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: 3. Will the Cabinet Minister set out the Welsh Government’s priorities regarding local government finance policy during this Senedd? OQ64434
documents.text_cy: 3. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet nodi blaenoriaethau Llywodraeth Cymru o ran polisi cyllid llywodraeth leol yn ystod y Senedd hon? OQ64434

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you. Within the Welsh Government, responsibility for local government lies with my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning. Working with local government, we have delivered our 100-day commitment to commission a review of the local government funding formula.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. O fewn Llywodraeth Cymru, mae'r cyfrifoldeb am lywodraeth leol yn dod o dan fy nghydweithiwr, y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Lywodraeth Leol, Tai a Chynllunio. Gan weithio gyda llywodraeth leol, rŷn ni wedi cyflawni ein hymrwymiad 100-diwrnod i gomisiynu adolygiad o fformiwla gyllido llywodraeth leol.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you for that answer, Cabinet Minister. In the wake of the announcement that the Welsh Government was going to review the local government funding formula, I know that you and the local government Minister received a letter from the leader of Merthyr Tydfil County Borough Council, and this firmly made the case that any review should not have a detrimental impact upon that council or the residents and communities that it serves. So, Cabinet Minister, I'm seeking similar assurances today that any review won't negatively affect either Merthyr Tydfil council or Rhondda Cynon Taf County Borough Council in view of the demographic challenges specifically that they face, and also that all councils will be fully involved in the process as it develops.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Yes, I can certainly give you the complete confidence that local government is a key partner in the work that we're doing on this review through its existing mechanisms, so that we do look properly at all aspects of work that need to feature in a review of this nature. And that does reflect on, and needs to reflect on, the patterns of need that we have throughout our communities and also the costs of delivering services across communities as well. So, it is a joint piece of work. I see it as a joint piece of work with local government. We want to be, as you were previously, a Government in partnership—working in partnership with local government. They are key to the delivery of public services in Wales. They're not key to it, they do it—they do the delivery of public services in Wales, and we need to make sure that they are funded in a way that enables that work to happen as effectively as possible in every community in Wales.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Minister, Plaid's inability to pass the budget has left councils in limbo. Local authorities needs as much time as possible to budget for the upcoming financial year. Audit Wales said that the Welsh Government's handling of restricted grants makes it hard for councils to plan. Audit Wales also found that £1.5 billion was allocated to councils in March 2025—the final month of the 2024-25 financial year. That represents 20 per cent of the annual total of this funding grant. So, Minister, what is the Welsh Government doing to give councils more certainty when setting their budgets, instead of leaving it to the last minute?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I agree 100 per cent with the need for us to be able to present a budget and to pass a budget in this place in as early as possible a way in order to provide that security and that lead-in time for planning and effective delivery of services by local authorities. We have a UK Government budget that happens at the end of October, and we are hoping to be able to pass a Senedd budget in the early part of January or February next year. I'm not going to miss the opportunity to say that the best way of giving certainty to local authorities, NHS, public services, public bodies, businesses in Wales, is that we can find a way of ensuring that a budget in this place has a majority to enable it to pass. Anything that stifles that process over the next few weeks and months will ultimately end in local authorities in Wales not having the ability to pass their own budgets in time.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I thank the Member for asking the question. The numerous small grants that are allocated to local authorities from year to year create real challenges in terms of advanced planning. By reforming the revenue support grant to make it fairer and more transparent, we can ensure that more money reaches front-line services. Now, I'm sure the Minister doesn't want to make any assumptions about any review, but does the Minister believe that simplifying the way that local government is funded could improve the current situation?
documents.text_cy: Diolch i'r Aelod am ofyn y cwestiwn. Mae'r llu o grantiau bach sy'n cael eu dyrannu i awdurdodau lleol o flwyddyn i flwyddyn yn creu heriau gwirioneddol o ran cynllunio ymlaen llaw. Trwy ddiwygio'r grant cynnal refeniw i'w wneud yn decach ac yn fwy tryloyw, gellid sicrhau bod mwy o arian yn cyrraedd gwasanaethau rheng flaen. Nawr, dwi'n siŵr nad yw'r Gweinidog eisiau rhagdybio unrhyw adolygiad, ond ydy'r Gweinidog yn meddwl, drwy symleiddio'r ffordd y caiff llywodraeth leol ei hariannu, y gallai hynny wella'r sefyllfa bresennol?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
Well, yes, I think those points are valuable for local authorities as they think about funding those programmes and services that they deliver. And it's that lens that we want to apply as to how the local government settlement could work more effectively, but also how the funding model could work more comprehensively too.

Providing that freedom to local government to decide on their own priorities is part of devolution within Wales of course, and, therefore, if we can deliver what we want to achieve by empowering local government to lead on how to develop and deliver services in their own areas, then we as a Government would be very pleased to hear of any ideas coming from local government, and coming from this Senedd, of course, so that we can ensure that the most effective package of funding is provided to local government, because, as I've said already, they deliver services, and they need those tools and those powers to do that effectively.
documents.text_cy:
Ie, dwi'n meddwl bod y pwyntiau yna'n sicr o werth i awdurdodau lleol wrth iddyn nhw feddwl amboutu ariannu'r cynlluniau yna a'r gwasnaethau yna y maen nhw'n eu delifro. Ac felly, y lens yna rŷn ni'n moyn ei roi ar siẁd mae'r setliad ar gyfer llywodraeth leol yn gweithio'n fwy effeithiol, ond hefyd siẁd mae'r model o ariannu yn fwy cynhwysfawr yn gweithio hefyd. 

Mae rhoi'r rhyddid yna i lywodraeth leol i fedru penderfynu ar eu blaenoriaethau nhw eu hunain yn bart o ddatganoli o fewn Cymru, wrth gwrs, ac felly, os ydyn ni'n gallu cyflawni yr hyn rŷn ni eisiau trwy rymuso llywodraeth leol i fod yn arwain ar siẁd mae datblygu a chyflenwi gwasanaethau yn eu hardaloedd nhw, yna, fel Llywodraeth, byddwn ni'n falch iawn i glywed am syniadau sy'n dod wrth lywodraeth leol, ac yn dod o'r Senedd yma, fel y gallwn ni sicrhau bod y pecyn mwyaf effeithiol o ariannu yn cyrraedd llywodraeth leol, achos, fel dwi wedi dweud eisoes, nhw sy'n delifro gwasanaethau, ac maen nhw angen yr arfau hynny a'r pwerau hynny i fedru gwneud hynny'n effeithiol.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: 4. How is the Cabinet Minister working with Cabinet colleagues to provide financial support to commoners and other people affected by the recent wildfires? OQ64453
documents.text_cy: 4. Sut mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn gweithio gyda chydweithwyr y Cabinet i ddarparu cymorth ariannol i gominwyr a phobl eraill sydd wedi'u heffeithio gan y tanau gwyllt diweddar? OQ64453

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I'm aware of the extensive impacts of the wildfires on commoners and farmers. And if appropriate, we will allow exemptions to planning conditions in order to help farmers that have been affected. Further consideration is given to how to support the resilience of the sector given the extensive pressures of this summer.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n ymwybodol o effeithiau helaeth y tanau gwyllt ar ffermwyr a commoners hefyd. Os yn briodol, byddwn yn caniatáu eithriadau i ofynion cynllunio er mwyn helpu ffermwyr sydd wedi eu heffeithio. Mae ystyriaeth bellach yn cael ei roi hefyd i sut i gefnogi gwydnwch y sector yn wyneb pwysau sylweddol yr haf hwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you very much for that, Cabinet Minister. The affected commoners in my constituency have already incurred almost £50,000 in direct costs and loss of earnings, with a further £20,000 needed for replacement fodder, and estimates for restoration work reaching around £89,000. In total, costs now exceed well over £100,000, with some family farms questioning their long-term liability. I've already written to your colleague the Cabinet Minister for rural resilience, looking for more support. And he came back and said pretty well that there wouldn't be any additional money because it was implied that sheep could just simply graze somewhere else, which I don't think were his words, but somebody had written on his behalf. And I'm sure he will disagree with that. I took great concern at that, as did many of the farming unions. However, we need a longer term solution to these issues. And given the scale of these losses—and across Wales—and the reality that these extreme events are likely to happen more often in the future, are you, Cabinet Minister, having discussions with ministerial colleagues about establishing a dedicated emergency fund designed to support farming businesses with managing short-term crises and financial challenges—not just a one-off, but a long-term fund?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
Thank you for the supplementary question, and I'm sure it must have been a terrible summer for those farmers and commoners in your area and elsewhere in Wales where they faced these fires with very real consequences on how they did their farming and livestock farming. 

I have had discussions, and they continue, with the rural resilience Minister about the financial implications of both the direct fires and also such a difficult summer in terms of harvest and growing that the drought led to here in Wales. So, we'll continue those discussions. I'll discuss that particular letter with him as well.

But also, to the point you make about the longer term implications of what we face as a country, as a world, in terms of the different challenges that have really struck home this year, I think, in a way, that we've seen bits of it in the past, over the past few years where we've had some intense periods of heat and wildfire consequences, but we've never seen it in such a sustained way over such a long period of time. And so, this asks questions of our sustainable farming scheme. Of course, we've made the long-term financial commitment, multi-year, of £1 billion on that scheme, but we do need to look at the content of that scheme, going forward, in order to meet some of the challenges that were discussed yesterday, actually, in this Senedd over how we manage our uplands and mountain areas in particular.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Minister, a fortnight ago, I attended the defence security and resilience conference in Newport, something rather naively described by opponents as an arms fair. It wasn't an arms fair. Resilience was a really key part of it, and some of these discussions we've had featured there highly in terms of flooding and wildfires. The First Minister yesterday quite rightly referred to resilience several times in his statement regarding the wildfires, and, indeed, we have a Cabinet member that has that word in the description. So, my question is, really: looking as to when these events occur in the future, and we do need to build into our land management more resilience—things like firebreaks and ponds, and so on—is the Minister prepared to talk about the financial impacts of the sustainable farming scheme, in particular, in terms of working into that scheme how we can build more resilience into our system so that we can prevent the extent of these fires in future?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
Yes, I agree, and I'm sure this summer has brought it home to the Minister, just as much as it has to farmers, how we manage land. Farmers knew this already, by the way. They were telling Ministers, I think, over the years about how some of the changes in support schemes are having effects on our uplands. But this year has brought to the forefront how there is a very direct relationship with how we farm our uplands and what happens in those uplands, both in terms of wildlife and regeneration of wildlife, but also in how we manage the uplands both in order to prevent floods downstream and also to ensure that we have adequate measures for limiting wildfires in these excessive heat situations that we have.

We are facing and we are likely to have to plan for these events to become possibly even annual events. We know that our climate is changing, and we as a Government and as a Senedd need to own up to that fact and to take the measures that we need to in order to make Wales resilient in the nature of the climate change that we are seeing in our society.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Minister, as I mentioned to the First Minister yesterday, the devastating fire in Pantside clearly demonstrated how the risk of wildfires has changed. Homes there were destroyed and, frankly, we were very fortunate that no lives were lost. The firefighters that I've spoken to through the FBU are clear that these incidents are increasing in terms of scale, complexity and the resources required to respond to them. Therefore, alongside the support for commoners and farmers who have suffered losses, what assessment have you made of the wider financial implications of this summer's fires?
documents.text_cy: Weinidog, fel gwnes i sôn wrth y Prif Weinidog ddoe, fe wnaeth y tân dinistriol yn Pantside ddangos yn glir iawn sut mae'r perygl o danau wedi newid. Cafodd cartrefi yn fanno eu dinistrio ac, a dweud y gwir, roeddem ni'n lwcus iawn bod neb wedi colli eu bywydau. Mae'r diffoddwyr tân dwi wedi siarad efo nhw trwy'r Fire Brigades Union yn glir bod y digwyddiadau hyn yn cynyddu o ran maint, cymhlethdod a'r adnoddau sydd eu hangen i ymateb iddyn nhw. Felly, ochr yn ochr â chymorth i'r commoners ac i'r ffermwyr sydd wedi dioddef colledion, pa asesiad ydych chi wedi ei wneud o oblygiadau ariannol ehangach tanau yr haf yma?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you for that question and thank you for reminding us of those terrible scenes that we saw in Pantside in your own constituency, with the fires affecting that community showing that property and homes are also at risk in scenarios such as this. The Minister for local government has already agreed to open the emergency financial assistance scheme and, therefore, that is available for local authorities and fire authorities in order to assess the scale of additional expenditure that they faced during this summer, and how they can, if necessary, use that programme. We accept that the work that they did as firefighters and local authorities and local communities is extremely important for our communities, and we are grateful for that work done over the summer. Therefore, we are willing to look, along with the appropriate authorities, as to the funding of any moneys that they require. We will be working with them on that.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn a diolch am ein hatgoffa ni o'r golygfeydd ofnadwy yna welon ni yn Pantside yn eich ardal chi, gyda'r tanau yna yn y gymuned yna yn dangos bod eiddo a thai hefyd mewn peryg mewn sefyllfaoedd o’r math yma. Mae’r Gweinidog llywodraeth leol eisoes wedi cytuno i agor yr emergency financial assistance scheme. Felly, mae hwnna ar gael ar gyfer yr awdurdodau lleol a’r awdurdodau tân i asesu maint y gwariant ychwanegol yr oedden nhw wedi gorfod ei wynebu yn ystod yr haf yma, a sut y gallan nhw, os oes angen, ddefnyddio’r cynllun yna. Rŷn ni’n derbyn bod y gwaith maen nhw wedi'i wneud fel diffoddwyr tân, fel awdurdodau lleol, fel cymunedau lleol, yn arbennig o bwysig yn ein cymdeithas ni, ac rŷn ni'n ddiolchgar am y gwaith yna yn ystod yr haf. Felly, rŷn ni'n barod i edrych gyda'r awdurdodau perthnasol ar sut mae'n bosib ariannu unrhyw arian sydd ei angen arnyn nhw. Byddwn ni'n cydweithio gyda nhw ar hynny.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: I'm very aware of time, but I would like to get at least halfway down our list. So I won't be able to take any supplementaries. Question 5, Anna Nicholl.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n ymwybodol iawn o'r amser, a hoffwn i gyrraedd o leiaf hanner ffordd lawr y rhestr. Felly, byddaf i'n methu â chymryd cwestiynau atodol. Cwestiwn 5, Anna Nicholl.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: 5. What work is the Cabinet Minister undertaking to reform business rates for hospitality businesses? OQ64459
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa waith y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet yn ei wneud i ddiwygio ardrethi busnes ar gyfer busnesau lletygarwch? OQ64459

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Yesterday, I was pleased to announce new non-domestic rates support for hospitality and leisure businesses, which are central to our ambition to regenerate town centres. From 1 April 2027 onwards, eligible businesses will benefit from a permanent 30 per cent reduction in their rates bills.
documents.text_cy: Ddoe, roeddwn i'n falch iawn i gyhoeddi cymorth ardrethi annomestig newydd i fusnesau lletygarwch a hamdden, sydd wrth galon ein huchelgais i adfywio canol trefi. O 1 Ebrill 2027 ymlaen, bydd busnesau cymwys yn elwa ar ostyngiad parhaol o 30 y cant yn eu biliau ardrethi.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you. I welcome the Cabinet Minister's announcement of a 30 per cent cut to business rates for hospitality and leisure businesses. This will be a vital lifeline to small hospitality and leisure businesses and has already been welcomed by businesses in Ceredigion Penfro. These small businesses play essential roles in our rural and coastal communities, protecting local jobs, strengthening local economies and building lasting prosperity. I'm happy to see that this announcement extends beyond just pubs, clubs and live music venues, like in England, to support visitor accommodation and leisure businesses like hotels, cinemas, theatres, museums and gyms. With this in mind, can the Minister explain what she anticipates now will be the practical impact of these measures for towns and high streets across Wales, as well as in our constituency of Ceredigion Penfro?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you. I was nudged by the Deputy Presiding Officer to keep my answers shorter, so I'll make an effort to do that. I won't repeat what I said yesterday in the Senedd when we were discussing this rate reduction of 30 per cent. But I do hope that it achieves two things. I hope that it makes a real difference to these businesses that will benefit from this, and that they will feel that it will enable them to plan more effectively for the future because this is a permanent cut. But also I hope that it delivers a message of support from this Government, and this Senedd if everyone agrees to the regulations, that we are serious about seeing this sector being supported and benefiting and developing in those communities across Wales that will benefit—not just those in coastal areas in our constituency, but also those town centres and suburbia too in our cities, towns and post-industrial communities.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Ces i gic gan y Dirprwy Lywydd, dwi'n meddwl, i gadw fy atebion i'n fyrrach. Felly, fe wnaf i ymdrechu i wneud hynny. Ni wnaf i ddim ail-ddweud dim gwnes i ei ddweud ddoe yn Senedd, pan oeddem ni'n trafod y gostyngiad treth yma o 30 y cant. Dwi'n gobeithio ei fod e'n cyflawni dau beth. Dwi'n gobeithio ei fod e'n gwneud gwahaniaeth realistig i'r busnesau yma a fydd yn elwa o hyn, ac y byddan nhw yn teimlo ei fod e'n eu galluogi nhw i gynllunio'n well ar gyfer y dyfodol oherwydd bod hyn yn barhaol. Ond hefyd gobeithio ei fod e'n cyflawni neges o gefnogaeth oddi wrth y Llywodraeth yma, a'r Senedd yma os bydd pawb yn cytuno i'r rheoliadau, ein bod ni o ddifri yn moyn gweld y sector yma yn cael ei chefnogi ac yn elwa ac yn datblygu yn y cymunedau yna ar draws Cymru sy'n mynd i elwa—nid dim ond y rhai arfordirol yn eich etholaeth chi a fi, ond hefyd y canol trefi yna, y swbwrbia yna hefyd, yn ein dinasoedd ni ac yn ein cymunedau ôl-lofaol ni.

documents.text: Question 6, Iain McIntosh.

documents.text: I appreciate this question may appear similar, on the face of it, to a similar question, but it is slightly different.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: 6. What assessment has the Cabinet Minister made of the financial sustainability of local government? OQ64463
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa asesiad mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'i wneud o gynaliadwyedd ariannol llywodraeth leol? OQ64463

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Within the Welsh Government, responsibility for local government lies with my colleague the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning, but we are aware across the Government that there is financial pressure on local authorities as they deliver important public services.
documents.text_cy: O fewn Llywodraeth Cymru, y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Lywodraeth Leol, Tai a Chynllunio sy'n uniongyrchol gyfrifol am lywodraeth leol, ond rŷn ni'n ymwybodol ar draws y Llywodraeth o'r pwysau ariannol ar gynghorau sir wrth iddynt ddelifro gwasanaethau cyhoeddus pwysig.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Diolch. Cabinet Minister, councils across Wales are at breaking point. Council tax rises this year have already added around £104 on average to band D bills across Powys, Neath Port Talbot and indeed Swansea, yet people are still paying more whilst roads crumble and front-line services disappear too. And now we are losing our primary schools. Cradoc primary school, for instance, in a nearby village to me, has already closed. When a primary school is closed, it's ripping out the heart of our communities. And clearly, under this Plaid Government, more school closures are coming too. My main question is this: as you have now commissioned a review of the funding formula, including rurality and sparsity, will you now admit that the current system is failing, and will you guarantee fairer funding, so taxpayers aren't continually asked to pay more for less, while our communities lose their services and more children lose their primary schools too? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
I represent a rural community, and have done over the years, so I'm very familiar with the fact that there are many factors that are at play in designing and deciding on the future of rural schools. It is not just the availability of public funding. Rural communities and aspects within those rural communities are a challenge, especially when we think about the depopulation, especially of our younger population, from many of our rural communities. How we look across Government as to how we can support that, not just in terms of money, but in how we are designing support, housing and economic opportunity for our rural areas, is important.

The important piece of work that this Government has started, though, is how we design a local government formula that meets the complexity of needs that our local authorities have. You rightly identified two of them in rurality and sparsity and the difficulty and expensive nature of delivering services across rural and sparse areas. We had reference made earlier to other priorities as well in terms of socioeconomic deprivation. Making sure that we strike a better balance in how we can deliver services effectively to all our communities in Wales is the journey that this Government has commenced in this piece of work, and hopefully all of us can involve ourselves in that.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: The final question to you, Minister, is question 7, Mike Hedges.
documents.text_cy: A'r cwestiwn olaf i chi, Weinidog, yw cwestiwn 7, Mike Hedges.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: 7. What assessment has the Cabinet Minister made of the adequacy of UK Government funding for the Welsh Government? OQ64438
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa asesiad y mae'r Gweinidog Cabinet wedi'i wneud o ddigonolrwydd cyllid Llywodraeth y DU ar gyfer Llywodraeth Cymru? OQ64438

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: The outlook for the Welsh budget remains extremely challenging. The expectation is that resource funding will fall 0.7 per cent in real terms in 2027-28 and that capital budgets will decline over the next three years, in contrast to the average real-terms growth of 3.5 per cent per year seen since the start of the decade.
documents.text_cy: Mae'r rhagolygon ar gyfer cyllideb Cymru yn dal i fod yn hynod heriol. Mae disgwyl i’r cyllid adnoddau ostwng 0.7 y cant mewn termau real yn 2027-28 a bydd cyllidebau cyfalaf yn gostwng dros y tair blynedd nesaf, o’i gyferbynnu â'r twf cyfartalog o 3.5 y cant y flwyddyn mewn termau real a welwyd ddechrau'r degawd.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: It's always interesting when you decide where you want to start something, because if you started in 2011, you'd have seen an entirely different figure. But let's not argue over that. Whilst every organisation believes it needs more money, fairness is important. What we know is that in devolved areas, Wales gets 20 per cent more than England for the same service. A commission led by Gerry Holtham calculated that Wales needs 15 per cent more than England for the same service. Wales has a Barnett floor set at that 15 per cent level. What evidence does the Minister have that the Holtham commission was wrong?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text:
I don't dispute the Holtham commission. I don't dispute the point you made at the start that wherever you start your analysis of any data, you can assess that. I'm trying to think of how we think about public service delivery now in the post-COVID period. That's why I was identifying this decade only. But you and I were in Senedds of the past where those austerity years of public finance in Wales, under a different political regime at a UK level, were particularly difficult at that time as well. So, I'm not pitching one difficult time against another. We have faced many of them in this place. I actually go back long enough to remember a time of plenty as well in this place, but that was another decade, almost in another century.

On the point you make, though, about needing to properly now assess where we are in terms of fiscal equality and meeting the economic and social needs of Wales through the Barnett formula as it is currently, our view as a Government is that the Barnett formula needs review. My immediate view on that—and it's something that I shared with the previous finance Minister—is that the Barnett formula especially needs its operational aspects to be strengthened. So, we need greater transparency on the Barnett formula as it exists, as well as independent oversight of the Barnett formula, so that we never ever again have to deal with the fiasco as it was of the decision on HS2 and how that has underfunded us as a country. And on that, if not on any other issue, I hope that we can all unite.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
documents.text: Thank you very much, Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi, Weinidog.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text: We'll move on now to the 90-second statements. Kiera Marshall.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen, felly, i'r datganiadau 90 eiliad. Kiera Marshall.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Diolch. I'd like to declare an interest, as I'm looking forward to becoming a trustee of the Living Room in the near future.

On 11 September this year, the Living Room in Cardiff celebrated 15 years of transforming people's lives. It was established by Wynford Ellis Owen with the support of the Welsh Council on Alcohol and Other Drugs, which itself is now marking 55 years of service. Since the beginning, the centre has offered hope to people living with addiction and harmful behaviours, as well as supporting their families and their local community.

Through counselling, therapeutic groups, peer support and education, thousands of people have had the opportunity to rebuild their lives. Stafell Fyw demonstrates that recovery is possible when people are treated with dignity, compassion and respect. It also highlights the value of investing in our community services, preventing problems from escalating and reducing pressure on our health, social care and criminal justice services.

As we mark this milestone, I'd like to thank the staff, volunteers, trustees and everyone who has contributed to the work of the Living Room over the last 15 years. Above all, I'd like to pay tribute to the individuals in recovery who remind us every day that change is possible and that hope is stronger than addiction.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
On Saturday, I was pleased to attend the official launch of the Football Museum of Wales and Wrexham Museum. As a member for Fflint Wrecsam, it was a real pleasure to be part of such an important occasion for the area and to join with colleagues in seeing the Cabinet Minister cut the ribbon on the museum.

The launch was a fantastic opportunity to celebrate the heritage of Wrexham and the history of Welsh football, and to see the new galleries and the stories they have to tell. I'm sure many of us agree that football is such an important part of communities across Wales. It brings people together, sometimes drives them apart, but creates shared opportunities and is a huge part of our national identity. The Football Museum of Wales provides a fantastic opportunity to preserve that history and share it with future generations.

The Wrexham Museum also plays an important role in celebrating the city, its people and its heritage. I was particularly pleased to meet those involved in making these museums a reality and to see the pride and enthusiasm surrounding the launch. These museums have huge potential to attract visitors, support the local economy and showcase Wrexham to people from across Wales and beyond. I hope the Welsh Government will recognise that potential and continue to work with and support both museums as they establish themselves and grow. They are important cultural assets for Wrexham and for Wales and deserve every opportunity to succeed.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
I would like to pay tribute to the work of the RSPCA during the summer hot weather and the work that they do to safeguard our pets and animals, especially dogs. Dogs can struggle badly in hot weather because they cool themselves mainly by panting, not sweating like humans. That means that even a warm day can become dangerous, especially for flat-faced breeds such as pugs and bulldogs, older dogs, overweight dogs and those with heart or breathing problems.

Owners should always make sure that dogs have constant access to fresh water, shade and a cool place to rest indoors or outside. Walks should be planned for the early morning or late evening when the ground and air are cooler. Hot pavements and asphalt can burn paws quickly, so it is wise to test the surface before going out. Dogs should never be left in a parked car, conservatory or other enclosed hot space, even for a few minutes, because temperatures can rise to fatal levels very fast. Grooming can also help in summer, but dogs should not usually be shaved without veterinary advice, as their coats can protect them from both sun and overheating.

It is also important to know the signs of heatstroke: heavy panting, drooling, weakness, vomiting, confusion and collapse, which are all warning signs that need urgent veterinary attention. If a dog seems overheated, move it to a cooler area, offer water and contact a vet immediately. The RSPCA in Wales deserves real praise for promoting practical, compassionate advice on dog welfare during hot weather. Its guidance is clear, accessible and focused on prevention, helping owners to understand simple but life-saving steps. By raising awareness about heatstroke, hot cars and safe summer care, the RSPCA continues to play an important role in protecting dogs across Wales.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Sir Billy Boston, who passed away last month at the age of 92, was one of rugby league's greatest ever players, an inspiration from Butetown in Cardiff, and I'm sure the whole Chamber will want to share our condolences with the Boston family.

Born on Angelina Street, just a stone's throw from this building, he first played rugby for Cardiff Internationals Athletic Club, and it's great to see the CIACs still going to this day. Billy dreamed of representing Cardiff and Wales through rugby union, yet despite his talent, he was overlooked by his hometown club and nation. As my predecessor Vaughan Gething said,

'It's hard to believe this was simply down to a scouting system failure and nothing to do with the colour of his skin.'

After being spotted during national service, he joined Wigan rugby league where he became a sporting legend. His remarkable achievements for Wigan, Great Britain and the game itself secured his place amongst rugby league's all-time greats. Last year, he became the first rugby league player to be knighted. Last week, Wigan renamed their central square in his honour.

I was immensely proud to work with members of the Butetown community, sports figures and local businesspeople to secure a lasting tribute to Billy and the other code breakers from Cardiff in the statue that was unveiled in Cardiff Bay. We were particularly delighted that we were able to achieve that during Billy's lifetime and have him there with us as we unveiled the statue to him, Clive Sullivan and Gus Risman, a fitting tribute to all the code breakers achieved and all they overcame. Rest in peace, Sir Billy Boston.
