Their experiences will be vital in learning lessons from these fires, but questions remain as to where their flocks will now graze and the support that they will receive for the recovery. So, my question is: how will the Government engage with these common land graziers to make sure that their experiences are given a fair hearing and their expertise considered in any decisions made in the wake of the summit? Diolch.

documents.item: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
documents.text:
Yes, I was very grateful to a number of the graziers on the land above Blaenavon for making time to speak with me. It was good that we were able to speak as Welsh Government, and with Senedd Members there too, about the stresses that had been placed on them. You could sense that there was a real tiredness after such a long period of the fire burning.

I am really keenly aware of the impact of the wildfires on Welsh farming and those grazing on common land. Welsh Government is exploring opportunities to bring together those relevant stakeholders in the coming months, as well as the summit itself, to consider how the resilience and recovery, of our commons specifically, to such events, can be strengthened. And as I signified, we're looking at all elements of the kinds of assistance that might be made possible through Government action.

documents.item: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
documents.text: Thank you, First Minister. Before we move on, I would like to remind the Chamber that Members have the right to speak in English or in Welsh at any time during our proceedings.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. Cyn symud ymlaen, hoffwn atgoffa'r Siambr fod gan Aelodau yr hawl i siarad yn Saesneg neu yn Gymraeg ar unrhyw adeg yn ystod ein trafodion.

documents.item: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
documents.text: Questions asked in English may be answered in Welsh, just as questions asked in Welsh may be answered in English.

documents.item: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
documents.text: Where there is a technical problem with interpretation equipment, we will of course always pause proceedings until the problems are resolved.
documents.text_cy: Os bydd problem dechnegol gyda'r offer cyfieithu, byddwn wrth gwrs yn oedi'r trafodion tan fod y broblem yn cael ei datrys.

documents.item: 3. Statement by the First Minister: Weather, wildfires, drought and resilience
documents.text: I hope that's a helpful clarification.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text: We will now move to item 4. Item 4, a statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: rebalancing the non-domestic rates system.
documents.text_cy: Rydym ni'n symud ymlaen at eitem 4. Eitem 4, datganiad gan y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Gyllid: ailgydbwyso'r system ardrethi annomestig.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
Thank you, Llywydd. Today, I'm pleased to announce changes the Welsh Government will make to reflect our manifesto commitments to rebalance the non-domestic rates system, and level the playing field for high-street businesses. We recognise the importance of vibrant retail, hospitality and leisure sectors, and these are central to our ambition to regenerate town centres and to breathe new life into our high streets.

Our work of rebalancing the rates system will be delivered through changes to the existing differential multipliers, improving support for selected hospitality and leisure businesses. An expanded scope for the lower multiplier will be funded by a marginal increase to the higher multiplier, applicable to the highest value properties in the tax base across all sectors.

From 2027-28, selected small to medium-sized hospitality and leisure properties will be subject to the lower multiplier currently applied to retail shops. This will bring eligible hospitality and leisure businesses in line with the permanent support introduced for retailers from this year. Eligible properties with rateable values below £51,000 will attract a 30 per cent reduction in their non-domestic rates bills.

This permanent support will replace and exceed the temporary discretionary relief of 15 per cent for food and drink hospitality properties that is currently being provided. It will mean that a wider range of hospitality and leisure businesses will get the long-term certainty that they need to invest and to grow.

The eligible food and drink hospitality properties are pubs, restaurants, cafes, bars, food courts, licensed clubs and live music venues. The eligible visitor accommodation properties are hotels, guest houses and hostels. And in the leisure sector, the eligible properties are cinemas, theatres, libraries, museums and gyms.

These businesses play important and complementary roles in vibrant high streets and town centres. Along with retailers, ratepayers for around 20,000 properties will therefore benefit from the expanded lower multiplier. Over 12,500 more properties of the relevant types already attract full relief, and that means that they therefore do not pay any non-domestic rates. Ratepayers for a majority of properties across Wales, particularly small businesses, will also continue to benefit from a range of permanent reliefs currently worth more than £200 million per year.

There is a balance to strike between the broader support that is provided through the lower multiplier and the resulting impact on the value of the higher multiplier. The higher multiplier will be set at just over 4 per cent above the standard multiplier from 2027-28 onwards. This is a small increase to the existing difference, and it's a fair way to redistribute liability so that we can better support the businesses that are at the heart of our high streets and town centres.

These changes to the differential multipliers are linked with the broader work of the town centres taskforce. This taskforce will take account of national policy frameworks, as well as considering the more tailored support that may be needed in individual town centres. Our approach recognises that needs will vary between places that may be facing different challenges that might go beyond the rate system.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch, Lywydd. Heddiw, rwy'n falch i gyhoeddi newidiadau y bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu gwneud i adlewyrchu'r ymrwymiadau yn ein maniffesto i ailgydbwyso’r system ardrethi annomestig, a sicrhau tegwch i fusnesau'r stryd fawr. Rŷm ni'n cydnabod pwysigrwydd sectorau manwerthu, lletygarwch a hamdden llewyrchus, ac mae'r rhain yn ganolog i’n huchelgais i adfywio canol trefi a rhoi bywyd newydd i'n stryd fawr.

Bydd ein gwaith o ailgydbwyso’r system ardrethi yn cael ei gyflawni drwy newidiadau i’r lluosyddion gwahaniaethol presennol, gan wella’r cymorth i fusnesau lletygarwch a hamdden penodol. Bydd cwmpas ehangach ar gyfer y lluosydd is yn cael ei ariannu gan gynnydd bach i’r lluosydd uwch sy’n gymwys i’r eiddo â'r gwerth uchaf yn y sylfaen drethu ar draws pob sector.

O 2027-28 ymlaen felly, bydd y lluosydd is sy'n cael ei ddefnyddio ar gyfer siopau manwerthu yn berthnasol hefyd i rai mathau o eiddo lletygarwch a hamdden bach a chanolig eu maint. Bydd hyn yn dod â busnesau lletygarwch a hamdden cymwys yn unol â'r cymorth parhaol a gyflwynwyd i fanwerthwyr eleni. Bydd eiddo cymwys sydd â gwerth ardrethol o dan £51,000 yn cael gostyngiad o 30 y cant yn eu biliau ardrethi annomestig.

Bydd y cymorth parhaol hwn yn disodli ac yn rhagori ar y rhyddhad dewisol dros dro o 15 y cant ar gyfer eiddo lletygarwch bwyd a diod sy’n cael ei ddarparu ar hyn o bryd. Bydd yn golygu bod ystod ehangach o fusnesau lletygarwch a hamdden yn cael y sicrwydd hirdymor sydd ei angen arnyn nhw i fuddsoddi a thyfu.

Y mannau lletygarwch bwyd a diod sy'n gymwys felly yw tafarndai, bwytai, caffis, bariau, cyrtiau bwyd, clybiau trwyddedig a lleoliadau cerddoriaeth fyw. Y mathau o lety ymwelwyr a fydd yn gymwys yw gwestai, tai llety a hosteli. Ac o ran hamdden, y mannau cymwys yw sinemâu, theatrau, llyfrgelloedd, amgueddfeydd a champfeydd.

Mae'r busnesau hyn yn cyflawni rolau pwysig sy'n ategu ei gilydd ar y stryd fawr a chanol trefi ffyniannus. Yn ogystal â manwerthwyr, bydd talwyr ardrethi ar gyfer tua 20,000 o safleoedd yn elwa ar y lluosydd is estynedig. Mae dros 12,500 yn fwy o'r mathau perthnasol o eiddo eisoes yn gymwys i gael rhyddhad llawn, sy'n golygu nad ydyn nhw'n talu unrhyw ardrethi annomestig. Bydd talwyr ardrethi ar gyfer y mwyafrif o eiddo ledled Cymru, yn arbennig busnesau bach, hefyd yn parhau i elwa ar sawl rhyddhad parhaol sy’n werth mwy na £200 miliwn y flwyddyn ar hyn o bryd.

Rhaid taro cydbwysedd rhwng y cymorth ehangach sy'n cael ei ddarparu drwy’r lluosydd is ac effaith hynny ar werth y lluosydd uwch. Bydd y lluosydd uwch yn cael ei osod ar ychydig dros 4 y cant yn uwch na'r lluosydd safonol o 2027-28 ymlaen. Mae hyn yn gynnydd bach i'r gwahaniaeth presennol, ac mae hi'n ffordd deg o ailddosbarthu atebolrwydd er mwyn inni allu rhoi gwell cefnogaeth i'r busnesau sy'n galon i'r stryd fawr a chanol trefi.

Mae’r newidiadau hyn i’r lluosyddion gwahaniaethol yn gysylltiedig â gwaith ehangach y tasglu canol trefi. Bydd y tasglu yma yn ystyried fframweithiau polisi cenedlaethol, yn ogystal â’r cymorth wedi’i deilwra a allai fod ei angen yng nghanol trefi unigol. Mae ein dull gweithredu yn cydnabod y bydd anghenion yn amrywio rhwng llefydd sy’n wynebu gwahanol heriau, tu hwnt i’r system ardrethi.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
I'll bring forward the regulations required to implement the changes to the differential multipliers in the coming weeks. The regulations will specify the properties that will be subject to the lower multiplier, and amend the value used to calculate the higher multiplier relative to the standard multiplier for any given year. Subject to the approval of this Senedd, the changes will take place on 1 April 2027.

The values of the multipliers for next year will be determined as part of our budget preparations for 2027-28, following the UK Government's autumn budget. I'm proposing to make these changes at the earliest opportunity in this Senedd, to prioritise the improvements that are deliverable and affordable in the short term. The Welsh Government will continue to consider further reforms to the non-domestic rates system that reflect our broader ambitions for Wales. I know that Members across the Chamber are interested in this matter, and ideas for further measures on non-domestic rates will receive a listening ear from me. Diolch.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
I'd first like to thank the finance Minister for taking the time out of her busy day to join us here in the Senedd, but if I'm truthfully honest, I'm not sure what the point was, given you'd already announced to the press in writing what you were going to do over 24 hours ago. I'm reminded of that excellent phrase from the former Plaid Cymru leader and current Government Minister, Adam Price, who said, when Labour did exactly the same thing, 'government by press briefing'. He also said it was disrespectful to the Llywydd and that, quote,

'it undermines this institution and our roles as elected Members'.

Strong words. Can the Minister confirm whether she aims to continue governing by press briefing?

Now, coming on to the content of your press release, I'd also like to thank the finance Minister for taking a policy straight out of Reform's manifesto. In it, we said:

'We will introduce a permanent lower multiplier for pubs, hotels and hospitality venues'.

Something that was not specified in Plaid Cymru's own manifesto. Look, if Reform provides the policy and Plaid Cymru delivers it, I won't complain. However, sadly, there must have been some misreading of our manifesto because, to afford the tax cut, you didn't end international spending or find savings in Government efficiencies; you just sent the bill directly to Wales's big businesses. As you were quoted in the press release, the

'burden will fall on the bigger businesses',

bigger businesses like Admiral, Wales's only FTSE 100 company; Airbus, one of Flintshire's biggest employers; and Tata Steel, providing an essential and strategic resource for the whole nation.

But of course, although the bill for the tax goes on the business's accounts, businesses don't pay taxes, in the same way as a house doesn't pay council tax, the same way this flooring doesn't pay VAT, and the same way this speech doesn't pay income tax. Do you know who pays taxes? People pay taxes. So, when you tax business, it has to be paid by somebody. Either it's paid by the owners or the customers or the workers. There is no other option. So, when Admiral's insurance premiums go up for its customers, and pay rises for Airbus's employees don't happen, and investment for Tata Steel's electric arc furnace dries up, will you take the blame? And will you correct your press release statement, Minister, to say that the burden falls on the millions of Welsh people associated with bigger businesses?

And the situation for them is even worse because, just across the border, businesses can run a factory or rent office space or use any other premises a large successful company needs for lower business rates, discouraging future businesses from an opportunity to come to Wales.

My final point on this press release is this: is this it? Plaid Cymru in their manifesto said business rates needed real reforms, and after eight weeks over the summer, all you could come up with was moving some industries into the eligibility for the lower threshold category that already existed. Minister, when will we see the real reforms of business rates promised in your manifesto? Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
Well, I'm sure I could have made this statement at any point during the summer term. The statement was ready to be made. I chose in particular to wait for the first day of the Senedd being back in session to make the statement, and I'm making it on the floor of the Senedd in order to receive questions from other parties and from Members here to see how they respond to the statement, and what else they think that this system should deliver. After that five minutes from the Reform representative, I'm not sure whether Reform are going to support this reduction of 30 per cent in business rates for this sector, which is a really important sector for our town centres, or not. It wasn't clear to me, from what you said, whether you would support it or not. But you'll have to decide on that, of course, before the voting happens on the floor of this Senedd one way or another on a change of this kind. 

But may I say why Plaid Cymru decided to take this initial step? Members across this Senedd continuously talk about the need to strengthen our town centres. Our town centres are important to the communities that we represent, whether that is in our industrial areas, in our Valleys, or in more rural areas. Providing support to those businesses that are, in their broad range, existing in town centres has been a manifesto commitment from Plaid Cymru, and today it is a commitment that we are delivering within Government. I hope that that strikes a chord that will be supported by people across the Senedd who represent communities all across Wales and of all political backgrounds as well.

You have been a bit too busy reading that press release, I think, rather than listening to what I said in my statement 5 ft away from you this afternoon. You asked the question, 'Is this it?', and I responded to that today in front of you. I responded when I said that this is an initial first step, and I'm keen to hear the views from other Members on what more this Government could be able to deliver in order to support those businesses. So, spend a bit less time reading the press releases and judging those press releases, and use a bit more of your time standing up in this Chamber listening to what's being said.
documents.text_cy:
Ie, wel, mae'n siŵr y gallwn i fod wedi gwneud y datganiad yma unrhyw bryd yn ystod tymor yr haf. Roedd y datganiad yn barod i'w wneud. Dewisais i yn benodol i aros tan ddiwrnod cyntaf y Senedd i fod nôl yn ymgynnull i wneud y datganiad, a dwi'n ei wneud e ar lawr y Senedd yma er mwyn cael cwestiynau gan bleidiau a gan Aelodau fan hyn i weld sut maen nhw'n ymateb i'r datganiad, a beth mwy maen nhw'n ei feddwl y dylai'r system yma ei gyflawni. Ar ôl y pum munud yna gan gynrychiolydd Reform, dwi ddim yn gwybod a ydy Reform yn mynd i gefnogi'r gostyngiad yma o 30 y cant mewn ardrethi busnes ar gyfer y sector yma, sy'n rili bwysig i'n canol trefi ni, neu beidio. Doedd hi ddim yn glir i mi, o'r hyn a ddywedoch chi, a fyddech chi'n ei gefnogi fe neu beidio. Fe fydd yn rhaid i chi benderfynu, wrth gwrs, cyn bod yna bleidleisio ar lawr y Senedd yma un ffordd neu'r llall ar newid o'r math yma.

Ond a gaf i ddweud pam fod Plaid Cymru wedi penderfynu cymryd y cam cychwynnol yma? Mae Aelodau ar draws y Senedd yma yn sôn yn barhaus am yr angen i gryfhau ein canol trefi ni. Mae ein canol trefi ni yn bwysig i'r cymunedau rŷn ni'n eu cynrychioli, p'un ai ydy hynny yn ein hardaloedd diwydiannol, yn ein Cymoedd, ni neu yng nghefn gwlad. Mae rhoi cymorth i'r busnesau yna sydd, yn eu hystod ehangach, yn bodoli'n benodol yng nghanol trefi wedi bod yn gomitment maniffesto gan Blaid Cymru, a heddiw yn gomitment inni ei ddelifro o fewn y Llywodraeth. Dwi'n gobeithio bod hwnna'n taro nodyn a fydd yn cael ei gefnogi gan bobl ar draws y Senedd yma, gan gynrychiolwyr o gymunedau o bob cwr o Gymru ac o bob cefndir gwleidyddol hefyd.

Rydych chi wedi bod bach yn rhy fisi yn darllen y press release yn hytrach na beth ddywedais i yn y datganiad, 5 tr oddi wrthych chi fan hyn y prynhawn yma. Roeddech chi'n gofyn y cwestiwn, 'Is this it?', ac fe atebais i hwnna yn y fan hyn o'ch blaen chi. Fe atebais i fe pan ddywedais i mai'r cam cyntaf yw hwn, a dwi'n awyddus i glywed beth yw barn Aelodau eraill ar beth yn fwy y gallai'r Llywodraeth yma ei gyflawni ar gyfer cefnogi busnesau. Felly, halwch bach llai o amser yn darllen press releases, yn beirniadu'r press releases, a defnyddio bach mwy o'ch amser ar eich traed yn y Senedd yma yn gwrando ar yr hyn sy'n cael ei ddweud.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
I don't know if I need to say this, but Cai made reference to Airbus, and I have a family member working for that company.

Welsh Labour has been clear that we at least intend to be a constructive opposition. That's why we do welcome the principles of today's announcement, recognising the permanent reduction of 30 per cent, providing valuable support and assurances to businesses in accommodation, hospitality and leisure that qualify for this reduction. This announcement, of course, builds on the policies of the previous Welsh Labour Government that provided over £1 billion of rate support for hospitality and leisure businesses since 2020-21.

But we do have to pay for this reduction, don't we? The Minister says that the proposals are cost neutral and that the burden will fall on the largest businesses. But we also have to recognise that non-domestic rates are based on the value of property, not the turnover of a company, its profit or its ability to pay. A business that has a high rateable value as a site isn't necessarily a large business or necessarily a very profitable business.
documents.text_cy:
Dwi ddim yn siŵr a oes angen dweud hyn, ond fe wnaeth Cai gyfeirio at Airbus, ac mae gen i aelod o'r teulu sy'n gweithio i'r cwmni hwnnw. 

Mae Llafur Cymru wedi bod yn glir ein bod ni o leiaf yn bwriadu bod yn wrthblaid adeiladol. Dyna pam ein bod ni yn croesawu egwyddorion y cyhoeddiad heddiw, gan gydnabod y bydd gostyngiad parhaol o 30 y cant yn rhoi cymorth gwerthfawr a mwy o sicrwydd i fusnesau lletygarwch, llety a hamdden sy'n gymwys. Mae'r cyhoeddiad hwn, wrth gwrs, yn adeiladu ar bolisïau'r Llywodraeth Lafur Cymru flaenorol a ddarparodd dros £1 biliwn o gymorth ardrethi i fusnesau manwerthu, hamdden a lletygarwch ers 2020-21.

Ond mae'n rhaid talu am y gostyngiad hwn, onid oes? Mae'r Gweinidog yn dweud bod y cynigion yn niwtral o ran cost ac y bydd y bwrdwn yna yn disgyn ar y busnesau mwyaf. Ond mae angen cydnabod hefyd fod ardrethi annomestig yn seiliedig ar werth eiddo, nid ar drosiant cwmni, ei elw nac ar ei allu i dalu. Nid yw busnes sy'n meddiannu safle â gwerth ardrethol uchel o reidrwydd yn fusnes mawr nac yn fusnes hynod broffidiol, o bosib.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
The Federation of Small Businesses says that some higher value hospitality and leisure premises have already faced increases of up to 70 per cent following revaluation. Some hotels could now be excluded from the 30 per cent reduction and made to pay the higher multiplier instead.

I'm also concerned about the unintended consequences of today's announcements. Few in this Chamber would, I think, challenge the notion of raising business rates on large out-of-town retailers, but these proposals will likely also impact valuable sites employing hundreds of workers each in places like the city centres of Cardiff, Swansea, Newport and Wrexham.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text: I was speaking earlier with Gwyn, regretting the loss of Marks and Spencer in Swansea. Will there be more retailers of that kind that are likely to take decisions to close their stores in the middle of our cities?
documents.text_cy: Roeddwn i'n siarad yn gynharach gyda Gwyn, yn gresynu ar golled Marks and Spencer yn Abertawe. Oes yna fwy o fanwerthwyr o'r math hynny mewn perygl o wneud penderfyniadau i gau eu siopau yng nghanol ein dinasoedd ni?

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
I'd point out here that Cardiff alone makes a net contribution of around £100 million to the Welsh national non-domestic rates pot. Will the Minister therefore share, in advance of the budget—today, if possible—the intended threshold for the higher multiplier, the number, type and location of the properties that will pay more, the average and largest expected increases, and her assessment of the effect on jobs, investment and prices? Can she also set out how she will avoid a cliff edge for businesses whose rateable value is just above £51,000?

What these questions demonstrate, I think, Minister, is that what's actually needed is wholesale reform of the business rates system in its totality. There was a commitment to that effect in Welsh Labour's manifesto, just as there was in Plaid Cymru's manifesto. I know that this new Government loves a review, it loves a commission. I wonder, Minister, if you could explain why your announcement today—welcome though it broadly is—is simply making tweaks at the margins and not getting into the more comprehensive changes that your party promised before the election. Our offer, as Welsh Labour, is to work with you so that we can make the system fair and so that we can incentivise businesses and local authorities to grow the value of NDR receipts and to drive wider economic growth. Thank you.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
Thank you for those comments and the welcome and the challenges that you set out there in your contribution. Of course, one of the advantages, hopefully, that the businesses that are eligible for this support will see is that it will be a 30 per cent reduction that will be permanent for them. The reduction that's in place for pubs at the moment is discretionary and is only 15 per cent, and therefore, this will excel compared to that and it will be automatic for those businesses. It will allow those businesses that are eligible to be able to plan on the basis of the guarantee that they will have that, if the regulations on this measure pass, this will be something that they can plan for ahead of time. Of course, we are adding to the system that's already in place for shops, that system that was introduced by the previous finance Minister under the Labour Government, so the use of the multiplier, the different multipliers, was introduced by my predecessor in that context. So what I'm doing is expanding the number of businesses that are eligible for this cut in non-domestic rates.

And it is a first step, as I mentioned, as we start to think about how we can go further with the town centre taskforce that has been set up in terms of developing the high street and supporting the high street as the heart of a number of communities. But also the challenge you set forward is a challenge that is about the system as a whole, of course. You speak particularly about city centres, which have large shops and have important anchor stores in the middle of those cities. It is important, of course, that we think about striking the right balance in terms of supporting the smaller businesses, which is a continuous call coming from Members in this Chamber, but with an eye to not disadvantaging the larger businesses too much. So striking that balance is important. In terms of publishing the exact multipliers that will be operational for 2027, that will have to wait until we have the budget for next year, when that is introduced. That is when that will become operational, will become known. 

And then on the point about the full reform of this system that is needed, I think, as a Senedd—. I hear it from different parties and from different Members: rather than making small changes here and there and sometimes making them in a reactive way, reacting to whatever issue is affecting the economy, we need to look at this area as a whole, in its entirety. I would hope, as we discuss and test out more of the ideas relating to business rates, we will come to a consensus across this Chamber with regard to the political appetite that there is to address this work. I would be happy to be part of that discussion.

On these cliff edges you mentioned—when £51,000 is the limit and if you're one side or the other of that, it's a 30 per cent difference in how much tax you pay—this is one of the considerations certainly that needs to be looked at in the future. So, there are further changes that I think the Government could look into making, with support from this Chamber, and then there is a broader question about addressing and reforming the system as a whole. I'm sure that the discussion on that will continue.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch am y sylwadau a'r croeso a'r heriau yn eich cyfraniad. Wrth gwrs, un o'r manteision, gobeithio, bydd y busnesau sydd yn gymwys ar gyfer y gefnogaeth yma'n ei weld yw y bydd e'n 30 y cant o ostyngiad parhaol iddyn nhw. Mae'r gostyngiad sydd mewn lle ar gyfer tafarnau ar hyn o bryd yn discretionary ac ond yn 15 y cant, ac felly fe fydd hwn yn rhagori ar hynny ac fe fydd e'n awtomatig ar gyfer y busnesau hynny. Bydd e'n caniatáu i'r busnesau sy'n gymwys i allu cynllunio ar sail y gwarant fydd yna, os bydd y rheoliadau a'r mesur yma'n pasio, fod hyn yn rhywbeth maen nhw'n gallu cynllunio ar ei gyfer o flaen llaw. Wrth gwrs, ychwanegu at y system sydd eisoes mewn lle ar gyfer siopau rŷn ni'n ei wneud, y system wnaeth gael ei gyflwyno gan y Gweinidog cyllid o fy mlaen i o dan Lywodraeth Lafur, ac felly mae'r defnydd o'r multipliers a'r gwahanol multiplier wedi cael ei gyflwyno gan fy rhagflaenydd i yn y cyd-destun yna. Felly ymestyn y nifer o fusnesau sy'n gymwys am y cwtogiad yma yn y trethi busnes ydw i.

Ac mae'n gam cyntaf, fel y gwnes i sôn, wrth inni feddwl ynglŷn â sut gallwn ni fynd ymhellach gyda'r tasglu ar ganol trefi sydd wedi'i sefydlu o ran datblygu'r stryd fawr a chefnogi'r stryd fawr fel calon i nifer o gymunedau. Ond hefyd, mae'r her rŷch chi'n ei rhoi yn her sydd yn sôn am y system yn ei chyfanrwydd, wrth gwrs. Rŷch chi'n sôn yn benodol, onid ydych, am ganol dinasoedd, sydd â siopau mawr ac sydd ag anchor stores pwysig yng nghanol y dinasoedd hynny. Mae'n bwysig, wrth ein bod ni'n meddwl ynglŷn â chael y balans yma'n iawn o ran cefnogi busnesau llai, sydd yn alwad sydd yn dod yn barhaus gan Aelodau yn y Siambr yma, ein bod ni'n gwneud hynny gyda golwg ar beidio ag anfanteisio mewn ffordd rhy ddifrifol y busnesau hynny sydd yn fwy. Felly, mae taro'r balans yna'n bwysig. O ran cyhoeddi'r union multipliers fydd yn weithredol ar gyfer 2027, fe fydd hwnna'n gorfod aros tan fydd y gyllideb ar gyfer y flwyddyn nesaf yn cael ei chyflwyno. Dyna pryd fydd hwnna'n dod yn weithredol, yn wybodus.

Wedyn, ar y pwynt ynglŷn â'r diwygiad llawn o'r gyfundrefn yma sydd ei angen, dwi'n credu, fel Senedd—. Dwi'n ei glywed e o wahanol bleidiau ac o wahanol Aelodau: yn hytrach na gwneud mân newidiadau fan hyn a fan draw ac ambell waith eu gwneud nhw'n adweithiol i ba bynnag fater sy'n bwrw'r economi, fod angen edrych ar y maes yma yn ei gyfanrwydd. Byddwn i'n gobeithio, wrth inni drafod a testio fwy o'r syniadau ynglŷn â threthi busnes, ein bod ni'n dod i ryw gonsensws ar draws y Siambr yma ynglŷn â'r appetite gwleidyddol sydd yna i fynd i'r afael â'r gwaith yma. Fe fyddwn i'n hapus i fod yn rhan o'r drafodaeth ynglŷn â hynny.

O ran y cliff edges yma rŷch chi wedi sôn amdanyn nhw—os ŷch chi un ochr neu'r llall o £51,000, mae e'n gwneud 30 y cant o wahaniaeth i chi o ran faint o dreth rŷch chi'n ei dalu—mae hwnna'n un o'r ystyriaethau yn sicr sydd angen edrych arnyn nhw yn y dyfodol. Felly, mae yna newidiadau pellach, dwi'n credu, y gall y Llywodraeth edrych i'w gwneud, gyda chefnogaeth yn y Siambr yma, ac wedyn mae yna gwestiwn mwy ynglŷn â mynd i'r afael â diwygio'r gyfundrefn yn ei chyfanrwydd. Mae'n siŵr y bydd y drafodaeth ar hynny yn parhau.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
Cabinet Minister, thank you for your statement today. I do share some of the concerns raised by our Reform colleague in terms of the way in which this information has been disseminated to Members of the Senedd. I think it is right and proper that in the vast majority of instances, information is shared in this Chamber first before being released to the press, just to show some respect to the Chamber itself and the Members within it.

But in terms of the meat of this statement, I certainly welcome the direction of travel from the Government on this and recognise that business rates represent a significant cost for businesses across Wales at a time when many are already under considerable pressures. Cabinet Minister, you'll be aware that our high streets have been struggling to adapt to changing consumer behaviour and the continued growth of online retail. The Welsh Conservatives have consistently argued that the tax burden on those businesses is far too high. We also need to be honest about the wider pressures that businesses are facing, dealing with taxation of all types alongside employee pressures and rising energy costs. Of course, business rates are only one part of a wider cost of doing business.

Colleagues have already raised a couple of questions I was interested in. I will point to three issues and questions, though. Respectfully, Cabinet Minister, I'm not sure if you fully responded to Huw Thomas's question, particularly around the cliff edge. You acknowledged it in your response, but, of course, there has potentially been the introduction of a new cliff edge here. I wonder what assurances you can give those businesses that they won't feel the pain of that, potentially, and that there may be some tapering that could take place so businesses aren't falling foul one way or the other. What confidence can you give to businesses that that is properly understood and recognised in terms of a potential tapering of this relief beyond that £51,000? A broader discussion you mentioned in regard to business rates, I think, does need to take place. I'd expect Welsh Government to lead on that.

There was one specific issue I'd be grateful for you to consider in this discussion, and that's one around the particular challenges faced by businesses who are just starting out. Business rates will ordinarily apply as soon as they start up, meaning firms can face a tax bill very soon after opening their doors without necessarily generating real income at that point. I wonder what consideration you might give to our proposal for business rate free periods for new retail businesses and others on the high street to give those entrepreneurs the opportunity to establish themselves before facing this additional cost.

Another consideration on which I'd be interested in your response is the role of local authorities in business rates. Of course, many people think that councils set those business rates, but they merely collect them on behalf of the Welsh Government. But I wonder if there's an opportunity to incentivise our local authorities by allowing them to retain an element of any non-domestic rates growth in their area, to allow our councils to invest in our town centres or incentivise our councils perhaps to invest in those town centres more than they currently do.

Finally, Minister, I'm interested—and it's back to this particular announcement today—in how it's going to impact businesses that offer mixed services. In my own constituency, Banana Ben's play centre and cafe may be impacted by this. They've been refused food and drink hospitality rate relief in the past, despite food and drink accounting for 60 per cent of their floor space and 61 per cent of their turnover. Companies House classify it as an unlicensed restaurant and cafe. The business provides indoor play alongside food and drink for families, and the two, of course, are not mutually exclusive, yet it will not, it seems, qualify for the equivalent relief. Businesses of a similar nature in England absolutely do. So, I wonder whether you could respond to that and what you might seek to do to address this disparity to ensure that Welsh businesses are not disadvantaged simply because they operate in Wales, perhaps offering more than one service to their customers. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text: Thank you for the contribution.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cyfraniad.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
I was obviously too keen to go to the pub to prepare for this statement, so I'll reflect on what everybody has united upon in thinking about the timing of statements. But just very genuinely from me, I could have made this statement during the summer recess, in the peak of the tourism season, but I quite deliberately left it until the first day back. But, yes, I'll consider the timing, and getting back in to the rhythm of the work of this place is something that I need to do.

Yes, just on the issue around a cliff edge, I do recognise that this is a very difficult issue for some businesses who fall the wrong side of a support package of this kind, and only very closely. So, the tapering issue is something that I will be interested in looking at, but I didn't want to delay the simplicity and the ability to make this statement and to move on this level of support of 30 per cent reduction for the hospitality and leisure sectors in this way by trying to do everything at the same time in one go. So, these are issues that I will be returning to, and they are issues, of course, that the high-street taskforce will also want to look at, I'm sure, as are many of the issues that you raise. The issue around whether new start-ups on the high street should be given a holiday period for that first six months to a year of trading as a kind of incentive for them to take up, quite often, empty shops, making local authorities more proactive in their local area to support business growth as well by incentivising growth of businesses and growth of business rate collection, with some payback back to local authorities—. I'm always interested in how we can make these systems include more incentives to do better all the time and to have more economic activity. So, those are some things that I hope the town-centres taskforce will look at, but also that we do in response to the issues that are raised in the Chamber here today and at other times.

On mixed businesses, I've come across this as an issue in my own constituency at different times as well, so I'm aware that it's an issue in the system and a tension. I will need to go back to my officials and see whether there is anything in the greater extent of the categorisation that we're now bringing into the 30 per cent reduction that will enable mixed businesses of the kinds you've described to qualify for this. But I can't give a guarantee on the floor here in any individual case or generally on mixed businesses, but I will look at it to see what is possible.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
As we know, high streets are at the heart of our communities, and the Cabinet Minister's announcement today to cut business rates by 30 per cent for hospitality and leisure businesses across Wales is a very welcome step to rebalance the non-domestic rate system. In addition to today's announcement, can you confirm whether any consideration has also been given to the small business rates relief threshold and, as Sam has already mentioned and you've touched upon, business rates holidays for new businesses, both of which would be a boost for our local entrepreneurs?

Whilst there would be a cost to such measures, one way to cover this, perhaps, would be to consider different valuation methods or multipliers for certain types of property, for example, data centres, which do not currently have their own classification. This way, some of the extractive profit generated from these properties could be retained and instead used to benefit local communities.

I look forward to working with the Cabinet Minister on longer term reforms that fall outside today's scope of this announcement.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text: Thank you for your contribution, and thank you for stretching the discussion to other areas that this Senedd will be interested in over the next months and years. As I've said, this is very much a first step to support businesses on our high street. It's a reasonably straightforward support package that we can offer at this time. But there are very many aspects of business rate support that need to be looked at and many ideas here this afternoon. The use of differential multipliers, as you've suggested, is new to the way we do our business rate support in this context. It was first introduced on retail properties and on shops by the predecessor Government; we're extending that today. But we need to, again, think about extending the categorisation and possibly categorising some for the first time, as new businesses and new properties develop within our economy. So, there is much still to do on this. This is a first step. For those businesses that will benefit from this, it is most definitely welcome in very challenging times. But there are an array of different measures that the Government currently works on to support businesses, and there is much that both this Government and the UK Government can do to support businesses in what is a very challenging time.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text: Thank you. Finally, Art Wright.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Yn olaf, Art Wright.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. First, I'd like to thank the Minister for the statement. Newport and Islwyn have seen a worrying number of pub and hospitality closures in the past few years. These businesses are at the heart of our communities, yet they continue to face mounting pressure from rising costs. Their closure results in lost jobs, reduced economic activity, lower footfall in our town centres and the loss of valuable community spaces. It also reduces the opportunity for young people to gain vital first-job experience and develop the skills needed to enter the wider workforce.

Whilst the Welsh Government's 30 per cent reduction in business rates is welcome, many hospitality businesses continue to face significant financial pressures. As David Chapman, and I'll quote, from UKHospitality Cymru has observed, running a hospitality business in this current climate is like

'plate spinning when you're riding an exercise bike'.

It's a good start, but we must go further. Given the continued loss of jobs in community pubs across Newport and Islwyn, does the Cabinet Minister believe that a 30 per cent reduction in business rates goes far enough? And what further action will the Welsh Government take to support the sector to prevent further closures? Diolch.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text:
The points you've made and the illustrations you've given as to how important the hospitality sector is in our various communities, and how important it is for different aspects of the economy, how many of our young people have their first jobs in pubs—. I had my first job in a pub, and I pulled my last pint in a pub in 1987. So, I hadn't done it until I pulled a pint just recently, and it showed that 30 years and more had passed since I pulled a pint.

But to be serious and to respond to the points that you've made, this will be a contribution that alleviates some of the pressure on our hospitality and leisure sector. It is more than just pubs, it is cafes and restaurants, and it is gyms and museums and libraries. So, it's the widest possible array, and when you add that to shops as well, it's the widest possible array of many of the businesses that feature in our town centres and some of our villages as well. So, it goes further than Government has done before in Wales. So, that's the important contribution of today. But I'm sure, as some have said already, that there are a myriad of different other issues that face our hospitality and leisure sectors. There are many pressures in our economy. The inflationary pressure that we are feeling today and will possibly be increasing again is something that puts particular pressure on so many of our high-street businesses. There are actions that the UK Government as well as the Welsh Government can take. But, hopefully, today will have been a strong signal that this Government and this Senedd believe that our small businesses that are trying to work so hard to keep going in our communities right throughout Wales in difficult times—this Government has their back and will try and take all initiatives that it can to support them in these testing times.

documents.item: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
documents.text: Thank you, Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Weinidog.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text: We will now move on to item 5, a statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: review of higher education. I call on the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education, Cefin Campbell.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen i eitem 5, datganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Sgiliau ac Addysg Drydyddol: adolygiad o addysg uwch. Galwaf ar y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Sgiliau ac Addysg Drydyddol, Cefin Campbell.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. I'm pleased to confirm the launch of the independent review of higher education in Wales, following the publication of the terms of reference on 4 August at the Garreg Las National Eisteddfod, in accordance with our commitment to do so within 100 days of the creation of this Government. This review forms part of our wider mission to build a stronger, fairer and more prosperous Wales through education, skills, research and opportunity.

Higher education is one of Wales's most important national assets. Our universities are educating future generations, driving research and innovation, supporting public services, strengthening communities and are making a significant contribution to our culture and language. They help create the skills, ideas and opportunities on which Wales's future prosperity depends.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr iawn, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Rwy'n falch iawn o gadarnhau ein bod ni wedi lansio adolygiad annibynnol o addysg uwch yng Nghymru, ar ôl cyhoeddi'r cylch gorchwyl ar 4 Awst yn Eisteddfod Genedlaethol y Garreg Las, yn unol â'n hymrwymiad ni i wneud hynny o fewn 100 diwrnod i sefydlu'r Llywodraeth hon. Mae'r adolygiad hwn yn rhan o'n cenhadaeth ehangach i adeiladu Cymru gryfach, decach a mwy ffyniannus drwy addysg, sgiliau, ymchwil a chyfleoedd.

Mae addysg uwch yn un o asedau cenedlaethol pwysicaf Cymru. Mae ein prifysgolion yn addysgu cenedlaethau'r dyfodol, yn llywio gwaith ymchwil ac arloesi, yn cefnogi gwasanaethau cyhoeddus, yn cryfhau cymunedau ac yn gwneud cyfraniad amhrisiadwy i'n diwylliant a'n hiaith. Maent yn helpu i greu'r sgiliau, y syniadau a'r cyfleoedd sy'n sail i ffyniant Cymru yn y dyfodol.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
But whilst our universities continue to transform lives and contribute to our economic, social and cultural life every day, they are currently, like universities across the United Kingdom, under significant financial pressure, caused by a range of complex and connected challenges. These include their funding model, the domestic and international student markets, looming demographic changes, the challenge created by artificial intelligence, a changing economy and new directions in UK research and innovation policy. Together they risk creating a perfect storm, one that our universities may not be able to navigate without fundamental reform.

The Welsh sector reported a collective underlying deficit of £82 million in 2024-25. Forecasts published by Medr suggest that financial pressures are likely to continue, raising significant questions about the long-term sustainability of parts of the sector. Total student enrolments at our universities declined by 11 per cent between 2022-23 and 2024-25. International enrolments also fell by around a third during that period, while enrolments of Welsh-domiciled students fell by 8 per cent. The Universities and Colleges Admissions Service data from the past two recruitment cycles show that these enrolment challenges have continued. Total research grants and contracts income to Welsh universities fell by £35 million between 2022-23 and 2024-25, primarily due to the final withdrawal of European Union structural and regional development funding.

Alongside these challenges, our student finance system has reached the limits of affordability within the spending controls imposed by UK Treasury. We must consider how to best target support for learners where it's most needed, whilst also ensuring the long-term sustainability of the system to the Government and without overburdening graduates with their loan repayments. The scale and complexity of these challenges mean that doing nothing is not an option.

All these challenges are interconnected and require a strategic response. Incremental adjustments alone will not be sufficient. We need a clear view of how higher education can continue to serve Wales in a changing world, while remaining financially sustainable and delivering the greatest possible benefit for learners, communities and the Welsh economy. That is why we are establishing this review. Its central purpose will be to recommend how Wales can secure a sustainable higher education sector and student finance system for future generations. We want public investment to deliver the strongest possible economic, social and cultural return for Wales, and for Wales to be a destination of choice for learners.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
The review will take a comprehensive view of the higher education system. It will examine student support, institutional funding, research and innovation, participation, graduate outcomes, and the organisation and resilience of the sector in Wales. But it will not limit itself to traditional full-time undergraduate study; it will also consider part-time provision, higher education delivered through colleges at level 4 and level 5 study, higher and degree apprenticeships, and postgraduate education. The review will also consider the commitments set out in our programme for government and election manifesto, including how we can increase the proportion of Welsh Government student support expenditure that benefits Wales, how to incentivise more Welsh students and graduates to study, work and train here and increase participation in Welsh-medium and bilingual higher education. Supporting the Welsh language will be a core consideration. We want to expand opportunities for learners to develop and use Welsh throughout their studies, and ensure that Welsh-medium and bilingual provision continues to flourish as part of a modern and inclusive tertiary education system.

The review will be conducted independently, because, as sector representatives have argued, a review of this significance should be evidence-led, objective and capable of taking a long-term view. As a Government, we have set out the challenge and the terms of reference, but the chair and panel will assess the evidence independently and develop their recommendations accordingly.

Dirprwy Lywydd, I am therefore delighted to announce that the review will be chaired by Professor Patrick Prendergast, former provost and president of Trinity College Dublin and the current chair of South East Technological University in Ireland. Professor Prendergast brings extensive experience of higher education leadership and institutional transformation in Ireland. He will be supported by a small panel of experts with experience across higher education policy, student finance, institutional sustainability, governance, and the intersection between universities and businesses. I will be confirming the full membership of the panel in the very near future and expect it to meet for the first time in early October.

Stakeholder engagement will be central to the review's work, and I want to remind Members that the sector itself has called for and has welcomed this review. University students, staff, employers, Medr, trade unions and wider partners will have opportunities to contribute evidence and perspectives throughout the process. We will be inviting key stakeholders to join a stakeholder advisory group to ensure a broad range of voices are heard while preserving the independence of the review. I will also ask the chair to engage with opposition parties in the Senedd and keep them informed of progress and emerging findings. I myself will be meeting with vice-chancellors once again in the autumn.

So, given the tight time frame for this review, I expect it to build upon the substantial evidence gathered through the previous Government's call for submissions on the future of tertiary education, as well as its published evaluation of the Diamond reforms, whilst also seeking further evidence, where required, on the specific issues identified in the terms of reference. I can today confirm that a summary of those submissions has been published on the Welsh Government website.

The work of this review will not be easy. Difficult choices and trade-offs will need to be considered, and recommendations must be both ambitious and realistic. They will need to operate within the financial constraints facing Welsh Government and the wider public sector. However, I believe, and I am encouraged from the conversations I've had with Professor Prendergast that he shares this view, that this review represents an important opportunity. It starts from a position of confidence in what higher education can and does contribute to Wales, whilst recognising that the status quo is not sustainable.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
To close, Dirprwy Lywydd, I saw this potential myself at last week’s European Association for International Education conference in Glasgow. There I met representatives from all our universities, and I had productive meetings with them and with international partners who are eager to work with them. I also heard about how rejoining Erasmus+ will provide new opportunities to students, staff and institutions for international study, work placements, exchanges, training and research in other countries.

Fundamentally, the aim of this review is to ensure that we have a higher education system that is financially resilient, that is internationally respected, that is rooted in communities, that is supportive of the Welsh language, and that is capable of helping to build a more prosperous Wales. I look forward very much to following the panel's progress and working with the sector and across the Senedd to shape a sustainable future for higher education in Wales.
documents.text_cy:
I gloi, Ddirprwy Lywydd, fe welais i'r potensial hwn fy hun yng nghynhadledd Cymdeithas Addysg Ryngwladol Ewrop yng Nglasgow wythnos diwethaf. Yno bues i'n cyfarfod â chynrychiolwyr ein holl brifysgolion, a chael trafodaethau cadarnhaol gyda nhw a chyda phartneriaid rhyngwladol sy'n awyddus i weithio gyda nhw. Fe glywais i hefyd sut y byddai ailymuno gydag Erasmus+ yn creu cyfleoedd newydd i fyfyrwyr, staff a sefydliadau ar gyfer astudio, hyfforddi, gweithio ac ymchwilio mewn gwledydd eraill.

Yn y bôn, nod yr adolygiad hwn yw sicrhau bod gennym system addysg uwch sy’n gadarn yn ariannol, sydd ag enw da yn rhyngwladol, sydd â gwreiddiau dwfn mewn cymunedau, sy’n cefnogi’r Gymraeg, ac sy’n medru helpu i adeiladu Cymru fwy ffyniannus. Rwy’n edrych ymlaen yn fawr at ddilyn cynnydd y panel a gweithio gyda’r sector ac ar draws y Senedd hon i lunio dyfodol cynaliadwy ar gyfer addysg uwch yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
I thank the Minister for the advance notice of today's statement, and I agree with the fundamental premise behind the review. We know that higher education in Wales at the moment is in an incredibly difficult position, and we all want to see it being in the best and strongest place it possibly can be. I declare an interest as somebody who has just finished a Master's degree from a Welsh educational institution, but I'm still awaiting award of the qualification so I can't quite use it for bragging rights just yet.

But one of the things that I found pertinent when speaking to some of my fellow students on the course is their perception around value for money when it comes to higher education at the moment. We know that tuition fees and student debt are incredible burdens for students going to university at the moment. My own level of student debt stands at just over £60,000 for an undergraduate and then a one-year Master's degree. I currently pay about £600 a month in student loan payments, and I'm one of the lucky ones, thanks to being in this job. But the average student who does graduate will work potentially for a decade—10 years or more—before they even begin to pay back more than just the interest on their student loans.

When it comes down to value for money for university graduates, that's one of the things that they consider when looking to go. When we look at the average earnings for university graduates after five years of graduating from their course, they were, in 2023-24, £31,500 for graduates from Welsh institutions. That compares to £33,000 from English institutions and £35,100 from Scottish ones. So, when we're asking the question about why should students choose universities in Wales, we also need to address the employability, the reward for that employment and the return on their investment into their education that they get when moving forward into Wales.

I'm glad that the review as well will consider the impact of AI as a crucial factor. I think that it's definitely contributing to the current graduate recruitment crisis that is ongoing across the UK, and it's clear to me that there needs to be at least some aspect of education in terms of AI in teaching our university students and our young people how to use it effectively, as it's likely going to be an embedded part of the modern economy for all graduates going forward.

I also think it's important that we look at how our university system can engage with technical education alongside. We know that there are certainly noises being made by the UK Government, and I think there is sentiment shared across the Chamber about the importance of technical education and education in trades and skills, and we should look at whether there is a part that our universities can play in bringing that technical education to bear for our young people.

Research and innovation is also an incredibly important aspect of our tertiary education system. We've seen the result of research and innovation. The AI craze that's going on in the economy at the moment has delivered incredible amounts of investment and value to the economy, and that's as a direct result of research undertaken by universities and recent graduates. So, I fundamentally support the objective of the review to see how we can strengthen our research and innovation in Wales.

I also welcome the overtures made within the review about strengthening the ties between employers and education, whether that is between the private sector and the public sector, and I hope that the review does take evidence from private sector employers in Wales to try and find out where the gaps may lie in between, why the entry-level jobs aren't existing and the opportunities don't exist in the same way as they have done in previous years when compared to the number of graduates.

Finally, I welcome the scope of the review, including colleges and degree apprenticeships, but I'd like to ask: will it also include fully remote university study? That’s something I'm noticing is an increasing trend—people who are studying their courses, whether it's undergraduate or postgraduate, fully remotely. And I note that the full report is due from the review from winter 2027-28, with the aim of measures being introduced for the start of the 2028-29 academic year. Given the funding deficit currently facing universities and the reduction in enrolment numbers, are there any actions planned or mechanisms in place to take shorter term actions if they are necessary? Because there will be some students who are either looking at starting university now or are currently involved in their courses who may be concerned about the future of their education given the funding shortfall, even though the review is not due to conclude for a couple of years yet. Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text: Well, thank you very much for those questions.
documents.text_cy: Wel, diolch yn fawr iawn am y cwestiynau.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
Thank you. There are so many different aspects there; I'll try to cover as many as I can.

Value for money and tuition fees. We recognise the importance of a fair and sustainable system of student support. I look at it in terms of three aspects, in many ways. The student fees are what keep our universities going. So they need those fees, unless we find other models of funding. There's also the aspect of making it fair for students as well, and you mentioned the burden of the debt that many young people carry. I should maybe also declare an interest. I have three children who went to university and are currently burdened with a huge amount of debt, which they will spend most of their working life repaying. And there are conversations going on amongst young people now as to whether it's worth them going to university or not. So, that is another aspect. And the third aspect, of course, is in terms of Welsh Government support. We want the benefits of that to be the best for Wales. So, when we look at those three aspects, it's a tightrope we have to walk in order to get that balance right.

You mentioned technical education. Now, I'm a firm believer in engaging with young people and educating them around the different pathways that are possible for them, not only the traditional work or university route, but there are other routes as well to further education, to work-based learning, apprenticeship schemes and so on. And in 2027, when we'll be introducing vocational certificates of secondary education as part of the Welsh curriculum, they will be exposed to opportunities to have vocational studies, which will engage a number of learners that are disengaged at the moment, and will open opportunities for them to maybe follow pathways that can lead to skills development and even apprenticeship degrees. I believe that our universities should look at providing more technical education. It's one of the interesting discussions I had with Professor Prendergast, because he is the chair of South East Technological University in Ireland. So I'm looking forward to him bringing his experience to bear on the work of the panel.

Research and innovation. We need to support our universities to have a greater share of that UK Research and Innovation funding. They currently only get about 2 per cent, whereas the Barnett consequential would be something around 5 per cent. So we need to support them to compete better for that funding.

And finally, you mentioned short-term actions. The panel will report back in about 18 months' time, but there will be a preliminary report in about six to nine months' time, especially around the financial support for students. Medr are keeping a close eye on what is going on in every university in Wales, and they feed that information back to me. So, if we need to step in and support, we will, but, at the moment, it's just a matter of monitoring the situation, keeping a close eye on what is happening and providing the best level of support we can. Diolch.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
Can I refer Members to my register of interests and the fact that I am an adult learner at Cardiff and Vale College? I wanted to start—. Thank you for your statement, Deputy Minister. But I think it would be remiss of me to start this statement without asking about what I think is the elephant in the room here, which is: what about further education? When you came into Government, you and the Cabinet Minister said you would take a systemic approach to education, combining higher education and further education, and I think that is the right approach. It runs from early years right the way through people's life course.

However, what we have here is one part of the system hived off, and that is in sharp contrast to the approach taken by the previous Labour Government, where we issued a comprehensive call for evidence on tertiary education. So, I suppose my first question to you is: you are very well aware—I don't need to remind you—of the funding pressures in FE, the participation pressures in FE. You'll have heard from the chief executives and principals in recent months. I know, too, that you are very well aware that FE is where some of our most disadvantaged, most vulnerable learners are educated—the learners who are most likely to have their life chances inhibited by becoming not in education, employment or training. You've said in the statement that there are finite resources and there will have to be trade-offs. Given that this review just looks at higher education, how will you measure any potential trade-offs for FE? How will you consider the pressures on FE, and how will you consider the need to look after those learners?

The statement commits to looking at part-time learners, and I've asked you previously about part-time learners. The Diamond reforms have been a huge success in terms of the numbers of part-time learners studying at our universities. What assurance can you give that the review will protect the interests of part-time learners in higher education?

There's no mention of Seren in this statement today, and when you issued the statement in the summer announcing there would be a review of higher education, there was a reference to Seren. You said there would be a review of Academi Seren, and indeed it's picked up in the Cabinet Minister's action plan on literacy. You said that it would be about bringing together Reaching Wider and the Seren programme. Now, I know that you are very well aware that Reaching Wider is a different kind of programme to Seren. Reaching Wider is participation; Seren is about stretch. It's about ensuring that our most able learners can go to the very furthest point that they can go. It is the only thing that we do in Wales that benefits our more able and talented learners.

So, I'd like to ask you whether this review—and I welcome that there's an independent chair and that we're going to be kept updated—is going to look at the Seren programme as well, or whether that is going to be done separately. Is it your intention, as part of the review of Seren, to engage with Oxford and Cambridge? Because if young people are capable of going to some of the very best universities, not just in the UK, but anywhere in the world, then they should be encouraged to do that.

We on these benches have always viewed Seren as a learner-focused programme designed to ensure that our young people can be the very best that they can be. I want to offer you a gentle warning that we will fight very hard on these benches to protect that aspect of Seren, and I want to ask you whether it is your intention, as part of the work that you're doing on Seren, or as part of this review, to try in any way to discourage young people from studying, whether it's over the border or wherever they want to go, to achieve their education and be the very best that they can be.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
Diolch yn fawr iawn. Thank you, Lynne. A number of important points. I'll start off with your first point around the pressures on FE colleges. We absolutely recognise that there are pressures, as there were last year, which is why Medr allocated an additional £6.25 million in this financial year to support those pressures.

In discussions I've had with Medr and ColegauCymru with regard to this academic term, we are seeing the pressures again in terms of increased enrolments, especially around levels 1 and 2. So, we will be considering the situation and making a decision around about November, when numbers will have settled down. We understand that funding pressures are acute on one or two FE colleges, but those discussions are ongoing.

We want to support the FE colleges as best as we can, because, for the reasons you outlined, they do provide opportunities for those young people, especially those at risk of becoming NEET, and we are acutely aware that we can't allow them to fall through the net in any way by not supporting them. So, we will take a considered view when we know the final numbers closer to November. But in terms of your wider point, we are well aware of the financial challenges.

Part-time learners: absolutely, the review will look at this. I believe in lifelong learning as being an opportunity for people to upskill, reskill, and to re-engage with education at any time in their life, and that can be done through part-time provision or through apprenticeship schemes or in-work provision through the trade union movement as well.

Seren: I'm hoping to make an announcement soon about Seren. You're right, I did say back on 11 June, I think it was, when I made a statement, that we are hoping to bring together the strongest elements of Academi Seren and also the Reaching Wider programme. And you're absolutely right to say that they are two different programmes. Academi Seren provides the stretch for the most able and talented pupils and we want to keep that, obviously, because we need to stretch our most academically gifted young people. And it's not a matter of discouraging them from studying wherever they choose. I would just want to flip that on its head: what we want to do as a Welsh Government is to encourage them to stay in Wales and to support our universities here. But it's not about discouragement at all, it's about encouraging them to stay, which is slightly different to what you were possibly alluding to.

The Reaching Wider programme is important as well, because it targets young people from disadvantaged communities, and you know and others know that the number of young people from disadvantaged communities going to universities is lower in Wales than in any of the other home nations. So, we want to encourage, through a cohesive programme, that to happen as well. So, I think that answers the main points, Lynne, and I'd be happy to have a conversation with you about any of these, moving forward. Diolch.

documents.text: Thanks. Sam Rowlands.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Sam Rowlands.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Apologies for my slight lapse in concentration, things seem to be more lively outside the Chamber today than they have been, perhaps, inside it.

Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement. Tertiary education is, of course, crucial in developing the skills and knowledge that our economy needs now and in the future, and the stakes for the higher education review could hardly be higher at this stage. And the many external reviews of Welsh higher education over recent decades, in my view, have failed to secure the long-term sustainability of the sector and have instead contributed to a cycle of managed decline.

But on this review specifically, you'll be aware, Cabinet Minister, that in Scotland when Ministers have sought to work with universities to develop solutions and secure their commitments to change, before holding them to account for delivery, there's been that close working relationship with those universities. So, I wonder how you will ensure and give assurances to our universities here in Wales that you'll be adopting a similar approach, working seriously with those universities as partners in developing and implementing these reforms, of course within the context of the independent panel that you're seeking to or you will be setting up.

There's already been mention of the central role that universities play in our economy and our growth in the future. We welcome the review's commitment to look at the role that alternative pathways, such as colleges and degree apprenticeships, should play in a wider education landscape. Of course, colleges can provide flexible modes of delivery and be more accessible to learners, and we know the increasing importance of a degree apprenticeship. So, will you direct the review to look specifically at what barriers there are in Wales to prevent our young people from accessing some of those alternative pathways that colleagues have already mentioned, those alternative pathways to higher education.

Within that context of economic growth, universities are important engines of place-based economic growth as well, not just the institution on its own. There are great examples of universities working closely in partnership with colleges and local industry to respond to the skills that are needed. Now, FE is not covered in the review, so how will you make sure there's a joined-up approach to meeting place-based skills requirements and opportunities across the tertiary systems? I appreciate that HE does need to be reviewed, but the context of their place is really important, particularly in a place like Wales.

Deputy Minister, in your terms of reference, you state that the scale and urgency of pressures on universities mean that the underlying funding sustainability of Welsh universities and the Welsh student support system must now be addressed. There's a real sense of urgency in your statements there, but the timeline that you're looking at is looking to make changes in the 2028-29 academic year. That's two years away. It doesn't really feel that urgent, quite frankly. Welsh students starting university in September will be entering the final year of their courses by the time any changes come in. Could you confirm whether you think that a two-year wait for this reform is acceptable to students, universities and businesses under pressure right now?

I just want to follow up on a comment that my colleague Lynne Neagle raised as well, Minister, in relation to this ambition of students seeking an education where it's best for them. Wales is already home to world-class universities. For many students, though, looking elsewhere in the UK or abroad is simply what's best for them and their future pathway. That should be a choice that is equally available to them. Higher education should allow our students to aspire to become the best that they can be, to be supported. They don't want to feel hemmed in by Wales-specific Government support or not. So, will you, on the floor of the Senedd today, commit to not holding back those Welsh student aspirations to study wherever is best for them? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
Diolch yn fawr iawn, Sam. Thank you. A number of points and I'll deal with them as you presented them. The first one, working with the university sector: since coming into post, I think I have had more meetings with the university sector than most sectors. I've met with all the vice-chancellors on more than one occasion. I've also had more than one meeting with the chairs of the universities as well, as well as Universities Wales as the umbrella body. In Scotland last week, in the international education conference that I attended, there was a stand where all the universities of Wales were present. I spoke to every one of them about the strengths they had and the offer they could give to students, not only in the United Kingdom but across the whole of the world. So, I'm in constant touch with every one of our university partners.

In terms of the economy and developing skills, skills is the bedrock of growing the economy. If we want a thriving, prosperous economy, if we want to meet the ambitions of this Welsh Government to increase productivity as well, skills is at the heart of that. It's why we are conducting a skills audit at present. The skills audit will end, in terms of inviting people to present evidence, at the end of this month, and hopefully the report will be published around about March or April of next year. That will inform employers, universities, FE colleges and work-based learning providers about emerging sectors, where we think the priorities in terms of skills growth are going to be in the future. Because we know that sectors like AI, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors and green energy are moving rapidly, so we need to recognise the skills pipeline that we need to meet those job opportunities coming down the line.

In terms of that skills development, we are holding a skills summit on 8 October in the Swansea.com Stadium. We’re hoping to get between 150 and 170 representatives from universities, FE and, crucially, employers as well. As it happens, this afternoon I had a meeting with organisations representing the biggest employers in Wales. I had an opportunity to tell them about this skills audit. I told them that their role in developing the Welsh economy with the Welsh Government, with HE, with FE, with apprenticeship providers, is absolutely crucial, and they were on board with that message.

On the final point you made, similar to Lynne, about curtailing choice, there's absolutely no intention to curtail choice. But it's incumbent on a Welsh Government to support our Welsh universities. What we want to do is to strengthen the offer that our Welsh universities are providing so that they can get more students from Wales and from the UK to come here to Wales to study and, potentially, to work as well. Diolch.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text: I'd also like to refer you to my register of interests, please. Until May, I used to work at a university in Wales, and I still have family members who work in the HE sector in Wales.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
documents.text:
Minister, this review comes at a vital time for higher education in Wales. The remit of the review is exciting and provides an opportunity to think boldly and creatively about how we want higher education to operate and, ultimately, deliver for Wales.

One of the issues that we have faced for some time now is the employability of graduates and, specifically, how we ensure that the skills and opportunities that are developed through our higher education system lead to successful careers in Wales. I believe that this review will bring those aspects together.

Often, SMEs face more challenges in terms of attracting and recruiting graduate talent. How does the Minister see the review helping us to better connect our graduates with the needs and opportunities of Welsh businesses, particularly SMEs, so that we can retain more graduate talent here in Wales, while also supporting the growth of our economy? Thank you.
