documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: I only wish that was true. There are no NHS jobs for three in 10 nurses graduating in Wales this summer. No-one has told me the wards have too many nurses; many have told me that the wards they have been treated on or visited patients needed more nurses. Student nurses have said they've felt let down, worried and angry after years of unpaid work in the NHS during training and taking out large loans to qualify. Will the health Minister provide, as requested by the Royal College of Nursing, a jobs guarantee for nursing graduates? And you'll want to know where the money is coming from: there's £247 million unallocated, and we only wanted £100 million of that for additional learning needs.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: The Member will be aware that—[Interruption.] The Member will be aware that we have a streamlining process in Wales, which is meant to ensure that they have jobs, that nurses and midwives and others have jobs when they finish their graduation. Unfortunately, because of the previous Government's failure to honour this, many nurses, midwives and paramedics in Wales today can't find those jobs, that's why we set up the graduate summit. So, I won't exercise that answer again; I've answered it once already, so forgive me if I don't go any further down that line.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: I'm sorry to be a type of Job's comforter, as my dear mother would say, but I'm going to add to your woes—your already considerable pile of woes—sorry. The situation isn't just nurses and midwives, but it actually involves medical trainees as well, speaking, again, from an ophthalmic perspective, which takes seven to 10 years of training in blood, sweat, tears and vitreous, as well as the actual cost of it as well. And we lose a third of our trainees to England because there's a lack of centralised planning for consultant vacancies for when people leave the system. So, then what we end up with in Wales is—and we already have the lowest number of specialist consultant ophthalmologists in Britain per head—we recruit from abroad to fill up the gaps. Whereas if only we could have a centralised authority to match trainees with their jobs, we would solve the problem. So, do you agree that you need central planning on a specialty basis to stop the brain drain from our country?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
The Member is absolutely right that, in the ophthalmic field, as in many other fields in health and care, in fact, we have many vacancies. The truth is that the system as it is, the one that we found when we got into position, doesn't record fully the whole workforce that we've got in Wales. So, some of the gaps that we've got, we are dependent on other bodies to inform us of their best-case situation.

So, we have to rectify this and make sure that we know the current situation and, moving forward, know what we will need. That's why we've set up two plans. First of all, a clinical plan for Wales so that we understand what the clinical needs of Wales are moving forward, and sitting beneath that clinical plan, we will have, and are developing now, the full comprehensive workforce plan—and I've mentioned this in this Chamber before—where I will be producing the first high-level part of that workforce plan and bringing it forward to the Senedd in the autumn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Minister, Swansea Bay University Health Board has recruited over 450 nurses from overseas in recent years. At the very same time, nurses graduating from Swansea University, who have completed thousands of hours of unpaid clinical training here in Wales, are unable to find employment within the Welsh NHS. We are training our own and then turning them away while recruiting from abroad to fill the gap. That cannot be sound workforce planning. So, Minister, why is the Welsh Government content to see Welsh graduates locked out of jobs while relying on overseas recruitment? Would it not be better to employ the nurses and midwives we have already trained here in Wales?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
This is slightly frustrating, because you're talking about two different things there that are going on. So, the situation with graduates, that goes back to 2022-23 and it will take a few years to work through the system. So, that's why we're finding an issue with the graduates now, because they started on their courses in 2022 when there were vacancies in the system, and the mapping and the modelling suggested that there would be vacancies in the system, but retention has improved because of the economic situation that the country finds itself in, which means that those positions are no longer available. So, that's dating back to 2022, when we did have those vacancies.

And the issue with having Indian nurses—. And once again, you're going on about Indian nurses, let's make sure that we show gratitude for the work of the nurses that come into this country, who treat your loved ones, my loved ones; they are there working, treating people who are sick, making sure that our loved ones improve. They've been recruited over the last few years before this year's graduate issue was recognised as a problem, which is a problem that lies with the previous Government.

So, yes, that's why we had a graduate summit, in order to make sure that this doesn't happen again. And, as and when we need to recruit more nurses, and if those nurses aren't available in Wales, absolutely, if those nurses want to come and work with us here in Wales from India, then we will welcome them, because they are helping us out here in Wales. The same as we have a number of Nigerian and Filipino nurses and carers working in the system, helping our loved ones, and we should show gratitude for the work that they do.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Low staffing numbers increase the length of waiting lists across many NHS services, but expectant mothers cannot join waiting lists, because babies don't wait. The Royal College of Midwives tell me that we now have unsafe staffing levels in maternity services across Wales. The impact of this situation is very serious. Not having a good birth experience is bad enough, but in some cases, it leads to medical complications. These complications can, of course, have a devastating effect on babies, their parents and, indeed, NHS staff. As well as the human impact, the costs to the NHS in treating conditions arising from birth complications and maternity cases are vast. I understand that a single maternity case typically costs £5 million. I understand also that to employ the 70 midwifery graduates who have not yet been offered jobs would cost less than £3.5 million. Not employing those midwives—

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: A question, Paul.
documents.text_cy: Cwestiwn, Paul.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: —feels like a false economy with an unjustifiable human impact. Will the Minister commit to placing all this year's midwifery graduates in jobs and making a plan to return midwifery services to a safe staffing level?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
The Member is absolutely right that we've seen a number of reports into maternity units and midwifery here in Wales that do highlight unsafe staffing levels and we have to get to grips with this. I'm glad that, for instance, recently, we've seen a new report by Audit Wales into Swansea bay show a significant improvement there, and that's to be welcomed. That's what we want to see, more improvement in those fields.

Once again, for fear of repeating myself, I'll say that the issues that we have with graduates this year lies with the fact that they started on their courses back in 2022 and it's a legacy of the previous Government we are now having to deal with. That is why I got that graduate summit together in order to bring together the RCM, HEIW and the health boards to try and find as many positions available as possible for those students, to make sure that those students who aren't midwives now do become full midwives when the time allows and when positions allow, and that we ensure that this doesn't happen again in the future.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: 5. What action is the Welsh Government taking to protect the continued availability of community beds in the Welsh NHS? OQ64403
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i ddiogelu argaeledd parhaus gwelyau cymunedol yn y GIG yng Nghymru? OQ64403

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Health boards are responsible for the planning and delivery of health services at a local level to meet the needs of their local population, working with their key stakeholders and partners.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Residents in my constituency are deeply concerned about the future of Maesteg Community Hospital. Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board has proposals for a new health and well-being centre that mean that services will be relocated from Maesteg, but the health board has confirmed that the new site will not house any community beds at the premises. Meanwhile, the health board says it has made no decisions regarding the future of the Maesteg Community Hospital site, effectively leaving both it and residents in the area in limbo, causing a great deal of distress. Will the Minister agree to meet with Cwm Taf Morgannwg health board to discuss how the continued availability of community beds in Maesteg can be protected? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
I understand the strength of feeling around the Maesteg Community Hospital. I expect any service change to be developed transparently with local people in line with national guidance and underpinned by robust evidence, options appraisals and impact assessments. I'm clear that services must be safe, sustainable and fit for purpose for the local population. In its preferred option for the development of a new health and well-being centre, the health board has highlighted that there will be an increased level and increased range of services available from the new proposed site. This is in addition to closer transport links with a bus stop and railway station in close proximity.

The health board has also committed to undertake further collaborative work on the Maesteg hospital building to ensure it is not lost. I understand that the board has requested an engagement plan on this to be presented at the July board meeting this month, in addition to an update on the plan for community beds within the Bridgend council area, and I have already met with the chair of Cwm Taf health board in order to discuss these.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
Gweinidog, in the case of Maesteg hospital that my colleague has referenced, Llais highlighted the strength of feeling locally about retaining community bed capacity, and, indeed, you've just referenced that strength of feeling. They also emphasised the importance of continued engagement with residents as proposals develop. There remains considerable worry locally about how alternative community provision, including step-down and respite care, will be delivered in practice.

I was grateful for your response earlier this month to a letter from myself and my fellow Plaid Cymru colleagues representing Afan Ogwr Rhondda, following the health board's decision to proceed with these proposals. In your reply, you noted that the Welsh Government officials would continue to engage with the health board as this work progresses. With that in mind, could you outline, please, what assurances the Welsh Government is seeking from Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board to ensure that any changes to community bed provision are supported by robust evidence, with solid working assumptions and meaningful engagement with local communities before any existing capacity is lost? Diolch.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Thank you for that question, and it reflects the strength of feeling in the Llynfi valley and other parts that are being served by the Maesteg hospital. And I understand that there are concerns around it; that's why I had that conversation with the chair of the health board in order to raise those concerns, concerns which have been raised in this Chamber, which I raised with the chair, making sure that they understood that that continued engagement is absolutely crucial, that they take on board the views of the residents, that we do get assurances that any decisions made are made by clinicians and are clinically led, and consider the distances of travel and the difficulty for some people to access some services in the area. So, we have to make sure, and health boards, especially when they present plans, have to make sure that these things are considered in the round and to the fullest possible extent in order to come to a decision.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
Prynhawn da, Weinidog. The issue of community beds in our communities and our local areas is really important, as you'll know, and I just wanted to focus in on Powys. I know we've had a discussion about this, but you'll know that there was a leak recently that Powys Teaching Health Board is considering stripping in-patient beds from eight out of our 10 community hospitals. That means that we will lose them from Ystradgynlais, Llandrindod, Builth, Knighton, Bronllys, Welshpool, Llanidloes and Machynlleth. That's up to 146 beds gone in a county with no district general hospital, where the population is older, more rural and further from alternative care than anywhere else in the country. We already know, don't we, that hospital stays in Powys average 40 days against the nationally agreed ambition of getting that down to 21.

So, Cabinet Minister, I realise these plans are not confirmed as yet, but could I just ask for your views on these potential plans? And also, would you consider intervening, as did your equivalent in 2013 in Hywel Dda health board, when there was concern about a similar issue? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
The health board has not yet made any decisions on its clinical services plan or any options for potential public consultation later this year, as this work remains under development. As part of the clinical services plan development process, the health board has been undertaking wider initial engagement across Powys over the last year, to help understand the strengths and weaknesses of current service provision and help inform and develop a future vision, potential models of care and options for change.

The clinical services plan will be a vital plan in delivering new ways of working that address critical service fragilities, ensuring services remain safe, sustainable, accessible and of high quality, which will have to be supported by evidence. The Welsh Government expects any service change to be developed transparently with local people in line with national guidance and underpinned by robust evidence, options appraisals and impact assessments to ensure services remain safe, sustainable and fit for purpose.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: 6. What support is Welsh Government providing to help parents return to work following a diagnosis of a serious health condition for a child? OQ64398
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa gymorth y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn ei ddarparu i helpu rhieni i ddychwelyd i'r gwaith yn dilyn diagnosis o gyflwr iechyd difrifol i blentyn? OQ64398

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Thank you for the question. We know that parents in this situation often face multiple and interconnected barriers to returning to work. Our Communities for Work Plus programme provides a one-to-one mentor to help parents to access a package of support and links into local networks, to address both employment needs and wider family circumstances.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn. Rydyn ni’n gwybod bod rhieni sydd yn y sefyllfa hon yn aml yn wynebu sawl rhwystr i ddychwelyd i’r gwaith, a’r rhesymau hynny’n rhyng-gysylltiedig yn aml. Mae ein rhaglen Cymunedau am Waith a Mwy yn darparu mentor un-i-un i helpu rhieni i gael gafael ar becyn o gymorth a dolen gyswllt â rhwydweithiau lleol, er mwyn delio ag anghenion cyflogaeth yn ogystal ag amgylchiadau teuluol ehangach.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Diolch, Weinidog. Last week, I met with Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, and I want to declare an interest: I have worked with this health board before when I worked at NHS Wales Performance and Improvement. So, last week, I met with Cardiff and Vale University Health Board's paediatric team to discuss the socioeconomic impact of a type 1 diabetes diagnosis in children and young people. I met with Ansruta Vijay Anand and Dr Ambika Shetty, and I'm very grateful for the work that they have both done in this area. Ansruta is a medical student, and she spoke to me about her research. Her findings were striking. In 68 per cent of cases where a child was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, there was a change to a parent's employment. This included reduced working hours, taking temporary leave from work and in some cases leaving employment altogether. And while this is recent research, I know that that anecdotally goes back decades as being other people's experiences as well. They also found that many children experience a significant delay in returning to school, nursery or other childcare settings following their diagnosis. Over the past decade, the number of children diagnosed with diabetes has increased by 29 per cent—

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: A question, please.
documents.text_cy: Cwestiwn, plis.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Given this evidence, what work is the Welsh Government undertaking to support families following a child's diagnosis of type 1 diabetes? And can I thank every person who works in the NHS, regardless of where they were born, for the work that they do for us? Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text:
I'd like to echo those sentiments put forward by the Member and thank the Member for bringing this to my attention. I welcome the research of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board on this issue. Clearly, the findings are sobering and shed new light on the insidious interrelationship between poor health and socioeconomics. We often talk about the social determinants of health and how they contribute to inequalities in health outcomes, but this study underlines that this dynamic can work both ways, whereby health conditions can, in and of themselves, lead to a deterioration in socioeconomic circumstances. 

We are committed to getting to grips with health-based inequalities. The Member will be aware that there is a first 100 days action on reviewing health-based inequalities in Wales, and I look forward to updating the Chamber on the findings. In the meantime, while the NHS does provide support packages to help families deal with a diagnosis and learn to manage their condition, including regular out-patient care by specialists, education programmes and technological solutions to reduce the burden of delivering insulin and monitoring glucose control, the evidence from the CVUHB research clearly shows that we must go further to strengthen these support mechanisms. I would welcome further engagement with both the Member and the researchers to understand how we can use these findings to learn, adapt and improve.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: And finally, question 7, Louise Emery.
documents.text_cy: Ac yn olaf, cwestiwn 7, Louise Emery.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to ensure NHS Wales uses existing technology to speed up access to patient consultations and associated services? OQ64423
documents.text_cy: 7. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod GIG Cymru yn defnyddio'r dechnoleg bresennol i gyflymu mynediad at ymgynghoriadau cleifion a gwasanaethau cysylltiedig? OQ64423

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: The Welsh Government is working with NHS Wales to make the most of existing technology to improve access to care. This includes strengthening the NHS Wales app, supporting virtual appointments and making use of ambient voice technology. Health boards and trusts are held to account on their performance to deliver patient outcomes and are expected to use existing technology as an enabler.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: That's great to hear, because obviously face-to-face initial consultations are still vital for most people, but for those who have got long-term conditions or those who are working full time or have transport issues, online consultations are really going to work. We've referred to Betsi Cadwaladr. They did a trial of Attend Anywhere. There were five patients in 2020—five patients in five years, and they haven't told the public a single thing about how this technology is performing in north Wales. So, I agree with your sentiment that we know it's a vital part of services for the NHS, but in Betsi Cadwaladr, could you please tell me what is going on in terms of how they're using Attend Anywhere and other technology to help my constituents?

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: I thank the Member for bringing this to my attention. It seems to be another case of one of the pieces of best practice that we have in parts of health boards across Wales that just isn't realised or isn't shared, or sits on a shelf somewhere. We need to learn from any piece of good practice out there and ensure that it's rolled out. So, I will raise this with the health board. I'm happy to keep you in the loop on any response I get back, because if it's good and it works, then we need to ensure that others benefit from it.

documents.item: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
documents.text: Thank you very much, Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr, Weinidog.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: We'll move on now to questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning. The first question is from Stephen Senior.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen i gwestiynau i'r Gweinidog Cabinet dros Lywodraeth Leol, Tai a Chynllunio. Cwestiwn 1, Stephen Senior.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: 1. What action is the Welsh Government taking to ensure that local government pension schemes are free to invest in key British defence and energy companies? OQ64395
documents.text_cy: 1. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod cynlluniau pensiwn llywodraeth leol yn rhydd i fuddsoddi mewn cwmnïau amddiffyn ac ynni Prydeinig allweddol? OQ64395

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much, and good afternoon, all. The UK Government is responsible for legislation and guidance on the local government pension scheme, including in relation to investments. The administering authorities and the Wales Pension Partnership are responsible for decisions on how this money is invested in Wales.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn, a phrynhawn da, bawb. Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Unedig sydd yn gyfrifol am ddeddfwriaeth a chanllawiau sy'n ymwneud â chynlluniau pensiwn llywodraeth leol, gan gynnwys buddsoddiadau. Yr awdurdodau gweinyddu a Phartneriaeth Pensiwn Cymru sy'n gyfrifol am benderfynu sut mae'r arian yma yn cael ei fuddsoddi yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Minister, whilst public sector pensions are not devolved, you know that the Welsh Government is responsible for oversight of local government and the £25 billion pot that is in the Welsh local government pension scheme. In recent years, there's been huge pressure from both elected members and pressure groups to divest from arms companies, from energy companies and from the banking system. Cabinet Minister, it was reported, just before the election in May, that you recently supported the Senedd Palestine pledge, which was produced by the Palestine Solidarity Campaign. That's a group connected with the Palestinian news agency, which I remind Members used to be part of the Palestine Liberation Organization, and also Stop the War, the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament and Extinction Rebellion. So, it's got a long history of various different groups. Three of your Cabinet Ministers supported that. Minister, now you've transitioned from being a campaigner to being in Government, can you give an assurance that the Welsh Government will exert no pressure on those local government pension schemes to divest from those key defence and energy companies, which we need in this great country of ours?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
The fact that I'm now a Minister in Government doesn't change my values at all. I continue to be a campaigner as well as a Minister in the Welsh Government, and I'm sure that other members of the Cabinet agree with that.

There is a place for pension funds in Wales to invest responsibly and locally. Of course, although, as you note, we don't have direct responsibility over pension funds, there are discussions that happen, and we do encourage pension authorities to invest responsibly and ethically, so that public sector pensions contribute positively to the future of Wales—economically, socially and environmentally.

One excellent use of pension funds is investing in the social housing stock, and you know that I'm campaigning for more social housing. I understand that the city and county of Swansea pension fund has just created a fund worth £51 million that will invest in social housing on a local level. I'm very supportive of that step.

The Wales Pension Partnership is responsible for explaining how they will invest. That doesn't mean not investing in the defence industry, for example, but it does mean not investing in companies that produce controversial arms. So, already there is an ethical framework for the Wales Pension Partnership.
documents.text_cy:
Dydy'r ffaith fy mod i rŵan yn Weinidog mewn Llywodraeth ddim yn newid fy ngwerthoedd i o gwbl. Dwi'n parhau i fod yn ymgyrchydd yn ogystal ag yn Weinidog o fewn Llywodraeth Cymru, a dwi'n siŵr bod Aelodau eraill y Cabinet yn cyd-fynd â hynny.

Mae yna le i gronfeydd pensiwn yng Nghymru fuddsoddi'n gyfrifol ac yn lleol. Wrth gwrs, er, fel rydych chi'n nodi, nad does gennym ni ddim cyfrifoldeb uniongyrchol dros y cronfeydd pensiwn, mae yna drafodaethau yn digwydd, ac rydyn ni'n annog awdurdodau pensiwn i fuddsoddi'n gyfrifol ac yn foesegol, fel bod pensiynau'r sector cyhoeddus yn cyfrannu'n gadarnhaol at ddyfodol Cymru—yn economaidd, yn gymdeithasol ac yn amgylcheddol.

Un defnydd gwych o gronfeydd pensiwn ydy buddsoddi yn y stoc tai cymdeithasol, ac rydych chi'n gwybod fy mod i'n ymgyrchu dros fwy o dai cymdeithasol. Dwi'n deall bod cronfa bensiwn dinas a sir Abertawe newydd greu cronfa effaith lleol gwerth £51 miliwn a fydd yn buddsoddi mewn tai cymdeithasol lleol, ymhlith pethau eraill. Dwi'n gefnogol iawn i hynny.

Partneriaeth Pensiwn Cymru sydd yn gyfrifol am esbonio sut y byddan nhw'n buddsoddi. Dydy hynny ddim yn golygu peidio â buddsoddi yn y diwydiant amddiffyn, er enghraifft, ond mae o'n golygu peidio â buddsoddi mewn cwmnïau sy'n cynhyrchu arfau dadleuol. Felly, mae yna, yn barod, fframwaith moesegol ar gyfer Partneriaeth Pensiwn Cymru.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: As you've explained, Welsh pension funds hold huge potential to be a force for good and drive moral and ethical investment. Another example would be the Norwegian wealth fund. But too often we hear that our pension funds are used to support the arms industry, fossil fuels or other get-rich-quick schemes that operate at the cost of the planet or contribute to the kind of human suffering that we've seen in Gaza, Lebanon and elsewhere. So, I'd like to ask what steps the Government will take to make sure that Welsh pension funds are invested ethically and deliver strong returns for pension holders whilst also supporting the well-being of our communities here in Wales and without profiting from harm done to others across the world. Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. Of course, the pension funds do need to invest in a way that is robust and safeguards those people who will benefit directly from those funds, but I do believe that we want to see responsible and ethical investment by pension authorities, so that public sector pensions do contribute in a positive way to the future of Wales, economically, socially and environmentally. Having passed the UK Pension Schemes Act 2026 earlier this year, the pension authority and the Welsh fund will agree on investment strategies over the next few months. So, those strategies haven't yet been defined in detail as of yet, but I do look forward to having discussions with them in line with this Government's values.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Wrth gwrs, mae angen i'r cronfeydd pensiwn fuddsoddi mewn ffordd sydd yn gadarn ac sydd yn gwarchod y rheini sydd yn elwa yn uniongyrchol o'r cronfeydd hynny, ond dwi'n credu ein bod ni eisiau gweld buddsoddiad cyfrifol a moesegol gan awdurdodau pensiynau, fel bod pensiynau'r sector cyhoeddus yn cyfrannu mewn ffordd gadarnhaol at ddyfodol Cymru, a hynny'n economaidd, yn gymdeithasol ac yn amgylcheddol. Ar ôl pasio Deddf Cynlluniau Pensiwn 2026 y Deyrnas Unedig yn gynharach eleni, mi fydd awdurdodau pensiwn a chronfa Cymru yn cytuno ar eu strategaethau buddsoddi dros y misoedd nesaf. Felly, dydy'r strategaethau yna ddim yn rhai sydd wedi cael eu diffinio yn fanwl eto, ond dwi yn edrych ymlaen at drafod efo nhw yn unol â gwerthoedd y Llywodraeth yma.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: This question reminds me, in a slightly odd way, of the days when many of us were fighting to convince our pension schemes—in my case the Universities Superannuation Scheme—to divest from fossil fuels, landmines, cluster bombs and tobacco. It's quite the converse of that fight. From time to time, a public sector pension executive would sidle up to me and quietly remind me that the best return on investment could be achieved from the lucrative international tobacco market, selling cigarettes to children in countries with less regulation than we have here in Wales. We pushed our pension schemes to invest positively in things like renewable energy and social housing, and the returns were good. Does the Minister agree with me that making positive, sustainable choices for our pensions is not only the moral thing to do, but it yields great, long-term returns for our pensions, returns that do not depend on global instability or risk stranded fossil fuel assets?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you very much. Yes, I do agree with you. That is why I'm eager to work with the Wales Pension Partnership to consider what further steps we can take together to strengthen the contribution of local government pension funds to Wales and to the kinds of investment that we want to see within our own country.

I'm talking specifically here of homes again, because I do think that social housing is one of those issues that you're referring to, which is not only the right thing to do, because we want to accelerate the process of providing more social homes, but there is also a consistent income flow coming in through rent from social housing. Therefore, it makes sense in general terms too for this investment here in Wales. I'm very pleased to hear that contribution from you supporting what we're doing within Government.

Dyna pam dwi'n awyddus i weithio efo Partneriaeth Pensiwn Cymru i archwilio pa gamau pellach y gallwn ni eu cymryd efo'n gilydd i gryfhau cyfraniad cronfeydd pensiwn llywodraeth leol Cymru i Gymru, ac i'r math o fuddsoddiadau rydym ni am eu gweld yn digwydd yn ein gwlad ni.

Dwi'n sôn am dai eto, oherwydd dwi yn credu bod tai cymdeithasol yn un o'r materion hynny rydych chi'n cyfeirio atyn nhw, sef nid yn unig y peth iawn i wneud, oherwydd ein bod ni eisiau cyflymu'r broses o gyflenwi mwy o dai cymdeithasol, ond hefyd mae yna lif cyson o incwm yn dod drwy'r rhent o dai cymdeithasol. Felly, mae'n gwneud synnwyr yn gyffredinol hefyd ar gyfer buddsoddi yma yng Nghymru. Dwi'n falch iawn o'r cyfraniad yna gennych chi yn cefnogi yr hyn rydym ni'n ei wneud o fewn Llywodraeth.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much for the question. The town centre taskforce that we're going to be announcing more about quite soon will address the structural challenges facing town centres, including looking at business rates and planning reform, and by working collaboratively with partners and maintaining a strong focus on delivery to help town centres adapt, attract investment and activity and thrive in the years ahead.

Bydd y tasglu canol trefi y byddwn ni'n cyhoeddi mwy amdano yn fuan iawn yn mynd i'r afael â'r heriau strwythurol sy'n wynebu canol trefi, gan gynnwys edrych ar ardrethi busnes a diwygio'r drefn gynllunio, a thrwy weithio ar y cyd â phartneriaid a chynnal ffocws cryf ar gyflawni i helpu canol trefi i addasu, denu buddsoddiad a gweithgarwch a ffynnu yn y blynyddoedd i ddod.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you for your answer, Minister. Given the range of issues and concerns that have been identified and brought to me, such as vacant and underused properties, no meaningful increase in footfall, and the need to support long-term private sector growth, alongside many other issues, it's essential that Members are provided with a comprehensive breakdown of how the Transforming Towns initiative money has been spent across Wales and how that is broken down by constituency or even by local authority area. As of last Thursday, this information was not currently available. Can you please tell us when you intend to publish this information so that Members can ensure that this money has been well spent?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. I can tell you this afternoon that Powys has benefited from more than £12.9 million in regeneration funding from the Welsh Government since 2021. This is under a previous administration, of course. This fund has been developing over the years. So, I am pleased to be able to announce that there is £12.9 million in Powys, including in Llandrindod, which is close to where you live, I believe, where support has been given to enable the restoration of a historic building, Auto Palace, creating a new business centre in the centre of town. In Newtown, I recently visited Hafan yr Afon, an important development that is transforming that part of the town. That has been supported with £1.1 million of funding. That building has been created, by the way, using the passive house approach, which is the most energy-efficient standard for building in the world, and that's happened in Newtown using some money from this fund. So, the information is there, and I'm sure that we can provide you with the full picture in each local authority too.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Medraf ddweud wrthych chi y prynhawn yma fod Powys wedi elwa ar fwy na £12.9 miliwn o gyllid adfywio Llywodraeth Cymru ers 2021. Mae hyn o dan y weinyddiaeth flaenorol, wrth gwrs. Mae'r gronfa yma wedi bod yn datblygu ar hyd y blynyddoedd. Felly dwi yn falch o fedru cyhoeddi bod £12.9 miliwn ym Mhowys, yn cynnwys yn Llandrindod, sydd yn agos i lle rydych chi'n byw, dwi'n credu, lle mae cymorth wedi cael ei roi i alluogi adfer adeilad hanesyddol Auto Palace, gan greu canolfan fusnes newydd yng nghanol y dre. Yn y Drenewydd, mi fues i yn ddiweddar yn Hafan yr Afon, datblygiad pwysig iawn sydd yn gweddnewid y rhan yna o'r dref. Mae hwnnw wedi cael ei gefnogi efo £1.1 miliwn o gyllid. Mae'r adeilad yna wedi cael ei greu, gyda llaw, efo dull passive house, sef y safon ddylunio fwyaf ynni effeithiol yn y byd, ac mae hwnna yn y Drenewydd ac wedi defnyddio peth arian allan o'r gronfa yma. Felly mae'r wybodaeth yna, a dwi'n siŵr y gallwn ni roi'r darlun cyfan fesul awdurdod lleol hefyd.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: I was delighted to hear yesterday of the Government's commitment to introduce the community right to buy. There are good examples of market towns that succeed in creating energy and activity, through a number of indigenous businesses rooted there. In my own constituency, there are a number of examples in Machynlleth of community groups buying community assets, such as churches and pubs and so on, and keeping them going for the benefit of the community and the local economy. Can the Cabinet Minister make a statement on community right to buy? Thank you.
documents.text_cy: Roeddwn i'n falch iawn i glywed ddoe am ymrwymiad y Llywodraeth i gyflwyno hawl y gymuned i brynu. Mae yna esiamplau da o drefi marchnad sy'n llwyddo creu bwrlwm ac egni, efo nifer o siopau a busnesau cynhenid wedi eu gwreiddio yno. Yn fy etholaeth i, mae yna nifer fawr o esiamplau ym Machynlleth o grwpiau cymunedol yn prynu asedau cymunedol, fel eglwysi a thafarndai ac ati, ac yn eu cadw'n fyw er lles y gymuned a'r economi leol. Gall y Gweinidog Cabinet wneud datganiad ar hawl y gymuned i brynu? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you very much for the question and I was very pleased to see that this announcement was part of the announcement on the Government's legislative programme. We are clearly committed to introducing a Bill on community right to buy and that will be a priority for us in the next few months now.

I am very aware of a great number of community groups that are keen to buy and to procure buildings that become empty in their communities, in order to turn them into assets that are of use to the community, to bring life to the community and to the high street quite often as well. I am very aware as well that there are barriers quite often to doing this, and sometimes they lose the opportunity to buy an asset and to transform it for community use. So, I do hope that we all will be able to agree on new legislation that will empower community groups, so that they can identify, in the first place, assets that are in their community that they might want to buy for the future, that we create a register identifying all of those, and that then, when they do come on the market, they get first offer on those properties, and then have an opportunity to make a business case and to continue with the process. That is not happening at the moment and opportunities are being missed.

I do intend to arrange a series of workshops over the summer now with partners, with communities, in order for us to have more detail in terms of this new legislation. I encourage you all to take part in that and encourage community groups in your constituencies to be part of this new important legislation.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr iawn am y cwestiwn ac roeddwn i'n hynod o falch o weld y cyhoeddiad yma yn rhan o'r cyhoeddiad am raglen ddeddfu y Llywodraeth yma. Dŷn ni wedi ymrwymo yn glir i gyflwyno Bil hawl cymunedol i brynu a bydd hynny'n flaenoriaeth gennym ni yn ystod y misoedd nesaf yma rŵan.

Dwi'n ymwybodol iawn o nifer fawr o grwpiau cymunedol sydd yn awyddus iawn i brynu ac i gaffael adeiladau sydd yn dod yn wag yn eu cymunedau nhw, er mwyn eu troi nhw'n asedau sydd o ddefnydd i'r gymuned, i fywiogi'r gymuned ac i fywiogi'r stryd fawr yn aml hefyd. Dwi'n ymwybodol hefyd fod rhwystrau yn dod ar draws hynny yn aml iawn, ac weithiau maen nhw'n colli'r cyfle i brynu ased ac i'w droi o at ddefnydd y gymuned. Felly, dwi yn gobeithio y byddwn ni i gyd yn gallu cytuno ar ddeddfwriaeth newydd fydd yn grymuso grwpiau cymunedol, fel eu bod nhw'n gallu adnabod, yn y lle cyntaf, asedau sydd yn eu cymunedau nhw y gallan nhw fod eisiau eu prynu i'r dyfodol, ein bod ni'n creu cofrestr yn nodi'r rheini i gyd, ac wedyn, pan maen nhw'n dod ar y farchnad, eu bod nhw'n cael y cynnig cyntaf i brynu, ac wedyn yn cael y cyfle i wneud achos busnes ac i fynd ymlaen efo'r broses. Dydy hynny ddim yn digwydd ar hyn o bryd ac mae yna gyfleoen yn cael eu colli.

Dwi yn bwriadu trefnu cyfres o weithdai dros fisoedd yr haf rŵan efo partneriaid, efo cymunedau, er mwyn inni gael mwy o gig ar yr asgwrn ar gyfer y ddeddfwriaeth newydd yma. Dwi'n eich annog chi i gyd i gymryd rhan yn hwnna ac annog grwpiau cymunedol yn eich etholaethau i fod yn rhan o'r ddeddfwriaeth newydd bwysig yma.

documents.text: Thank you. I now call on the party spokespeople to question the Cabinet Minister. Reform UK spokesperson, Francesca O'Brien.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Minister, England's Building Safety Act 2022 provided leaseholders with remediation orders and cost protection since 2022. Wales has only now delivered those same powers through the 2026 Act, and secondary legislation remains out to consultation until September—four years behind England, with only four out of 161 buildings being fully remediated. Given that England ran this exact same consultation process first, is the Welsh Government using the evidence and models already established to assess what's needed here and finally speed up the process?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
The new legislation that I was involved in drawing up in the last Senedd is more far-reaching than the legislation in England, which came into force some years ago. We are consulting on new regulations. I pushed the previous administration to include the ability to do that. So, we are consulting on new regulations that will mean that those people living in buildings that haven't been remediated, or who are facing additional costs because their service charges have increased because of work that has to be done—those people will have a route to tribunal, once those new regulations are in place. Now, that is a significant step forward, and it's going to take a little time, a few months, before we bring those regulations into force. I hope that everyone will support—I'm sure that you will support—those regulations.

There are three aspects of this in reality, aren't there? There is the new legislation in Wales, but there is also the remediation work, which is extremely slow in happening; it is extremely slow—we accept that. I have invited the companies that are continuing with this work to meet with me next month, where they will get a very clear message that this Government insists that that remediation work should be accelerated, and that the pace should go up.
documents.text_cy:
Mae'r ddeddfwriaeth newydd, yr oeddwn i'n rhan o'i chreu yn y Senedd ddiwethaf, yn fwy pellgyrhaeddol na'r ddeddfwriaeth yn Lloegr a ddaeth i rym rai blynyddoedd yn ôl. Mi ydyn ni yn ymgynghori ar reoliadau newydd. Fe wnes i wthio'r weinyddiaeth flaenorol i gynnwys y gallu yna. Felly, dŷn ni'n ymgynghori ar reoliadau newydd a fydd yn golygu bod pobl sydd yn byw mewn adeiladau sydd ddim wedi cael eu hadfer, neu sydd yn wynebu costau ychwanegol drwy fod eu costau gwasanaeth nhw wedi cynyddu'n sgil gwaith sydd yn gorfod cael ei wneud—bydd gan y bobl yna, unwaith mae'r rheoliadau yna'n dod i rym, lwybr i fynd â materion i dribiwnlys. Rŵan, mae hynny'n gam sylweddol ymlaen, ac mae o'n mynd i gymryd ychydig bach o amser, ychydig o fisoedd, tan ein bod ni'n dod â'r rheoliadau yna i rym. Dwi'n gobeithio y bydd pawb yn cefnogi—dwi'n siŵr y byddwch chi'n cefnogi—y rheoliadau yna.

Mae yna dair agwedd mewn gwirionedd, onid oes? Mae'r ddeddfwriaeth newydd sydd yng Nghymru, ond mae hefyd y gwaith adfer, sydd yn hynod o araf deg; mae o'n hynod o araf deg—dŷn ni'n derbyn hynny. Dwi wedi gwadd y cwmnïau sydd yn dal wrthi'n gwneud y gwaith i'm cyfarfod i fis nesaf, lle byddan nhw'n cael neges hollol glir fod y Llywodraeth yma yn mynnu bod y gwaith adfer yna yn cyflymu, a bod pace y gwaith yn cyflymu.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you, Minister. I believe you met with the Welsh Cladiators recently, so thank you for that. I'm sure that legislation does take time, but people are living in unsafe buildings, so I urge you to put pressure on those in the coming weeks. So, thank you for your answer to that.

I'd like to turn to housing. I note your statement on Monday confirmed your commitment, or reconfirmed your commitment, to create 20,000 social homes. Another statement, though, without an annual target means there is no way to measure your Government's performance. But, of course, housing is a question of supply and demand. There is a severe lack of accountability and transparency on who is actually living in our council and social housing. Data in England shows that significant amounts of housing are being allocated to people who are foreign nationals. So, Minister, will you commit your department to collect accurate nationality data from councils and housing associations so the people of Wales can know who will be living in these houses that taxpayers are subsidising?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you very much. To return to your point on the Cladiators, yes, I had a very constructive meeting with them on Monday. I was delighted to meet with them and to hear their concerns directly from them.

I made a written statement on Monday that confirmed the 20,000 social homes that are desperately needed in Wales, for everyone living in Wales. The way that social housing is allocated is a matter for local authorities. Local authorities have a housing register and homes are allocated according to need, and that's how it should be too. Therefore, I look forward to the work now of supplying more social homes. That's what's at the heart of the problem; the core of the housing crisis in Wales is that we don't have enough social homes. The supply isn't adequate to meet demand, and that is where we should be focusing our efforts always.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr. I fynd yn ôl at eich pwynt chi am y Cladiators, do, mi ges i gyfarfod adeiladol iawn efo nhw ddydd Llun. Roeddwn i'n falch iawn o'u cyfarfod nhw a chlywed eu pryderon nhw'n uniongyrchol ganddyn nhw.

Mi wnes i ddatganiad ysgrifenedig ddydd Llun a oedd yn cadarnhau yr 20,000 o dai cymdeithasol newydd sydd mawr eu hangen yng Nghymru, i bawb sydd yn byw yng Nghymru. Mae'r ffordd y mae tai cymdeithasol yn cael eu dynodi yn fater i awdurdodau lleol. Mae awdurdodau lleol yn casglu cofrestr tai ac mae tai yn cael eu dyrannu yn ôl angen, ac felly y dylai hi fod hefyd. Felly, dwi'n edrych ymlaen i'r gwaith rŵan o gyflenwi mwy o dai cymdeithasol. Dyna ydy gwraidd y broblem; gwraidd y broblem, gwraidd yr argyfwng tai yng Nghymru, ydy bod gennym ni ddim digon o dai cymdeithasol. Dydy'r cyflenwad ddim yn ddigonol i ateb y galw, ac yn y fan yna y dylem ni fod yn rhoi ein hymdrechion ni drwy'r amser.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you, Minister, for your answer. So, I take that as a 'no', but, don't panic, I thought that would be the reason, or the answer. But my team and I have been hard at work collecting this data from councils. We take Cardiff Council as an example; I'm sure our friend in the corner there will be listening with interest to this. The figures I've obtained under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 are shocking. I have them right here, and they will be made public as we speak.

So, let's look at the council's social housing stock of over 14,000 homes, where nationality is actually recorded. More than 31 per cent of lead tenants are foreign nationals. On the waiting list of over 9,000 properties, non-British applicants are 22 per cent of those recorded. And of the new tenancies handed out last year, almost 30 per cent of recorded allocations went to non-British applicants. Meanwhile, 35 per cent of those in temporary accommodation are foreign nationals, where the data is actually recorded. This equates to thousands of foreign national households in one city, which is being subsidised.

documents.text: A question, please.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: But here is the real scandal, that, of the 14,000 homes, the nationality—

documents.text:
Yes, I'm coming to it, thank you.

The nationality of 11,000 tenants, a whopping 70 per cent, is simply not recorded.

documents.text: Francesca, please can I have a question?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: So, will the Minister—? Instead of providing homes for nationalities, let's do for the people of Wales—

documents.text: A question, please.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Yes, absolutely. Will you commit to amending the allocation of housing and homelessness regulations, to restrict the eligibility and give preference to British applicants? And will you use your legal powers to set a standard compelling every registered social landlord in Wales to record and publish the nationality of applicants and tenants?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Before you respond, Minister—if I ask for a question, I do expect to hear a question. I don't expect someone to go 45 seconds over time. Thank you. Minister.

documents.text: I'm extremely disappointed with that question. Certainly, I don't know whether those statistics are accurate or not. But I am disappointed that you are insisting on pursuing this time and time again in this Chamber. As I said, the housing crisis has been created because of a shortage of social housing to meet demand. Everyone in Wales deserves a roof over their head and a safe place to live. So, I don't want to pursue this issue any further.

Mae pawb sydd yng Nghymru yn haeddu cael to uwch eu pen a lle saff i fyw. Felly, dwi ddim eisiau mynd ar ôl y mater yma ymhellach.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Mike Hedges.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer, and I will be under a minute.

When we discussed the current budget during the last Senedd, there was widespread support from Plaid Cymru, including you, Minister, that local government has substantial pressures. We overcame the ludicrous idea of a former finance Minister that the consumer price index indicated local government inflation, as if the change in price of items such as hummus, alcohol-free beer, pet grooming, motor homes, dashboard cameras, sheets of wrapping paper and bottled premium lager affected the cost of running local government services.

It is my understanding that the areas of local government expenditure on additional learning needs, social services, including elderly care and childcare, homelessness and prevention services are causing pressure on council budgets. Minister, is that your understanding, or do you wish to change that list?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. The final part of your question in terms of the great pressures facing local government is accurate, yes. You talk about ALN, you talk about social services, care services. Local government is under great pressure and has been cutting budgets for many years, and has had to cut budgets in some areas that are now under genuine pressure—planning, for example, and building regulations. Those services have reached a very difficult point, but, of course, they've done that in order to safeguard some of the services that support the most vulnerable people in our society. They haven't had a choice other than to do that, because of the austerity policies of the Conservatives across so many years, policies that have been emulated by the UK Labour Government as well.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Mae rhan olaf eich cwestiwn chi ynglŷn â'r pwysau mawr sydd yn wynebu llywodraeth leol yn gywir, ydy. Dŷch chi'n sôn am anghenion dysgu ychwanegol, dŷch chi'n sôn am wasanaethau cymdeithasol, gwasanaethau gofal. Mae llywodraeth leol o dan bwysau mawr iawn ac wedi bod yn cwtogi cyllidebau am flynyddoedd lawer, ac wedi bod yn gorfod cwtogi cyllidebau mewn rhai mannau sydd wirioneddol dan bwysau rŵan, o ran cynllunio, er enghraifft, a rheolau adeiladu. Mae'r gwasanaethau yna wedi cyrraedd pwynt anodd iawn, ond, wrth gwrs, maen nhw wedi gwneud hynny er mwyn diogelu rhai o'r gwasanaethau sydd yn cefnogi'r bobl fwyaf bregus o fewn ein cymdeithas ni. Doedd ganddyn nhw ddim dewis o ran gwneud hynny, oherwydd polisïau llymder y Torïaid ar draws cymaint o flynyddoedd, polisïau sydd wedi cael eu dilyn gan Lywodraeth Lafur y Deyrnas Unedig hefyd.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you for that answer; it was longer than I expected. We have agreed there is an increasing demand for certain council services. There are also environmental health and trading standards—vital services that need to be supported. Things like food safety and trading standards protect consumers. Minister, how much extra money have you and fellow Ministers asked for from the finance Minister to meet this increased demand out of the £247 million unallocated?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Well, you may remember that, in your budget as the Labour Government, Plaid Cymru did come to a position where we could abstain on that budget by negotiating, responsibly and maturely, £112.8 million, I believe, in additional funding for local government. That enabled your Government to pass a budget. It was very disappointing for me yesterday that that spirit of compromise and negotiation wasn't realised by your party. Plaid Cymru did bring a proposal worth £120 million over three years to the table, and that was rejected by Labour. That was for ALN, as you mentioned. You've decided that you don't want to go down that route.

For me, yesterday was a very sad day for Wales, where that spirit of trying to create some kind of collaboration for the benefit of the people of Wales—that got thrown out of the window yesterday, unfortunately. But I do hope that we can return to a situation where we put the people of Wales first in everything that we do.

Wel, mi fyddwch chi'n cofio, adeg eich cyllideb chi fel Llafur, fe wnaeth Plaid Cymru ddod i sefyllfa lle roeddem ni yn gallu atal ein pleidlais ar y gyllideb honno drwy negodi, yn gyfrifol ac yn aeddfed, £112.8 miliwn, dwi'n meddwl, yn ychwanegol ar gyfer llywodraeth leol. Mi alluogodd hynny i'ch Llywodraeth chi sefydlu cyllideb. Roedd yn hynod o siomedig gen i ddoe fod yr ysbryd yna o negodi a chyfaddawdu ddim wedi cael ei wireddu gan eich plaid chi. Mi oedd Plaid Cymru wedi dod â chynnig gwerth £120 miliwn dros dair blynedd i'r bwrdd, a chafodd hwnna ei wrthod gan Lafur. Roedd hwnna ar gyfer yr anghenion dysgu ychwanegol dŷch chi'n sôn amdano fo. Dŷch chi wedi penderfynu nad ydych chi ddim eisiau mynd lawr y llwybr yna.

I fi, roedd ddoe yn ddiwrnod trist iawn i Gymru, lle mae'r ysbryd yna o geisio creu cydweithio er mwyn pobl Cymru—fe aeth hwnna drwy'r ffenestr ddoe, mae arnaf i ofn. Ond dwi yn gobeithio y gallwn ni ddychwelyd at sefyllfa lle dŷn ni'n rhoi pobl Cymru yn gyntaf ym mhopeth dŷn ni'n ei wneud.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Welsh Conservatives' spokesperson, Peter Fox.
documents.text_cy: Llefarydd y Ceidwadwyr Cymreig, Peter Fox.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Cabinet Minister, thank you for your statement on Monday. I was hopeful that a statement like that would have come to this Chamber for a deeper debate, so I'll use one of my questions on it. While the ambition to increase the supply of social housing is absolutely welcomed, your written statement confirms that acquired properties will count towards the 20,000 homes target, alongside new-build developments. Now, many people will hear this announcement and assume it means 20,000 newly built social homes. However, by including the acquisitions, the target appears to rely in part on existing properties already within Wales's housing stock, rather than wholly on the creation of new homes. Cabinet Minister, can you tell us how many of the 20,000 additional social homes you expect to be delivered through acquisitions and how many will be genuinely new-build properties?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you very much for that question and for an opportunity to explain some of what was contained within the written statement issued on Monday. You're exactly right, we want that target of 20,000 to include vacant properties above shops on our high streets, and this will be part of the work of the town centre taskforce, of course, and how we accelerate the process to allow more vacant properties to come into our housing stock.

I do emphasise that I think it's important to be entirely transparent and, therefore, I have said that only homes that will remain as social homes for communities and families will be counted as part of that 20,000 target. Now, what exactly the percentage will be between new builds and acquisitions in terms of vacant properties and so on, I can't give you an exact figure on that. But, also in that statement made on Monday, I have spoken of community-led housing and I would like to include housing that's created through community groups—through the community right to buy, for example—and that we also include those within the target because they do provide a solution that is in keeping with those communities in rural areas and where the Welsh language prospers.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn yma ac am gyfle i esbonio ychydig bach am beth oedd yn y datganiad ysgrifenedig ddydd Llun. Yn hollol, mi ydyn ni am i'r targed o 20,000 yma gynnwys eiddo gwag uwchben siopau yn ein strydoedd mawr ni, a bydd hyn yn rhan o'r gwaith mae'r tasglu canol trefi yn mynd i fod yn edrych arno fo, wrth gwrs, a sut ydyn ni'n cyflymu'r broses i alluogi mwy o eiddo sydd yn wag ar hyn o bryd i ddod i mewn i'r stoc.

Dwi'n pwysleisio fy mod i'n meddwl ei fod o'n bwysig i fod yn hollol dryloyw ac, felly, dwi wedi dweud mai dim ond cartrefi fydd yn aros yn gartrefi cymdeithasol i gymunedau ac i deuluoedd fydd yn cael eu cyfrif fel rhan o'r 20,000. Rŵan, beth yn union fydd y canran rhwng y rhai newydd a'r rhai fydd yn dod drwy ddulliau eraill o ran eiddo gwag ac yn y blaen, allaf i ddim rhoi ffigwr i chi ar hynny yn union. Ond dwi hefyd, yn y datganiad yna ddydd Llun, wedi sôn am dai o dan arweiniad y gymuned, ac mi fyddwn i'n hoffi cynnwys tai sydd yn cael eu creu drwy grwpiau cymunedol—drwy'r hawl i brynu, er enghraifft—a'n bod ni'n cynnwys y tai yna hefyd o fewn y targed oherwydd maen nhw'n cynnig ateb cydnaws â chymunedau yn yr ardaloedd gwledig ac yn yr ardaloedd lle mae'r Gymraeg yn ffynnu.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. Very clearly, then, there needs to be quite a lot of data gathered so that we can ascertain just how many new houses we do need to build, and I hope that that work is ongoing. Turning back to town-centre regeneration, we know that town centres—and you'll agree—are the beating heart of our communities but continue to face those significant challenges. If we are to increase footfall, we need an environment in which businesses can thrive. Now, Cwmbran is a good example. It continues to demonstrate the importance of convenience for shoppers, with businesses there citing free parking as one of the factors behind strong visitor numbers. However, businesses across Wales continue to raise concerns about the high business costs, declining footfall, restrictive regulations and the difficulty of attracting customers back into the town centre. Now, regeneration isn't just about bringing new initiatives to the towns, but it's about preserving existing businesses and enabling them to survive. Cabinet Minister, working with the Cabinet Minister for Finance and through your town-centre task group, what specific measures are you prepared to consider or introduce to incentivise businesses to locate back in our town centres and help regenerate those struggling high streets?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you for that question and for your interest in this particular area. During this Government's first 100 days, we will be making a full announcement on the purpose of the new taskforce that we're currently establishing and its membership. Of course, it's the taskforce that will consider its specific remit, and I'm very eager for that to happen, rather than us, as a Government, setting out certain criteria. It's the people in that taskforce, in consultation with others, that will set the remit for that work. But I assume, having been involved in this sort of work for years, that looking at business rates and how we can make sustaining a shop in a town centre more attractive than being located in an out-of-town centre would be one area that they would look at, along with planning and how we can accelerate the process in order to convert vacant buildings in our town centres. But there's also this desire to look holistically at what public services can be brought into our town centres and how we can accelerate the planning process around that too. There's a great job of work to be done, but it's very exciting, and I look forward to working with the taskforce.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn ac am eich diddordeb chi yn y maes penodol yma. Yn ystod 100 niwrnod cyntaf y Llywodraeth yma, mi fyddwn ni'n gwneud cyhoeddiad llawn ynglyn â phwrpas y tasglu ac aelodaeth y tasglu newydd rydyn ni wrthi'n sefydlu. Wrth gwrs, y tasglu fydd yn edrych ar ei gylch gorchwyl yn benodol, felly, a dwi'n awyddus iawn i hynny ddigwydd, yn hytrach nag ein bod ni, fel Llywodraeth, yn gosod rhyw fath o feini prawf. Y bobl yn y tasglu yna, yn ymgynghori efo eraill, fydd yn gosod y cylch gorchwyl ar gyfer y gwaith. Ond mi fyddwn ni'n cymryd yn ganiataol, o fod wedi ymwneud â'r math yma o waith am flynyddoedd, y bydd edrych ar drethu busnes a sut gallwn ni wneud cynnal siop yng nghanol tref yn fwy atyniadol nag ydy hi i fod ar y cyrion mewn canolfan siopa, y byddai hwnna'n un maes, byddwn i'n meddwl, y byddan nhw'n edrych arno fo. Mae cynllunio hefyd a sut i gyflymu'r broses er mwyn trosi adeiladau gwag yng nghanol ein trefi ni. Ond hefyd, bydd yr awydd yma, mae'n siŵr, i edrych yn holistaidd ar ba wasanaethau cyhoeddus a allai ddod i mewn i ganol ein trefi ni a sut i gyflymu'r broses gynllunio o gwmpas hynny. Mae yna dasg fawr yna, ond mae'n dasg gyffrous, a dwi'n edrych ymlaen i gydweithio efo'r tasglu.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: 3. When will the Welsh Government update 'Planning Policy Wales'? OQ64366
documents.text_cy: 3. Pryd fydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn diweddaru 'Polisi Cynllunio Cymru'? OQ64366

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. 'Planning Policy Wales' is kept under continual review to ensure that it remains effective, relevant and responsive to emerging evidence. Officials are currently reviewing planning guidance, and they are doing so to identify which aspects may need to be updated in future to ensure that the planning framework reflects the priorities of this Welsh Government.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Mae 'Polisi Cynllunio Cymru' yn cael ei adolygu yn barhaus i sicrhau ei fod o'n parhau yn effeithiol, yn berthnasol, a’i fod o'n ymateb i’r dystiolaeth sy’n dod i’r amlwg. Mae swyddogion yn adolygu canllawiau cynllunio ar hyn o bryd. Maen nhw’n gwneud hyn gan nodi pa agweddau y gall fod angen eu diweddaru yn y dyfodol i sicrhau bod y fframwaith cynllunio yn adlewyrchu blaenoriaethau y Llywodraeth Cymru yma.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you. One area that I could say that definitely needs updating is the way that the Welsh Government's energy policy is in planning policy, especially regarding 'Future Wales: the national plan 2040'. We all know that is outdated in regard to industrial-scale wind turbines and pylons across a vast part of rural mid and west Wales. We all know about the 220m turbines that are going to be erected if Bute Energy have their way. That would absolutely decimate my communities. But, in 'Future Wales', it doesn't actually take into consideration the current size of those turbines that are currently being proposed. It also doesn't take into consideration the low-frequency noise that they generate as well. So, I'm asking you, Minister: are you willing to put a moratorium on these large-scale industrial plans for rural mid and west Wales, because unless planning policy is updated, we are going to see something potentially approved that will have devastating long-term impacts on communities without having updated planning guidance to make an informed decision?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you for the question, and I'm pleased that we do agree that we need to look seriously at 'Future Wales', namely the national plan, the top-tier plan on developments in Wales. It's under that, of course, that 'Planning Policy Wales' lies. So, we need to do the work on that highest level around the national spatial strategy and to include in that the current priorities for growth, infrastructure and regional development and transport. So, it does have statutory status, and I'm very eager, as the work has started to look at that highest level, to then see what needs to be changed in terms of the planning policies, including energy policy, electrification and new electrical lines, and so forth. So, I can assure you that that work is happening.
documents.text_cy: Diolch am y cwestiwn, ac rwy'n falch ein bod ni'n cytuno bod angen edrych o ddifrif ar 'Cymru'r Dyfodol', 'Future Wales', sef y cynllun cenedlaethol, yr haen uchaf yna o ddatblygu a datblygiadau yng Nghymru. O dan hwnna, wrth gwrs, mae 'Polisi Cynllunio Cymru' yn gorwedd, felly rydym ni angen gwneud y gwaith ar y lefel uchel yna o gwmpas strategaeth ofodol genedlaethol, gan roi yn hwnna y blaenoriaethau cyfoes ar gyfer twf, seilwaith, ynni, trafnidiaeth a datblygu rhanbarthol. Felly, mae ganddo fo statws statudol, a dwi'n awyddus iawn—mae'r gwaith wedi dechrau i edrych ar yr haen uchaf yna—wedyn i weld beth sydd angen ei newid o ran y polisïau cynllunio, gan gynnwys, wrth gwrs, y polisi ynni a pholisi ynglŷn â thrydaneiddio a llinellau trydan newydd, a'r materion yna i gyd. Felly, gallaf eich sicrhau chi fod y gwaith yn digwydd ar hwnna.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Diolch, Weinidog, for your commitment to championing a community-centred planning system and strengthening the voice of local people. Cymru is emerging as a significant location for data-centre development, with two designated UK Government AI growth zones. However, they have no dedicated use class and no mention in 'Planning Policy Wales', even though their scale and energy and water demands raise important questions for our environment and our planning system beyond their immediate locality. As you know, in my own constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, a data centre is proposed in Llanrumney, replacing the Cardiff east park and ride, which serves the University Hospital of Wales, and this has given rise to a controversy beyond the immediate locality. The proposed 150 MW facility, only a short distance from primary schools and local homes, will rely on fossil-fuelled gas turbines as well as polluting standby diesel generators. Will the Minister, therefore, set out what plans the Government has to review the planning requirements for data centres, and in particular look into the Cardiff east park-and-ride application, so that communities like Llanrumney don't end up paying the social and environmental price while the profit goes elsewhere? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. Unfortunately, I can't comment on specific developments in specific constituencies. Welsh Ministers are responsible for making decisions in those areas, and who knows with this particular issue, so I can't talk about that specifically. But you do bring forward an important point about how our planning policies and our strategies look at issues relating to data centres, which bring us back to the point made by James Evans, namely the need to look again at the main national development framework, 'Future Wales'. We do need to reform that. This is one example of why, and so that work is happening. During our first 100 days, there will be a specific announcement about the process that needs to happen with that. There is a specific process; we can't just sit down and change it. We have to go through a process, and we will be making an announcement about that during the first 100 days.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Yn anffodus, fedraf i ddim sôn am ddatblygiadau penodol mewn etholaethau penodol. Mae Gweinidogion Cymru yn gyfrifol am wneud penderfyniadau mewn meysydd fel yna, a phwy a ŵyr efo'r mater penodol yma, felly fedraf i ddim sôn yn benodol. Ond rydych chi'n dod â phwynt pwysig ymlaen ynglŷn â sut mae'n polisïau cynllunio ni, ein strategaethau ni, yn edrych ar faterion i wneud efo canolfannau data, sy'n mynd yn ôl at y pwynt roedd James Evans yn ei wneud—yr angen i fod yn edrych eto ar y prif fframwaith datblygu cenedlaethol, 'Future Wales'. Mae angen ei ddiwygio fo. Mae hon yn un enghraifft o pam, ac felly mae'r gwaith yna yn digwydd. Yn ystod ein 100 niwrnod cyntaf ni, mi fydd yna gyhoeddiad penodol ynglŷn â'r broses sydd angen digwydd efo hwnna. Mae yna broses benodol; fedrwn ni ddim jest eistedd i lawr a'i newid o. Mae'n rhaid mynd drwy broses, ac mi fyddwn ni'n cyhoeddi mwy am hynny yn ystod y 100 niwrnod cyntaf.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Wales needs more houses. You've said that today, Minister, but we heard in the press over the weekend developers and housing associations saying that it can take between three and five years to secure planning consent.
documents.text_cy: Mae ar Gymru angen mwy o dai. Rydych chi wedi dweud hynny heddiw, Weinidog, ond fe glywom ni yn y wasg dros y penwythnos ddatblygwyr a chymdeithasau tai yn sôn ei bod hi'n gallu cymryd rhwng tair a pum mlynedd i sicrhau caniatâd cynllunio.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: As you update 'Planning Policy Wales', can you confirm your intention, therefore, to make the planning system more permissive so that we can build the homes Wales needs and, indeed, build the industrial developments that Wales needs? Will you make it more permissive, or will you continue to risk letting the not-in-my-backyard brigade stop developments and delay developments that have overwhelming public benefit?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you very much. I do agree with you that we do need to accelerate the planning process, particularly in the area of housing. It's not acceptable that it takes years sometimes for developments to bear fruit. So, it is my intention to announce during the first 100 days that we will be making a call for evidence for reform of the planning system in the area of housing specifically, so that we can try to get professional people—people like you who have been council leaders and who understand the planning barriers at the grass roots—to bring evidence forward so that we can proceed to reform 'Planning Policy Wales', and to make it more fit for purpose and more swift in response to the needs of our communities.

There were two Acts that were passed at the end of the last Senedd that bring planning policies together, and I do think that that in itself is going to help issues, but it doesn't go halfway far enough.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr iawn. Dwi'n cytuno efo chi—mae angen cyflymu'r broses gynllunio, yn enwedig yn y maes tai. Dydy o ddim yn dderbyniol ei bod hi'n cymryd blynyddoedd weithiau i ddatblygiadau ddwyn ffrwyth. Felly, mae hi'n fwriad gen i i gyhoeddi yn ystod y 100 niwrnod cyntaf y byddwn ni'n gwneud galwad am dystiolaeth ar gyfer diwygio'r drefn gynllunio yn y maes tai yn benodol, er mwyn ceisio cael pobl broffesiynol—pobl fel chi sydd wedi bod yn arwain cyngor ac sydd yn deall ar lawr gwlad beth ydy'r rhwystrau cynllunio hynny—i ddod â thystiolaeth ymlaen, fel ein bod ni'n gallu mynd ati o ddifrif i ddiwygio 'Polisi Cynllunio Cymru' ac i'w wneud o'n fwy pwrpasol ac yn fwy cyflym ar gyfer anghenion ein cymunedau ni.

Mae yna ddwy Ddeddf wedi cael eu pasio ar ddiwedd y Senedd ddiwethaf sydd yn dod â'r polisïau cynllunio ynghyd, a dwi'n meddwl bod hwnna yn ei hun yn mynd i fod yn help, ond dydy o ddim yn mynd hanner digon pell.
