documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: 4. What steps is the Welsh Government taking to ensure that local government procurement supports Welsh businesses and maximises the economic benefits of public spending within Wales? OQ64389
documents.text_cy: 4. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod caffael llywodraeth leol yn cefnogi busnesau Cymru ac yn gwneud y mwyaf o fanteision economaidd gwariant cyhoeddus yng Nghymru? OQ64389

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much, and, again, this is an important question. This Government does want to go further than we currently go in this area, and to provide greater flexibility to local government to use procurement to support Welsh businesses and strengthen local supply chains. This isn't directly in my portfolio, but I have sought information about it. So, I hope I can respond to your supplementary question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr, ac mae hwn eto'n gwestiwn pwysig. Mae'r Lywodraeth yma eisiau ein gweld ni'n gallu mynd ymhellach nag ydyn ni ar hyn o bryd yn y maes yma, a rhoi mwy o hyblygrwydd i lywodraeth leol ddefnyddio caffael i gefnogi busnesau Cymru a chryfhau cadwyni cyflenwi lleol. Dydy hwn ddim yn fy mhortffolio i'n uniongyrchol, ond dwi wedi chwilio am wybodaeth amdano fo. Felly, gobeithio y medraf i ateb eich ail gwestiwn chi.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Diolch, Minister. I've been approached by A.N. Richards, a well-established Welsh supplier based in Froncysyllte in my constituency, which has raised concerns about the increasing use of England-based procurement frameworks by Welsh local authorities, and the barriers steering procurement officers towards them. The company says the English procurement portal, used, in this case, for fleet purchasing, is more user friendly and efficient than its Welsh equivalent. As a result, procurement officers may be drawn towards England-based frameworks, creating a structural disadvantage for Welsh suppliers and undermining the Welsh Government's aim of maximising the economic benefit of public spending within Wales. What assessment has the Welsh Government made of the impact that the design and usability of Welsh procurement systems have on local authority procurement decisions? And what steps is it taking to improve Wales-based procurement routes and ensure more local authority spending is retained in the Welsh economy?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much for that supplementary question, and the relevant Minister has just walked into the Chamber. [Interruption.] Oh, it's you. Good. The finance Minister, rather, has heard your request, and, having sought information, I am given to understand that there will be a new procurement policy statement published to actually increase public expenditure in Wales. Things have improved, and there was the procurement Act 2023, passed in this Senedd, which has made it easier for SMEs to actually bid for opportunities, and for Business Wales, which provides tailored support for Welsh businesses to help them to expand, grow and strengthen, and to understand the complex procurement processes. But I do know that the Minister for finance is very eager, as am I, to go much further within our powers in this Senedd. So, thank you.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi am y cwestiwn atodol yna, ac mae'r Gweinidog perthnasol newydd gerdded i mewn i'r Siambr. [Torri ar draws.] O, ti ydy o. O, da iawn. Mae'r Gweinidog cyllid, felly, wedi clywed eich cais chi, a dwi'n deall, ar ôl holi am wybodaeth, fod yna ddatganiad polisi caffael newydd yn mynd i fod yn cael ei gyhoeddi yn adlewyrchu'r cynllun uchelgeisiol i gynyddu gwariant cyhoeddus yng Nghymru. Mae pethau wedi gwella, ac roedd yna Ddeddf caffael 2023, a basiwyd yn y Senedd yma, sydd wedi'i gwneud hi'n haws i fusnesau bach a chanolig gystadlu am gyfleoedd, ac i Fusnes Cymru, sy'n cynnig cymorth wedi’i deilwra i fusnesau Cymru i'w helpu nhw i ehangu, i dyfu a chryfhau, ac i ddeall y prosesau caffael cymhleth sydd yna. Ond dwi'n gwybod bod y Gweinidog cyllid yn awyddus iawn, fel ydw i, i fynd llawer iawn pellach o fewn ein grymoedd ni yn y Senedd yma. Felly, diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you for that and obviously this will probably go to the financial Minister as well, so I'm going to carry on, as the Member just carried on. Small businesses are the backbone of our community in Wales, but many are effectively shut out of public sector contracts before the process has even begun. Large companies have dedicated teams to deal with procurement, legal requirements and lengthy tender documents. Small local businesses may have one person trying to do all of that while also running a day-to-day business. If the Welsh Government genuinely wants more public money to stay in Wales, it must make sure that local businesses have a fair chance to compete. So, my question is: what practical support will the Welsh Government provide to simplify the procurement process and help Welsh businesses bid successfully for local authority contracts? And will the Minister support publishing council-by-council figures showing how much public spending is awarded directly to Welsh businesses in respect of transparency? Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you very much for that question, and for your support too in increasing public procurement for local businesses. Now, we know that there is work to be done in this area—there are so many examples of where it isn't currently working. As I say, things have improved a little, but the pace of that improvement has been slow since the Social Partnership and Public Procurement (Wales) Act was passed in 2023. That legislation does place a duty on contracting authorities to improve economic, social, environmental and cultural well-being through procurement, including considering access for SMEs, and fair work is addressed in the legislation too.

But, of course, there is some way to go, as you say. I also hope that the new food strategy will address some of these issues, because local food production and creating local supply chains for the public sector again is a way of strengthening local businesses and the agricultural sector and so on. So, there are a number of different issues that can coalesce here, including, of course, the work that the national development body will do to support businesses so that they feel that they can access these contracts that are offered.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn yna ac am eich cefnogaeth chithau hefyd i gynyddu'r caffael cyhoeddus i fusnesau lleol. Mae rhywun yn gwybod bod yna waith i’w wneud yn y maes yma—gymaint o enghreifftiau lle dydy o ddim yn gweithio ar hyn o bryd. Fel dwi'n dweud, mae pethau wedi gwella ychydig, ond araf ydy pace y gwella yna ers pasio'r Ddeddf Partneriaeth Gymdeithasol a Chaffael Cyhoeddus (Cymru) yn 2023. Mae'r Ddeddf yna yn gosod dyletswydd ar awdurdodau contractio i wella llesiant economaidd cymdeithasol, amgylcheddol a diwylliannol drwy gaffael, gan gynnwys ystyried mynediad ar gyfer busnesau bach a chanolig, a hefyd gwaith teg yn cael sylw yn y Ddeddf yna.

Ond, wrth gwrs, mae yna le i fynd, fel rydych chi'n dweud. Dwi hefyd yn gobeithio y bydd y strategaeth bwyd newydd yn cyfarch rhan o hwn, oherwydd mae cynhyrchu bwyd yn lleol a chreu cadwyni cyflenwi lleol ar gyfer y sector cyhoeddus hefyd yn ffordd o atgyfnerthu busnesau lleol a’r sector amaethyddol ac yn y blaen. Felly, mae yna nifer o wahanol faterion medrith dod ynghyd yn fan hyn, gan gynnwys hefyd, wrth gwrs, y gwaith y bydd yr awdurdod ddatblygu cenedlaethol newydd yn gallu ei wneud i gefnogi busnesau er mwyn teimlo eu bod nhw'n cael mynediad at y contractau yma sydd yn cael eu cynnig.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: 5. What action is the Welsh Government taking to meet its social housing targets? OQ64420
documents.text_cy: 5. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gyrraedd ei thargedau tai cymdeithasol? OQ64420

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. We are already taking action through the social housing grant and the transitional accommodation capital programme. This will tackle homelessness, reduce reliance on temporary accommodation and ensure that people across Wales have access to quality homes that are energy efficient. We're also establishing Unnos to accelerate the delivery of social housing across Wales.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Rydym ni eisoes yn cymryd camau drwy'r grant tai cymdeithasol a rhaglen gyfalaf llety trosiannol. Mi fydd hyn yn mynd i'r afael â digartrefedd, yn lleihau dibyniaeth ar lety dros dro ac yn gwneud yn siŵr bod gan bobl ledled Cymru fynediad at gartrefi o safon sy'n effeithlon o ran ynni. Rydym ni hefyd yn sefydlu Unnos i gyflymu'r broses o ddarparu tai cymdeithasol ar draws Cymru.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Diolch, Minister. Following on from what our Reform spokesperson has already said, I would like to urge you further to have annual targets so that any progress on delivering those 20,000 social homes can be easily tracked. We all know that Rome wasn't built in a day, but we would like to know how many homes will be built in Wales in a year.

Minister, following alongside those aims to get people into social housing as soon as possible, I was wondering whether the pots of money currently given to registered social landlords to adapt old stock—current old stock—to meet the demand and needs of those on current waiting lists will continue.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
Thank you very much. I do understand the point about having annual targets, but often work can happen towards the end of the period. So, setting rigid annual targets, therefore, the same target every year, wouldn't reflect the reality of the situation, because it doesn't happen in a linear way. Often, the process starts and it accelerates towards the end of the period. But I will look to see how transparent—. I want to be transparent, and I want to provide you with as much information as possible. I'm going to be asking to have an operational role in some of the meetings that are happening with civil servants for me to understand exactly what's going on.

And in terms of the housing associations bringing old stock up to standard, there is another grant available for that, the optimised retrofit scheme, which is very successful in terms of improving the condition of our social housing. We need to accelerate that, and we also need to see the private sector stock progressing as well, so that the quality of our housing everywhere and across all tenacies improves.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr iawn. Dwi'n deall y pwynt ynglŷn â chael targedau blynyddol, ond yn aml mae yna waith yn gallu digwydd tua diwedd y cyfnod. Felly, fuasai roi targedau blynyddol rigid mewn ffordd, felly, yr un un targed bob blwyddyn, ddim yn adlewyrchu realiti'r sefyllfa, achos dydy o ddim yn digwydd mewn ffordd linear. Yn aml iawn, mae'r broses yn cychwyn ac mae'r cyflymder yn digwydd tua diwedd y cyfnod. Ond mi wnaf i edrych i weld pa mor dryloyw—. Dwi eisiau bod yn dryloyw, a dwi am roi cymaint o wybodaeth i chi ag sy’n bosib. Dwi’n mynd i fod yn gofyn rŵan i fod yn rhan weithredol o rai o’r cyfarfodydd yma sydd yn digwydd efo’r gweision sifil imi gael deall yn union beth sydd yn mynd ymlaen.

Ac o ran y cymdeithasau tai yn dod â hen stoc i fyny i bwrpas, mae yna grant arall ar gyfer hwnna, yr optimised retrofit scheme, sydd yn llwyddiannus iawn yn gwella cyflwr ein tai cymdeithasol ni. Mae eisiau cyflymu hynny, ac mae eisiau hefyd gweld y stoc yn y sector preifat yn gallu symud ymlaen hefyd, fel bod ansawdd ein tai ni ym mhob man ac ar draws pob deiliadaeth yn gwella.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: 6. What progress has the Welsh Government made towards establishing a tenure-neutral retrofitting programme? OQ64397
documents.text_cy: 6. Pa gynnydd mae Llywodraeth Cymru wedi'i wneud tuag at sefydlu rhaglen ôl-osod niwtral o ran deiliadaeth? OQ64397

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. That takes us on very neatly from that previous response, because progress is being made, and, certainly, in our manifesto, you will recall that establishing a tenure-neutral retrofit programme was a crucial part of that. So, I hope that that will lead to a supplementary question—I forget that there's a supplementary question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Mae hwnna’n cario ymlaen yn daclus iawn o’r ateb diwethaf yna, achos mae yna gynnydd yn cael ei wneud, ac, yn sicr, yn ein maniffesto ni, byddwch chi'n cofio bod sefydlu rhaglen ôl-osod sydd yn niwtral o ran deiliadaeth yn hollbwysig. Felly, gobeithio bod hynny'n arwain at ail gwestiwn—dwi'n anghofio bod yna ail gwestiwn.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: I warmly welcome the Welsh Government's commitment to a national home retrofitting programme. Good housing is good health. Better-insulated homes will not only reduce energy bills and carbon emissions, they also improve people's health and reduce pressure on the NHS. Public Health Wales estimates that tackling excess cold in Welsh homes alone can save the NHS more than £40 million a year. Living in cold, damp and mouldy homes also increases the risk of respiratory illnesses, particularly in children and older people. So, Cabinet Minister, can you outline how the Welsh Government's retrofitting programme will prioritise tackling damp, mould and excess cold in homes so that it improves public health, reduces pressure on the NHS and lowers energy bills for families across Wales?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. There are a number of reasons why it's important that we improve the standard of our housing. One is to decarbonise so that we in Wales contribute less to climate change through our housing sector. Housing contributes around 11 per cent of carbon emissions in Wales, and I am very eager to see that reduced, and having a plan to decarbonise homes is very important. But there are benefits in terms of reducing bills as a result of making our homes more energy efficient—it's important that we consider that—and fuel poverty is also an issue in Wales, and it'll help us tackle poverty more generally. But also there is the impact on health, which is crucially important, and I am having discussions with the Deputy Minister in relation to preventative work, because, for me, housing is central to improving people's health, and we can improve health outcomes for our nation by having a clear focus on improving our housing standards. I will be going on Thursday to see—it's social housing—how retrofit programmes have helped a particular family there, and I'll be making further announcements on this specific area in our first 100 days.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn. Mae yna nifer o resymau, onid oes, pam mae hi’n bwysig inni fod yn gwella cyflwr ein tai ni. Un rheswm ydy er mwyn eu datgarboneiddio nhw er mwyn ein bod ni yng Nghymru yn cyfrannu llai drwy ein tai ni tuag at newid hinsawdd. Mae tai yn cyfrannu 11 y cant o allyriadau carbon yng Nghymru ar hyn o bryd, a dwi'n awyddus iawn i weld hynna yn gostwng, ac mae cael cynllun i datgarboneiddio tai yn hollbwysig. Ond mae manteision ynglŷn â biliau, costau biliau yn dod i lawr oherwydd ein bod ni'n gwneud ein tai yn fwy ynni effeithiol—mae'n bwysig i ni edrych ar hynny—ac mae hefyd tlodi tanwydd yn broblem yng Nghymru, so mae o'n mynd i fod yn ein helpu ni i daclo tlodi. Ond hefyd mae'r effaith ar iechyd yn hollbwysig, a dwi yn cael trafodaethau efo'r Dirprwy Weinidog ar waith ataliol, oherwydd, i fi, mae tai yn hollol ganolog i wella iechyd pobl, ac mi fedrwn ni wella deilliannau iechyd ein gwlad ni drwy roi ffocws clir ar wella cyflwr ein tai ni. Dwi'n mynd dydd Iau i weld—tŷ cymdeithasol ydy o—sut mae'r cynlluniau gwella wedi helpu teulu penodol yn y fanna, ac mi fyddaf i'n gwneud mwy o gyhoeddiadau ynglŷn â'r maes penodol yma hefyd yn y 100 diwrnod cyntaf.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you. And the last question, Minister, Anna Nicholl.
documents.text_cy: Diolch. A'r cwestiwn olaf, Weinidog, Anna Nicholl.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: 7. Will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the Government’s plans to review the funding formula for local government? OQ64400
documents.text_cy: 7. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf am gynlluniau'r Llywodraeth i adolygu'r fformiwla ariannu ar gyfer llywodraeth leol? OQ64400

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you very much. I discussed this particular review of the funding formula with the finance sub-group on 8 July. The finance sub-group is the sub-group of the WLGA dealing with these issues.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Mi wnes i drafod yr adolygiad penodol yma ar y fformiwla gyllido efo'r is-grŵp cyllid ar 8 Gorffennaf. Yr is-grŵp cyllid ydy'r is-grŵp o dan y WLGA sydd yn ymdrin â'r materion yma.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you. Ceredigion and Pembrokeshire are among the most rural authorities in Wales. People in rural Wales face higher living costs while often earning lower wages, and an ageing population is increasing the pressure on public services that are already under immense strain. For too long, rural councils have had to do more with less. The current funding formula does not reflect the true cost of delivering services across dispersed rural communities. Rural councils need a fair deal. Will the Cabinet Minister, therefore, commit to working in partnership with rural councils throughout this funding formula review?
documents.text_cy: Diolch. Mae Ceredigion a sir Benfro ymysg yr awdurdodau mwyaf gwledig Cymru. Mae pobl yng Nghymru wledig yn wynebu costau byw uwch tra, yn aml, yn ennill cyflogau is, ac mae poblogaeth sy'n heneiddio yn cynyddu'r pwysau ar wasanaethau cyhoeddus sydd yn barod dan straen enfawr. Am rhy hir, mae cynghorau gwledig wedi gorfod gwneud mwy gyda llai. Nid yw'r fformiwla cyllid presennol yn adlewyrchu'r gwir gost o ddarparu gwasanaethau ar draws cymunedau gwledig gwasgaredig. Mae angen bargen deg ar gynghorau gwledig. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet, felly, ymrwymo i weithio mewn partneriaeth gyda chynghorau gwledig drwy gydol yr adolygiad fformiwla cyllid yma?

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text:
I will. I will commit to work not only with the rural councils, but with councils across Wales—urban councils too, because I am entirely clear that this is work that should be undertaken collaboratively. As you mentioned, the rural aspect is important, but deprivation is also important, and there is, of course, deprivation in rural areas too.

Now, the purpose of the review is to decide whether change is needed, and, if we are to make changes, that that fairly reflects needs across Wales in different areas. The work has commenced, and, to date, the council leaders have been providing very constructive input to that work, and we will continue with that work. We will be commissioning an external review in order to ensure that the evidence is accurate and that the work is happening in a way that is transparent, and that everyone can understand what is happening. So, I look forward to seeing that bear fruit too. They will be looking at experiences in other countries—as well as focusing on Wales, they will look to see how distribution formulas work in different countries. Thank you.
documents.text_cy:
Gwnaf. Gwnaf i ymrwymo i weithio nid yn unig efo cynghorau gwledig, ond efo cynghorau ar draws Cymru—cynghorau trefol hefyd, oherwydd dwi yn hollol glir mai gwaith rydym ni'n ei wneud efo'n gilydd ydy hwn. Fel rydych chi'n sôn, mae'r agwedd wledig yn un bwysig, ond mae amddifadedd yn bwysig hefyd, ac, wrth gwrs, mae amddifadedd yn digwydd hefyd mewn ardaloedd gwledig.

Pwrpas yr adolygiad ydy ceisio gweld a oes angen newid, ac, os ydym ni'n mynd i newid, fod hynny'n adlewyrchu'n deg yr anghenion ar draws Cymru mewn gwahanol feysydd. Mae'r gwaith wedi dechrau ac, hyd yma, mae arweinwyr cyngor wedi bod yn rhoi mewnbwn adeiladol iawn i mewn i'r gwaith, ac mi fyddwn ni'n para efo'r gwaith. Mi fyddwn ni'n comisiynu adolygiad allanol i wneud yn siŵr bod y dystiolaeth yn gywir a bod y gwaith yn digwydd mewn ffordd sydd yn dryloyw ac i bawb gael deall beth sydd yn mynd ymlaen. Felly, dwi'n edrych ymlaen at weld ffrwyth y gwaith yna hefyd. Byddan nhw'n edrych ar brofiadau mewn gwledydd eraill—yn ogystal â rhoi ffocws ar Gymru, byddan nhw'n edrych i weld sut mae fformiwlâu dosbarthu yn gweithio mewn gwledydd eraill. Diolch.

documents.item: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
documents.text: Thank you, Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Weinidog.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: We move on now to topical questions—Mair Rowlands.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn ymlaen i gwestiynau amserol—Mair Rowlands.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: 1. Will the Cabinet Minister make a statement on the wildfire in Sychnant Pass? TQ1484
documents.text_cy: 1. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet ddatganiad ar y tân gwyllt ym Mwlch Sychnant? TQ1484

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Thank you very much. The fire is under control now, thanks to the efforts of the North Wales Fire and Rescue Service and all of the partners. This reminds us of the climate change threat and the need for all public services to adapt to that.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Mae'r tân bellach dan reolaeth, a diolch i ymdrechion Gwasanaeth Tân ac Achub Gogledd Cymru a'r holl bartneriaid. Mae hyn yn ein hatgoffa ni o fygythiad newid hinsawdd a'r angen i bob gwasanaeth cyhoeddus addasu i hynny.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text:
Thank you, Minister. The frightening sights that we saw on Conwy mountain over the weekend have not only had a direct impact on residents, communities, farmers, local businesses and nature, but they have also raised serious questions about the very real impact that climate change is having on the planet.

I'd like to start by placing on record once again my sincere thanks to the emergency services, the local authority and to nearby communities for their swift and determined response in the face of the crisis over recent days. Dirprwy Lywydd, as I mentioned in the Chamber yesterday, I'm pleased that the worst of the crisis is now behind us. However, many of my constituents are still asking questions about what the response will be to the damage and challenges posed by this wildfire. I would appreciate, therefore, if the Cabinet Minister could provide further details on how the Welsh Government will co-ordinate efforts with local stakeholders to start the work of restoring the 200 acres of agricultural and forestry land that was destroyed. I'd also like to know if measures will be put in place to safeguard residents who have respiratory problems as a result of the damage done to air quality in the local area.

And finally, the events of the weekend will have certainly been a blow to farmers and local businesses. I would appreciate it, therefore, if the Minister could tell us of any support that may be available to support them. And as I said earlier, we should all in this Chamber be concerned about what the events on the Conwy mountain, as well as similar incidents at Braichmelyn forest in Bethesda, tell us about the existential threat of climate change. I was pleased to hear the Trefnydd agree yesterday that we need a more comprehensive plan in place for such incidents in the future. I would appreciate, therefore, if the Cabinet Minister could expand on what measures the Welsh Government will put in place to prevent such incidents from becoming common across Wales, and to ensure that we are as well prepared as possible if these incidents do arise in future. Thank you.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch. Mae'r golygfeydd brawychus a gwelsom ar fynydd Conwy dros y penwythnos nid yn unig wedi cael effaith uniongyrchol ar drigolion, cymunedau, ffermwyr, busnesau lleol a byd natur, ond maent hefyd wedi codi cwestiynau difrifol ynglŷn â'r effaith gwirioneddol mae newid hinsawdd yn ei gael ar y blaned.

Hoffwn ddechrau drwy roi ar y cofnod unwaith eto fy niolch diffuant i'r gwasanaethau brys, yr awdurdod lleol ac i gymunedau cyfagos am eu hymateb cyflym a phendant yn wyneb yr argyfwng dros y dyddiau diwethaf. Ddirprwy Lywydd, fel y soniais yn y Siambr ddoe, rwy'n falch bod y gwaethaf o'r argyfwng y tu ôl i ni erbyn hyn. Serch hynny, mae nifer o fy etholwyr yn dal i ofyn cwestiynau am beth fydd yr ymateb, rŵan, i'r difrod a'r heriau a grëwyd gan y tân gwyllt. Gwerthfawrogwn, felly, pe gallai'r Gweinidog Cabinet roi mwy o fanylion ar sut bydd Llywodraeth Cymru'n cydlynu ymdrechion gyda'r rhanddeiliad lleol i ddechrau ar y gwaith o ail-adfer y 200 erw o dir amaethyddol a choedwigol a ddifethwyd. Hoffwn hefyd wybod os bydd mesurau'n cael eu cyflwyno i warchod trigolion sydd gyda phroblemau anadlu a resbiradaeth yn sgil y difrod a wnaed i ansawdd aer yr ardal leol.

Ac yn olaf, bydd digwyddiadau'r penwythnos yn sicr wedi bod yn ergyd i ffermwyr a busnesau lleol. Byddwn yn gwerthfawrogi, felly, pe gallai'r Gweinidog sôn am unrhyw gymorth fydd ar gael i'w cefnogi nhw. Ac fel y dywedais ynghynt, dylem ni i gyd yn y Siambr hon fod yn bryderus o'r hyn mae digwyddiadau ar fynydd Conwy, ynghyd â digwyddiadau tebyg yng nghoedwig Braichmelyn ym Methesda, yn ei ddweud wrthym am fygythiad dirfodol newid hinsawdd. Roeddwn yn falch o glywed y Trefnydd yn cytuno ddoe fod angen cynllun mwy cynhwysfawr yn ei le ar gyfer digwyddiadau tebyg yn y dyfodol. Gwerthfawrogwn, felly, pe gallai'r Gweinidog Cabinet ymhelaethu ychydig ar ba fesurau bydd Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cyflwyno i atal digwyddiadau tebyg rhag bod yn gyffredin ar draws Cymru, a sicrhau ein bod ni wedi paratoi gymaint â phosib, os ydy digwyddiadau fel hyn yn codi yn y dyfodol. Diolch.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text:
Thank you very much for bringing this issue forward before the Senedd. One thinks about the people who were affected by this fire. I can only imagine how frightened they must have been during that period when the flames were roaring on the mountain in Penmaenmawr, an area I've very familiar with. Thirty-six households had to flee their homes during the work of putting out the fire, but luckily they could return home on Monday evening. Conwy council provided temporary accommodation for those who needed it, so we are very grateful to Conwy council for their work and very grateful to Natural Resources Wales, and, of course, to the fire service. Fighting wildfires is very difficult and dangerous work, and we need to pay tribute to all the firefighters in north Wales and the partner agencies who responded so quickly to this event and kept communities and people safe.

You asked what support the Welsh Government can provide. Well, of course, we are working with local partners. The county council is in all likelihood the first port of call in terms of understanding the problems that may continue now because of what's happened, and also NRW in terms of restoring the land and any work that needs to happen on the nature side of things. But you're right, this is shocking and makes us realise the severity of the situation in terms of the climate, the nature emergency and climate emergency that we're facing here. I don't think anybody could start to deny that that's very real. Between these fires and this incredible heat that we've had, which is also affecting people in very negative ways, we genuinely have to tackle this crisis facing us in Wales.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr iawn i chi am ddod â'r mater yma gerbron y Senedd. Mae rhywun yn meddwl am y bobl gafodd eu heffeithio gan y tân yma. Dwi ond yn gallu dychmygu gymaint o ofn roedden nhw'n byw ynddo fo yn ystod y cyfnod yna pan oedd y fflamau yn rhuo ar y mynydd ym Mhenmaenmawr, ardal dwi'n gyfarwydd iawn â hi. Mi fu'n rhaid i 36 o aelwydydd adael eu cartrefi yn ystod y gwaith diffodd y tân, ond yn lwcus mi oedd modd iddyn nhw fynd yn ôl adref nos Lun. Mi wnaeth cyngor Conwy ddarparu llety dros dro i'r rhai oedd ei angen, felly rydyn ni'n hynod o ddiolchgar i gyngor Conwy am eu gwaith nhw ac yn ddiolchgar i Gyfoeth Naturiol Cymru, ond wrth gwrs i'r gwasanaeth tân. Mae ymladd tanau gwyllt yn waith hynod o anodd a pheryglus, ac mae eisiau talu teyrnged i holl ddiffoddwyr tân y gogledd a'r asiantaethau partner sydd wedi gweithredu mor gyflym i ymateb i'r digwyddiad yma a chadw pobl a chymunedau yn ddiogel.

Rydych chi'n holi pa gefnogaeth gall Llywodraeth Cymru ei rhoi. Wel, wrth gwrs, rydyn ni'n gweithio efo'r partneriaid lleol. Y cyngor sir ydy'r lle cyntaf, debyg, i fod yn deall beth ydy'r problemau sydd efallai'n parhau rŵan oherwydd beth sydd wedi digwydd, a hefyd Cyfoeth Naturiol Cymru ynglŷn ag adfer y tir ac unrhyw waith sydd angen digwydd o ran yr ochr natur o bethau. Ond rydych chi'n iawn, mae hwn yn ein dychryn ni ac yn gwneud i ni sylweddoli difrifoldeb y sefyllfa o ran yr hinsawdd, yr argyfwng natur a hinsawdd rydyn ni'n wynebu yma. Dwi ddim yn meddwl y medrith neb ddechrau bod yn gwadu bod hwnna yn real iawn. Rhwng y tanau yma, rhwng y gwres llethol yma, sydd hefyd yn effeithio pobl mewn ffyrdd sydd yn negyddol iawn, mae'n rhaid i ni yn wirioneddol daclo'r argyfwng sydd yn ein hwynebu ni yng Nghymru.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Will the Welsh Government follow in the footsteps of the Scottish Government and develop a strategic action plan to address escalating wildfire threats in Wales?

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Thank you for your question, and I'm glad that—.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: I am pleased that you, like me, are concerned about the growth in the number of wildfires, not only in your constituency but across the whole of Wales. The Cabinet, the Government, this week have been discussing our carbon plan as a Government, how we in Wales will contribute to the huge task  of not only of tackling climate change, but also mitigating and adapting to it, as you've mentioned. I'm not sure exactly what Scotland has done, but we will certainly look at that.
documents.text_cy: Dwi'n falch eich bod chi yn poeni yr un fath â fi am y twf mewn tanau gwyllt, nid yn unig yn eich etholaeth chi ond ar draws Cymru. Mae'r Cabinet, y Llywodraeth, yr wythnos yma wedi bod yn trafod ein cynllun carbon ni fel Llywodraeth, sut ydyn ni yng Nghymru yn mynd i fod yn cyfrannu tuag at y dasg anferth, nid yn unig o daclo newid hinsawdd ond o liniaru ac addasu, fel rydych chi'n sôn. Dwi ddim yn siŵr beth mae'r Alban wedi'i wneud yn union, ond yn sicr mi fyddwn ni'n edrych ar hynny.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text:
Thank you, Mair, for putting your question in. We actually did table an emergency question ourselves, the Welsh Conservatives, first thing on Monday morning; somehow that seems to have been rejected. But I'm glad that you put one in as well. So, I would like to endorse all the thanks that have gone before me: North Wales Fire and Rescue Service, Conwy County Borough Council and other partner agencies. Their incredibly fast response saved considerably more acres.

I'd also like to pay tribute to local residents who evacuated quickly, but also did what they could to try and help. It could have been far more serious, though it was incredibly serious in itself. Our farmer, Gareth Wyn Jones, who had to go himself in searing heat to try and rescue pigs from up on the uplands. The impact that this fire has had on local residents who have been forced out of their homes, there have to be questions now, asking how we can support them, because it's a frightening experience. There were 36 homes evacuated, one family noting it was actually in their driveway, and 200 acres of land have been affected.

We all have to be cautious. I wonder whether some messaging could go out in terms of graphics or something. Do you know, you only need, these days, glass? If you're carrying clear glass on hot, dry grass, it can easily turn into a fire. Not a fully extinguished cigarette butt: we should not be having people, you know—. They can unintentionally spark a fire, leading to significant damage whilst also putting lives at risk.

It was a very, very resource-intensive, financial-resource-intensive operation for all those partner agencies. I suppose what I'm asking for is: will you put some resources forward now for the aftermath of this? Will you contact those partner agencies and see how your Government can financially support them? But we also need a strategic plan. I'm not a lover of strategic plans, but we need something in place, because this could happen again. We're only halfway through the summer; this could happen again and again, and I want to be sure that all those partner agencies and rescue services are not stuck for finance in any way, shape or form. Diolch.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Thank you very much, Janet, and I do agree with you. That family there, where the fire was very close to their home, that was very frightening, wasn't it? It's too early to know at present what caused this specific fire on the mountain in Penmaenmawr. Usually these fires happen earlier in the year, don't they? They happen between March and May, but they're increasingly happening in the summer now, which is also an indication of the climate change that is happening. And you're right, I think that we do need to get that messaging out that people need to be very careful when using barbecues, when discarding cigarette butts and when leaving glass behind—glass can cause a fire when there is sunlight on it, and that can spread across the vegetation, which is very dry at this time of year, and we've had very little rain. So, as I said, we really do need to think about prioritising tackling climate change, and think about the mitigation measures and the adaptations that we need to undertake in all our lives. In terms of the support and financial support, Welsh Government officials will be talking to all the agencies now to see exactly where we can help and what exactly the implications of the fire are.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr iawn, Janet, a dwi'n cyd-fynd efo chi. Y teulu yna lle roedd y tân yn agos iawn at eu cartref nhw, roedd hynny yn ddychrynllyd iawn, onid oedd? Mae'n rhy gynnar i wybod ar hyn o bryd beth wnaeth achosi'r tân penodol yma ar y mynydd ym Mhenmaenmawr. Fel arfer, mae'r tanau yma yn digwydd yn gynt yn y flwyddyn, onid ydyn? Maen nhw'n digwydd rhwng mis Mawrth a mis Mai, ond maen nhw yn gynyddol yn digwydd yn yr haf, sydd eto yn arwydd o'r newid hinsawdd sydd yn digwydd. Ac mi ydych chi'n iawn, dwi'n meddwl bod eisiau i ni gael y neges yna allan, bod eisiau i bobl fod yn hynod ofalus wrth ddefnyddio barbeciws, wrth daflu pennau sigaréts, wrth adael gwydr ar ôl—mae gwydr yn gallu tanio pan fydd haul arno fo, ac yn gallu lledaenu ar draws y llystyfiant sydd yn sych iawn yr adeg yma o'r flwyddyn, a dydyn ni ddim wedi cael fawr ddim glaw. Felly, fel roeddwn i'n dweud, mae eisiau i ni wirioneddol feddwl ein bod ni'n blaenoriaethu taclo'r newid hinsawdd, a'n bod ni'n meddwl am y lliniaru a'r addasu sydd angen digwydd i ni i gyd yn ein bywydau ni. O ran y gefnogaeth a'r cymorth ariannol, mi fydd swyddogion Llywodraeth Cymru yn siarad efo'r asiantaethau i gyd rŵan i weld lle'n union y medrwn ni fod yn helpu, beth yn union ydy goblygiadau y tân sydd wedi digwydd.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Thank you, Minister. And the second question is from Lynne Neagle.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Weinidog. A'r ail gwestiwn, Lynne Neagle.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: 2. Will the Cabinet Minister make a statement on the Teachers' Pay Award 2026-27? TQ1485
documents.text_cy: 2. A wnaiff y Gweinidog Cabinet ddatganiad ar y Dyfarniad Cyflog Athrawon 2026-27? TQ1485

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: I made a written statement on Monday, announcing my intention to consult after the summer holidays on a 3.5 per cent pay award for teachers and leaders, and a 5 per cent pay award for unqualified teachers. I will provide additional funding to support local authorities and schools with implementing the pay award.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text:
Thank you. As you've indicated, you made that written statement on Monday, announcing that you would consult from September. This is later than stakeholders would like. As you're aware, there's previously been a commitment to consult ahead of the school holidays, so that teachers can receive their pay rise as soon as possible, although I do welcome your commitment to start the process earlier in future years.

As we discussed yesterday, the Welsh Government is now in a pay dispute with both school leadership unions in Wales, with pay as well as additional learning needs funding cited as the reasons for the dispute. It was really worrying to see the written statement issued immediately after the debate yesterday, saying there would be no money for ALN, even though the Welsh Government could allocate that money, as they are doing with their priorities. But it's crucial now that the Government gets around the table with trade unions in order to prevent industrial action in the autumn.

Can I ask the Cabinet Minister what steps you'll take to ensure that this dispute focused on pay and ALN is urgently resolved?

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text:
If I can take the point on the pay award timings first: yes, it would have been easier to consult at an earlier point. She may have noticed that there was an election. There was a period when these consultations could not have gone ahead, which is precisely why I made the announcement on the 3.5 per cent pay award for teachers and 5 per cent for unqualified teachers, because in representations to me, they said very clearly that an early indication—admitting the consultation would need now to happen in the autumn—early certainty, and an early certainty for local government that funding would be available to pay for these pay rises, was the desire of the workforce. That's why I made that statement at that point.

On ALN, I think that we are revisiting a conversation from yesterday. As my colleague said earlier on, we are very aware of the pressures in funding on both local government and on schools, and I have no doubt that those will be continuing conversations. On ALN specifically, what we set out to do, in conversation with you—and I thought that we were talking about the same thing, which was how to arrive at a sustainable model for ALN. For a number of years, it has been clear that that is not where we are. We are constantly told, by parents, families, schools and local authorities, that the current system is facing significant difficulty, and it was on that basis that we presented an argument for £40 million this year, £40 million next year and at least £40 million in the third year, in order to bring us to a point where we had a sustainable ALN system that we could be proud of. You voted against that yesterday.

On the trade dispute itself, I was obviously disappointed to receive a letter from the NAHT and the Association of School and College Leaders, entering into a trade dispute, given that we have been working together and I have been committed to the social partnership now and throughout my career. And I hope that we can move forward quickly to resolve these issues. I remain committed to the social partnership, and I'm currently considering the issues and the response.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: I welcome the Gweinidog's acknowledgement that improving educational outcomes requires meaningful engagement with teachers, ensuring they feel supported, valued and listened to. It is somewhat ironic that when similar pay uplifts were offered to teachers in previous years, under previous Governments, they did not attract the same level of scrutiny. For too long, Wales has faced persistent challenges in retaining teachers. If we are serious about raising standards, we must work in genuine partnership with our education workforce. Teachers are central to our education system and should be able to focus on teaching and supporting learners, rather than being overwhelmed by unnecessary pressures. Therefore, Gweinidog, at a time when teachers face growing demands and expectations, how will the Welsh Government work with teachers, unions and local authorities to ensure that the profession is properly supported, teacher well-being is prioritised and schools can attract and retain the staff they need?

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Diolch yn fawr, and I think she's quite right to point to the value we put on the teaching profession, and we are determined to work in partnership. I have existing relationships with teachers and school leaders across Wales, and I am in constant dialogue, formally and informally, with them, and we have a great deal that we want to do together around workload, around retaining and recruiting teachers, around the ideas we have on literacy and numeracy and clarity of expectation, looking at the curriculum. These are things that the teaching profession has welcomed, and it is a continuing dialogue that will touch on all the areas the Member mentioned. It will include the unions and as wide as possible an input from the people who deliver on the ground and who matter to us.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: As a former teacher, I know first-hand the challenges facing our schools and the immense commitment shown by teachers and school leaders across Wales, and I'd like to thank Lynne Neagle for bringing forward this question. Of course, supporting teachers is vital, and fair pay is an important part of that, but we must also recognise that the pressures facing the profession go far beyond pay alone. There is workload, recruitment and retention, additional learning needs provision and the increasing demands placed on schools all requiring attention. I note that the NAHT, the school leaders' union, and the Association of School and College Leaders have now written to the education Minister, herself a former leader of the NAHT, to formally register a dispute with the Welsh Government over the pay settlement, alongside concerns with ALN funding. What makes this particularly significant is that neither union has previously been in a formal dispute with the Welsh Government; these are unprecedented circumstances. Therefore, can the Minister outline how the Welsh Government intends to rebuild consensus with these unions, resolve the issues that have led to this dispute, and what further action can be taken to support teachers and school leaders across Wales?

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Thank you, and I'm sure the former Minister will be grateful for your support. On the trade dispute, I am anxious to resolve this as quickly as possible, as I said earlier on, and I remain committed to working in social partnership with them. I think there is ground that we can build on here and I am determined to resolve that matter as quickly as I can.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text:
I'm grateful to Lynne Neagle for tabling this item here today. As you know, Cabinet Minister, schools across Wales are increasingly feeling overlooked and undervalued when it comes to funding. And, of course, you've already noted the serious challenges surrounding funding for additional learning needs, with many schools struggling to provide the support that learners deserve.

You've again mentioned the offer from the Welsh Government of that £40 million per year. But let's not forget that, last night, this Senedd rejected that as an option, because this Senedd believed that that was not enough to support ALN across Wales. And now we're seeing again a Welsh Government unwilling to meet the recommended pay award for teachers. It goes back to that point of them feeling overlooked and undervalued. Cabinet Minister, we cannot risk a strike in the autumn because of this situation.

I think that what's happening at the moment really sends the wrong message to a profession that's already feeling that immense pressure. Teachers, as already described by your Plaid Cymru colleague, are at the heart of our education system and there's a real risk of this general issue around funding affecting recruitment, retention and ultimately outcomes for our children and young people.

I'm particularly concerned about how school leaders are having to manage this situation at the moment, and I declare an interest as a school governor myself. School governing bodies are having to manage stretched budgets, and if schools are left to bridge the funding gap themselves, it's children who ultimately feel the impact of this. So, Cabinet Minister, can you explain what reassurance you can give headteachers and governing bodies that they won't have to choose between rewarding their staff fairly and appropriately and protecting the support and opportunities available to pupils?

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text:
Thank you. I think we have rehearsed the reasons why the ALN funding for this year will be difficult in this particular context, but I am committed to working with my colleague the finance Minister on building the sustainable ALN system that we committed to in our manifesto and that I know has support across Wales.

On schools funding more broadly, part of the announcement I made on Monday about the pay award was that we would provide local authorities with additional funding in order that that would not be an additional pressure on school budgets. But we remain committed too to making sure that school leaders and the wider school workforce do feel valued and consulted under this Government, and it is in that spirit that I propose to proceed.

documents.item: 3. Topical Questions
documents.text: Thank you, Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Weinidog.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text: We'll move now to item 4, the 90-second statements. The first is from Llŷr Powell.
documents.text_cy: Symudwn nawr at eitem 4, datganiadau 90 eiliad. Yn gyntaf, Llŷr Powell.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I was sad and shocked on the weekend to find out about the passing of the Rt Hon Ann Widdecombe. I'm not going to comment today on the circumstances, but will celebrate the person that she was.

Ann was the MP for Maidstone for 23 years. She served in Government, serving the country that she loved as Minister of State for employment and Minister of State for prisons. Ann became a Member of the European Parliament for South West England in 2019. Her words were that she was there to ensure that the largest democratic vote the United Kingdom has had is fulfilled, and she pushed it through. She became an unlikely national treasure through her appearances on Strictly Come Dancing. She was on Big Brother. She appeared in several pantomimes across the country during the seasons, and even appeared in a production at the Royal Opera House.

She was a dedicated campaigner for animal causes. Ann went against her own party and friends when she was outspoken in supporting the ban on fox hunting, claiming it was immoral not to do so. She stood up for animals like donkeys and their welfare. She fought for the end of the use of animals in circuses. Ann showed us that you could be a true Conservative, a 'small c' conservative, but you can also stand up for your principles, you can go against your party. In tributes, we've heard that Ann was a maverick; she was. She was fearless in debate, she was kind-hearted, she was true to her faith at all times.

I had the pleasure of meeting Ann in 2019. It was a friendship that I cherish more than anything. I walked the streets of Ebbw Vale with her, where I saw women leaving a hair salon and nail bar quickly to have a selfie with the Strictly Come Dancing star that was Ann Widdecombe. She looked perplexed at how she was a star—she just saw herself as Ann. That's the person I knew every time I met her. She's a loss to this country, to our party and to Britain as a whole. We on these benches, and, I hope, across the Chamber, will pay tribute to her family and to the person whom we will long miss. Rest in peace, Ann.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Following Thursday's Remembering Srebrenica commemoration, attended by Members across this Senedd, we pause to honour the victims and survivors of the Srebrenica genocide. This year's theme, 'We are here', reminds us that, while the genocide sought to erase a people, survivors continue with dignity, courage and strength, and their stories continue to educate and inspire future generations.

We remember the 8,372 Muslim men and boys murdered in the town of Srebrenica alone. We remember the more than 100,000 people murdered across Bosnia and Herzegovina. We remember the 2 million people forced from their homes. And we remember the more than 50,000 women who were the victims of genocidal rape between 1992 and 1995. Because we know that behind every number is a name, a life lost and a family changed forever.

We also recognise the vital work of Remembering Srebrenica Wales. Continued investment in education, including support for more school and college visits to Bosnia and Herzegovina, is essential to ensure future generations learn these lessons and help realise the ambitions of our 'Anti-racist Wales Action Plan'. As His Majesty King Charles III said himself in his own words, by remembering the pain of the past and learning its lessons, we can together resolve that it must never happen again.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
As we look forward to welcoming Eisteddfod y Garreg las to Llantood in Pembrokeshire, I'd like to extend a very warm welcome to this special festival. In two weeks' time, we will once again celebrate and take pride in our culture, our history and our local communities, which will be displayed on a national stage for the whole of Wales.

I would like to express my sincere appreciation to all the people, communities, organisations and local businesses that have come together to support this Eisteddfod. Their commitment and hard work has been a vital part of the success of the preparations. A target of £400,000 was set, and the communities of Pembrokeshire, south Ceredigion and west Carmarthenshire smashed that target, raising over £500,000—more money than any National Eisteddfod has ever raised, clear evidence of the strength of our communities and their support for the Welsh language and our culture.

It has also been a pleasure to see the celebrations that have highlighted the historical significance of this Eisteddfod, especially as we remember Lord Rhys, who held the first Eisteddfod in Cardigan castle 850 years ago. It is a privilege to be able to welcome the Eisteddfod back home to Ceredigion Penfro, and I'm looking forward to welcoming all Members of the Senedd to the maes during the first week of August. Thank you.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text: I would like to congratulate and celebrate the anniversary of the BAWSO charity at 30. For three decades, BAWSO has been supporting people the length and breadth of Wales at some of the most difficult periods of their lives.
documents.text_cy: Hoffwn i longyfarch a dathlu pen-blwydd yr elusen BAWSO yn 30 mlwydd oed. Am dri degawd, mae BAWSO wedi bod yn cefnogi pobl ledled Cymru ar rai o achlysuron mwyaf anodd eu bywydau.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text:
Founded in Cardiff by a small group of black and minoritised women, BAWSO recognised that survivors of domestic abuse needed services that understood their experiences and the barriers they faced in seeking help. They've grown from a rented room with just a desk, chair and phone to a Wales-wide organisation, supporting thousands of people every year, with a free-access helpline, available 24 hours a day, every day. BAWSO has often led the way in tackling issues such as forced marriage, female genital mutilation, honour-based violence, modern slavery and human traffic, long before many of these issues received the attention they deserved.

As BAWSO marks its thirtieth anniversary, I want to thank staff, volunteers and trustees for everything they do. I particularly want to acknowledge the contribution of their founding chief executive, Mutale Merrill, and their present chief exec, Samsunear Ali, both of whom I've worked closely with over the years. I understand there's a gala celebration event on Friday, and I'm sure all of us here are very welcome there. Diolch.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text: And finally, Rebeca Phillips.
documents.text_cy: Ac yn olaf, Rebeca Phillips.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text: Diolch, Lywydd. Gaynor Hopkins was born on 8 June 1951 in Skewen, Neath, one of six children to her father, Glyndwr Hopkins, a coal miner, and her mother, Elsie Hopkins. From humble beginnings, she became known all over the world for her distinctive raspy voice, immense emotional range and timeless anthems. Yes, Bonnie Tyler was a legend. With her well-known hits such as 'Total Eclipse of the Heart' and 'Holding Out for a Hero', Bonnie Tyler went on to sell millions of records all over the world. Not just a singer, Bonnie was an ambassador for many charities and used her global profile to champion them, supporting events and making appearances at charitable functions. Once saying, 'I'm just a girl from a small town in Wales who just loves to sing', she never forgot her Skewen roots. Sadly, on 9 July 2026, at the age of 75, we heard of the singer's passing. Our thoughts are with her family, friends and all those affected by her death.

documents.item: 4. 90-second Statements
documents.text: Thank you, Bonnie, for being an inspiration to us all with your talent and kindness, and for showing the next generation that dreams can come true. Rest in peace.
documents.text_cy: Diolch i ti, Bonnie, am fod yn ysbrydoliaeth i ni i gyd gyda dy dalent a dy garedigrwydd, ac am ddangos i'r genhedlaeth newydd fod breuddwydion yn bosib. Cwsg mewn hedd.

documents.item: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
documents.text: Item 6 is next, a Member debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv), young people and employment. I call on Shav Taj to move the motion tabled in her name and in the names of Jane Dodds and Paul Rock.
documents.text_cy: Eitem 6 nesaf, dadl Aelodau o dan Reol Sefydlog 11.21(iv), pobl ifanc a chyflogaeth. Galwaf ar Shav Taj i gyflwyno'r cynnig, a gyflwynwyd yn ei henw hi ac yn enwau Jane Dodds a Paul Rock.

documents.item: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
documents.text:
Sorry, I'm just taking my jacket off, it's really hot. Diolch, Lywydd. I just wanted to say that I'm really pleased to move this motion today. It's my first individual Member debate, and I'm really pleased that it is on this issue, because it is such a big issue. I'm really happy that it was co-submitted by both the Greens and the Lib Dems. I just want to declare an interest—I have said this previously—I am the former general secretary of TUC Cymru, so this issue, in terms of young people and employment, is very much close to my heart and really important for me.

Can I start by noting that today, in fact, is World Youth Skills Day? This is really a chance for us to celebrate the potential of the next generation of young people in Wales and make sure that this new Government is setting them up to succeed. All of us, ultimately, have responsibility in this area, and, in the spirit of cross-party collaboration, I want to thank my co-sponsors for this debate, Jane Dodds and Paul Rock, for helping to get this issue onto the agenda. On World Youth Skills Day, the timing really couldn't be any better.

It's often said that young people are our future, but I want to remind everyone that the underlying issues related to young people and employment are not problems for the future, they're for the here and now. When it comes to mental health and physical health, a lack of job opportunities, a lack of well-paid and secure work, bullying, harassment and discrimination, or even not being able to catch a bus in time, get to a bus or a train to where jobs actually are, and the impact of AI on entry-level jobs, these are the real obstacles, and they're happening in the here and now, which makes these issues just as urgent as anything else that we may be discussing in the Senedd.

documents.item: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
documents.text:
Now, younger generations today may want all of the same things that we wanted back in the days. I mean, I remember my first official paid job when I was 17 or 18 in the Sweater Shop in town. I was paid £2.65 and it really was an awful job. But the first thing that I got to do was to buy my first pair of Nike trainers, because up until then, it was Matchstick all the way, because that was what my parents could afford to buy me from Woolworths. But, of course, young people now want the same things. They want to make their own money. They want to make sure that they can pay their way in life and, of course, start building a future, not only for themselves, but also for many others. Many of them have caring responsibilities. They want to be able to buy a house or even start a family.

Now, Llywydd, as the former health Secretary Alan Milburn has set out in his review, we risk a lost generation of young people. One in eight between the ages of 16 and 24 are not in employment, education or training, otherwise known as NEETs, and I was shocked, really, to find that the data from the end of last year showed that the situation in Wales is actually even worse. One in six young people are not in work, not in education or training, and that should really wind each and every one of us up and make us angry enough to want to do something about it and to work together on these issues, because youth unemployment is not a fringe issue. It is actually the symptom of a systemic failure, bigger than any one policy, bigger than any department or Government, and clearly, now, it demands an even bigger and better response.

Now, I saw during my time at TUC Cymru that the last Welsh Government took some really positive steps. The young person's guarantee that was rolled out, when we were coming out of the COVID pandemic, helped around 10,000 young people to get into work; 30,000 apprenticeships were started; and more people were helped to further their education or even start their own business. But clearly, though, that guarantee hasn't been universally effective. So, it hasn't done all the things that we were hoping to do. Only around half of the people that were supported through these various schemes actually went on to achieve a positive outcome. And that's just the people who were even aware that this support existed in the first place and were able to take advantage of it and to navigate through it as well. But what about the people who weren't aware, who weren't able to navigate the systems that were set up?

Now, as set out by the previous skills and social partnership Minister, Jack Sargent, the various schemes that make up the young person's guarantee are going to be replaced by a new employability support programme, starting next year. I think that if we do this right, it genuinely can be a golden opportunity for us to do things differently here in Wales, to take what works and to streamline it with a real laser focus on moving young people into good, fair work jobs and other opportunities. The UK Government also operates a number of schemes for young people in Wales. The youth jobs grant, which started last month—that gives a real financial incentive for some employers to hire young people who have been out of work and are claiming universal credit. And, of course, there is the economic inactivity trailblazer scheme, which has been piloted in Blaenau Gwent, Denbighshire and Neath Port Talbot, and is currently being reviewed, as I understand it. This scheme, which looks at the underlying big causes of long-term unemployment, gives people the tailored support that they actually need, whether that's for mentoring, counselling or any other kind of special support that that person may need.

Now, despite all of the good work, all of the stuff that we've done so far, the issue with youth unemployment is not unique to Wales, but we can lead from the front when it comes to finding those solutions and implementing them. And we have to start, of course, with the evidence. Let's listen to the people who know best, and that is the young people who are actually at that sharp end, who are facing these real challenges on a day-to-day basis, because we don't have all of the answers, and that is the truth. Some people, young people in particular, are being let down more than others.

The latest stats, the official stats from the Welsh Government, show that 40 per cent of people with disabilities between the ages of 19 and 24 are not in education, employment or training. We know it's not because they lack skills or aspiration or any of those things. It is actually a failure, an abject failure of society, a lack of opportunity and a lack of proper support that's being given. In reality, one in three disabled workers are not getting the reasonable adjustments that they actually need in the first place. Relatively few public sector organisations even have the highest level of Disability Confident accreditation. And according to Mencap, 86 per cent of young people with learning disabilities want to be in paid work, and in reality, it's only 5 per cent—5 per cent—who actually are. This is mind-boggling, and that's just not right.

So, yes, while we have these schemes and they are transforming some lives, there are clearly gaps in the provision, and we know they exist and we need to do something about them. Now, when young people with disabilities consistently say that the systems that they're meant to be using, that are meant to be there—. Well, they say, 'They're not actually built with us in mind.' And that's not an opinion, that's their own individual lived experience. These are the people who know the issues best, and the systems would work better if we did a better job of listening to the people who use them. So, that should always be our starting point—for this Welsh Government, for all of us in this Senedd, we really need to, always, get out into our communities, listen and learn and act.

documents.item: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
documents.text:
And what else do young people need in Wales? One simple answer: more jobs embedded. But not any old job—good jobs, good jobs that are well paid, secure and give people a real opportunity for progress into that career, whatever that career may be that they choose. And Wales has a lower jobs density than England and Scotland. So, that's a problem, the availability of jobs. But the quality of jobs has actually been very much lacking too. Now, according to research by the Health Foundation, of all the nations and regions, it is Wales where workers are most likely to face multiple aspects of job quality. Lots of young people are actually overqualified for the roles that are open to them, and they're less likely than older colleagues to access any training and development.

Now, there's always a demand for young people in sectors like retail, hospitality and social care. But once they actually get into those jobs, what actually happens to them? They find themselves trapped in jobs with limited training and not able to actually progress. Now, TUC Cymru has raised concerns, and I've constantly been in front of one committee after the other where I've said that precarious jobs are shaping a generation. Bullying, harassment and poor treatment remain very real issues and are concerns for young people at work.

Working parents are struggling to even help their own children to navigate the world of work, and lots of young workers are also, of course, parents themselves, so it's a struggle for them to balance work and caring responsibilities. So, yes, we need to create more job opportunities for young people, but we need work that is well paid, that is secure, and we need to have welcoming workplaces in the first place, and cultures in workplaces where people feel that they can speak up and that they will be supported in the first place. Not just some warm words, not another policy, not another perfected way of doing things—we need tangible actions. It's so important that young people actually understand, of course, what is acceptable in the workplace and the rights and protections that they have. People who have been paid under the minimum wage, who haven't been given breaks or have experienced harassment in the workplace—they are at risk of thinking, 'This is just the way things are and there is nothing that I can do to change it.'

Now, for some young people, there is a lack of understanding around the jobs that are available, even when they're studying or training to work in a particular industry. For lots of young people, ideas about future careers and the opportunities that they can get are based on their own connections. That can make job seeking even harder, especially if they're from disadvantaged backgrounds. Now, TUC Cymru has done some good awareness work with the Welsh Government teaching young people about their rights at work, the role of trade unions, issues like health and safety and artificial intelligence, and that's through the World of Work programme that's been rolled out in schools, in youth clubs and many other places as well. And I hope that the current Government will continue to support that work.

Another Welsh Government scheme, which deserves praise, of course, is Taith. Now, that was and still is, actually, a distinctly Welsh programme that gives young people from disadvantaged backgrounds the opportunity to actually travel. Now, last week, I visited Ysgol Gyfun Gymraeg Glantaf in my constituency and I spoke to some of the pupils who have benefited from this scheme. And I was actually honestly genuinely so inspired by the new skills and the confidence that Taith has given them, and this is clearly not a one-off investment—it's a lifelong investment in young people all over Wales. So, again, I really hope that the Government will back this project beyond the current funding, because it definitely has a place in Wales, alongside, I believe, Erasmus+, reaching out to schools, and youth and adult organisations. Those who never thought that they'd have opportunities to even travel—so many of the young kids that I spoke to said they didn't even have a passport. They didn't even believe that this was going to be a real trip. They had the opportunity to go to Malaysia, and now there's going to be a delegation of children that are going to be visiting here. And it was, honestly, just amazing what they talked about.

Now, the new employability support programme coming in next year is a chance for us to build a better system that actually reflects the needs of the people it intends to help. And that gives a real helping hand to anyone who might need it. We need to seize the opportunities in front of us. Where there are jobs being created in sectors like clean energy, in digital and tourism—of course, the electric arc furnace in Port Talbot or the Cardiff parkway project—we need to make sure that young people from every single part of Wales are able to get to where they need to be, both literally, but also in the sense of public transport—affordable public transport—but also that they have the opportunity of good jobs and that they have the chance to progress.

So, while I'm proud to put forward this debate, the real work is for each and every one of us to do when we leave the Chamber. And I know that there are Members from all parties who are genuinely extremely passionate about helping young people—Members with different experiences, working with and on behalf of young people before they even came into the Senedd, with lots of different insights. So, let's come together and let's use those. Let's get out into our constituencies over the summer, let's listen to the people who are facing these challenges and look at what's working. Let's think about what we could do better and then let's get on with it and do it, so that Wales is the best place that it can be for young working people, where no young person is left behind. Diolch, Lywydd.

documents.item: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
documents.text:
I'd also like to declare an interest. It might surprise a few people to know that I'm a former young person myself. It was a while ago now, but—. I will say, I think when you think about the journey that young people go through, for too long, they've been kind of mis-sold a promise that if you go to university, then on the other side awaits a golden nirvana, a good job and big success, but the reality is that it hasn't—. Instead, thousands of young people across Wales, and indeed the UK, go into that process and they leave having to go for unpaid or low-paid jobs at the end of it in an unrelated field, because the degree that they had isn't valued by employers or wanted by the economy. They leave with debt. And the harsh reality is that the dreams of those young people going into those university courses have often been broken, and there's a lot of disappointment on the other side. And on both sides of the M4, young people have been mis-sold degrees, pushed through the system and leave with tens of thousands of pounds-worth of debt that they carry with them for decades. An economy of skilled workers that those employers have to go out to the world to look for to fill that—we could be filling right here in Wales. And many people in that generation are really paying the price for the decisions that we, as the older generation, have been making, and, certainly, in this Chamber.

Now, as has already been mentioned, 17 per cent of Welsh young people in Wales are NEET, and that, for a supposed advanced economy, is not an acceptable position to be in. Unlike many of them, I actually started my career with an apprenticeship, and I would say it was easily one of the best decisions I ever made. I would actually like to take the opportunity to pay tribute to those men and women at the civilian technical training school that I went on to work with. They've gone on throughout the world to achieve some remarkable things. It's just a shame that we couldn't keep them employed here in Wales, and that's what we have to look to do. I was able to earn and learn at the same time, and it led to a long and successful 30-year career across aerospace and defence. First of all with the Ministry of Defence at St Athan—a three-year apprenticeship that taught me and my colleagues the fundamentals of aerospace engineering. I then went on to the defence sector at another Welsh success story at General Dynamics, and various senior management positions soon after. So, apprenticeships may well be vocational in nature, but they can lead to some really exciting places for young people.

I know first-hand what apprenticeships can achieve. I understand the power of apprenticeships, for employers and for young people. They have dual value, and it's important that we consider that. Now, I want every young person in Wales to have those same opportunities. I think we can all agree to that premise. I think there will be consensus around the Chamber on that. I think there's power in that. That means shifting our focus away from low-value degrees and putting skilled trades back at the heart of where they belong, which is at the heart of Welsh education, so that people are aware of what those trades mean to the economy as they're coming through school and making those choices.

Now, today, young people who want to become electricians, engineers, plumbers and technicians are fighting over a handful of apprenticeship places. Despite skyrocketing demand, apprenticeship starts in Wales have actually fallen by around 37 per cent over the last decade. The last Government claimed they delivered 100,000 apprenticeships over the last term, but as we all now know, the figures were fiddled and the public were misled on that, and that's a terrible legacy to leave. Terrible delivery and a misrepresentation of data. But we need to turn that around.

Now, this debate today is an attempt to reclaim that narrative; we understand that. But I do think that we can all come together to recognise that programmes like Jobs Growth Wales and ReAct aren't enough to get our students through the process into producing high-quality jobs for employers. Too often these programmes have become a revolving door of courses, placements and paperwork, rather than a genuine route into secure employment and training. Now, of course it's not enough for me to say what we wouldn't do; we are the party that tells the public exactly what we would do. Reform Wales would expand high-quality degree apprenticeships, work with employers and make vocational skills just as respected as academic qualifications.

We also need to have an honest conversation about the impact of uncontrolled immigration on our jobs market. To not acknowledge the direct correlation is not to acknowledge the reality of the pressures that people face. Four hundred Welsh nurses, for example, paramedics and midwives who were trained here in Wales, ready, willing and able to work in our NHS, are unable to find work, while we import staff from abroad. Now, that's completely unacceptable to the men and women who are looking for jobs in our NHS. But that's what happens when Welsh workers aren't put first. Now, we appreciate anyone that wants to work in our NHS and contribute, but it can't be to the detriment of our own Welsh young people. Warm words aren't enough. We need better than the young person's guarantee. That's why—
