documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text:
Diolch yn fawr. I really do welcome the support. I'm really excited about this policy, and we saw that excitement on the doors, didn't we? Because I think you can compare it. When we deliver this, it will be up there with the most—well, the most—generous offer in the UK, certainly—world leading, actually. There are nations that are very much ahead of us, but I think that this is something that should be a real badge of honour for Wales. More than that, it won't be an empty badge of honour; this will be something that makes a real difference to people's lives. So, I think it's great to see the enthusiasm for this expansion. I'm hearing it from stakeholders and partners.

It is a significant commitment, and, yes, it will require a substantial increase in workforce numbers. So, as I said, this is a key theme of the work of our expert group. We are developing those projections of how many staff we're going to need, where we're going to need them as we're working through these phases. A specific phase of that expansion is to extend the funded childcare to nine months to two years. We know that will require a step change in provision. This is completely new. The first two phases are building on something that is already provided in part. This will be new, so there will be specific actions needed there to grow the workforce. That'll be informed by the work we're currently doing. I'll update colleagues regularly as we reach that phase.

Of course, Welsh-medium provision, as you would expect, is a core element of this expansion and a core concern of this Government. So, we're working closely with Mudiad Meithrin. The chief executive, Dr Catrin Edwards, is a member of the expert steering group. We are already taking measures now. We announced a new pilot scheme, which is coming through the National Centre for Learning Welsh, to build the Welsh language skills of our childcare workforce in order to increase that capacity.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text:
We have a statement on early years childcare and play, but I note in it that play is not mentioned once. When we look back to our own childhoods, play develops resilience, communication skills and emotional well-being. For many children, particularly those that are facing disadvantage, play can be the difference between isolation and inclusion, between struggling and thriving.

In my constituency, I've had people complain—this is Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni—about play services there. So, I took the opportunity last week to go over to Torfaen, where they've got absolutely excellent play services. Torfaen Play are offering to young people of all ages—so, these are little ones as well—they support children with additional needs, care-experienced children, young carers and families across the community. What stood out for me was not only the breadth of work, but the life-changing impact.

So, what we've got is, in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, we've got children that are really struggling through lack of play facilities, but, in Torfaen, it's the opposite way round. So, for a Government who talks persistently about equality, could I ask what measures they are taking to ensure that high-quality play opportunities are available for everybody, regardless of where they live, and is there funding specifically for play?

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text: This statement is specifically on the childcare expansion, but I accept, of course, that these things are linked. Play is within my portfolio; I'm not speaking about that today, but I would encourage you to ask me questions about that when I am here to answer questions on my broader portfolio. But I would say that ensuring children have access to childcare absolutely helps to socialise them, to bring out that play, which we know is absolutely key to children's development. As I said before, this is about making children also more ready for school and learning, getting into that foundation phase. But I would encourage you to perhaps ask me a question or write to me specifically about your concerns as regards play.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text:
Cabinet Minister, families in Cardiff already face some of the highest childcare costs in Wales, with average fees significantly above those in other areas. One constituent of mine in particular, Lizzie, recently told me that she is paying £92 a day for a local nursery. She says, in her words, 'Childcare is single-handedly the biggest financial issue for my family and the reason we cannot yet afford to have a second child. We currently pay over £1,400 a month, which is £400 more than our mortgage.'

Llywydd, given the significant childcare costs faced by many families in Cardiff specifically, it is crucial that the expanded offer reflects the pressures being felt in our higher cost communities, in addition to the needs of the rest of Wales. So, I wanted to ask: when can Lizzie and other families across Cardiff, specifically, expect to be included in the expanded offer, what factors are determining which areas are being prioritised, and how can you ensure fairness for families in higher cost areas like Cardiff in the meantime?

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text: Thank you very much for the question.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr am y cwestiwn.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text:
I absolutely agree that childcare costs across Wales are prohibitively high. One of the reasons for this policy is understanding that it will be a mitigation against the high cost of living for families. It will put money back in people's pockets, and parents, especially mothers, of course, can find themselves locked out of the labour market, and children then, of course, prevented from accessing all the benefits of quality childcare. So, as regards prioritisation, we're committed to make progress on the expansion as soon as we can. As I mentioned in my statement, we're making very good progress to offer childcare to all two-year-olds all over Wales, and we're urging all local authorities to work with us to complete this stage, and, as I say, the vast majority of them are there and will be there.

So, at the moment, thousands of children across Wales don't get any childcare support, and so we're going to go from that current reality to a system where all families are able to access support, but we have to add to that support incrementally until we reach our full commitment. But by proceeding with and getting early momentum with this initial phase, I think, of getting 12.5 hours funded childcare to all two-year-olds, we're really laying the foundations of that truly universal funded childcare offer, which, as I say, is something only a handful of countries in the world have achieved.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text: I'd like to thank Kiera Marshall for her excellent question on capacity. The Minister has characterised these benches as focused on worst-case scenarios. I asked whether she'd modelled for very high demand, because planning for a policy that succeeds beyond expectation isn't negativity, it's prudence, but today my question is about proving success. Last week, the Minister told this Senedd we're not able to measure the difference in Wales that having early years education makes. You stated last week that early years provision transforms children's potential, but I'm asking about benchmarking, yet she has told us Wales cannot currently measure that difference. So, this roll-out is happening now. How will the Minister prove that this £375 million policy delivers the transformation she describes when the children reached first will have received the offer before any baseline would have been analysed or met? So, this is about benchmarking.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text:
Thank you for the question. I think I just answered the question in that we absolutely recognise the need for better benchmarking; we simply haven't got that in place. It exists in parts, but it isn't satisfactory and isn't measuring what we think we need it to measure.

Having seen learning from childcare provision both in the UK and internationally, we can see that, for instance, 100 per cent is unlikely. However, as work continues on developing this policy, we are, as I said, going to respond to any emerging trend, and that will include demand. And we remain ready and willing—and that's why this work has to be planned and phased in this way, in order to respond to those things—to adjust and refine our plans. But this is an ambitious Government, as I said, and we fully hope that as many children as possible take up the offer that we'll be able to give them.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text:
I do welcome this statement. Thank you very much for all of the work that's gone into it. You've said that you've got a laser focus on delivering this, having had the ambition that many of the parties here in this Siambr had. So, I really take issue with Reform UK and your spokesperson criticising the ambition, because you never had an ambition—nothing in your manifesto talked about childcare whatsoever. So, the criticism of the ambition is actually without any foundation. 

My question to you, though, if I may, is about our private providers. We do rely on private providers across Wales, and particularly in rural areas we see that they're really up against it. So, how will their interests be represented on your panel, because currently it's only through Cwlwm? Will you be looking to get more views from independent providers? And also how will that be rolled out in rural areas? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

documents.item: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
documents.text:
Thank you very much to the Member for the question, and thank you very much for the support and for the campaigning work that you and others in this Chamber have done on this crucial policy area. I'm pleased that you share our ambition for the children of Wales, and I know you do. 

In terms of that voice on the panel, Cwlwm, as you mentioned, are represented on the panel, but also there is a representative from the WLGA, who of course represents all of Wales's local authorities. So, they are vocal and taking those messages from their councils in terms of the particular situation in the many diverse areas of Wales. And as I mentioned, this group is not limited. There is a core membership, and what we are doing and have done—we've met twice already—is that we ask people to join us. So, looking at the rural picture will certainly be part of that, and, as I said, those differing needs that will exist across Wales will be one of the things that we will certainly be considering.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: We'll move on, therefore, to item 6, a statement by the Deputy Minister for Public Health and Preventative Health, priorities for public and preventative health. I call on the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health, Nerys Evans.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Dirprwy Lywydd, today I am setting out my ministerial priorities for public and preventative health for this Senedd term. As we celebrate 78 years since Aneurin Bevan established the NHS, built on the radical principle that the circumstances of your birth should never determine the quality of your care, it is worth recalling Bevan's own words,
documents.text_cy: Ddirprwy Lywydd, heddiw dwi'n nodi fy mlaenoriaethau gweinidogol ar gyfer iechyd cyhoeddus ac ataliol dros dymor y Senedd hon. Wrth inni ddathlu 78 mlynedd ers i Aneurin Bevan sefydlu'r NHS ar sail yr egwyddor radical na ddylai amgylchiadau eich genedigaeth fyth benderfynu ansawdd eich gofal, mae'n werth cofio geiriau Bevan ei hun,

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: 'the victories won by preventive medicine are much the most important for mankind.'

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
More than seven decades on, that message remains as relevant as ever. But treating illness is never enough on its own. Preventative and public health are the key to unlocking a more sustainable future for our health system and our wider population. In an age where demands on services are increasing, people's needs are becoming more complex and financial pressures are intensifying, we must shift away from managing sickness to treating the root causes. For the first time since devolution, Wales now has a Minister with specific responsibility for preventative health. That is a significant step forward. It represents a clear statement of intent from the First Minister that preventing ill health is a national priority. This approach also reflects manifesto commitments to a wider shift towards preventative spending across all portfolio areas.

The need to make this change is not new. What has been missing is the determination to deliver it. For too long, our models, processes and ways of working have been focused on responding to crises, rather than preventing them and helping people to live healthier and happier lives. This changes now. Under this Government, success will be measured not by the number of hospital admissions, but by the number of people who stay healthy enough to avoid hospital altogether.

This isn't a standalone initiative. We are embedding this work across Government through a series of strategic measures to ensure it's reflected in everything that we do. I have already had discussions with all Cabinet Ministers and Deputy Ministers to consider how we embed prevention more effectively and focus on improving the health of everyone in Wales.

But every journey begins with a first step, and those early steps matter just as much as the destination. This statement sets out the foundations that have already been laid to put us on the right path.

Nid menter ar ei phen ei hun mo hon. Rŷn ni'n gwreiddio'r gwaith hwn ar draws y Llywodraeth drwy gyfres o gamau strategol er mwyn sicrhau ei fod yn cael ei adlewyrchu ym mhopeth a wnawn. Ond mae pob taith yn dechrau gyda'r cam cyntaf, ac mae'r camau cynnar hynny yr un mor bwysig â phen y daith. Mae'r datganiad hwn yn nodi'r sylfeini sydd eisoes ar waith wrth inni fynd ar y trywydd cywir.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
I have agreed with the First Minister that Government decision making will be informed by a shared focus on public and preventative health. Official and ministerial-level cross-Government governance arrangements are being established to support this. These arrangements will provide the foundations for a comprehensive new public health strategy and framework for Wales. Embedding prevention and health into decision making will be supported with the guidance and support for public bodies in preparing for when the Health Impact Assessment (Wales) Regulations 2025 come into force next year.

Being serious about prevention also means having the budgetary mechanisms to match, and in line with our first 100 days commitments, officials are in the process of exploring better defining preventative spending within the Welsh budget, with the aim of instilling greater coherence in the deployment of resources. I have also held discussions with the Cabinet Minister for Finance and Treasury officials on options for the introduction of a designated preventative departmental expenditure limit—PDEL—within the Welsh Budget.

In addition to the strategic cross-Government work, there are immediate priorities that we will be tackling, in addition to rolling out the 100-day commitments. I fully recognise the need for us to provide healthy environments that support people to make healthier choices and maintain a healthy weight, to reduce the risk of severe, life-threatening conditions, including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke and certain cancers. This includes the roll-out of prevention programmes to encourage and support children and adults to be more active in line with the recent changes to the UK Chief Medical Officers' evidence-based physical activity guidelines.

I recognise that weight-loss medications have a place for some patients, but we cannot simply medicate our way out of the high levels of obesity that we see across Wales and the UK. It must form part of a blended approach that includes looking at the food systems, regulation, availability and promotion of physical activity, alongside more medicalised interventions.

We're getting to work straight away, through our first 100 days commitments. Firstly, on advancing the active mile and the Daily Mile Foundation work across primary schools, with preliminary work well under way with stakeholders to begin the roll-out. Secondly, I have discussed with the Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport strengthening partnership working between health services and sport organisations, and the wider role both arts and sports can have in health pathways, and have agreed we will embed a workstream for this work within our new cross-Government structures.

I will also be working closely with my colleague the Cabinet Secretary for Rural Resilience and Sustainability on the development of the food strategy for Wales. Together, we will consider the fundamental changes needed to strengthen our food systems and the opportunity this presents to improve access to affordable, nutritious food, support locally produced Welsh food, and embed healthy, sustainable food choices, education and awareness within our schools.

Alongside this, we will be examining how we create healthier food environments across Wales. This includes considering the levers available to us to support healthier choices in the retail sector, across the out-of-home food settings, and within our communities, helping to make the healthy choice the easy choice.

I am firmly committed to addressing the concerning rise in vaping among children and young people. Nearly one in four of our 11 to 16-year-olds has tried vaping, despite these products having been developed as a smoking cessation aid for adult smokers. The unintended consequences of their widespread availability and appeal to young people are deeply concerning, and this Government is determined to take action. The consultation we launched last week marks the first step in delivering the robust measures needed to protect the health of the next generation.

Lung cancer disproportionately affects those from the most deprived communities, with a higher incidence rate in these areas. I am committed to improving outcomes with the development of a national lung cancer screening programme with integrated smoking cessation services. Smoking remains one of the leading causes of preventable illness and deaths in Wales and highlights stark inequalities. And through the groundbreaking Tobacco and Vapes Act 2026, we will progress towards the goal of creating the first smoke-free generation in Wales, and this will include work to further reduce smoking rates during pregnancy, which in Wales are the highest amongst the UK nations.

My approach to addiction includes tackling substance misuse and is based on the principle of harm reduction, to support and protect families and communities from the problems associated with harmful substance use. I am focused on working across the Welsh Government to do all that we can to tackle the risk factors for substance misuse, alongside work to strengthen support for those that need it, ensuring our work is informed by the voices of those with lived experience.

Reducing the equity gap will play a key role in my future vision for preventative services. This includes work to promote vaccinations and screening, which are disproportionately less prevalent amongst our most deprived communities. This will involve better engagement with our underserved communities, better access to services, and digital enablement. I have already taken action to introduce a time-limited meningitis B vaccination programme ahead of the winter peak, and an expansion to the respiratory syncytial virus programme to include those aged 65 to 74 who are immunosuppressed or with chronic respiratory disease. Both these actions will help reduce those affected by serious disease this winter.

This national focus on prevention will be informed by and will support local action, working with local government and the community and third sector. I'll be building on the work of the Marmot places under the Health Equity Wales initiative that builds on learning from Torfaen and Blaenau Gwent in taking a more preventative approach with communities to the delivery of services and tackling inequalities.

The importance of having a healthier, more resilient population is also clear in the context of the increasing frequency and severity of public health risks. The impacts of climate change on the health of the population have come to the fore with the recent extreme heat, but other linked risks include antimicrobial resistance, environmental hazards, and outbreaks of communicable diseases. A fundamental priority of any Government is to protect its population. This will include work to plan, prepare, and respond to existing and emerging public health risks, working with colleagues and partners to embed a one-health approach across human health, animal health and the environment, and looking internationally to share and learn best practice.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Llywydd, we firmly believe that building a healthier population is not only a moral imperative, particularly in tackling deep-rooted inequalities, but is also fundamental to improving the wider prosperity and resilience of our nation. That is why we are embedding this principle across the Government, that every part of Government, not just those with health within their portfolio, have a shared responsibility to support this ambition. I look forward to updating Members on the progress we are making when we return in the autumn.

Dyna pam rŷn ni'n gwreiddio'r egwyddor hon ar draws y Llywodraeth, fod gan bob rhan ohoni, nid jest y rhai sydd ag iechyd yn eu portffolio, gyfrifoldeb ar y cyd i gefnogi'r uchelgais hon. Dwi'n edrych ymlaen at roi'r wybodaeth ddiweddaraf i'r Aelodau am gynnydd y gwaith pan fyddwn yn dychwelyd yn yr hydref.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
I'd like to welcome the Minister to her post. I'll stop the pleasantries here because people are watching the clock and we'll be here all night. So, anyway, I'll move on to your statement, Minister.

It says here that you've had bilaterals with Cabinet Ministers and Deputy Ministers across Government. That's lovely, but I'd like to know what the next steps of those are going to be, really, because if we don't know what's coming out of it, they're just lovely meetings to have, aren't they? You said here as well that you've talked to the First Minister and that Government decision making will be informed by a shared focus on public health. Well, I think we can all agree with that, but what does that look like in practice? We've heard these things before, and it would be quite good if we could get some understanding today as to what actually that looks like.

You did say that officials and ministerial and cross-governance and arrangements are all being established. Fantastic, but what does this mean? How much is this going to cost the Welsh civil service, in terms of having all these cross-ministerial portfolios? Is this more civil servants to do this? Is this going to be managed within the current health portfolio? You also mentioned, further down in your statement, creating a new budget line within the Government's overall budget-setting process. Is there a risk with that, even though I'm not against it in principle, that we could end up with a bit of silo working here: that, actually, other departments are all chipping in, trying to look for this pot of money, while, actually, if it sat directly within the departments, it would be easier to spend? If the cross-governmental work was focused on prevention, you maybe wouldn't need a budget line there. I'm sure the Finance Committee would be quite pleased if it wasn't there, as it's something else to look at.

You also talked about weight-loss medication. This is something I've been quite involved in, actually. I haven't taken it personally. But I think one thing we have to be careful with, with weight-loss medication, is that, yes, it is changing lives, but it's not changing lifestyles. It cannot be seen as a silver bullet to losing weight long term, because we do know about the longer term health impacts, with osteoporosis in women, with people with cardiovascular problems emerging from these jabs, so I'd just like to know—. There needs to be a way for people to get off the treadmill, as such, of taking these jabs. So, I'd like to know what work you're doing with primary care to understand how you can work with local gyms, leisure facilities, so that when people are accessing weight-loss medication, their lifestyle is changing along with their life, because if you don't, it's just a vicious circle: you'll come off it, you'll put weight back on again, and you're back on the jabs and then end up in A&E with longer term problems, and that's no way to help our health service.

You did talk about working quite closely with the wider portfolio across health. I'd be interested to know how much money you're intending to move into the prevention agenda. I know the Cabinet Minister for sport is here as well, and the Government talked an awful lot during the election period about moving money into that portfolio. So, it would be quite good today to get some figures on how much of that prevention agenda is going to be delivered there and what proportion of that is the budget. I think that's really important.

You also mentioned working with the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability. I think it's very important. We talk about healthy food; I'm a big advocate of that. I know there were Members in the Conservative Party who brought forward a food Bill, which was supported across the Chamber, which is really important. But I think we need to make sure we've got good-quality food in schools. We've all seen the scandal with Thai chicken in our schools. That's not the sort of food we want to be putting into our kids. So, the prevention agenda is moving money into the schools' budget, so you can make sure that they can afford those good things in schools, and not imported food from across the world.

What else here? Lung screening. You talked about a lung screening programme. Well, we had the pilot in the previous Senedd. That was a good success story that came out of it. I'm pleased you're rolling that out further and going to develop that. The one thing that was raised at the time was chronic obstructive pulmonary disease screening. If we don't embed COPD screening as part of that lung cancer screening process, you're literally having another test for something else. So, sometimes, it's cheaper to do it all at the same time. Yes, you might be double-diagnosing somebody, but if someone's got lung cancer, you can almost, at the same time, say they've got COPD, or they're developing it, or they have COPD and do not have cancer. So, to get it done first time is the right approach, rather than having numerous different tests for people. Treat it once and get it done with.

Then you also talked about substance misuse. I know the Deputy Minister for mental health is also sat to your side. To deal with substance abuse—I think we have to look as well—you have to treat the individual, not the offence, as such. And if you are going to move to try and address this problem, mental health support has to be there. I know when Lynne Neagle, for example, was the Minister for mental health, she actually laboured on this quite a lot: that if you do not put the mental health support in place to support people on their substance misuse journey, whether that's drugs or alcohol, you're just going to have the revolving door of people getting clean and then coming back in again, because you've not dealt with the trauma that's led people there in the first place.

And in the interests of time, Deputy Presiding Officer, I think I've taken my five minutes, even though I said I was going to be quite brief. So, if you could answer some of those questions, Deputy Minister, I'd be very much obliged. Diolch.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Thank you. You could have had another 10 seconds of pleasantries at the—

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Oh, no, we wouldn't want that. I'd have taken 10 minutes then.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
Thanks for the contribution and for the welcome into the role. In terms of the bilaterals and the shared Government understanding, I think this is the first time we've ever had this discussion across Government level. I think there have been lots of pockets of good practice over a number of years, but nothing embedded, nothing strategic, no discussion about the impact of spend on the population of Wales in other portfolio areas.

So, the bilaterals have been really good to kick that process off in terms of just seeing where we can work together. For example, you mentioned food and a discussion with the Cabinet Minister for rural resilience. That's not just a bilateral between me and that Cabinet Minister; we're talking about education, we're talking about our planning system, we're talking about the economy and supporting our food businesses. So, that's what this approach is absolutely about, to make sure we don't miss those opportunities. And if we look at the approach to food during the last Government, it was quite narrowly focused, and this is absolutely building on the work that you mentioned by your previous colleague on the food Bill, to make sure that it is a whole-system approach.

I absolutely agree with you in terms of the quality of food in schools, but also teaching our young people about food skills and making sure that we understand where our food comes from, supporting our brilliant agricultural industry, and looking at our procurement rules. So, this is not just something for food; this is absolutely health prevention, looking at the economy. So, those bilaterals have kicked off that discussion while we work out how we make sure that these are embedded discussions early on in every policy development—that we look at preventing ill health and reducing the health inequality that we've got and making sure it's a cross-Government approach. And that's my role—to make sure that we don't miss those opportunities while we work out the mechanics, and that that is replicated on the official level as well. These conversations, potentially, have never happened before in these policy areas, so it's making sure that that's embedded so that it's systematic and strategic that we really do look at health inequality and look at preventative health measures. 

In terms of the budgets and the costs, you raise some interesting points there in terms of how that will be developed. You're right in terms of a new budget line. I think the first step that we're grappling with now is the definition of 'prevention', especially if we are committed to increased spend on prevention over this Senedd term. How do we define that is really important—how do we define current activity within health and social care, but also in the other portfolio areas as we move to shift resources towards prevention. Getting that definition of prevention is absolutely key. There are different mechanisms then of identifying that spend. The Scottish Government are currently looking at how you tag some spend as prevention—so, not necessarily creating a budget line but tagging it as 'preventative' and those definitions within preventative spend. We are exploring those options, with the key fundamental principle that transparency is key. Without us knowing what we're spending, how we're spending it, and, ultimately, what the outcomes of that spend are in terms of population health, it's not as impactful as it should be, and that's why I'm in this role. 

In terms of the weight loss medication, absolutely—it's creating that system of support around individuals for those lifestyle choices. They are right in some instances: preparing people for treatment in the NHS, for example, or certain body mass indexes. But making sure we've got that whole-system approach around the individual, to make sure there's a sustained improvement, is really important, and we're keeping that under review. Public Health Wales have been successful recently in co-ordinating a Wales-wide bid for funding through the obesity pathway innovation programme. That's £8 million of funding in order to look at these issues, to develop and test approaches that could form part of that delivery model going forward. We want to be looking at treating obesity as a chronic condition, and, obviously, the changes that would mean in terms of how the NHS would respond to that would be key. 

I've mentioned the food issue. On substance misuse, absolutely. I'm pleased to hear your approach in terms of the person-centred approach—not just dealing with the substance misuse issue, but, absolutely, mental health and making sure that all the services around that individual are there. Following on from the last Government's harm reduction method, we will absolutely be taking that forward and working closely with the Deputy Minister for mental health. If I've missed anything, as I know time is tight—[Interruption.] I'll come back to you on the COPD screening specifically. Thank you.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
Thank you to the Deputy Minister for her statement today. As Welsh Labour's spokesperson, I welcome the cross-Government approach to preventative health, but I'm interested in what outcomes will be delivered for people across Wales. You've mentioned today the designated preventative departmental expenditure line within the Welsh budget for 2027-28, but I'm sure you'd agree, Minister, that it isn't just the creation of the budget line itself that we should be focused on, but rather how people's overall health and well-being will improve. I, like many others, challenge the Government to go beyond the process. We want to know what exactly will change and how success will be measured during this Senedd term.

I'm glad the Deputy Minister mentioned two very effective interventions: screening and vaccinations. It's good to hear the Deputy Minister supports the continuation of the national lung cancer screening programme, which was introduced by the Welsh Labour Government. I'm surprised there's no mention today of the HPV vaccine. Since it was introduced in 2008, the HPV vaccine has reduced cervical cancer rates by almost 90 per cent in women in their 20s, and that has saved hundreds of lives every year across the UK. So, I'd like to know how the Government will engage with schools across Wales to encourage participation in vaccination programmes like this.

Cervical screening also saves lives, and there's work to be done to make that more accessible. So, I'd like to see the Government learn from areas where there have been increases in screening uptake. You did give one example of screening uptake best practice, but I think there have been some other ones, particularly in London, where GPs have adapted to offer appointments for their clinics that fit in with people's work and family lives, such as on weekends and late evenings. So, I'd be interested to hear if you've been able to look into that.

Encouragement to help break down stigma is also key to increasing screening uptake. So, I'd like to know how Public Health Wales is focusing screening delivery that is tailored to local communities, for instance consistent breast screening opportunities in each geographical area throughout the year to support local health board demand. There's also work to be done engaging with businesses and organisations to support their workforce to attend all screening as a priority.

Targeted communications and education are important, breaking down stigma for everyone, but specifically for those attending their first screening appointment. We all know the way people access information is changing, and I'd like to know how national screening programmes are adapting to fit into those communication methods to reflect this.

Inclusion health is a globally recognised approach to address and prevent the health inequalities facing marginalised groups who struggle to access health services and experience far poorer health outcomes. We know that there's a huge human cost to these inequalities, as well as a cost to public services such as blue light services, A&E and emergency inpatient treatment. A stark example is people experiencing homelessness who experience acute physical and mental health problems and die 30 years younger than the general population.

There are some fantastic examples of inclusion health work led by Public Health Wales and services such as Cardiff and Vale inclusion service, and the partnership work between Ysbyty Gwynedd and Cyngor Sir Ynys Môn. However, this is often reliant on passionate individuals going above and beyond the remit of their roles, rather than inclusion health being prioritised, systematic and integrated with health services. Prioritising inclusion health is key to preventative health, as well as delivering significant savings to emergency health services. So, will you commit to making inclusion health one of your ministerial priorities, and consider developing an inclusion health strategy?

Finally, we know that sport helps to tackle obesity and to prevent physical and mental health conditions. Professional and grass-roots sport clubs play a leading role, and their impact is far-reaching. They are trusted places at the heart of our communities. I'd also recommend to you the Fit Fans programme, which works across our football league clubs. In Plaid Cymru's manifesto, you said you would invest in sports and physical activity as part of the preventative health agenda, and you've mentioned today your discussions with the Minister for culture and sport. However, any new work stream does need funding. The health minister couldn't give an answer when I previously asked how much that investment will be and where the money will come from. So, can you, Deputy Minister, today tell us that? Diolch.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
Diolch. Thanks for those questions. In terms of the outcomes, we're going to be working on a public health strategy that brings all of this together in terms of what we're trying to achieve across portfolios, and looking at those objectives and those outcomes in the short, medium and longer term. As you mentioned, in terms of the budget, the budget increases transparency on what's actually happening. We don't have that now. Over the last 27 years, we don't know what's been spent on prevention. We don't know the impact. It has not been embedded. So, ensuring that we have transparency in terms of what we're spending does drive activity in terms of being transparent and putting those outcome measures in place to make sure that we are really clear what the expectation is in terms of public and preventative health.

In terms of the HPV vaccine, absolutely, and there will be a statement by the Cabinet Minister on the cancer strategy this week, which will include details on that.

You're right in terms of working with education, and we've been discussing with the Cabinet Minister for education how we can improve those messages to schools. Schools are under pressure with lots of demands on their time, but making sure that they understand their role in promoting vaccine uptake in schools is really important, and something that we are working on.

One of the things that worries me is the differences within our deprived communities in terms of screening and vaccine uptake. The work you mentioned there on inclusion health is really important. There hasn't been a systematic look at this up until now. So, we really need to be making sure that the work that Public Health Wales are doing on screening and vaccinations really understands at that community level what the barriers are for uptake in terms of screening and vaccination. Because we know the benefits of making sure that people undertake screening and vaccination when they're meant to be part of that. 

So, there is definitely good work happening, especially on the stigma side as well, but we do need to do more. We do need to better understand it, and we do need to better make sure that the good work that's happening now is better understood across the health service as well.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
Can I also thank the Deputy Minister for bringing this statement here to the Chamber today? We've seen a lot of proposals flying around the Chamber when it comes to health and social care over the past few months, outlining summits and following clinically led decisions, but less about when and how these proposals are going to be actioned. Take, for example, the shift towards primary care and prevention. It's great that the Government is proposing an extra 100 GPs, but when GP practices are saying they do not have the physical space to be able to train up new GPs, we have a problem.

We also know the scale of the challenges that Wales is facing, from one in three adults living with obesity, which costs Wales £5.2 billion in health spending and lost productivity, to nearly 4,000 preventable deaths each year because of smoking. I know the Deputy Minister has already launched a consultation on vaping as part of the four-nation approach to prevent children and young people from starting to smoke or vape, so I'd like to know what other actions you're going to be taking on both of these issues and when we are likely to be seeing delivery.

Also, are you considering the work and recommendations of the previous Health and Social Care Committee's inquiry in relation to obesity? I welcome that you are focusing on activity as part of weight loss and prevention, but sometimes green spaces and safe walking routes are inaccessible to communities across all of our constituencies. According to the Ramblers Association, councils in my constituency spend an average of just 44p per resident on maintaining public paths. Therefore, will the Deputy Minister commit to continuing the access improvement grant so that more communities get the benefit of walking regularly and safely?

Deputy Presiding Officer, I see that there will be a food strategy for Wales. My colleague Peter Fox—I know his name has been mentioned quite a few times—was strident in his work regarding the food Bill in the last Senedd, which focused on sustainable and secure food sources and increasing the proportion of Welsh food and drink served in hospitals and schools across Wales. Sadly, this was voted down by Labour and Plaid in the last Senedd term. So, Deputy Minister, will you make a commitment to revisit my colleague's proposals as part of your food strategy now?

Deputy Presiding Officer, I believe that prevention is better than cure, and I know many of us say it enough here in the Chamber, but we should also be looking at what we can learn from the past. It's now over six years since COVID-19 hit Wales, and we still are none the wiser as to how well or badly our health and social care system coped, and vitally, how we prevent another virus from nearly collapsing Wales. The fallout from COVID is also clear when it comes to those who suffer from long COVID, as well as the health of those who have had misdiagnoses due to lengthy shutdowns of routine exams. As the Deputy Minister will be aware, both Plaid Cymru and the Welsh Conservatives supported calls for a Wales-only COVID inquiry. Now that you're in government, will the Deputy Minister be initiating a Wales-only inquiry as well?

Additionally, I see the mention of building on the Marmot initiative, but I note from the findings that although it provides a successful framework, it's failing to rapidly change lives because councils don't have sweeping macroeconomic powers or huge cash reserves to apply it. So, Deputy Minister, are you committing to more powers to local authorities and further cash to apply Marmot across Wales?

Finally, Deputy Presiding Officer, child oral health is a huge component of prevention and public health, and I don't see any specific mention of this in your statement today. Because we are seeing one in four children aged five being affected by tooth decay, rising to one in three in the most deprived areas across Wales. Therefore, Deputy Minister, will you be making a commitment on record to embedding oral health in nursery and school settings? I also note that the dental contract has a massive impact on child oral health. So, Deputy Minister, how are you going to be working with the Cabinet Minister to change the dental health contract and provide a better deal for both dentists and NHS patients here in Wales? Thank you.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
Thank you. On the first point there, in terms of tobacco and vaping, you've referenced the consultation that we launched last week. I mentioned that a key priority is making sure that we tackle the increasing number of children and young people who are vaping. Vaping is seen as a cessation tool for adults who smoke, it was never intended—. These are unintended consequences with dire impacts. Talking to parents and teachers, they really want us to step up and support tackling this issue. So, I'd urge people to respond to the consultation, which looked at changing the packaging of vaping products, making them plain packaging, similar to tobacco, removing the ability of companies to call them flavours that would be attractive to young people, and also the design of them, making them less appealing to young people, and also restricting where they're sold in shops so that they're under the counter. That's the first step, and I've asked officials to give us an outline of the other powers that we have in order to tackle tobacco and vaping, and making sure that we really do tackle these issues.

On obesity and green spaces, absolutely, I think social prescribing, where it happens, is fantastic, and it's making sure that we embed that, share the best practice and make sure that people understand the benefits of linking to their local communities, not just in terms of green spaces, but physical activity and community groups, making sure that that is seen as a central part of the prescribing tool that our GPs have.

On the food strategy, we are working at pace on this and we will be sharing information on it. It is going to be comprehensive, as I mentioned in the answer to James. It's not just looking at food in terms of what we produce, but also looking systematically at healthy food, supporting our rural industries, looking at production, and also, in terms of healthy foods, looking at schools and our young people. I think also, going further than that, I'm keen to look at healthy food environments and making sure that we talk to food producers and manufacturers about what more they can be doing and what more we can be asking them to do in terms of reformulation, product placement, and really looking at retail spaces and out-of-home food outlets to make sure that we are really committed in terms of tackling this, making sure that the healthy choice is the easy choice. We know that we are not eating as much fresh fruit and veg as we should be doing. We know we've got a fantastic agricultural industry, and we should be looking at procurement rules as well, which will be part of that.

In terms of COVID, you mentioned our manifesto call. We made a clear manifesto call to establish a Wales-specific review of the COVID response, focused on matters not fully addressed by the UK-wide inquiry. With the report out today, of course, we'll be studying the report's findings and the recommendations in depth and publishing a response to that within six months. Responsibility lies with my Cabinet colleague.

And in terms of children's public health, in terms of the demographics, in terms of the outlook for children's public health, this is an absolute area we need to be focusing on, and that's why, as part of the public health strategy, there'll be a specific public health strategy for children that we'll be developing in the months ahead.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Diabetic eye screening is a vital preventative service. In England, OCT, or optical coherence tomography, has been introduced in diabetic eye screening, with an estimated 120,000 hospital eye appointments a year saved, while improving diagnostic accuracy. In Wales, patients are often referred from diabetic eye screening into the hospital eye service, and then, in some cases, into the Wales general ophthalmic service pathway back to the screening service. For patients, that means additional travel, time away from work and caring responsibility. For the NHS, it means administrative appointments and costs. Much of this would be potentially avoided earlier if there is earlier access to simple non-invasive OCT scans during the screening. So, will the Cabinet Secretary work with Diabetic Eye Screening Wales to develop a pathway of introducing OCTs into Diabetic Eye Screening Wales to improve efficiency, reduce unnecessary referrals and help improve avoidable sight loss?

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text:
Diolch. As you will well know—and thank you for your work in this area—everyone aged 12 and over diagnosed with diabetes and registered with a GP in Wales is invited for screening through the Diabetic Eye Screening Wales service. The OCT you mentioned, delivered with the diabetic eye screening programme, may reduce referrals for inadequate images to hospital eye services, which would improve participant experience. However, the introduction of OCT would need a new service delivery model, which would require additional specialist workforce and equipment.

Scoping of the introduction of OCT is part of the wider Diabetic Eye Screening Wales transformation plan, which is planned for future years, and would determine the potential benefits of introduction and requirements in relation to resource and funding. So, the focus at the moment is currently on improving the stability of the diabetic eye screening for existing screening pathways. As you will know, Diabetic Eye Screening Wales is delivered in accordance with the recommendations of the UK National Screening Committee, and that committee is currently consulting on the use of digital imaging within the screening programme, and we will consider the advice of the committee when that is received.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Nobody in this Chamber disputes that preventing illness is better than treating it. But look at the evidence in my constituency. Swansea bay has been under targeted intervention for cancer since 24 January, and on the latest published figures, its bowel screening uptake is the lowest in Wales, at around 57 per cent in the most deprived communities, compared with around 72 per cent in the least deprived. Prevention is falling short precisely where it is needed most. Analysis by the future generations commissioner also found that less than 10 per cent of the previous Welsh Government's budget was directed towards evidence-based primary prevention. Warm words about prevention have never been in short supply in this Chamber; budgets and screening programmes have. So, Deputy Minister, will your Government do better? When will eligible people across Wales begin receiving invitations for the national lung cancer screening programme? And will the first budget increase the proportion spent on evidence-based primary prevention? Thank you.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Thank you. You're right to point out the cancer inequalities. I think that's one of the clearest examples of the wider health inequalities that we face in Wales, especially in some of the communities in south Wales. Evidence shows that people living in more deprived communities are more likely to develop cancer, more likely to die from cancer, and less likely to survive cancer than those living in the least deprived communities. So, it's an absolute imperative that we tackle that issue, and tackle the issue you mentioned there in terms of screening as well. These inequalities are driven by many of the same factors that underpin health inequalities, including poverty, smoking, obesity, housing, employment and access to services. That's why this is a cross-governmental approach, and that's why this Government is taking a very, very different approach to previous Governments by having a designated Minister with responsibility for looking at these issues across Government. The Cabinet Minister for health will be setting out a statement on the plans for cancer this week, with the aim of developing a cancer plan, as we set out ahead of the election.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Prevention must be central to turning around the NHS and improving services for staff and patients, and I welcome your statement today. This issue arose repeatedly in the cross-party group on substance use and addiction, which I chaired in the last Senedd and intend to re-establish in September, working with Kaleidoscope as the secretariat and Members from across this Chamber. If anybody else is interested, please get in touch. The group heard expert, lived-experience evidence on harm reduction, including wider access to naloxone, the international impact of safer consumption facilities, and the urgent need to educate people, particularly young people, about ketamine. Although Westminster's outdated drugs legislation limits what Wales can do, would the Deputy Minister explore further harm-reduction measures within her remit? In particular, will the Government consider a national ketamine awareness campaign to challenge myths about its perceived safety and explain the serious risks of frequent use, including bladder and kidney damage, pressure on GPs and urology services, and the potential life-changing harm developed over a relatively short period for users? Diolch.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Thank you very much. There are serious concerns about the use of ketamine and the increase in the use of ketamine, of course, particularly among young people, and the harm that that can cause. Thank you for your work during the last Senedd in this area. I look forward to engaging with you in the cross-party group when it is established. I'd be more than happy to do that.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr. Mae yna bryderon sylweddol ynglŷn â'r defnydd o cetamin a'r cynnydd yn y defnydd o cetamin, wrth gwrs, yn enwedig ymysg pobl ifanc, a'r niwed y gall hwnna beri. Diolch i chi am eich gwaith yn ystod y Senedd ddiwethaf yn y maes yma. Dwi'n edrych ymlaen at gysylltu gyda chi yn y grŵp trawsbleidiol pan fydd wedi cael ei sefydlu. Byddwn i'n hapus iawn i wneud hynny.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Across Wales, the area planning boards have developed a range of information about ketamine, mainly focused on awareness raising, harm reduction, reducing risks and ensuring information is being disseminated widely. Areas are also adapting services to address these issues and these developing needs, with treatment pathways specifically for those using ketamine, with some areas implementing joint assessments for those using the drug. This allows access to clinical support and consultation from the substance misuse service, and quicker access to GP support and community mental health referral teams where appropriate. Given the concerns, and the rise of the concerns, on the use of ketamine in our communities, we've established a ketamine working group with key stakeholders and clinical leads to take this work forward. The aim of the group is to share best practice and to inform a co-ordinated approach across Wales. This includes informing treatment pathways and prevention, but also how we raise awareness of the harms, building on the local work already being led by the boards. The first meeting of the working group took place on 13 July. I'd like to reiterate I'm more than happy to work with the cross-party group to share information about that working group and how we can work together to raise awareness of this really important issue and the harms associated with it.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Minister, for your statement, and welcome to your role. Minister, everyone agrees that prevention is better than cure, but prevention only works if people can actually access the services they need. In west rural Wales, too many residents face long journeys, limited appointment availability and growing difficulty accessing GPs, community healthcare and screening programmes. Reform UK believes that public money should be focused on delivering effective front-line services, not expanding bureaucracy. Rural communities contribute just as much to the public purse as anyone else and deserve the same standard of healthcare. If we are serious about preventative health, we need practical action that improves access, shortens waiting times and ensures services reach people where they live, rather than expecting patients to travel even greater distances. Deputy Minister, what specific changes will the Welsh Government make to improve access to preventative healthcare in west rural Wales? And can you guarantee that future investment will be directed towards strengthening front-line services in rural communities, rather than increasing administration costs? Diolch.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Well, I'm glad you agree with the priority that we've put on tackling waiting lists and the investment that we've set out in the supplementary budget in order to do that. I hope, indeed, that Members would reflect on what voting against that supplementary budget would mean in terms of the investment that we need in our NHS and across other preventative health measures. There's investment in the supplementary budget on the swimming initiative for schools as well. So, voting against the supplementary budget this afternoon does have serious consequences in terms of the ability of our NHS to respond to the demands it's facing now and the backlog that we have inherited from the previous Government, which absolutely impacts on the issues that you mentioned about the provision of health services in our rural communities. I am also from rural west Wales and know the challenges. As the First Minister set out earlier this afternoon, our ambition is to make sure that we look at rural-proofing, to make sure that the cost of delivery of services really does adequately reflect the actual costs in terms of what's being funded, and that is a key central part. But I'd urge Members across this Chamber to make sure that they support the supplementary budget, to make sure of exactly what you mentioned, in terms of tackling the waiting lists and making sure our health and social care system is on a sustainable footing.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: And finally, Deputy Minister, Gwyn Williams.
documents.text_cy: Ac yn olaf, Ddirprwy Weinidog, Gwyn Williams.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. Gaining access to dental care is vital to prevent dental and health problems more generally in the future, and I welcome our commitment to review the NHS dental contract to resolve vital issues affecting the profession in Wales and the experience of our patients. We met with leaders in the field of dentistry in Wales last week to listen to their concerns, and reviewing the contract, as set out in our manifesto, is one of their main priorities. I'd like to pay tribute to Mike Hedges from the Labour Party, because he was in the meeting as well. Will the Deputy Minister commit to undertaking this task as soon as possible, as well as contacting leaders in the field of dentistry in Wales to seek short-term solutions to stabilise dental services in the meantime? Thank you.
documents.text_cy: Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Mae cael mynediad at ofal deintyddol yn hollbwysig er mwyn atal problemau deintyddol ac iechyd yn gyffredinol, a dwi'n croesawu ein hymrwymiad i adolygu contract deintyddol y GIG er mwyn datrys materion hollbwysig sy'n effeithio ar y proffesiwn yng Nghymru ac ar brofiad ein cleifion. Fe wnaethom gyfarfod ag arweinwyr ym maes deintyddiaeth yng Nghymru yr wythnos diwethaf i wrando ar eu pryderon, ac mae adolygu'r contract, fel a nodir yn ein maniffesto, yn un o'u prif flaenoriaethau. Hoffwn dalu teyrnged i Mike Hedges o'r Blaid Lafur, achos roedd e yn y cyfarfod hefyd. A fydd y Dirprwy Weinidog yn ymrwymo i wneud hyn cyn gynted â phosib, yn ogystal â chysylltu ag arweinwyr ym maes deintyddiaeth yng Nghymru i geisio atebion clou i sefydlogi gwasanaethau deintyddol yn y cyfamser. Diolch yn fawr.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Diolch. The NHS dental contract arrangements that came into force on 1 April this year represent the most significant changes to NHS dentistry in two decades. Health needs and prevention are at the heart of the new system, creating an opportunity to improve access to care and to ensure resources are targeted towards those with the greatest need. We are, as you would expect, keeping the new contract under continual review to assess its impact on patients, practitioners and access to services, but we do need to give it some time to bed in. As evidence emerges, we will work with stakeholders to identify where further refinements may be required to ensure that the system is delivering the intended improvements and remains an attractive place to provide NHS dental care.

documents.item: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health: Priorities for Public and Preventative Health
documents.text: Thank you, Deputy Minister.
documents.text_cy: Diolch, Ddirprwy Weinidog.

documents.item: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Priorities for Skills and Tertiary Education
documents.text: Moving on now to item 7, a statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: priorities for skills and tertiary education. I call on the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education, Cefin Campbell.
documents.text_cy: Rydym yn symud ymlaen, felly, at eitem 7, datganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Sgiliau ac Addysg Drydyddol: blaenoriaethau ar gyfer sgiliau ac addysg drydyddol. Galwaf ar y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Sgiliau ac Addysg Drydyddol, Cefin Campbell.

documents.item: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Priorities for Skills and Tertiary Education
documents.text:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd, and good afternoon, everyone. Today, I will be setting out this Government's priorities for skills and tertiary education. Our tertiary education sector supports young people taking their first steps after compulsory education, adults returning to learning, workers seeking to upskill or re-skill, and communities seeking confidence, resilience and social prosperity. The sector also supports our economy by developing the knowledge, skills and research capacity that Wales needs to support our businesses and industry, and to build, also, for the future. 

I am committed to working closely with the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language to deliver a shared vision of one education and skills system for Wales, with Welsh-medium provision at the core of this vision. And I have seen first-hand, through my experience of teaching adults at Welsh universities, the impact the tertiary sector can have on people’s lives. I want learners to progress through the system with confidence, with clear, visible and Welsh-medium development pathways. Academic, vocational and work-based routes should be understood as complementary parts of each learner’s journey, aligned with the needs of Wales today and the ambitions we have for tomorrow.
documents.text_cy:
Diolch yn fawr iawn, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Prynhawn da, bawb. Heddiw, byddaf i'n nodi blaenoriaethau'r Llywodraeth hon ar gyfer sgiliau ac addysg drydyddol. Mae ein sector addysg drydyddol yn cefnogi pobl ifanc sy'n cymryd eu camau cyntaf ar ôl addysg orfodol, oedolion sy'n dychwelyd i ddysgu, gweithwyr sy'n ceisio gwella eu sgiliau neu ddysgu sgiliau newydd, a chymunedau sy'n ceisio hyder, gwytnwch a ffyniant cymdeithasol. Mae’r sector hefyd yn cefnogi ein heconomi drwy ddatblygu'r wybodaeth, y sgiliau a'r capasiti ymchwil sydd eu hangen ar Gymru i gefnogi ein busnesau a'n diwydiant, ac adeiladu, hefyd, ar gyfer y dyfodol.

Dwi wedi ymrwymo i weithio'n agos gyda Gweinidog y Cabinet dros Addysg a'r Gymraeg i gyflawni gweledigaeth gyffredin o un system addysg a sgiliau i Gymru, gyda darpariaeth cyfrwng Cymraeg wrth wraidd y weledigaeth hon. A dwi wedi gweld drosof fi fy hun, trwy fy mhrofiad o addysgu oedolion mewn prifysgolion yng Nghymru, yr effaith y gall y sector trydyddol ei chael ar newid bywydau pobl. Dwi am i ddysgwyr symud ymlaen drwy'r system yn hyderus, gyda llwybrau datblygu clir, gweladwy a chyfrwng Cymraeg. Dylai llwybrau academaidd, galwedigaethol a seiliedig ar waith gael eu deall fel rhannau ategol o daith pob dysgwr, sy'n cyd-fynd ag anghenion Cymru heddiw a'n huchelgeisiau ar gyfer yfory.

documents.item: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Priorities for Skills and Tertiary Education
documents.text:
Our future economic success depends on developing a highly skilled workforce. I will work closely with the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy to ensure that the skills system supports our wider economic ambitions. A comprehensive national skills audit is currently under way. It will bring together evidence, analyse available data and gather views from employers, industry representatives, providers and other stakeholders. Its purpose is to provide a clear, cross-Government view of current and future workforce needs across Wales, including where shortages exist, where demand is likely to grow, and how the system can respond for learners, employers and the economy. The findings will help us target investment more effectively and align education, employment and training pathways with Wales’s priorities. Early findings will inform the future skills summit this autumn, bringing together business, the tertiary sector, training providers and other stakeholders to develop a shared vision and strategic direction for the future skills system and its funding. We will take an employer-led approach to identifying skills needs and we'll work together with business and industry to co-design solutions that meet key sector needs.

Our manifesto also commits to developing a national strategy for skills and vocational education. This will draw on evidence from the skills summit and the skills audit, supporting learners in a changing labour market, strengthening economic growth and promoting genuine parity between vocational and academic pathways. It will also build on the priorities set out in the strategic direction for vocational education and training.

On higher education, we are aware of the challenges that universities face, including rising costs and constrained income. That is why one of our first 100-day commitments is to take forward a review of higher education funding, and we will publish the terms of reference for that review in the summer. I am grateful for the responses to the recent call for submissions on the future of tertiary education in Wales. These views are informing our thinking. I will publish a summary report of those responses, followed by a fuller report in the autumn, to support transparent, evidence-led policy development. 

I am also examining options for reforming Seren, so that it has a stronger focus on addressing participation gaps, on supporting learners from Wales’s most disadvantaged communities and strengthening pathways so that learners can reach their full potential. I will issue a written statement in due course setting out our next steps.

documents.item: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Priorities for Skills and Tertiary Education
documents.text:
Wales has always been an outward-looking nation, and we are determined to maximise opportunities for young people in Wales to live, study and work in Europe. We are working closely with the UK Government to ensure that the benefits of rejoining Erasmus are realised, and we are considering future options for Taith.

I want to emphasise the importance of Welsh-medium and bilingual provision across the tertiary system. Learners should have the opportunity to develop, maintain and use their Welsh language skills at every stage. We work, of course, with Medr, the Coleg Cymraeg Cenedlaethol, providers and employers to expand Welsh-medium and bilingual apprenticeship provision, to strengthen career pathways and increase bilingual delivery and to build capacity as well so that more young people who enter the workplace are able to work bilingually and provide key services through the medium of Welsh.

There is more to do, but the direction is clear: Welsh-medium and bilingual provision must be built into the future of tertiary education and skills, not treated as an add-on. Medr will consult on a national plan for the Welsh language in the autumn, and I look forward to engaging with Medr and the sector as we work towards our Welsh language goals.
